Across three representative dLLMs and four datasets, BlockBatch reduces denoising NFEs by 26.6% on average and achieves a 1.33\times average end-to-end speedup, with comparable average accuracy.

title: Mitigating False Credit Propagation: Probabilistic Graphical Reward Aggregation for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
author: Can Lv; Mingju Chen; Heng Chang; Shiji Zhou
abstract: Rubric-based rewards are increasingly used for open-ended language model post-training, but criterion-level scores are commonly aggregated as independent utilities. This flat scalarization ignores semantic dependencies among criteria, allowing downstream credit or penalties to be counted even when the conditions that license them are absent. We call this structural failure False Credit Propagation (FCP). We propose GEAR (Graphical Event Aggregation for Rubric rewards), a dependency-aware aggregation framework for rubric rewards. GEAR represents rubric criteria as latent events in a typed dependency graph, uses monotone retention factors to infer dependency-adjusted criterion marginals, and computes a normalized expected-utility reward. This preserves compatibility with standard rubric-based reinforcement learning while adding only linear-time aggregation over criteria and edges. Experiments on HealthBench, WritingBench, and PLawBench with two policy backbones show that GEAR consistently improves over flat aggregation and hard gating, both in controlled aggregation-only settings and as a plug-in module for existing rubric-guided RL pipelines. FCP diagnostics further show that GEAR substantially reduces invalid downstream utility while avoiding the over-suppression of deterministic gating.

title: Rubric-as-Experts: Case-Specific MQM Rubrics for Translation Error Span Detection
author: Weilu Xu; Yunzhi Shen; Xinye Wang; Renfei Dang; Shujian Huang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown potential for reference-free span-level translation quality estimation (QE), yet existing approaches based on Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) typically rely on fixed rubric configurations shared across translation instances. However, translation instances often differ substantially in error complexity, ambiguity, and required evaluation granularity, making static rubric allocation suboptimal for span-level error detection. We find that larger MQM subtype spaces improve error coverage but also introduce more false positives, while different translation instances prefer different rubric granularities, suggesting that evaluation spaces should be allocated dynamically for each case. Therefore, we propose a case-specific dynamic rubric framework that adaptively constructs MQM evaluation spaces for individual translation instances. Unlike methods that generate fully free-form rubrics, our framework remains grounded in the predefined MQM taxonomy while dynamically selecting suitable subtype spaces and evaluation granularity for different cases. Experiments on span-level QE benchmarks from the Conference on Machine Translation (WMT) across multiple model scales demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves F1 and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC).

title: Rethinking the Role of Efficient Attention in Hybrid Architectures
author: Ziqing Qiao; Yinuo Xu; Chaojun Xiao; Zhou su; Zihan Zhou; Yingfa Chen; Xiaoyue Xu; Xu Han; Zhiyuan Liu
abstract: Modern language models increasingly adopt hybrid architectures that combine full attention with efficient attention modules, such as sliding-window attention (SWA) and recurrent sequence mixers. However, how these efficient modules shape model capabilities remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic analysis across hybrid architectures from three perspectives: scaling behavior, mechanism analysis, and architecture design. First, from a scaling perspective, we find that efficient-attention design primarily affects how fast long-context capability emerges, while different hybrids eventually converge to comparable long-context performance under sufficient training. Second, mechanistically, we show that long-range retrieval is mainly carried by full attention, whereas efficient attention shapes its optimization trajectory. This explains a counter-intuitive phenomenon we call Large-Window Laziness: larger SWA windows can delay the formation of retrieval heads in full-attention layers. Third, guided by this mechanism, we show that applying No Positional Encoding (NoPE) to only the full-attention layers of a small-window SWA hybrid substantially improves long-context performance with negligible impact on short-context performance.

title: What Does a Language Model Know If It Has Never Seen the Future? Temporal Isolation as a Natural Experiment in Knowledge Attribution
author: Azizur Rahman; Rushikesh Hiray; Shubham Srivastava; Mohammad Hijjawi; Laraib Hasan
abstract: How much of a language model’s apparent knowledge reflects general linguistic competence, and how much reflects memorisation of facts seen during pretraining? Disentangling the two is normally confounded by data contamination, because modern corpora overlap with the benchmarks used to evaluate them. We exploit a natural experiment that removes exact benchmark exposure by construction. TALKIE-1930 is a 13B-parameter transformer trained exclusively on approximately 260 billion tokens of English published before 1931; TALKIE-WEB is an architecture-, tokeniser-, and compute-matched twin trained on an equivalent volume of FineWeb. Because every modern NLP benchmark postdates 1930, any post-1930 capability TALKIE-1930 exhibits cannot arise from benchmark contamination. We study this model pair along three axes. First, syntactic competence transfers across eras with only a modest gap (BLiMP: 76.9% for TALKIE-1930 vs. 82.0% for TALKIE-WEB), and an OCR-noise ablation shows that this gap is not an artefact of character-level corruption in the historical corpus. Second, in-context learning is largely preserved by temporal isolation: TALKIE-1930 matches TALKIE-WEB on SST-2 (91.2% vs. 90.9% at k=32), exceeds it on MNLI (47.3% vs. 37.8%), and learns post-2006 genres it cannot have seen (tweet sentiment and emotion) with learning-rate slopes statistically indistinguishable from TALKIE-WEB’s. Third, linear probes recover the temporal provenance of a factual statement from hidden states at 98.2% accuracy (TALKIE-1930) and 99.5% (TALKIE-WEB); a three-way probe on TALKIE-1930 that adds a suspected-leaked class reaches 96.0% accuracy (chance approximately 33%), well above lexical and permutation baselines, though this figure is carried mainly by the temporal contrast and the leaked class is only partially recovered. Finally, we document a dissociation between representation and behaviour: although TALKIE-1930’s hidden states linearly encode temporal-boundary information, its greedy decodings do not, confabulating post-1930 facts with fluent, confident anachronisms such as dating the iPhone to 1876. We frame these findings as a controlled case study of a rare temporally isolated model pair, providing evidence that exact benchmark exposure is not necessary for in-context learning on modern tasks, and that base language models contain linearly decodable representations of the temporal provenance and, in part, the epistemic status of their knowledge that need not surface in their outputs.

title: From Rollouts to Recipes: Self-Contained Post-Training for LLMs
author: Yifei Li; Lingling Zhang; Muye Huang; Zihan Ma; Jiashuai Liu; Jun Liu
abstract: Post-training large language models usually apply a single training recipe to all samples, even though the model’s own rollouts reveal different sample-level learning states. We propose Self-Routing, a behavior-conditioned post-training framework that uses rollout correctness and confidence to decide how each sample should be optimized. Depending on its behavior state, a sample is routed to GRPO, on-policy self-distillation, regularization, or skipping, allowing training to adapt without external teachers, extra annotations, or additional sampling. Experiments on mathematical reasoning across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 backbones show that Self-Routing consistently improves over uniform GRPO, uniform OPSD, fixed mixtures, and simpler routing baselines. Further analyses show that the routing distribution changes over training and reduces unnecessary updates on low-signal or already stable samples.

title: CWM: Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting for Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Reasoning Ability
author: Keuntae Kim; Eunhye Jeong; Yong Suk Choi
abstract: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant attention due to their strong language understanding and generation capabilities, demonstrating impressive reasoning abilities as well as effective utilization of external knowledge. Many studies have proposed methods that specialize in improving performance for individual tasks. However, ironically, only a limited number of attempts have explored general-purpose, task-agnostic methods. In this work, we present a unified framework integrating reasoning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) tasks. We further propose Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a low-cost white-box method for adaptive RAG tasks previously dominated by black-box approaches, without requiring external decision modules or multi-sampling. CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across recent LLMs, including GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, and Llama3.1-8b, while also demonstrating strong generality by extending to reasoning tasks. In addition, CWM provides controllability by enabling retrieval decisions to be regulated through the manipulation of internal model signals. Our code is available at https://github.com/JeongEunhye00/CWM.

title: DynaWeb: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning of Web Agents
author: Hang Ding; Peidong Liu; Junqiao Wang; Ziwei Ji; Meng Cao; Rongzhao Zhang; Lynn Ai; Eric Yang; Tianyu Shi; Lei Yu
abstract: The development of autonomous web agents, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning (RL), represents a significant step towards general-purpose AI assistants. However, training these agents is severely hampered by the challenges of interacting with the live internet, which is inefficient, costly, and fraught with risks. Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) offers a promising solution by learning a world model of the environment to enable simulated interaction. This paper introduces DynaWeb, a novel MBRL framework that trains web agents through interacting with a web world model trained to predict naturalistic web page representations given agent actions. This model serves as a synthetic web environment where an agent policy can dream by generating vast quantities of rollout action trajectories for efficient online reinforcement learning. Beyond free policy rollouts, DynaWeb incorporates real expert trajectories from training data, which are randomly interleaved with on-policy rollouts during training to improve stability and sample efficiency. Experiments conducted on the challenging WebArena and WebVoyager benchmarks demonstrate that DynaWeb consistently and significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art open-source web agent models. Our findings establish the viability of training web agents through imagination, offering a scalable and efficient way to scale up online agentic RL.

title: ChapterRL: Chapter-Aware Reward Framework for Novel Generation Reinforcement Learning
author: Bingqian Sun; Jingchao Yang; Xiangyu Wu; Zhang Yunfei; Tingting Gao; Han Li
abstract: Multi-chapter novel generation requires models to balance two quality dimensions simultaneously: chapter-level reader engagement and global narrative rhythm. Existing approaches have mainly focused on planning, memory, and execution, while paying limited attention to the mismatch between training signals and reader experience. We propose **ChapterRL**, which reformulates multi-chapter generation as a reward design problem. Specifically, ChapterRL introduces two complementary reward signals. **Reading Depth Residual** (RDR) derives debiased chapter-level quality signals from reader continuation and completion behavior through genre–position stratified normalization. **Dynamic Rhythm Trajectory** (DRT) uses an arousal estimator to impose a threshold-gated penalty on systematic rhythm collapse in the later part of a story. The two signals correspond to chapter attractiveness and global narrative momentum, and are jointly integrated into reinforcement learning training. We evaluate the full ChapterRL policy on three automatic benchmarks and separately validate its RDR reward model on task-aligned narrative domains of the Chinese WritingPreferenceBench. Results show that ChapterRL improves chapter quality and rhythm stability over supervised fine-tuning and single-reward variants, while RDR exhibits strong narrative preference alignment as an efficient scalar reward model.Code is available at [ChapterRL](https://github.com/SorBetQ/ChapterRL).

title: JPhonABX: Japanese Phonological Discrimination Dataset for Moraic and Accentual Minimal Pairs
author: Yurie Koga; Shunsuke Kando; Yusuke Miyao
abstract: Self-supervised speech models are known to encode phonological information, yet it remains underexplored whether they capture phonological properties characteristic of Japanese, such as mora and pitch accent. This paper introduces JPhonABX, a Japanese phonological discrimination dataset targeting moraic and accentual contrasts. It consists of 192,000 moraic and 98,000 accentual ABX test items, covering various types of contrasts such as those involving moraic nasal, geminate consonant, vowel length, and pitch accent. Our human evaluation by native Japanese speakers shows high discrimination accuracy and inter-rater agreement, validating the quality of the dataset. We further evaluate several self-supervised speech models and find that while almost all of them show no significant difference from humans in mora discrimination, they perform significantly worse in accent discrimination, and even models trained on Japanese fail to reach human-level performance.

title: From Gaps to Active Retrieval : Open-Domain Iterative Timeline Completion via Historical Trajectory Analogy and Dynamic Ontology
author: Yunhui Zheng; Chenlong Bao; Shasha Li; Ting Wang; Jin-Tao Tang
abstract: Open-Domain Timeline Summarization (Open-TLS) seeks to construct coherent evolutionary narratives for a topic by distilling information from large, unstructured web streams. Existing retrieve-and-generate pipelines often fail to capture logically necessary but semantically distant evidence, resulting in macro-level causal gaps (missing intermediate stages) and micro-level element gaps (underspecified milestones). We propose Active Timeline Completion (ATC), an iterative framework that converts implicit narrative gaps into targeted retrieval questions, enabling reflection-driven evidence acquisition. ATC leverages three complementary mechanisms—parametric causal gap detection, historical trajectory analogy, and dynamic ontology-guided completion—while a Logical Utility Verification module ensures only evidence directly addressing these gaps updates the timeline. Experiments on Open-TLS demonstrate that ATC consistently outperforms strong baselines in both content coverage and temporal alignment, showing that active, question-driven retrieval improves the completeness and coherence of open-domain timelines.

title: FLOUR: Mixing the Right Ingredients for LLM Unlearning in Latent Space
author: Thuy Dung Nguyen; Giang Nguyen; Taylor T Johnson; Kevin Leach
abstract: As large language models are deployed at scale, the ability to selectively remove knowledge has become critical for privacy, safety, and legal compliance. Existing post-training unlearning methods suffer from a persistent tension: unbounded divergence signals over-unlearn, degrading utility and producing incoherent outputs, while fixed sample-agnostic targets and reference-relative penalties under-unlearn, leaving traces recoverable under paraphrase or membership-inference attacks. We attribute both failures to a common structural cause: the forgetting objective is decoupled from any sample- or parameter-level notion of what retention requires. We present FLOUR (Forgetting via Learned On-manifold Unlearning Representations), a latent unlearning framework in which a lightweight encoder produces a per-sample suppression direction. This direction is anchored to the null region of the reference model’s activations, keeping it on-manifold and disentangled from retention-critical directions, which enables forgetting while preserving coherent generation and enhancing privacy. Results on the Open-Unlearning benchmark suite show that FLOUR most closely matches the retrain oracle across the unlearning trilemma of forgetting, retention, and privacy, substantially outperforming prior baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ judydnguyen/flour-unlearning.

title: TriAlign: Towards Universal Truth Consistency in Personalized LLM Alignment
author: Thi-Nhung Nguyen; Linhao Luo; Rollin Omari; Junae Kim; Thuy-Trang Vu; Dinh Phung
abstract: Personalized large language models adapt responses to users’ preferences and social attributes, but can introduce substantial universal truth inconsistencies across social groups, where some groups systematically receive less accurate responses on objective tasks. Existing alignment methods either ignore personalization or mainly focus on subjective preference alignment, largely overlooking fairness and consistency in universal truths. To address this gap, we study Truth-Invariant Alignment (TIA), an alignment problem for personalized LLMs that aims to ensure universal truths remain consistent across social groups while preserving personalization. We propose TriAlign, the first offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for TIA, where each social group is modeled as an agent interacting. TriAlign jointly optimizes universal truth accuracy, cross-group truth consistency, and personalization through a fairness-aware objective and an explicit inconsistency penalty. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that TriAlign achieves a stronger balance among these three objectives than strong baselines, reducing universal truth disparities across social groups while improving both objective task performance and personalization quality.

title: THE-Tree: Can Tracing Historical Evolution Enhance Scientific Verification and Reasoning?
author: Xin Wang; Jiyao Liu; Yulong Xiao; Junzhi Ning; Hairong Zhang; Lihao Liu; Junjun He; Botian Shi; Kaicheng Yu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are accelerating scientific idea generation, but rigorously evaluating these numerous, often superficial, AI-generated propositions for novelty and factual accuracy is a critical bottleneck; manual verification is too slow. Existing validation methods are inadequate: LLMs as standalone verifiers may hallucinate and lack domain knowledge (our findings show ~60% unawareness of relevant papers in specific domains), while traditional citation networks lack explicit causality and narrative surveys are unstructured. This underscores a core challenge: the absence of structured, verifiable, and causally-linked historical data of scientific evolution. To address this, we introduce THE-Tree (Technology History Evolution Tree), a computational framework that constructs such domain-specific evolution trees from scientific literature. THE-Tree employs a search algorithm to explore evolutionary paths. During its node expansion, it utilizes a novel "Think-Verbalize-Cite-Verify" process: an LLM proposes potential advancements and cites supporting literature. Critically, each proposed evolutionary link is then validated for logical coherence and evidential support by a recovered natural language inference mechanism that interrogates the cited literature, ensuring that each step is grounded. We construct and validate 88 THE-Trees across diverse domains and release a benchmark dataset including up to 71k fact verifications covering 27k papers to foster further research. Experiments demonstrate that i) in graph completion, our THE-Tree improves hit@1 by 8% to 14% across multiple models compared to traditional citation networks; ii) for predicting future scientific developments, it improves hit@1 metric by nearly 10%; and iii) when combined with other methods, it boosts the performance of evaluating important scientific papers by almost 100%. By constructing explicit, verifiable pathways of scientific progression, THE-Tree provides a robust historical foundation for evaluating new hypotheses (human or AI-generated) and enables a computable science history, fostering evidence-based AI-driven scientific discovery.

title: HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification
author: Xianzhi Li; Xiaodan Zhu
abstract: Large language models can often generate plausible mathematical reasoning traces, but reliably identifying the correct solution among multiple candidates remains a key challenge. Existing test-time reasoning pipelines typically rely on text-based verifiers that re-read each generated solution, making verification an expensive component of inference. Prior work has shown, however, that LLMs often encode correctness-related signals in their internal representations, including awareness of when their own answers are likely to be wrong. Building on this observation, we introduce HSRM, a lightweight hidden-state reward model that verifies candidate solutions by directly reading the generator’s internal representations rather than re-processing its text. HSRM extracts hidden states from a frozen generator at reasoning-step boundaries and uses a small Transformer encoder to rank candidates. It is trained from self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring neither human-written process supervision nor a large pretrained verifier. Across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator–dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters, providing an efficient alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation.

title: Beyond Planning: Sparse Context Reset for Long-Horizon GUI Agents
author: Weiyao Huang; Xinye Wu; Zeming Liu; Xiaoyu Shen; Yunpu Ma
abstract: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for computer-use automation, but remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks. Existing planner–executor frameworks address this by shifting more reasoning to the planner, thereby decomposing rather than decoupling long-horizon reasoning. Our failure analysis reveals that many long-horizon failures are not pure capability gaps: from the same failure state, executors recover substantially more often when their accumulated context is reset with a locally executable subtask. To bridge this gap, we propose SCoR, a sparse context reset framework that restores the executor’s short-horizon capability by resetting its accumulated task context. At subtask boundaries, a lightweight Refiner emits a locally executable subtask and resets the Executor’s context; the executor then autonomously executes multiple GUI actions within the reset context. We train the Refiner with turn-level GRPO. In OSWorld, SCoR achieves a success rate of 53.16%, yielding a 25.41% relative improvement over the standalone EvoCUA-8B executor. Our code is available at https://github.com/huia711/SCoR.

title: Cleansing the Artificial Mind: A Self-Reflective Detoxification Framework for Large Language Models
author: Kaituo Zhang; Zhimeng Jiang; Na Zou
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in Large Language Models (LLMs) have revealed remarkable generative capabilities and emerging self-regulatory mechanisms, including self-correction and self-rewarding. However, current detoxification techniques rarely exploit these built-in abilities; instead, they rely on external modules, labor-intensive data annotation, or human intervention –factors that hinder scalability and consistency. In this paper, we introduce a fully self-reflective detoxification framework that harnesses the inherent capacities of LLMs to detect, correct toxic content, and refine LLMs without external modules and data annotation. Specifically, we propose a Toxic Signal Detector—an internal self-identification mechanism, coupled with a systematic intervention process to transform toxic text into its non-toxic counterpart. This iterative procedure yields a contrastive detoxification dataset used to fine-tune the model, enhancing its ability for safe and coherent text generation. Experiments on benchmark datasets such as DetoxLLM and ParaDetox show that our method achieves better detoxification performance than state-of-the-art methods while preserving semantic fidelity. By obviating the need for human intervention or external components, this paper reveals the intrinsic self-detoxification ability of LLMs, offering a consistent and effective approach for mitigating harmful content generation. Ultimately, our findings underscore the potential for self-regulated language models and more responsible text generation systems. Code: https://github.com/KaituoZhang/SRD Warning: this paper may contain offensive content.

title: The Grammar of Transformers: A Systematic Review of Interpretability Research on Syntactic Knowledge in Language Models
author: Nora Graichen; Iria de-Dios-Flores; Gemma Boleda
abstract: We present a systematic review of 337 articles evaluating the syntactic abilities of Transformer-based language models (TLMs), reporting on over 3,000 datapoints spanning a wide range of syntactic phenomena, languages, models, and methods. We take the data to collectively show that TLMs encode a non-trivial amount of syntactic knowledge. Behavioral evidence shows strong performance on formal syntactic phenomena, but weaker and more variable performance on phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface. Performance is also consistently lower for languages with less digital support. Probing and mechanistic studies further support the presence of syntactic knowledge in TLMs. Yet, because most work remains observational and methodologically heterogeneous, insight into the detailed computational mechanisms underlying syntactic processing remains limited. At the same time, the literature remains heavily concentrated on English and BERT-like models. We discuss the implications of our results and provide recommendations for future research.

title: UltraVoice: Scaling Fine-Grained Style-Controlled Speech Conversations for Spoken Dialogue Models
author: Wenming Tu; Guanrou Yang; Ruiqi Yan; Wenxi Chen; Ziyang Ma; Yipeng Kang; Kai Yu; Xie Chen; Zilong Zheng
abstract: Spoken dialogue models currently lack the ability for fine-grained speech style control, a critical capability for human-like interaction that is often overlooked in favor of purely functional capabilities like reasoning and question answering. To address this limitation, we introduce **UltraVoice**, the first large-scale spoken dialogue dataset engineered for multiple fine-grained speech style control. Encompassing over 830 hours of spoken dialogues, UltraVoice provides instructions across six key speech stylistic dimensions: emotion, speed, volume, accent, language, and composite styles. Fine-tuning leading models such as SLAM-Omni and VocalNet on UltraVoice significantly enhances their fine-grained speech stylistic controllability without degrading core conversational abilities. Specifically, our fine-tuned models achieve improvements of 29.12-42.33% in Mean Opinion Score (MOS) and 14.61-40.09 percentage points in Instruction Following Rate (IFR) on multi-dimensional control tasks designed in the UltraVoice. Moreover, on the URO-Bench benchmark, our fine-tuned models demonstrate substantial gains in core understanding, reasoning, and conversational abilities, with average improvements of +10.84% on the Basic setting and +7.87% on the Pro setting. Furthermore, the dataset’s utility extends to training controllable Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, underscoring its high quality and broad applicability for expressive speech synthesis. The complete dataset and model checkpoints are available at: [https://github.com/bigai-nlco/UltraVoice](https://github.com/bigai-nlco/UltraVoice).

title: RoleArena: Autonomous Plot Progression for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Role-Playing
author: Qi Zhao; Jian Li; Yizhang Jin; Dongqi Liu; Hang Ding; Qi Song; Xiang-Yang Li
abstract: Improving the plot progression ability of role-playing language agents (RPLAs) plays a critical role in enhancing user experience and dialogue immersion. However, research on plot progression in role-playing language agents is still limited. Existing datasets often contain too few dialogue turns and lack large-scale sentences with clear deterministic plot turns, which restricts further model development and evaluation. To bridge this gap, we propose RoleArena, an innovative multi-agent role-playing environment. By introducing a critic agent and combining discrete plot lines with environment-agent-based dynamic judgments, the system generates long multi-turn dialogues with key markers for plot progression. Based on RoleArena, we construct the PlotStream dataset, which contains 39.3k characters and 170k dialogues, with annotations for key plot progression sentences. In addition, based on PlotStream, we further develop PlotRole-7B and PlotRole-72B, RPLAs built upon the Qwen2.5 model and specialized in plot progression capabilities. Extensive experiments show that RoleArena and PlotRole improve dialogue generation with plot progression and strengthen the ability of plot progression.

title: Escaping the Frequent Finding Shortcut: Pathology-Aware Curriculum Learning for Radiology Report Generation
author: Ziming Song; Mingyang Shen; Chi Man Vong
abstract: Radiology Report Generation (RRG) has benefited from stronger encoder-decoder pipelines and particularly Large Language Model (LLM) report generators, but most methods still perform training through random mini-batches. This practice is poorly matched to chest radiology corpora, where common normal statements and frequent findings dominate the optimization signal, while clinically important pathological attributes appear in the long tail. We argue that random sampling pushes report generators toward a frequent-finding shortcut, where models quickly learn fluent report narratives and high-frequency disease phrases, then receive limited pressure to recover rare attributes that contribute little to aggregate cross-entropy. To address this problem, we propose ParaC, a pathology-aware replay curriculum for long-tail RRG. ParaC ranks training reports with pathology labels and structured medical knowledge, expands the training process from simple reports to complex long-tail cases, and replays prototype anchors to preserve basic cross-modal grounding. Extensive experiments on IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR confirm the superiority of ParaC on several existing methods, with further ablations analyzing the large gains brought by our pathology-aware curriculum to cover rare pathological findings.

title: Grounded Token Initialization for New Vocabulary in LMs for Generative Recommendation
author: Daiwei Chen; Zhoutong Fu; Chengming Jiang; Haichao Zhang; Ran Zhou; Tan Wang; Chunnan Yao; Guoyao Li; Rui Cai; Yihan Cao; Ruijie Jiang; Fedor Borisyuk; Jianqiang Shen; Jingwei Wu; Ramya Korlakai Vinayak
abstract: Language models (LMs) are increasingly extended with new learnable vocabulary tokens for domain-specific tasks, such as Semantic-ID tokens in generative recommendation. The standard practice initializes these new tokens as the mean of existing vocabulary embeddings, then relies on supervised fine-tuning to learn their representations. We present a systematic analysis of this strategy: through spectral and geometric diagnostics, we show that mean initialization collapses all new tokens into a degenerate subspace, erasing inter-token distinctions that subsequent fine-tuning struggles to fully recover. These findings suggest that token initialization is a key bottleneck when extending LMs with new vocabularies. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose the **Grounded Token Initialization Hypothesis**: linguistically grounding novel tokens in the pretrained embedding space before fine-tuning better enables the model to leverage its general-purpose knowledge for novel-token domains. We operationalize this hypothesis as **GTI** (Grounded Token Initialization), a lightweight grounding stage that, prior to fine-tuning, maps new tokens to distinct, semantically meaningful locations in the pretrained embedding space using only paired linguistic supervision. Despite its simplicity, **GTI** outperforms both mean initialization and existing auxiliary-task adaptation methods in the majority of evaluation settings across multiple generative recommendation benchmarks, including industry-scale and public datasets. Further analyses show that grounded embeddings produce richer inter-token structure that persists through fine-tuning, corroborating the hypothesis that initialization quality is a key bottleneck in vocabulary extension.

title: Emotion Understanding in Streaming Video with Trajectory-Aware Reliability
author: Qingsong Wang; Qigong Lei; Zitong Wang; Bohan Yu; Zhiang Dong; Jian Liu; Weiqiang Wang; Chang Yao; Jingyuan Chen
abstract: Video emotion understanding is commonly studied as an offline classification problem, where the complete video segment is available before prediction.Real-time interaction, however, requires emotion decisions from incomplete and evolving evidence.This paper studies streaming video emotion understanding as a reliability-aware decision process over evolving emotion beliefs. In this setting, a single confident prefix prediction can still be unreliable when the underlying belief trajectory is unstable or repeatedly switches across emotion classes. We propose TRACE, a trajectory-aware reliability framework that forms low-latency emotion beliefs from streaming audio prefixes, estimates reliability from confidence, entropy, stability, and class-switching patterns, and selectively invokes contextual belief reinterpretation with visual, textual, and neighboring-utterance evidence. TRACE keeps stable cases in the low-latency online pathway while allocating stronger multimodal reasoning to uncertain cases that remain ambiguous. Experiments on StreamMER, MELD, and MER2024 show that TRACE improves the accuracy-cost trade-off, retaining most full-context gains while reducing unnecessary contextual reasoning.

title: Prompt Revision as a Source of Cultural Bias in Text-to-Image Systems
author: Aleksandra Urman; Elsa Lichtenegger; Salima Jaoua; Azza Bouleimen; Robin Forsberg; Corinna Hertweck; Stefania Ionescu; Nicolò Pagan; Ancsa Hannak; Joachim Baumann
abstract: Commercial text-to-image systems silently revise user prompts before generating images, a step users typically cannot disable or even see. Existing audits of cultural bias examine only the final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, so they cannot tell where the bias originates. We introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language–context pairings. Using it, we audit the revision layer in three systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5) through a three-step analysis of how heavily it marks each cultural context, whether it flattens that context into a narrow vocabulary, and whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Relative to a no-context English baseline, the US is the least-marked context, while non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked far more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across topically diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. Comparing images from original versus revised prompts on models without a revision layer, we identify the layer itself as a previously undocumented, causal source of this stereotyping. To locate cultural bias, and fix it, we must audit the system as deployed, not the model alone.

title: DITING: Evaluating Sentence-Level Cultural Meaning in Web Novel Translation
author: Enze Zhang; Jiaying Wang; Mengxi Xiao; Jifei Liu; Zhiwei Hu; Ziyan Kuang; Rui Dong; Youzhong Dong; Mohsinul Kabir; Victor Gutierrez Basulto; Min Peng; Qianqian Xie; Sophia Ananiadou
abstract: Large language models are increasingly regarded as strong translators, yet it remains unclear what their success establishes beyond overall translation quality. This question is especially consequential in Chinese web novel translation, where sentence-level cultural meaning shapes tone, characterization, and reader experience. Existing evaluation provides only indirect evidence, as benchmarks emphasize overall quality and available metrics do not explicitly assess the cultural and pragmatic phenomena underlying reader experience. We introduce DITING (a mythological creature known for discerning truth), the first comprehensive evaluation framework for this problem, supported by an expert-annotated benchmark of over 18K Chinese-English sentence pairs, a reasoning-driven multi-agent evaluator, AgentEval, and a 1,440-pair meta-evaluation benchmark, MetricAlign. AgentEval achieves the strongest correlation with human judgments among eight representative automatic metrics. Applying DITING to 14 translation systems shows that current progress is selective rather than general: frontier LLMs lead overall, but their gains concentrate in a subset of dimensions, while zero-pronoun resolution remains the clearest bottleneck. Overall, our results show that aggregate rankings substantially overstate how broadly sentence-level cultural meaning has been solved in web novel translation. All the code and data in https://github.com/whunextgen/DITING.

title: HiSVR: Hierarchical Semantic Visual Reconstruction for Unified Multimodal Models
author: Tailai Chen; Weining Wang; Yuchen Liu; Jun Fu; Jie Jiang; Yiming Cheng; Jing Liu
abstract: Unified multimodal models use a shared Transformer backbone for visual understanding and image generation. Existing post-training signals primarily constrain final outputs, output-side representations, or task-level behavior, providing limited supervision for how visual semantics are organized across intermediate layers. We propose HiSVR, a hierarchical semantic visual reconstruction method for post-training unified multimodal models. A frozen semantic visual tokenizer extracts residual semantic codes from each training image, which supervise image-associated hidden states at different Transformer depths. Shallow layers predict shorter semantic-code prefixes, while deeper layers reconstruct longer prefixes, yielding coarse-to-fine supervision over intermediate representations. To balance the differing optimization difficulty across depths and prefix lengths, we introduce an uncertainty-weighted progressive reconstruction loss. HiSVR is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving the original architecture and inference cost. Experiments on unified multimodal backbones show that HiSVR improves visual understanding while maintaining image generation quality. These results indicate that hierarchical semantic reconstruction effectively regularizes intermediate representations in unified multimodal models.

title: GutenBench: A Taxonomy-Based Dataset for Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
author: Marcio Monteiro; Denys Senkin; Abhilasha Ravichander; Marius Kloft; Sophie Fellenz
abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) relies on retrieved evidence to mitigate hallucination, its reliability is constrained by retrieval quality and diagnosing where retrieval fails remains difficult. Existing benchmarks typically report a single aggregate score over heterogeneous query sets and are often dominated by queries whose relevant passages can be identified through simple lexical overlap, concealing the failure modes that matter most in practice. We introduce GutenBench, a fine-grained, zero-shot evaluation dataset built around a four-level retrieval taxonomy: lexical, semantic, explicit aggregation, and latent conceptual retrieval. It pairs queries with relevance judgments adjudicated by subject-matter experts, enabling precise and controlled comparisons of retrievers. We evaluate several off-the-shelf retrievers in an asymmetric, English-to-target cross-lingual setting across 272 Bible translations (141 languages) and find that performance is strong on lexical and semantic queries, but degrades when models must aggregate information across passages or recognize conceptually relevant passages with no surface overlap.

title: COGTRL: Training LLMs for Scientific Discovery Assistance using Cognitive Traces via Reinforcement Learning
author: Shrinidhi Kumbhar; Santosh Mashetty; Divij Handa; Kevin Coutinho; Siddharth Sambhaji Ghule; Chitta Baral
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on extensive scientific research are increasingly integrated as assistants for scientific discovery. However, most research papers omit the fine-grained cognitive process of examining constraints, failed alternatives, and iterative decisions required to achieve the desired goal. Such cognitive processes are vital for real-world scientists working toward specific goals under constraints. In this paper, we show that LLMs, when trained to produce such cognitive traces, perform better as scientific discovery assistants than when trained solely on scientific literature. We propose COGTRL, a trajectory-level reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to emulate cognitively grounded reasoning by jointly optimizing cognitive traces and the scientific steps produced in an interleaved manner. Across two 3B-parameter models and two scientific domains (AI and Materials Science), COGTRL improves method quality by an average of 7.85 points over comparable 3B model baselines and achieves competitive performance relative to 70B parameter models. Moreover, analysis by domain experts shows a preference for methods generated by COGTRL over the baselines.

title: How Cognitive Biases Propagate in LLM Clinical Differential Diagnosis
author: Soma Bálint Nagy; Richard Farkas
abstract: Clinical diagnostic reasoning is a sequential process: a working hypothesis is formed early in an encounter and updated as new evidence arrives, and biases at one stage can compound across the stages that follow. In human clinicians, anchoring and premature closure account for a large share of preventable diagnostic errors. As large language models are increasingly considered for clinical decision support, an analogous question arises: how do they handle wrong context that enters mid-encounter - whether from their own prior outputs, an earlier clinician’s note, or pushback from a user? Existing evaluations of LLM cognitive bias use single-shot question answering and cannot speak to this dynamic. We introduce a temporal-replay benchmark over MIMIC-IV in which 686 patient timelines are replayed step by step to three open-weight LLMs, with each step’s structured assessment carried forward as the prior for the next. At three clinically meaningful anchor points we inject the same wrong diagnosis through four structurally distinct channels. The most damaging is corruption of the model’s own previous assessment, with effects roughly twice those of any other channel. When this manipulation derails the correct answer, the model lands specifically on the planted diagnosis about half of the time.

title: From Prompts to Trees: Effective LLM-Guided Tree Generation for Few-Shot Tabular Classification
author: Yue Qiu; Zekang Du; Yiqun Diao; Bingsheng He; Qinbin Li
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) possess rich world knowledge and impressive generalization capabilities, their direct application to tabular data classification is hindered by high inference costs and limited interpretability. In contrast, decision trees are fast and transparent but often underperform in low-data regimes. In this work, we propose a novel framework that bridges these paradigms by distilling LLM knowledge into interpretable decision trees under a few-shot learning setting. Instead of directly prompting the LLM to generate full trees, which is often unstable and inefficient, we develop a three-stage paradigm that prompts the LLM to generate rules and organize the rules into a tree. Experiments on multiple real-world tabular datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy and interpretability with significantly lower prompting overhead compared to existing baselines.

title: From Expressions to Needs: Hierarchical Interpretive Reasoning for Emotional Support Conversation
author: Xinjie Zhang; Haotian Fan; Zhaopei Huang; Shujie Ren; Wenxuan Wang; Qin Jin
abstract: Existing emotional support conversation (ESC) systems often react directly to surface-level distress expressions, generating reassurance or advice without adequately modeling the underlying psychological needs driving the distress. However, effective emotional support requires an interpretive process that connects what is expressed with why it is expressed and ultimately what support is needed. We argue that current ESC systems lack such an interpretive layer between observation and supportive intervention. To address this gap, we propose HierINT, a psychologically grounded hierarchical interpretive schema for emotional support conversations. HierINT distinguishes observable communicative intentions from the underlying psychological interpretations that drive them, including cognitive appraisals and unmet fundamental psychological needs. Building on this schema, we construct HierINT-Dlg, a dataset with hierarchical interpretive annotations and need-aligned support strategies. We further propose HierINT-CoRe, a collaborative reasoning framework that operationalizes HierINT by jointly modeling psychological interpretation and support strategy planning prior to response generation. Experiments on ESConv and HierINT-Dlg demonstrate consistent improvements over surface-level and intention-aware baselines, particularly on empowerment and personalization metrics. Our results suggest that effective emotional support requires moving beyond reactive response generation toward psychologically grounded need-informed intervention. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/43zxj/HierINT.

title: Evaluating Style-Personalized Text Generation: Challenges and Directions
author: Anubhav Jangra; Bahareh Sarrafzadeh; Silviu Cucerzan; Adrian de Wynter; Sujay Kumar Jauhar
abstract: With the surge of large language models (LLMs) and their ability to produce customized output, style-personalized text generation–"write like me"–has become a rapidly growing area of interest. However, style personalization is highly specific, relative to every user, and depends strongly on the pragmatic context, which makes it uniquely challenging. Although prior research has introduced benchmarks and metrics for this area, they tend to be non-standardized and have known limitations (e.g., poor correlation with human subjects). LLMs have been found to not capture author-specific style well, it follows that the metrics themselves must be scrutinized carefully. In this work we critically examine the effectiveness of the most common metrics used in the field, such as BLEU, embeddings, and LLMs-as-judges. We evaluate these metrics using our proposed style discrimination benchmark, which spans eight diverse writing tasks across three evaluation settings: domain discrimination, authorship attribution, and LLM-generated personalized vs non-personalized discrimination. We find strong evidence that employing ensembles of diverse evaluation metrics consistently outperforms single-evaluator methods, and conclude by providing guidance on how to reliably assess style-personalized text generation.

title: From Specialization to Generalization: Instruction-tuned LLMs for Robust Harmful Content Mitigation
author: Lukas Edman; Daryna Dementieva; Alexander Fraser
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance across a wide range of general NLP tasks; however, their effectiveness in sensitive domains, such as hate speech detection, remains less clear. Prior studies comparing prompted LLMs with state-of-the-art encoder-based models (e.g., BERT variants (Roy et al., 2023; Dönmez et al., 2024)) have shown only marginal gains, suggesting that LLMs may not excel in hate speech detection or mitigation. In this work, we revisit this question through the lens of instruction tuning. By thoroughly unifying 36 English hate speech datasets spanning multiple labeling schemes, we fine-tune a generalist LLM, based on Qwen3 (Qwen Team, 2025), specifically for hate speech mitigation. Our results demonstrate not only state-of-the-art performance on in-domain benchmarks but also substantial improvements in cross-domain and cross-lingual generalization—areas where encoder-based specialist classifiers often struggle.

title: Calibrating Student Models via Uncertainty-Integrated Distillation
author: Ruixuan Zhang; Hongye Tan; Zhiwei Hu; XiaoQi Han; Ru Li; Jeff Z. Pan; Victor Gutierrez Basulto
abstract: Model calibration aligns a model’s confidence with the accuracy of its predictions, directly influencing reliability and user trust. Surprisingly, existing research on knowledge distillation has paid little attention to the calibration of student models. In this paper, we evaluate calibration across diverse knowledge distillation settings and demonstrate that student models distilled from black-box teachers generally exhibit poor calibration. We attribute this to the fact that distillation fails to convey well-calibrated confidence, which serves as a crucial expression of predictive uncertainty. To address this limitation, we propose an ***U**ncertainty-**I**ntegrated **K**nowledge **D**istillation* (**UIKD**) method comprising two key components: (1) *uncertainty estimation*, which leverages the collective intelligence of multiple LLMs via a debate mechanism to quantify uncertainty in the distillation data; and (2) *uncertainty integration*, which employs an adaptive weighted loss function to integrate this data uncertainty into the student model effectively. Experiments on common-sense reasoning and natural language inference benchmarks demonstrate that UIKD consistently improves student model calibration while maintaining predictive accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuixuanZhang127/UIKD.

title: REFOCUS: Training-Free Attention Sparsification via Uniform-Reference Filtering
author: Fengyuan Fan; Rena Wei Gao; Yanbei Jiang
abstract: Dense softmax attention assigns non-zero probability mass to many task-irrelevant keys, which can dilute useful signals in the attention output. We present REFOCUS, a training-free and plug-and-play inference-time sparsification method that keeps attention entries above a row-wise, context-length-aware threshold and renormalizes the remaining weights. This design is stable, simple to deploy, and requires no model retraining. REFOCUS is integrated in HuggingFace via attn_implementation="refocus" without model-code modification. On Qwen3-4B under 0-shot greedy decoding, REFOCUS matches or outperforms dense eager attention on full-test GSM8K, HumanEval, WinoGrande, and AQuA-RAT, and improves RULER-4k by +0.52 percentage points overall, including +3.20 points on aggregation tasks. These results indicate that a single row-wise threshold can remove diffuse long-tail attention while preserving or improving accuracy.

title: Auditing Chinese Web-scale Corpora via Sampled BPE Token Statistics
author: Qingjie Zhang; Ziqi Tang; Jie Zhang; Gelei Deng; Jinfeng Li; YueFeng Chen; Yitong Yang; Hui Xue; Tianwei Zhang; Han Qiu
abstract: Chinese web pollution has surfaced in LLMs, motivating audits of upstream Chinese corpora. However, auditing such corpora faces three challenges: (1) their web-scale size makes full scan costly; (2) prior analyses are often too coarse to expose token-level pollution; (3) Chinese web pollution is implicit and rapidly changing. We propose Sampled-BPE, a lightweight token-level auditing pipeline that sample a small subset and train BPE tokenizer to surface polluted tokens. Experiments show that Sampled-BPE preserves usable estimates while substantially reducing runtime and memory: a 148.4 \times speedup and a 35.8 \times memory reduction induce only 4.25% relative error for pollution categories. We apply the pipeline to 11 open Chinese corpora and 6 Chinese Common Crawl snapshots from 2021 to 2026. The audit reveals widespread but uneven pollution across open corpora, as well as highly polluted and temporally shifting Chinese web content. We further release a hierarchical Chinese web token dataset with 660k+ token records, each with web context, category, and explanation fields, organized as trees to support review and tracing of pollution.

title: The Autonomy Tax: Defense Training Breaks LLM Agents
author: Li Li; Yue Zhao
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external tools (file operations, API calls, database transactions) to autonomously complete complex multi-step tasks. Practitioners deploy defense-trained models to protect against prompt injection attacks that manipulate agent behavior through malicious observations or retrieved content. We reveal a fundamental capability-alignment paradox: defense training designed to improve safety systematically destroys agent competence while failing to prevent sophisticated attacks. Evaluating defended models against undefended baselines across 97 agent tasks and 1,000 adversarial prompts, we uncover three systematic biases unique to multi-step agents. Agent incompetence bias manifests as immediate tool execution breakdown, with models refusing or generating invalid actions on benign tasks before observing any external content. Cascade amplification bias causes early failures to propagate through retry loops, pushing defended models to timeout on 99% of tasks compared to 13% for baselines. Trigger bias leads to paradoxical security degradation where defended models perform worse than undefended baselines while straightforward attacks bypass defenses at high rates. Root cause analysis reveals these biases stem from shortcut learning: models overfit to surface attack patterns rather than semantic threat understanding, evidenced by extreme variance in defense effectiveness across attack categories. Our findings demonstrate that current defense paradigms optimize for single-turn refusal benchmarks while rendering multi-step agents fundamentally unreliable, necessitating new approaches that preserve tool execution competence under adversarial conditions.

title: Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval: A Large-Small Model Collaboration Framework for Multimodal Entity Alignment
author: Xiongnan Jin; Jianming Lin; Tiantian Mei; Tiantian Zhu; Changxin Huang; Jinpeng Chen; Chaoqun Hong; Jianqiang Li
abstract: Multimodal Knowledge Graphs (MMKGs) provide structured multimodal grounding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), while Multimodal Entity Alignment (MMEA) is essential for integrating heterogeneous MMKGs. However, existing MMEA methods remain vulnerable to noisy modalities and unreliable pseudo-supervision. We propose CRMEA, a large–small collaborative framework for unsupervised MMEA that unifies PTM-based retrieval and MLLM-based reasoning through a closed-loop optimization process. CRMEA introduces a text-centric adaptive cross-modal coordination mechanism to regulate noisy visual evidence, together with a retrieve-and-vote strategy for reliable pseudo-supervision. Extensive experiments show that CRMEA consistently outperforms existing unsupervised MMEA methods and achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art supervised approaches, while maintaining strong robustness, adaptability across heterogeneous backbones, and substantially improved cost-effectiveness over exhaustive MLLM-based alignment. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nsai-szu/CRMEA.

title: Can Heterogeneous Language Models Be Fused?
author: Shilian Chen; Jie Zhou; Qin Chen; Wen Wu; Xin Li; Feng Qi; Liang He
abstract: Model merging aims to integrate multiple expert models into a single model that inherits their complementary strengths without incurring the inference-time cost of ensembling. Recent progress has shown that merging can be highly effective when all source models are homogeneous, i.e., derived from the same pretrained backbone and therefore share aligned parameter coordinates or compatible task vectors. Yet this assumption is increasingly unrealistic in open model ecosystems, where useful experts are often built on different families such as Llama, Qwen, and Mistral. In such heterogeneous settings, direct weight-space fusion becomes ill-posed due to architectural mismatch, latent basis misalignment, and amplified cross-source conflict. We address this problem with HeteroFusion for heterogeneous language model fusion, which consists of two key components: topology-based alignment that transfers knowledge across heterogeneous backbones by matching functional module structures instead of raw tensor coordinates, and conflict-aware denoising that suppresses incompatible or noisy transfer signals during fusion, with a small replay set used to assist transfer-operator optimization. We further provide analytical and empirical evidence for preserving the target adapter basis while predicting structured updates. Across heterogeneous transfer, multi-source fusion, noisy-source robustness, and cross-family generalization settings, HeteroFusion consistently outperforms strong merging, fusion, and ensemble baselines.

title: ReBound: Relevance-Boundary Supervision for Distractor-Robust Mathematical Reasoning
author: Jiahui Long; Lidan Shou; Huan Li; Ke Chen
abstract: Mathematical word problems with plausible irrelevant context expose a failure mode in which language models reason from facts that should not support the target solution. We formulate distractor-robust mathematical reasoning as relevance-boundary supervision: a model should separate Signal facts from Distractor facts before solving, and then ground the solution in Signal facts only. We introduce ReBound, a post-training framework that constructs paired clean–distractor examples, trains boundary-first traces with supervised fine-tuning, and applies correctness-guided reinforcement learning to discourage Distractor use. Across three open base LLMs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ReBound consistently improves distractor robustness over CoT prompting and strong training-based baselines; on Qwen3-0.6B, the distractor benchmark average increases from 34.92 to 48.29. ReBound also preserves competitive clean and perturbation performance. Process diagnostics, ablations, and output-length analysis show that these gains are tied to better fact use and boundary behavior, rather than longer generations or answer-only optimization.The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Rebound-5FB8

title: MP-Bench: Evaluating Voice Agents as a Multiparty Conversation Participant
author: Yi-Jen Shih; Shih-Yun Shan Kuan; Guan-Ting Lin; Kai-Wei Chang; Siddhant Arora; Shu-wen Yang; Abdelrahman Mohamed; Shinji Watanabe; Hung-yi Lee; David Harwath
abstract: Conversational voice agents have advanced significantly, offering increasingly natural human-machine interactions through both cascaded and end-to-end architectures. However, while recent benchmarks extensively evaluate dyadic interactions and passive audio comprehension, they largely overlook a prevalent real-world scenario: multi-party conversations. Evaluating agents in these settings is fundamentally more challenging than in dyadic interactions due to the exponentially greater conversational complexity. For voice agents to integrate seamlessly into human group dynamics, they must not only generate contextually appropriate responses but also demonstrate a nuanced understanding of open turn-taking. To address this gap, we introduce Multiparty Bench (MP-Bench), the first benchmark specifically designed to objectively evaluate conversational speech systems as active participants within multi-party contexts. MP-Bench assesses agent behavior along two primary dimensions: turn-taking awareness and response appropriateness. Additionally, we incorporate comprehension-based question-answering tasks as a complementary evaluation. By benchmarking 12 voice agents, we find that real-time voice agents stay at or below 22% on multiparty comprehension and remain near chance on multiparty turn-taking, exposing an open challenge for real-time voice agents under multiparty scenario.

title: Forewarned Is Not Forearmed: How Coordinated LLMs Shift Reader Opinions in News Comment Sections
author: Wooyoung Go; Yujin Potter; Hyoungshick Kim; Seungjin Ryu; Yongdae Kim
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate human-like online comments at scale, raising concerns that coordinated AI campaigns could manipulate public opinion. While prior work has shown that single AI messages can persuade individual readers, it remains untested whether coordinated multi-agent LLM campaigns, in which multiple agents jointly plan, divide roles, and manage visibility, can shift reader opinions in news comment sections, and whether per-comment AI labels can mitigate such influence. We address these questions through a controlled experiment with 1,000 U.S. adults reading news articles on a Reddit-like platform. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of six conditions, crossing three comment sources (human, independently generated AI, or coordinated multi-agent LLM) with two label settings (per-comment "Likely AI-generated" badges from a deployed detector, shown or hidden). Coordinated LLM comments did not increase average persuasion over independently generated AI comments, but disproportionately converted readers who initially disagreed and compressed opinion diversity by 12%, manufacturing apparent consensus where genuine disagreement existed. The labels reduced the perceived believability of comments but did not reliably reduce actual opinion change. These findings reveal what we call a Knowing-Resisting dissociation between source recognition and behavioral resistance, and indicate that per-comment disclosure alone is insufficient to counter coordinated LLM opinion campaigns.

title: STEEREVAL: Inference-time Interventions Strengthen Multilingual Generalization in Neural Summarization Metrics
author: Silvia Casola; Ryan Soh-Eun Shim; Felicia Körner; Yuchen Mao; Barbara Plank
abstract: An empirical bottleneck for Natural Language Generation tasks such as summarization is the lack of accurate and robust evaluation metrics for many languages, which hinders progress. While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted as evaluators with the advent of LLM-as-a-Judge approaches, their agreement with human judgments remains low across many languages. We take inspiration from recent studies suggesting that multilingual language models often use English as an internal pivot language, and that misalignment with this pivot can lead to degraded downstream performance during text generation. Motivated by this hypothesis, we ask whether steering the activations of neural metrics with respect to an English pivot can improve their correlation with human judgments in multilingual summarization evaluation. We experiment with encoder- and decoder-based metrics across five languages. We find that activation steering is effective for neural metrics, and that a single, language-independent steering vector improves metric–human agreement. Steering also results in improvements when applied to COMET, a small encoder-based metric, showing notable human agreement despite its small scale.

title: DIANOIA: Diagnostic Decomposition and Joint Optimization for Multi-Agent Reasoning
author: Yiming Yang; Zhuoyuan Li; Fanxiang Zeng; Hao Fu; Yue Liu
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems can outperform single-agent baselines, yet practitioners still cannot predict which design works for a new task or diagnose why one fails. We argue this gap persists largely because the field lacks a diagnostic framework with measurable primitives and testable predictions. We introduce DIANOIA, a three-channel decomposition of multi-agent reasoning gain into coverage, fidelity, and synthesis, each of which is empirically measurable. From this decomposition, we propose a diagnostic protocol that forms qualitative hypotheses about bottleneck channels for tasks with measurable quality signals. We instantiate the protocol as a multi-agent system whose three components mirror the channels: role-diverse proposers for coverage, execution- or pseudo-verification-grounded review for fidelity, and iterative synthesis. On GSM8K, MBPP, and BFCL-SP, our method outperforms strong multi-agent baselines under matched standard configurations; on MBPP, it matches the strongest baseline with approximately 5{\times} fewer tokens and dominates the measured accuracy–token Pareto frontier. Full-scale MBPP replications on Qwen, DeepSeek, and Gemini consistently improve over the corresponding single-model baseline. A prospective held-out evaluation on VitaBench, whose bottleneck hypothesis was recorded before running DIANOIA, improves pass rate from 29.5% to 45.0%. DIANOIA reframes multi-agent design as channel-aware resource allocation: diagnose the likely bottleneck, then invest tokens accordingly.

title: Improving Parameter Utilization by Sharing Neural Experts Across Layers in Transformers
author: Dian Jiao; Jiaxin Duan; Shuai Zhao
abstract: Transformer-based large language models often suffer from inter-layer parameter redundancy, where functional transformations are redundantly learned across network depths. We propose CS-MoE, a novel Transformer architecture featuring cross-layer expert sharing to address this inefficiency. Deviating from the widely used Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture that terminates each Transformer block with layer-isolated experts, CS-MoE combines layer-independent experts with concurrent access to a centralized, globally shared expert pool. This Global Experts Sharing mechanism enables elastic control over token-level parameter activation and computational consumption (FLOPs). Experiments demonstrate that CS-MoE achieves lower perplexity than equal-scale dense Transformers while activating only 55% of parameters. Furthermore, its performance scales monotonically with an increased number of activated experts and approaches MoE counterparts that consume more FLOPs by expanding the shared pool without increasing FLOPs. CS-MoE also establishes a flexible Pareto frontier between computational cost and model capacity, offering an efficient alternative for computation-constrained environments.

title: Investigating the Laws of Synonymy Evolution through a Fine-Grained Lemma-Based Framework
author: Eduardo Calò; Pierluigi Cassotti; Stefano De Pascale; Nina Tahmasebi; Pablo Mosteiro
abstract: We investigate how synonyms evolve over time, focusing on two apparently contradictory tendencies: the Law of Differentiation, whereby synonyms diverge in meaning, and the Law of Parallel Change, whereby they co-evolve. We develop a framework that breaks down the laws into a fine-grained taxonomy, which we use to construct a diachronic dataset based on the Oxford English Dictionary. We rely on definition embeddings and the use of LLM-as-a-Judge to link synonyms. We validate our methodology by performing a human evaluation on a subset of the constructed dataset. Finally, we populate the taxonomy and conduct extensive analyses across different time spans to investigate the predominance of each law in English over time. We find that while the Law of Differentiation is larger in absolute numbers, it is driven by the general tendency for meanings to disappear from the language rather than by a property unique to synonymy.

title: CMPA-SLU: A Benchmark for Chinese Mobile Personal Assistant Spoken Language Understanding
author: Di Wu; Zhongqiu Li; Zetao Zhu; Sishi Xiong; Ruiyu Fang; Shuangyong Song
abstract: China has over 1.116 billion mobile Internet users, whose demands continue to evolve rapidly. However, existing Chinese spoken language understanding (SLU) benchmarks are outdated and cover limited domains, failing to reflect real-world mobile assistant scenarios. To this end, we introduce CMPA-SLU, a Chinese SLU dataset for mobile personal assistants collected from real-world applications and annotated with rigorous quality control. CMPA-SLU contains 50 domains, 247 intents, and 74 slot types, expanding the diversity of existing Chinese SLU benchmarks. To better simulate practical deployment scenarios, we further introduce a Partial Category setting, where candidate labels are dynamically filtered using a Bidirectional Guided Embedding (BGE)-based retrieval strategy. We further adopt a label mapping strategy for joint intent and slot prediction within a single generation process. We evaluate multiple large language models (LLMs) under both Full Category and Partial Category settings. Experimental results show that the Partial Category setting improves performance by reducing the candidate label space.

title: How Correct Is Your Answer? A Semantic Correctness Framework for Open QA Evaluation
author: Elitsa Yotkova; Violeta Kastreva; Petar Velkov; Hristo Boyanov; Dimitar Iliyanov Dimitrov; Preslav Nakov; Ivan Koychev
abstract: Reliable evaluation of open-ended question answering remains a bottleneck for measuring answer correctness of modern LLMs. Unlike multiple-choice tasks, free-form answers may be correct in many surface forms and may fail in qualitatively different ways, including incompleteness, contradiction, overgeneration, and endorsement of false premises. Existing judgment-based and similarity-based metrics often collapse these distinctions. We address this gap with three reusable contributions. First, we introduce a semantic correctness taxonomy that assigns open-ended answers to eight ordered classes, separating verbose-but-correct answers from those contaminated by hallucinated content. Second, we release CAP-Correctness, an 8.8k-example benchmark spanning widely used QA datasets, and CAP-Statements, an 11k-example dataset for converting question-answer pairs into declarative statements for natural language inference (NLI) training and statement-based evaluation. Third, we introduce CAP (Context-Aware Precision), a reference-based metric that scores question-conditioned statements using bidirectional NLI. Under a monotonicity protocol testing whether metrics respect the taxonomy’s intended ordering, CAP outperforms established baselines.

title: APEX : Adaptively Balancing Off-Policy Guidance and On-Policy Exploration for LLM Reasoning
author: Yuchen Wang; Zikang Zhang; Duo Xu; Kunpeng Xu; Qihui Zhu; Wei Huang; Siying Wu; Caihong Cheng; Xin He; Yang Yang; Guanjun Jiang; Xiaoyan Sun
abstract: In post-training large language models (LLMs), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides expert guidance but can overfit, while reinforcement learning (RL) enables exploration but often suffers from cold-start and sparse-reward issues. Although combining SFT with RL is intuitive, naively mixing off-policy expert data into on-policy RL can induce distribution shift and destabilize optimization. We propose APEX, a framework that harmonizes off-policy guidance and on-policy exploration via a Cognitive State Awareness mechanism. Specifically, APEX leverages a perplexity-based Student’s -test to compare the sequence-level perplexity distributions of on-policy generations against candidate offline data. This comparison diagnoses whether failures reflect sampling stochasticity or missing knowledge. Guided by this diagnosis, APEX adaptively gates GRPO optimization and modulates SFT supervision. The framework preferentially selects offline samples that are statistically consistent with the current on-policy distribution to guide RL updates, while filtering out high-shift data and verifiably incorrect samples that could destabilize training. APEX also uses a dynamically weighted SFT loss when needed. Extensive experiments show that APEX improves over SFT-then-RL by +7.10 points in average pass@1 on six math benchmarks and by +15.50 points on three general reasoning benchmarks.

title: RFCLLM: Evaluating LLMs’ Reasoning Ability of Network Protocol State Machines
author: Anqi Chen; Dan Goldwasser; Cristina Nita-Rotaru
abstract: Mapping textual specifications into formal representations is essential for ensuring the correctness of protocol designs and implementations. LLM-generated mappings, used for networking security or testing, are assumed to capture a perfect understanding of the specification, which may not hold in practice. The goal of this paper is to assess the extent to which LLMs can interpret the specification correctly. We examine the degree to which an LLM’s implicit representation of a finite-state transition system–defined via natural language descriptions–aligns with a manually generated ground-truth model. We designed 4 tasks and 1482 task queries for 16 protocols. We evaluated different judge biases, observed the inherent difficulty gaps between tasks, looked into the effect of 4 context types, and the influence of protocol characteristics. Our work contributes to a step toward verifying whether LLMs can really be trusted in FSM (Finite State Machine) reasoning of protocol specifications.

title: Managing Evidence at Document Scale: A Survey of Multi-Page Visually Rich Document Understanding
author: Lewei Xu; Yihao Ding; Zihan Xu; Siwen Luo; Daochang Liu; Wei Liu
abstract: Documents spanning tens to hundreds of pages are pervasive in real-world workflows, from scientific papers to financial reports and technical manuals. In this setting, answer-relevant evidence is sparse and distributed across pages, and the document itself often exceeds a backbone MLLM’s context window, making MP-VRDU a distinct problem from single-page VRDU. We survey MP-VRDU through the lens of evidence management, the organising principle that distinguishes multi-page from the single-page setting: the problem of deciding how document-scale evidence is selected and reasoned over when it cannot all be held at once. We introduce a taxonomy spanning four architectural families, multimodal representation, inference-time adaptation, and training strategies for cross-page evidence. We further consolidate MP-VRDU datasets and outline open challenges in efficiency, faithfulness, evidence pipelines, supervision integrity, and reproducible evaluation that define the frontier.

title: QTEA: Ternary LLMs with Sparse Residual Salient Weight and By-Column Optimization
author: Yipin Guo; Jie Fu; Arun M George; Tareq Mahmoud; Siddharth Joshi
abstract: Weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) can alleviate the computational burden of serving large language models (LLMs) at scale. However, existing PTQ methods often fail to generalize across models and suffer severe accuracy loss below 2 bits. Many leverage unstructured sparsity to mitigate this loss, but at the cost of regularity and GPU-friendly execution. We present QTEA, a sub-2-bit PTQ framework that quantizes weights into ternary values and uses salient weights as residual error compensators. To maintain hardware efficiency, residuals are assigned to selected columns with semi-structured 1:4 sparsity within the salient columns. We further add column-wise rescale refinement to GPTQ-style column-by-column quantization, alternately updating per-column scales and ternary assignments to reduce reconstruction error. We also identify order-dependent error propagation in GPTQ and introduce error decay to attenuate late-stage error accumulation. On Qwen3-14B, QTEA compresses all weights to an effective 1.7 bits per weight while improving average accuracy over the strongest ternary PTQ baseline by 16.7%. It also achieves 1.40× and 2.61× lower perplexity on WikiText and C4 respectively. This trend holds on Llama3-8B, where QTEA obtains a 6.6% accuracy gain and 1.34×/1.95× lower perplexity on the same datasets. Finally, we develop a lookup-table based kernel that achieves 7.2× faster per-token generation over an FP16 baseline.

title: SchemaToken: Tokenizing Database Schemas for Efficient and Robust Text-to-SQL Linking
author: Weibin Liao; Jingwen Liu; Rihong Qiu; Xin Gao; Xinyu Ma; Hongxin Ding; Yue Fang; Yifan Zhu; Yuheng Huang; Junfeng Zhao; Yasha Wang
abstract: Schema linking is a crucial step in Text-to-SQL systems, connecting natural language mentions to relevant database tables and columns. Despite recent advances in LLM-based Text-to-SQL models, current approaches face two fundamental limitations: (1) providing detailed column descriptions inflates the input context, often exceeding the model’s effective sequence length, and (2) predicting multi-token column names increases output complexity, making the task fragile to generation errors. To address these challenges, we propose SchemaToken, which represents each database column as a dedicated token in the LLM’s vocabulary. This design compresses column semantics into single embeddings, reducing context length and simplifying prediction. We introduce a two-stage training paradigm: (i) Semantic Alignment, which enables the LLM to understand the newly added schema tokens via structured embeddings, and (ii) Pseudo-task Alignment, which trains the LLM to generate these tokens as an unordered set using reinforcement learning with a Jaccard-based reward. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that SchemaToken significantly improves schema linking performance, particularly for large and complex schemas, while maintaining computational efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MrBlankness/SchemaToken.

title: Vendi-RAG: Adaptively Trading-Off Diversity And Quality Significantly Improves Retrieval Augmented Generation With LLMs
author: Mohammad Reza Rezaei; Adji Bousso Dieng
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for multi-hop question answering is limited by retrieving semantically redundant documents, when reasoning instead needs diverse, complementary sources. We introduce Vendi-RAG, which treats set-level semantic diversity as a first-class retrieval objective. It combines an eigenvalue-based diversity score (the Vendi Score) with query relevance into a single Vendi Retrieval Score, embedded in an iterative loop that uses an LLM-based answer-quality signal to adaptively rebalance diversity and relevance. On HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, Vendi-RAG improves accuracy by +2.4, +1.6, and +2.4 points over the strongest diversity-aware iterative baseline (Adaptive Retrieval + MMR). A fixed-s variant captures most of the gain at no extra inference cost, while the LLM-judge loop adds a smaller but significant gain on hard queries. Results hold across five instruction-tuned backbones and two dense retrievers, identifying set-level retrieval diversity as a primary, controllable axis for improving multi-hop RAG.
