Building on this representation, TSA-RAG navigates evidence through a progressive Expand-Route-Retrieve paradigm, which expands query-focused subgraphs under path-consistency constraints, routes the query to structural entry points within relevant documents, and retrieves subtree-structured evidence preserving discourse continuity. Extensive experiments on seven QA datasets demonstrate that TSA-RAG consistently outperforms strong baselines while yielding more compact retrieval contexts. Quantitative analyses further confirm the scalability and robustness of our framework. Code is available at https://github.com/ZKYQUQ/TSA-RAG.

title: Bridging Time Series and Language via Query-Adaptive Multi-Granularity Routing for Temporal Reasoning
author: Hyuna Jeon; Jaeyoung Lee; Misuk Kim
abstract: Time-Series Question Answering (TSQA) aims to interpret time-series information and generate answers according to the intent of natural language questions. However, in TSQA, the required temporal granularity and reasoning scope vary across queries, making it crucial to effectively organize the time-series information needed for each query. In this study, we propose TiMER (**Ti**me-series and language alignment with **M**ulti-granularity **E**xpert **R**outing), a time-series-language alignment framework that selectively constructs multi-granularity time-series information according to query intent and connects it to the LLM input space. Experimental results on a large-scale TSQA benchmark show that TiMER achieves an overall accuracy of 81.02% using only a small number of external alignment modules while keeping the LLM frozen, outperforming various LLM-based baselines. In addition, extensive ablation studies verify the effectiveness of each component. This study presents an effective direction for natural language-based time-series understanding and temporal reasoning by dynamically organizing and utilizing time-series information according to query intent. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hyuna0926/TiMER_paper.

title: PaperScout: An Autonomous Agent for Academic Paper Search with Process-Aware Sequence-Level Policy Optimization
author: Tingyue Pan; Jie Ouyang; Mingyue Cheng; Qingchuan Li; Zirui Liu; Daoyu Wang; Mingfan Pan; Shuo Yu; Qi Liu; Enhong Chen
abstract: Academic paper search is a fundamental task in scientific research, yet most existing approaches rely on rigid, predefined workflows that struggle with complex, conditional queries. To address this limitation, we propose PaperScout, an autonomous agent that reformulates paper search as a sequential decision-making process. Unlike static workflows, PaperScout dynamically decides whether, when, and how to invoke search and expand tools based on accumulated retrieval context. However, training such agents presents a fundamental challenge: standard reinforcement learning methods, typically designed for single-turn tasks, suffer from a granularity mismatch when applied to multi-turn agentic tasks—where token-level optimization diverges from the granularity of sequence-level interactions—leading to noisy credit assignment and unstable training dynamics. We introduce Proximal Sequence Policy Optimization (PSPO), a process-aware, sequence-level policy optimization method that aligns optimization with agent–environment interaction. Comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that PaperScout significantly outperforms strong workflow-driven and RL baselines in both recall and relevance, validating the effectiveness of our adaptive agentic framework and optimization strategy.

title: Agreement Is Not Truth: Characterizing and Controlling Consistent-but-Wrong Reasoning in LLMs
author: Minje Kim; Keeheon Lee; Chi-Guhn Lee
abstract: Self-consistency treats agreement among sampled chains of thought as evidence that the answer is correct. We show that this reading fails predictably. Across 5 reasoning datasets and 5 generators, consistent-but-wrong (CBW) rates track the task rather than the generator, and the pattern holds across agreement thresholds and sample budgets. On StrategyQA, at least 15% of answers are wrong at 90% self-agreement. We prove that no procedure reading only the answer distribution can always separate a question whose majority is right from one whose majority is wrong. We propose Risk-Controlled Self-Consistency (RISC), which combines the majority ratio with a verifier signal and calibrates an acceptance threshold by Learn-then-Test. It certifies the risk target in domain at finite sample size, and accepts nothing when no threshold qualifies. Against self-consistency alone, pooled selective error falls 3.01pp at 0.50 coverage; per-task gains are mixed. At 0.9 coverage, a local generator with a lightweight verifier costs ~9× less than an all-API baseline and shows no detectable selective-error gap on four of five datasets. It trails on MATH500. Higher agreement is not always higher accuracy. Calibration narrows the gap, but more sampling usually does not.

title: ReasoningFlow: Discourse Structures for Understanding LLM Reasoning Traces
author: Jinu Lee; Shivam Agarwal; Amruta Parulekar; Siddarth Madala; Dilek Hakkani-Tür; Julia Hockenmaier
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) produce reasoning traces with non-linear structures, such as backtracking and self-correction, that complicate the evaluation and monitoring of the reasoning process. We introduce ReasoningFlow, a framework that captures the discourse structures of LRM reasoning traces into fine-grained directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). We develop and validate our annotation schema through careful manual annotation of 31 traces (2.1k steps), achieving high inter-annotator agreement, then scale to automatic annotation of 1,260 traces (247.7k steps) spanning three tasks (math, science, argumentation) and five models (Qwen2.5-32B-Inst, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-oss-120B). By analyzing ReasoningFlow graphs, we find: (1) LRMs exhibit structurally similar traces, despite being trained from different base models and potentially non-overlapping post-training data. (2) ReasoningFlow reveals diverse fine-grained reasoning behaviors (e.g., local verification, self-reflection, and assumptions) that can be used for better reasoning trace monitorability. (3) In LRMs, most of the erroneous steps are not used to derive final answers. (4) Mechanistic causal dependencies between steps do not reflect the language-level discourse structure.

title: BiNSGPS: Geometry Problem Solving via Bidirectional Neuro-Symbolic Interaction
author: Qi Wang; Peijie Wang; Fei Yin; Cheng-Lin Liu
abstract: Geometry problem solving poses distinct challenges in artificial intelligence. Existing approaches typically fall into two paradigms: symbolic methods, which exhibit limited adaptability, and neural methods, which are prone to hallucinations. Recent neuro-symbolic hybrids predominantly rely on a unidirectional pipeline where neural outputs are fed into solvers without feedback, making system brittle to early-stage errors. To break this unidirectional bottleneck, we propose BiNSGPS, a framework that establishes Bidirectional Neuro-Symbolic Interaction (BiNS) between a MLLM Adviser and a Symbolic Solver. MLLM Adviser actively incorporates feedback from the symbolic solver to dynamically rectify inconsistent formal representations or propose auxiliary hypotheses, resolving symbolic conflicts and facilitating complex deductions. Experiments show that BiNSGPS achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 90.5% completion accuracy on Geometry3K and 90.1% on PGPS9K, while maintaining 96% step-wise logical coherence to balance capability with mathematical rigor.

title: Charting Empirical Patterns for LLM Fine-Tuning in Scientific Multi-Discipline Learning
author: Lintao Wang; Zhuqiang Lu; Yilin Zhu; Kun Hu; Zhenfei Yin; Shixiang Tang; Zhiyong Wang; Wanli Ouyang; Xinzhu Ma
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly after adaptation within individual scientific domains, their learning dynamics in multi-disciplinary contexts remain poorly understood, despite the promise of improved generalization and broader applicability through cross-domain knowledge synergy. We present a systematic study of multi-discipline LLM fine-tuning across five scientific disciplines and compare the learning dynamics of full fine-tuning, LoRA, LoRA-MoE, and LoRA composition. In our naturally imbalanced setting, we show that multi-disciplinary learning is substantially more variable than single-discipline training and distill four empirical patterns: (1) Balance-then-Diversity: increasing scarce-domain exposure helps, but broad source-pool diversity must be preserved; (2) Merge-then-Align: general instruction data restores instruction-following behavior needed for effective joint adaptation; (3) Optimize-then-Scale: increasing trainable capacity offers limited gains without prior design optimization; and (4) Share-then-Specialize: asymmetric LoRA-MoE improves multi-discipline performance through a shared low-rank projection. Together, these patterns form a practical recipe for principled multi-discipline fine-tuning and provide actionable guidance for developing generalizable scientific LLMs.

title: Logic Tree: Topology-Aware Backtracking for DeepResearch Agents
author: Tianwen Lyu; Zhengke Gui; Peilong Zhao; Ling Zhong; Yiwen Zhang; Lei Liang; Mengshu Sun; Jun Zhou; Qiang Zhang; Huajun Chen
abstract: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong potential for open-ended information-seeking tasks. However, existing agent frameworks primarily rely on sequential execution, making them vulnerable to error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning. Recent plan-and-execute approaches partially alleviate this issue, but their fixed planning strategies still struggle to recover from intermediate failures. We propose Logic Tree, a non-linear agentic reasoning framework formulated as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Instead of following a fixed plan with sequential execution, Logic Tree models complex task solving as a dynamically evolving and recoverable graph search process. The framework decomposes queries into parallel execution branches and incorporates a two-level self-correction mechanism. Local backtracking performs targeted rollback to repair failed reasoning states, while global replanning revises high-level execution strategies and preserves verified intermediate conclusions through a knowledge sanitation process. Experiments on BrowseComp, GAIA, and XBench show that Logic Tree consistently outperforms both sequential and plan-and-execute baselines. Further ablation studies demonstrate that combining DAG-based parallel execution with dynamic error recovery substantially improves robustness in long-horizon research tasks.

title: Confident Rankings with Fewer Items: Adaptive LLM Evaluation with Continuous Scores
author: Esma Balkir; Alice Pernthaller; Marco Basaldella; Jose Hernandez-Orallo; Nigel Collier
abstract: Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) has proven effective for efficient LLM evaluation on multiple-choice benchmarks, but modern LLM evaluation increasingly relies on generation tasks where outputs are scored continuously rather than marked correct/incorrect. We present a principled extension of IRT-based adaptive testing to continuous bounded scores (ROUGE, BLEU, LLM-as-a-Judge) by replacing the Bernoulli response distribution with a heteroskedastic normal distribution. Building on this, we introduce an uncertainty aware ranker with adaptive stopping criteria that achieves reliable model ranking while testing as few items and as cheaply as possible. We validate our method on five benchmarks spanning n-gram-based, embedding-based, and LLM-as-judge metrics. Our method improves ranking correlation by 0.13 \tau over random sampling and has 99% accuracy on confident predictions while using 2% of the items after a one-time calibration step

title: From Final Artifacts to Trajectories: Retrospective Process Supervision for Evidence-Grounded Long-Form Generation
author: Junjie Huang; Jiarui Qin; di Yin; Weiwen Liu; Yong Yu; Xing Sun; Weinan Zhang
abstract: Trajectory data is getting more vital for training large language models for boosting the agentic abilities. Unlike the verifiable domains such as coding or mathematics, scaling trajectory data for open-ended tasks are much more difficult because these tasks lack singular ground truth and are costly to annotate or verify. In this paper, we propose RetroGen, a self-improving framework of retrospective process supervision. Our key observation is that although expert trajectories are scarce, high-quality final artifacts such as literature reviews, analyst reports and legal judgments, are abundant in pre-training data and can be viewed as compressed traces of the evidence-seeking processes that produced them. RetroGen reconstructs candidate latent trajectories from expert artifacts, verifies them against both the artifact and supporting evidence, and trains models on their own successful reconstruction data, without requiring trajectory data from stronger models. Experiments show that RetroGen improves grounding, faithful synthesis, and long-form evidence-seeking agent tasks.

title: GradSentry: Gradient Spectral Entropy for Backdoor Sample Filtering in Large Language Model Fine-Tuning
author: Haodong Zhao; Tianyi Xu; Tianhang Zhao; Zhuosheng Zhang; Gongshen Liu
abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models with untrusted data exposes models to backdoor attacks, where poisoned samples cause targeted misbehavior. Existing sample-filtering defenses rely on clustering, which requires sufficient data and can fail at extreme poison ratios. We propose GradSentry(Gradient Sentry), a backdoor sample filtering method based on the spectral entropy of per-sample gradients. Our key finding is that poisoned samples produce gradients with higher spectral entropy compared to clean samples. GradSentry captures output-altering backdoor signatures using per-sample gradient spectra, avoiding pairwise sample comparisons and clustering during feature construction. Importantly, our method is training-agnostic: it works for both parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA and full-parameter tuning, as the gradient analysis operates independently of which parameters are being updated during training. GradSentry requires no clustering, operates effectively across all poison ratios (1%–90%), and introduces minimal computational overhead (20–50ms per sample for a 7B model). Evaluation on four QA datasets and four attack types demonstrates the effectiveness of spectral entropy for backdoor detection.

title: CMIE: Cross-Modal Interaction Erasure for MLLM Safety Unlearning via Counterfactual Localization and Subspace Nullification
author: Jiatian Cao; Linyi Cai; Mengqi Wang; Jinduo Liu; Junzhong Ji; Yongping Du; Honggui Han
abstract: Safety unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fails when it treats danger as an object, topic, or prompt template. A useful MLLM must still recognize risky visual evidence and answer benign educational or preventive questions about the same content. The safety-critical target is narrower: the post-fusion interaction that converts risky visual evidence and unsafe textual intent into actionable harmful assistance. Existing refusal-oriented and unlearning objectives reach this mechanism only indirectly, widening refusal boundaries or leaving recoverable multimodal harmful pathways. We propose CMIE, Cross-Modal Interaction Erasure, a mechanism-level method that directly treats the harmful image-text interaction as the object of erasure. CMIE first estimates harmful interaction directions with intent-matched counterfactual contrasts that cancel unimodal main effects. It then localizes behaviorally active post-fusion layers and estimates a safe-whitened low-rank harmful subspace. A closed-form minimum-distortion weight edit erases this subspace, and projection-constrained recovery restores benign utility without rewriting erased directions. Across SafeEraser, VLGuard, and MSSBench, CMIE achieves the best overall mean rank and outperforms strong baselines on multiple safety, utility, visual selectivity, and paired-context metrics. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language and images, and reader discretion is recommended.

title: Beyond CTC Spikes: LLM-Driven Gloss-Temporal Supervision for Continuous Sign Language Recognition
author: Junfeng Zhu; Cheng Jin; Yuchun Fang
abstract: Continuous Sign Language Recognition aims to predict gloss sequences from unsegmented sign language videos. Existing methods typically rely on Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss for implicit alignment, which is the most dominant loss function for current sequence alignment tasks but causes low-entropy alignment and weak visual-semantic correspondence learning. To address this issue, we propose an explicit temporal-semantic supervision framework that provides dense signals beyond CTC. Specifically, we design the Gloss-Temporal Module (GTM) to construct sustained gloss-to-frame interval supervision by using an LLM to integrate three types of information from RGB videos. We further introduce a joint optimization method with frame-level and sequence-level objectives, coupled with a curriculum learning strategy, enabling a transition from local to global alignment and improving the model’s learning of visual-semantic features. The results show that dense temporal supervision substantially alleviates alignment collapse and enables even simple RGB-only baseline models to achieve competitive performance among state-of-the-art methods without extra cues, while the recognizer converges significantly faster.

title: Towards Reliable Long-Context Reasoning: Detecting Unanswerable Questions via FactGuard
author: Qian-Wen Zhang; Biao Liu; Fang Li; Jie Wang; Lingfeng Qiao; Yifei Yu; di Yin; Xing Sun
abstract: Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in long-context tasks, their reliability in recognizing unanswerable questions remains a critical challenge. In information-seeking scenarios, models often suffer from overconfidence and hallucinations when evidence is missing or misleading. In this paper, we propose FactGuard, a systematic multi-task workflow for generating evidence-grounded answerable and unanswerable questions. We introduce FactGuard-Bench, a benchmark comprising 25,220 examples with context lengths up to 128K, specifically targeting Lack of Evidence and Misleading Evidence scenarios. Evaluations of eleven representative open-source and proprietary LLMs reveal a significant reliability gap: models struggle to reject unanswerable questions as context scales, with the leading model achieving only 71.62% accuracy. By training with FactGuard-Bench, we improve overall accuracy to 81.17% and significantly enhance models’ reasoned rejection capabilities. Our work provides a scalable path toward building more faithful and trustworthy long-context LLMs. Our source is publicly available at https://github.com/biaoliu-kiritsugu/FactGuard.

title: Benchmarking Language Models for Statistical Problem Formulation
author: Chen Wang; Junzhe Zhao; Xin Cong; Wanlu Deng; Ke Deng
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as assistants for statistical and data science work, yet existing evaluations largely assume the analysis target is already specified. In practice, users arrive with informal goals and heterogeneous data, leaving the model to decide what statistical task is implied and which data are relevant. We first formalize this upstream step as Statistical Problem Formulation and decompose it into two subtasks: (1) Statistical Problem Classification and (2) Variable Identification Role Assignment. We then introduce StatFormBench, a benchmark built from five cross-domain statistics textbooks and a data science case library, covering diverse problem types, data representations, and scenario styles. It contains 1,013 samples spanning 20 coarse-grained and 85 fine-grained statistical problem categories. Across 14 open- and closed-source LLMs, the best zero-shot models reach only 72.0 fine-grained classification accuracy and 63.2 variable set overlap. No model performs consistently best across the two subtasks, while enhanced prompting strategies yield only limited or inconsistent gains. We release the benchmark data on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/THU-CongLab/StatFormBench and the evaluation code on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-CongLab/StatFormBench.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge: Concerning Rubric Artifacts in LLM-based Automated Text Generation Evaluation
author: Anshul Bagaria; Sowmya S Sundaram; Gokul S Krishnan; Balaraman Ravindran
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are increasingly used to evaluate AI-generated text, based on the assumption that judgments arise from reasoning over candidate responses with respect to a rubric. We show that this assumption warrants further scrutiny. Classifiers trained only on rubric text, without access to any evaluated response, achieve nontrivial predictive performance on judge outputs. This suggests that rubric formulations encode recoverable evaluative signals, allowing scores to be partially anticipated independently of model outputs. Finally, counterfactual perturbations reveal that judges often fail to reliably update their decisions when either the candidate response or the rubric criterion is reversed. Our findings raise concerns about the reliability of rubric-based LLM evaluation and highlight the need for further methodological study of automated evaluation via LLMs.

title: Can LLMs Follow Medical Expert Logic? A Benchmark for Hierarchical Logical Consistency in Risk-of-Bias Assessment
author: Jiayu Huang; Zichen Tang; Qianhui Ling; Zemin Kuang; Haihong E
abstract: Evidence-based medicine (EBM) demands strict logical consistency, yet current evaluations of large language models (LLMs) prioritize superficial label matching over genuine reasoning. We introduce LogiMed-RoB, a benchmark grounded in Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) 2.0 expert logic, comprising 860 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 14,820 queries. It evaluates models under the Hierarchical Logical Consistency (HLC) framework across four dimensions: Atomic Consistency, Domain Consistency, Aggregation Consistency, and Evidential Faithfulness. Experiments on 10 state-of-the-art LLMs reveal a catastrophic Error Compounding Effect: despite the top model reaching 98.88% Atomic Consistency, its end-to-end consistency collapses to 45.13%, with several open-weight architectures plummeting to nearly 0%. We further uncover a systematic evidence-reasoning gap: even when models retrieve high-quality evidence, they fail to deduce correct outcomes in 18.63–40.05% of cases, while Blind Guess Rates reach 48.28%. LogiMed-RoB demonstrates that high outcome accuracy can conceal critical reasoning flaws, underscoring the necessity of white-box logical verification for clinical deployment.

title: Han2Han: Efficient Language-Specific Character Representation through Script-Aware Pre-Training for Historical Text Analysis
author: Cellik Adams; EunKyoung Jo; Juae Kim
abstract: Language models learn semantic similarity from shared context; however, when a single word has multiple orthographies that rarely appear in the same context, models cannot learn their equivalence. This is a structural problem that cannot be solved with scale. Korean presents a clear case: 20th-century print media used Hanja (Sino-Korean script), while contemporary models train on Hangul-only (Korean alphabet) text. Multilingual models inherit script segregation from their training distribution, where Hanja appears almost exclusively outside Korean text, and monolingual Korean models assign separate vocabulary entries to script variants, forcing distinct representations from initialization. We introduce Han2Han, a 169M parameter encoder-decoder model trained with a language-aware recipe—jamo and character-level embedding fusion, morpheme-aware denoising, and bidirectional Hanja-Hangul transcription—that forces orthographic alignment as a prior to distributional learning. The resulting representations are script-invariant: the same content receives the same representation regardless of script. On temporal classification of mixed-script historical newspapers, evaluated on an article-level held-out split, Han2Han reaches 76.0 macro F1 against 54.3 for the strongest baselines (KLUE-BERT and the 4.7\times larger T5Gemma 2 alike), a 21.7-point margin, demonstrating that language-specific pre-training yields capabilities not addressed by current Korean-inclusive multilingual training at this scale.

title: Online Language Adaptive Sampling for Better Distributed Cross-lingual Gains
author: Quang Phuoc Nguyen; Félix Gaschi; David Anugraha; Santiago Martínez Novoa; En-Shiun Annie Lee
abstract: Realignment is a promising approach for improving the cross-lingual transfer ability of multilingual language models, particularly for extremely low-resource languages (LRLs). However, existing realignment methods rely on uniform and random sampling of parallel sentences across languages, which may be suboptimal under limited batch sizes. In practice, models may benefit from seeing certain languages more frequently, especially those that are poorly aligned, and the optimal distribution can evolve throughout training. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective adaptive sampling strategy that assigns trainable sampling probabilities to each language. Languages that contribute more to the realignment loss are sampled more frequently in subsequent batches, and the optimal distribution can evolve throughout training. Our method employs an inner–outer optimization loop with a small overhead, leading to consistent performance improvements and, more importantly, distributing the gains across languages. We observed a +0.67 average performance increase on all tasks with XLM-R, and +0.60 with Gemma 2 9B compared with uniform realignment. Furthermore, our method is robust across different models.

title: MobQA: A Benchmark Dataset for Semantic Understanding of Human Mobility Data through Question Answering
author: Hikaru Asano; Hiroki Ouchi; Akira Kasuga; Ryo Yonetani
abstract: This paper presents MobQA, a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the semantic understanding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) for human mobility data through natural language question answering. While existing models predict human movement patterns well, their ability to interpret underlying reasons or semantic meaning remains unclear. To address this gap, we annotated 14,260 trajectory points from the GeoLife dataset with 30,703 semantic labels covering points of interest, mobility modes, and visit reasons, grounding semantics-dependent questions and reference answers. Building on these annotations, MobQA provides 5,800 question–answer pairs from daily and weekly GPS trajectories, spanning factual retrieval, multiple-choice semantic inference, and free-form interpretive explanation. Our evaluation of major LLMs reveals strong performance on factual retrieval but notable limits in semantic reasoning and explanation, with trajectory length substantially impacting effectiveness. These findings demonstrate both achievements and limitations of recent LLMs for semantic mobility understanding.

title: GAC: Noise-Aware Adaptive Mixing for Hybrid SFT-RL Post-Training
author: Yuelin Hu; Wei Liu; Zhenbo Yu; Zhengxue Cheng; Li Song
abstract: Hybrid post-training combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) is the standard paradigm for aligning large language models, yet fixed mixing schedules cannot adapt when the relative noise of the two signals evolves. We derive a noise-aware mixing weight by minimizing an MSE upper bound on the mixed stochastic gradient, yielding a closed-form that balances gradient noise variance and SFT–RL disagreement. Building on the token-wise reweighting of CHORD (CITATION)

title: Subspace Alignment Score: Locating Domain-Relevant Important Parameters in Large Language Models
author: Le Wu; Jiayi Wu; Jixiang Xiong; Mengfa Mo; Jingmin Xin
abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) possess powerful general capabilities, their insufficient domain expertise limits their application in high-reliability scenarios. The sparse activation patterns of neurons in LLM feed-forward layers suggest that structured fine-tuning strategies for domain adaptation can be constructed by identifying important parameters, thereby enhancing domain-specific performance while preserving general capabilities. However, due to high computational costs or weak scalability, current studies struggle to support large-scale and fine-grained domain-relevant parameter analysis. To address this, we investigate the distribution patterns and hierarchical evolution patterns of domain knowledge within the hidden state space of LLMs, and propose a novel parameter evaluation method: Subspace Alignment Score. Intervention experiments across three models and six domains illustrate that, compared with baseline methods, our method demonstrates superior performance in locating domain-relevant important parameters. Furthermore, structured fine-tuning strategies based on the important parameters achieve performance comparable to full fine-tuning while substantially reducing training costs, which is helpful for understanding efficient and interpretable domain adaptation. Our code is available at https://github.com/lewu0723/subspace-alignment-score.

title: Language Identification for Non-Standard Varieties: Language Varieties as Geolects on a Geodesic Grid
author: Sina Ahmadi; Rico Sennrich
abstract: Language identification is a critical preprocessing step for curating multilingual corpora. While current approaches treat language varieties as clearly bounded categories, such discrete labels obscure the continuous nature of linguistic variation in practice. We propose reframing non-standard variety identification as a geographically-grounded task, representing varieties as geolects, that is, linguistic data anchored to geographic coordinates. Rather than classifying texts into predefined labels, we place them on a geodesic grid, where predictions are points on the earth’s surface and variety distinctions emerge from spatial structure. We introduce GeoVar, a fine-grained dataset of 517,985 samples spanning 929 geolects across 20 languages and seven dialect continua in Europe and the Middle East, and develop a grid-based framework with three geolect-to-cell mapping strategies of increasing spatial smoothness: centroid, uniform, and Gaussian. We compare various geolocation methods, with the best model reaching 0.97 accuracy on compact continua such as Basque and Caspian. Accuracy decreases with the geographic dispersion of varieties, with North Germanic being the hardest case. Our model handles non-standard variety text more reliably than current LID tools, while additionally operating at sub-language granularity.

title: EEMA: Experience-Evolving Meta Agents for AutoML
author: Kai Tian; Weizhi Wang; Kaikai Zhao; Che Jiang; Junlin Yang; Zhenzhao Yuan; Jincheng Zhong; Guoli Jia; Yuru Wang; Xinwei Long; Ning Ding; Bowen Zhou; Kaiyan Zhang
abstract: Open machine learning engineering tasks require agents to interpret data, build models, debug code, and produce valid competition submissions. Although current coding agents can generate runnable programs, they often rediscover solutions across tasks and repeat engineering mistakes across feedback rounds. We propose EEMA, an experience-evolving meta-agent framework that organizes accumulated experience by purpose and routes it during multi-round solving. Its static component distills public competition material and historical failure traces into compact Skills: task-level modeling priors for improving solution quality and failure-prevention contracts for maintaining execution validity. Its dynamic component, Experience Routed Search (ERS), operates above a lower-level coding agent. At each round, ERS selects a draft, debug, or improve action, routes the corresponding Skill, and updates task memory, allowing cross-task experience to guide code generation while task-level feedback shapes later decisions. On MLE-bench Lite (22 tasks), EEMA achieves a 77.3% medal rate, 20.1% average leaderboard Grade, and 96.0% execution success, outperforming all baselines including GPT-5.5-xhigh. Ablations show that task Skills improve solution quality, failure-prevention Skills improve reliability, and ERS coordinates both effectively. The materials will be released at https://github.com/FrontisAI/OpenRSI.

title: MessageSieve: Runtime Message Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM-Based Multi-Agent Communication
author: Nianhao You; Yubo Dong; Jun Wang; Hehe Fan; Yi Yang
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) improve reasoning through specialized collaboration, but dense multi-round communication can increase prompt cost and expose agents to outdated, redundant, or noisy context. A prominent line of MAS communication-efficiency work reduces communication through agent-, edge-, or topology-level structural decisions, which operate on graph structure rather than the realized text entering a specific receiver prompt. Such structural decisions are too coarse for runtime communication: messages sent over the same edge may carry useful evidence in one query, redundant content in another, or only a few useful spans. We introduce MessageSieve, a training-free runtime message pruning policy for fixed-graph MAS that operates on message instances rather than agents or edges. Before prompt assembly, it uses lightweight state cards and local message comparisons to preserve original text, retain compact evidence, or omit messages, without a trained selector or additional LLM call. We evaluate MessageSieve on two backbone models and five benchmarks covering expert QA, math reasoning, and code generation. Experiments show that MessageSieve improves the macro-average score over dense Full MAS by 4.10 points on Qwen3-8B and 2.59 points on Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, while reducing evaluation tokens by 19–49%.

title: Adaptive Boundaries: Context-Aware Detection for Synthetic Text
author: Haorong Li; Ruitao Ni; Haihui Yang; Shiping Gao; Yang Liu; Xiaojun Quan
abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) has created an urgent need for accurate and robust detection of AI-generated text. However, existing statistical detectors often rely on a fixed decision boundary, which hinders their ability to generalize across topics, styles, and model variants. In this paper, we propose preference calibration with context-aware thresholding (PC-CAT), a novel framework that integrates preference calibration with context-aware thresholding to improve detection reliability. PC-CAT first applies Simple Preference Optimization (SimPO) to maximize the log-probability gap between paired human-written and AI-generated texts, enhancing discriminability. It then tailors instance-specific thresholds using a lightweight regressor trained with a hybrid centering and ordinal objective. Experiments across diverse domains and generators show that PC-CAT consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves new state-of-the-art results. Moreover, it exhibits strong robustness under distribution shifts and adversarial attacks. These findings highlight the critical role of adaptive thresholding in advancing the robustness of AI-generated text detectors.

title: AfriSUD: A Dependency Treebank Collection for Evaluating Models on African Languages
author: Happy Buzaaba; Cheikh Mouhamadou Bamba Dione; David Ifeoluwa Adelani; Sylvain Kahane; Bruno Guillaume; Kim Gerdes; Shamsuddeen Hassan Muhammad; Kevin Guan; Anuoluwapo Aremu; Naome A Etori; Utitofon Inyang; Peter Nabende; David Sabiiti Bamutura; Andiswa Bukula; Idris Akinade; Chinedu Uchechukwu; Rooweither Mabuya; Christiane Fellbaum
abstract: Despite their linguistic diversity and global significance, African languages remain underrepresented in research and resources to support NLP. We aim to bridge this gap by introducing AfriSUD, the first multilingual collection of syntactically annotated treebanks for nine diverse African languages spanning major language families and regions across Sub-Saharan Africa. Using the Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD) framework, our community-led effort provides high-quality, native-speaker-verified data that capture typological key features such as agglutination and tone. We evaluate a range of models on AfriSUD for part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing, including non-transformer baselines, multilingual pretrained encoders, and LLMs. Our results reveal a significant syntax gap, where models still show clear limitations across the nine languages, suggesting that existing architectures may not fully capture the structural diversity of African-language syntax.

title: To Copy or Not to Copy: Copying Is Easier to Induce Than Recall
author: Mehrdad Farahani; Franziska Penzkofer; Richard Johansson
abstract: Language models used in retrieval-augmented settings choose between parametric knowledge stored in their weights and contextual information in the prompt. This work presents a mechanistic study of that choice: using an approach based on steering vectors, we carry out interventions at selected layers and token spans, and we are able to toggle the model’s behavior in two directions: Copy→Recall (suppressing context use) and Recall→Copy (inducing the model to copy any token from the context). Experiments on three architectures (decoder-only and encoder/decoder) and two open-domain QA benchmarks show consistent behavior shifts under moderate scaling while monitoring accuracy and fluency. Mechanistic analyses of attention routing, MLP contributions, and layer-wise probability trajectories reveal an asymmetry: inducing copying is an easy "reactivation" process that can be triggered at different locations in the input, while restoring recall is a "suppression" process that is more fragile and strongly tied to object-token interventions.

title: Informed Masking: Structure-Aware Perturbation for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Large Language Models
author: Xiaoyi Yu; Enver Sangineto; Pei Fu; Fiorenzo Parascandolo; Wenhui Tan; Ruikang Zhang; Rita Cucchiara; Ruihua Song; Jian Luan
abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as an efficient alternative to autoregressive models, yet aligning them via Reinforcement Learning (RL) requires likelihood surrogates estimated from masked reconstruction subproblems under a small Monte Carlo budget per rollout. Existing methods construct these subproblems by uniform random masking, leaving open the question of which subproblems to prioritize. We identify a systematic upstream/downstream structure in dLLM rollouts. Some tokens, when revealed, trigger large confidence changes in nearby undecoded positions; we call them upstream. Others induce only small local changes and are therefore downstream. We find masking downstream tokens yields substantially better-posed subproblems than masking upstream tokens, a phenomenon we term subproblem difficulty asymmetry. Based on the observation, we propose Informed Masking (IM), which derives a per-token priority score from the denoising trajectory at zero extra inference cost and biases mask sampling toward downstream tokens. IM is plug-and-play: when plugged into three state-of-the-art dLLM RL methods on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, it delivers up to 2.01%, 8.68%, and 5.77% relative average gains on math and planning benchmarks with improved training stability.

title: Black-Box Dataset-Level Source Ranking via Context Mixture Factorization
author: Milad Fotouhi; Mohammad Taha Bahadori; Payman Arabshahi; Oluwaseyi Feyisetan
abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) for large language models is dominated by gradient- and retraining-based methods that require model internals, ruling out the most widely deployed closed-weight systems. We study TDA in the strictly black-box setting, observing only input output behavior accessed through retrieval- augmented prompting. We introduce Context Mixture Factorization (CMF), which models the LLM’s output distribution as a mixture of a base component and dataset-specific components and recovers per-dataset contribution weights by regularized matrix factorization via alternating projected least squares. CMF explicitly decomposes background (π0) and dataset- specific influence and requires only K+1 prompts per query for K candidate datasets. As a comparison method we also formulate the Shapley Context Method (SCM), a residual- similarity attribution score aggregated via Shapley values. We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs (GPT-4, Bloomz, Mistral-7B, Phi-3mini) on BoolQ, a synthetic FakeQ variant, and a post-cutoff Olympic2024 dataset against three baselines (TRAK, ContextCite, retrieval cosine similarity). CMF and SCM recover the ordering predicted by our exposure-proxy setup (BoolQ>FakeQ>Olympic2024); ContextCite shows the opposite ordering, attributing most to Olympic2024 because the model relies on context most when it has no parametric knowledge — supporting the claim that span-level context attribution and dataset-level exposure attribution answer different questions. A synthetic identifiability experiment, controlled fine- tuning sweeps, and a multi-checkpoint unlearning case study provide supporting evidence that the metrics behave as exposure-sensitive source-ranking proxies.

title: HEMP: Hierarchical Entity-aligned Memory Prompting for CT Report Generation
author: Tong Xu; Yiming Qian; Zhe Shan; Xia Xie
abstract: Automated CT report generation remains challenging because it requires both fine-grained grounding of pathological entities in multi-view volumetric evidence and clinically coherent language that reflects diagnostic priors from historical cases. Existing methods often rely on noisy cross-modal alignment or underutilize retrieved report knowledge during decoding. We propose HEMP, which is a Hierarchical Entity-aligned Memory Prompting framework for LLM-based CT report generation. HEMP first performs two-stage entity-visual alignment where graph-constrained entity-conditioned attention retrieves initial evidence and an optimal transport refinement enforces principled coupling between entity nodes and visual tokens under marginal constraints. To inject case-conditioned linguistic priors, we design a Conditional Dual-Hopfield Memory module that retrieves case-conditioned report priors and integrates them through both implicit feature-level fusion into entity representations and explicit memory tokens appended to the prompt. Finally, we enforce clinical consistency via hierarchical severity supervision at the entity, region, and sign-group levels. Comprehensive Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms previous methods and achieves SoTA performance.

title: IGTF: Intent-Guided, Game-Inspired Structured Intent Calibration for LLM-Assisted Fake News Detection
author: Kun Xu; Zongyuan Mou; Yuan Rao; Yufei Xin; Tingting Xin
abstract: Fake news detection increasingly relies on LLMs to extract semantic and pragmatic signals. We study a narrower problem than factual hallucination: when an LLM scores multiple intent dimensions, the resulting vector may contain internally inconsistent labels. We present IGTF, an intent-guided, game-inspired structured intent calibration framework for LLM-assisted fake news detection. IGTF defines an expert-validated nine-dimensional intent taxonomy, extracts intent-aware text representations with a Mixture-of-Experts encoder, and calibrates LLM-produced intent vectors through a fixed graph of cooperative and conflicting intent relations. The refinement is motivated by a potential-game formulation, whereas the deployed algorithm is a differentiable fixed-point update rather than an exact Nash-equilibrium solver. We prove convergence to a unique fixed point under a contraction condition and evaluate the refinement empirically. Across four benchmark datasets, IGTF improves over supervised GPT-4+BERT fusion baselines by 4.07 F1-macro points on average, with the largest gains when raw intent vectors show stronger relation-level inconsistency. Human evaluation and graph-perturbation controls suggest that these gains come from structured intent calibration rather than LLM features alone.

title: Subtraction Gets You More: Gap-Aware Retrieval for Multimodal Multi-Hop QA
author: Sunah O; Jay-Yoon Lee
abstract: In multimodal multi-hop question answering, we focus on the initial retrieval stage via two distinct tasks: (1) evidence set completion, retrieving missing evidence given context, and (2) sequential pool construction, iteratively building the top-K pool from the scratch. Under these settings, we point out that conventional iterative retrieval frameworks often suffer from Semantic Anchoring, where previously fetched evidence traps the retriever and yields entity-centric redundancy. To break this trap, we propose GRAIL (Gap-aware Retrieval via Adaptive Implicit Localization), a paradigm that performs implicit query rewriting directly at the embedding level. By context-subtractive query steering, GRAIL excels at compositional cross-modal reasoning, while additive embedding updates show strength on localized information aggregation. To leverage these complementary strengths, we propose a Task-Adaptive Hybrid Framework, achieving a 35.7% macro-averaged performance gain on the MultimodalQA evidence set completion task. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that sequential GRAIL retrieves in a superior, noise-resilient manner, significantly expanding the search horizon through iterative gap-aware optimization.

title: BOW: Training Language Models to Reason Over Plausible Next Words
author: Ming Shen; Zhikun Xu; Jacob Dineen; Xiao Ye; Ben Zhou
abstract: Next-word prediction (NWP) trains language models against a single observed continuation, even though many contexts admit multiple plausible next words. Recent RL-based next-word reasoning methods make this tension explicit: they reward a model for producing a rationale that supports one context-conditioned continuation, which can turn a pre-existing preference into a confident, self-justifying trajectory. We introduce BOW, an RL framework that instead trains models to produce self-contained, neutral, and comprehensive descriptions of the plausible next-word space. The policy generates a next-word reasoning trajectory from the full context, but a frozen scorer computes the core reward from that trajectory alone, without separately receiving the context. BOW-Reg adds a lightweight breadth regularizer to this core reward to discourage premature collapse. On two model backbones, BOW remains competitive with the original models and often outperforms trained baselines across ten general reasoning benchmarks. On benchmarks testing ambiguous references and word meanings, BOW-Reg achieves the highest SharedRef correctness and the lowest HoWN-Simple single-sense collapse on both backbones. Human evaluation further shows that BOW-Reg produces broader next-word reasoning trajectories, while direct next-word-prediction evaluation shows that these trajectories remain predictive.

title: Linguistics-Aware Non-Distortionary LLM Watermarking
author: Shinwoo Park; Hyejin Park; Hyeseon An; Yo-Sub Han
abstract: Watermarking should identify language-model output without degrading quality or limiting verification to the model provider. Multilingual deployment makes this harder because morphology, segmentation, and script change where watermark evidence can be naturally embedded. We introduce LUNA, a linguistically adaptive watermark that combines model-free detection with single-token non-distortion under the standard random-key model. LUNA estimates normalized next-tag entropy from part-of-speech contexts in an external corpus and uses it to set the depth of a non-distortionary binary tournament sampler; the detector reconstructs the same schedule from text, a tokenizer, a tagger, and a secret key. We evaluate LUNA on six typologically diverse languages and two domains against eight primary baselines. LUNA attains an AUROC of 0.9959 and the lowest mean absolute median perplexity shift, 0.045, across the 12 settings; its 95% bootstrap interval [0.022, 0.073] lies below all baseline intervals. LUNA also records the lowest mean on Self-BLEU, Distinct-1, surprisal, and entropy shifts; it is the only method that simultaneously achieves AUROC > 0.99 and |ΔPPLmed| < 0.1 in a majority of settings, reaching this regime in 9 of the 12 settings while no baseline reaches it in more than 2. Our code is available at https://github.com/Shinwoo-Park/luna_watermark.

title: Entity tracking emerges in sub-billion parameter language models and exceeds human performance in naturalistic narratives
author: Karolina Drożdż; Micha Heilbron
abstract: Understanding language requires tracking entities across discourse - i.e., knowing where things are and how they change, even when not explicitly stated. Whether language models perform such tracking in a human-like fashion remains unclear, in part because existing evaluations rely on artificial tasks, far removed from natural language comprehension, and lack comparisons to humans. Here, we evaluate entity tracking in both language models and humans (N=48) using naturalistic narratives at multiple levels of complexity. In humans, we find that entity tracking degrades specifically with narrative complexity, not narrative length. In language models, we find that human-level entity tracking is already present at 410 million parameters - well below the multi-billion parameter, code-specialised models identified by prior work - and improves with scale, with contemporary models far exceeding human performance. Together, these results demonstrate that entity tracking, a core component of language understanding, emerges at model scales far smaller than previously thought.

title: Inter-3D VQA: A Roadside Multimodal Benchmark for 3D Spatiotemporally Grounded Visual Question Answering
author: Shaozu Ding; Linan Song; Dajiang Suo
abstract: Recent advances in visual question answering (VQA) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled natural-language reasoning over traffic scenes. However, existing benchmarks are largely built from ego-vehicle views or 2D roadside videos, limiting their ability to evaluate 3D-grounded reasoning over real-world distances, trajectories, infrastructure topology, and safety-critical interactions. We introduce Inter-3D VQA, a large-scale roadside multimodal benchmark for 3D spatiotemporally grounded VQA at intersections. Built from synchronized point clouds and multi-view images, Inter-3D VQA contains 407K QA pairs covering lane-level positions, object relationships, motion patterns, and near-miss-oriented interaction reasoning. We further propose Inter-Geo, an MLLM baseline that integrates object- and scene-level aligned LiDAR representations, and Inter-Metrics, a unified evaluation framework for textual consistency, numerical accuracy, and semantic correctness. Experiments show that Inter-Geo outperforms image-based VLMs, especially on grounded spatial and temporal reasoning tasks.

title: IndicDetect: Evaluating Cross-Lingual LLM-Generated Text Detection for Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil
author: Bhaskar Ganesh Devalla; Junchao Wu; Nilesh Dokuparthi; Greeshma Yaluru; Tatiana Muniz Rodriguez; Lidia S. Chao; Derek F. Wong
abstract: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has further heightened the necessity to develop dependable AI-generated text detection, especially beyond English. Nevertheless, current benchmarks pay little attention to Indic languages and test detectors in idealized settings that do not represent the real world. We present a generalized benchmark for AI-generated text detection in Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil, which we name IndicDetect is a benchmark designed to assess the robustness of detectors under realistic distribution shifts. IndicDetect comprises highly curated human-written texts matched with LLM-generated counterparts across various domains and generators, and systematically evaluates detectors in the presence of domain shift, generator shift, and adversarial perturbation. Using a single and repeatable evaluation scheme, we evaluate a wide range of statistical and neural detectors. We find substantial robustness failures: supervised neural detectors perform well in-distribution, but most training-free methods fail catastrophically on unseen generators and adversarial attacks, with larger failures observed for Telugu and Tamil than for Hindi. These results highlight that the primary weakness of existing detectors in Indic settings lies in their robustness, not peak accuracy. IndicDetect provides standard data splits, an evaluation protocol, and baselines to establish a robust, language-aware foundation for AI-generated text detection in Indic scripts.

title: Activation-Space Anchored Access Control for Multi-Class Permission Reasoning in Large Language Models
author: Zhaopeng Zhang; Pengcheng Sun; Lan Zhang; Chen Tang; Jiewei Lai; Xirong Zhuang; Yunhao Wang; Hui Jin; Li Liu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed over knowledge bases for efficient knowledge retrieval and question answering. However, LLMs can inadvertently answer beyond a user’s permission scope, leaking sensitive content and complicating deployment under fine-grained access-control requirements. We identify a geometric regularity in intermediate activations: representations associated with different permission scopes exhibit consistent and distinguishable structure in activation space. Building on this observation, we propose Activation-Space Anchored Access Control (AAAC), a training-free framework for multi-class permission control. AAAC constructs a compact bank of permission-specific activation anchors from a small offline calibration set and requires no model fine-tuning. At inference time, the trusted permission metadata is used by the controller to steer query activations toward authorized anchors and away from unauthorized ones, thereby mitigating the risk of over-privileged generation. Across three LLM families, AAAC achieves permission violation rates of 0.005–0.009 and prompt-based attack success rates of 0.084–0.101, while maintaining competitive utility with 10.3%–25.2% inference overhead.

title: Robust and Efficient Guardrails with Latent Reasoning
author: Siddharth Sai; Xiaofei Wen; Muhao Chen
abstract: Maintaining the safety of large language models (LLMs) is crucial as they are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. Existing safety guardrails typically rely on single-pass classification or, more recently, distilled reasoning. Reasoning-based guardrails significantly outperform classification-only baselines, but they incur substantial query latency and token overhead that make them impractical for high-throughput deployment. To address this challenge, we propose CoLaGuard, a guardrail model that transfers multi-step safety reasoning into a continuous latent space through a stage-wise training curriculum, enabling direct hidden-state propagation at inference. Evaluated across ten prompt and response moderation settings from eight unique safety benchmarks on ten prompt- and response-moderation settings spanning eight safety benchmarks, CoLaGuard improves macro-F1 by 8.24 points over Llama Guard 3 and matches our explicit reasoning baseline, GuardReasoner, in macro-F1 while delivering a 12.9\times speedup and 22.4\times reduction in token usage. Our results suggest that latent reasoning offers a practical alternative to explicit rationale generation for deployable guardrails, jointly improving safety robustness and inference efficiency rather than treating them as competing objectives.

title: When Seeing Is Not Enough: Benchmarking Interactive Visual Grounding in LVLMs
author: Zhengxiang Wang; Owen Rambow
abstract: Visual grounding is typically evaluated as a one-shot mapping from an informative referring expression to a visual target. This formulation misses a central property of real-world reference: initial referring expressions are often incomplete or ambiguous, requiring participants to establish shared understanding through interaction. We introduce a controlled evaluation framework for interactive visual grounding in large vision-language models (LVLMs), varying how much target information is provided upfront and how much must be acquired through dialogue. Across four human-grounded visual contexts and four interaction protocols, current LVLMs perform significantly below task-level human baselines. Interaction can help when follow-up questions refine or repair an initial target description. Performance is lowest when no initial description is provided and target information must be acquired through questions, indicating that proactive question-driven grounding remains difficult. LVLMs are also poorly calibrated, often reporting confidence that exceeds their empirical accuracy. Follow-up studies confirm these patterns across varied description sources (human versus AI), reasoning efforts, repeated interactions, description providers, and visual contexts. Overall, interactive visual grounding remains challenging, requiring visual matching, information seeking and synthesis.

title: DuplexGen: Adaptive Synthesis of Human-AI Turn-Taking Dialogues
author: Takyoung Kim; Kang-wook Kim; Tony Woo; Julia Hirschberg; Gunhee Kim; Dilek Hakkani-Tür
abstract: Effective spoken AI assistants must decide not only what to say, but also when to say it. Although appropriate AI turn-taking behavior is inherently scenario-dependent, current approaches fall short in complementary ways: human-human speech corpora capture natural timing phenomena but provide little AI-role grounding or scenario-specific norms, while heuristic or prompted synthesis methods inject turn-taking behaviors without grounding them in human preferences. We introduce **DuplexGen**, a human-calibrated framework that generates synthetic human-AI dialogues with scenario-adaptive turn-taking. DuplexGen transforms text dialogues into spoken-style transcripts, marks candidate intra-utterance action slots, and calibrates LLM predictions using a small set of slot-level human preference annotations. Across six tasks spanning cooperative and competitive interactions, DuplexGen aligns substantially more closely with human preferences than uncalibrated prompting and models trained solely on generic human-human data; furthermore, a full-duplex model trained on DuplexGen-generated data exhibits distinctive, human-preferred turn-taking behaviors across scenarios.

title: When Seekers Are Hard to Help: Evaluating Emotional Support Dialogue Systems in Worst-Case Interactions
author: Jiajie Yang; Yangchun Li; Guanyi Chen; Rui Fan; Xin Bai; Tingting He
abstract: Emotional Support Dialogue Systems (ESDSes) are increasingly evaluated and trained with LLM-simulated seekers. However, such simulated seekers often behave as cooperative, average-case users who disclose clearly, respond constructively, and accept support within a few turns. This can lead to overly optimistic evaluation and obscure whether ESDSes can handle difficult help-seeking interactions. In this work, we study ESDS evaluation under worst-case interactions, where seekers are hard to help due to low engagement, resistance, limited self-disclosure, emotional volatility, or rigid negative interpretations. We first conduct an expert simulation study with eight experienced counselling professionals, who simulate difficult seekers, interact with existing Chinese ESDSes, provide scale ratings, and participate in semi-structured interviews. Based on this study, we derive worst-case seeker behaviours and identify key limitations of current systems. We then propose a worst-case evaluation framework consisting of an LLM-based worst-case seeker simulator and four worst-case-oriented metrics: Deep Emotional Understanding, Guided Exploration, Balanced Emotional Support, and Authentic and Grounded Support. Evaluating 17 systems, we find that nearly all models suffer substantial performance drops under worst-case interactions. Large general-purpose LLMs are generally more robust than specialised ESDSes, but even the strongest models struggle to sustain engagement and improve seekers’ emotional states. Finally, we show that worst-case simulation can also generate useful training data, improving the robustness of smaller models.

title: SAMAC: Collaborating with Multi-Disciplinary Team for Adaptive Medical Decision-Making
author: Maosheng Li; Xiao Wu; Hu Wang; Imran Razzak; Yutong Xie
abstract: Multi-agent large language model systems offer a promising paradigm for multidisciplinary medical decision support by integrating heterogeneous expert perspectives. However, existing frameworks often rely on loosely structured interactions, where disagreement is insufficiently diagnosed and discussion may collapse into superficial consensus or parallel opinion aggregation. We propose Structured Adaptive Multi-disciplinary Collaboration (SAMAC), a structured and strategy-aware multi-agent framework for adaptive MDT-style medical reasoning. SAMAC introduces Structured Deliberation to detect opinion disagreement and majority not confident, along with a Consensus Purification mechanism that transforms disagreement into constructive and collaborative refinement. When disagreement arises, SAMAC adaptively selects between Self-refinement and Counter-questioning to enable evidence-grounded negotiation. Experiments on three medical datasets—RADCURE, HANCOCK, and OSCCPI—show that SAMAC consistently improves overall performance and collaborative gains over existing multi-agent baselines. In particular, SAMAC improves the Average Score by 4.29 points on the RADCURE dataset and achieves higher Relative Self-Correction Scores (RSS), indicating more effective resolution of disagreement and stable collective decisions. These results highlight the importance of controlled and diverse interaction dynamics in multi-agent medical reasoning. Code will be released upon publication.

title: Implicit Hierarchical Modeling for Cross-System Legal Case Retrieval
author: Zhengjia Zhong; Hongyi Lan; Yuhong Chen; Shengjia Hua; Kaiyan Liang; Xiaodong Li; Xianming Lin; Hui Li; Rongrong Ji
abstract: Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) identifies relevant precedent cases to support legal reasoning and sentencing. A core challenge for cross-system LCR is the structural divergence between legal systems: civil-law systems provide explicit statutory hierarchies but lack inter-case citations, while common-law systems offer rich citation networks but lack uniform codified semantic hierarchies. Existing methods exploit only one side of this divide, remaining system-specific. We propose DSLaw, which unifies both systems by implicitly modeling hierarchical semantics through residual quantization and using the resulting discrete representations as semantic anchors for cross-case graph reasoning. By progressively decomposing legal semantics from coarse concepts to fine-grained distinctions, DSLaw constructs implicit connections even without explicit citations. Experiments on COLIEE2025 (common law) and ELAM (civil law) show DSLaw consistently outperforms strong baselines, while joint training further validates cross-system generalization. The implementation is provided at https://github.com/KDEGroup/DSLaw.

title: PatientAct: Theory-Grounded Mental Health Client Simulation
author: Sahand Sabour; NG Tsz Yam; Yaqian Chen; Guanqun Bi; Minlie Huang
abstract: LLM-based simulated clients are increasingly used to train novice counselors, evaluate LLM therapists, and generate synthetic data. However, current simulators produce overly cooperative clients that disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within a single session. We trace these issues to profiles that lack causal depth and behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible. We present PatientAct, a framework for client simulation grounded in established clinical theories. Our profiles integrate the 5Ps clinical case formulation, providing causal depth without tying the design to any single therapeutic modality. During simulation, profiles include a dynamic memory layer in which items carry trust thresholds (e.g., symptoms are available early, whereas formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, we model the client’s emotional reaction and behavior before generating a response. If the therapist approaches gated content, PatientAct expresses resistance in terms of quantity, content, and style rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern. We evaluate our framework on 40 clinical situations and demonstrate that it generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility. Moreover, PatientAct significantly outperforms the baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism. Our code and data are publicly available via github.com/Sahandfer/PatientHub.

title: Fake It Till You Make It: Training Deep-Search Agents in Synthetic Search Environments
author: Yibo Xue; Pin Zheng; Chengyu Wang; Yukun Kang; Yuanjie Lyu; Ming Wang; Jian Peng; Jun Huang; Changliang Xu
abstract: Deep-search agents are commonly trained via repeated interaction with real-world search APIs and browser environments. While realistic, this paradigm is expensive, difficult to reproduce, and sensitive to external drift. Existing simulator-based alternatives reduce dependence on live retrieval, but they largely inherit task distributions from pre-existing QA datasets, limiting their alignment with the behaviors required for deep search. We introduce SynSearch, a framework for training deep-search agents entirely within a synthetic search–browse environment. Our core idea is to jointly design the environment and the training-task distribution, enabling the synthesis of environment-aligned tasks and reinforcement learning of compact language models in multi-turn search settings. By grounding task validity in executable environment trajectories rather than surface-level plausibility alone, SynSearch unifies task generation, trajectory verification, and policy optimization within a low-marginal-cost and reproducible framework. Experiments on multi-hop QA and deep-search benchmarks show that SynSearch consistently improves both answer accuracy and search behavior, with especially large gains on deep-search tasks. Moreover, SynSearch offers low marginal cost, reproducibility, controllability, and strong performance under real-search evaluation, highlighting synthetic environments as an effective substrate for training deep-search agents.

title: TRACE: Table–Text Relationalization and Completion of Evidence for Coverage-Sensitive QA
author: Sunho Cha; Sungho Park; Wook-Shin Han
abstract: Table–Text question answering asks systems to answer natural-language questions whose evidence is split between structured tables and linked unstructured passages. Many realistic questions in this setting are coverage-sensitive: the answer depends on a set of evidence items distributed across table rows and linked passages, and the same failure mode that appears in aggregation also surfaces in joins, multi-row filters, list questions, and universal or existential queries. Existing hybrid systems retrieve and read such evidence, yet leave passage-derived facts as strings in the LLM context rather than as typed, joinable, and repairable relational values that SQL can operate on. We propose TRACE (Table–Text Relationalization And Completion of Evidence), a completeness-aware query-processing framework built on two relational state transformations. Schema-Guided Relationalization (SGR) turns linked passages into typed, foreign-keyed side tables, exposing textual evidence as SQL-visible relational values; Question-Conditioned Relational Completion (QCRC) then repairs this state per question by adding missing attributes and filling incomplete cells. SQL performs set-oriented operations over the completed state, while a lightweight passage fallback handles residual gaps. On the coverage-sensitive SPARTA benchmark, TRACE more than triples the strongest baseline F1 (60.5 vs. 19.2 with gpt-4o-mini); on lookup-heavy HYBRIDQA, it stays competitive while substantially reducing the drop on questions that require many evidence items.

title: DiffNeCTIS: Diffusion-based Nested Compound Type Identification for Sanskrit
author: Pretam Ray; Sinchani Chakraborty; Sriram Krishnan; Manoj Balaji Jagadeeshan; Pawan Goyal
abstract: Sanskrit multi-component compounding presents a severe structured prediction challenge: the space of valid parse structures grows exponentially with compound length, implicit semantic relations are highly context-sensitive, and accurate type assignment demands simultaneous global structural coherence and local morphological precision across a fine-grained label typology. Existing systems address Nested Compound Type Identification for Sanskrit (NeCTIS) discriminatively, predicting dependency edges and semantic types in a single greedy pass. Reformulating NeCTIS as iterative generative refinement via diffusion over the full label sequence resolves this structural inconsistency but exposes a complementary bottleneck - coarse global attention that suppresses the localized morphological signals necessary for fine-grained type discrimination. We address this through a local refinement mechanism within a restricted window. We further provide the first systematic evaluation of large language models on NeCTIS, finding consistent and substantial failures under zero-shot and few-shot conditions - attributable to the absence of structural inductive biases, Sanskrit under-representation in pretraining, and morphological sensitivity requirements that broad-coverage models are fundamentally ill-equipped to satisfy.

title: OneVision: An End-to-End Generative Framework for Multi-view E-commerce Vision Search
author: Zexin Zheng; Huangyu Dai; Lingtao Mao; Xinyu Sun; Zihan Liang; Ben Chen; Chenyi Lei
abstract: Traditional vision search follows the multi-stage cascading architecture (MCA) paradigm to balance efficiency and conversion, yet optimization objectives collide across stages, making it difficult to achieve Pareto optimality. Meanwhile, pronounced multi-view discrepancies of the same item undermine retrieval accuracy, as embedding-similarity methods fail to bridge large appearance variations. In this paper, we propose OneVision, an end-to-end generative framework that addresses both challenges. OneVision introduces VRQ, a vision-aligned residual quantization method that assigns consistent shallow-level codes to visually similar images of the same item while preserving fine-grained differences at deeper levels. It further employs a multi-stage training pipeline to retrieve all relevant items across views for a query image and incorporates user-specific signals for personalized preference modeling. In offline evaluations, OneVision performs on par with online MCA. Dynamic pruning further reduces its inference latency by 18% over the unpruned variant. In A/B tests, it achieves significant improvements: +3.61% item CTR, +2.43% CVR, and +5.89% order volume. The code will be publicly available.

title: CASCADE Against Jailbreaks: Combination Across Stages with Controlled Attack-Defense Evaluation
author: Jiale Luo; Han Liang Wee Eric
abstract: Defenses against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) operate at different pipeline stages, such as input modification or output guard, but it remains unclear which defenses to deploy at each stage and how to combine them. Prior empirical studies, fragmented by inconsistent attack-success-rate definitions and experimental settings, have evaluated defenses largely in isolation. Here we present the first systematic study, to our knowledge, of defense combinations both within and across pipeline stages, under a consistent threat model of direct, black-box, single-turn attacks. Our decision framework standardizes evaluation through a principled attack-success-rate formulation with controlled query budgets, together with explicit fairness rules. Across 19 attacks and 15 defenses, we find that no single defense is universally best, but well-chosen combinations achieve substantial safety with minimal utility degradation, yielding practical recommendations for layered defense pipelines.

title: I Wrote This Because of That: Interpretable Radiology Report Generation via Visual Prototypes
author: Marco Salmè; Federico Siciliano; Fabrizio Silvestri; Paolo Soda; Rosa Sicilia; Valerio Guarrasi
abstract: Automated Radiology Report Generation (RRG) could substantially reduce documentation workload by supporting physicians in routine clinical practice. Clinical adoption, however, requires each generated finding to be supported by inspectable evidence that a physician can verify. Existing systems either provide only post-hoc explanations weakly coupled to the prediction, or require costly region-level supervision to achieve spatial grounding. To address this gap, we introduce ProtoRRG, an RRG framework that grounds generation in visual prototypes. Specifically, each generated finding is tied to a dual form of evidence: localised image exemplars learned without anatomical supervision, and retrieved prior reports that supply case-based linguistic precedents. A multi-task training strategy reconciles the competing representational demands of prototype-based prediction and autoregressive decoding within a shared architecture. On MIMIC-CXR, ProtoRRG improves state-of-the-art clinical F1 and recall by 2.9% and 10%, respectively, with gains also demonstrated on IU X-Ray. An evaluation against anatomical annotations confirms that prototype activations localise within the correct regions, indicating spatially faithful evidence for the generated findings. These results demonstrate that combining visual prototypes with case-based retrieval improves both diagnostic accuracy and report quality while preserving the inspectable evidence that clinical deployment demands.

title: Beyond My Own Shadow: Collaborative Latent Prompting for Personalized Question Answering
author: Yinghan Shi; Kai Fu; Xinyu Liu; Quanyou Chu; Ming Du; Hongya Wang; Yanghua Xiao; Bo Xu
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in general question answering, they typically generate uniform responses, ignoring users’ diverse intents. Current Personalized Question Answering (PQA) methods face dual limitations: individual-based prompting struggles with data sparsity, while collaborative explicit prompting suffers from inaccurate user matching and attention dispersion caused by text concatenation. To tackle these challenges, we propose Collaborative Latent Prompting (CLP), a PQA framework that fuses collaborative knowledge within a dynamic latent space rather than relying on explicit textual concatenation. First, our Multi-Grained Collaborative Retrieval (MGCR) module ensures precise retrieval of relevant reference users through a three-stage refinement. Next, the Dynamic Q-Former (DQ-Former) utilizes question-modulated dynamic latent queries to extract compact personalized features from noisy texts. Finally, these features are projected into dense soft prompts to implicitly steer a frozen LLM. Experiments across three PQA domains and three backbone LLMs show consistent improvements over representative PQA baselines.

title: RASPER: Reward-Aligned Summarization of Clinical Notes for EHR Outcome Prediction
author: Arya Hadizadeh Moghaddam; Mohsen Nayebi Kerdabadi; Chen Chen; Dongjie Wang; Zijun Yao
abstract: Unstructured discharge notes in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) often carry signal complementary to structured medical codes, holding patient-specific evidence that standardized cohort-level codes alone cannot capture. However, this evidence in notes is frequently buried in lengthy, noisy text that is not intentionally written with any specific clinical prediction in mind. Summarization is an obvious mitigation, but generic summaries, tuned for fluency rather than the outcome, routinely omit decisive evidence while retaining plausible but uninformative detail. To this end, we propose RASPER, a Reward-Aligned Summarizer for Prediction in EHR, that optimizes note summarization directly against the downstream clinical task. RASPER employs a tunable LLM-based summarizer to extract task-relevant evidence from discharge notes and trains it via reinforcement learning from prediction feedback, using a reward derived from the downstream predictor’s loss. To ground the summarizer, a longitudinal encoder converts structured codes into soft prompts that incorporate each patient’s clinical context into note summarization. By rewarding the quality of the resulting multimodal prediction, RASPER encourages the summarizer to retain patient-specific evidence that complements, rather than duplicates, information captured by structured codes. RASPER consistently outperforms strong baselines on both readmission prediction and medication recommendation across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV.

title: D2C-Routing: Dimension-to-Composition Evidence Routing for Mixed-Origin AI-Generated Text Detection
author: Xin Chen; Fuwei Zhang; Yiqi Tong; Wei Guo; Yutian Xiao; Fuzhen Zhuang
abstract: AI-generated text detection is commonly framed as a binary document-level judgment about whether a text is human-written or machine-generated. This framing breaks down for mixed-origin writing, where content origin and expression origin may differ. We cast mixed-origin detection as dimension-to-composition source attribution, inferring content origin and expression origin before composing them into four collaboration types. We propose *Dimension-to-Composition Routing* (**D2C-Routing**), which routes content-side and expression-side evidence to supervised dimension heads before a learned gated composition layer predicts the final label. On MixD2C, a reconstructed split derived from the HART mixed-origin benchmark, our disclosed D2C-Routing-based detector system reaches 0.8603 four-way Avg TPR@1%FPR, 6.5 points above the same-split RACE-local rerun. Core ablations support the routing design, while error analysis shows that distinguishing AI-content/human-expression from fully AI-generated text remains the hardest boundary. Code is available at https://github.com/bystander563/d2c-routing-artifact.

title: MemoNoveltyAgent: A Historical-Memory-Augmented Multi-Agent System for Paper Novelty Assessment
author: JiaJun Hou; Hexuan Deng; Wenxiang Jiao; Xuebo Liu; Xiaopeng Ke; Derek F. Wong; Min Zhang
abstract: To alleviate the heavy burden of paper screening, researchers increasingly rely on existing AI agents, such as AI reviewers or DeepResearch, for paper evaluation and novelty assessment. However, lacking specialized mechanisms for processing scholarly literature, their analyses often produce superficial results with noticeable deficiencies in quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemoNoveltyAgent, a multi-agent system designed to generate comprehensive and faithful novelty reports.
