Beyond retrieving concrete prior-paper evidence via RAG, our system incorporates a high-level abstract memory constructed from large-scale scholarly corpora. This memory organizes research into hierarchical trees to distill field-specific evolutionary trajectories, thereby providing a broader historical context. Furthermore, we decompose papers into discrete novelty points for fine-grained analysis and retrieval, while employing a self-validation mechanism to improve report faithfulness. Finally, to address the evaluation challenges of such open-ended generation tasks, we propose a RAG-augmented checklist evaluation method that enables reliable and evidence-grounded assessments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemoNoveltyAgent outperforms GPT-5 DeepResearch by 13.69%. Code and demo are available at https://github.com/SStan1/MemoNoveltyAgent.

title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources
author: Jaeyoung Lee; Misuk Kim
abstract: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.

title: LLMTrace: A Corpus for Classification and Fine-Grained Localization of AI-Written Text
author: Irina Tolstykh; Aleksandra Tsybina; Sergey Yakubson; Maksim Kuprashevich
abstract: The widespread use of human-like text from Large Language Models (LLMs) necessitates the development of robust detection systems. However, progress is limited by a critical lack of suitable training data; existing datasets are often generated with outdated models, are predominantly in English, and fail to address the increasingly common scenario of mixed human-AI authorship. Crucially, while some datasets address mixed authorship, none provide the character-level annotations required for the precise localization of AI-generated segments within a text. To address these gaps, we introduce LLMTrace, a new large-scale, bilingual (English and Russian) corpus for AI-generated text detection. Constructed using a diverse range of modern proprietary and open-source LLMs, our dataset is designed to support two key tasks: traditional full-text binary classification (human vs. AI) and AI-generated interval detection, facilitated by character-level annotations. We believe LLMTrace will serve as a vital resource for training and evaluating the next generation of more nuanced and practical AI detection models.

title: Doc-CoB: Enhancing Document Understanding with Visual Chain-of-Boxes Reasoning
author: Ye Mo; Kai Ye; Xianwei Mao; Zirui Shao; Gang Huang; Bo Zhang; Hangdi Xing; Kehan Chen; Zhou Huan; Zixu Yan; Jiajun Bu; Sheng Zhou
abstract: Document understanding aims to perform question answering and information extraction over document images, where the visual content is highly information-dense and most queries rely on only a few relevant layout regions. However, existing methods either adopt a one-pass strategy that implicitly assumes all layouts are equally important, or focus excessively on small regions at the cost of losing critical layout information. To address these limitations, we introduce Doc-CoB (Chain-of-Boxes), a simple-yet-effective framework that integrates coarse-to-fine layout-aware visual reasoning into multimodal large language models. Instead of directly zooming into small regions, Doc-CoB progressively focuses on query-relevant layouts while preserving global document information. Specifically, it first selects key layout boxes and then focuses on them for further understanding with visual prompting. To support this paradigm, we introduce two reasoning tasks for box recognition and box reasoning, with an automatic pipeline that constructs 249k training samples with intermediate visual supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks with four popular models show that Doc-CoB significantly improves performance, demonstrating its effectiveness and wide applicability. The code and the data are available at https://github.com/Doc-CoB/Doc-CoB.

title: CePRM: Generative Process Reward Modeling with Calibrated Values and Repair-Aware Supervision
author: Zongxuan Li; Yixiang Dong; Bo Hu; Gonghao Cao; Yanzhen Chen; Huan Liu
abstract: Generative process reward models (PRMs) improve step-level verification of mathematical reasoning, yet their effectiveness is limited by the quality of process supervision. The dominant Monte Carlo (MC) estimation derives step labels from final-answer accuracy rather than semantic correctness, producing systematic label noise, while standard pipelines discard the implicit tree structure of rollout data that encodes informative failure patterns. We propose CePRM, which addresses both limitations through Step-Cognitive MC Value Scaling, calibrating raw MC scores with step-level semantic signals via multiplicative adjustment, and pivot-step-directed repair mining, which exploits value cliffs in failed trajectories to construct same-prefix contrastive correction pairs via Sibling Advantage filtering. Experiments on ProcessBench and PRMBench show that CePRM, with a 4B backbone, achieves competitive or superior error localization and process verification against 7B-scale baselines, with notably strong error-side recognition.

title: Quantifying Retriever-Generator Alignment in RAG with Local Explanations
author: Korbinian Randl; Guido Rocchietti; Aron Henriksson; Ziawasch Abedjan; Tony Lindgren; John Pavlopoulos
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems combine dense retrievers and language models to ground outputs in external documents. However, the interaction between these components remains opaque, creating challenges for deployment in high-stakes domains. We present RAG-E, an end-to-end explainability framework that quantifies retriever-generator alignment through mathematically grounded attribution methods. Our approach adapts Integrated Gradients for retriever analysis, proposes a Monte Carlo-stabilized Shapley Value approximation for generator attribution, and introduces the *Weighted Alignment between Retriever and Generator* (WARG) metric to measure how closely the generator’s document usage aligns with retriever rankings. Experiments on PopQA, QAMPARI, and TREC CAST datasets reveal substantial misalignment: depending on the model and setting, generators often ignore top-ranked documents and rely on documents ranked as less relevant. We show that WARG captures retriever-generator alignment better than Pearson and Spearman correlations and can serve as an indicator of RAG performance. RAG-E and WARG provide a practical framework for auditing this interaction, enabling more reliable and transparent RAG systems.

title: Roles with Rails: Contract-Preserving Role Evolution in Multi-Agent Structured Reasoning
author: Ling-Yue Ge; Lan-Zhe Guo
abstract: Role-based LLM multi-agent systems need adaptive role pools, yet adapting such systems is not merely a matter of prompt optimization: roles often carry structural obligations, including capability coverage, message compatibility, validation, final-answer aggregation, and parser-compatible output protocols. Existing systems either fix the role inventory and lose adaptivity, or allow unconstrained generation to induce role drift, removing structurally necessary roles and breaking answer contracts. We formulate this as contract-preserving role evolution, requiring every committed edit to preserve five structural contracts (capability, communication, validation, aggregation, output protocol). We instantiate this formulation in SERO, a \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{E}volving \textbf{R}ole \textbf{O}rchestration framework that evolves a typed role-card pool through credit-guided retrieval, a credit-ranked communication DAG with a protected terminal aggregator and conditional validator repair, and a contextual-bandit controller whose LLM-proposed edits are committed only when they preserve the contracts and improve task score. Experiments on real-world reasoning benchmarks across three LLM backbones confirm the value of contract-preserving role evolution.

title: PrivAgentFlow: Agentic Workflow for Automating Privacy Preservation in Web Agents
author: Tianyi Tang; Tianyi Ma; Yueming Lyu; Yew-Soon Ong; Ivor Tsang; Haiyan Yin
abstract: Autonomous web agents increasingly operate over sensitive personal data, yet existing privacy-preserving approaches rely on static filtering and globally enforced safeguards misaligned with compositional agent execution. We introduce PrivAgentFlow, a memory-guided agentic workflow framework that formulates privacy preservation as adaptive node-level governance over compositional web-agent workflows. PrivAgentFlow decomposes complex tasks into compositional workflow nodes, where each node operates under a distinct privacy policy conditioned on its execution role and information access requirements, enabling privacy governance to be localized at the execution level rather than globally enforced. Such localized governance is refined through execution memory, where historical task failures and privacy violations serve as corrective signals for improving node-level privacy control without exposing raw user data during planning. We provide theoretical insights showing that compositional web-agent workflows induce subtask-specific privacy–utility trade-offs, formally characterizing the advantage of heterogeneous node-level governance over uniform privacy control. Across 246 web-agent tasks on three platforms, PrivAgentFlow improves task utility by 23.1 percentage points (0.415→0.646), cuts environment-level privacy leakage by 92.3% (0.366→0.028), and reduces API-level leakage from 100% to 3.7% over the strongest prior baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/haorentang/PrivAgentFlow.

title: COIN: A Live, Large-scale Benchmark for Semantics-to-Input Code Reasoning
author: Jiho Kim; Cen Zhang; Youngjoon Kim; Dongkwan Kim; Brian Junekyu Lee; Dae R. Jeong; Taesoo Kim
abstract: Constructing inputs that drive execution to chosen code locations underpins many dynamic-analysis tasks in software engineering and security. It is a generalized constraint-solving challenge that requires agents to reason about the semantic mapping between input and code. We built COIN, the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this ability in modern code agents. By leveraging OSS-Fuzz’s long-running coverage data and maintainer-written harnesses, COIN constructs reachability challenges across over 1000 real-world projects in nine languages, and is contamination-resistant and self-refreshing as upstream code and OSS-Fuzz coverage evolve. To keep challenges non-trivial yet solvable, COIN samples two target families: lines OSS-Fuzz has covered but baselines miss, and lines never be reached but with static evidence of a reachable harness path. Across five independent runs on 137 targets from 15 projects in six languages, the strongest agent (Claude Code with Opus 4.6) reaches on average only 26.6% of the C/C++ targets and 39.7% of the Go/JVM/Python/Rust targets, never half of either set in any run, and the weakest (DeepSeek V3.2) stays below 9%, indicating substantial room for improvement.

title: Continual Graph Memory for Adaptive Recommendation under Intent Drift
author: Hao Nguyen Ngoc; Tung Nguyen; Nguyen Thi Hanh; Dinh Thai Hoang; Nguyen Xuan Tung
abstract: This paper studies adaptive recommendation under intent drift, where feedback from each recommendation outcome can reveal whether the relational evidence used for ranking is useful, missing, or misleading. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide essential semantic structure to handle these shifts, traditional KG-enhanced systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making it brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation. CGM-Rec treats the graph state as a writable memory and maintains two complementary components. Therein, a Semantic Graph Memory is updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable and high-confidence relational knowledge. Meanwhile, an Episodic Lesson Memory acts as a fast reactive memory that learns recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. We evaluate CGM-Rec under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol, where encoders and prompts remain fixed during testing and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. Experiments across multiple recommendation settings show that CGM-Rec improves over evaluated neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Particularly, under sampled-candidate reranking, CGM-Rec improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.

title: Old Memories Die Hard: Unveiling Shallow Forgetting and Ripple Effects in Privacy Unlearning
author: Xiaoyi Chen; Haoyuan Wang; Siyuan Tang; Sijia Liu; Liya Su; XiaoFeng Wang; Haixu Tang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often memorize personally identifiable information (PII) during training, raising serious privacy concerns. While machine unlearning has emerged as a promising mitigation, its effectiveness against privacy attacks remains unclear. We introduce PrivUn, an evaluation framework for privacy unlearning under recovery attacks, paired with three measurement tools: forgetting scores, association metrics, and layer-wise analysis of forgetting depth. This framework studies not only whether a model forgets, but also how forgetting propagates and where it fails. Using PrivUn, we make two findings. (i) The PII ripple effect is gradient-driven, not semantic. Graph-based proximity is uncorrelated with PII forgetting, while gradient-based association is more strongly correlated. (ii) Label-based unlearning is typically shallow, while PII is stored across deeper layers. Layer-wise evidence suggests that label-based methods mainly change the final layers, explaining why they reduce direct retrieval but remain vulnerable to stronger recovery attacks.

title: Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning
author: Anna Karnysheva; Dietrich Klakow; Ji-Ung Lee
abstract: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

title: ThinkLeap: Reasoning Optimization Through Confidence-Guided Cognitive Leap Extraction
author: Yijia Zhu; Zhenning Shi; Junhan Shi; Xun Zhang; Yong Jiang; Qing Li
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) show remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning tasks through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) mechanisms. However, their reasoning processes frequently suffer from overthinking, generating inefficient patterns and substantial overhead without improving quality. Existing pruning approaches typically rely on computationally expensive external teacher models or aggregated sequence-level metrics, failing to capture the fine-grained, intrinsic cognitive state of individual reasoning steps. In this paper, we propose ThinkLeap, a novel confidence-guided optimization framework that identifies and retains only critical cognitive leaps within reasoning chains. Our approach is grounded in the observation that a model’s internal confidence dynamics serve as a fine-grained structural signal: rising confidence often reflects evidence accumulation, while declining confidence signals doubt or redundancy. By leveraging these dynamics, ThinkLeap autonomously replaces inefficient steps with ellipsis markers, preserving the logical flow while signaling omitted deliberation. Extensive experiments across three challenging reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkLeap establishes a new paradigm for efficient reasoning, achieving an average 19.4% reduction in reasoning length while maintaining comparable accuracy.

title: Assessing the Impact of Language Disparity on Multilingual Linguistic Ability in Large Language Models
author: Zhanyu Chen; Jaap Jumelet
abstract: Claims about the grammatical competence of multilingual language models vary sharply with how competence is measured, yet the interaction between evaluation paradigm, post-training, and language resource availability has not been systematically examined. We evaluate base and post-trained models from six families on MultiBLiMP, a syntactic minimal-pair benchmark covering 101 languages, using four evaluation methods. We report three principal findings. First, post-training degrades grammatical competence, but the magnitude of this effect is determined by post-training recipe rather than model scale, and scaling reduces it unevenly, with low-resource languages bearing the highest cost. Second, post-trained models retain grammatical knowledge they cannot articulate through explicit prompting, yet this is measurable only in high-resource languages, because near-chance baselines in low-resource settings leave little knowledge to hide. Third, native-language prompting recovers otherwise hidden competence on low-resource languages, demonstrating that only high-resource languages can be probed directly from unprompted probabilities. We conclude that multilingual grammatical evaluation must adopt language-informed, multi-paradigm protocols to avoid systematically underestimating low-resource abilities.

title: GeoPrune: A Robust and Engine-Friendly Importance Signal Beyond Attention for Vision Token Pruning in VLMs
author: Kang Lou; Shijin Zhang; Ming Chen; Junzhe Cao
abstract: Vision token pruning can accelerate vision language model inference by removing redundant visual tokens. However, we observe that ViT attention based pruning drops sharply on Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5. Empirically, we identify the root cause: the last-block MLP of the vision encoder significantly alters the spectral structure of hidden states and induces spectral collapse. Thus, pre-MLP attention rankings no longer reflect downstream token importance. Through further analysis of vision token selection when ViT attention based pruning still succeeds, we find that selected tokens strongly anti-correlate with raw L2 norm in the vision encoder output space S_{out} , while favoring tokens with larger residual energy. Motivated by shared components mask token-specific importance, we propose GeoPrune, a new importance-based pruning method that operates in S_{out} , applies deflation to remove dominant components, and ranks tokens by residual L2 norm. At aggressive pruning rates, GeoPrune is more robust and surpasses ViT attention based pruning by +4.4/+6.3 recovery points on Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5. We further integrate GeoPrune into the production-grade inference engine vLLM, delivering 5.4%-10.5% mean E2E latency reductions with only slight accuracy drops, advancing vision token pruning toward practical deployment.

title: PLC-DPO: Posterior Label Correction in Noisy and Ambiguous Preference Optimization
author: Boryeong Cho; Sumyeong Ahn; Se-Young Yun
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies alignment through pairwise comparisons but assumes all observed preferences are reliable. Real data often violates this assumption, leading to reversed, weak, or ambiguous labels that cause harmful policy updates. To address this, we propose Posterior Label Correction DPO (PLC-DPO) to robustly optimize preferences by routing each pair’s training signal as a clean, flip, or tie case. The key idea is to use the calibrated policy-reference margin as online evidence to take appropriate correction actions. This reframes noisy preference learning as actively correcting supervision direction and strength rather than merely filtering suspicious examples. Across 57 dataset-model-benchmark cells, PLC-DPO obtains the best mean win rate against DPO (60.5 vs. 55.5 for the next-best method). Injected-noise and tie stress tests, human disagreement analysis, and self-confirmation diagnostics further show that the routing remains stable and distinguishes flipped from weakly directional pairs.

title: How Do People Challenge Racial Stereotypes Online? Counter-Story Detection Across Reddit Communities
author: Uma Gunturi; Jimin Mun; Maarten Sap; Maria Antoniak
abstract: Counter-storytelling is a powerful mechanism people use to challenge dominant narratives. Unlike other forms of counterspeech that have been widely studied in computational social science, counter-storytelling has largely been overlooked. Counter-stories are difficult to detect automatically; they are relational (defined with respect to expressions of racial stereotypes) and structurally diverse (drawing on stories that describe lived experiences, witnessed events, exemplars, and hypotheticals). We introduce a first framework for detecting and characterizing counter-storytelling against racial stereotypes at scale. This includes (1) a three-dimensional taxonomy grounded in narratology and Critical Race Theory and (2) a multi-stage pipeline that identifies relational pairs of stereotypes and counter-stories in noisy Reddit discourse. Using this pipeline, we annotate 25,549 Reddit posts across 615 communities and identify 1,312 counter-stories. Our analysis shows that speaker identity and post context shape how counter-stories are told. For example, in-group writers favor first-person testimony, often adopting the role of self-reflective insiders. Our work shows how computational methods can scale qualitative approaches to identify and characterize counter-storytelling as a contextual narrative practice, with implications for content moderation, narratology, and racial discourse analysis.

title: From Bugs to Fixes: Self-Evolving Hierarchical Knowledge Graphs for LLM-Based Code Repair
author: Haoyue Ran; Junguo Zhu; Hongyu Ge
abstract: Large Language Models have shown remarkable potential in automated code generation, yet the programs they produce frequently fail due to logical flaws or unhandled edge cases. To address this, we propose RA-CRF, a Retrieval-Augmented Code Repair Framework that explicitly integrates a structured Error-Repair Knowledge Graph (ERKG). Unlike existing methods that rely on unstructured self-reflection or raw execution feedback, our framework constructs a hierarchical taxonomy connecting error types to specific repair strategies. By leveraging execution feedback, the framework retrieves relevant knowledge to generate structured repair documents, effectively decoupling error diagnosis from targeted code editing. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive self-evolution mechanism that continuously refines the ERKG by persisting verified repair results. Experimental results on single-function benchmarks including BigCodeBench demonstrate that RA-CRF achieves significant performance gains across various open-source and closed-source models. Notably, RA-CRF lifts DeepSeek-V3 to 65.52% Pass@1, a new best on the official BigCodeBench leaderboard. Our findings indicate that integrating explicit and evolvable error-correction knowledge is a robust path to enhancing the reliability and interpretability of code generated by large language models.

title: Evaluate-as-Action: Self-Evaluated Process Rewards for Retrieval-Augmented Agents
author: Jiangming Shu; Yuxiang Zhang; Ye Ma; Xueyuan Lin; Jitao Sang
abstract: Retrieval-augmented agents can query external evidence, yet their reliability in multi-step reasoning remains limited: noisy retrieval may derail multi-hop question answering, while outcome-only reinforcement learning provides credit signals that are too coarse to optimize intermediate steps. To address these limitations, we propose EvalAct (Evaluate-as-Action), which converts implicit retrieval quality assessment into an explicit action and enforces a coupled Search-to-Evaluate protocol so that each retrieval is immediately followed by an explicit evaluation score, yielding process signals aligned with the interaction trajectory. To leverage these signals, we introduce Process-Calibrated Advantage Rescaling (PCAR), a GRPO-based optimization method that rescales advantages at the segment level according to evaluation scores, emphasizing reliable segments while updating uncertain ones conservatively. Experiments on seven open-domain QA benchmarks show that EvalAct achieves the best average EM across multiple model scales, with the largest gains on multi-hop tasks. Ablations verify that the explicit evaluation loop drives the primary improvements, while PCAR provides consistent additional benefits. Code is available at https://github.com/DBMing/EvalAct.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Survey
author: Yongcan Yu; Kuangpu Guo; Jian Liang; Lingxiao He; Meng Wang; Ran He
abstract: Large reasoning models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data serves as a crucial foundation for eliciting and enhancing their reasoning abilities. Despite rapid progress in both improving and analyzing reasoning-oriented SFT, the field still lacks a systematic survey that consolidates its fast-growing literature. To fill this gap, we present a comprehensive review of recent advancements in reasoning SFT, examining the literature through the dual lenses of methodological design and analytical investigation. First, we review methodological improvements across the SFT pipeline and categorize them into data-centric approaches and algorithm-centric innovations. Second, we reorganize analytical studies along three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. Finally, by synthesizing current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks, we outline promising future directions for reasoning SFT. We hope this survey deepens the understanding of reasoning SFT and paves the way for advanced reasoning models.

title: An Image Is Worth Ten Thousand Words: Verbose-Text Induction Attacks on VLMs
author: Zhi Luo; Zenghui Yuan; Daizong Liu; Wenqi Wei; Pan Zhou
abstract: With the remarkable success of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on multimodal tasks, concerns regarding their deployment efficiency have become increasingly prominent. In particular, the number of tokens consumed during the generation process has emerged as a key evaluation metric. Prior studies have shown that specific inputs can induce VLMs to generate lengthy outputs with low information density, which significantly increases energy consumption, latency, and token costs. However, since output length is non-differentiable, existing methods mainly prolong the generated content by disrupting the distribution of the next-step token following the prompt, thereby steering the output away from the original normal response. This strategy neglects the subsequent autoregressive generation process, which makes the attack effect unstable and difficult to control. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel gray-box verbose-text induction attack (VTIA) to inject imperceptible adversarial perturbations into benign images via a two-stage framework. Specifically, we first perform adversarial prompt search, employing reinforcement learning strategies to automatically identify adversarial prompts capable of inducing the LLM component within VLMs to produce verbose outputs. We then conduct vision-aligned perturbation optimization to craft adversarial examples on input images, maximizing the similarity between the perturbed image’s visual embeddings and those of the adversarial prompt, thereby constructing malicious images that trigger verbose text generation. Comprehensive experiments on five popular VLMs demonstrate that our method achieves significant advantages in terms of effectiveness, efficiency, and generalization capability.

title: TTT-Sparse: Test-Time Training of Sparse Attention for Long-Context Understanding
author: Xuehao Wang; Huayu Deng; Linhao Zhong; Yanbin Wei; Hengyu Zhao; Mingyu Liu; Hao Chen; Chunhua Shen
abstract: Pretrained LLMs excel across diverse tasks, yet standard attention remains a major bottleneck for long-context understanding. Recent test-time training (TTT) methods alleviate this by encoding context into internal model parameters, but they typically require specialized architectures, meta-learned initialization, or continual post-training, preventing plug-and-play use on off-the-shelf LLMs. We propose test-time training sparse attention (TTT-Sparse), a plug-and-play alternative that performs test-time training over external memory while keeping the internal parameters frozen. For each input, TTT-Sparse constructs contextual chunk key states from the KV cache and learns a lightweight query adapter to induce a task-specific sparse attention pattern, which is used during generation to attend only to the most relevant context chunks and suppress interference from irrelevant context. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that TTT-Sparse improves long-context understanding while reducing generation-time attention cost.

title: ASSAY: Reconciling Stability and Validity in Reference-Free Scientific LLM Judges
author: Soyeon Hong; Heegyu Kim; Ji Hoon Hong; Jindong Hwang; Juhyeon Ha; Sung Beom Cho; Hyunsouk Cho
abstract: LLM judges have emerged as a key approach to evaluating open-ended scientific outputs that resist automated verification, yet their faithfulness in reference-free settings remains underexplored, particularly for fields such as novel materials synthesis where no ground-truth reference exists. Such judges produce false positives that accept scientifically invalid recipes and false negatives that penalize semantically equivalent ones in unfamiliar notation. We introduce ASSAY, a probe suite built on domain-grounded augmentations of ground-truth synthesis recipes, and reveal that these two failure modes form a systematic Stability–Validity trade-off across thirteen judge models. To resolve this trade-off, we train SynthJudge-8B via DPO on contrastive pairs derived from the same augmentations, improving judgment accuracy from 51.4% to 85.1% while maintaining agreement with domain experts. We release our probe suite and trained model to support faithful automated evaluation in scientific fields beyond materials synthesis at https://github.com/SoyeonHH/ASSAY.

title: From Process Loss to Assembly Bonus: Human-Grounded Diagnosis of Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
author: Ala N. Tak; Teruhisa Misu; Kumar Akash; Zhaobo Zheng; Kevin Joo; Jonathan Gratch
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for collaborative problem solving and human-group simulation. This makes outcome-only evaluation insufficient: if LLM groups are used as models of human groups, we need to know whether they succeed or fail through human-like deliberative mechanisms. We compare human group chats with matched LLM deliberation traces on Wason-style deductive reasoning, then test whether the same process signatures generalize to analogical, abductive, and analytical tasks. Humans and LLMs show the same assembly bonus asymmetry: discussion improves the average member more often than the best initial member. Initial-answer diversity accounts for the effect of model heterogeneity, increasing movement in both corrective and destructive directions. The main differences are process-level. Compared with humans, LLM groups follow majorities more often, surface less unique information, and converge earlier; correct minority signals succeed mainly when re-expressed early. Interventions motivated by human group-decision research yield modest improvements in collective outcomes, but do not remove the coordination bottleneck. Together, these results suggest that LLM groups can reproduce some outcome-level patterns of human deliberation while diverging in the mechanisms that generate assembly bonus and process loss, with implications for human-group simulation and human-AI collaboration.

title: Evaluating Second-Order Bias of LLMs Through Epistemic Entitlement
author: Ramaravind Kommiya Mothilal; Terry Jingchen Zhang; Raiyan Ahmed; Zhijing Jin; Shion Guha; Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed
abstract: Evaluations of social bias in LLMs largely focus on whether models generate or imply biased content. However, as LLMs are increasingly used as judges of bias, they may exhibit social biases in subtler ways in how they evaluate biased content, which current methods do not systematically capture. We call this second-order bias: social bias in an LLM’s judgment about social bias, which we evaluate through a novel, philosophically grounded reasoning task. Drawing on entitlement epistemology, we conceptualize bias as misplaced foundational knowledge that shapes an agent’s rational inquiry, and derive a logical reasoning task for LLMs to judge to whom a biased text is acceptable or non-acceptable. We develop two simple metrics to measure how biased LLM judges are in inferring demographics for acceptability without sufficient support, and how these inferences vary across groups targeted by biased texts. Evaluating open and closed models, we find that our task evades safety guardrails by surfacing bias in model judgment. It varies systematically across target groups, reflects implicit social maps, and shows how models are still triggered by demographic labels. Our work points to the need for LLM bias evaluation in judgment tasks and broadly, for more theoretically grounded approaches to bias evaluation in NLP. We release our code and model responses at https://github.com/uofthcdslab/second-order-bias.

title: Seeing Failure In Advance: Pre-Generation Failure Diagnosis for Multi-Modal Retrieval-Augmented-Generation
author: Chan-Wei Hu; Shuo Xing; Ryan A. Rossi; Zhengzhong Tu
abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (MMRAG) systems can fail even when relevant evidence is retrieved, exposing a gap between retrieval and generation. We formulate MMRAG failure diagnosis as an online single-fire decision problem over prefill hidden states, which is distinct from static probing of model internals or post-hoc self-correction. Across InfoSeek, E-VQA, and VISA, we show that hidden states encode both failure occurrence and failure type, with failure detection reaching around 90% accuracy and recall on InfoSeek and E-VQA. We further introduce a Fire-Then-Type prober that separates failure detection from failure typing, improving typed diagnosis over direct classification. Finally, our method matches the response accuracy of final-layer repair on InfoSeek and E-VQA while diagnosing before answer decoding. The available prefill depth varies substantially across models, from 4.6% to 24.3%, and is limited for Qwen3-VL and InternVL on VISA.

title: SaFeR-Steer: Evolving Multi-Turn MLLMs via Synthetic Bootstrapping and Feedback Dynamics
author: Haolong Hu; Hanyu Li; Tiancheng He; Huahui Yi; An Zhang; Qiankun Li; Kun Wang; Yang Liu; Zhigang Zeng
abstract: MLLMs are increasingly deployed in multi-turn settings, where attackers can escalate unsafe intent through the evolving visual-text history and exploit long-context safety decay. Yet safety alignment is still dominated by single-turn data and fixed-template dialogues, leaving a mismatch between training and deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose SaFeR-Steer, a progressive multi-turn alignment framework that combines staged synthetic bootstrapping with tutor-in-the-loop GRPO to train a single student under adaptive, on-policy attacks. We also introduce Trajectory-Consistent Summative Reward (TCSR), which aggregates the historical minimum and average of turn rewards so that any low-quality turn affects the trajectory-level return. I. Dataset. We release STEER, a multi-turn multimodal safety dataset with STEER-SFT (12,934), STEER-RL (2,000), and STEER-Bench (3,227) dialogues spanning 1–10 turns. II. Experiment. Starting from Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, SaFeR-Steer substantially improves Safety/Helpfulness on both single-turn (48.30/45.86 → 81.84/70.77 for 3B; 56.21/60.32 → 87.89/77.40 for 7B) and multi-turn benchmarks (12.55/27.13 → 55.58/70.27 for 3B; 24.66/46.48 → 64.89/72.35 for 7B), shifting failures to later turns and yielding robustness beyond scaling alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Ed-Bg/SaFeR-Steer-full

title: PlanBench-XL: Evaluating Long-Horizon Planning of LLM Tool-Use Agents in Large-Scale Tool Ecosystems
author: Jiayu Liu; Qihan Lin; Cheng Qian; Rui Wang; Emre Can Acikgoz; Xiaocheng Yang; Qing Zong; Jiateng Liu; Zhenhailong Wang; Xiusi Chen; Heng Ji; Dilek Hakkani-Tür
abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in large tool ecosystems, where real-world tasks require discovering relevant tools, inferring implicit sub-goals, and adapting to dynamic environments over long horizons. However, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate planning under retrieval-limited tool visibility. To address this gap, we introduce **PlanBench-XL**, an interactive benchmark of 327 retail tasks over 1,665 tools that tests whether agents can iteratively retrieve usable tools, invoke them to uncover intermediate evidence for subsequent calls toward the final goal. PlanBench-XL further features an optional blocking mechanism that simulates real-world unpredictability through missing, failing, or distracting tool functions, forcing agents to detect disrupted paths and adapt at runtime. Experiments on ten leading LLMs show that massive-tool planning remains challenging: while GPT-5.4 achieves 51.90% accuracy in block-free settings, it collapses to 11.36% under the most severe blocking condition. Further analysis shows that agents are especially vulnerable when failures lack explicit error signals or when recovery requires longer alternative tool-use paths. These results establish PlanBench-XL as a testbed for diagnosing agentic planning failures and highlight the need for robust adaptive planning in long-horizon tasks with large, imperfect tool environments.

title: ParaSpeechRAG: A Benchmark for Robust Speech Retrieval under Paralinguistic and Acoustic Perturbations
author: Alexandre Costa Ferro Filho; Marcos Paulo C M Queiroz; Matheus Franco Medeiros; Gabriel Orlow De Oliveira Sene; Murilo Alvares Silva; Diogo Fernandes Costa Silva; Arlindo Rodrigues Galvão Filho
abstract: Speech Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Speech RAG) systems are increasingly used in real-world settings where spoken queries vary across speakers, emotions, and acoustic conditions. However, current evaluations primarily focus on clean-condition retrieval accuracy, leaving unclear whether these systems remain semantically invariant under paralinguistic variation. We introduce ParaSpeechRAG, a counterfactual robustness benchmark that isolates non-semantic acoustic factors while preserving lexical content. The benchmark spans controlled perturbations across speaker identity, emotion and prosody, additive noise, speaking rate, and codec compression, enabling systematic evaluation of semantic invariance in speech retrieval. We evaluate three retriever families: ASR-based cascades, speech-text multimodal retrievers (CLASP), and general-purpose audio-language models (GLAP). Results reveal a consistent robustness–accuracy trade-off: multimodal retrievers achieve higher performance under clean conditions but are substantially more sensitive to paralinguistic and acoustic perturbations, particularly emotion and noise. In contrast, ASR-based cascades are more robust to these variations due to their text-centric bottleneck, though with reduced expressive capacity. These findings highlight an overlooked dimension of instability in Speech RAG systems and underscore the need for robustness-aware evaluation beyond clean-condition benchmarks.

title: APPSim-Bench: Bridging Real-world Apps and Reproducible Evaluation for Mobile GUI Agents
author: Jintian Feng; Long Chen; Xiao Yu; Jiayi Dai; Chenglong Liu; Haoru Wang; Zizhen Xue; Yuxuan Shi; Ziyang Wang; Yichen Gong
abstract: Mobile GUI agents can execute tasks from natural-language instructions, but their evaluation remains difficult to make both realistic and reproducible. Existing benchmarks typically trade off these goals: simplified apps lack real-world mobile complexity, whereas live commercial apps introduce uncontrolled variation from recommendations, advertisements, accounts, and changing content. We propose AppSim-Bench, which addresses this trade-off through controllable simulated apps that preserve task-relevant interaction logic while supporting deterministic evaluation. Built through a coding-agent-assisted and human-verified workflow, it contains 557 tasks across 17 high-frequency Chinese and English apps. Its controllable backend data and outcome-based verification remove major sources of environmental stochasticity, enabling reproducible cross-model comparison. Evaluating 19 GUI agents, spanning general-purpose and GUI-specialized systems, we find that autonomous mobile execution remains far from solved. The best model completes only 50.27% of tasks, and 28.55% of tasks are not solved by any agent. Further analysis shows that failures concentrate in longer workflows, numerical reasoning tasks, and inefficient trajectories marked by high action overhead and budget exhaustion. Our project is available at https://github.com/Acrab-Lab/AppSim.

title: Do LLM-Generated Web Apps Behave Correctly? A Contract-Grounded Benchmark for Behavioral Conformance
author: Chansung Park; Juyong Jiang; Jiasi Shen; Sunghun Kim
abstract: Large language models and coding agents can produce web applications that appear functional, yet surface plausibility is an unreliable proxy for behavioral conformance under interaction. We introduce ConformWeb, a contract-grounded protocol and benchmark that operationalizes public behavioral contracts to construct hidden interaction scenarios, evaluating whether agent-generated applications preserve strict conformance under dynamic execution. By decoupling hidden interaction sequences from the public behavioral scope, the protocol guarantees a fair held-out workflow evaluation without relying on undisclosed reference implementations. Evaluated across 24 validated instances scaling to 756 evaluation scenarios and 6,433 semantic steps, only 252 of the 2,160 total execution runs achieve full conformance, yielding a strict pass rate of 11.7%. While scenario-level conformance reaches 36.7% and step-level progress averages 49.4%, this quantitative gap demonstrates that generative systems frequently achieve substantial partial progress but fail to maintain the critical behavioral invariants required for end-to-end conformance. All code and data are released at https://github.com/deep-diver/ConformWeb.

title: LaME: Learning to Think in Latent Space for Multimodal Embedding via Information Bottleneck
author: Peixi Wu; Biao Yang; Feipeng Ma; Bosong Chai; Bo Lin; Wei Yuan; Fan Yang; Tingting Gao; Hebei Li; Xiaoyan Sun
abstract: Reasoning-driven universal multimodal embedding has advanced rapidly by introducing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into the embedding pipeline. Despite the strong performance across both general and complex tasks, this paradigm suffers from two core limitations: (i) autoregressive CoT reasoning incurs high computational cost, making it impractical for low-latency retrieval; and (ii) embedding performance is heavily coupled with CoT annotation quality, making large-scale training unreliable. These raise fundamental questions:Is textual CoT the optimal form of reasoning for embedding, and can effective embedding reasoning be accomplished in latent space? To this end, we propose LaME (Latent Reasoning Multimodal Embedding), which formulates embedding-oriented latent reasoning as a weakly supervised information bottleneck. LaME employs K learnable reason tokens as a fixed-capacity bottleneck, completing all reasoning within a single forward pass. The two weak supervision signals structurally decouple contrastive from autoregressive objectives and eliminate dependence on CoT annotations, while a two-stage training pipeline ensures stable convergence. Experiments on MMEB-v2 and MRMR show that LaME achieves competitive performance, surpassing some explicit CoT-based models, while delivering 60× faster inference than explicit CoT methods and 2× faster than latent baselines with throughput comparable to discriminative embedding models. The code is available at https://github.com/PeppaWu/LaME.

title: InfoQuant: Shaping Activation Distributions for Low-Bit LLM Quantization
author: Ke Li; Dong AN; Xiaoling Zang; Can Ye; Liang Xie; Qibo Qiu; Chen Shen; Xiaofei He; Wenxiao Wang
abstract: Low-bit activation quantization remains a major bottleneck in efficient large language model (LLM) deployment. The difficulty is not only that activations contain outliers, but that their transformed distributions often remain poorly matched to a low-bit uniform quantizer. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods suppress peaks, balance channels, or minimize reconstruction error, yet they rarely specify what activation distribution is actually easy to discretize. As a result, activations may appear numerically smoother while still incurring large quantization error because the quantization range remains wide or most values collapse into a few levels near the mean. We recast activation transformation as quantizer-facing distribution design and analyze quantization error from an information-theoretic perspective. Our analysis shows that quantization-friendly activations should jointly have a smaller numerical range and sufficient dispersion within that range. Guided by this analysis, we propose InfoQuant, a train-free method that employs Peak Suppression Orthogonal Transformation (PSOT) to shape activations into more quantization-friendly distributions. We further introduce adaptive outlier-token selection to improve the robustness of PSOT during optimization. Across multiple LLM families, InfoQuant consistently outperforms prior PTQ and end-to-end training baselines. Under W4A4KV4, InfoQuant preserves approximately 97% of the floating-point zero-shot accuracy on average. Code is available at: https://github.com/LLIKKE/InfoQuant.

title: MEMORA: Embodied Action Memory from Egocentric Videos for Reasoning and Planning
author: Zihao Yu; Xiu Yuan; Chongjie Zhang
abstract: Embodied agents must reason and act from experience accumulated before future questions or goals are known, yet existing memory systems often treat such experience as flat text, retrieved clips, or static graphs. We introduce MEMORA, an embodied memory framework that forms persistent participant-specific world memory from continuous egocentric video. MEMORA instantiates a formation–consolidation lifecycle: online memory editing maintains typed stores for spatial context, object identity and state, and temporal action evidence, while offline consolidation abstracts repeated experience into reusable routines, habits, and preferences. We evaluate MEMORA with MEMORA-Bench, a 45-hour egocentric-video suite for retrospective memory faithfulness and prospective memory-grounded planning. Across four open-weight answer models, MEMORA improves over no-memory, flat-text, and graph-structured memory baselines under matched perception and retrieval. The gains are largest on out-of-distribution planning, where MEMORA improves robot-grounded planning score by up to , showing that formed memory can compose new goals from remembered procedures, objects, and preferences. A physical-robot demonstration further suggests that memory formed from human egocentric video can guide participant-grounded action without in-domain robot data.

title: POISS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Point-of-Interest Search
author: Nicola Maritan; Alessandro Moschitti; Federico Borazio; Xiaokun Zhou; Zhengwei Bai
abstract: Points-of-Interest (POI) search, the task of retrieving and ranking geographically situated entities in response to a query issued from a specific location, underpins major mapping and navigation services. We present POI Search Suite (POISS), the first large-scale dataset designed for this task, pairing over 300K geo-anchored natural language queries across 7 languages and 14 locales with more than 4M graded relevance labels across over 90M candidate POIs drawn from the 72M-entity Overture Maps Places index, jointly capturing semantic match, geographic proximity, and entity quality. Our experiments assess the utility of the proposed dataset for advancing research on POI search.

title: ClinicalReTrial: Clinical Trial Redesign with Self-Evolving Agents
author: Sixue Xing; Kerui Wu; Xuanye Xia; Haoyu He; Meng Jiang; Jintai Chen; Tianfan Fu
abstract: Clinical trials constitute a critical yet exceptionally challenging and costly stage of drug development (2.6B per drug), where protocols are encoded as complex natural language documents, motivating the use of AI systems beyond manual analysis. Existing AI methods accurately predict trial failure, but do not provide actionable remedies. To fill this gap, this paper proposes ClinicalReTrial, a multi-agent system that formulates clinical trial optimization as an iterative redesign problem on textual protocols. Our method integrates failure diagnosis, safety-aware modifications, and candidate evaluation in a closed-loop, reward-driven optimization framework. Serving the outcome prediction model as a simulation environment, ClinicalReTrial enables low-cost evaluation and dense reward signals for continuous self-improvement. We further propose a hierarchical memory that captures iteration-level feedback within trials and distills transferable redesign patterns across trials. Empirically, ClinicalReTrial turns 56.7\% of failed protocols into predicted successes under the simulation environment, with a mean success probability gain of 7.4\% at negligible cost (0.156 per trial). Extensive retrospective case studies further show that ClinicalReTrial recovers clinically meaningful modification patterns that align with real-world expert-driven protocol changes.

title: Discourse-Aware Policy Analysis with Argumentation: A Hybrid LLM–Symbolic Framework for Disaster Governance
author: Stylianos Loukas Vasileiou; Olga Derendiaeva
abstract: Policy documents shape governance outcomes, but their reasoning is often implicit, with tensions between participatory commitments and managerial control rarely stated directly. Existing computational approaches to policy discourse cannot express the frame-mediated relations that drive these tensions, where one argument narrows or instrumentalizes another, and end-to-end summarization by large language models offers little structure that domain experts can inspect or contest. To address this, we present **D-APA** (Discourse-aware Argumentative Policy Analysis), a hybrid LLM–symbolic pipeline that operationalizes critical discourse policy analysis as a quantitative argumentation graph. Given a policy text, an LLM first extracts its arguments, where each argument is classified into a *deliberative* or *managerial* frame and scanned for discourse features such as agency type and verb class. Deterministic rules over these features then connect the arguments through four frame-mediated relation subtypes, namely *agency reduction*, *agenda shift*, *instrumental support*, and *normative support*. Finally, argumentation semantics propagates linguistically grounded base scores through the resulting graph, yielding a final strength for every argument. We release a novel dataset of 100 sub-documents of disaster-risk-reduction policy from the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia, and show that our pipeline produces argument graphs that are accurate, interpretable, and consistent across jurisdictions.

title: ATC-Bench: A Simulation-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Generated Air Traffic Control Instructions
author: Jinjun Cai; Jiaxing Li; Xingyue Wang; Weihuang Zheng; Youyong Kong; Hui Ding
abstract: Air traffic control (ATC) requires structured, safety-critical decision making whose effects unfold through aircraft trajectories, so text-level correctness alone is insufficient for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in this domain. We introduce ATC-Bench, a simulation-grounded benchmark for ATC instruction generation with Chinese-facing scenario descriptions and controller-style instruction fields. Given a structured Chinese traffic situation, a model generates a JSON control plan that is translated into BlueSky commands and evaluated through closed-loop simulation against separation, no-fly-zone (NFZ) avoidance, and route-recovery constraints. The benchmark spans four task families that form a controlled complexity gradient: single-aircraft NFZ avoidance, pairwise conflict resolution, joint conflict-airspace constraints, and multi-aircraft conflict graphs. Experiments with 11 representative LLM endpoints show that while most models produce format-valid instructions, task success varies widely across models and task families: the highest-scoring endpoint under our fixed protocol achieves 63.5% macro-average task success rate (TSR), while the two lowest endpoints fall below 25%, with the largest gaps appearing under joint constraints and multi-aircraft coordination. These results expose a persistent execution gap between static validity and simulation-passing behavior, motivating simulation-in-the-loop evaluation for LLM-based decision making in safety-critical aviation settings.

title: GLARE: Repository-Level Code Optimization Agents for Heterogeneous CPU-GPU Systems
author: Junfeng Gong; Cheng Liu; Junying Chen; Xiaowei Li; Huawei Li
abstract: Recent LLM-based GPU code generation methods have shown promising results on CUDA and Triton kernels, but they typically operate on pre-isolated operators. Such a pre-isolated setting falls short in real-world CPU-GPU heterogeneous optimization, where the target computation is embedded in a larger repository and must be discovered, contextualized, selectively offloaded, and integrated. Such optimization requires repository-level context—including data structure definitions, caller patterns, build configurations, and profiling signals—that is largely absent from operator-level tasks and benchmarks. In this work, we propose GLARE, a profiling-guided framework for repository-level CPU-GPU heterogeneous optimization. GLARE anchors repository context in dynamic profiling signals, builds a multi-granular code dependency graph, extracts hotspot-centered active subgraphs, and uses an agentic loop to decide CPU-GPU partitioning and refine heterogeneous patches with execution feedback. On a GPU-acceleration subset of GSO with 63 tasks, GLARE improves OPT@1 from 74.6% to 87.3% over the strongest baseline under GPT-5.2, and achieves an 11.6% average end-to-end speedup. Ablation studies confirm that profiling-guided context construction is the primary driver of these gains.

title: Beyond Text Following: Repairable Arbitration Reversals in Audio-Language Models
author: Yichen Gao; Yiqun Zhang; Zijing Wang; Yujia Li; Heng Guo; Xi Wu; Xiaocui Yang; Shi Feng; Yifei Zhang; Daling Wang
abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) often follow text that conflicts with audio, even when the audio evidence is clear. This behavior leaves an important question unresolved: is the audio-supported answer unavailable, or is it represented but overridden by the conflicting text? We test this question with a same-audio counterfactual that keeps the audio fixed, removes only the conflicting text, and measures the resulting shift in model preference. Across five ALMs and four conflict tasks, 64.1% of conflict samples exhibit a sign flip: the same-audio branch prefers the audio-supported answer, whereas the joint branch prefers the text-supported answer. This pattern suggests that the relevant audio evidence is encoded but loses during arbitration. Activation patching further localizes the reversal to answer-position computation, and patching effects closely track output candidate-score differences (Spearman ρ=0.93). Based on this diagnostic, we propose Gated Audio Counterfactual Logit Correction (GACL), a training-free decoding rule that interpolates between joint and same-audio scores. Under a strict 5 pp faithfulness-drop budget, GACL improves nAUC by 17.8 points over the best contrastive baseline and transfers without retuning to vision-text arbitration (up to +40.5 pp).

title: SAFEGuard: Detect Optimization-Based Jailbreak Atacks Through Harmful Semantic Analysis and Fluency Measurement
author: Quoc Viet Vo; Trung Le; Damith Ranasinghe; Ehsan Abbasnejad
abstract: Despite the significant efforts devoted to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and ensuring safe deployment, recent work has revealed that LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreak attacks that can bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful responses. Many defense methods are proposed to detect jailbreaks but they are limited in their effectiveness to counter wide-range optimization based jailbreak mechanisms that can yield highly fluency-optimized or harmful semantic obfuscated prompts. To tackle this challenge, we propose a unified detection framework—SAFEGuard—which incorporates a hybrid fluency measurement based on cross-layer distribution distance and perplexity, and the analysis of harmful semantics through gradient matching. Our method is grounded in a paramount observation: high fluency prompts maintain their malicious intention close to harmful prompts while harmful semantic obfuscated prompts often inject gibberish token sequences. Our evaluation demonstrates that SAFEGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves significant improvement in accuracy across different optimization-based jailbreaks. This underscores the effectiveness of SAFEGuard against evolving jailbreak attacks.

title: BenchCompass: From Scores to Signals for Training and Harness Decisions in Payment-Domain LLMs
author: Sijie Dong; Wei Ren; Xuanwei Hu; Jiawei Luo; Zifan Wang; Xiaoyun Feng; Hui Cai; Lyuxin Xue; Peng Lu; Wei Wu; Xin Zhang
abstract: Payment operations are a critical financial infrastructure, but the value of large language models in this domain remains unclear because payment rules change quickly, evidence is fragmented, and decisions depend on transaction state, participant role, region, and payment rail. Existing benchmarks do not isolate whether failures come from missing payment-rule knowledge, poor use of supplied evidence, or brittleness under imperfect harness inputs. We introduce BenchCompass, a payment-domain benchmark whose construction pipeline builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, applies LLM-based quality checks, creates task-input attack variants, and reserves final item admission for domain experts. The release contains an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark covering payment knowledge, context-grounded scenario reasoning, and Attacked Open robustness, plus a lower-assurance Normal pool for inspection and future curation. Across 16 model variants, BenchCompass shows qualitatively different failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows. The benchmark remains unsaturated: the best frontier model reaches 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs, while a representative 32B open-weight model reaches 69.8% and 42.6%. The benchmark, data, and code are publicly available at https://github.com/ant-intl/BenchCompass.

title: Cross-Attention Eigenvalues Know the Word Order in Multilingual Machine Translation
author: Nikolai Prudnikov; Oleg Kachan
abstract: Multilingual machine translation models must adapt to the grammatical structure of the target language, yet how structural information shapes decoder computation remains unclear. Using the eigenvalue spectra of per-(layer, head) attention Gram matrices instead of raw attention weights, we show that cross-attention geometry in NLLB-200 is organized around the target language: these spectral features carry a strong, distributed signal about target-language word order (SVO vs. SOV) when English is the source, with near-perfect decodability across cross-validation. The signal is not concentrated in a small subset of heads, but is broadly distributed across layers and heads—yet it degrades sharply at every level of aggregation when English is the target. This asymmetry suggests that cross-attention geometry reflects the demands of target-side generation rather than source-side structure. Leave-one-language-out evaluation confirms that the signal generalizes to unseen languages, ruling out language identity as a confound.

title: Shortcut-Controlled Evaluation for AI-Generated Text Detection
author: Hee-Young Jung; Jae-Eon Ahn; Seong-Jin Park; Kang-Min Kim
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed in writing assistance for online text, making AI-generated text (AIGT) detection a critical challenge for managing text provenance. However, it remains unclear whether the high detection performance reported in existing AIGT benchmarks reflects a detector’s ability to capture essential differences between human-written and AI-generated text. Rather, this high performance might be driven by easily measurable shortcuts in benchmark settings. To address this question, we decomposed the detection signals in AIGT and systematically analyzed the role of shortcuts in existing benchmark settings. Our analysis reveals that a simple logistic regression classifier trained solely on surface shortcut features (e.g., formatting style and lexical usage) achieves strong classification performance without relying on any semantic signals. Furthermore, the consistent performance degradation of existing detectors when such shortcuts are removed suggests that current AIGT evaluations are influenced by shortcut signals. Motivated by these findings, we present AIGT-SignalBench, a shortcut-controlled benchmark designed to reflect realistic AI-assisted writing scenarios.

title: PercepLog-0: LLM-Augmented Backward Chaining for Legal Reasoning
author: Parisa Kordjamshidi; Sai Amrit Bulusu; Madhavan Seshadri; Samer Aslan; Leslie Barrett; Enrico Santus
abstract: In-depth logical reasoning in domains such as legal analysis remains challenging for large language models (LLMs), exhibiting brittle and inconsistent performance on tasks requiring multi-step deductive inference. This limitation is expected, as LLMs primarily rely on learned distributional associations rather than performing explicit step-by-step logical inference through formal rule application. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework, called PercepLog, that incorporates a classical deductive reasoning algorithm, backward chaining, within an outer control loop, while utilizing LLMs for primitive operations such as substitution and unification. By following the backward chaining algorithm, the framework benefits from the interpretability and explainability of symbolic reasoning procedures while retaining the flexibility of LLM perception for processing natural-language legal text. We evaluate the proposed method on statutory reasoning tasks across a range of legal domains as well general logical reasoning. The results demonstrate that our approach enables more robust, explainable, and principled reasoning over unstructured legal text, where exhaustive formalization is often brittle and prone to hallucination. Our method yields average relative performance improvements of 58% over direct LLM reasoning and 16% over formal LLM-based translation and Prolog inference pipelines.

title: More Context, Larger Models, or Moral Knowledge? A Systematic Study of Schwartz Value Detection in Political Texts
author: Víctor Yeste; Paolo Rosso
abstract: Detecting Schwartz values in political texts is hard: cues are often implicit, and neighboring values differ by fine distinctions. Two remedies are widely assumed to help: more surrounding document text, and explicit moral knowledge. Knowledge-based retrieval has improved benchmarks elsewhere, but whether either transfers here is untested, because published systems vary context, knowledge, and model family at once. We separate these factors under matched conditions on the ValuesML/Touché ValueEval format. The input ranges from the target sentence to a local window to the full document. Retrieval is either absent or drawn from a curated moral knowledge base, injected by early, late, or cross-attention fusion. Supervised DeBERTa-v3 encoders are compared against zero-shot LLMs from 12B to 123B. More context is not uniformly better: full-document input improves the encoders by 2.5-3.8 macro-F1 points but does not consistently help the LLMs. Retrieved knowledge helps more reliably, improving every model family and context under early fusion. A control substituting random knowledge-base entries shows the families gain differently: LLMs from relevance, encoders from exposure to the value ontology. Neither larger encoders nor larger LLMs guarantee gains, and early fusion outperforms both trainable variants. Value-sensitive NLP should evaluate context, knowledge, and model family jointly.

title: PRISM: Private Rank-Invariant Subspace Memory for Federated Continual Fine-Tuning under Local Differential Privacy
author: Ziyi Wang; Liang Liu; Zhu Meng; Zhicheng Zhao
abstract: Privacy-preserving adaptation of pretrained language models requires continual fine-tuning as private client distributions shift, while protecting individual samples under local differential privacy (LDP). In streaming differentially private federated learning, full-rank Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters expose many trainable directions to DP noise, and later domains may overwrite directions that remain relevant to earlier domains. We propose Private Rank-Invariant Subspace Memory (PRISM), a fixed-rank LoRA framework that schedules the active plastic rank over the stream and applies shrinkage-gated memory writes to DP-protected aggregate updates. Server-side consolidation stores retained high-SNR directions in an orthogonal memory and remains pure post-processing of LDP updates. On MNLI genre and Sentiment3, PRISM stabilizes adaptation under strict privacy budgets while preserving a strong public initialization. At \epsilon=2 , it reaches 79.8% and 92.3% final average accuracy, compared with 52.3% and 85.0% for full-rank DP-FedSVD. Ablations indicate that rank scheduling accounts for most strict-budget recovery, and shrinkage-gated memory contributes a smaller retention gain and modestly improves over the strongest static low-rank control on MNLI.

title: BiMTokenizer: Preserving Semantic-Acoustic Balance in Low-Bitrate Speech Tokenization via Bidirectional State-Space Modeling
author: Xin Zhang; Lin Li; Chuanbo Liu; Jianquan Liu; Kong Aik Lee
abstract: Speech codecs serve as bridges between continuous speech signals and large language models, yet face an inherent conflict between acoustic fidelity and semantic preservation. To mitigate this conflict, recent works increasingly adopt dual-tower architectures to decouple semantic and acoustic modeling with separate encoders. However, these dual-tower designs incur substantial architectural overhead. To avoid such complexity, we revisit the single-tower paradigm and propose \textbf{BiMTokenizer}, a low-bitrate speech codec (around 1.1 kbps) combining a \textbf{bidirectional state-space backbone} with \textbf{Residual Spherical Leech Quantization (RSLQ)}. The bidirectional backbone strengthens temporal modeling, while RSLQ offers a fixed, well-separated lattice bottleneck for robust semantic and acoustic tokenization without learned-codebook collapse. Experiments show that BiMTokenizer achieves superior acoustic reconstruction and the lowest WER among low-bitrate codec baselines across both clean and noisy environments, while using less than half the parameters of recent dual-tower baselines. Furthermore, its robust semantic representations yield strong performance on downstream speech understanding tasks, confirming that a well-designed single-tower codec can preserve the semantic–acoustic balance at low bitrates. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/ZhangXinWhut/BiMTokenizer.

title: RegionDoc-R1: Reinforcing Semantic Layout-Aware Reasoning for Document Understanding
author: Chao Wang; Hehe Fan; Huichen Yang; Zhengdong Hu; Sarvnaz Karimi; Lina Yao; Yi Yang
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has proven effective in eliciting reasoning abilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and is emerging in document understanding. However, existing approaches usually lack fine-grained region-level grounding supervision, while the key challenge in document reasoning lies in linking visual evidence within precise regions directly to question–answer semantics. We introduce RegionDoc-R1, a novel framework for document understanding that enhances MLLMs’ reasoning with step-wise feedback. Instead of previous OCR-based text positions, we encourage the model to predict question-relevant Regions of Interest (RoIs) and ground the answer in these regions. Specifically, we first propose the Region-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (RA-GRPO), which encourages models to utilize region-level spatial information in documents for reasoning. Correspondingly, we construct a hybrid training corpus, named SR-Doc, containing Semantic Reasoning (SR) examples enriched with cross-page and region-level reasoning layout annotations. Meanwhile, we also introduce an Adaptive Chain-of-Thought (Ada-CoT) strategy, which dynamically adjusts the reasoning process according to different tasks, enabling more efficient and flexible step-wise document understanding. Experiments on several document reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RegionDoc-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance across tasks such as form document understanding, table-based QA, and layout-sensitive information extraction.

title: Online Self-Weighted Fine-Tuning
author: Haiquan Wen; Yiwei He; Bei Peng; Guangliang Cheng
abstract: Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) assigns the same explicit loss weight to every expert demonstration, regardless of the model’s changing competence over training queries. Reinforcement learning (RL) based methods adapt update strength using model-generated rollouts, but often require substantially more sampling and can be unstable on hard tasks. We propose Online Self-Weighted Fine-Tuning (OSW-FT), a simple method that augments SFT with online, trajectory-level weighting. For each query, OSW-FT estimates the model’s current success rate using a small number of inference-only rollouts and rescales the standard SFT loss accordingly. The optimization direction remains anchored to the expert trajectory, while the update magnitude adapts online. For binary-verifiable reasoning, we connect this weighting to SFT and RL at the gradient level, inspired by variance-reduction principles. The resulting estimator is unbiased for the exact OSW-FT surrogate update for any finite rollout count, and we analyze convergence with respect to the corresponding surrogate objective. Evaluated across Qwen3 series ranging from 0.6B to 4B on multiple challenging benchmarks (e.g., AIME), OSW-FT consistently improves over SFT on small-to-medium scale models. OSW-FT offers a favorable compute-performance trade-off as a practical approach for fine-tuning small-to-medium LLMs on binary-verifiable reasoning tasks with only 2 online rollouts.

title: AuroraCounsel: A Multi-Agent Large Language Model Collaboration Framework for Psychological Counseling
author: Yuean Zhu; ZiChao Song; Haiming Luo
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in alleviating mental health resource shortages, existing approaches struggle with complex emotional dynamics and maintaining theory-grounded counseling trajectories. In particular, they fail to adapt interaction rhythms across counseling phases, often resulting in excessive exploration or premature interventions. To address these limitations, we propose AuroraCounsel, an agent-based counseling framework that models professional counseling workflows. The framework integrates an emotion-sensing agent for affect recognition, a reflection agent for structured psychological analysis, and a guidance agent for response generation. Through emotion-driven dynamic routing, AuroraCounsel selectively activates reflective reasoning only when negative emotions are detected, enabling accurate problem tracing while avoiding unnecessary computation. Building on this architecture, we further align counseling behaviors by optimizing the guidance agent with Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), allowing it to regulate questioning and supportive strategies across dialogue phases and overcome the limitations of supervised fine-tuning in capturing clinical counseling rhythms, such as those prescribed by REBT. Evaluations using LLM-based evaluators and expert assessments by professional counselors demonstrate consistent improvements over existing approaches in professionalism, empathy, and interaction appropriateness.

title: Think-Probe-Respond: Improving Large Language Models as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
author: Tim Schopf; Tobias Schreieder; Akiko Aizawa
abstract: Automated novelty judgment can accelerate scientific discovery by enabling efficient evaluation, refinement, and comparison of research ideas. While large language models are increasingly adopted for this task, we investigate a previously overlooked limitation in their judgment capabilities: despite generating reasoning rationales that closely mirror those of human experts, their final novelty judgments often diverge substantially. We demonstrate that this miscalibration stems from a systematic bias towards judging ideas as "medium novel". To mitigate this, we propose **T**hink-**P**robe-**R**espond (TPR), a lightweight approach that probes latent novelty judgments from hidden states during the reasoning phase and uses the probed judgments to condition the final response. Across strong baselines, TPR improves novelty judgment performance by 22.30% and successfully mitigates the prevalent "medium novelty" bias.

title: Copy First, Translate Later: Interpreting Translation Dynamics in Multilingual Pretraining
author: Felicia Körner; Maria Matveev; Florian Eichin; Gitta Kutyniok; Barbara Plank; Michael A. Hedderich
abstract: Large language models exhibit impressive cross-lingual capabilities. However, *how* cross-lingual generalization emerges has only been analyzed through isolated factors and at sparse points during training, limiting our understanding — particularly of the early phases of learning. To study the early trajectory of linguistic and translation capabilities, we pretrain a multilingual 1.7B model on nine diverse languages, capturing checkpoints at a much finer granularity. We use word-level translation as a testbed, introducing a novel dataset to trace how translation develops over training through behavioral analyses, model-component analysis, and parameter-based ablations. We find that the model quickly acquires basic linguistic capabilities in parallel with token-level copying, while translation develops in two distinct phases: an initial phase dominated by copying and surface-level similarities, and a second phase in which generalizing translation mechanisms develop and copying is refined. Together, these findings provide a fine-grained view of how cross-lingual generalization develops during multilingual pretraining.

title: CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases
author: Sil Hamilton; Albert Sun; Oscar J. Romero; Carl-Leander Henneking; David Mimno; Bishan Yang; Igor Labutov
abstract: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don’t want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

title: Beyond Binary: Turning Partial Success into Dense Verifiable Rewards for Reinforcement Learning in Code Generation
author: Longwen Wang; Yirui Liu; Xuaner Wu; Xiaohui Hu; Yuankai Fan; Kaidong Yu; Qizhen Weng; Wei Xi; Xuelong Li
abstract: Effective reward design is a central challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for code generation. Mainstream test-suite-level outcome rewards enforce functional correctness but induce sparsity, while external Reward Models (RMs) provide dense supervision at the cost of misalignment and additional overhead. Since code evaluation naturally yields multiple test-case-level outcomes, partial success—passing a subset of test cases—offers an intrinsic, verifiable source of dense supervision. In this paper, we propose VeRPO (Verifiable Dense Reward Policy Optimization), an RL framework that systematically turns verifiable partial success into reliable dense rewards.
