Real user requests are challenging to benchmark because they often depend on local execution environments, involve implicit or underspecified intent, and require nontrivial verification. RealClawBench addresses these challenges with two core mechanisms: reconstructed execution environments and deterministic verifiable scorers, which together convert real sessions into reproducible, automatically scored tasks. The resulting release contains 281 executable tasks sampled from a much larger real-session pool while preserving the source distribution, with maximum final-vs-source Jensen-Shannon divergence of 0.0448. Evaluating 14 contemporary models shows that the best system solves only 65.8% of tasks, revealing substantial headroom on realistic developer-agent workloads. By turning real deployed sessions into controlled evaluation instances, RealClawBench provides a practical path toward benchmarks that better measure agent capability in actual use.

title: HiMed: Incentivizing Hindi Reasoning in Medical LLMs
author: Dingfeng Jiang; Han Yan; Chenze Ma; Amit Kumar Jaiswal; Ang Li; Yunxiang Jiang; Xinlei Xiong; Juhao Liang; Hongru Xiao; Xiang Li; Fan Bu; Jiale Han; Ruchir Gupta; Prayag Tiwari; Benyou Wang
abstract: Medical large language models hold promise for reducing healthcare disparities, yet Hindi remains severely underrepresented. While medical LLMs excel in high-resource languages, their performance degrades sharply in Hindi, particularly on Indian systems of medicine. We argue that robust cross-lingual medical transfer requires Hindi reasoning. To this end, we introduce HiMed, a Hindi reasoning medical corpus and benchmark suite covering both Western and Indian medicine. We further propose HiMed-8B, a Hindi-form medical reasoning LLM, through the design of decaying scaffolding reward. Extensive experiments demonstrate improvement in Hindi medical reasoning performance and a reduction in the English–Hindi accuracy gap. Ablation studies validate the contribution of each training stage and reward component. All code, data, and weights are available.

title: Analyzing Reasoning Shifts in Audio Deepfake Detection Under Adversarial Attacks
author: Binh Nguyen; Charles Fleming; Thai Le
abstract: While Audio Language Models (ALMs) offer a promising shift towards explainable audio deepfake detection (ADD) via generated reasoning, whether these explanations reflect faithful perceptual grounding or fragile post-hoc rationalizations under adversarial attack remains under-explored. To address this gap, we introduce **SARA** (**S**hift **A**nalysis of **R**easoning in **A**udio), a diagnostic framework that evaluates the reasoning of five ALMs across three dimensions: acoustic perception, reasoning-verdict coherence and dissonance. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, current ALMs exhibit weak acoustic perception (< 50% accuracy), and generating explicit rationales imposes an accuracy penalty (reducing real F1 score by up to 21%). Second, adversarial attacks show a modality asymmetry: acoustic attacks severely degrade reasoning-verdict coherence (average drop of 14.20%), whereas linguistic attacks achieve higher attack success (61.73%) while preserving fluent coherence (a drop of only 3.91%). Third, we demonstrate that decomposing reasoning shifts into prediction confidence and reasoning-verdict coherence enables a secondary defense layer that can detect adversarially perturbed audio with a 74.41% F1 score even with unseen attack strategies and speaker profiles. These findings suggest that reasoning traces also provide diagnostic utility that persists even when final classification outputs are compromised. Our code is available at [https://github.com/nqbinh17/sara_reasoning_shifts](https://github.com/nqbinh17/sara_reasoning_shifts).

title: CoFGraph: Interleaving Reciprocal Calibration with Confidence Feedback for LLM-Augmented Graph Learning
author: Feng Zhao; Tiewen Chen; Xianggan Liu; Ruilin Zhao; Yifan Song
abstract: Graph learning requires jointly leveraging node semantics and graph structure, but traditional methods often suffer from label scarcity and shallow semantic utilization. Although LLMs provide strong semantic reasoning for graph learning, existing LLM-augmented pipelines face two major challenges: their semantics-only outputs can inject semantic noise that conflicts with graph topology, and they often incur substantial overhead due to LLM fine-tuning or repeated LLM calls at training/inference. We propose CoFGraph, a confidence-feedback framework that interleaves reciprocal calibration between semantic and structural views to enable reliable and efficient LLM-augmented graph learning. To avoid expensive LLM adaptation, we keep the LLM frozen and train a lightweight Interpreter as a semantic proxy, eliminating the need for LLM fine-tuning and continual test-time prompting. To further mitigate semantic noise and the lack of structural feedback, we introduce confidence-based dual-view learning with node-wise confidence estimation and dynamic role switching, allowing the more reliable view to correct the other. Experiments on four public benchmarks validate the effectiveness of CoFGraph and demonstrate strong stability across varying training label ratios, with particularly consistent gains in low-resource regimes.

title: Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data
author: Teagan Johnson; Elliott Ash; Andrew Piper; Maria Antoniak
abstract: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored, even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After curating and hand-annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we create an LLM-labeled dataset of 25K passages, and finally, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, two RoBERTa-based models for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to \sim13M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find that narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data and narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources, topics, and formats in ways that current data curation practices neither measure nor account for. Our framework, dataset, and analyses provide a foundation for understanding how narrative qualities are distributed in LLM pretraining data.

title: FSA-GRPO: Teaching Auditory LLMs to Use Few-Shot Demonstrations
author: Haolong Zheng; Siyin Wang; Xulin Fan; Zengrui Jin; Mark A. Hasegawa-Johnson
abstract: Few-shot prompting provides an effective way to adapt auditory large language models to low-resource tasks such as children’s speech recognition. However, most auditory large language models are not explicitly trained to perform inference in this demonstration-conditioned format, limiting the extent to which they can benefit from In-Context Learning (ICL). To address this limitation, we introduce Few-Shot Aware GRPO (FSA-GRPO), an RL-based post-training recipe that uses a specially designed reward to encourage the model to leverage few-shot demonstrations, thereby strengthening its few-shot adaptation ability. Notably, training with only 2k high-resource adult ASR utterances improves the model’s general few-shot adaptation ability, yielding gains not only in children’s speech recognition (53.9% relative WER reduction without any in-domain training) but also in multilingual ASR (including low-resource languages), speech translation, and audio understanding. We further study data selection and the weight and similarity cutoffs of the auxiliary reward to identify an effective training recipe. Our experiments show that when in-domain data are unavailable or cannot be used for training, FSA-GRPO is more effective than direct tuning on related out-of-domain data.

title: SIGHT: Gaze-Guided Attention-Head Selection for Head-Sparse PEFT
author: Xinyu Gao; Shaonan Wang; Jiajie Zou; Li Zhao; Nai Ding
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces trainable parameters, yet head-sparse PEFT still requires deciding which attention heads should receive updates. We introduce SIGHT, **S**parse **I**dentification of **G**aze-aligned **H**eads for **T**uning, a gaze-guided head selector for head-sparse PEFT. Using eye-tracking data during reading comprehension tests, SIGHT ranks heads by correlating word-level gaze metrics with the attention heads of large language models. Specifically, the comprehension question appears either before or after the passage so that the readers either read the passage with a clear goal or for general understanding. The eye-tracking data from these two conditions are both correlated with attention heads and are fused by an offline-calibrated layer-wise gating module. When applied to Qwen3-based models, updating only the top 10% SIGHT-selected heads generally outperforms other head selectors and all-head PEFT references on reasoning and syntax benchmarks. These results suggest that gaze information during human reading can move beyond post hoc interpretation and serve as an external criterion for allocating adaptation capacity.

title: CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation
author: Yunzhe Li; Richie Yueqi Feng; Tianxin Wei; Chin-Chia Hsu
abstract: Evaluating multi-turn conversational systems remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional pipelines rely on manual rubrics and fixed context, a static approach that limits coverage and fails to capture emergent dialogue behaviors. To address this, we introduce CoReflect (A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation), which unifies dialogue simulation and evaluation into an adaptive, iterative process. CoReflect employs a conversation planner that generates structured templates to guide a user simulator through diverse, goal-directed dialogues. Subsequently, a reflective analyzer processes these dialogues to identify systematic behavioral patterns and automatically refine the evaluation rubrics. Crucially, the insights from the conversation analysis are fed back into the planner to update conversation templates for subsequent iterations. This co-evolution loop ensures that the complexity of test cases and the diagnostic precision of rubrics improve in tandem. By minimizing human intervention, CoReflect provides a scalable and self-refining methodology that allows evaluation protocols to adapt alongside the rapidly advancing capabilities of dialogue models.

title: SUGAR: Spectral and Geometry-Aware Alignment for Matryoshka Representation Distillation
author: Hai An Vu; Phung Gia Huy; Minh-Phuc Truong; Linh Ngo Van; Thanh Hong Nguyen; Thanh-Toan Do; Trung Le
abstract: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) produces nested embeddings whose prefixes remain semantically meaningful, allowing representations to be truncated at inference time and enabling a single model to operate across multiple dimensional budgets. This paradigm has been adopted in several modern embedding models such as Qwen3-Embedding and OpenAI text-embedding-3. However, distilling MRL teachers into compact students remains largely unexplored, as conventional knowledge distillation methods focus on aligning single-scale embeddings and do not account for the multi-scale structure of Matryoshka representations. We introduce Matryoshka Representation Distillation and propose SUGAR, a new framework that preserves the structural properties of MRL embeddings during knowledge distillation. SUGAR aligns point-wise semantic fidelity, spectral capacity via effective-rank matching, and global subspace geometry through Grassmannian alignment. Our extensive experiments show that SUGAR produces compact students that retain strong performance across multiple embedding dimensions while preserving deployment flexibility.

title: PTCG: Persona-guided Tree-based Counterargument Generation
author: Eunbeen Son; Yohan Jo; Joonsuk Park; JinYeong Bak
abstract: The ability to generate counterarguments is important for critical thinking and balanced discourse, yet existing approaches typically produce only a single counterargument, failing to capture the diversity and persuasiveness required in real-world debates. To address this limitation, we propose Persona-guided Tree-based Counterargument Generation (PTCG), a framework that combines Tree-of-Thoughts–inspired step-wise generation and pruning with speaker persona selection. By estimating the author’s persona from the original argument and incorporating speaker personas representing distinct perspectives, PTCG operationalizes perspective-taking and enables the generation of diverse counterarguments. Results from LLM-as-a-Judge, classifier-based assessment, and human evaluations indicate that PTCG shows consistent improvements in both the diversity and persuasiveness of counterarguments compared to baseline methods.

title: NARRATOR: Narrative-Aware Routing and Evaluation of Large Language Models
author: Ahmed Hamdi; Jose G Moreno; Antoine Doucet; Fabio A. González
abstract: Narrative NLP encompasses a diverse set of competencies such as detecting whether a text contains a narrative, classifying its genre or function, completing its plot, and judging similarity between stories. However, the relationship between model capabilities across these sub-tasks remains poorly understood and no unified benchmark exists to evaluate large language models across these dimensions simultaneously. In this paper, we introduce NARRATOR, a unified benchmark of 96,818 multiple-choice questions derived from six narrative datasets spanning detection, classification, story completion, and similarity. Evaluating 50 open-weight LLMs in a zero-shot setting reveals that LLM performance profiles are highly heterogeneous and no model dominates across all sub-tasks. To exploit this complementarity efficiently, we learn compact narrative competence embeddings of LLMs using a matrix factorisation over a binary correctness matrix, without accessing model weights. A single linear layer on top of these frozen embeddings supports model routing (71.1%), correctness forecasting (65.3%), and benchmark accuracy prediction (mean Kendall’s \tau = 0.72) at near-zero inference cost.

title: Reinforcement Learning Can Amplify Emergent Misalignment from Harmless Rewards
author: Magnus Jørgenvåg; David Kaczér; Lasse Ruttert; Marvin Gülhan; Lucie Flek; Florian Mai
abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) is the surprising tendency of language models to become broadly misaligned after fine-tuning on narrowly misaligned examples. While EM has been extensively studied in the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) setting, evidence that it also arises from reinforcement learning (RL) is limited to large, closed-source models, leaving the phenomenon expensive to study and difficult to reproduce. We characterize EM from RL in small, off-the-shelf open-weight models along three axes. First, we show that rewarding narrow, overtly misaligned behavior produces substantially higher general-domain misalignment than sample-matched SFT. Second, we show that EM from RL can be induced by reward signals that could plausibly arise naturally, such as unpopular aesthetic preferences or poor rhetorical appeals. Third, we evaluate in-training mitigations developed for SFT-induced EM and find that they broadly transfer, with preventive steering with persona vectors, interleaving safety data and inoculation prompting all performing well.

title: MetaCLASS: Metacognitive Coaching for Learning with Adaptive Self-regulation Support
author: Naiming Liu; Richard Baraniuk; Shashank Sonkar
abstract: Large language models can generate fluent explanations, but effective tutoring requires supporting the learner’s thought process, not just delivering content. Metacognitive tutoring targets this gap by prompting planning, monitoring, debugging, and evaluation, and, crucially, deciding when to be active versus minimally present, based on learner signals and trajectory. We introduce MetaCLASS, a learning-science grounded framework that formulates metacognitive tutoring as move selection over 11 interpretable actions aligned to self-regulated learning (SRL) processes. MetaCLASS uses a two-phase procedure that first plans a pedagogical trajectory conditioned on learner profiles (calibration, help-seeking) and then generates natural dialogue consistent with that plan. This process yields 1,015 conversations spanning 7,711 turns, each annotated with turn-level metacognitive labels and supported by comprehensive validation analyses. We benchmark nine open-source LLMs on predicting the next coach move given a question and dialogue context. The best model achieves only 43.2% accuracy in coach move prediction, and models exhibit compulsive intervention bias: in turns where effective metacognitive tutoring requires silence (41.7% of cases), models predict "no intervention” only 6.6% of the time, while severely over-predicting high-intervention moves. These results show that traditional content-based tutoring ability does not translate to metacognitive tutoring competence, positioning MetaCLASS as a testbed for developing tutors that promote SRL.

title: MLOps-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Production ML Engineering in Real Repositories
author: Quoc Co Tran; Hitesh Laxmichand Patel; Diwakar Mahajan; Kshitij Bakliwal; Avi Sil; Katrin Kirchhoff
abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to modify and maintain machine-learning systems in production, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate either competition-style ML experimentation or generic repository issue resolution. We introduce MLOps-Bench, a repository-grounded benchmark for production ML engineering. Unlike prior ML-agent benchmarks, MLOps-Bench evaluates executable lifecycle changes inside real ML repositories, spanning data pipelines, feature engineering, model training, model serving, monitoring, CI/CD and governance, and end-to-end integration. Each task is grounded in repository evidence and includes a natural-language requirement, oracle patch, plausible buggy baseline, fail-to-pass tests, pass-to-pass tests, and provenance metadata. The benchmark contains 212 validated tasks from 31 public ML repositories, with 636 fail-to-pass tests and 856 pass-to-pass tests. We evaluate five agents and find that the best system solves 27.3% of tasks while passing 67.1% of tests, showing that current agents often make partial progress but still fail production-relevant behavioral requirements.

title: EpiPersona: Persona Projection and Episode Coupling for Pluralistic Preference Modeling
author: Yujie Zhang; Weikang Yuan; Zhuoren Jiang; Pengwei Yan
abstract: Pluralistic alignment is essential for adapting large language models (LLMs) to the diverse preferences of individuals and minority groups. However, existing personalized reward models often mix stable personal traits with episode-specific factors, limiting their ability to generalize across episodes. To address this challenge, we propose EpiPersona, a framework for explicit persona–episode coupling. EpiPersona first projects noisy preference feedback into a low-dimensional persona space, where similar personas are aggregated into shared discrete codewords. This process separates enduring personal characteristics from situational signals without relying on predefined preference dimensions. The inferred persona representation is then coupled with the current episode, enabling episode-aware preference prediction. Extensive experiments show that EpiPersona outperforms the baselines. It achieves notable performance gains in hard episodic-shift scenarios, while remaining effective with sparse preference data.

title: Who Speaks for the Pruned? Visual Token Pruning as Coverage Optimization
author: Qingchan Zhu; Weihang You; Hanqi Jiang; Changdi Yang; Tianming Liu; Geng Yuan
abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of vision-language models (VLMs), but most methods only ask which tokens to keep. This retained-token view can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. We propose CoverPruner, a training-free pruner that asks the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM? CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), covering the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. Across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, with the largest gains usually appearing under aggressive compression.

title: Zero-Shot Tabular Learning via Hypergraph Reasoning with LLMs
author: Geon Lee; Kyungho Kim; Dongwon Choi; Juyeon Kim; Shinhwan Kang; Kijung Shin
abstract: Tabular data are prevalent across diverse domains such as healthcare and finance. Zero-shot tabular learning aims to make predictions without labeled data. However, existing LLM-based approaches rely on row-wise prompting, resulting in high inference cost and limited use of inter-row dependencies. In this work, we propose TabHGR+, an efficient relation-aware zero-shot framework for tabular data that leverages LLM-generated rules to label and group rows. Specifically, based on column and task descriptions, we use LLMs to generate rules that assign weak labels to all rows. To refine these noisy weak labels, we construct a hypergraph by grouping semantically related rows using LLM-generated rules and perform hypergraph-based label propagation. Lastly, we further enhance the LLM-generated hypergraph for propagation, which is potentially suboptimal, by assigning label-adaptive weights to hyperedges. By requiring only a constant number of LLM calls independent of dataset size, TabHGR+ substantially reduces inference cost while achieving higher classification accuracy than zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.

title: CoDR: Training-Free Confidence-Drift Remasking for Diffusion Language Models
author: Yue Wu; Qinghe Zheng; Yu Zhang; Jian Huang
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) decode by repeatedly committing tokens to masked positions, but these commitments are usually irreversible. A token chosen under sparse, partial context is kept fixed, even when later context no longer supports it. Existing samplers mainly decide when to commit a token, but rarely check whether an already committed token should still be kept, allowing early mistakes to propagate. We trace this issue to confidence drift, where the model’s confidence in a committed token drops from its sparse commit-time context to the denser context available later. Based on this signal, we propose CoDR (Confidence-Drift Remasking), a training-free and sampler-agnostic refinement pass. CoDR estimates drift for all committed positions in only k forward passes via k-partition probing, then remasks and regenerates only the tokens the model no longer endorses. Across two backbones, four reasoning and coding tasks, and three base samplers, CoDR improves accuracy on nearly every combination with modest overhead. Controlled experiments show that the gains come from targeted confidence-drift remasking rather than extra compute alone, and that CoDR uses far fewer forward passes than prior remasking methods.

title: OrchDebate: Adaptive Orchestration for Multi-Agent Debate via Self-Evolving Skills
author: Kaiyu Zhou; Yongsen Zheng; Xuanye Zhang; Kwok-Yan Lam
abstract: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for eliciting stronger inference-time reasoning, yet most existing systems still use fixed interaction protocols across instances. Such static designs can suffer from anchoring bias, overthinking on easy problems, and rigid coordination across tasks of varying difficulty. We present OrchDebate, a framework that recasts multi-agent debate as structured-state orchestration over reusable debate-control skills. Instead of following a pre-defined template, OrchDebate uses an orchestrator to examine the current debate state and select the next coordination action, such as introducing agents under different visibility settings or terminating deliberation with an adaptive readout rule. This skill-based view makes debate control modular and state-dependent. The orchestrator operates through a structured control interface rather than directly generating reasoning content, helping reduce reliance on early answers. OrchDebate further maintains a self-evolving skill bank whose reusable realizations are refined through outcome-guided updates on an evolution stream, without additional external training data. Across diverse benchmarks, OrchDebate delivers a better accuracy-cost trade-off than representative fixed and adaptive debate methods by allocating debate compute more selectively.

title: Learning Personalized Prompts for Healthcare Guidance
author: Ruize Shi; Hong Huang; Wei Zhou; Kehan Yin; Kai Zhao; Yun Zhao
abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has transformed many industries, including healthcare. In practice, hospitals and patients increasingly seek LLM-based systems capable of interpreting personal health records and providing healthcare guidance. However, existing approaches mainly rely on general medical knowledge and often fail to account for individual variability, limiting their ability to provide personalized guidance. To address this, we propose personalized prompt learning (PPL), a framework that learns individualized prompts to guide LLMs in generating personalized healthcare recommendations. PPL constructs initial personalized prompts by leveraging both self-informed patient information and peer-informed signals derived from clinically similar cases. These prompts are then refined using reinforcement learning (RL) to better align the generated responses with physician recommendations written for each patient. PPL operates with hard prompts, enabling seamless integration with proprietary LLMs without modifying the underlying models. We evaluate PPL on real-world obstetrics and gynecology data. The results show that our approach produces more personalized healthcare guidance and wins 97 out of 100 comparisons in expert evaluation, demonstrating its potential for broader healthcare applications. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/PPL.

title: SCARV: Structure-Constrained Aggregation for Stable Sample Ranking in Redundant NLP Datasets
author: Feiyu Wu; Xu Zheng; Zhuocheng Wang; YIMing Dai; Hui LI
abstract: Sample-level ranking is widely used for data selection, debugging, and training-data attribution, but redundant NLP corpora—exact and near duplicates, paraphrases, and templated examples—can make proxy-induced rankings unstable across random seeds. We study stable sample-level ranking under redundancy and propose SCARV, a modular aggregation layer that operates on top of existing scoring proxies. SCARV normalizes scores within each run, can regularize redundant examples through cluster-level aggregation and allocation, and aggregates across seeds with a robust operator. Across synthetic redundancy, naturally mined QQP redundancy, multiple proxy families, classification and sentence-pair tasks, and end-to-end DistilBERT fine-tuning, stability-aware aggregation improves over bare proxy rankings and yields more reproducible ranking-based decisions, such as selected subsets and suspicious-example sets. Matched mechanism analysis shows that cross-seed aggregation is the dominant generic stabilizer. The incremental effect of structural regularization is small, map-dependent, dataset-dependent, and sometimes negative; a meaningful redundancy map is useful mainly when group-consistent treatment is operationally desired. These results position SCARV as a stability-oriented aggregation framework rather than a universal data selector and emphasize decision reproducibility over uniform gains in downstream utility.

title: COPE: Continual Personalization of LLMs under Sparse User Feedback via User Embeddings and Self-Evaluation
author: Ruike Cao; Fugen Yao; Liang Dong; Jian Xu; Guanjun Jiang; Li Xiao
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable results across various benchmarks, their alignment with normative values often results in homogenized responses that fail to address diverse user preferences. Existing training-free methods often occupy valuable context windows through prompt engineering, while training-based methods typically remain static post-training, failing to support the continual optimization required in real-world settings. To address these challenges, we propose **COPE** (**C**ontinual **O**ptimization with **P**ersonalized embedding and self-**E**valuation), a novel optimization framework tailored for real-world-motivated interaction settings with sparse user feedback. Our framework assigns learnable personalized embeddings to each user and synergistically integrates preference capture, self-evaluation calibration, and personalized response optimization within a single update step. A key innovation of our method is the use of self-evaluation to generate proxy rewards, enabling continuous model updates even when explicit user feedback is unavailable. Experiments show that COPE consistently outperforms strong training-free and training-based baselines under sparse feedback, and remains complementary to Retrieval-Augmented Prompting (RAP). Further analyses confirm COPE’s reliable self-evaluation, meaningful preference patterns, stable general capabilities, and robustness under shifting preferences and alternative evaluators.

title: Pair Difficulty Matters: Rethinking Pairwise LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation and Consistency
author: Bruno Brocai; Maria Becker
abstract: Large Language Model judges are widely used to rank texts and text-generating systems through pairwise comparison, and their reliability is typically assessed via three proxies: position bias, transitivity, and pairwise agreement (self- or human-labeled). Because these proxies drive judge selection and benchmarking, a substantial literature reporting that judges perform poorly on them risks steering practitioners away from otherwise capable evaluators. We argue this assessment is misleading. Under the Bradley–Terry geometry underlying pairwise aggregation, each proxy is dominated by close-rank-gap pairs, where inconsistency is information-theoretically expected and individual verdicts contribute little to the aggregate ranking; far-gap pairs carry the ranking signal but barely move the proxies. We formalize this argument and validate it in a controlled simulation and on two human-rated corpora: the proxies correlate only weakly with ranking accuracy against gold, and their predictive component concentrates in the far-gap regime. Judges should therefore be assessed on rank-gap-conditional metrics, ideally against human rankings. Code in the supplementary zip archive.

title: WebWorld: The Browser as a World Model for Self-Improving Web Code
author: Jiajun Wu; Jian Yang; Yaxin Du; Wei Zhang; Haowen Wang; Junhang Cheng; Yuxuan Zhang; Tuney Zheng; Xianglong Liu; Ming Zhou
abstract: VLM-driven self-improvement of web code has a structural flaw: the model that proposes the repair is the model that judges it, and visual plausibility under that judge is a poor proxy for whether the page actually works. What the loop is missing is a counterparty the VLM cannot fool, and the browser already is that counterparty: a deterministic, executable simulator of how an HTML artifact behaves under user actions, and in everything but name a world model for web code. We present WEBWORLD, the interface that lets a VLM prior interact with this browser-as-world-model autonomously and decides which interactions become supervision. Each round, the VLM emits a critique that the planner compiles into a typed interaction contract; the browser re-executes the candidate and issues an acceptance certificate only when both target progress and preservation of every previously verified capability hold; certified transitions accumulate as a quality ratchet that is the only thing the SFT export ever sees. Under matched training, WEBWORLD-27B improves Raw-27B by 5.3 points on HTMLBench-400 and 14.9 points on MiniAppBench-Val, and reaches the level of strong frontier systems such as Kimi-K2.6 and GPT-5.4 on interactive HTML generation. Equal-size ablations show that browser-backed admission carries the gain: without the certificate, the matched 9B lift nearly disappears.

title: Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis
author: Junchi Liao; Jiawen Deng; Fuji Ren
abstract: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

title: Beyond Chunking: Efficient Global Pooling for Holistic Long-Document Representation
author: Hoin Jung; Xiaoqian Wang
abstract: Effectively representing long documents is a persistent challenge in natural language processing, as foundational encoders are constrained by limited context windows. Prevailing methods like truncation and independent chunk aggregation can discard content or lose cross-chunk context, hindering downstream performance. To address this problem, we introduce **Spectral Attention Token Pooling (SATPool)**, a novel, encoder-agnostic module that generates a single, fixed-size vector from variable-length sequences of locally encoded tokens. SATPool operates in two stages: it first uses efficient linear attention to model global token interactions after chunk encoding, then employs **Spectral Token Compression (STC)** to compress these globally-aware token representations into a compact, context-aware vector. Across long-document classification, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and multimodal RAG, SATPool achieves strong overall improvements and robust top-tier performance across datasets and encoder backbones. The pretrained encoder remains frozen, while the lightweight SATPool module and task-specific heads are trained for each downstream task.

title: Balancing Faithfulness and Performance in Reasoning via Multi-Listener Soft Execution
author: Nithin Sivakumaran; Shoubin Yu; Hyunji Lee; Yue Zhang; Ali Payani; Mohit Bansal; Elias Stengel-Eskin
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning sometimes fails to faithfully reflect the true computation of a large language model (LLM), hampering its utility in explaining how LLMs arrive at their answers. Moreover, optimizing for faithfulness and interpretability in reasoning often degrades task performance. To address this tradeoff and improve CoT faithfulness, we propose Reasoning Execution by Multiple Listeners (REMuL), a multi-party reinforcement learning approach. REMuL builds on the hypothesis that reasoning traces which other parties can follow will be more faithful. A speaker model generates a reasoning trace, which is truncated and passed to a pool of listener models who “execute” the trace, continuing the trace to an answer. Speakers are rewarded for producing reasoning that is clear to listeners, with additional correctness regularization via masked supervised finetuning to counter the tradeoff between faithfulness and performance. On multiple reasoning benchmarks (BIG-Bench Extra Hard, MuSR, ZebraLogicBench, and FOLIO), REMuL consistently and substantially improves three measures of faithfulness – hint attribution, early answering area over the curve (AOC), and mistake injection AOC – while also improving accuracy. Our analysis finds that these gains are robust across training domains and are associated with shorter and more direct CoTs.

title: TUX: Measuring Human–AI Tacit Understanding
author: Yueshen Li; Hanyi Min; Vedant Das Swain; Koustuv Saha
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as collaborative partners, human–AI alignment is often evaluated through explicit task success, accuracy, or reward optimization. Yet many collaborative settings depend on tacit understanding: whether an agent can align with a human’s evaluative stance or representational priors without clear objectives, communication, or feedback. To study this capacity, we develop a spectrum-placement task inspired by the social party game Wavelength, in which humans and agents independently place concepts along subjective spectra. We operationalize the Tacit Understanding Index (TUX) as a pairwise behavioral measure of similarity between human and agent judgments, and evaluate it with 241 human participants and 200 profile-conditioned LLM agents across four models. We find that nearest human–agent pairs in trait space achieve significantly higher TUX, suggesting that tacit alignment is associated with person-level characteristics rather than reflecting only random similarity. Regression analyses show that TUX becomes more explainable as predictor sets become richer, with individual traits, decision-making styles, and confidence improving over aggregate trait-distance baselines. These findings suggest that TUX provides a measurable behavioral signal of human–LLM tacit understanding, while revealing the limits of profile-based conditioning for capturing deeper representational alignment.

title: Can Scientific Claims Be Removed from Large Language Models? A Systematic Evaluation of Claim-Level Unlearning
author: Snigdha Paul; Manasi Patwardhan; Arman Cohan
abstract: Language models (LMs) are trained on static scientific corpora, whereas scientific knowledge continuously evolves through correction and revision. Scientific claims encoded within these models may later become retracted, disproven, or updated by subsequent research, creating the risk of disseminating outdated information in scientific workflows. This creates a need for LMs to forget obsolete scientific claims. Machine unlearning offers a promising solution by enabling knowledge removal while maintaining overall model utility. Existing studies primarily investigate instance-level forgetting; however, scientific claims introduce additional challenges because they are interconnected, and continually evolving. To address this gap, we introduce the task of Scientific Claim Unlearning and present a new benchmark, SciUnlearn. We show that current unlearning approaches are unable to effectively eliminate claim-level knowledge and often achieve only superficial suppression, highlighting the need for specialized methods designed for structured knowledge removal.

title: Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy: Bootstrapping Intent-Based Persona Routing with PRISM
author: Zizhao Hu; Mohammad Rostami; Jesse Thomason
abstract: Persona prompting can steer LLM generation towards a domain-specific tone and pattern. This behavior enables use cases in multi-agent systems where diverse interactions are crucial and human-centered tasks require high-level human alignment. Prior works provide mixed options on their utility: some report performance gains when using expert personas for certain domains and their contribution to data diversity in synthetic data creation, while others find near-zero or negative impact on general utility. To fully leverage the benefits of the LLM persona and avoid its harmfulness, a more comprehensive investigation of the mechanism is crucial. In this work, we study how model optimization, task type, prompt length, and placement can impact expert persona effectiveness across instruction-tuned and reasoning LLMs, and provide insight into conditions under which expert personas fail and succeed. Based on our findings, we developed a pipeline to fully leverage the benefits of an expert persona, named PRISM (Persona Routing via Intent-based Self-Modeling), which self-distills an intent-conditioned expert persona into a gated LoRA adapter through a bootstrapping process that requires no external data, models, or knowledge. PRISM enhances human preference and safety alignment on generative tasks while maintaining accuracy on discriminative tasks across all models, with minimum memory and computing overhead.

title: Understanding Training Data Attribution in RLVR: From the Perspective of Causal Inference
author: Chi Zhang; Jian Zhao; Wei Wang; Kai Wang; Yao Zhao; Xuelong Li
abstract: Training data attribution is increasingly used to filter, reweight, and prioritize rollouts in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). However, these interventions often assume that individual samples, transitions, or trajectories can be attributed independently of the other data used in the same update. We show that this assumption is not merely a property of the attribution estimator, but a structural property of the training objective. We recast training data attribution as individual treatment effect estimation and use the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) to determine when a proposed attribution unit is well-defined. This yields a simple criterion that attribution is only valid at the level where the algorithm assigns a stable contribution to that unit. Applying this criterion to RLVR, we show that the PPO objective admits trajectory-level attribution, whereas naive trajectory-only attribution is not well-defined for GRPO unless peer context is modeled. Experimental results support this distinction and provide preliminary evidence for group-level attribution under GRPO.

title: Exposía: Teaching and Assessment of Academic Writing Skills for Research Project Proposals and Peer Feedback
author: Dennis Zyska; Alla Rozovskaya; Ilia Kuznetsov; Iryna Gurevych
abstract: We present Exposía, the first public dataset that connects writing and feedback in higher education, enabling research on educationally grounded computational approaches to teaching and evaluating academic writing. Exposía includes student research project proposals and peer and instructor feedback consisting of comments and free-text reviews. The dataset was collected in the "Introduction to Scientific Work" course of the Computer Science. Exposía reflects the multi-stage nature of the academic writing process that includes drafting, receiving feedback, and revising the writing based on the feedback received. Both the project proposals and peer feedback are accompanied by human assessment scores based on a fine-grained, pedagogically-grounded schema for writing and feedback assessment that we develop. We use Exposía to benchmark state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) on two tasks: automated scoring of (1) the proposals and (2) the student reviews. We find that the two tasks are best served by different LLMs. Furthermore, closed-source models consistently outperform open-weight models, motivating further research on improving the performance of open-weight models preferred in classroom settings. Finally, we establish that a prompting strategy that scores multiple aspects of the writing together is the most effective, paving the way for more effective classroom deployment of modern LLMs.

title: R^3 -MDT: A Retain-Rerank-Revise Framework Based on Uncertainty and Consistency for Medical Decision Tree Extraction
author: Boyu Qiu; Xiaolong Weng; Zehua Wang; Buzhou Tang; Ying Xiong; Min Zhang
abstract: Automatic extraction of Medical Decision Trees (MDTs) is an important task for Clinical Decision Support Systems, but remains challenging due to the complex logical structures involved. Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) commonly adopt generate-then-revise pipelines with self-correction to improve reasoning accuracy. However, we find that applying revision uniformly across all samples can be harmful, as it often alters already correct and stable predictions, leading to over-correction on simple cases. To alleviate this issue, we propose R^3-MDT, an adaptive inference framework that dynamically selects reasoning strategies based on sample difficulty. We use model uncertainty and output consistency as internal signals to estimate difficulty and route samples into Easy, Medium, and Hard categories. For Easy samples with confident and consistent predictions, we directly retain the initial outputs. Medium-difficulty samples, which exhibit ambiguity among multiple plausible candidates, are handled via reranking to select the optimal decision tree. Hard samples, characterized by high uncertainty and structural inconsistency, are revised to rectify intractable generation failures. By adaptively selecting inference strategies based on difficulty levels, R^3-MDT avoids unnecessary revisions while effectively correcting underlying reasoning failures. Experiments on the Text2DT benchmark show that R^3-MDT alleviates the over-correction problem and achieves state-of-the-art performance, while auxiliary language- and task-shift evaluations indicate the broader transferability of its routing principle.

title: Beyond the Illusion of Consensus: From Surface Heuristics to Knowledge-Grounded Evaluation in LLM-as-a-Judge
author: Mingyang Song; Mao Zheng
abstract: Agreement among LLM judges is widely used as evidence that automated evaluation is reliable. Yet consensus may be stable without reflecting a shared understanding of quality. We call this Evaluation Illusion: judges can produce detailed critiques while relying on overlapping surface cues or a common evaluation instrument. In a fully crossed baseline study, three frontier judges conduct 105,600 evaluations of 32 models. First, for the two highest-scoring models, moving from a shared five-dimension rubric package to independently generated rubrics reduces agreement by 62%, a joint contrast we term the Rubric Commensurability Problem. Second, nearly identical model-level rankings coexist with substantially weaker criterion-level agreement under non-equivalent metrics and sample sets, yielding the Resolution Paradox. We further introduce MERG, a four-stage protocol that elicits task knowledge and potential biases before scoring. In a controlled comparison on the same models at t{=}0.0, agreement decreases under independently generated MERG rubrics. These results do not establish that MERG scores are more accurate; they show that consensus depends on the evaluation instrument and analytical resolution at which it is measured.

title: StateSwap: Probing Support–Elimination Hidden States in Multiple-Choice Questions
author: Chao Gao; Haijiang Liu; Qiyuan Li; Caicai Guo; Frank van Harmelen; Jinguang Gu
abstract: Large language models often answer the same multiple-choice question inconsistently when it is posed under support-oriented and elimination-oriented framings. We investigate whether these discrepancies arise from different internal representations induced by the two framings. We introduce a dual-framing protocol with minimally varied prompts that use either support- or elimination-oriented framing while keeping the evaluation target fixed. To probe the internal computation, we append an untrained special token, [STATE], and treat its residual-stream activation as an intervention interface. Across both models, the two framings induce separable [STATE] activations concentrated in intermediate layers. Swapping these activations between paired prompts systematically changes predictions and improves cross-framing agreement, providing intervention-based evidence that the activations are behaviorally relevant. Beyond instance-level substitution, mean-difference steering directions derived from the dual-framing contrast exhibit more bounded layer-wise responses than matched contrastive activation addition directions under the evaluated protocol.

title: QUORUM: QUality-Optimized Routing Using Multiple annotators
author: Antonio Purificato; Maria Sofia Bucarelli; Andrea Bacciu; Amin Mantrach; Fabrizio Silvestri
abstract: Data annotation remains a central bottleneck in natural language processing, requiring human effort to obtain high-quality labels at scale. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a fast and cost-effective alternative, their reliability is highly instance-dependent: they perform well on simple inputs but often fail on examples requiring nuanced reasoning or contextual understanding. In this work, we address this challenge with QUORUM (QUality-Optimized Routing Using Multiple annotators), a budget-aware routing framework that dynamically assigns each instance to human or LLM annotators under a fixed annotation budget. Unlike prior approaches relying on model confidence or uncertainty estimates, QUORUM leverages feature-based signals to estimate instance difficulty and supports multiple annotations per instance, combining them through agreement-based rewards to improve reliability. We evaluate QUORUM across diverse closed- and open-ended annotation tasks in English and multilingual settings, and QUORUM improves annotation quality by up to 34.4% while reducing costs by 8.8% over competing methods. Code can be found at https://github.com/amazon-science/QUORUM.

title: TRONTOR: To RoPE or Not to RoPE for Long-Context Modeling
author: Youngjun Son; Jongyeon Park; Jaejin Lee
abstract: While Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely used in large language models, its inductive biases can impair long-context reasoning and lead to attention sinks. In this work, we propose TRONTOR, a method that effectively combines RoPE and No Positional Encoding (NoPE) through a simple fine-tuning phase, bypassing the need for expensive pretraining modifications. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that mixing RoPE and NoPE at the attention-head level can enhance long-context capabilities, while static selection strategies fail to capture the varying complexity of inputs. Based on this observation, TRONTOR employs a lightweight context-aware routing method that dynamically switches each attention head between RoPE and NoPE at every token step. This router-only configuration provides an efficient operating point, yielding long-context performance gains with minimal inference overhead. For further gains, we extend TRONTOR to TRONTOR-Agg, which applies simple unweighted averaging over multiple RoPE bases within RoPE-active heads while avoiding learnable intra-head routing. Evaluated on the RULER benchmark using Llama-3.2 (1B and 3B) and Qwen3 (1.7B and 4B), TRONTOR improves long-context performance by mitigating attention sinks and dynamically reallocating attention toward relevant mid-context tokens.

title: Generating Complete Court Judgments with Large Language Models: A Study on CMML
author: Zhongyi Guan; Zhitian Hou; Nanli Zeng; Kun Zeng
abstract: Given the criminal fact, a complete legal judgment usually contains two parts: Court View Generation (CVG) for the case and Legal Judgement Prediction (LJP) for each defendant. However, existing studies still cannot support unified modeling and evaluation of complete legal judgments. First, at the data level, existing legal datasets mostly cover either single-defendant scenarios or multi-defendant scenarios, and the attributes predicted by LJP are not rich enough, making it difficult for models to generalize to real-world complete legal judgments. Second, CVG and LJP are usually modeled independently, ignoring their intrinsic connection. Third, the role of auxiliary articles has not been explored. To address these issues, we build CMML (Chinese Mixed-Defendant Multi-Attribute Legal Judgment Dataset), a large-scale dataset that mixes single- and multi-defendant cases with multi-attribute annotations. Based on CMML, we propose a new task, LJP-x, which extends LJP with additional prediction attributes. We further systematically study the interaction between CVG and LJP-x, and explore how auxiliary articles influence both tasks. Our dataset is available at: https://github.com/magicalpig2003/CMML.

title: From Proprietary to Public: Dataset Declassification for Question Answering
author: Stefano Campese; Alessandro Moschitti; Ivano Lauriola
abstract: Training Question Answering (QA) systems on real customer interaction data is often infeasible to reproduce or share due to privacy and intellectual property constraints. We introduce dataset declassification, a framework that replaces proprietary QA datasets with public, semantically equivalent counterparts that preserve training and evaluation utility while satisfying typical legal and privacy requirements. The approach maps proprietary questions to public equivalents via large-scale retrieval and reconstructs answers from domain-matched corpora using LLM-based annotation. Experiments on four QA benchmarks show that models trained and evaluated on declassified datasets achieve performance within \Delta \approx 0 of the original data. The method targets datasets whose underlying information needs already exist in public knowledge sources (e.g., knowledge available on the web and used by public-facing services). We further provide explicit applicability conditions showing that declassification succeeds when sufficient semantic overlap exists between proprietary and public corpora, and degrades predictably when it does not.

title: Counterfactual Self-Distillation: A Distribution-Shaping Framework for Entity-Fact Unlearning in Large Language Models
author: Ying Zhao; Yihui Zhang; Mengyi Deng; Xin Li; Yuan Tian; Wei Wang; Yi Chang
abstract: Entity-fact unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove the binding between a target entity and a forgotten fact, producing a model that behaves like one retrained without the forgotten data while preserving neighboring knowledge and overall model utility. We frame this problem as distribution shaping: such a retrained model would yield a plausible distribution at forget queries, fluent, semantically appropriate, and reflective of residual knowledge, which we take as the appropriate target. Existing objectives provide only narrow token-level or semantically uninformative supervision, falling short of this target. We propose Counterfactual Self-Distillation (CSD), a self-distillation framework that approximates the retrained distribution by constructing a counterfactual teacher through type-consistent entity substitution. The resulting teacher is decoupled from the target identity while preserving type-level relational structure, enabling directed probability reallocation without an external oracle. Experiments on TOFU and RWKU show that CSD achieves a strong forget-utility trade-off, including the best overall forgetting on RWKU and strong performance on TOFU.

title: iFlip: Iterative Feedback-driven Counterfactual Example
author: Yilong Wang; Qianli Wang; Nils Feldhus
abstract: Counterfactual examples are minimal edits to an input that alter a model’s prediction. They are widely employed in explainable AI to probe model behavior and in natural language processing (NLP) to augment training data. However, generating valid counterfactuals with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging, as existing single-pass methods often fail to induce reliable label changes, neglecting LLMs’ self-correction capabilities. To explore this untapped potential, we propose iFlip, an iterative refinement approach that leverages three types of feedback, including model confidence, feature attribution, and natural language. Our results show that iFlip achieves an average 57.8% higher validity than the three state-of-the-art baselines, as measured by the label flipping rate. The user study further corroborates that iFlip outperforms baselines in completeness, overall satisfaction, and feasibility. In addition, ablation studies demonstrate that three components are paramount for iFlip to generate valid counterfactuals: leveraging an appropriate number of iterations, pointing to highly attributed words, and early stopping. Finally, counterfactuals generated by iFlip enable effective counterfactual data augmentation, substantially improving model performance and robustness.

title: RAGSentinel: Certifiable Geometric Consensus for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: Yueyang Quan; Anjun Gao; Yufei Xia; Minghong Fang; Zhuqing Liu
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models by grounding responses in external documents, but it also exposes a critical security vulnerability: adversarial documents injected into the knowledge database can enter the context window and steer the model toward targeted incorrect answers. Existing post-retrieval defenses rely on instruction following, parametric knowledge, or text-level consistency, all of which can be imitated or optimized against by adaptive attackers. We propose RAGSentinel, a training-free, label-free defense for black-box RAG systems. RAGSentinel uses a surrogate encoder to measure query-conditioned hidden-state shifts induced by retrieved documents, removes shared topic directions, and filters poisoned documents as geometric outliers from a robust majority consensus. We prove that, under an honest-majority assumption and a representation-level separation condition, RAGSentinel exactly recovers a poison-free majority-sized context. Experiments across three question-answering datasets, three LLM families, and multiple poisoning attacks show that RAGSentinel consistently achieves low attack success rates while preserving competitive accuracy and remaining effective against adaptive attacks with full pipeline knowledge.

title: ParentingLLM : Pacing Reasoning Maturity for Bidirectional Test-Time Scaling under Token Budgets
author: Seunghwan Jeong; Sugi Lee; WeiJin Park; Ikjun Yeom; Honguk Woo
abstract: Reasoning LLMs under fixed token budgets often commit before verification finishes, or spend the budget on deliberation that never reaches a final answer. Existing inference-time controllers regulate reasoning length, which does not indicate whether the current prefix is ready to be finalized. We introduce ParentingLLM, an inference-time controller that paces reasoning maturity, defined as the prefix’s readiness to commit given the remaining budget, against a user-specified target schedule, without fine-tuning the underlying LLM. The maturity estimate combines consumed budget with a forked forced-commit probe; the controller injects Wait when the estimate runs ahead of the schedule and Hurry when it lags. On MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, AIME 24+25, and GSM-Hard with three Gemma-4 models and Qwen3.5-9B, ParentingLLM improves over prior inference-time baselines, with the largest gains on AIME 24+25 under a tight budget (-22.6 burst rate, +4.0 to +7.3 accuracy at B=1024).

title: Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets
author: Paul He; Elke Kirschbaum; Shiva Kasiviswanathan
abstract: NLP systems increasingly aggregate claims from retrieved passages, documents, and generated reasoning steps. Yet current factuality methods mostly verify claims individually or compare pairs of claims, leaving open the question of whether the entire aggregated claim set can be retained coherently. This misses a fundamental failure mode: claims may be locally plausible and pairwise compatible while still being jointly inconsistent. We formalize global consistency repair: given an inconsistent natural-language claim set, preserve the largest coherent subset while localizing the compact sources of inconsistency. We introduce QXR, an adaptive diagnosis-and-repair framework that treats an LLM as a noisy set-level consistency judge, localizes minimal conflicting subsets, and repairs the claim set by deleting a small hitting set of claims. Across LLM judges and benchmarks derived from VitaminC, FEVER, and conflicting-evidence RAG, QXR preserves substantially more valid claims than direct all-at-once judging while maintaining high precision. These results suggest that factuality in claim aggregation systems should be treated as a set-level repair problem, not only as local verification.

title: Chain-of-Thought Hurts When the Answer Speaks for Itself
author: Shlok Shelat; Shrey Vimalbhai Salvi; Manas Gaur; Souvik Roy
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision has become a default assumption in fine-tuning large language models for reasoning tasks, with the intuition being that exposing models to intermediate reasoning steps leads to deeper learning than training on answers alone. We challenge this assumption. We introduce answer backtrackability, a measurable quantity capturing the degree to which a question can be reconstructed from its answer, and argue it is a key determinant of whether CoT supervision helps or hurts during fine-tuning. To test this, we construct two novel benchmarks derived from automata theory (NFA and DFA), where answers are transition tables from which the question is largely recoverable, and fine-tune three LLMs using LoRA on CoT and No-CoT versions of five datasets: GSM8K, MathInstruct, MATH, and our two formal-language benchmarks. On mathematical datasets, CoT consistently outperforms No-CoT. Within MathInstruct, Program-of-Thought (PoT) problems, where executable code answers are high-backtrackability, favour No-CoT, while CoT-format problems favour CoT. On our benchmarks, the pattern reverses: No-CoT outperforms CoT across all models and difficulty tiers. When the answer encodes sufficient structure to reconstruct the reasoning process, intermediate supervision adds noise rather than signal.

title: M-GOAL: Toward Accurate and Language-Consistent Reasoning in LLMs via English-Only Post-Training
author: Dingyuan Dai; Yuxi Chen; Jiayuan Wang
abstract: Reasoning-oriented language models inherit strong English-centric biases from pre-training, which are further reinforced by English-only post-training. This creates a dual failure mode where models fail both to reason correctly and to maintain reasoning traces in the query language. We study reasoning accuracy and language consistency under English-only post-training. SFT primarily improves language consistency with limited or inconsistent accuracy gains, while group relative policy optimization (GRPO) substantially improves accuracy at the cost of language consistency. Although translated multilingual GRPO improves both objectives, it requires translating reasoning post-training data into multiple languages and may introduce translation noise and information loss. We find that the language-consistency capability acquired by SFT and the accuracy capability acquired by GRPO are approximately orthogonal in the model’s update space. By merging an English LoRA-SFT adapter with an English GRPO checkpoint trained from the same base model, M-GOAL improves MGSM accuracy from 39.1 to 57.8 and language consistency from 17.1 to 75.2 without translated reasoning supervision. This composition outperforms sequential training, its merge coefficient exposes a tunable operating point along the accuracy–consistency frontier, and the pattern holds beyond mathematical reasoning and on benchmarks whose non-English problems are natively authored rather than translated. Our results suggest that multilingual reasoning post-training does not necessarily require multilingual post-training data.

title: HiDiffTIR: Hierarchical Difficulty-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning
author: Yucan Guo; Xiaohan Wang; Miao Su; Saiping Guan; Zhongni Hou; Jiajun Chai; Wei Lin; Guojun Yin; Xiaolong Jin; Jiafeng Guo; Xueqi Cheng
abstract: Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) is a fundamental capability for LLM agents to solve complex tasks by interacting with external tools iteratively. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become the dominant paradigm for enabling this capability. However, existing approaches typically assign uniform trajectory-level advantages and treat all correct tool calls equally, ignoring the varying difficulty and learning value across trajectories and reasoning steps. This can lead to imprecise learning signals that do not adequately distinguish between trivial and challenging tool-use patterns. To address this limitation, we propose HiDiffTIR, a Hierarchical Difficulty-aware policy optimization framework for multi-turn TIR. HiDiffTIR performs difficulty-aware credit assignment at both trajectory and turn levels, enabling the policy to focus on more informative trajectories and harder reasoning steps. Notably, this fine-grained optimization is achieved without additional supervision, relying solely on group-level statistics derived from standard RL rollouts. Extensive experiments on three tool-using benchmarks demonstrate that HiDiffTIR consistently improves multi-turn TIR performance and tool invocation accuracy over strong RL baselines, highlighting the necessity of difficulty-aware credit assignment for effective policy optimization in tool-integrated LLM agents.

title: SVR-MAD: A Bayesian-Inspired Framework for Posterior-Guided Multi-Agent Debate
author: Weifan Jiang; Rana Shahout; Minghao Li; Zhenting Qi; Yilun Du; Michael Mitzenmacher; Minlan Yu
abstract: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves LLM-agent accuracy but suffers from rapid context growth, limiting scalability in larger multi-agent settings. Existing methods prune low-utility communications using prior signals, such as token-level log-likelihoods or LLM self-reported confidence. However, these signals become unreliable under hallucination, degrading the accuracy of MAD methods that rely on them. We propose SVR-MAD, a Bayesian-inspired MAD framework that treats pre-debate signals as priors and debate outcomes as posterior-style evidence for estimating agent correctness. SVR-MAD uses this evidence to incrementally construct the communication graph, prioritizing agents whose answers survive peer challenges. Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks show that SVR-MAD reduces token cost by up to 61% while matching or improving accuracy relative to the most accurate competing MAD baseline.

title: CAGE: Concept Algebra for Guardrail Evasion and Jailbreak Attacks via Lexical-Semantic Decoupling
author: Zekai He; Yuxiang Chen; Jun Shao; Xiao Song; Haibo Hong
abstract: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) depend heavily on surface-level lexical filters for safety alignment, exposing a critical lexical-semantic gap: harmful intent can be fully decoupled from explicit wording. Motivated by this vulnerability, we propose CAGE (Concept Algebra for Guardrail Evasion), a single-turn black-box jailbreak leveraging the victim’s reasoning to reconstruct masked harmful intent. Through slot masking and concept equations, CAGE eliminates explicit triggers while guiding the target model to internally deduce the payload. Because standard evaluations conflate generic harmfulness with precise intent execution, we introduce the Strict Attack Success Rate (sASR), a metric that mandates verbatim slot recovery to measure reconstructive controllability beyond mere compliance. Across seven frontier models and three benchmarks, CAGE achieves an average ASR of 93.7% and sASR of 85.1%. Defense stress tests and keyword-recovery analysis reveal that existing token-level guardrails remain largely ineffective against reasoning-driven semantic evasion, suggesting that robust alignment must go beyond surface token filtering to address threats at the reasoning level. WARNING: THIS PAPER CONTAINS UNSAFE CONTENTS.

title: CArtBench: A Museum-Grounded Benchmark for Evidence-Faithful Chinese Art Understanding
author: Xuefeng Wei; Wang Zhixuan; Xuan Zhou; Zhi Qu; Hongyao Li; Yusuke Sakai; Hidetaka Kamigaito; Taro Watanabe
abstract: We introduce CARTBENCH, a museum-grounded benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on Chinese artworks beyond short-form recognition and QA. CARTBENCH comprises four subtasks: CURATORQA for evidence-grounded recognition and reasoning, CATALOGCAPTION for structured four-section expert-style appreciation, REINTERPRET for defensible reinterpretation with expert ratings, and CONNOISSEURPAIRS for original-copy discrimination under visually similar confounds. CARTBENCH is built by aligning image-bearing Palace Museum objects from Wikidata with authoritative catalog pages, spanning five art categories across multiple dynasties. Across evaluated VLMs, high overall CURATORQA accuracy can mask sharp drops on evidence-heavy and style-to-period questions; long-form appreciation remains far from expert references; and original-copy discrimination remains near chance. A held-out protocol-replication pilot on 120 artworks from five external institutions reproduces the main task-difficulty pattern, while not preserving the exact overall model ranking.

title: Back on Track: Aligning Rewards and States for Reasoning in Diffusion Large Language Models
author: Yawen Shao; Jie Xiao; Kai Zhu; Yu Liu; Hongchen Luo; Xueyang Fu; Yang Cao; Wei Zhai; Zheng-Jun Zha
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds immense promise for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of diffusion large language models (dLLMs). However, progress is fundamentally constrained by a dual misalignment between authentic generation trajectory and the gradient update process: (i) Process-reward misalignment. Sparse, terminal rewards are indiscriminately assigned to all intermediate steps of the generation process, failing to provide discriminative credit assignment. (ii) State-trajectory misalignment. Policy updates are often diverted toward artificial, out-of-trajectory states, squandering gradients on less informative samples. To address these limitations, we introduce Process Aligned Policy Optimization (PAPO), a novel framework that holistically aligns the RL update with the dLLM’s generative trajectory via Step-Aware Process Rewards (SPR) that transform sparse terminal rewards into dense, step-wise credit, and Entropy-Guided Historical Re-enactment (EHR) that replays authentic trajectories at high-uncertainty steps. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that PAPO significantly outperforms baselines, achieving gains of 4.5% on GSM8K, 4.8% on MATH500, 42.2% on Countdown and 16.1% on Sudoku.

title: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis
author: Cheonbok Park; Jihwan Kim; Shinyoung Joo; Joosung Lee; Hwiyeol Jo; Jeonghoon Kim; Jaegul Choo
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. Using fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice QA (FIM-MCQA) as a seed task format, we synthesize automatically verifiable tasks from domain passages and reshape them into cross-lingual variants. These variants preserve the same evidence-answer relation but change how English and target-language evidence are presented during RLVR. On Korean medical benchmarks and cybersecurity benchmarks across four target languages, code-switched training outperforms matched monolingual and bilingual-mixture baselines on average target-language performance while maintaining comparable English performance. Additional analyses provide evidence of better target-language input understanding and stronger cross-lingual alignment in both model outputs and internal representations. These results suggest that code-switched training helps target-language inputs access domain reasoning learned more strongly in English.

title: EviDx: Evidence-Aware Active Diagnosis with Scaffolded LLM Agents
author: Lihang Zeng; Shaoting Zhang; Xiaofan Zhang
abstract: Clinical diagnosis is an active evidence-seeking process in which clinicians acquire evidence, update competing hypotheses, and decide when the available evidence is sufficient for diagnosis. Yet many medical diagnosis systems built around large language models (LLMs) still formulate diagnosis as static case-to-answer prediction, with limited support for evidence acquisition. Agentic LLMs offer a dynamic alternative through tool use and intermediate diagnostic trajectories, but existing systems often under-specify how patient evidence should be exposed, scaffolded, and controlled at runtime. We introduce EviDx, an evidence-aware active diagnosis framework that pairs patient-specific diagnostic environments with a clinical diagnostic scaffold and an observer-guided runtime harness. In EviDx, \mathcal{E}-Synthesis constructs interactive environments from raw clinical cases; the scaffold organizes role-specialized agents, evidence tools, and evolving evidence states; and the harness regulates diagnostic termination by tracking uncertainty and evidence coverage. A 3-level evaluation pyramid assesses execution robustness, reasoning dynamics, and diagnostic outcomes. Experiments show that EviDx improves diagnostic performance and process stability while revealing model-dependent capability boundaries.

title: A Unified Framework to Elicit Structured Feedback for Interpretable Multi-Trait Essay Scoring
author: Shihang Yang; Sanwoo Lee; Ningning Zhao; Yunfang Wu
abstract: Multi-trait Automated Essay Scoring (AES) requires rubric-grounded reasoning across interdependent traits, rather than isolated score prediction. Existing feedback-enhanced methods often decouple feedback from scoring or assess traits independently, weakening score–feedback consistency and rubric alignment. We propose HiFTS, a unified autoregressive framework that generates hierarchical CoT feedback before predicting trait-level and holistic scores. HiFTS distills rubric-grounded hierarchical CoT feedback from a teacher LLM and trains student models to jointly generate feedback and scores. HiFTS further applies Group Relative Policy Optimization with a composite reward balancing score agreement, calibration, feedback quality, and structural validity. At inference, a lightweight global prior provides holistic guidance to reduce drift during long-form reasoning. We also introduce CFMS-34, a Chinese multi-trait AES dataset with 951 essays annotated with holistic scores and 34 rubric-based traits. Experiments on CFMS-34 and ASAP++ show that HiFTS achieves strong holistic and trait-level scoring while producing coherent, rubric-aligned feedback.

title: Are Large Language Models Suitable for Graph Computation? Progress and Prospects
author: Yuting Zhang; Yi Han; Kai Wang; Wei Ni; Angela Bonifati; Wenjie Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly explored for graph computation, where tasks require reasoning over structured relationships and algorithmic operations. Yet, it remains unclear when LLMs can reliably support such computation and how they should be incorporated into graph-solving pipelines. Existing surveys at the intersection of LLMs and graphs primarily focus on graph learning, text-attributed graphs, or graph-language modeling. To bridge this gap, we provide a comprehensive review of LLMs for graph computation through a role-based taxonomy. Specifically, we identify two major paradigms: i) LLMs as executors, where models directly solve graph tasks from graph descriptions and instructions; and ii) LLMs as planners, where models formulate problems, decompose reasoning steps, and invoke external tools or agents for execution. Based on this taxonomy, we analyze the strengths and limitations of current methods. Our review indicates that LLMs are promising for simple, small-scale tasks, but remain unreliable for large-scale and exactness-demanding tasks. Finally, we summarize available datasets and suggest four future directions.

title: UrduMMLU: A Massive Multitask Benchmark for Urdu Language Understanding
author: Ahmer Tabassum; Sarfraz Ahmad; Hasan Iqbal; Owais Aijaz; Momina Ahsan; Preslav Nakov
abstract: Meaningful multilingual evaluation must test models in the target language and educational context. Urdu, spoken by more than 230 million people, lacks a broad MMLU-style benchmark built from native educational sources. We introduce UrduMMLU, a benchmark of 26,389 Urdu MCQs across 26 subjects and five domains, collected from native Urdu MCQ banks and public examination PDFs. Unlike translation-based benchmarks, UrduMMLU combines academic subjects with content specific to Urdu and regional education. We label the exam-derived portion through dual human annotation with strict consensus filtering. We evaluate 30 LLMs under English and Urdu prompts, yielding 60 zero-shot evaluations, and further evaluate four open-source LLMs under multiple few-shot settings across both prompt languages. Gemini-3.5-Flash performs best, reaching 90.23% and 90.45% accuracy, while no other model exceeds 85%. The strongest open-source model trails by 7.78 and 9.12 points, and many models lose 25 to 40 points on Urdu-centered Humanities subjects compared with STEM. Few-shot prompting yields only modest gains. Results on UrduMMLU show that current LLMs have uneven Urdu knowledge, particularly for content grounded in the regional context.

title: AgentCVR: Active Multi-Agent Cross-Video Reasoning via Script-Simulated Reinforcement Learning
author: Yilun Qiu; Jiahe Wang; Cilin Yan; Jiayin Cai; Xiaolong Jiang; Yao Hu; Chun Yuan
abstract: Cross-Video Reasoning (CVR) has emerged as a critical frontier in multimodal intelligence, requiring models to retrieve, align, and aggregate evidence distributed across multiple videos. Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often struggle with CVR, as simple single-pass strategies encode multiple videos into a shared compressed context, potentially obscuring rare but critical evidence. In this paper, we propose AgentCVR, a multi-agent framework that treats CVR as an active evidence-acquisition task. AgentCVR employs a Master Agent to iteratively coordinate specialized Visual and Audio Agents for targeted evidence extraction. To ensure efficient training, we introduce Script-Simulated RL, which optimizes the agent’s policy with LLM-generated semantic scripts and a lightweight text-based simulator, bypassing costly multimodal inference during online exploration.
