Experiments on our held-out predicted-state matching benchmark show that our approach outperforms world models trained with supervised next-state prediction. We further show that our approach improves PRM-style action ranking on WebPRMBench compared with action-only PRMs and PRMs augmented with supervised-next-state world models. Finally, on WebArena-Lite, using our world model for test-time action selection improves end-to-end task success. Our project page is available at: https://dhruvpendharkar.github.io/dwm/.

title: Beyond Transfer Accuracy: Mechanism-Guided Controlled Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages
author: Khumaisa Nur’aini; Ayu Purwarianti; Alham Fikri Aji; Derry Tanti Wijaya
abstract: Existing circuit discovery methods rely on templated tasks with clean counterfactuals, limiting their use on diverse natural text. We adapt Contextual Decomposition for Transformers (CD-T) for unstructured settings via label-balanced activation means and task-directional relevance scoring, enabling counterfactual-free circuit discovery. We leverage the discovered circuits for Circuit-Targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (CT-SFT), restricting parameter updates to task-relevant heads and LayerNorm. Experiments on NusaX cross-lingual sentiment transfer show that CT-SFT is highly competitive for low-resource adaptation. While non-circuit sparse updates and full fine-tuning sometimes match target accuracy through capacity recruitment, CT-SFT most consistently avoids catastrophic forgetting, preserving source-language and related-task performance. Extensions to XNLI support the source-retention and intervention findings on a harder task and two model families, showing that circuit-targeted adaptation provides a more controlled, intervention-supported alternative to global fine-tuning.

title: Why Do LLM Agents Fail in Exploring New Environments? A World-Modeling Perspective
author: Shiqi Chen; Tongyao Zhu; Zian Wang; Jinghan Zhang; Kangrui Wang; Ruochen Zhou; Siyang Gao; Teng Xiao; Yee Whye Teh; Junxian He; Manling Li
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) as agents often fail to improve in new environments. We identify and characterize a failure mode we call exploration collapse: under reinforcement learning (RL) in environments whose states are unfamiliar to the policy, Pass@k, the probability that at least one of k sampled trajectories succeeds, drops markedly over training even as Pass@1 edges up, revealing increasingly brittle exploration; environments closer to the pretraining distribution show no such decline. We trace this collapse to weak grounding in environment states and dynamics, and study a simple remedy: explicitly teaching the agent to estimate the current state and predict its transitions before optimizing for reward. We instantiate it as SPA, an explore-then-exploit recipe that cold-starts the policy with a Self-Experience supervised finetuning (SFT) stage, collecting the model’s own interaction trajectories and supervising state and next-state prediction, and then runs standard RL. The resulting world model serves as a grounded initialization for RL rather than an inference-time planner. Across unseen environments, SPA consistently and substantially improves over vanilla RL: for example, it raises the Sokoban success rate from 25.6% to 59.8% on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, letting sub-3B models surpass a 20B baseline on these tasks. Controlled studies indicate that the gains track four factors: grounded state representations, explicit transition modeling, self-experience trajectories from a sufficiently strong exploration policy, and adequate coverage of transition data.

title: Over-Refusal and Representation Subspaces: A Mechanistic Analysis of Task-Conditioned Refusal in Aligned LLMs
author: Utsav Maskey; Mark Dras; Usman Naseem
abstract: Aligned language models that are trained to refuse harmful requests also exhibit over-refusal: they decline safe instructions that seemingly resemble harmful instructions. A natural approach is to ablate the global refusal direction, steering the hidden-state vectors away or towards the harmful-refusal examples, but this corrects over-refusal only incidentally while disrupting the broader refusal mechanism. In this work, we analyse the representational geometry of both refusal types to understand why this happens. We show that harmful-refusal directions are task-agnostic and can be captured by a single global vector, whereas over-refusal directions are task-dependent: they reside within the benign task-representation clusters, vary across tasks, and span a higher-dimensional subspace. Linear probing suggests that the two refusal types are representationally distinct from the early transformer layers. These findings provide a mechanistic explanation of why global direction ablation alone cannot address over-refusal, and establish that task-specific geometric interventions are necessary.

title: Rethinking the Role of Tensor Decompositions in Post-Training LLM Compression
author: Artur Zagitov; Alexander Miasnikov; Maxim Krutikov; Artem Tsedenov; Vladimir Aletov; Gleb Molodtsov; Nail Bashirov; Aleksandr Beznosikov
abstract: Post-training compression is essential for deploying large language models (LLMs) under tight resource constraints. Tensor decompositions have emerged as a promising direction, offering compact parameterizations well suited to Transformer weight structures. However, existing studies evaluate these methods in narrow settings, leaving unclear whether tensorization is effective at large-scale deployment. We systematically evaluate tensor compression across dense and MoE architectures, establishing performance trade-offs grounded in both empirical analysis and theoretical analysis. % We identify a fundamental mismatch between the shared subspaces assumed by tensor decompositions and the heterogeneous representations learned by modern LLMs, thereby delineating their practical limits and clarifying their viable role in large-scale deployment. We identify a fundamental mismatch between the shared subspaces assumed by tensor decompositions and the heterogeneous representations learned by modern LLMs, thereby delineating their practical limits that persist across an extensive range of mainstream dense and MoE deployment settings evaluated in this work. The code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/TT-LLM.

title: BID-SPO: Rethinking Multi-Agent Prompt Optimization as Information Contracting via Bidding-based Shapley Values
author: Weiqiang Jin; Yuxin Cheng; Tingting Sun; Shixiang Tang; Jing Gao; Jinhu Qi; Wentao Zhang; Junli Wang; Biao Zhao; Guoshuai Zhao; Guang Yang
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems decompose complex tasks across specialist agents, yet joint prompt optimization remains difficult because agents are coupled through structured information handoffs. We identify interface mismatch as a structural failure mode that existing optimizers cannot diagnose: their scalar attribution signals conflate reasoning quality with format incompatibility, and the inter-agent contract is left entirely implicit. We propose BID-SPO (Bidding-based Shapley Prompt Optimization), which makes the inter-agent contract an explicit optimization variable. Each agent declares an Output Bid and an Input Demand, and a contract-aware cooperative-game characteristic function yields an attribution signal whose Shapley decomposition exposes three interpretable dimensions (global task contribution, downstream interface alignment, and upstream adaptation cost), turning attribution into a targeted diagnosis for prompt repair. A bid-conformance constraint keeps declared contracts feasible with respect to actual agent behavior throughout optimization. Across seven benchmarks and different model configurations, BID-SPO outperforms MASPO and AgentDropout, with accuracy gains of +2.93% under the Qwen3-8B + Gemini-2.5-pro configuration and +4.38% under the DeepSeek-v4 flash / pro configuration. Our findings emphasize that reliable multi-agent LLM optimization requires optimizing inter-agent interfaces as explicit objects, not just improving agents in isolation.

title: DeARAG: Decoupled Agentic RAG for On-Device and Precise Multi-Hop Question Answering
author: Qiuchang Shi; Tianqi Liu; Feng Zhang; Peng Chen; Jianjun Liu; Gaoyun An
abstract: Although cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced complex multi-hop question answering, they pose severe data privacy risks. On the other hand, simply migrating such compute-intensive systems to edge devices with limited computational resources inevitably triggers context overload and the “lost-in-the-middle” phenomenon. To resolve the privacy-accuracy dilemma, we introduce DeARAG, a fully decoupled, local agentic framework. By shifting heavy hypergraph construction entirely offline, DeARAG substantially condenses the required context during inference. Consequently, the agent’s exploration is strictly grounded in the retrieved hypergraph topology, ensuring rigorous, evidence-based reasoning without overwhelming local resources. Evaluated on multiple datasets, our framework consistently outperforms massive, cloud-dependent baselines (e.g., achieving a gain of 6.47 F1 points on HotpotQA) using only consumer-grade GPUs, enabling highly precise on-device reasoning.

title: Teacher-Guided Policy Optimization for On-Policy Reasoning Distillation under Large Policy Divergence
author: Xinyu Liu; Kechen Jiao; Chunyang Xiao; Runsong Zhao; Junhao Ruan; Bei Li; Jiahao Liu; Qifan Wang; Xin Chen; Jingang Wang; Chenglong Wang; Tong Xiao; JingBo Zhu
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for reasoning-oriented post-training of large language models (LLMs), especially when combined with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). Existing OPD methods rely on reverse KL (RKL)-based teacher supervision over trajectories sampled from the student policy. However, we identify a critical limitation: under large teacher–student policy divergence, RL-driven exploration often produces trajectories that the teacher assigns low probability, resulting in uninformative negative feedback. To address this, we propose Teacher-Guided Policy Optimization (TGPO). Unlike existing OPD methods that evaluate student-sampled actions using the teacher, TGPO directly guides next-token generation using the teacher’s predicted distribution on student-generated contexts, yielding an on-policy forward-KL objective. Combined with RLVR, this guidance steers exploration toward improved continuations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that TGPO outperforms existing RKL-based OPD methods and remains robust across different teacher models. Furthermore, we find that teacher top-1 predictions suffice for effective guidance, without requiring the full teacher distribution.

title: DRNash: Efficient and Robust Multi-Task Learning for Financial Sentiment Analysis
author: Hongcheng Ding; Xuanhuang Liu; Deshinta Arrova Dewi; Shamsul Nahar Abdullah; Qingyu Liu; Xuanze Zhao
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for sentiment polarity regression often suffers from severe data distribution imbalance. Financial texts typically concentrate in the neutral range, leaving extreme sentiments underrepresented, yet traditional techniques offer limited remedy since such extremes are inherently rare. We introduce an auxiliary classification task to provide complementary supervision, but this multi-task formulation faces two challenges: (1) sentiment group construction for the classification task, and (2) gradient conflicts between tasks that fixed weights cannot resolve. These challenges are coupled: improper group boundaries yield biased gradients, which amplify task conflicts. We propose the DRNash framework as a unified solution to jointly address both challenges and the underlying data distribution imbalance, including Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) and Nash Task Coordinator (NTC). DRO partitions the sentiment space into quantile-based groups and performs worst-case aggregation over group losses, automatically assigning higher weights to underperforming sentiment regions. NTC formulates task weighting as a Nash bargaining game, deriving closed-form weights that achieve scale-invariant balancing. Experiments demonstrate that DRNash achieves average improvements of 14.1% in MSE and 1.92% in accuracy (ACC) across multiple financial datasets, with cross-domain experiments confirming generalizability beyond financial texts.

title: MedReaMM: Evaluating Large Multimodal Models on Expert-Level Clinical Diagnostic Synthesis
author: Lai Wei; Yuchao Chen; Zhenbiao Cao; Xiaojin Zhang; Zhongyu Wei; Bangting Wang; Wei Chen; Xiang Bai
abstract: The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to diagnostic decision-making has garnered growing interest. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on textual reasoning or isolated visual question-answering (VQA) tasks, lacking holistic integration of clinical narratives and medical imaging, and thus failing to assess the multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability central to expert clinical judgment. To bridge this gap, we introduce **MedReaMM**, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate models’ ability to synthesize heterogeneous clinical evidence consisting of detailed patient histories alongside multiple medical images into accurate differential diagnoses under a complete-information paradigm. Constructed from case reports sourced from top-tier medical journals and curated clinical case databases, MedReaMM comprises 625 expert-validated cases with an average of 2.79 medical images per case and a total of 1,042 standardized diagnoses annotated with ICD-11 codes. These cases predominantly represent rare, atypical, or multi-system presentations that demand expert-level evidence integration beyond routine pattern recognition. We evaluate 23 Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) and find that most achieve diagnostic accuracy scores below 50%, underscoring a substantial gap in multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability. Further analysis reveals that medical knowledge proficiency, medical image understanding, and evidence integration are all highly correlated with diagnostic performance.

title: RULER: Instance-aware Rubric Rewards for SVG Generation
author: Hangyu Ran; Yuhao Zheng; Yingying Zhang; Kevin Qinghong Lin; Han Peng
abstract: Generating Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) code from natural-language instructions is an open-ended task without absolute visual ground truth, leaving both evaluation and policy optimization without a faithful signal. Scalar metrics (CLIP, Aesthetic) calibrated on natural images transfer poorly to stylized vector content, and reusing them as RL rewards triggers reward hacking. We address both limitations with rubric-based scoring. We first establish empirically that prompting a vision–language judge with a multi-axis rubric correlates with human judgments far better than scalar metrics, both across samples and within instructions. Building on this finding, we introduce **RULER** (Instance-aware **Ru**bric Rewards for Reinforcement **Le**a**r**ning), which converts each instruction into an instance-aware rubric of six items spanning semantic, visual, and stylistic axes; a judge VLM scores rendered rollouts item-by-item, and the weighted satisfactions form a fine-grained reward optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization. Because the rubric is derived from text alone, RULER requires neither paired SVG ground truth nor human preference labels. On MMSVG-Illustration and MMSVG-Icon, RULER lifts the rubric score from 0.432/0.395 to 0.693/0.683, surpassing dedicated SVG specialists and matching the substantially larger DeepSeek-V3, with ablations identifying rubric design as the active lever for RL on open-ended SVG generation.

title: Difficulty-Adaptive Tree-Structured Policy Optimization for Expanding Reasoning Coverage in RLVR
author: Youngjun Yu; Sanghwan Jang; Hwanjo Yu
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been central to the recent success of Large Reasoning Models. However, while RLVR significantly improves single-sample accuracy, it often fails to expand the model’s intrinsic reasoning coverage (pass@k) due to limited exploration during training. To address this, we optimize the structural design of train-time rollouts to enhance pass@k. Our analysis identifies three key design principles: (1) difficulty-adaptive rollout can play an important role in expanding pass@k, beyond serving as an efficiency heuristic; (2) tree-based rollout outperforms parallel sampling in discovering correct answers; and (3) sentence-entropy-guided forking overcomes the localization phenomenon of token-level branching to maximize semantic diversity. Building on these insights, we propose DATPO (Difficulty-Adaptive Sentence-entropy-guided Tree-structured Policy Optimization). DATPO integrates difficulty-adaptive tree search with a sibling-diversity advantage term, explicitly promoting semantic diversity to expand reasoning coverage during training. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DATPO outperforms baselines especially in pass@k, which directly translates to superior test-time scaling performance.

title: Evaluating Inquiry Learning in LLM-Based Agents: Hypothesizing, Reasoning, and Exploration
author: Marta Knežević; Seyed Parsa Neshaei; Jibril Frej; Vinitra Swamy; Tanja Käser
abstract: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs’ inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.

title: Atomicity for Agents: Exposing, Exploiting, and Mitigating TOCTOU Vulnerabilities in Browser-Use Agents
author: Linxi Jiang; Zhijie Liu; Haotian Luo; Zhiqiang Lin
abstract: Browser-use agents automate everyday web tasks through structured DOM interfaces or vision-language models operating on page screenshots. However, web pages can change between observation and action execution due to advertisements, asynchronous loading, and timed updates, causing agents to act on stale assumptions. We frame this temporal mismatch as a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability in browser-use agents, where page changes during planning can alter the target, value, or validity of a planned action before execution. We introduce DYNWEB, a benchmark spanning synthesized and real-world websites, and evaluate 10 open-source agents as well as Codex’s computer-use feature across different observation and action modalities. All 11 evaluated systems exhibit at least one TOCTOU violation, showing that the vulnerability is not limited to a particular agent design. To reduce this exposure, we design a lightweight pre-execution validation mechanism that reduces the exploitable window from approximately 10 s to 0.13 s. Across three agent frameworks, the mechanism reduces the number of vulnerable DYNWEB cases to 0 out of 14. Adaptive attacks further show that stealthy single-mutation attacks succeed in at most 2.2% of trials, while event-driven timing reveals the limits of pre-execution validation.

title: Hallucination-Aware Multi-Agent RAG via Internal Attention Rewards
author: Runsong Jia; Qian Chang; Mengjia Wu; Ciprian Doru Giurcaneanu; Jie Lu; Yi Zhang
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds language models in retrieved evidence, but its outputs often contain claims unsupported by that evidence. Recent multi-agent RAG systems decompose the pipeline into cooperative decisions, yet they typically optimize all agents under a shared task reward such as EM or F1, which measures answer overlap rather than faithfulness to evidence. We propose a hallucination-aware multi-agent RAG framework that combines the task reward with an internal hallucination-risk signal computed from the generator’s attention-head norms. Three role-specific LoRA adapters, a query planner, an evidence selector, and an answer generator, share a frozen backbone. A lightweight critic is trained once on TruthfulQA truthful/false pairs and then kept frozen, providing a complementary risk score that is added to the shared reward during cooperative PPO training. Across three backbones (Qwen3-8B, Llama3-8B, Llama2-13B) and three benchmarks (RAGTruth, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), our method improves task performance and reduces hallucination rates over the strongest multi-agent baseline. Ablations and critic diagnostics show that the TruthfulQA-calibrated signal provides useful reward shaping that transfers across RAG tasks.

title: CoreMem: Riemannian Retrieval and Fisher-Guided Distillation for Long-Term Memory in Dialogue Agents
author: Jiaqi Chen; Yongqin Zeng; Shaoxiong Zhan; Shaoshen Chen; Yijian Zhang; Chunxia Ma; XiuTeng Zhou; Hai-Tao Zheng
abstract: Personalized dialogue agents require continuous long-term memory to maintain coherent interactions across multiple sessions. However, deploying these capabilities on consumer-grade hardware (e.g., 8 GB VRAM edge devices) introduces severe memory and compute bottlenecks. Existing systems typically rely on isotropic cosine similarity for retrieval and heuristic rules for context compression. These approaches lack a unified theoretical foundation, frequently suffering from the hubness problem in high-dimensional retrieval and syntactic fragmentation during compression. To overcome these limitations, we propose CoreMem, a resource-efficient edge-cloud memory architecture fundamentally unified by information geometry. First, Riemannian retrieval replaces cosine matching with a locally adaptive Fisher-Rao metric, effectively penalizing hub memories via Mahalanobis distance with O(Ndr) Woodbury acceleration for real-time search. Second, Fisher-guided discrete token distillation (FDTD) introduces a hierarchical sentence-to-token compression mechanism. It derives sensitivity scores from Fisher information traces, providing a principled compression-KL tradeoff augmented with explicit structural syntax protection. Evaluated on the LOCOMO and LongMemEval-S benchmarks, CoreMem achieves strong accuracy improvements, yielding substantial gains in Open-domain (+4.51 pp) and Temporal (+4.17 pp) reasoning. Extensive profiling confirms that the lightweight MiniLM-L6 configuration of CoreMem operates within a strict 8 GB VRAM budget, successfully bridging the gap between resource-constrained edge devices and the demand for theoretically grounded, lifelong memory agents.

title: Diagnose, Then Refine: A Closed-Loop TTS System with AudioLLM-guided Correction
author: Zeyang Song; Tianchi Liu; Tianrui Wang; Chenglin Xu; Steven Y. Guo; Haizhou Li
abstract: Current TTS systems typically rely on open-loop, single-pass generation and can produce sporadic local prosodic defects, such as misplaced stress, unnatural pauses, or flattened intonation, that utterance-level metrics often fail to expose. We present LoopTTS, a judge-guided Filter-Judge-Refiner framework for recovering low-quality TTS outputs diagnosed by an AudioLLM. Given an initial utterance from a base TTS model, an AudioLLM Judge identifies salient prosodic issues and generates structured refine instructions; a Refiner, our fine-grained instruction-following TTS model, then performs guided expressive re-synthesis conditioned on the initial utterance, target text, and instruction. To train the Refiner, we construct Refiner-DB, a 42K-example AudioLLM-annotated dataset with word-level prosodic weak supervision. Human evaluation on diagnosed low-quality utterances shows that LoopTTS can detect perceptually salient errors and correct them with the Refiner, outperforming raw generated audio and practical open-loop re-generation baselines in recovery quality. The Refiner also demonstrates stronger instruction-following ability for stress and pause control in targeted prosody modification. LoopTTS is available at https://github.com/Pooookeman/LoopTTS.

title: WebCompass: Evaluating Multimodal Code Agents in Web Development from Vision, Instruction, and Interaction to Implementation
author: Xinping Lei; Xinyu Che; Junqi Xiong; Chenchen Zhang; Yukai Huang; Chenyu Zhou; Haoyang Huang; Minghao Liu; Letian Zhu; Hongyi Ye; Ken Deng; Zizheng Zhan; Han Li; Yifan Yao; Ming Sun; Zhaoxiang Zhang; Jiaheng Liu
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as interactive coding agents for end-to-end web development, yet existing benchmarks evaluate narrow slices of this workflow—typically text-conditioned generation with static correctness metrics—overlooking visual fidelity, interactivity, and codebase-level reasoning. We introduce WebCompass, a benchmark that covers the full web development lifecycle by spanning three input modalities (text, image, video) and three task types (generation, editing, repair). To match the diverse nature of these tasks, we pair checklist-guided LLM-as-a-Judge for patch-based evaluation with a novel Agent-as-a-Judge protocol that executes generated websites in a real browser and synthesizes targeted test cases. Experiments on ten models reveal a 25-point gap between the best closed- and open-source models, persistent weaknesses in visual aesthetics even among frontier systems, and divergent performance profiles across task types that challenge the notion of a single "best" web coding agent.

title: G-STAR: End-to-End Global Speaker-Tracking Attributed Recognition
author: Jing Peng; Ziyi Chen; Haoyu Li; Yucheng Wang; Mengtian Li; Duo MA; Yu Xi; Yunfan Du; Kai Yu; Shuai Wang
abstract: We study timestamped speaker-attributed automatic speech recognition (SA-ASR) for long-form, multi-party speech with overlap. In this setting, chunk-wise inference must preserve meeting-level speaker identity consistency while producing time-stamped, speaker-labeled transcripts. Prior Speech-LLM systems tend to prioritize either local diarization or global labeling, lacking the ability to jointly model fine-grained temporal boundaries and robust cross-chunk identity linking. We propose G-STAR, an end-to-end framework that couples a cache-conditioned speaker-tracking module with a Speech-LLM transcription backbone. The tracker provides structured speaker cues with temporal grounding, and the LLM generates attributed text conditioned on these cues. G-STAR supports component-wise optimization and joint end-to-end training, enabling flexible learning under heterogeneous supervision and domain shift. Under chunk-wise decoding protocols, experiments on both oracle-segmented local evaluation and full-meeting global evaluation show strong speaker-attributed transcription performance.

title: ExecRubrics: Executable Tool-Augmented Rubrics for Verifiable, Efficient and Explainable Evaluation
author: Kaustubh Dhole; Charles L. A. Clarke; Eugene Agichtein
abstract: Rubrics aim to make language-model evaluation transparent by decomposing response quality into interpretable criteria. However, natural-language rubrics are often ambiguous, require LLM judges, and typically assume criteria aggregated through linear weighted sums, limiting their ability to capture dependencies, alternatives, penalties, and override conditions. We propose ExecRubrics, a framework for representing rubrics as compact executable programs. ExecRubrics encodes evaluation logic as verifiable Python scoring functions, giving natural-language rubric intent an operational semantics: a fixed decision procedure that can be inspected, executed, and edited. On three long-form response benchmarks – HealthBench, HelpSteer, and ArgQuality – we show that ExecRubrics can recover substantial preference signal without an LLM judge at evaluation time. On ArgQuality and HelpSteer, the strongest executable variants are within 1.1 and 4 percentage points, respectively, of the direct GPT-5.5 agentic baseline. Executable rubrics are also considerably faster, achieving a 192× average speedup. We show that incorporating external logic and resources from text processing libraries such as NLTK and spaCy can further improve preference accuracy. Our results suggest a novel way of approaching automated evaluation, by offering a faster, more explainable, and less ambiguous alternative to black-box rubric evals, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and banking where precision and auditability are critical.

title: ACTOR: Agentic CT Reasoning with Radiologist-Aligned Actions
author: Xingyu Qian; Yu Sun; Songyou Li; Zongzhao Li; Jiacheng Cen; Wenqian Wu; Tingyang Xu; Yu Rong; Deli Zhao; Wenbing Huang
abstract: Radiologists read CT as a sequential decision process, actively scrolling, zooming, adjusting windows, comparing with prior scans, and measuring structures, where each observation guides the next action. Current VLMs instead answer from passively sampled views, missing the multi-step reasoning that clinical reading demands. We address this by aligning the agent’s action space to the radiologists’ operations within the Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS), enabling active, multi-step CT reading with inherently transparent reasoning for clinical decision support. In particular, we build **ACTOR**, a unified framework comprising: (1) a PACS-like interactive CT environment with five radiologist-aligned tools; (2) **ActiveCTR-Bench**, spanning 7 tasks across a Perception–Interpretation–Reasoning hierarchy (7,112 items with visual ground truth and verified vision necessity); and (3) **ActiveCTReasoner**, a 7B model trained on 108K synthesized trajectories via SFT and reinforcement learning. ActiveCTReasoner achieves 73.2% close-ended accuracy, outperforming GPT-5.4 (47.3%) remarkably. In open-ended evaluations, it scores 44.2% compared to 23.8% for the best baseline. A radiologist collaboration study provides preliminary evidence for the decision-support utility of radiologist-aligned agentic reasoning.

title: The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images
author: Zhiheng Wang; Bo Peng; Lai Wei; Chaochao Lu
abstract: The “thinking-with-images” paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain into per-group contributions and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

title: Controllable Affective Generation via Latent Vector Steering
author: Xixian Yong; Siyuan Chang; Yingying Zhang; Xian Wu; Xiao Zhou
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce emotionally flattened responses after alignment, limiting their effectiveness in affect-sensitive applications. In this paper, we propose EmoVec, a lightweight framework for controllable affective generation via latent vector steering. EmoVec extracts emotion-specific directions from paired neutral and emotion-conditioned responses using contrastive activation addition, and further purifies them through task-specific debiasing and principal subspace removal. During inference, these vectors are injected into the final residual stream with static or scenario-adaptive scaling, enabling continuous control over emotional intensity without updating model weights. Experiments across three LLMs and eight emotions show that EmoVec consistently improves emotional salience while largely preserving semantic content, fluency, and coherence. Ablation studies and human evaluation further confirm the effectiveness of vector purification and adaptive scaling, demonstrating EmoVec as a practical inference-time method for affective control in deployed LLMs.

title: How Many Instances Are Enough? Minimum Subsample Size Prediction for Stereotype Evaluation
author: Bora Bozdogan; Soroush Vosoughi; Weicheng Ma
abstract: Stereotype evaluation for large language models relies on heavily annotated benchmarks, yet such evaluations are constrained by limited instance availability and are often sensitive to which examples are included. We propose a framework for predicting the minimum number of evaluation instances needed to preserve benchmark-level stereotype scores under specified error and confidence criteria. Our method provides a statistically grounded way to determine how much a benchmark can be reduced without materially changing the resulting evaluation outcome. We support the framework with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on three widely used stereotype benchmarks, CrowS-Pairs, StereoSet, and BBQ. Across datasets, models, and tolerance settings, the proposed method provides reliable subsample-size guidance without exception. As an additional extension, we show that our approach can also guide compact synthetic stereotype evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that benchmark-level stereotype evaluation can often be conducted with far fewer instances than the original datasets require, offering a practical and principled approach to more efficient bias assessment.

title: SciEmbed: Citation-Context Supervision for Scientific Document Embeddings
author: Jonas Wilinski; Michael Färber
abstract: Open scientific document embedders are typically trained on binary citation edges between paper title-abstract pairs. This signal discards the citation context sentence: a domain-expert description of the cited paper, written by the citing author. We use these sentences as the primary contrastive supervision signal to train SciEmbed, an open 149M ModernBERT-base encoder. On the official SciRepEval benchmark it reaches 66.85 over three seeds, surpassing prior open scientific embedders such as SPECTER2 and SciNCL. To isolate what the supervision source contributes, we compare against IBM Granite R2, a same-size ModernBERT peer trained on general retrieval data. Using only open citation-context data, SciEmbed matches Granite R2 to within 0.6 on the SciRepEval macro overall while specialising in the opposite direction: it leads regression tasks tied to paper impact by 2.3 points, where Granite R2 instead leads classification, proximity, and search. A 28-configuration sweep over recipes and alternative supervision signals does not improve on this result, consistent with the specialisation tracking the supervision source rather than the training recipe. Training at longer contexts yields monotonic gains on a body-fact retrieval probe within our recipe. We release the model, training pipeline, and evaluation harness as a fully open, citation-context-supervised baseline with a distinct, reproducible specialisation pattern.

title: LLM Abstention Can Be a Prompt Artifact, in Addition to Genuine Uncertainty
author: Zipeng Ling; Shuliang Liu; Yuehao Tang; Junqi Yang; Shenghong Fu; Seonil Son; Chen Huang; Kejia Huang; Yao Wan; Zhichao Hou; Xuming Hu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to abstain from answering questions they are unsure about. However, this ability is often misused: in real-world applications, input prompts sometimes contain uncertainty elements, and driven by this, LLMs are inclined to abstain even on problems they are capable of solving. We argue that LLM abstention is not only an expression of genuine uncertainty; it is also an artifact that can be largely influenced by prompts. We name this phenomenon *Abstention Inflation*. We add "Unknown" as an extra option for LLMs to choose from; experiments show serious accuracy drops on True/False Questions (TFQs). Replacing "Unknown" with an unrelated random word produces an identical effect. We argue that LLMs are trained to imitate the surface pattern of abstention, rather than to express genuine uncertainty. Based on ten experiments, we support four claims that form a progressive argument: **(C1)** *Abstention Inflation* is triggered by the structural presence of an extra option, not by genuine uncertainty; **(C2)** further, it makes the model deny it can answer even when it can; **(C3)** at the representation level, this manifests as a later-layer output override; **(C4)** finally, this bias is stable and emerges through instruction tuning, rather than stochastic noise.

title: Hybrid Linear Attention Done Right: Efficient Distillation and Effective Architectures for Extremely Long Contexts
author: Yingfa Chen; Zhen Leng Thai; Zihan Zhou; Zhu Zhang; Xingyu Shen; Shuo Wang; Chaojun Xiao; Xu Han; Zhiyuan Liu
abstract: Hybrid architectures that combine softmax attention blocks and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown a desirable performance-throughput tradeoff for long-context modeling, but their adoption and studies are hindered by the prohibitive cost of large-scale pre-training from scratch. Some recent studies have shown that pre-trained softmax attention blocks can be converted into RNN blocks through parameter transfer and knowledge distillation. However, these transfer methods require substantial amounts of training data (more than 10B tokens), and the resulting hybrid models also exhibit poor long-context performance, which is the scenario where hybrid models enjoy significant inference speedups over Transformer-based models. In this paper, we present HALO (Hybrid Attention via Layer Optimization), a pipeline for distilling Transformer models into RNN-attention hybrid models. We then present HypeNet, a hybrid architecture with superior length generalization enabled by a novel position encoding scheme (named HyPE) and various architectural modifications. We convert the Qwen3 series into HypeNet using HALO, achieving performance comparable to the original Transformer models while enjoying superior long-context performance and efficiency. The conversion requires just 2.3B tokens, less than 0.01% of their pre-training data.

title: High Scores, Hidden Failures: Evaluating Codebook-Based LLM Content Analysis
author: Elena Senger; Yuri Campbell; Rob Van Der Goot; Barbara Plank
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for codebook-based content analysis in computational social science, where codebooks translate theoretical concepts into labeling schemes. While prior work reports strong predictive performance, it remains unclear whether these systems produce reliable and robust annotations. We conduct a large-scale empirical failure-mode analysis of LLM-based coding pipelines across three datasets and five models by systematically evaluating their stability, robustness, and conceptual validity under controlled perturbations, domain shifts, and optimization procedures. We uncover multiple failures that are largely invisible under standard metrics, showing that high aggregate scores frequently coexist with severe label-level disparities, instability across runs, domain sensitivity, and shifts in label interpretation. Importantly, these failure modes persist under widely used optimization strategies and remain largely invisible under standard metrics such as accuracy and micro-F1. Our results demonstrate that current LLM-based coding pipelines cannot be treated as stable measurement tools without targeted validation beyond aggregate performance.

title: CARD: Cluster-level Adaptation with Reward-guided Decoding for Personalized Text Generation
author: Yutong Song; Jiang Wu; Weijia Zhang; Chengze Shen; Shaofan Yuan; Weitao Lu; Jian Wang; Yu Wang; Nikil Dutt; Amir M. Rahmani
abstract: Adapting large language models to individual users remains challenging because systems must capture fine-grained personal preferences while serving many users efficiently. We introduce CARD, a hierarchical personalization framework that first learns preferences shared across user groups and then captures how individual users depart from those shared patterns. CARD trains a parameter-efficient adaptation module for each group, providing a reliable prior even when a user has limited history. It then learns a compact user preference vector by contrasting user-authored responses with outputs from the corresponding group model, without requiring manual annotations. During inference, both the backbone and the group adaptation module remain frozen, while the user vector applies a low-rank correction to the token logits during decoding. Experiments on personalization benchmarks show that CARD consistently outperforms competitive baselines while requiring only a compact vector for each user.

title: Attention-Aligned Reasoning for Large Language Models
author: Hongxiang Zhang; Yuan Tian; Tianyi Zhang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to generate a long reasoning chain when solving complex tasks. However, as the reasoning chain extends, critical intermediate steps and the original prompt will be buried in the context, receiving insufficient attention and leading to errors. In this work, we present ATAR, a novel reasoning method that leverages the inherent reasoning structure to steer LLM attention. Our experiments show that ATAR outperforms SOTA methods across six benchmarks, achieving up to 15.39% absolute improvement. Furthermore, with ATAR, “non-reasoning” models achieve comparable or even better performance compared to reasoning models of the same size in most benchmarks. Finally, our ablation studies show that the attention alignment component contributes significantly, and that these improvements are persist under different attention-steering backends.

title: Tree-of-Concerns: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Debate for Unstated-Limitation Extraction in Scientific Critique
author: Sahil Mishra; Niranjan Rajeev; Tanmoy Chakraborty
abstract: As scientific literature grows and papers increasingly under-report limitations, multi-agent LLMs offer a promising approach to systematically uncover these hidden failure modes. Here, we introduce Tree-of-Concerns, a multi-agent framework that deploys specialized skeptic personas, each operating through a category-specific analytical lens, as parallel debate trees to extract unstated limitations from scientific papers. Each persona conducts structured, evidence-grounded argumentation, while a Panel Review mechanism re-evaluates each surviving claim from all five perspectives to correct category drift and severity miscalibration. Through retrieval-free, single-paper experiments on ToC-Bench, our benchmark of 414 research papers with 1,905 unstated limitations, sourced from reviewer-reported weaknesses and follow-up citation critiques, we demonstrate that ToC improves precision by 79% and coverage by 11% relative to the strongest baseline, surfacing specific, evidence-grounded concerns that support reviewers in systematic evaluation.

title: DisCon4Gen: A Semantic Alignment Framework Through Discriminative Conditioning for Generation
author: Caiwei Yang; Yanping Chen; Shuai Yu
abstract: Generative language models (GLMs) excel at text generation and instruction following, while discriminative language models (DLMs) provide strong semantic representations for understanding tasks. Under the manifold hypothesis, natural language semantics can be regarded as lying on a shared latent semantic manifold, while DLMs and GLMs learn different representations of this manifold in their respective latent spaces. However, due to differences in training objectives and modeling strategies, these representation spaces are not naturally aligned, preventing discriminative representations from being directly utilized by GLMs through simple concatenation or linear transformation. To address this issue, a semantic alignment framework through discriminative conditioning for generation (DisCon4Gen) is proposed. From a manifold-based perspective, DisCon4Gen transforms DLM semantics into continuous conditions for GLMs. It further incorporates both global semantic signals and fine-grained discriminative cues to guide generation, enabling GLMs to better exploit external discriminative semantics. Experiments on five downstream datasets show that DisCon4Gen improves over strong supervised fine-tuning baselines and achieves competitive performance across both semantic understanding and generative reasoning tasks.

title: CapGeo-Bench: Decoupling Visual Perception from Reasoning and Evaluating Geometric Understanding
author: Yuying Li; Siyi Qian; Hao Liang; Leqi Zheng; Ruichuan An; Linzhuang Sun; Jiajun Zhang; Wentao Zhang
abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success in difficult purely textual mathematical reasoning tasks, even advanced closed-source models such as GPT-o3 still struggle with geometric problems. This discrepancy motivates us to investigate the root cause: is the bottleneck of multimodal geometric reasoning rooted in reasoning itself, or in the perception of geometric information from diagrams? To answer this question, we conduct an exploratory experiment and find that providing high-quality captions consistently and substantially boosts performance of MLLMs, empirically validating the visual perception bottleneck in geometric reasoning. However, MLLMs’ capabilities in visual geometric perception remain insufficiently evaluated. To fill the gap, we propose CapGeo-Bench, a benchmark of 4,641 high-quality figure–caption pairs equipped with a fine-grained keypoint-based evaluation metric. Specifically, CapGeo-Bench encompasses three geometric classes and is devided into four difficulty levels according to the complexity of geometric primitives. Captions are scored at a fine-grained level by extracting keypoints along three dimensions-geometric elements, spatial relationships, and numerical attributes. CapGeo-Bench provides a reliable instrument and guideline for evaluating and advancing MLLMs’ geometric perception capabilities. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/YuYingLi0/CapGeo.

title: The Analyst in the Prompt: Role, Retrieval, and Memory Biases in LLM Financial Analysis
author: Ahmed Asaad; Amr Mohamed; Yang Zhang; Omneya Abdelsalam
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) use persistent user context such as memory, profiles, and role prompts. This enables personalization, but can destabilize evidence-based judgment: the same evidence may yield different conclusions under different user contexts. Finance offers a high-stakes long-document setting where evidence reading is central. We test this on 3,575 SEC filings across twelve models. By comparing persona-conditioned retrieval, neutral retrieval, and memory-framed context, we find that bias comes from how models interpret identical evidence under role-style context, not from which evidence they retrieve. As mitigation, user-memory framing of the same mindset and dual-output scoring reduce the effect, with model-specific effectiveness across models.

title: LoopViT: Scaling Visual ARC with Looped Transformers
author: Wen-Jie Shu; Xuerui Qiu; Rui-Jie Zhu; Harold Haodong Chen; Yexin Liu; Harry Yang
abstract: Recent ARC-AGI systems have shown that pure vision can solve abstract grid reasoning without language backbones, but most strong models still rely on fixed-depth feed-forward computation. We study whether recurrent computation is a better scaling axis for this setting. We propose Loop-ViT, a vision-native recurrent model that reuses a weight-tied Hybrid Block across multiple steps, with local convolutions for image-token refinement and attention for global rule induction. We also use an entropy-based exit rule to reduce unnecessary iterations at inference time. On ARC-AGI-1, Loop-ViT improves the parameter-efficiency trade-off over fixed-depth vision baselines and reaches 65.8% accuracy with an 18M model. Overall, the results suggest that repeated computation is a useful inductive bias for ARC-style visual reasoning. The code is available at https://github.com/WenjieShu/LoopViT.

title: LatentMem: Customizing Latent Memory for Multi-Agent Systems
author: Muxin Fu; Xiangyuan Xue; Yafu Li; Zefeng He; Siyuan Huang; Xiaoye Qu; Yu Cheng; Yang Yang
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered multi-agent systems (MAS) demonstrate remarkable collective intelligence, with multi-agent memory serving as a pivotal mechanism for continual adaptation. However, existing multi-agent memory designs remain constrained by two fundamental bottlenecks: (i) memory homogenization caused by limited role-aware customization, and (ii) information overload induced by exposing agents to excessively fine-grained textual memories. To address these limitations, we propose LatentMem, a learnable multi-agent memory framework that customizes agent-specific experiential memories while reducing textual context. Specifically, LatentMem comprises an experience bank for lightweight storage of raw interaction trajectories and a memory composer that synthesizes compact latent memories conditioned on retrieved experience and agent-specific contexts. Further, we introduce Latent Memory Policy Optimization (LMPO), which propagates task-level optimization signals through latent memories to learn compact, high-utility latent representations. Extensive experiments across six benchmarks and four mainstream MAS frameworks show that LatentMem improves vanilla settings by up to 19.36% and consistently outperforms existing memory architectures, without requiring modifications to the agent-layer workflows.

title: Beyond Static EHRs: Dynamic Examination Feedback for LLM-based Virtual Patients
author: Renwei Xiao; Wen He; Hongzhou Yu; Qingqiu Li; Yuejie Zhang; Rui Feng; Xiaobo Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant promise in healthcare applications. To better mirror real-world settings for LLM evaluation, dynamic longitudinal diagnosis-and-treatment simulation with virtual patients has recently emerged as a focal point of research. However, existing simulation frameworks are limited by clinical trajectory uniqueness, where virtual patients can only provide feedback based on information available in static electronic health records (EHRs). This limitation leads to simulation failures when unrecorded but medically sound examinations are ordered. In this paper, we formulate the task of Examination Feedback Simulation, which aims to dynamically augment the unique trajectory by simulating medically plausible examination results in response to clinical orders. To support this largely unexplored research area, we construct ClinTrack, a dataset curated from MIMIC-IV. We further propose a structure-aware evaluation metric SimScore to quantitatively assess the quality of simulated results, which shows promising initial alignment with expert judgment. Building on this framework, we develop ClinSim, a tailored generative model for this task. Experiments demonstrate that our 4B ClinSim model significantly outperforms flagship models with up to 235B parameters on this task, providing a critical foundation for creating more dynamic and realistic virtual patients. Code and other resources are available at GitHub.

title: ProcessLight: Process Supervision for Large Language Model Based Traffic Signal Control
author: Shuaitao Zhao; Tianlong Zhou; Weijie Wang; Shi Jiasheng; Weixiong Rao
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been introduced into traffic signal control (TSC) as decision agents due to their strengths in human-readable reasoning generation. Yet, existing LLM TSC methods optimize only from final outcomes and fail to distinguish valid from flawed reasoning steps, causing useful or misleading steps to be jointly updated and thus impairing the model’s learning of effective reasoning. To bridge this gap, we propose an LLM-based framework ProcessLight to decompose signal decisions into verifiable semantic steps. Building on ProcessLight, we further develop Step-wise Traffic Process Policy Optimization (STeP-PO), a novel reinforcement learning framework that optimizes structured reasoning processes through step-level credit assignment. Specifically, STeP-PO uses step quality scores to evaluate local reasoning quality and step importance to measure each step’s influence on the final action, and then assigns step-level advantages over a semantic step tree structure. The resulting step-level advantages are propagated to reasoning tokens, enabling fine-grained policy optimization beyond outcome-only rewards. Extensive experiments over multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/wenzhaoabc/processlight.

title: Disentangling In-Language Alignment and Cross-Lingual Safety Borrowing in Low-Resource Languages
author: Zeguang Huang; Zhenma Spenpa; Mio Yip Sien Chu; Xi Cao; Nuo Qun; Nyima Tashi
abstract: We study two modes of low-resource language safety: in-language alignment, where models refuse harmful instructions in the target language, and cross-lingual safety borrowing, where they rely on a better-aligned proximate high-resource language, including via response-language fallback. We evaluate 11 commercial APIs on English, Mandarin, Cantonese, Tibetan, and Russian, plus 3 Tibetan-specialized open-source models, using native-speaker-verified datasets. Results reveal two patterns: Tibetan, for which response-language fallback provides limited aggregate protection in our setting, shows a safety cliff with ASR of 12.69–60.96%, far above English; Cantonese, which shares script and vocabulary with Mandarin, keeps aggregate ASR in single digits, but Cantonese-reply ASR exceeds aggregate ASR for all 11 models (sign test, p < 0.001), exposing in-language safety gaps concealed by aggregate metrics. We release Cantonese-AdvBench and Tibetan-AdvBench.

title: HarmEvoSkill: Skill-Memory Self-Evolution for Zero-shot Multimodal Harmful Meme Detection
author: Jianyu Zhou; Weihai Lu
abstract: Multimodal harmful meme detection is challenging because harmful intent is often expressed through implicit image-text associations, cultural references, rhetorical framing, and context-dependent targets. Existing methods mainly rely on supervised multimodal models, MLLM prompting, or fixed agent workflows. However, they still lack experience accumulation and rely on static skill design, making it difficult to reuse prior judgments or adapt to emerging meme templates and long-tail harm patterns. To address these limitations, we propose HarmEvoSkill (Harmful Meme Evolving Skill-Memory), a label-free self-evolving Skill-Memory framework for harmful meme detection. HarmEvoSkill converts unlabeled reference memes into Case Memory, Insight Memory, and Risk Memory. It then automatically discovers candidate skills, abstracts recurring reasoning patterns, and induces executable skill cards without predefined skill labels. During inference, a Skill Planner retrieves relevant memories, selects task-specific skills, and generates structured evidence packets. A graph-assisted judge organizes the evidence into a harmful–harmless claim graph, makes the final prediction, and updates memory through graph diagnosis. Extensive benchmark evaluations show that HarmEvoSkill achieves consistently strong performance among evaluated methods. On HarM, it improves Accuracy by 9.33% and Macro-F1 by 17.97% over the direct MLLM baseline.

title: LSC-Pattern: Interpretable Lexical Semantic Change Analysis via Diachronic Sense Distributions
author: Zhidong Ling; Mamoru Komachi
abstract: Lexical semantic change detection identifies words whose meanings change over time, but it often cannot explain which senses and semantic properties are responsible for the change. We propose LSC-Pattern, a framework for interpretable lexical semantic change analysis that combines dictionary-grounded diachronic sense distributions with interpretable semantic dimensions. The framework first assigns each target-word usage to an explicit dictionary sense and then analyzes the resulting sense distributions along dimensions such as valence, semantic scope, and metaphoricity. We instantiate it for Japanese with LLM-based word sense disambiguation, which reaches 0.815 accuracy against majority-vote human annotation and outperforms five baselines; its sense-distribution change scores correlate with JaSemChange human judgments (Spearman’s ρ of 0.821 on seven overlapping entries and 0.580 on all 20). Case studies illustrate how sense redistribution and operationalized semantic signals can jointly support the discovery and interpretation of candidate types of change.

title: LangMAP: A Language-Adaptive Approach to Tokenization
author: Clara Meister; Suchir Salhan; Andrzej Szablewski; Pietro Lesci; Paula Buttery; Tiago Pimentel
abstract: Language-specific tokenizers improve tokenization quality and the downstream performance of models on those languages. Using one with an existing pretrained model requires either training a new model from scratch or adapting the vocabulary of the pretrained one. We propose Language-adaptive Maximum a Posteriori (LangMAP) Tokenization, which extends the UnigramLM algorithm to the multilingual setting by replacing its single distribution over the vocabulary with one distribution per language over the same vocabulary. LangMAP can be used to train a multilingual language model from scratch, or to adapt a pretrained model’s tokenizer to individual languages without changing its vocabulary. Language labels are required to estimate the per-language distributions; at inference, the algorithm selects the highest-probability segmentation across languages, i.e., it does not need a language label. In experiments where we adapt a pretrained tokenizer with LangMAP, we observe that LangMAP’s new segmentation has consistently higher morphological boundary recall than the original tokenizer. In code data, it improves alignment with abstract syntax tree (AST) leaf boundaries in all configurations we try. Despite ostensible improvements in segmentations, in language model fine-tuning experiments, we do not observe significant differences in performance for most language-task pairs.

title: Reformulating Radiology Report Error Detection as Sentence-Level Vision-Language Learning
author: Dabin Min; Kyungmin Jeon; Dongheon Lee; Chang Min Park
abstract: Accurate alignment between chest X-ray (CXR) images and radiology reports is essential for clinical safety, yet automatic radiology report error detection from paired CXRs remains challenging. Prior approaches typically compare the entire report with the image, limiting the model’s ability to learn fine-grained vision-language correspondences at the level of individual findings. We reformulate report error detection as a sentence-level vision-language learning problem by decomposing reports into atomic finding statements, thereby reducing semantic entanglement and supervision noise. We propose SenRED (Sentence-level Report Error Detector), which uses sentence-conditioned patch aggregation to associate each statement with localized visual evidence. To supervise learning, we generate sentence-level synthetic errors reflecting clinically relevant categories—false positives, false negatives, and mislocalization—along with consistent image-sentence pairs. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and Open-i show that SenRED consistently outperforms task-specific baselines and zero-shot instruction-tuned VLMs in both sentence-level and exam-level evaluations. Radiologist-confirmed evaluations further show that these gains are maintained on clinically reviewed subsets. Comparative experiments support the benefit of sentence-level reformulation, while ablations demonstrate that sentence-conditioned patch aggregation improves fine-grained consistency checking.

title: TTS-Guard: Black-Box Ownership Verification of Text-to-Speech Models via Adaptive Adversarial Speaker-Pair Fingerprints
author: Xubin Yue; Zhenhua Xu; Zhebo Wang; Mengting Li; Zijie Zhou; Wenpeng Xing; Dezhang Kong; Meng Han
abstract: The rapid maturation of zero-shot Text-to-Speech (TTS) models has turned high-quality voice cloning into a widely available capability, raising acute concerns over unauthorised replication, fine-tuning and resale of proprietary speech models. Yet ownership verification for TTS remains largely open: speech is a continuous waveform whose perturbations are easily destroyed by routine signal processing, and the human auditory system imposes a much tighter perceptual budget than vision. We present TTS-Guard, a black-box ownership verification framework for TTS models built on adversarial speaker-pair fingerprints. TTS-Guard(i) selects key speaker pairs in a dual embedding space for architecture-agnostic stealth;(ii) optimises a perturbation through an adaptive curriculum of shadow models covering fine-tuning, pruning, quantisation and distillation; and (iii) aggregates black-box queries into a calibrated Verification Confidence Score. On five mainstream TTS systems, TTS-Guard reaches an average Fingerprint Success Rate of 96.4% at a False Positive Rate of 5.8%, while preserving intelligibility and naturalness. The fingerprint remains effective against ten audio attacks, six model modifications, and two state-of-the-art adversarial purifiers.

title: ProactiveEngine: Proactive Learning with Lifelong Memory via World Models
author: Python Song; Xiaoying Liao
abstract: Large language models have shown promise in assisting humans, but most real-world AI remains reactive, responding only to explicit user prompts. Current proactive AI agents often fail in multimodal reasoning over long-term memory, which requires agents performing temporal reasoning over long-horizon multimodal histories and continual knowledge update, and thus struggle to predict users’ needs and intent. To address this challenge, we present ProactiveEngine, the first foundation model designed for proactive multimodal agents, which generates proactive responses in long-horizon settings. ProactiveEngine supports both video plus text and text-only input. Our model achieves an F1-score of 83.3%, substantially outperforming current commercial models. Our model also achieves strong performance on the public Proactive Benchmarks in a zero-shot setting without further training, while enabling a 7.8× increase in token context window and over 100× more historical events for long-horizon proactive prediction. We also introduce NeuroAuroraBench, a multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate long-term memory proactive prediction. The benchmark resulted in 24.8k annotated sessions capturing dynamic changes.

title: Cascade-SC: A Pareto-Efficient Cross-Model Cascade for Test-Time Reasoning
author: Minghan Li; Siqi Zhao; Luoliang Hua; Guodong Zhou
abstract: In test-time reasoning, pairing a weak local generator with a strong but expensive teacher makes deployment cost hinge on when additional teacher computation is worthwhile. We propose Cascade-SC, a containment-gated cascade that accepts the teacher’s independently solved answer when it matches the generator’s candidate set and draws additional teacher samples otherwise. The cross-model gate fires roughly 5× less often than within-model unanimity, concentrating teacher compute on harder cases. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and AIME-2024, Cascade-SC improves over self-consistency by 11–37%. On GSM8K, it matches ModelSwitch within 0.46% at roughly one-third the teacher-inference cost and beats matched-compute Teacher-only SC by 1.71%. On low-recall AIME-2024, it reaches 40.00% versus the candidate-restricted Oracle@8 ceiling of 11.11%. It also outperforms trained 7B process-reward rerankers by 4–11% without verifier training. Self-consistency and Teacher-greedy arise as special cases, while a teacher-only versus union-vote ablation shows that aggregation is a separate design choice. Source codes are available at https://github.com/SUGAR-NLP/Cascade-SC.

title: Keeping Eyes on the Image: Dynamic Visual Attention Recalibration for Vision-Language Reasoning
author: Yuna Jeong; Junhyeong Park; Mingyu Kang; Hyein Seo; Keon Kim; Yong Suk Choi
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieve strong performance on various vision-language tasks, yet Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation often weakens attention to visual tokens, degrading evidence-grounded reasoning. During the later stages of autoregressive decoding, models tend to increasingly rely on previously generated text rather than visual evidence, leading to plausible but visually inconsistent rationales. We propose DVAR (Dynamic Visual Attention Recalibration), a training-free method that selectively amplifies visually relevant tokens to mitigate visual attention decay during decoding. DVAR operates at three levels: (i) prompt level structure to encourage visually grounded reasoning; (ii) embedding level relevance weights derived from image–text alignment; and (iii) decoding level scheduling that adjusts recalibration by tracking shifts in visual attention. Without sensitive model-specific hyperparameter retuning, DVAR yields consistent performance improvements across six benchmarks on LLaVA and Qwen-VL models, and better preserves visual attention throughout decoding.

title: Encoder-only and decoder-only models exhibit distinct patterns of linguistic bias
author: Suet-Ying Lam; Qingcheng Zeng; Rob Voigt
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) based on encoder and decoder architectures exhibit strong performance across a range of tasks, yet systematic comparisons of how training objectives shape their behavior remain limited. Building on prior work establishing systematic comparison between decoder-encoder differences (Weller et al., 2026), we ask whether this difference shapes different linguistic bias using two production-related tasks: semantic role assignment and syntactic structure choice (actives vs. passives). Across architectures, LLMs exhibit a robust animacy-first bias, preferring to place animate entities in subject position, diverging from human bias. However, when animacy cues are removed, encoders generalize better than decoders and show a stronger preference for passive constructions. We argue that these differences reflect training objectives: encoders’ sensitivity to contextual compatibility supports flexible mapping from semantics to structure, whereas decoders’ reliance on surface frequency favors dominant patterns and disfavors infrequent structures such as passives.

title: DIPLOMAT: Dialogue-Span-Aware Direct Preference Optimization for Polite Persuasive Workplace Negotiation Dialogues
author: Bibhuti Jha; Rishikant Chigrupaatii; Priyanshu Priya; Asif Ekbal
abstract: Effective workplace negotiation requires balancing multiple objectives, including achieving task goals, preserving professional relationships, and resolving conflicts constructively. However, misunderstandings, misaligned preferences, and interpersonal friction often impede successful outcomes. Politeness mitigates these challenges by fostering trust, reducing tension, and preventing escalation, and persuasive communication helps overcome resistance, align preferences, and guide participants toward mutually beneficial agreements. Motivated by these insights, we present **DIPLOMAT**, a dialogue system for polite and persuasive workplace negotiation. To support its development, we introduce **PROWESS**, a dataset of multi-turn workplace negotiation dialogues generated via a multi-agent framework and enriched with negotiation strategies, politeness levels, and persuasive strategies. **DIPLOMAT** is trained using Dialogue-Span-Aware Direct Preference Optimization (DSA-DPO), a novel preference learning objective that identifies key dialogue spans for preference alignment. This enables **DIPLOMAT** to generate contextually coherent responses that employ intended negotiation strategies, maintain politeness, and incorporate effective persuasion strategies throughout interactions. Automatic and human evaluations on **PROWESS** confirm that **DIPLOMAT** consistently outperforms baselines in generating coherent, polite, and persuasive negotiation responses.

title: LatCom: Cross-Agent Latent Compression for Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration
author: Shinan Zhang; Tao Zhang; Qihui Zhu; Mengjie Zhang; Dong Jin; Yunpeng Hou; Shuangwu Chen; Xiaobin Tan; Quan Zheng; Jianyang
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) increasingly use latent collaboration to avoid the information loss and repeated encoding-decoding overhead of natural-language communication. However, directly forwarding all sender latents makes the receiver-side context scale with both the number of agents and the reasoning length, increasing computation, memory usage, and collaboration latency. A natural solution is latent compression. But we find that cross-agent redundancy remains unresolved in existing latent compression approaches, which typically compress each sender independently and then concatenate the results. We propose LatCom, a cross-agent latent compression framework for efficient multi-agent latent collaboration. LatCom maps multiple sender latents into a fixed number of receiver-readable and task-relevant slots. Rather than reconstructing all sender hidden states, it optimizes the compressed latents for receiver-side task utility. LatCom trains the compressor in two stages: single-sender readability learning first establishes a latent interface interpretable by the frozen receiver, and multi-sender fusion learning then trains the compressor to fuse complementary evidence and remove redundancy across agents. Experiments on multiple benchmarks with the Qwen-4B model show that LatCom improves average inference speed by 2.46x over LatentMAS, reduces token usage by 70.3%, and increases average accuracy by 0.46%.

title: LadderEdit: Edit-Level Residual Compression for Memory-Efficient Lifelong Editing of LLMs
author: Xiaobing Yu; Peijie Qiu; Jin Yang; Xuanzhao Dong; Weiwei Ma; Zhaoqi An; Xiaoqi Zhao; Xiaofeng Liu
abstract: Lifelong editing of LLMs requires storing thousands of edits after acquisition. A widely used family of approaches attaches one LoRA adapter per edit, which preserves behavior but grows linearly in storage. To address this challenge, we propose LadderEdit, a method that compresses each LoRA adapter after it is acquired. Each edit is first stored at low rank as a cheap sketch. We then check whether this sketch still satisfies the rewrite, generalization, and locality contract on probe prompts. Edits that pass keep the sketch; those that fail are promoted to a higher rank along a ladder until the contract is met. Because every edit retains some representation, coverage is maintained, and only hard edits consume more rank. Across ZsRE, CounterFact, and WikiBigEdit benchmarks on LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B, LadderEdit tracks exact LoRA storage at 5.2\times less memory and remains effective at 50{,}000 sequential edits.

title: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing
author: Anuj Kumar; Shintaro Ozaki; Yamuna Prasad; Katsuhiko Hayashi; Hidetaka Kamigaito; Taro Watanabe
abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved the performance of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers, yet determining when their outputs can be trusted remains largely unexplored. This work presents the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting using top-k beam-search candidates. Uncertainty is estimated from pairwise candidate similarities and evaluated using the Prediction Rejection Ratio. This work characterises the relationship between parsing performance and uncertainty, evaluates the reliability of beam candidate distributions, analyses the effect of evaluation metrics on uncertainty assessment, and identifies parsers that provide the strongest balance between performance and reliability. Experimental results show the value of uncertainty estimation as a complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers.

title: Scale or Reason? A Compute-Equivalent Analysis of Reasoning Distillation
author: Nicolas Boizard; Hippolyte Gisserot-Boukhlef; Kevin El Haddad; Celine Hudelot; Pierre Colombo
abstract: Distilling reasoning traces from strong teacher models has become the standard recipe for building capable small language models. Yet reasoning traces are 5-20\times longer than standard instruction fine-tuning (IFT) outputs, meaning every practitioner who chooses reasoning distillation implicitly forgoes training a larger IFT model on the same compute budget. Whether this trade-off is worthwhile remains unaddressed. We study it with a controlled experiment: a single teacher generates paired IFT and reasoning outputs for identical prompts by toggling only its reasoning mode, isolating supervision format as the sole variable. Training students at five scales (0.5B to 14B) and evaluating on 18 benchmarks, we find that at matched FLOPs, IFT lies on or near the Pareto frontier across the majority of configurations. Reasoning reaches the Pareto frontier only on open-ended tasks at 7B and above. Even there, a sequential curriculum mixing just 25-50% reasoning data with IFT captures most of the accuracy benefit at far lower compute cost.

title: EviGen: Predictive Evidence Scaffolding for Verifiable Clinical Rationale Generation
author: Fengnan Li; Heman Burre; Liwen Sun; Roshni Varma; Matthew M. Engelhard
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) capture years of patient history across notes, codes, labs, and procedures, and contain evidence needed to reason about likely clinical outcomes. However, comprehensive clinician review of these records is impractical, and LLM-based processing is costly and often unreliable, missing some relevant observations while hallucinating others. We therefore propose **EviGen**, a three-layer framework for verifiable clinical rationale generation that addresses these challenges. The **first layer** is a patient-conditioned retriever that uses learnable queries to find evidence predictive of, not just textually relevant to, a clinical outcome and ranks it by prediction attribution scores. The **second layer** is an LLM generator that consumes this ranked evidence as a scaffold to produce a clinical rationale grounded in the retrieved spans. The **third layer** is a process-supervised verifier that checks the generated rationale at the reasoning-step level, flagging unreliable claims. Across three medical prediction datasets, EviGen improves prediction performance and rationale faithfulness over full-context LLM and RAG baselines, and is preferred by clinical reviewers in a usability evaluation.

title: CForce: Boosting Parallel Decoding for dLLMs via Consistency Forcing
author: Yuji Ren; Chenkai Xu; Zhuocheng Gong; Jianguo Li; Zhijie Deng
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) accelerate language generation by predicting multiple masks in a single forward pass.However, existing dLLMs can suffer from unreliable predictions in early denoising stages under aggressive parallelism strategies, leading to errors that can propagate to later stages. To tackle this issue, we present Consistency Forcing (CForce) for dLLMs, a distillation method to force the mask predictions of early stages to align with those of later stages. CForce trains the model on pre-collected self-rollout trajectories, thereby improving training-inference alignment.We introduce Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence as a distillation objective to conjoin the merits of forward and reverse KL.We further provide a theoretical analysis for the consistency objective to explain why CForce can approximately minimize the prediction error of early stages.Critically, the same formulation applies to both mask-to-token decoding and edit-capable decoding; in the edit-capable case, later token-to-token refinements provide additional supervision for earlier masked-state predictions. Experiments on non-edit and edit-capable LLaDA models show improved speed-quality trade-offs, especially under high-parallelism decoding budgets.

title: Fact-Checking the Jailbreak: A Claim-Level Framework for Structured Misinformation Assessment
author: Jia Yee Tan; Rong Fu; Yongtai Liu; Kaiyi Hu; Simon James Fong
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit structured, credible misinformation. Existing benchmarks primarily track binary refusals, often overlooking the severity and exposure risk of the misinformation payload itself. In this work, we introduce Misinfo-Jailbreak Bench, a comprehensive framework that systematically maps diverse attack strategies to a claim-level scoring pipeline for precise risk quantification. Building on this diagnostic foundation, we propose Selective LoRA Ethical Surgery, a parameter-efficient defense mechanism. Instead of broad parameter updates, our approach identifies safety-relevant subspaces via contrastive representations to confine LoRA edits and employs inference-time gating to preserve benign capabilities. Experimental results on state-of-the-art models (e.g., Qwen2.5, Llama-4) demonstrate that our method reduces high-severity risk by 60-70% while limiting general capability degradation to less than 1%, offering a precise and minimally invasive paradigm for post-hoc alignment.

title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
author: Cantao Su; Anna Wegmann; Esther Ploeger; Dong Nguyen
abstract: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization.
