Meanwhile, supervised fine-tuning relies on mimicking filtered, compliant data, which fails to establish the priority asymmetry at the algorithmic level. In this paper, we introduce HIPO, a novel alignment framework that formulates HIF as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. HIPO elevates system prompts from mere input context to strict algorithmic boundaries. Using a primal-dual safe reinforcement learning approach, the algorithm dynamically enforces system prompt compliance as an explicit constraint, maximizing user utility strictly within this feasible region. Extensive evaluations across diverse model architectures (e.g., Qwen, Phi, Llama) demonstrate that HIPO significantly improves both system compliance and user utility. Furthermore, mechanistic analysis reveals that this constrained optimization autonomously drives the model to shift its attention toward long-range system tokens, providing a principled foundation for reliable LLM deployment in complex workflows.

title: OriGround: Orientation-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
author: Haochen Li; Jiaxin Shi; Ruonan Liu; Luo Liufu
abstract: Zero-shot 3D visual grounding (3DVG) aims to localize a referred object in a 3D scene without task-specific grounding supervision. Existing training-free methods commonly reason over object categories, centers, and bounding boxes, but these representations do not encode the local reference frames needed to interpret viewpoint-dependent expressions such as left of, behind, or facing the door. We propose OriGround, an orientation-aware neuro-symbolic framework that explicitly models object-centric orientations and infers observer viewpoints for zero-shot 3DVG. OriGround parses each query into a viewpoint-aware symbolic program, estimates object-centric orientation bases from multi-view observations, performs anchor- and observer-specific geometric relation scoring, and constructs a reference-frame-aligned visual prompt for final VLM-based disambiguation. On Nr3D, OriGround improves over the strongest training-free baseline by 8.4 points in overall accuracy, with larger gains of 8.9 points on hard queries and 5.6 points on view-dependent queries. On ScanRefer, OriGround further improves overall Acc@0.5 by 17.3 points over VLM-Grounder. Project page: https://origround.github.io/

title: Intrinsic Attention as Navigator: A Non-Generative Retrieval Method for Multi-Hop Queries
author: Linwei Song; Weijie Zhang; WeiDi Chen; Huixia Lai; Shi Zhang; Ruliang Xiao
abstract: For multi-hop queries in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), it is crucial to accurately obtain evidence pieces. In this study, we propose a training-free method for multi-hop query retrieval, named Intrinsic Navigating-based Non-Generative Retrieval (IN-Retriever). Instead of generating intermediate reasoning text, the method extracts the bridging clue from the internal attention of the embedding model based on the current context and retrieved candidate documents. During iterative clue extraction and document retrieval, IN-Retriever strips away revealed clues from the embedded query vector and then reranks candidate documents in a targeted manner, thereby steering retrieval toward hidden next-hop evidence. In the experiments, we confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of using intrinsic attention signals to guide external multi-hop retrieval. Experimental results show that our method precisely collects sufficient documents to support multi-hop queries and significantly outperforms sparse and dense retrieval methods.

title: Emergent Backdoors in Agentic Recursive Training
author: Xuan Wang; Yuliang Lu; Kejiang Ye; Cheng-zhong Xu; Xitong Gao
abstract: Agentic recursive training systems increasingly reuse model-generated tasks, proxy feedback, and selected trajectories to refine policies over multiple rounds. This creates feedback loops in which small conditional biases can accumulate across training and alter later selection and updates. We study whether trigger-conditional proxy-feedback biases can produce emergent backdoors in a controlled recursive training loop. A Curriculum Agent proposes tasks, an Executor Agent generates rollouts, and environment feedback is selectively biased on rare markers, affecting reward, selection, and curriculum updates. Under matched biased supervision, Reward Hacking + SFT and Reward Hacking + RLHF reach 31.27% and 53.85% ASR, while the full loop reaches 97.62% at comparable clean accuracy. The effect persists across Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3-8B, BLIP-2-OPT-2.7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, transfers to GSM8K, BBH, and HotpotQA, extends to a tool-augmented setting, and is only partially reduced by post-hoc defenses. These results suggest that feedback and curriculum mechanisms in agentic recursive training should be audited for long-horizon bias amplification.

title: Meta-Prompt Optimization for LLM-Based Sequential Decision Making
author: Mingze Kong; Zhiyong Wang; Yao Shu; Zhongxiang Dai
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been employed as agents to solve sequential decision-making tasks such as Bayesian optimization and multi-armed bandits. These works usually adopt an LLM for sequential action selection by providing it with a fixed, manually designed meta-prompt. However, numerous previous works have found that the prompt has a significant impact on the performance of the LLM, which calls for a method to automatically optimize the meta-prompt for LLM-based agents. Unfortunately, the non-stationarity in the reward observations during LLM-based sequential decision making makes meta-prompt optimization highly challenging. To address this challenge, we draw inspirations from adversarial bandit algorithms, which are inherently capable of handling non-stationary reward observations. Building on this foundation, we propose our EXPonential-weight algorithm for prompt Optimization (EXPO) to automatically optimize the task description and meta-instruction in the meta-prompt for LLM-based agents. We also extend EXPO to additionally optimize the exemplars (i.e., history of interactions) in the meta-prompt to further enhance the performance, hence introducing our EXPO-ES algorithm. We use extensive experiments to show that our algorithms significantly improve the performance of LLM-based sequential decision making.

title: Adaptive Reasoning for Efficient Generative Retrieval
author: Yingchen Zhang; Ruqing Zhang; Jiafeng Guo; Wenjun Peng; Sen Li; Fuyu Lv; Xueqi Cheng
abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) retrieves documents by directly generating document identifiers (DocIDs) from queries using a sequence-to-sequence model. Recent reasoning-enhanced GR methods improve retrieval effectiveness by generating intermediate reasoning before DocID decoding. However, they typically apply reasoning uniformly to all queries, even though many queries can already be handled effectively through direct DocID decoding. This introduces unnecessary token generation and retrieval latency when reasoning provides little additional benefit. In this work, we propose Generative Retrieval with Adaptive Reasoning (GEAR), a retrieval framework that dynamically allocates reasoning computation based on query-specific needs. Instead of treating reasoning as a fixed pre-retrieval procedure, GEAR learns when to reason, what retrieval-oriented context to generate, and when to transition from free-form generation to constrained DocID decoding. This adaptive behavior is implemented through a learnable retrieval transition policy optimized jointly for retrieval quality and reasoning cost. Experiments on NQ, MS MARCO, and TREC DL 2022 show that GEAR maintains retrieval effectiveness comparable to strong reasoning-enhanced GR methods while substantially reducing reasoning overhead, triggering non-trivial reasoning for only 37.1% of queries and reducing both generated tokens and retrieval latency.

title: ConvDeck: Conversational Paper-to-Slide Generation via Stage-Specific User Feedback
author: Tarik Can Ozden; Sachidanand VS; Furkan Horoz; Ozgur Kara; Dilek Hakkani-Tür; Junho Kim; James Matthew Rehg
abstract: Automatic academic paper-to-slide generation is inherently iterative, because creating an effective presentation requires repeated cycles of generation, critique, and revision. Recent multi-agent systems partially acknowledge this through internal critique-and-revise loops, while conversational approaches allow users to refine generated slide decks through dialog. However, these refinement processes either remain largely closed to the user or introduce feedback only after a complete deck has been produced, limiting the user’s ability to participate in the iterative refinement of narrative flow, content allocation, and presentation emphasis. To address this gap, we introduce ConvDeck, a multi-agent pipeline for conversational paper-to-slide generation that distributes interaction across the pipeline through stage-specific loops, allowing users to iteratively refine both the presentation outline and the final slide deck at the stages where each kind of decision is made. These loops are driven by a refinement mechanism in which agents can think, speak, and act, enabling them to either directly apply edits or respond conversationally to clarify user feedback and discuss revision options. Our evaluation shows that stage-specific conversational feedback improves user-goal satisfaction while preserving narrative coherence, content quality, and visual presentation.

title: Small Models, Fewer Heads, More Forgetting: Sparse Attention Fine-Tuning for SLM Continual Learning
author: Hao Xu; Shezheng Song; Long Peng; Xiaodong Liu; Xiaopeng Li; Ma Jun; Shasha Li; Jie Yu
abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) have been widely deployed in edge computing and mobile devices. Generally, these models need to be continuously updated to adapt to dynamic environments and evolving user needs. Therefore, the performance of SLMs in continual learning has become a critical research focus. Compared to LLMs with rich redundant representation spaces, SLMs are more likely to overwrite previous representations during new task learning due to their fewer attention heads and layers. To address this issue, we propose LightLoRA, a sparse fine-tuning method specifically designed for SLMs. This method constructs a conflict-aware importance mechanism by combining raw importance from SVD decomposition with task conflict degrees based on gradient direction consistency. By selecting and updating heads that provide high contributions and low conflicts, LightLoRA successfully maintains sufficient space for knowledge preservation. Experimental results show that the proposed method reaches state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks without adding extra parameters. Code is released on https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LightLoRA-077C.

title: How Do We Engage with Other Disciplines? A Framework to Study Meaningful Interdisciplinary Discourse in Scholarly Publications
author: Bagyasree Sudharsan; Alexandria Leto; Maria Leonor Pacheco
abstract: With the rising popularity of interdisciplinary work, there is a growing need to understand how publications incorporate ideas from multiple disciplines. Existing computational approaches, such as affiliation diversity, keyword matching, and citation patterns, do not account for how individual citations are used to advance the citing work. Prior studies have proposed taxonomies to classify citation purpose. However, these frameworks are not well-suited to interdisciplinary research and do not provide general measures of engagement depth. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for evaluating citation engagement in scholarly publications. We introduce a citation purpose taxonomy tailored to interdisciplinary work, supported by an annotation study and model for automatically predicting a citation’s purpose. We then leverage signal from a citation’s purpose and the sections in which it appears to predict a single measure of how deeply a publication engages with a citation. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through a large-scale analysis of publications at the intersection of NLP and Computational Social Science.

title: Making Clinical Language Models Auditable: Concept-Guided Fine-Tuning for Robust Prediction
author: Jin Mu; Guanhua Chen
abstract: Clinical language models can achieve strong in-hospital accuracy yet fail under deployment shifts because they exploit note-specific artifacts (e.g., templates, separators, boilerplate) that do not reflect patient state. We propose CAST (Concept-guided Artifact Suppression Tuning), an SAE-based framework for auditable clinical text classification. CAST uses Sparse Autoencoders to expose sparse, human-auditable features from intermediate Transformer activations, labels SAE latents with an LLM-assisted interpretation pipeline and ICD-10 retrieval constraints, suppresses verified artifact latents via residual subtraction during fine-tuning, and provides post-hoc perconcept attributions for auditing model decisions. On MIMIC-IV discharge-note mortality prediction, CAST improves over its corresponding fine-tuned encoder baselines and remains competitive with strong LLM baselines, while producing a feature-level audit trail of the clinical concepts that support each prediction and the artifact concepts suppressed during training.

title: The Role of Entropy in Visual Grounding: Analysis and Optimization
author: Shuo Li; Jiajun Sun; Zhihao Zhang; Xiaoran Fan; Senjie Jin; Hui Li; Yuming Yang; Junjie Ye; Lixing Shen; Tao Ji; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xuanjing Huang
abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning–based fine-tuning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have highlighted the importance of entropy control for stable optimization. While entropy has been extensively studied in reasoning-centric settings, its behavior and optimization role in perception-oriented tasks remain insufficiently understood. In this work, we reveal that entropy exhibits fundamentally different roles in perception tasks compared to reasoning, particularly under continuous prediction and reward. Using visual grounding as a case study, we show that entropy can remain misaligned with optimization objectives due to persistent low-probability yet high-advantage samples. Building on these findings, we introduce ECVGPO (Entropy Control Visual Grounding Policy Optimization), an interpretable algorithm designed for effective entropy regulation. Through entropy control, the trade-off between exploration and exploitation is better balanced. Experiments show that ECVGPO achieves broad improvements across various benchmarks and models.

title: When the Specification Emerges: Benchmarking Faithfulness Loss in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
author: Lu Yan; Xuan Chen; Xiangyu Zhang
abstract: Current coding-agent benchmarks usually provide the full task specification upfront. Research-code implementation may instead re- quire an agent to preserve design commitments disclosed progressively across a long session. We introduce SLUMP, a controlled benchmark for testing implementation faithfulness when a mathematically structured machine-learning target is disclosed through synthetic, paper- grounded multi-turn interactions rather than in a single canonical implementation specification. The benchmark contains 20 recent ML papers, 371 atomic verifiable components, and approx- imately 60 coding requests per paper. An expo- sure audit verifies whether scored components are recoverable from the visible interaction. On Claude Code and Codex, the single-shot control achieves higher overall implementation fidelity on 16/20 and 14/20 papers, respectively. Struc- tural integration degrades under progressive dis- closure on both platforms, while semantic com- ponent faithfulness degrades substantially on Claude Code and remains approximately sta- ble on Codex. These conclusions persist under stricter exposure filters and a targeted human correction of judge false-absence errors. As a mitigation case study, ProjectGuard main- tains external semantic and structural project state and recovers 90% of Claude Code’s mea- sured faithfulness gap. Code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/lunaryan/drift-benchmark.

title: Sufficiency-Aware Adversarial Evidence Masking for Textual Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction in Conversations
author: Mengqiang Hu; Qian Chen; Xin Guo; Suge Wang
abstract: Textual Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction in Conversations (TECPE) requires identifying emotion utterances, their categories, and the textual cause spans that explain them. Although recent systems improve aggregate scores, clean supervision can induce evidence bias: models exploit explicit emotion cues, cause–emotion proximity, and speaker/discourse priors rather than evidence sufficient for causal explanation. We introduce \textbf{SAAM-EC}, a sufficiency-aware adversarial evidence masking framework for span-grounded TECPE. SAAM-EC adversarially masks high-impact conversational evidence units during training, but treats masking as a semantic intervention rather than a label-preserving perturbation. When masking removes the cause span or necessary bridge context, the original span may no longer be extractable or justified. SAAM-EC therefore combines adversarial masking with a sufficiency gate and an extractability guard, training masked examples to recover the original span only when the remaining dialogue still supports the emotion–cause relation and preserves the annotated span; otherwise, it trains the model with an unanswerability objective. All auxiliary components are discarded at inference, leaving the backbone unchanged. Experiments on span-level TECPE and utterance-level ECPE benchmarks show consistent performance gains over clean backbones and masking-based alternatives. Diagnostics further show better recovery on distant and cross-speaker causes and stronger abstention under destructive masks.

title: TCHV: Type-Conditioned Hypothesis Verification for Multimodal Named Entity Recognition
author: Feiyu Han; Yang Liu; Yongxiu Xu; Yixiao Jiang; Zhaoqi Zhou; Chuan Zhou
abstract: Multimodal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) uses supplementary images to resolve ambiguity in entity mentions in noisy, short-form social-media text. Prevailing approaches typically fuse text with visually aligned features, but such cues often lack sufficient discriminative power and may support conflicting entity-type hypotheses. To address this issue, we propose TCHV, a lightweight framework grounded in a type-conditioned hypothesis-verification perspective. By formulating each span-type pair as a distinct hypothesis during inference, TCHV predicts the latent feature evidence expected under each hypothesis and validates it against observed multimodal representations through bidirectional text-image matching, using a visual relevance gate to suppress unin- formative images. Verification scores serve as surrogate evidence statistics; TCHV improves over established non-VLLM multimodal baselines on Twitter-2015/2017, and TCHV† leads the compared VLLM-based methods on Twitter-2017. Extensions demonstrate applicability to grounded and fine-grained settings. Code: https://github.com/ hanfeiyu703/ImaginE.git.

title: From Benchmarking to Failure Diagnosis: Diagnosing Classical Chinese Understanding in LLMs via IRT and Error Attribution
author: Jiong Wang; Tengju Li; Shengquan Yu
abstract: Literary Chinese reading comprehension is a challenging task for large language models (LLMs), requiring understanding of implicit meanings, contextual reasoning, and discourse-level integration in a low-resource setting. However, existing evaluations rely primarily on aggregate accuracy, which provides limited insight into model capabilities, error sources, and reliability under uncertainty. We propose DELit, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond aggregate metrics by introducing a hierarchical capability–error taxonomy, a Deep-MIRT-based ability estimation model, and a capability-decoupled residual analysis for behavioral diagnosis. Together, these components enable fine-grained interpretation of model performance at both capability and error-type levels. Experiments on mainstream LLMs reveal that (i) discourse-level understanding remains a consistent bottleneck despite strong performance on local semantic tasks; (ii) similar overall accuracy can correspond to substantially different capability profiles; and (iii) overconfident errors on difficult items concentrate on logically constrained reasoning, highlighting reliability risks that are not captured by standard evaluation metrics.

title: Proactive for Uncertainty: Cause-Aware Error Diagnosis and Interactive Clarification for Spoken Dialogue Systems
author: Yizhou Peng; Ziyang Ma; Changsong Liu; Yi-Wen Chao; Xie Chen; Eng Siong Chng
abstract: Cascaded Automatic Speech Recognition — Large Language Model (ASR-LLM) pipelines remain popular for industrial Spoken Dialogue Systems (SDS), primarily because their decoupled design ensures perceptual verifiability. However, cascaded systems suffer from error propagation, as transcription failures inevitably cascade to subsequent components, thereby degrading the final interaction quality. Although ASR confidence scores offer a simple filter for unreliable inputs, this approach is fundamentally limited because it typically fails to detect deletion errors or to distinguish between acoustic (inability to hear clearly) and linguistic (inability to understand) mismatches, both of which require targeted recovery strategies. In this paper, we propose a cause-aware error recovery paradigm that fundamentally rethinks robustness in SDS. Unlike traditional confidence filtering, we introduce a suite of small precision-focused detectors that exploit deep ASR latent representations to disentangle token-level errors into perception, comprehension, and deletion failures. This fine-grained diagnostic intelligence empowers the LLM to orchestrate targeted, multi-turn clarification strategies, effectively transforming ambiguous signals into seamless user interactions. Experimental results validate the precision of our approach, which more than doubles the recall on domain-shift errors (57.96% vs. 23.66%) compared to baselines. Crucially, this diagnostic precision yields up to a 31% reduction in WER and a 19% improvement on the downstream task across diverse accents, distortions, and domains.

title: Hidden Threat in Synthetic Data: Covert Targeted Bias Injection through Benign Text
author: Minkyung Cho; Jihyo Kim; SeungWoo Song; Junghun Yuk; Minjoon Kee; Hoyun Song; KyungTae Lim
abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used to train large language models (LLMs), yet its security implications remain poorly understood. Prior work on subliminal learning suggests that models can inherit behavioral traits from seemingly unrelated training data. In this work, we investigate whether such mechanisms can be exploited to inject targeted social biases into aligned models through semantically benign synthetic data. We construct a pipeline in which a misaligned teacher model generates filtered synthetic datasets across domains such as creative writing and code generation, which are then used to fine-tune aligned student models. Our experiments show that benign-looking synthetic data can act as a covert channel for transmitting targeted biases while largely preserving the student model’s general task capabilities. These results reveal a previously underexplored security risk in synthetic data–driven LLM training pipelines and highlight the need for improved safeguards. As one possible step toward this goal, we suggest that log-linearity-based scoring may provide a useful signal for screening seemingly benign synthetic data.

title: AgSynth: A Multi-Agent Reverse Synthesis Framework for Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning Data Generation
author: Yaxuan Wang; Lingfeng Zeng; Jiatu Hu; Guojie Lin; Boyu Yang; Bing Zhao; Lin Qu; hu Wei
abstract: Multimodal large language models show significant potential in mathematical reasoning, yet they remain constrained by a scarcity of high-quality training data for visually grounded problems. Existing approaches commonly suffer from narrow coverage, image-text inconsistency, and heavy imitation of seed problems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes AgSynth, a multi-agent collaborative reverse synthesis framework. It first constructs solution logic programmatically and renders the corresponding images, then generates problem statements backward from the visual facts, thereby embedding answer correctness and image-text consistency directly into the generation pipeline. Meanwhile, AgSynth distills the core competencies tested in seed problems and performs divergent reconstruction, enabling synthesized problems to be substantially novel in both structure and visual presentation. Based on this framework, we construct the AgSynth-10K dataset, comprising 10{,}477 multimodal mathematical reasoning problems that have undergone two-tier quality control, spanning four major domains: geometry, algebra, combinatorics, and number theory. Experiments demonstrate that reinforcement learning training on AgSynth-10K significantly improves model performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks (WeMath +7.42, LogicVista+9.15), validating the effectiveness of this traceable synthesis paradigm. The framework is publicly available at https://github.com/Yaxuan7690/AgSynth.

title: Compressing Only What Is Compressible: Memory-Efficient Multiscale Muon via Selective Low-Rank Projection
author: Ren Lianhai; Yeyun Gong
abstract: Multiscale Muon maintains K momentum EMAs at different decay rates \beta_k, doubling or tripling the optimizer-state memory of Muon. We show that the EMA update is a first-order low-pass filter and Multiscale Muon is therefore a filter bank on the gradient stream, with each band tuned to a different temporal scale. Under this view, the empirical fact that Multiscale Muon outperforms any single-\beta filter is a direct consequence of multi-band coverage; and a sharp, asymmetric compressibility property follows from the bandwidth—the narrow-band (high-\beta) buffer is dominated by the slow, low-rank component of the gradient and is safe to project, while the wide-band (low-\beta) buffer carries high-frequency content whose effective rank is large and cannot be compressed without hurting convergence. We formalize this asymmetry, instantiate it in SMuG (Selective Multiscale Muon with GaLore) by applying GaLore only to high-\beta buffers, and prove an algebraic impossibility result ruling out any non-negative linear spectral score from predicting the band-mixing coefficient \lambda^\star in closed form. On 200,M GPT-2 pretraining (n{=}4 seeds), SMuG (K{=}2, r/n{=}0.125) reaches PPL 21.66{\pm}0.05, statistically tied with full-rank Multiscale Muon (21.69{\pm}0.03), at 1.25\times Muon’s optimizer memory (including the persistent GaLore basis V) versus 2.00\times for full Multiscale Muon—recovering 75% of the added overhead at no average quality cost.

title: Diffusion-Proof: Recipe for Formal Theorem Proving Beyond Auto-Regressive Generation
author: Ruida Wang; Rui Pan; Pengcheng Wang; Shizhe Diao; Tong Zhang
abstract: Enhancing the formal math reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) has become a key focus in both mathematical and computer science communities in recent years. While significant progress has been made in using state-of-the-art Auto-Regressive (AR) LLMs for formal theorem proving, these models suffer from inherent limitations. Their next-token prediction generation methods may yield suboptimal performance due to the challenges of long-range coherence and the compounding of errors over long sequences. Recent advancements in diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which generate text through iterative denoising of a multi-token block, offer a promising alternative. However, the application of dLLMs to formal mathematics, where maintaining long-range coherence is critical, remains largely understudied. To address the challenges above, we propose Diffusion-Proof, to the best of our knowledge, the first framework to train and apply dLLMs for formal theorem proving. Our frameworks contain training and inference methods for two models. The first one is dLLM-Prover-7B, which performs whole-proof writing with long-range coherent tactic usage. The second one is dLLM-Corrector-7B, which is a novel large block diffusion-based correction model. It leverages the in-filling capabilities of dLLMs to perform local proof correction using bi-directional information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Diffusion-Proof relatively significantly outperforms the AR LLM baseline trained under the same dataset. Diffusion-Proof achieves an absolute improvement of 1.61% on ProofNet-Test and 6.14% on MiniF2F-Test benchmarks compare to the baseline. Notably, Diffusion-Proof successfully resolves one IMO problem that more advanced thinking model DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B could not solve, showcasing the unique advantage of dLLMs in formal theorem proving.

title: Can Large Language Models Still Explain Themselves? Investigating the Impact of Quantization on Self-Explanations
author: Qianli Wang; Nils Feldhus; Pepa Atanasova; Fedor Splitt; Simon Ostermann; Sebastian Möller; Vera Schmitt
abstract: Quantization is widely used to accelerate inference and streamline the deployment of large language models (LLMs), yet its effects on self-explanations (SEs) remain unexplored. SEs, generated by LLMs to justify their own outputs, require reasoning about the model’s own decision-making process, a capability that may exhibit particular sensitivity to quantization. As SEs are increasingly relied upon for transparency in high-stakes applications, understanding whether and to what extent quantization degrades SE quality and faithfulness is critical. To address this gap, we examine two types of SEs: natural language explanations (NLEs) and counterfactual examples, generated by LLMs quantized using three common techniques at distinct bit widths. Our findings indicate that quantization typically leads to moderate declines in both SE quality (up to 4.4%) and faithfulness (up to 2.38%). The user study further demonstrates that quantization diminishes both the coherence and trustworthiness of SEs (up to 8.5%). Compared to smaller models, larger models show limited resilience to quantization in terms of SE quality but better maintain faithfulness. Moreover, no quantization technique consistently excels across task accuracy, SE quality, and faithfulness. Given that quantization’s impact varies by context, we recommend validating SE quality for specific use cases, especially for NLEs, which show greater sensitivity. Nonetheless, the relatively minor deterioration in SE quality and faithfulness does not undermine quantization’s effectiveness as a model compression technique.

title: Seeing with You: Perception-Reasoning Co-evolution for Multimodal Reasoning
author: Ziqi Miao; Haonan Jia; Lijun Li; Chen Qian; Yuan Xiong; Wenting Yan; Jing Shao
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially enhanced the reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing RLVR approaches typically rely on outcome-driven optimization that updates both perception and reasoning using a shared reward based solely on the final answer. This shared reward blurs credit assignment, frequently improving reasoning patterns while failing to reliably enhance the accuracy of upstream visual evidence extraction. To address this perception bottleneck, we introduce PRCO (Perception-Reasoning Co-evolution), a dual-role RLVR framework with a shared policy. PRCO consists of two cooperative roles: an Observer that generates an evidence caption tailored to the question and a Solver that predicts the final answer based on this caption. Crucially, PRCO employs role-specific reward signals: the Solver is optimized using verifiable outcome rewards on the final answer, while the Observer receives a utility reward derived from the Solver’s downstream success. Extensive experiments across eight challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PRCO yields consistent improvements across model scales by over 7 points on average accuracy compared to the base model, outperforming prior open-source RL-tuned baselines.

title: FinGuard: Detecting Financial Regulatory Non-Compliance in LLM Interactions
author: Huaixia Dou; Jie Zhu; Minghao Wu; Shuo Jiang; Junhui Li; Lifan Guo; Feng Chen; Chi Zhang
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in financial services, a single non-compliant interaction can expose institutions to regulatory penalties and direct consumer harm. Existing guard models are built around general harm taxonomies and overlook violations grounded in specific financial regulations. We address this gap with a regulation-driven pipeline that operates directly on regulatory documents, inducing a financial compliance risk taxonomy and synthesizing grounded training data without any predefined violation categories. Instantiating the pipeline on Chinese financial regulations, we release \textbf{FinGuard-Bench}, to our knowledge the first benchmark for financial regulatory compliance detection, with expert-annotated labels at both the query and response levels. We further train \textbf{FinGuard}, a financial compliance detection model built on Qwen3-8B and trained on the regulation-grounded data via supervised fine-tuning and self-play reinforcement learning. On FinGuard-Bench, FinGuard substantially outperforms all baselines, including dedicated guard models and much larger general-purpose LLMs such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and GPT-5.1. Furthermore, FinGuard also preserves general safety capabilities and adapts to unseen institution-specific policies using policy documents alone. We will publicly release the code, prompts, and resources used in this work on GitHub.

title: Multi-Faceted Interactivity Alignment in Full-Duplex Speech Models
author: Atsumoto Ohashi; Neil Zeghidour; Alexandre Défossez; Eugene Kharitonov
abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models can listen and speak simultaneously, making them a promising architecture for natural conversation. However, current models are trained solely with supervised learning through token-level likelihood maximization, which does not directly optimize interaction-level behaviors, causing interactivity issues such as excessive silence and ill-timed turn-taking. Recent work has applied reinforcement learning (RL) to improve interactivity, but existing methods address only a limited set of interactive behaviors in their rewards. In this work, we propose a post-training alignment method that comprehensively improves the interactivity of full-duplex spoken dialogue models through RL. We address the four canonical axes of interactivity: pause handling, turn-taking, backchanneling, and user interruption. For each axis, we extract short audio segments from human conversation corpora and optimize the model with axis-specific reward functions. An extra LLM-based reward for response quality prevents semantic degradation. We apply our method to two open-source models, Moshi and PersonaPlex, demonstrating consistent improvements in interactivity on both offline evaluation with pre-recorded audio and real-time multi-turn dialogue evaluation.

title: STAMP: Provenance-Guided Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
author: Ke Xu; Han Xu; Xinran Chen; Yuqian Wang; Zhixuan Li; Xiaojian Liu; Changwo Wu; Jianqiang Xia; Yuchen Li
abstract: Reinforcement learning for deep-search agents has largely focused on trajectory-level scoring—outcome correctness, citation-aware rewards, and evidence coverage. Yet the actions that expose supporting documents receive no targeted credit, a gap we call the reward-credit mismatch. We propose STAMP, in which a reference-based verifier judges whether each cited document supports an entity or relation in a training-time evidence graph, and first-exposure attribution traces each supported citation back to the action that first surfaced it. This step credit is injected through sign-preserving advantage modulation, which redistributes advantage across steps without changing the trajectory-level reward or the relative ranking of trajectories within each group. On BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, and xbench-DS, STAMP improves the strongest GRPO baseline by +2.0/+5.5/+3.0 points under matched SFT initialization, training data, and search tools, and composes with both outcome-only and citation-rubric base rewards. Component ablations confirm that the provenance-based credit signal and the sign-preserving advantage modulation each contribute to the gains.

title: Pigeonholing: how bad prompts hurt models, causing collapse and mistakes
author: HyunJi Nam; Keertana Chidambaram; Dorottya Demszky; Natasha Jaques
abstract: While in-context learning is generally shown to be effective for Large Language Models (LLMs), misleading or flawed contexts can cause performance degradation and mode collapse, an empirical phenomenon we term "pigeonholing". Unintentionally bad contexts can happen without jailbreak intent. For example, a user prompts the model to justify an incorrect math theorem or fails to correct buggy agent code. Specifically, we investigate pigeonholing in two settings: (1) when a user suggests an incorrect solution, and (2) when the multi-turn dialogue history contains the assistant’s incorrect answers from prior turns. Our evaluations across 10 verifiable and open-ended tasks with 10 different models show that pigeonholing manifests in three distinct ways: (1) repeating the incorrect answers from the context (causing a 38-40% performance drop), (2) reducing answer diversity in open-ended text generation, and (3) reversing stances on controversial topics to align with the previous user or assistant’s perspective. Further, we find that pigeonholing worsens almost monotonically with context length (i.e., conversation turns). Finally, while standard RLVR-trained models show improvements on clean prompts, they fail to maintain performance on corrupted contexts. We take a step towards mitigating model vulnerability by training with RLVR on synthetic errors, improving model performance on bad contexts by 43–60% over vanilla baselines.

title: SAFE: An LLM-as-Verifier Framework for Evidence-Grounded Multi-Hop Reasoning
author: Daeyong Kwon; Soyoung Yoon; Seung-Won Hwang
abstract: Multi-hop QA benchmarks often reward Large Language Models (LLMs) for spurious correctness, where models reach correct answers through invalid intermediate reasoning. We propose SAFE, an LLM-as-verifier framework for evidence-grounded multi-hop QA. Rather than judging only the final answer after generation, SAFE verifies reasoning during generation by checking intermediate steps against the provided passages and previous reasoning trajectory. To make this process checkable, SAFE decomposes reasoning into atomic, evidence-grounded units represented with Knowledge Graph (KG) triples. At train-time, SAFE verifies benchmark supervision under KG-grounded constraints and constructs reliable verifier training data. At inference-time, an external verifier checks each generated step, identifies invalid reasoning, and provides correction feedback before errors propagate. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, SAFE improves accuracy by 8.8 pp on average. These results show that evidence-grounded multi-hop QA benefits from shifting LLM-based evaluation from post-hoc answer judgment to stepwise reasoning verification.

title: FactNLI: Dynamic and Automated Fact-Based Augmentation of NLI Benchmarks
author: Yihan Lu; Junzhe Zhang; Huixuan Zhang; Xiaojun Wan
abstract: Natural Language Inference (NLI) is a core task for language understanding, yet existing NLI datasets are static and increasingly saturated, allowing current Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform well without fully revealing their capabilities and shortcomings. To address this problem, we propose a new data augmentation framework that automatically builds more challenging NLI datasets by iteratively fusing rich facts into the premise and hypothesis of an NLI instance. We use a strict fact filter to ensure that fused facts are non-contradictory and non-redundant. Applied to SNLI and MNLI, our augmentation substantially increases data length and complexity, and the performance of a range of LLMs on the augmented datasets drops significantly (up to 30%). Ablation experiments and human quality checks confirm the high quality of the generated data.

title: Reconstructing the Right Episode: Evaluating Interleaved Conversational Memory Beyond Long Context
author: Zhexi Feng; Ruiyi Zhang; Yongbo Yang; Pengtao Xie
abstract: Conversations with chat assistants increasingly span many topics in a single long-running thread, challenging memory systems. Existing long-context and memory benchmarks often expose session or topic boundaries, or probe direct personal-memory questions. These settings understate a harder assistant-memory regime: a flat mixed-topic thread where the system must infer which earlier episode makes a later task decision valid. We introduce SCALE-QA, a constraint-grounded task QA benchmark for flat unsegmented threads targeting episode integrity failure. The dataset contains 3,000 audited questions across 10 domains, uses deterministic four-way multiple-choice grading, and includes a deterministic runtime builder; experiments use all 3,000 questions through 128k and a stratified 400-question diagnostic at 1M. SCALE-QA questions are ordinary task-oriented requests whose correct answer depends on causally related evidence introduced earlier in the conversation. We also propose Temporal-Semantic Interleaved Memory Reconstruction (TSIM), which segments the turn stream into coherent episodes and indexes them through a hierarchical multi-view memory stack with deterministic episode-level summary and cluster-routing views. Experiments show that SCALE-QA challenges strong RAG baselines and long-context LLMs alike; across three open-source and proprietary LLM backends, TSIM achieves the highest accuracy in every backend setting, gaining 5.6–17.6 accuracy points over the strongest corresponding baseline.

title: ForeDreamer: A Self-Evolving Dual-Agent Memory Architecture for Future Event Prediction
author: Linhao Zhong; Zongze Du; Linyu Wu; Yu Bo; Hourong Li; Chenchen Jing; Hao Chen; Yuling Xi; Chunhua Shen
abstract: Open-web future event prediction requires agents to distill reliable signals from noisy, redundant, and incomplete evidence. Existing retrieval/memory mechanisms directly feed retrieved information to agents or rely on simple memory functions such as storing and reusing prior information for prediction, leaving them insufficient for open-web forecasting. We propose to transform raw web evidence into structured memory before prediction, enabling agents to reason over distilled, question-specific evidence rather than noisy retrieval results. This paper presents ForeDreamer, a self-evolving dual-agent framework for managing memory over open-web evidence. ForeDreamer separates factual memory, a question-specific evidence state for the current forecast, from experiential memory, persistent agent experience accumulated across forecasting episodes. It uses a main agent for search and prediction, and a memory-processing subagent to convert search results into factual memory with dedicated tools. ForeDreamer further evolves experiential memory through two tracks, improving both forecasting decisions and factual-memory construction. Experiments on Prophet Arena and FutureX demonstrate the effectiveness of ForeDreamer.

title: MM-VeriRubric: Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Rubrics for Multimodal Reward Models
author: Zhiyong Cao; Bo Wang; Jintao Li; Shuxia Liu; Kairan Zhang; Aijia Wang; Yi-Liang Wei; Sicheng Zhou
abstract: Reward modeling is essential for multimodal alignment, yet most existing reward models only provide outcome reward, which is sparse and fails to capture human preferences. Rubrics can provide structured and fine grained evaluation signals, but building effective rubrics for multimodal tasks is challenging. In this work, we propose **MM-VeriRubric**, a framework for scalable construction of training data for multimodal rubric generation and rubric-based reward models. To better use visual evidence in images, we introduce task-aware visual clue extraction, which makes rubric generation more grounded in task-relevant visual information. MM-VeriRubric then generates evidence-grounded rubrics and constructs rubric-aligned rejected responses with controlled error dimensions, enabling the quality of each rubric to be verified through consistency checking. The verified data are used to train both a rubric generator and a rubric-based reward model. Experiments on multimodal reward model benchmarks and downstream Best of N tasks show that MM-VeriRubric improves preference judgment (+16.4% on VL-RewardBench) and provides more interpretable and diagnostic reward signals for multimodal alignment (+13.1% on MMMU-Pro using Best of 5 selection). Code is available at: https://github.com/TraceLite-AI/MM-VeriRubric.

title: Agent Planning Benchmark: A Diagnostic Framework for Planning Capabilities in LLM Agents
author: Haoyu Sun; Wenxuan Wang; Mingyang Song; Jujie He; Weinan Zhang; Yang Liu; Yang Yang; Yu Cheng
abstract: Planning is central to LLM agents: before acting, an agent must decompose goals, select tools, reason over constraints, and decide when a task is infeasible. Yet existing agent evaluations often report only end-to-end success, making it difficult to determine whether failures stem from planning or execution. We introduce Agent Planning Benchmark (APB), a planning-specific diagnostic benchmark with 4,209 multimodal cases across 22 domains and five settings, covering holistic planning, feedback-conditioned step-wise planning, and robustness under extraneous tools, broken tools, and unsolvable tasks. Across 12 MLLMs, APB reveals systematic weaknesses in long-horizon planning, tool-noise robustness, calibrated refusal, and inference-time refinement. We further validate APB on 200 ToolSandbox tasks and 200 \tau^2-bench tasks, where APB-guided refinement consistently improves plan correctness, plan grade, and downstream execution metrics across three representative models. APB thus serves as an upstream diagnostic complement to execution benchmarks. The APB benchmark and code are available in this URL.

title: AU-Harness: An Open-Source Toolkit for Efficient and Unified Evaluation of AudioLLMs
author: Hoang H Nguyen; Sidharth Surapaneni; Akshay Kalkunte Suresh; Jash Mehta; Aman Tiwari; Oluwanifemi Bamgbose; Khyati Mahajan; Jash Shah; Shruthan Radhakrishna; Sathwik Tejaswi Madhusudhan; Vikas Yadav; Sai Rajeswar
abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) are rapidly advancing, but evaluating them remains challenging due to inefficient and non-standardized toolkits that limit fair comparison and systematic assessment. Existing evaluation frameworks exhibit three critical limitations: (1) slow and inefficient processing pipeline that bottlenecks large-scale studies, (2) inadequate multi-turn dialogue support, leaving fundamental questions about cross-turn context integration and performance dynamics over extended conversations in LALMs unanswered; and (3) the absence of unified and scalable evaluation framework capable of keeping pace with the rapid growth of both LALMs and audio benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce **AU-Harness**, an efficient and comprehensive evaluation framework for LALMs. Our empirical studies demonstrate that AU-Harness achieves 77% reduction in evaluation processing time over existing evaluation toolkits, enabling large-scale LALM evaluations previously considered impractical. We provide standardized evaluation protocols and flexible configurations for fair model comparison across diverse scenarios. AU-Harness unlocks a range of in-depth analyses difficult to conduct without a unified foundation, including multi-turn dialogue dynamics, enabling the study of true audio reasoning capabilities in existing LALMs. AU-Harness provides both practical evaluation tools and insights into model limitations, advancing systematic LALM development.

title: Omanic: Towards Step-wise Evaluation of Multi-hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
author: Xiaojie Gu; Sherry T. Tong; Aosong Feng; Sophia Simeng Han; Jinghui Lu; Yingjian Chen; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo; Chanjun Park; Rex Ying; Irene Li
abstract: Evaluating the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) solely from final answers can obscure failures in intermediate steps, especially in multi-hop QA benchmarks without step-level annotations. To address this gap, we introduce Omanic, an open-domain 4-hop QA benchmark designed not only to measure final-answer accuracy but also to diagnose where reasoning breaks down. Omanic contains 10,296 machine-generated training examples (OmanicSynth) and 967 expert-reviewed human-annotated evaluation examples (OmanicBench), with each evaluation question decomposed into single-hop sub-questions, intermediate answers, and structured graph topologies. Experiments with proprietary and open-source LLMs show that Omanic is challenging, while step-wise analysis reveals a later-hop bottleneck, factual knowledge floor, and error propagation along reasoning chains. Fine-tuning on OmanicSynth transfers to six reasoning and mathematics benchmarks, yielding a 7.41-point average gain and validating its effectiveness as supervision for reasoning-capability transfer. We release the data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/li-lab/Omanic.

title: P-Search: A Parallel Plan–Act–Verify Framework with Decoupled GRPO for Deep Research
author: Pin Zheng; Yibo Xue; Ming Wang; Yukun Kang; Haonan Zheng; Chengyu Wang; Jian Peng; Jun Huang; Changliang Xu
abstract: Open-web deep research is limited not only by how long an agent searches, but also by how it organizes evidence into independent, verifiable branches. Existing systems often scale single-path ReAct trajectories or long-context search, which can deepen one hypothesis while leaving alternative entities, constraints, or falsifying evidence underexplored. We propose P-Search, a parallel plan–act–verify framework that first builds a grounded background state, then decomposes the task into independently executable evidence branches, runs branch-specific search agents in parallel, and iteratively verifies unresolved constraints before final synthesis. For training, we avoid end-to-end credit assignment over a full multi-stage rollout. Instead, P-Search-React learns reusable grounded search-report behavior from raw-question search instances and is reused for branch execution and targeted supplementary search, while P-Search-Plan learns schema-constrained routing, decomposition, and verification decisions. We supervise this structure with star-shaped subgraph data and role-specific GRPO rewards. Experiments show that instantiating P-Search with open-source backbones such as GLM-5 and Tongyi-DR-30B improves their reported baselines on most open-web benchmarks, while the trained 8B P-Search-React + P-Search-Plan system reaches 59.2% on GAIA and 70.0% on Xbench-DeepSearch. Ablations confirm the complementary roles of Plan, ReAct, and Verify, as well as the transferability of the trained planner across ReAct backbones.

title: How Much Do LLMs Know About Chinese Zero Pronouns?
author: Yifei Li; Guanyi Chen; Tingting He
abstract: Zero Pronouns (ZPs) are a pervasive linguistic phenomenon in pro-drop languages such as Chinese and have long posed a challenge for natural language processing systems. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on many Chinese language tasks, their ability to process ZPs remains poorly understood. We conduct a systematic investigation of LLMs’ handling of Chinese ZPs through a sequence of linguistically motivated tasks, including identification, referentiality classification, referential type classification, resolution, and translation. A diverse set of LLMs is evaluated across all tasks. Our results show that Chinese ZPs remain highly challenging for current LLMs, particularly for upstream tasks such as identification and referentiality classification. Performance on downstream tasks, such as ZP translation, is also consistently low: even state-of-the-art reasoning-oriented LLMs correctly translate fewer than half of Chinese ZPs into English.

title: UCO: A Multi-Turn Interactive Reinforcement Learning Method for Adaptive Teaching with Large Language Models
author: Shouang Wei; Min Zhang; Xin Lin; Bo Jiang; Kun Kuang; Jingyuan Chen; Zhongxiang Dai
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are shifting from answer providers to intelligent tutors in educational settings. However, current supervised fine-tuning methods only learn surface-level teaching patterns without dynamic adaptation. Recent reinforcement learning approaches address this, yet two key challenges remain. First, they evaluate teaching effectiveness solely based on whether students produce correct outputs, unable to distinguish whether students genuinely understand or echo teacher-provided answers. Second, they cannot perceive students’ evolving cognitive states through dialogue, failing to adapt teaching strategies accordingly. We propose Unidirectional Cognitive Optimization (UCO) to address these challenges. UCO employs a multi-turn interactive reinforcement learning paradigm with two synergistic reward functions: the Progress Reward captures cognitive advancement, evaluating students’ transition from confusion to comprehension, and the Scaffold Reward dynamically identifies each student’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), encouraging the teacher to conduct productive teaching within this zone. We evaluate UCO against 11 baseline models on BigMath and MathTutorBench. Results demonstrate that UCO outperforms all equivalent-scale models and achieves performance comparable to leading closed-source models. Code is available at https://github.com/ECNU-RAIL/UCO-EMNLP2026.

title: DynSess: Dynamic Session-Level Evaluation and Optimization Framework for Role-Playing Agents
author: Rongsheng Zhang; Jiji Tang; Junnan Ren; Zuyi Bao; Weijie Chen; Ruofan Hu; Tangjie Lv; Zhou Zhao; Yan Zhang
abstract: Role-playing with large language models is fundamentally a *session-level* task, requiring agents to sustain character identity and interaction quality across extended multi-turn conversations. Yet existing evaluation and optimization methods remain largely turn-level, failing to capture long-horizon quality. We propose **DynSess**, a unified session-level framework for role-playing agents. **DynSess-Eval** scores complete dialogue sessions via rubrics targeting long-horizon behaviors. Leveraging its session-level rewards, we construct high-quality training trajectories through multi-turn lookahead search and train **DynSess-Character** with two complementary variants: DSPO (off-policy) and GSRPO (on-policy). Experiments show that DynSess-Eval aligns with human judgments substantially better than prior evaluators, and blind human evaluation further shows that DynSess-Character matches the strongest character model despite using substantially fewer parameters, while maintaining strong role consistency and interactive ability. The dataset and code are publicly available in https://github.com/Collab-Gen/DynSess.

title: When Attention Escapes: Diagnosing and Mitigating Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: Wencheng Su; Qinglong Wang; Zhongjie Ba; Zhixuan Chu; Zhenyu Zhong; Liu Yan; Kui Ren
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations by grounding generation in retrieved evidence, yet failures persist when models underutilize the retrieved context. While prior work attributes this to conflicts between external context and internal parametric knowledge encoded in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs), our empirical analyses reveal that FFN-derived signals are unstable and insufficient for reliable diagnosis across diverse contexts. We therefore propose the Attention Escape Score (AES), a training-free diagnostic framework that provides a mechanistic lens on RAG hallucinations via dynamic attention routing failures. We models the failures as weakened Semantic Anchoring, increased Contextual Distraction, and heightened Generation Inertia, moving beyond static component-level analyses. Extensive experiments show that AES significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with robust cross-model generalization. Furthermore, we introduce Pruning Escape Routes (PER), a lightweight inference-time intervention that suppresses hallucinations by attenuating identified escape pathways, achieving improved faithfulness with negligible degradation to complex reasoning and general capabilities.

title: Role Consistency in Role-Playing Agents: A Survey of Evaluation, Memory, Reasoning, Alignment, and Safety
author: Chenghao Li; Xueqin Xiao; Yinuo Xiao; Zihan Xu; Xinzhao Li; Yuxuan Luan; Jiwei Wei; Yang Yang; Chaoning Zhang
abstract: Large language models have made role-playing agents viable as interactive characters, virtual companions, game agents, and social actors. The harder problem, however, is not producing one convincing response but sustaining a coherent role through long, changing, and sometimes adversarial interactions. This survey examines recent work on role consistency: the maintenance of identity, character knowledge, expressive style, memory, values, behavioral logic, and safety boundaries over time. We organize the literature around role specification, role-state maintenance, role-aware reasoning, role-consistent alignment, and evaluation.

title: Doc2Weight: In-Weights Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Parameter Injection
author: GyuSik Jang; Wonkee Lee; Seung-Hoon Na
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically incorporates external knowledge by appending retrieved documents to the input prompt. While effective for knowledge-intensive tasks, this in-context formulation increases memory use and serving cost as the retrieved context grows. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Doc2Weight, an in-weights RAG framework that injects retrieved information into model parameters rather than the textual context. Doc2Weight converts retrieved documents into parameter-efficient low-rank updates and fuses them in weight space according to their relevance to the query. This enables retrieval augmentation with a query-only prompt, decoupling retrieval depth from prompt length while allowing multiple retrieved passages to influence generation within a single forward pass. We evaluate Doc2Weight on instruction-tuned language models of different scales, including LLaMA-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and LLaMA-3-8B, across major QA benchmarks. Experiments show that Doc2Weight achieves the best average F1 among standard in-context RAG and prior in-weights RAG baselines across backbones and prompting settings, while matching the throughput of in-context RAG once document signatures are cached. Our code is publicly available.

title: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
author: Zefeng Wu; Weiwei Qi; Jielong Chen; Tianhang Zheng; Di Hong; Chaochao Lu; Liang He; Zhan Qin; Kui Ren
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs.Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6% with sample filtering and 32.3% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

title: ChemVA: Bridging Visual and Semantic Gaps in Multimodal LLM Chemical Diagram Reasoning
author: Mingyang Rao; Kehua Feng; Zhihui Zhu; Jiangzhen Fu; Hao Yu; Keyan Ding; Huajun Chen
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized scientific text processing, they exhibit a significant capability gap when interpreting chemical reaction diagrams. We identify two bottlenecks restricting current systems: a Visual Deficit, where generic vision encoders struggle to resolve the strict topological connectivity of dense molecular graphs, and a Semantic Disconnect, where standard linear strings (e.g., SMILES), although structurally precise, are often poorly aligned with the chemical semantic abstractions used by LLMs for reasoning. To bridge these gaps, we propose the Chemical Visual Activation (ChemVA) framework, which employs a novel Visual Anchor mechanism to ground functional groups via hybrid-granularity detection, followed by a semantic alignment approach that translates recognized structures into language-accessible chemical representations for downstream LLM reasoning. We evaluate our approach on OCRD-Bench, a newly constructed benchmark spanning recognition, chemical knowledge, and mechanistic reasoning. Experiments show that ChemVA achieves 92.0% structural recognition accuracy. It further delivers a consistent performance gain of approximately 20 percentage points across 9 diverse LLMs, allowing open-weights models to approach strong proprietary systems on complex chemical reasoning tasks.

title: When Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty Remember They Are on the Same Team
author: Gautam Siddharth Kashyap; Mark Dras; Usman Naseem
abstract: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) requires simultaneously satisfying Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty (HHH). Existing works-including SFT, MoEs, RLHF, and orchestrator-based steering-operate on standard 1-to-1 transformer architectures and show systematic trade-offs across objectives. While such works can steer behaviour post hoc, they remain fundamentally additive and therefore suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While recent mechanistic interpretability have helped characterise this behaviour, they expose a deeper structural failure-transformers lack an mechanism to negotiate incompatible objective signals, resulting in a mechanistic blind-spot. Therefore, we test the hypothesis that these failures are architectural-driven rather than optimisation-driven via NegotiaX, a 1-to-N transformer architecture that separates and reconciles alignment objectives via two modules. Module I (Transformer Module) allocates independent representational pathways to each objective-mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Module II (Mechanistic Alignment Circuit (MAC)), embeds objectives into dedicated subspaces and performs a learned negotiative operation prior to decoding-mitigating mechanistic blind-spot. Across four 7B backbones, NegotiaX remains competitive with SOTA-improving Avg by up to 6.3%, Helpfulness by 6.2%, Honesty by 5.6%, and Harmlessness by 4.7%.

title: What AI Gets to See: Auditing the Loss of Multilingual Community Knowledge in Machine-Facing Metadata on Wikimedia Commons
author: Yihan Yu; Aylin Caliskan
abstract: AI systems increasingly inherit what public knowledge infrastructures make machine-visible. Yet multilingual NLP still tends to frame data responsibility around new corpora, annotations, and benchmarks, even though public knowledge communities have already produced rich multilingual knowledge that may be lost when AI-facing infrastructures compress it into narrower metadata layers. We study this problem on Wikimedia Commons, where multilingual captions and descriptions coexist with the English-dominant category system and Wikidata-linked Structured Data on Commons. Using 2,500 featured images across five domains, we introduce a representational recovery framework that audits lexical, semantic, and retrieval-based recovery from current machine-facing metadata layers. Across these tests, we find a consistent asymmetry. After removing the exact query text from the gold image’s free-text document, Commons categories plus Wikidata entity labels outperform the remaining free text for English retrieval. For non-English retrieval, however, the remaining multilingual captions and descriptions outperform categories plus Wikidata entity labels rendered in the query language. Entity-label rendering improves non-English retrieval, but does not fully recover the meaning already present in contributor-written multilingual text. These results show that multilingual NLP should not only collect new data, but also audit, identify, and repair recovery gaps in public knowledge infrastructures as they increasingly feed large-scale AI training pipelines.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation
author: Sheldon Yu; Junda Wu; Xintong Li; Nikki Lijing Kuang; Sizhe Zhou; Tong Yu; Jiawei Han; Jingbo Shang; Julian McAuley
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) tool-use policies select actions from a finite candidate set at each reasoning step. We observe that this action-selection interface is already a linear contextual scorer: under a restricted output vocabulary, the LM head computes per-action scores from the last-layer hidden state, exactly the structure assumed by linear contextual bandits. Existing online adaptation methods for LLMs operate indirectly through prompts or retrieved memories, leaving this decision layer fixed and providing no explicit mechanism for action-level credit assignment or uncertainty-aware exploration. We propose OLIVIA, a lightweight online adaptation layer that replaces the frozen action-selection head with a per-action contextual linear bandit, selects actions via LinUCB exploration on the LLM’s hidden state and updates only its per-action sufficient statistics from step-level feedback via a rank-one Sherman–Morrison rule. Without backbone fine-tuning and additional LLM calls per step, OLIVIA adds negligible overhead relative to LLM inference. Across four tool-use benchmarks ToolBench, TaskBench, TaskBench-MM, BFCL and two backbones Qwen3-4B, Mistral-7B, OLIVIA outperforms prompt-based online adaptation and contextual-bandit variants.

title: Online Strategic Reasoning for LLM-Based Negotiation via Opponent-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search
author: Chen-Cheng Huang; Yi-Cheng Wang; Hung-Lin Hu; Yi-Ren Yeh; Chu-song Chen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong reasoning abilities in mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and code generation. However, negotiation requires interactive reasoning, where each action can influence the opponent’s future behavior. Agents must therefore look beyond the current dialogue state and consider the long-term effects of their actions. Existing LLM-based negotiation agents often rely on prompting or fine-tuning from self-play trajectories. These methods can produce fluent responses and help models learn useful bargaining patterns. Yet at decision time, they often remain reactive, responding mainly to the current dialogue without reasoning about how different actions may shape future negotiation paths. We introduce an online strategic reasoning method that combines Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based lookahead planning with opponent simulation. Before responding, our agent uses a proxy opponent agent to simulate future interactions and evaluate candidate strategies by their expected long-term outcomes. To make opponent simulation more precise, we proposed a Theory-of-Mind-inspired opponent modeling module that infers latent opponent attributes from dialogue history and conditions the proxy opponent agent during search. Experiments on CraigslistBargain and A2A-NT show that our method improves negotiation efficiency and profitability.

title: CentralKV: Compressing Long-Context LLMs via Attention-Graph Centrality
author: Yusen Wu; Huang Yinjun; Jia Yee Tan; Hao Li; Rongfeng Guo; Liang Fan; Jiachen Luo; Guangyuan Dong; Sike Xiang
abstract: Long-context inference in large language models is limited by the linear memory growth of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing eviction methods typically retain tokens with high accumulated attention or remove semantic redundancy, but may discard low-frequency tokens that connect distant dependencies. We propose CentralKV, a training-free framework that models attention as a dynamic sparse causal graph. Its Stream-Influence algorithm updates token centrality online and preserves structurally important bridge tokens during KV compression. The attention graph is constructed directly from the attention operation without separate similarity computation. Experiments on LongBench show that CentralKV improves over H2O, SnapKV, and GraphKV under strict physical memory constraints, particularly on reasoning-intensive tasks, with minimal latency overhead.

title: Continual Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models via Program Memory
author: Hung Le; Svetha Venkatesh
abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), particularly Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), has become a standard approach for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) under limited compute. However, in continual settings where models are updated sequentially with small datasets, conventional LoRA updates struggle to balance rapid adaptation and knowledge retention. Existing methods typically treat the low-rank space as a homogeneous update region, lacking mechanisms to regulate how short-term updates are consolidated over time. We propose a continual LoRA framework with Program memory, inspired by Complementary Learning Systems in neuroscience. Our approach, dubbed ProCL, organizes LoRA adapters into structured program memory slots that are dynamically retrieved through input-conditioned attention. This enables rapid and localized adaptation, encouraging similar inputs to reuse shared adapter regions while reserving unused capacity for future data. The slots are then combined with the underlying adapter, which maintains a distributed representation that gradually accumulates knowledge across tasks to balance plasticity and stability. Our method operates entirely within the LoRA parameterization and incurs no additional inference cost. Experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate improved retention and reduced catastrophic forgetting over other continual LoRA strategies.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
author: Maximo Rulli; Thomas V. Fontanari; Simone Petruzzi; Federico Alvetreti; Giorgio Strano; Donato Crisostomi; Giorgos Nikolaou; Tommaso Mencattini; Andrea Santilli; Emanuele Rodolà; Simone Scardapane; Alessio Devoto
abstract: Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, MDLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that MDLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to controlled and predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is manipulated by these models.

title: SAGE: How Well Do LLMs Align with Classical Chinese Philosophy?
author: Yuying Zhao; Sirui Chen; Yixin Liu; Xuemei Jia; Lingxi Min; Zheng Wang
abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in socially consequential settings makes it increasingly important to understand the value systems they encode and the moral judgments they produce. However, existing evaluations are largely grounded in Western ethical traditions, leaving non-Western moral perspectives underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce Sage, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs through the lens of Classical Chinese philosophy. Sage is grounded in major Pre-Qin philosophical debates and represents normative alignment in a continuous six-dimensional value space. It includes three task types and is constructed from over 4,000 passages spanning ten philosophical schools. Experiments on eight leading LLMs reveal that models occupy highly similar regions in the proposed value space, exhibit a clear gap between self-declared philosophical identities and benchmark-measured behavior, and show systematically different reasoning patterns across task granularities. Code and data will be released after publication.

title: Patch the Distribution Mismatch: RL-Based Data Rewriting for Stable Downstream SFT
author: Jiacheng Wang; Zhijie Liu; Ping Jian; Zirong Chen; Ke Ren Liao; Zhen Yang; Zhongbin Guo
abstract: Large language models are commonly adapted to downstream tasks through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but substantial distribution mismatch between downstream supervision and a model’s generation distribution can intensify catastrophic forgetting. Data rewriting offers a data-centric way to narrow this mismatch before SFT. Existing methods, however, typically sample rewrites from a prompt-induced conditional distribution, which need not align with the backbone’s natural question-answering generation distribution, and fixed templates can reduce output diversity. We formulate data rewriting as a policy-learning problem and train a lightweight LoRA rewriting policy with reinforcement learning. The policy optimizes question-answering-style distributional alignment and semantic diversity under a hard task-consistency gate, producing verified supervision for downstream SFT. Across three instruction-tuned backbones, the resulting models attain downstream gains broadly comparable to standard SFT while reducing degradation on non-downstream benchmarks in every evaluated setting. Additional experiments on logical reasoning and medical question answering provide preliminary evidence that a rewriting policy can be reused across domains for the same backbone.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Retrieval-Based Fact-Checking: Detecting and Mitigating Evidence Contamination
author: Alamgir Munir Qazi; John Philip McCrae; Jamal Abdul Nasir
abstract: Retrieval-based fact-checking systems ground verification in large document collections, creating a critical vulnerability: adversarial evidence contamination. We demonstrate that factually inconsistent but contextually coherent evidence generated to satisfy both retrieval-similarity and linguistic-fluency constraints can systematically mislead verification models. Contaminating just 3.1-7.4% of training corpora with five label-specific strategies causes adversarial content to penetrate up to 35.2% of top-k retrievals, degrading verification accuracy by up to 46.9% relative F1. Existing retrieval-stage defenses, validated against gradient-optimized or syntactically anomalous attacks, transfer poorly to this threat model: detection rates collapse and F1 recovery exhibits high variance across seeds. We propose GLAD (Geometric-Lexical Adversarial Defense), which fuses dense embedding peer-coherence with lexical distributional isolation. Across two benchmarks, two embedding models, and five random seeds, GLAD achieves the highest detection rates (70-86%) and the most consistent F1 recovery, reclaiming 73-80% of contamination-induced degradation on LIAR-RAW while approaching clean baselines on RAWFC. Crucially, unlike defenses that trade clean performance for robustness, GLAD imposes negligible cost on uncontaminated corpora.

title: AR-Bench: Benchmarking Legal Reasoning with Judgment Error Detection, Classification and Correction for Chinese Criminal Cases
author: Yifei Li; Richong Zhang; Wanyu Tu; Zhijie Nie; Haokun Luo; Chuantao Yin
abstract: Legal judgments may inadvertently contain errors, yet human appellate review faces immense pressure to improve efficiency. While current legal AI focuses on legal judgment prediction or document generation, judgment review is fundamentally a retrospective diagnostic task. In this paper, we introduce Appellate Review to assess large language models’ (LLMs) legal diagnostic reasoning underlying appellate review. We specifically target Chinese criminal cases, under the assumption that their highly structured logic, which maps explicit facts to strict statutory penalties, provides a verifiable ground truth. We decompose Appellate Review into three subtasks: error detection, error classification, and error correction. To support this, we construct AR-Bench, a controlled benchmark comprising 8,700 judgments with counterfactually introduced errors spanning charges, prison terms, and fines. Evaluations of 16 LLM variants reveal substantial limitations: models classify known errors relatively well but struggle with unguided detection and precise correction. Further analyses of a representative model show that it identifies explicit textual contradictions but fundamentally fails at holistic deductive reasoning and rule-based arithmetic.

title: Video-DeepResearch: Towards the Next-Generation Multimodal Deepresearch Agent
author: Zhen Fang; Yu Zeng; Wenxuan Huang; Yiming Zhao; Shiting Huang; Tianfei Ren; Qi Lu; Qingnan Ren; Qisheng Su; Lionel Z. Wang; Qingyu Yin; Shuang Chen; Zehui Chen; Lin Chen; Zhenfei Yin; Yao Hu; Shaohui Lin; Wanli Ouyang; Shaosheng Cao; Feng Zhao
abstract: We introduce Video-DeepResearch (Video-DR), extending multimodal agents from static images to continuous video streams, a setting that demands dense spatiotemporal grounding coupled with open-web exploration. Preliminary evaluations reveal two critical bottlenecks in current models: (1) modality bias, where agents bypass visual tools in favor of textual search, and (2) parametric knowledge leakage, where models rely on internal memory rather than genuine tool-augmented execution. To address these challenges, we propose Video-DeepResearch, featuring a decoupled perception-exploration pipeline with stage-wise tool unlocking that compels exhaustive cross-frame visual grounding prior to web retrieval.
