In this work, we study how to make LLMs natively generate TTS-friendly text, which we frame as a preference alignment problem: instead of relying on downstream rewriting modules, we directly align LLMs to generate text optimized for spoken delivery. We introduce two preference datasets spanning different target domains, CORA and Recipe, which contain paired TTS-friendly and TTS-unfriendly responses. We further propose an evaluation suite combining a pattern-based heuristic metric, a TTS→ASR evaluation pipeline, and a MUSHRA listening study with human judges. Our experiments compare the recently proposed Feature-aware Sampling and Tuning (FaST) framework – leveraging interpretable features instead of a black-box reward model – against an array of alignment baselines on the TTS-friendly generation task. Notably, we found that FaST achieves the best overall tradeoff between TTS-friendliness and helpfulness across various settings. We also identified a strong correlation between our different metrics, highlighting the ability to reliably assess TTS-friendliness via an efficient heuristic.

title: Relevance as a Vulnerability: How Web Retrieval Degrades Safety Alignment in LLM Agents
author: Aditya Nawal; Manit Baser; Mohan Gurusamy
abstract: AI agents augment large language models with external tools such as web retrieval, enabling grounded and up-to-date responses. However, incorporating external content into the generation pipeline can weaken the safety alignment mechanisms that govern model outputs. Prior work shows that enabling retrieval in agents increases compliance with harmful requests. We introduce AgentREVEAL, a diagnostic framework for analyzing retrieval-induced safety degradation in LLM agents. The framework examines two axes: how retrieval is integrated into the agent pipeline and the properties of the retrieved content. Along the integration axis, we find that binding tool invocation and response generation in a single step amplifies harmful outputs. Along the content axis, we uncover the Safe Source Paradox: even oppositional or safety-oriented sources, such as pages containing warnings or risk disclaimers, can increase harmful compliance by an average of 25% compared to the no-retrieval baseline. Finally, we show that relevance acts as a shared activation condition for both vulnerabilities. We observe that several agents retrieve information for harmful requests in the autonomous retrieval setting, while harmful compliance remains elevated despite several retrieval-pipeline interventions and defenses. Because relevance is also what makes retrieval useful, these results expose a safety-utility trade-off for retrieval-enabled agents. We introduce HarmURLBench, a benchmark containing 1,405 real-world URLs paired with 320 harmful behaviors to support future evaluations.

title: Ability-Aligned Skill Evolution for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning
author: Fei Huang; Tianyu Chen; Zhongyu He; Yuanfan Li; Meng Hsuan Yu; Xingyang Li; Lu Pan; Ke Zeng; Xunliang Cai
abstract: Large Language Model agents augmented with external skill banks have demonstrated remarkable performance on sequential decision-making tasks. However, existing methods update skills in an undirected, unverified manner and prematurely penalize agents for failing to utilize immature skills. We introduce a structured cognitive representation that decomposes both general and task-specific skills into four dimensions—D-PLAN, D-TRACK, D-EXEC, and D-GUARD—enabling precise failure attribution. Building upon this representation, we propose A^2SE, an ability-aligned skill evolution framework that synchronizes skill bank updates with the agent’s learning trajectory. Specifically, A^2SE concentrates evolution on the identified bottleneck dimension, safeguards updates via a causal verification mechanism with per-task-type rollback, and employs a competence-aligned skill reward to alleviate premature penalization. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that A^2SE achieves 11.0% and 7.1% improvements over the strongest baselines, respectively, with ablation studies confirming the necessity of each proposed component.

title: VisCopilot: Assisting Data-Driven Article Authoring with Fact-Based and Intent-Aligned Autocompletion
author: Tzu-Wei Yu; Che-Wei Chang; Evelyn Yi-Ting Hung; Jia-Yu Pan; Wen-Chieh Lin
abstract: Data-driven articles combine narrative text with visualizations to communicate insights but are time-consuming to produce, requiring both narrative composition and accurate text–chart linking. Existing automated linking methods struggle with accuracy, and automated narrative generation often misaligns with user intent and may contain hallucinations. We present VisCopilot, which leverages retrieval-augmented generation and large language models to provide fact-based, intent-aligned suggestions. As users write, the system supports narrative completion and text–chart linking in a single step, with a human-in-the-loop approach ensuring reliability. Technical evaluation on a benchmark dataset of data-driven articles authored by journalists confirmed the accuracy and quality of VisCopilot’s links. A user study further showed that VisCopilot outperforms baselines in usability, accuracy, and user confidence, with participants valuing its fact-based autocompletes for aligning suggestions with their writing intent. VisCopilot contributes: (1) an autocomplete-based design for assisting data-driven article authoring that balances efficiency, accuracy, and user autonomy; and (2) a reframing of text–chart link generation as a data-fact recommendation problem, enabling intent-aligned retrieval and systematic evaluation.

title: TopoAlign: A Framework for Aligning Code to Math via Topological Decomposition
author: Yupei Li; Philipp Borchert; Gerasimos Lampouras
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at both informal and formal (e.g. Lean 4) mathematical reasoning but still struggle with autoformalisation, the task of transforming informal into formal mathematical statements. Yet, the performance of current Math LLMs is constrained by the scarcity of large-scale corpora, particularly those containing pairs of informal and formal statements. Interestingly, the formal languages used in autoformalisation share structural similarities with programming languages, and code data is available at scale. However, current models trained on code do not transfer effectively to formal math, due to structural and syntactic differences between them. To address this, we propose TopoAlign, a framework that unlocks widely available code repositories as training resources for Math LLMs. TopoAlign decomposes code into docstrings, main functions, and dependency functions, and reassembles these components into analogues that structurally mirror formal statements. We train three state-of-the-art models, , and , and evaluate them on the , , and benchmarks. TopoAlign provides substantial gains for , improving performance by 17.77% on BEq@10 and 68.82% on typecheck@10, and also measurably improves by 0.12% on BEq@10 and 1.09% on typecheck@10 despite introducing no new mathematical knowledge.

title: Mitigating Exploration Bias in RL for Multi-Instruction Following
author: Mian Zhang; Yueqin Yin; Kaiyu He; Peilin Wu; Xinlu Zhang; Mingyuan Zhou; Zhiyu Chen
abstract: RL has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing the instruction following capabilities of LLMs. While existing training recipes achieve substantial gains, we find that they suffer from **exploration bias towards easy instructions** when the training data has multiple instructions in a prompt. This bias is caused by two main reasons: 1) **the policy model’s initial ability to satisfy hard instructions is too low** to trigger successful exploration during RL training, so the optimization is biased to easy instructions and 2) canonical RL training recipes typically employ a cumulative reward (the number of instructions fulfilled), **treating all the instructions equally**; the policy model is biased to fulfill the easy instructions to get the same amount of rewards. To address these, we first propose two metrics to measure the exploration bias of instruction following and then introduce a two-stage framework to alleviate it: 1) Behavioral Bootstrapping: a lightweight rejection sampling fine-tuning before RL to activate hard instructions and 2) Scarcity-Aware Rewards: a new RL reward function that assigns rewards to instructions based on their empirical scarcity. Experiments show that the proposed metrics are highly correlated with model performance and our methods unleash the potential of RL training: our best models outperform the baselines by a significant margin across three verifiable instruction following benchmarks.

title: GRASP: Gated Regression-Aware Skill Proposer for Self-Improving LLM Agents
author: Johannes Moll; Jean-Philippe Corbeil; Jiazhen Pan; Martin Hadamitzky; Daniel Rueckert; Lisa C. Adams; Keno Bressem
abstract: LLM agents acting in structured environments fail in operational rather than conversational ways, and reliability depends on procedural knowledge of the environment. Prior self-improvement methods accumulate natural-language guidance without checking that each new item preserves previously correct behavior, so a note that fixes one trajectory can silently regress another. We introduce GRASP (Gated Regression-Aware Skill Proposer), which treats agent improvement as a sequence of edits to a bounded skill library, admitting each candidate only if it produces a net improvement on a balanced held-out probe under a hard regression budget. We evaluate GRASP across five base models (gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.4) on two FHIR-based clinical benchmarks. On MedAgentBench, GRASP lifts gpt-oss-120b from 40.6% to 88.8%, exceeds the strongest of five self-improvement baselines by 21.0 points, and improves every other base model by 17.2 to 40.3 points. Ablations attribute the gain to comparative proposal generation, the acceptance gate, and the hard regression budget rather than to skill writing itself, which without validation is no better than using no skills. The mechanism generalizes beyond the clinical domain, improving agents on three of four non-clinical environments and remaining flat only where the action space is open-ended. Frozen libraries transfer across models, where skills from a stronger model improve weaker executors beyond what they learn for themselves while the reverse does not, an asymmetry that no ungated baseline reproduces.

title: Adaptive Hierarchical Representation Alliance for Multimodal Learning
author: Chunlei Meng; Pengbin Feng; Jacqueline J. Pang; Chih-Ting Liao; Rong Fu; Zhaolu Kang; Zhongxue Gan; Chun Ouyang
abstract: Multimodal models often align language, vision, and audio in a single final-layer latent space, implicitly assuming that task-relevant evidence emerges at the same semantic depth across modalities. Using layer-wise CKA analysis, we observe that this assumption leads to semantic granularity mismatch: textual cues usually require deeper contextual abstraction, whereas visual and acoustic cues often provide discriminative perceptual evidence in shallow or middle layers. This mismatch can flatten fine-grained modality-private cues and reduce reliability under noisy, imbalanced, or missing inputs. To address this, we proposed Adaptive Hierarchical Representation Alliance (AHRA), a hierarchical shared–private expert framework. AHRA factorizes each modality into shared and private streams across semantic levels, regularizes them with shared alignment and private decorrelation, routes shared information through a cross-modal expert, and enhances task-relevant private tokens with modality-specific experts guided by a sparsity-controlled soft-gating mechanism (foreground exam). A hierarchical co-fusion module then performs intra-level expert coordination and inter-level semantic selection. Experiments on six benchmarks across image-text classification, multimodal intent recognition, and trimodal sentiment analysis show that AHRA consistently improves over strong baselines and remains robust under noisy and missing-modality settings.

title: AdapTools: Adaptive Tool-based Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic LLMs
author: Che Wang; Jiaming Zhang; Ziqi Zhang; Zijie Wang; Yinggui Wang; Jianbo Gao; Tao Wei; Zhong Chen; Wei Yang Bryan Lim
abstract: As open-source large language models (LLMs) become increasingly powerful, they are rapidly evolving into Agentic LLMs capable of automating complex daily tasks. However, this paradigm shift entails severe security risks, as the agents’ necessary integration with external real-time data sources creates a direct pathway for indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks. Existing attack methods are limited by their reliance on static patterns and evaluation on simple language models, failing to address the fast-evolving nature of modern Agentic LLMs. We introduce AdapTools, a novel adaptive IPI attack framework that selects stealthier attack tools and generates adaptive attack prompts to create a rigorous security evaluation environment. Our approach comprises two key components: (1) Adaptive Attack Strategy Construction, which develops transferable adversarial strategies for prompt optimization, and (2) Attack Enhancement, which identifies stealthy tools capable of circumventing task-relevance defenses. Comprehensive experiments on both open-source and commercial agentic LLMs show that AdapTools achieves a per-model average improvement of 2.08× in attack success rate over the strongest baseline under state-of-the-art defenses (MELON, Pi-Detector), with gains reaching up to 3.06× on the most resistant reasoning agents. The framework further transfers to black-box commercial agents (GPT, Qwen, Gemini), with ASR ranging from 4.2 to 20.3 (peak on the in-family Qwen-MAX), exposing systematic vulnerabilities in modern Agentic LLMs.

title: How Well Do Vision-Language Models Understand Movies?
author: Emmanouil Zaranis; António Farinhas; Saul Santos; Beatriz Canaverde; Miguel Moura Ramos; Wafaa Mohammed; Giuseppe Attanasio; Chrysoula Zerva; Nithin Sivakumaran; Shoubin Yu; Elena Bueno-Benito; Aditya K Surikuchi; Ben Peters; Danae Sanchez Villegas; Andre G. Viveiros; Pavlo Vasylenko; Baohao Liao; Sonal Sannigrahi; Jaehong Yoon; Elias Stengel-Eskin; Mariella Dimiccoli; Oswald Lanz; Alessandro Suglia; Mohit Bansal; Sandro Pezzelle; Stella Frank; Vlad Niculae; Desmond Elliott; Raffaella Bernardi; Raquel Fernández; Andre Martins
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can increasingly handle extended contexts and answer questions about long videos—but can they understand the narrative structure of movies as humans do? To investigate this question, we introduce {MF}^2 (\textit{Movie Facts and Fibs}), a fully manually curated benchmark designed to evaluate whether models can identify, recall, and comprehend information central to the movie’s storyline, using both the visual and textual modalities. {MF}^2 includes over 50 \textit{open-licensed} movies, each paired with manually constructed sets of claim pairs: one true claim (\textit{fact}) and one plausible but false (\textit{fib}), totaling over 850 pairs. Our analysis across 20 open-source and 2 proprietary models reveals a substantial gap relative to human performance. While subtitles provide a strong signal for narrative understanding, other textual sources (e.g., synopses) are less informative. In contrast, when visual information is distributed across the entire movie and jointly embedded with subtitles, models struggle to identify and effectively use the relevant content. However, when the visual input is restricted to claim-relevant visual content, models improve significantly, indicating substantial room for improvement in processing large multimodal contexts and distinguishing relevant from irrelevant information. Overall, our findings highlight persistent challenges in multimodal narrative understanding for current VLMs. We release our data and code to support further research in this direction.

title: The Scientific Contribution Graph: Automated Literature-based Technological Roadmapping at Scale
author: Peter Jansen
abstract: Scientific contributions rarely develop in isolation, but instead build upon prior discoveries. We formulate the task of automated technological roadmapping as extracting scientific contributions from scholarly articles and linking them to their prerequisites. We present the Scientific Contribution Graph, a large-scale resource containing 6 million detailed scientific contributions extracted from 655k open-access papers spanning computer science, medicine, biology, physics, chemistry, and other sciences, and connected by 36 million prerequisite edges. We further introduce scientific prerequisite prediction, a scientific discovery task in which models predict which existing technologies can enable future discoveries, and show that contemporary models are rapidly improving on this task, reaching 0.48 MAP when evaluated using temporally-filtered backtesting. We anticipate technological roadmapping resources such as this will support scientific impact assessment and automated scientific discovery.

title: MedSPA: Self-planning Medical Agents
author: Luu Van Huy; Bowen Wang; Fumio Okura; Yuta Nakashima
abstract: Reliable medical diagnosis requires a precise final prediction, which is strictly supported by observable evidence. Recent large vision-language models perform well on medical image understanding tasks, yet they often lack explicit control over which evidence to inspect before making a prediction. To facilitate flexible planning of evidence exploration, we propose MedSPA, a self-planning medical reasoning framework that separates diagnostic evidence acquisition from evidence-grounded prediction with two cooperative agents: a planning-and-reasoning agent that adaptively decides what to inspect and when to stop, and a summary agent that generates the final output from the accumulated evidence. MedSPA distills medical knowledge from strict diagnostic procedures but acquires flexibility through reinforcement learning to generate optimal outputs. Experiments on medical report generation and medical visual question answering show that MedSPA improves clinical performance, faithfulness, and controllability over existing reasoning baselines.

title: On the (In)effectiveness of AMR Augmentation for Large Language Models
author: Hoa Quynh Nhung Nguyen; Jacopo Staiano; Michael Sullivan
abstract: While Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has historically improved performance on a range of NLP tasks, the benefit—or lack thereof—of AMR augmentation for modern LLMs is thus far unclear. In this paper, we attempt to reproduce recent work that reported substantial downstream gains from AMR augmentation, finding that these are likely due to specific choices in the experimental settings used: using a consistent and unified protocol for hyperparameter selection, we observe that text-only baselines consistently match or exceed the performance of AMR-augmented models. To investigate this null result, we introduce a perplexity-based probe measuring the degree to which AMR provides an LLM with supplemental relational knowledge not already available to the model. We find that AMR augmentation does not help LLMs improve their understanding of relational content in the sentence, indicating that augmenting these models with AMR offers no clear benefit on downstream tasks.

title: iPOE: Interpretable Prompt Optimization via Explanations
author: Jiahui Li; Yarik Menchaca Resendiz; Sean Papay; Roman Klinger
abstract: Prompt optimization has often been framed as a discrete search problem to find high-performing and robust instructions for a large language model (LLM). However, the search result might not make it transparent why and where specific prompt changes lead to performance gains. This is in contrast to how humans are instructed for annotation tasks. Here, researchers carefully design annotation guidelines, leading to enhanced annotation consistency. Our paper aims at joining these two approaches and introduces iPOE, a novel interpretable prompt optimization strategy via explanations. We guide the prompt optimization process by automatically created guidelines from explanations of annotation decisions (either automatically generated or from humans). This set of guidelines is furthermore optimized by a series of operations, including removing, adding, shuffling, and merging. The resulting prompt includes guidelines that instruct the annotation, making the decision process of the LLM and the optimization transparent. It therefore supports also laypeople in prompt optimization. In our experiments on four datasets, we find that iPOE can improve over the evaluated baselines by up to 39% and LLM explanations can replace human explanations in the proposed method. Moreover, our interpretability validation study demonstrates that humans and LLMs substantially agree on which guidelines contribute to their annotations, achieving a Cohen’s kappa score between annotators and LLMs of up to 0.68, 0.80, and 0.95 for the emotion classification, medical fact-checking, and hate speech detection tasks respectively.

title: Fast Block Diffusion Training via Multi-Mask Context Sharing
author: Tengyu Pan; Weilin Zhao; Yutao Sun; Yanghao Li; Jianyong Wang; Xu Han
abstract: Block Diffusion Language Models generate multiple blocks of text sequentially, while tokens within each block are denoised in parallel, enabling efficient parallel decoding. However, their training suffers from low computational utilization: each sample is duplicated into a clean context and a masked copy, yet only the masked portion contributes to the training loss, resulting in merely 50% compute utilization. In this paper, we propose Multi-Mask Training (MMT), a simple yet effective training paradigm that significantly improves computational efficiency through context sharing. Our key idea is to generate K different mask patterns for the same clean text and process them together in a single forward pass via a sparse attention mechanism, where each masked segment attends to the shared clean context while remaining isolated from other segments. In pretraining, our proposed approach yields better performance under matched compute, despite being exposed to fewer unique training instances. Under a matched-step protocol, MMT maintains comparable downstream quality while improving training efficiency in AR-to-Diffusion adaptation. This reveals a compelling trade-off between data uniqueness and training efficiency in block diffusion models, demonstrating that the rich training signals from diverse mask samplings can effectively compensate for reduced exposure to unique data.

title: IRIS: Iterative Refinement of Internal States for Safer Language Models
author: Beize Zhang; Yuchen Feng; Peize Li; Zhitong Zhu; Peng Fu; Mu Weimin; Zheng Lin; Weiping Wang
abstract: Attack success rate (ASR) is insufficient for evaluating the safety of large language models (LLMs). Many defenses rely on surface-level refusal behavior, which can over-refuse benign-sensitive prompts and remain brittle: once the initial refusal boundary is bypassed, the model may still follow a harmful continuation trajectory. We analyze model activation spaces to examine the limits of static interventions, finding substantial overlap among useful, benign-sensitive, and harmful representations. This suggests that a single global intervention may suppress harmful outputs only by perturbing general utility. We propose IRIS, Iterative Refinement of Internal States, a routing-conditioned internal correction method. To address this, IRIS leaves low-risk states unaltered while routing high-risk states to a shared module for multi-step latent refinement. To make the refinement module learn behavior-level correction, we introduce model-owned base-source prefix recovery, which trains IRIS to recover from base-model failure prefixes toward safe continuations. Extensive evaluations on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B demonstrate that IRIS drastically reduces ASR from around 70% to around 10% and successfully defends against prefilling attacks. Furthermore, IRIS preserves general benchmark utility and maintains near-zero over-refusal rates.

title: Beyond Isolated Behaviors: Hierarchical User Modeling for LLM Personalization
author: Liang Wang; Xinyi Mou; Xiaoyou Liu; Tiannan Wang; Yuqing Wang; Zhongyu Wei
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, yet personalizing their outputs to individual users remains an open challenge. Existing approaches predominantly adopt a flat behavioral paradigm, aggregating user behaviors without an explicit account of how they are organized into deeper behavioral structures. In this work, we draw on Pierre Bourdieu’s Theory of Practice to propose PHF (Practice-Habitus-Field), a sociologically grounded framework that reconceptualizes LLM personalization through three hierarchical levels: individual behaviors as practices, their temporal accumulation into stable dispositions as habitus, and shared regularities across similar users as fields. We instantiate PHF through PHF Compass, a lightweight and model-agnostic implementation based on a frozen LLM. Experiments on the Language Model Personalization (LaMP) benchmark demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse tasks, while further analyses validate the interpretability and extensibility of the learned behavioral structures.

title: Chiaroscuro for Emotions: A Contrastive Emotion Benchmark Grounded in Appraisal Theory
author: Divyesh Bommana; Mohammad Saim; Tianyu Jiang
abstract: Emotion recognition benchmarks predict one emotion per text, missing many real-world scenarios where two people arrive at opposing emotions from a single shared trigger. For example, a child kicks her seat in excitement while the passenger ahead feels mounting irritation. We introduce Chiaro, a 1,000 human-annotated sentence benchmark for contrastive emotion inference grounded in appraisal theory. Each scene describes one causal trigger eliciting a positive emotion in one person and a negative emotion in the other, drawn from a ten-class taxonomy. We benchmark seven frontier LLMs and four off-the-shelf emotion classifiers, where the strongest LLM reaches 67.3 macro-F1, well below human agreement, while existing emotion classifiers score near chance. Beyond evaluation, Chiaro also serves as a training signal: combined with an existing emotion corpus, the resulting downstream classifier improves on Chiaro itself and on six of ten external emotion benchmarks, positioning Chiaro as a complementary signal for emotion recognition.

title: CAVD-Guard: Defending Against Token Fragmentation Jailbreaks via Attention Footprints
author: Junjie Xu; Zicheng Zhao
abstract: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks that hide harmful intent from safety screening. A recent family of highly effective attacks exploits this weakness by splitting harmful keywords into recoverable fragments; we refer to this family as Token Fragmentation Jailbreaks. The success of these attacks stems from a mismatch between screening and generation: safety screening may no longer observe complete harmful keywords, while the target model can reconstruct them during generation. We show that instructions containing fragmented words leave a measurable attention footprint inside the model. Attention concentrates among the fragmented keyword pieces, while links from those pieces to complete words are weak. Based on this finding, we introduce Calibrated Attention-Void Detection (CAVD), a training-free detector that measures this footprint with length-conditioned calibration. We then combine guard models with CAVD in CAVD-Guard. When CAVD flags an instruction as unreliable for original-view safety screening, CAVD-Guard maps it to multiple canonical views and applies guard-based classification to the recovered views. Extensive experiments show that CAVD-Guard substantially reduces attack success and improves guard blocking while maintaining low false-positive rates on benign inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/serendipity098/CAVD-Guard.

title: Agentic Open-Domain Tabular Question Answering with Self-Supervised Multi-Table Retriever
author: Jianwei Wang; Mengqi Wang; Qing Liu; Xiwei Xu; Zhenchang Xing; Liming Zhu; Wenjie Zhang
abstract: Open-domain tabular question answering (TQA) aims to answer natural language queries over a data lake that contains a large corpus of heterogeneous tables. Unlike closed-domain TQA, this task operates without pre-provided tables, making it particularly challenging. Existing methods usually first retrieve relevant tables and then answer the question based on the retrieved tables. However, it faces challenges in effectively and efficiently preparing tables from the low-quality, heterogeneous data lake and in operationalizing table information. To address these limitations, we present ArrTab (Agentic retrieval and reasoning on Tables) for open-domain TQA. ArrTab leverages MuRe, a self-supervised Multi-table Retriever trained on questions synthesized by translating table-derived SQL queries into natural language via large language models. Based on MuRe, ArrTab proposes a multi-agent system for open-domain TQA that consists of the Table Retriever Agent, the Table Integration Agent, the Information Extraction Agent and the Answer Agent. Furthermore, to enhance accuracy, a lazy execution strategy is adopted where operations are described in natural language but executed only during the information extraction stage, allowing for globally consistent reasoning. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of ArrTab.

title: Accelerating Constrained Decoding with Token Space Compression
author: Michael Sullivan; Alexander Koller
abstract: To guarantee that an LLM’s outputs conform to a specified structure, context-free grammar (CFG) decoding engines force the selection of next tokens to produce strings that conform to a given CFG. Current CFG-constrained decoding engines are highly optimized, but still suffer from the inherent costs arising from their massive per-step search space—i.e. the entire token vocabulary. This results in intractably high overhead for more complex CFGs, which is precisely the situation where CFG engines are most useful. In this paper, we introduce CFGzip, an offline technique for compressing the token search space, which massively reduces CFG engine overhead. In experiments, we report latency reduction of up to 75x during batched inference, cutting overhead down to ~1.2-2x on the hardest grammars: with CFGzip, constrained decoding is now possible at scale for complex CFGs.

title: GSPR: Aligning LLM Safeguards as Generalizable Safety Policy Reasoners
author: Haoran Li; Jingru Zeng; Yulin Chen; Huihao Jing; Wenbin Hu; Hao Peng; Haochen Shi; Xi Yang; Ziqian Zeng; Sirui Han; Yangqiu Song
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are integrated into numerous applications, LLMs’ safety becomes critical for both application developers and intended users. Currently, great efforts have been made to develop safety benchmarks with fine-grained taxonomies. However, these benchmarks’ taxonomies are disparate with different safety policies. Thus, existing safeguards trained on these benchmarks are either coarse-grained to only distinguish between "safe” and "unsafe,” or constrained by the specified narrow risk taxonomies. To leverage these fine-grained safety policies across multiple safety taxonomies, we propose GSPR, a Generalizable Safety Policy Reasoner to identify unsafe inputs and outputs with violated safety taxonomies and concise explanations. Unlike prior safeguards which only cover a fixed set of risk factors, GSPR incentivizes its reasoning capability with varied safety taxonomies through reinforcement learning. Our GSPR can be trained across multiple safety benchmarks with distinct taxonomies and naturally exhibits powerful generalization ability. We conduct extensive experiments to show that GSPR significantly improves existing safety guardrails’ reasoning capabilities for both safety and category prediction tasks. Moreover, GSPR also achieves the least inference token costs with explanations.

title: ReasonMap: Making Implicit Mathematical Knowledge Explicit in Long Chain-of-Thought Traces
author: Haodong Wu; Yuhang He; Yongqi Zhang
abstract: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces provide observable natural-language rationales for mathematical problem solving, but they rarely expose the named definitions and theorems that justify the written solution. We treat each problem–trace pair as carrying a recoverable knowledge footprint: a trace-grounded support set of named definitions and theorems. Inspired by formal proofs, where supporting premises are recorded more explicitly than in free-form CoT, we formulate Mathematical Support Set Extraction (MSSE): given a problem and a completed long CoT trace, recover the canonical support set that supports the written solution. We propose ReasonMap, which attributes this support set to make solutions auditable, reusable, and easier to repair. ReasonMap follows a two-stage pipeline: proof-to-CoT support transfer adapts premise-explicit proof supervision to premise-implicit long CoT traces, and hard-negative support calibration applies preference optimization against plausible-but-wrong support sets. Experiments show that ReasonMap improves support-set extraction over strong baselines and that ReasonMap-generated support hints aid downstream reasoning in both frontier-model and self-generated settings. The GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/kui253/ReasonMap.

title: Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity
author: Zhuofan Ying; Peter Hase; Nikolaus Kriegeskorte
abstract: Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report a nearly perfect linear relationship between a probe’s MCS to a reference probe trained on out-of-distribution (OOD) data and its OOD AUROC (R^2=0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove it in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are near-linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe’s signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

title: Learning How to Align: Elastic Domain Adaptation for Improving Reasoning Robustness of Large Language Models
author: Yujie Hou; Mei Wang; Yaoyao Zhong; Guozhang Li; Qiannan Zhu; Hua Huang
abstract: Despite exceptional performance on static benchmarks, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit significant brittleness when evaluated on perturbed variants of the original questions. Current extrinsic interventions, prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, overlook an important intrinsic factor underlying this degradation: the distributional shifts in layer activations between original and perturbed questions. To address this, this work formulates the reasoning robustness challenge as an Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) problem and proposes the Elastic Domain Adaptation (EDA) method. Unlike rigid strategies that enforce a uniform alignment constraint, EDA dynamically aligns layer activations based on the specific layers and perturbation types. Specifically, EDA incorporates an Adaptive Layer Selection (ALS) to identify pivotal layers and employs an Elastic Shift Module (ESM) to selectively pull or push layer representations depending on the perturbation types. Extensive experiments across six LLMs and 15 perturbation types demonstrate that EDA achieves state-of-the-art performance on most perturbed benchmarks while preserving reasoning capability on original benchmarks.

title: SLIT: Execution-Grounded Small Language Models for Issue-Reproducing Test Generation
author: Runlin Liu; Zhe Zhang; Zeren Chen; Xiang Gao; Lu Sheng; Ping Yang; Mu Li; Hailong Sun
abstract: Automatically generating issue-reproducing tests is essential for debugging and regression prevention. Recent advances show that large language models can effectively perform this task, but their reliance on extremely large parameter scales limits practical deployment. In this paper, we propose SLIT, an execution-grounded framework that enables small language models to generate effective issue-reproducing tests. SLIT formulates issue reproduction as an execution-guided exploration problem and optimizes policies with reinforcement learning over execution-based rewards. To improve inference-time exploration, SLIT further introduces diversity-augmented test construction and a learned scoring model to select effective reproducing tests. Experimental results on SWT-Bench-Verified indicate that the 14B-parameter model achieves a resolve rate of 46.2%, achieving competitive performance against prior approaches that rely on larger models. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of SLIT and highlight the viability of execution-grounded small language models for issue-reproducing test generation.

title: Cross-lingual Clustering of News Stories using Embeddings-based Community Detection
author: Nikolaos Nikolaidis; Kristina Kovacikova; Ion Androutsopoulos
abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models has accelerated news content generation, yet methods to help readers contextualize and responsibly consume news content lag behind. Existing approaches to clustering news articles face significant limitations. Methods based on dense representations often struggle with robustness and efficiency, while those based on sparse (n-gram) representations are unsuitable for cross-lingual applications. Additionally, LLM-based methods are expensive to apply at the needed scale, restricting their use to only well funded organizations. We present a novel method for efficient clustering of news articles using cross-lingual, sentence-level embeddings and community detection on similarity graphs. Our method can construct a document-level similarity graph from sentence-level embeddings, avoiding the use of sub-optimal embeddings of entire documents. The proposed method can be executed on consumer hardware, enabling practical news analysis for personal use and research. We also release a manually curated dataset of clustered news articles, providing a valuable resource for future research. We use the dataset to benchmark our method using nine text embedding models with cross-lingual capability and propose various practical configurations.

title: AgentEHR: Advancing Autonomous Clinical Decision-Making via Retrospective Summarization
author: Yusheng Liao; Chuan Xuan; Yutong Cai; Lina Yang; Zhe Chen; Yanfeng Wang; Yu Wang
abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated profound utility in the medical domain. However, their application to autonomous Electronic Health Records (EHRs) navigation remains constrained by a reliance on curated inputs and simplified retrieval tasks. To bridge the gap between idealized experimental settings and realistic clinical environments, we present AgentEHR. This benchmark challenges agents to execute complex decision-making tasks, such as diagnosis and treatment planning, requiring long-range interactive reasoning directly within raw and high-noise databases. In tackling these tasks, we identify that existing summarization methods inevitably suffer from critical information loss and fractured reasoning continuity. To address this, we propose RetroSum, a novel framework that unifies a retrospective summarization mechanism with an evolving experience strategy. By dynamically re-evaluating interaction history, the retrospective mechanism prevents long-context information loss and ensures unbroken logical coherence. Additionally, the evolving strategy bridges the domain gap by retrieving accumulated experience from a memory bank. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that RetroSum achieves performance gains of up to 29.16% over competitive baselines, while significantly decreasing total interaction errors by up to 92.3%.

title: SimRule: Collaborative Similarity-Driven Rule Learning for Interpretable Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting
author: Wenshuo Liu; Shufeng Hao; Ziyu Li; Chongyang Shi
abstract: Rule-based methods for temporal knowledge graph (TKG) forecasting are valued for the interpretability of their explicit logic chains. However, they suffer from a severe cold-start coverage gap: exact-match closed walks terminate at sparse entities, leaving many queries without any rule evidence. Existing similarity-based remedies are unreliable because their similarity is derived from static structural co-occurrence or shallow embeddings with no temporal calibration and hand-tuned thresholds. To address these limitations, we propose SimRule, a collaborative recommendation framework for TKG rule mining. SimRule first mines both exact rules and collaborative-surrogate rules through a temporally calibrated dual-view entity similarity index. An adaptive dual-branch fusion then ranks candidate objects from their aggregated evidence, and each forecast remains fully auditable as an explicit rule chain with quantified time gaps. On ICEWS14, ICEWS18, and ICEWS05-15, SimRule achieves state-of-the-art MRR and Hits@K (K \ge 3) among rule-based methods.

title: DELTA: Decoupling Latent Heterogeneity in Asymmetric Low-Rank Compression
author: Jialin Zhan; Fangxin Liu; Junjie Wang; Ning Yang; Li Jiang; Haibing Guan
abstract: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is a promising post-training compression technique for large language models (LLMs), as it is training-free, hardware-friendly, and preserves regular dense computation. However, existing SVD-based methods suffer from severe accuracy degradation under aggressive compression. This is mainly because hard rank truncation discards useful singular directions, while the two resulting SVD factors are usually compressed symmetrically despite their different roles, shapes, and quantization sensitivities. In this paper, we propose DELTA, an asymmetric low-rank compression method that decouples the latent heterogeneity between the two SVD factors. Under a fixed memory budget, the proposed method jointly determines the retained rank, factor-wise quantization bit-widths, and quantization directions, allowing more effective singular directions to be preserved with low-bit representations. To efficiently select compression configurations, we use an activation-aware reconstruction error as a layer-wise proxy objective. Experiments on multiple LLMs and datasets show that DELTA consistently outperforms existing post-training SVD-based compression methods, especially under high compression ratios. Compared with the strongest SVD-based baseline at the same compression ratio, DELTA reduces perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4 by up to 68.2% and 53.2%, respectively, and improves average zero-shot accuracy by up to 11 percentage points. These results demonstrate that asymmetric factor-aware compression can effectively mitigate the accuracy degradation of SVD-based LLM compression at high compression ratios. Code is available at https://github.com/BlacksheepJane/DELTA.

title: Predicting LLM Training and Inference Runtime: A Survey of Methods, Datasets, and Open Challenges
author: Kangda Wei; Ziqian Bi; Ashish Molakalapalli; Haonan Duan; Xiaowei Zou; Vincent Du; Alex Carter; Ruihong Huang
abstract: Large language models have become the dominant workload in modern GPU clusters, driving unprecedented demand for compute during both training and inference. Yet GPU clusters typically operate at only 30–50% utilization, largely because schedulers rely on user-provided runtime estimates that are notoriously inaccurate. Running thousands of LLM inference requests through shared datacenters further compounds this underutilization. Accurate runtime prediction is a key enabler of LLM efficiency: it supports shortest-job-first scheduling, backfilling, dynamic resource allocation, and cost-aware instance selection, while providing NLP practitioners with reliable completion estimates for training runs and serving latency guarantees. However, LLM workloads pose unique prediction challenges: attention complexity scales quadratically with sequence length, autoregressive decoding produces variable-length outputs, and 3D parallelism creates intricate performance interactions. This survey systematically reviews runtime prediction methods with emphasis on LLM training and inference workloads, presenting a feature taxonomy, analyzing design choices of existing prediction methods, surveying public datasets and highlighting their limitations. We identify applications critical to LLM efficiency and key open challenges including generalization to rapidly evolving model architectures and hardwares.

title: CauTab: Counterfactual Tabular Data Synthesis with Functional and Causal-Dependency Constraints
author: Xingyu Yang; Mingchuan Ma; Dexuan Xu; Xiangyang Long; Yu Huang
abstract: High-quality tabular data is essential for data-driven tasks, yet often limited by scarcity and privacy concerns. While synthetic data generated by recent Deep Generative Models and LLMs improves fidelity, existing methods struggle to preserve rigorous attribute dependencies. As a result, the generated data may appear statistically realistic but lack logical consistency. To address this challenge, we propose CauTab, a novel counterfactual framework for tabular data synthesis that preserves functional dependencies and causal-dependency structures. CauTab operates in a three-stage pipeline: (1) it employs an LLM-guided mining strategy to efficiently identify functional dependencies; (2) it constructs a causal-dependency graph by integrating data-driven optimization with LLM-based semantic reasoning; and (3) it executes a dependency-constrained generation process via the Abduction-Intervention-Prediction paradigm. By enforcing deterministic constraints and using the learned graph for structured propagation, CauTab improves statistical fidelity while preserving logical consistency. Experiments demonstrate that CauTab outperforms baselines in data utility and fidelity, while maintaining competitive empirical privacy and strong logical consistency.

title: A Robust Evaluation of Probe Robustness: Lessons for Reliable OOD Uncertainty Quantification
author: Joe Stacey; Hadas Orgad; Kentaro Inui; Benjamin Heinzerling; Nafise Sadat Moosavi
abstract: Recent work has shown that the hidden states of large language models contain signals useful for uncertainty estimation, motivating a growing interest in efficient probe-based approaches. Yet it remains unclear how robust existing methods are, with prior work reporting conflicting conclusions under substantially different evaluation settings. We address this by introducing ProbeDrift, a systematic evaluation framework for supervised uncertainty probes covering a wide range of OOD settings across models, tasks, and distributional shifts. Using ProbeDrift, we train over 2,000 probes to disentangle the effect of key design choices, showing poor robustness of current methods beyond near-OOD settings. We find that robustness is driven by design decisions that have a largely invisible effect in-distribution, including the choice of feature type, aggregation strategy, and training signal. We argue that robust uncertainty estimation requires robust evaluation. To support this, we release ProbeDrift as a lightweight Python library that contains the train and test splits underpinning our extensive evaluation. We also show how insights from our evaluation can directly lead to more robust methods through a simple Hybrid Back-Off (HBO) strategy.

title: Breaking Bored? SciMemeX: Towards Automatic Generation of Scientific Memes from Research Articles
author: Sandeep Kumar; Asif Ekbal
abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature makes it increasingly difficult to communicate a paper’s core novelty in a concise and accessible manner. While prior work has explored visual summaries such as graphical abstracts, emerging informal formats such as scientific memes remain largely unstudied from a computational perspective. Scientific memes rely on concise visual–textual juxtaposition and contrast to highlight how new work differs from prior approaches, making them a challenging test case for controlled abstraction, contrastive reasoning, and creative compression in generative models. We formalize scientific meme generation as a novel multimodal, contrastive generation task and propose SciMemeX, a modular multi-agent framework that extracts core innovations, selects contextually appropriate meme templates, and iteratively generates and refines captions through contrastive feedback-guided refinement. We evaluate generated memes along three complementary dimensions—scientific fidelity, clarity, and engagement potential—and conduct extensive automatic and human evaluations on 1.5k computer science papers. Our results show that SciMemeX consistently outperforms strong single-agent prompting and existing multi-agent baselines across all evaluation dimensions, suggesting that scientific meme generation provides a constrained setting for exploring controlled creative generation in scientific communication context. We make the code public.

title: REAT: A Reflective Experience-Augmented Tutoring Framework for Multi-turn Mathematical Instruction
author: Jianheng Zhou; Chaoli Zhang; Xingjun Wei; Xinliang Zhou; Giancarlo Fortino; Xing Fan; Yanfeng Wang; Qingsong Wen; Haoyang Li
abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at solving complex mathematical problems, yet this proficiency does not inherently translate into effective tutoring. While advanced LLM tutors may leverage multi-agent frameworks or fine-tuning, most still lack a mechanism to systematically accumulate and reuse pedagogical experience over time, limiting their adaptability to diverse student needs during fluid, multi-turn interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose the Reflective Experience-Augmented Tutoring (REAT) framework, which couples experience distillation from historical dialogues with real-time adaptive retrieval. Driven by a multi-agent Observer-Critic-Mentor (OCM) distillation pipeline, REAT reviews past conversational trajectories and distills raw interactions into structured, problem-agnostic pedagogical experiences. During live tutoring, a state-aware retrieval module injects these curated experiences to provide adaptive scaffolding based on the student’s cognitive state. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms both prompt-only and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines, particularly in improving complex, low-scoring teaching scenarios. Crucially, the distilled experiences exhibit robust generalization across diverse model architectures and mathematical datasets.

title: NOSA: Native and Offloadable Sparse Attention
author: Yuxiang Huang; Pengjie Wang; Jicheng Han; Weilin Zhao; Zhou su; Ao Sun; Hongya Lyu; Hengyu Zhao; Yudong Wang; Chaojun Xiao; Xu Han; Zhiyuan Liu
abstract: Decoding throughput gains from larger inference batches are often limited by GPU memory, mainly due to the large size of KV cache. Training-free KV cache offloading mitigates this issue by storing redundant context on the CPU and fetching sparse KV subsets, but often harms long-generation quality due to training-inference mismatch of sparse patterns. Trainable sparse attention can improve quality, yet its unconstrained KV accesses are inefficient for offloading and may incur excessive CPU–GPU transfers. To this end, we propose NOSA, a trainable sparse attention mechanism designed for KV cache offloading. NOSA explicitly bounds CPU–GPU KV transfers, enabling low communication overhead and high decoding throughput. We further develop NOSI, an offloading inference system that realizes these efficiency gains. Experiments on 1,3,8B LLMs show that NOSA outperforms KV cache offloading baselines on general, long-input, and long-generation tasks, while improving decoding throughput by up to 5.04\times, 1.92\times, and 1.83\times over FullAttn, InfLLMv2, and ShadowKV, respectively.

title: GRACE: Gradient-guided Coreset Selection for LLM Unlearning
author: Praveen Bushipaka; Andrea D’Angelo; Lucia Passaro; Tommaso Cucinotta
abstract: Machine Unlearning methods for Large Language Models typically assume pre-specified forget and retain sets. In realistic settings, however, requests may provide only a few examples of undesired behaviour, requiring forget and retain sets to be inferred from heterogeneous corpora. We study this data-selection problem and propose GRACE, a gradient-guided coreset selection method that constructs both forget and retain sets for LLM unlearning. GRACE first computes a forget direction from seed examples that elicit the undesired behaviour, then selects a compact forget coreset whose gradients approximate this direction using non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit. To preserve model utility, it selects retain examples after projecting out the forget direction and applying clustered orthogonal matching pursuit in the remaining gradient space. Across two target domains, two model families, and four unlearning algorithms, GRACE improves model utility while maintaining comparable forget quality, with particularly consistent gains over prior gradient-based selection methods.

title: Taming the Thinker: Conditional Entropy Shaping for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
author: Shuyu Wei; Jian Sun; Delai Qiu; Yining Wang; Shengping Liu; Jerry Liang; Ying Fu; Wei Huang; Jitao Sang
abstract: Entropy-based deep reasoning has emerged as a promising direction for improving the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing methods often either increase response length indiscriminately or shorten responses at the cost of accuracy. To better balance this trade-off, we introduce Conditional Entropy Shaping (CES), a framework that dynamically controls token-level response entropy, enabling LLMs to produce concise solutions on simple problems while encouraging deeper exploration on hard ones. Built on DAPO, CES uses token-level entropy as an uncertainty signal and applies a conditional bidirectional policy: it penalizes high-entropy "forking point" tokens on correct reasoning paths to improve conciseness, and rewards them on incorrect paths to encourage exploration and error correction. We implement CES on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and evaluate it on 12 mathematical benchmarks. CES consistently improves average accuracy while reducing response length relative to DAPO, and supplementary experiments show similar trends on a smaller 1.5B backbone and on out-of-domain benchmarks.

title: Visual Preference Optimization with Rubric Rewards
author: Ya-Qi Yu; Fangyu Hong; Xiangyang Qu; Hao Wang; Gaojie Wu; Qiaoyu Luo; Nuo Xu; Huixin Wang; Wuheng Xu; Yongxin Liao; Zihao Chen; Haonan Li; Ziming Li; Dezhi Peng; Minghui Liao; Jihao Wu; Haoyu Ren; Dandan Tu
abstract: The effectiveness of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) depends on data pairs that capture task-relevant quality differences. Existing data pipelines often rely on *off-policy* perturbations or *coarse* outcome-based signals, which are not well suited to fine-grained visual reasoning. We propose *rDPO*, a rubric-based data pipeline for DPO-based visual preference optimization. For each image-instruction pair, we create a checklist-style rubric of essential and additional criteria to score responses from any possible policies. The instruction-rubric pool is built *offline* and reused during the construction of *on-policy* preference data. On public reward modeling benchmarks, rubric-based prompting massively improves a 30B-A3B judge and brings it close to GPT-5.4. On public downstream benchmarks, rubric-based filtering raises the macro average to 82.69, whereas outcome-based filtering drops it to 75.82 from 81.14. In scalability evaluation on a comprehensive benchmark, rDPO achieves 61.01, markedly outperforming the style-constrained baseline (52.36) and surpassing the 59.48 base model. Together, these results show that visual preference optimization benefits from combining on-policy data construction with instance-specific criterion-level feedback.

title: SkillMe: Evolving Agent Skills for Recurring Personal Workflows
author: Xiuqi Lu; Jie Zhang; Yuanfu Liu; Lewen Yan; Yutong Zhi; Jing Shao
abstract: Skills help LLM agents reuse procedural knowledge in recurring workflows, but broad transferability alone does not guarantee workflow fit: a reusable skill may be semantically relevant yet fail under local tools, files, formats, and failure modes. We propose SkillMe, a workflow-situated skill evolution framework that adapts agent skills through repeated use in matched workflow recurrences. A Publisher induces and validates an initial skill from a successful execution, while Executors use the skill in agent-native sessions and provide trace-grounded feedback. SkillMe activates the matched skill on demand as workspace files, allowing agents to inspect and adopt guidance progressively without permanently installing it as a local skill. On the 71-task skill-needed subset of PinchBench with OpenClaw, SkillMe improves the overall mean score of all eight Executors over their paired no-skill baselines, with mean gains of +25.7 points. Comparisons show that evolved task-scoped skills are more stable than static skills and more reliable than broadly reusable skills. SkillMe thus provides an agent-native path to evolve reusable skills into effective workflow guidance through situated use.

title: Cross-Cultural Value Attribution in Large Vision-Language Models
author: Phillip Howard; Xin Su; Kathleen C. Fraser
abstract: The rapid adoption of large vision-language models (LVLMs) in recent years has been accompanied by growing fairness concerns due to their propensity to reinforce harmful societal stereotypes. While significant attention has been paid to such fairness concerns in the context of social biases, relatively little prior work has examined the presence of stereotypes in LVLMs related to cultural contexts such as religion, nationality, and socioeconomic status. In this work, we aim to narrow this gap by investigating how LVLM judgments about a person’s moral, ethical, and political values vary across cultural contexts presented in images. We conduct a multi-dimensional analysis of such value judgments in popular LVLMs using counterfactual image sets, which depict the same person across different cultural contexts. Our evaluation framework pairs descriptive analyses (Moral Foundations Theory categorization, lexical analyses, and value sensitivity) with a novel grounding analysis that compares LVLM cross-context variation against two large-scale human surveys (MFQ-2 and WVS Wave 7). Across 4.8 million LVLM generations, we identify three survey-grounding bias patterns that replicate across multiple architecturally diverse models. Additional ablations show that nationality grounding is text-dominant while religion and socioeconomic grounding depend strongly on the image, and that image conditioning can amplify survey-grounding bias patterns.

title: From Enumeration to Principle: Robust Prompt Optimization via Semantic Reflection and Multi-Objective Evolution
author: Gang Xie; Dongming Shan; Kai Li; Ziyuan Huang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in adversarial environments, yet current automatic prompt optimization methods often suffer from "shortcut learning"—overfitting to specific samples rather than learning generalizable principles. We argue that, compared to scalar reward optimization or few-shot enumeration alone, the interpretability of language offers a useful medium for inducing robust decision logic. To study this, we introduce PROSE, a robust prompt optimizer that uses semantic reflection and multi-objective evolution to reduce over-reliance on enumerated examples. Facing adversarial tasks, PROSE employs an operational proxy for explicit case enumeration as an additional optimization objective. By exploring the Pareto frontier between performance and this proxy, it adds a regularization signal against sample fitting and favors more reusable rule descriptions. It employs ensemble-based de-biasing strategies and a semantic greedy selection mechanism to reduce inductive bias and premature "semantic collapse," while leveraging LLM-based reflection to summarize concise, high-level rules from failure patterns. Across the evaluated benchmarks, PROSE achieves higher average performance than the strongest baseline by up to 14.6 percentage points in accuracy on Short-Text and up to 11.84 percentage points in F1 score, while showing stronger held-out content-category generalization and reducing the F1 degradation from 29.7 points for GEPA to 13.0 points.

title: SecAgent: Efficient Mobile GUI Agent with Semantic Context
author: Yiping Xie; Chensong; Jingxuan Xing; Wei Jiang; Zekun Zhu; Yingyao Wang; Pi Bu; Jun Song; Yuning Jiang; Bo Zheng
abstract: Mobile Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents powered by multimodal large language models have demonstrated promising capabilities in automating complex smartphone tasks. However, existing approaches face two critical limitations: the scarcity of high-quality multilingual datasets, particularly for non-English ecosystems, and inefficient history representation methods. To address these challenges, we present SecAgent, an efficient mobile GUI agent at 3B scale. We first construct a human-verified Chinese mobile GUI dataset with 18k grounding samples and 121k navigation steps across 44 applications, along with a Chinese navigation benchmark featuring multi-choice action annotations. Building upon this dataset, we propose a semantic context mechanism that distills history screenshots and actions into concise, natural language summaries, significantly reducing computational costs while preserving task-relevant information. Through supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning, SecAgent outperforms similar-scale baselines and achieves performance comparable to 7B-8B models on our and public navigation benchmarks. Our dataset and benchmark are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/alibabagroup/CMGUI.

title: When Accuracy Aligns and Fails: Diagnosing Human–LLM Response Alignment at Population Scale
author: Seoyoon Park; Hyeji Choi; Subin An; Xiaonan Wang; Heejae Kim; Joeun Kang; Hansaem Kim
abstract: We propose CAPE, a Choice-Distribution Alignment and Performance Evaluation framework for diagnosing human–LLM response alignment using population-scale human choice distributions. CAPE separates outcome-level difficulty alignment from response-distribution alignment with four metrics: OA, MAE, PA, and DA. We apply CAPE to 609 Korean CSAT items with item-level response distributions from approximately 300K examinees per item, and evaluate 16 LLMs. Results show that model capability is the strongest predictor of alignment, with accuracy closely tied to both full-choice and distractor-only alignment. However, group-level scores are affected by aggregation size and model composition, and neither reasoning augmentation nor Korean adaptation yields consistent residual advantages. Bloom-level analyses further suggest that capability-linked alignment varies across item types. CAPE thus enables evaluation beyond accuracy by diagnosing how model success and failure patterns relate to human population responses.

title: Language Modeling Across Script Variants: The Case of Japanese
author: Go Inoue; Nizar Habash; Timothy Baldwin
abstract: We investigate the effect of script variants on language modeling in Japanese, which uniquely combines logographic (kanji) and phonetic (kana) writing systems. Motivated by educational curricula in which learners are gradually exposed to increasing numbers of logographic characters, we simulate this staged exposure during training to study its effect on model behavior. We construct multiple versions of a corpus with controlled script transformations, including fully transliterated kana text and intermediate variants corresponding to curriculum-based kanji levels, and train language models under different schedules that vary the timing and progression of script exposure during pre-training. In addition, we propose a cross-script evaluation framework using multiple versions of a minimal-pair benchmark with systematically varied kanji usage to assess the robustness of language models to script variation. Our results show that training on a mixture of two extreme script variants improves robustness across script conditions, whereas curriculum-based progression does not consistently improve performance.

title: From Debate to Decision: Conformal Social Choice for Safe Multi-Agent Deliberation
author: Mengdie Flora Wang; Haochen Xie; Guanghui Wang; Aijing Gao; Guang Yang; Ziyuan Li; Qucy Wei Qiu; Fangwei Han; Hengzhi Qiu; Yajing Huang; Bing Zhu; Jae Oh Woo
abstract: Multi-agent debate improves LLM reasoning, yet agreement is not evidence of correctness. When agents converge on a wrong answer through social reinforcement, consensus stopping commits that error to automated action with no recourse. We introduce Conformal Social Choice, a post-hoc layer that converts debate outputs into calibrated act-versus-escalate decisions. Verbalized probability distributions from heterogeneous agents are aggregated via a linear opinion pool and calibrated with split conformal prediction, yielding fixed-round marginal coverage: at any pre-specified round, the correct answer is included with probability {\geq}1{-}\alpha, without assumptions on individual model calibration. A hierarchical action policy maps singletons to autonomous action and larger sets to human escalation. Across eight MMLU-Pro domains and two additional benchmarks, fixed-round coverage stays close to target. The key finding is not that debate becomes more accurate, but that the conformal layer makes its failures actionable: at the final round, 81.9% of wrong-consensus cases are flagged by non-singleton sets at \alpha{=}0.05. Separately, among cases that reach a singleton before the final round, accuracy reaches 90.0–96.8% on MMLU-Pro (up to 22.1pp above consensus stopping): a selection effect, not a reasoning improvement. Simple probability- and entropy-threshold rules attain comparable interception; conformal’s distinct value is a finite-sample fixed-round coverage guarantee together with explicit candidate sets for escalation. Adaptive first-singleton stopping is evaluated empirically and not covered by this guarantee.

title: Definitional Sensitivity in Media Bias Detection: A Multi-Definition Dataset and Benchmark
author: Martin Paul Wessel; Timo Spinde; Jürgen Pfeffer; Gianluca Demartini
abstract: Media bias detection relies on definitions and examples that specify what counts as bias, yet these specifications often vary across datasets or remain implicit, even when given the same name. Such variation makes it unclear whether models trained for the same bias category learn the same construct or different phenomena, a problem largely overlooked in prior work. We examine how definition choice affects bias annotation in a between-subjects experiment with 354 participants and a parallel evaluation with four LLMs. Participants and models rate six news articles across four bias categories using definitions that vary in conceptual framing and elaboration. Across 8,496 human and 28,800 LLM ratings, we find that the conceptual target of a definition drives annotation divergence, while construct-preserving elaboration does not: conceptual framing significantly shifts annotations for humans and does so even more strongly for LLMs. We discuss implications for construct specification in annotation protocols and prompt-based measurement, and consider how definitional sensitivity may propagate to downstream classification beyond media bias. We also release MUDD, the Multi-Definition Bias Detection Dataset.

title: Beyond Prefix Answering: Parallel Infilling Reading for Long Contexts with Diffusion Language Models
author: Han Peng; Zican Dong; Peiyu Liu; Jingyuan Zou; Pengfei Li; Xin Zhao
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, showing strong non-autoregressive generation abilities. Although the masked denoising objective trains DLMs to recover tokens at arbitrary positions, current long-context usage still mostly follows a prefix-based paradigm: the full context is given as a prefix, and the answer is generated only at the end, leaving the model’s infilling ability underutilized. To investigate whether DLMs can read long contexts by infilling, we introduce Parallel Infilling Reading (PIR), a training-free method that inserts extraction slots into long contexts to generate intermediate reading states. Our empirical study shows that naive PIR improves over prefix-based DLM inference, but suffers from slot repetition, where multiple slots generate redundant evidence. To mitigate this issue, we propose Slot-Isolated PIR, which blocks direct slot-to-slot attention, and PIR-SFT, which uses fine-grained evidence supervision to teach DLMs effective evidence extraction while reading. Experiments on long-context question answering benchmarks show that our methods improve answer accuracy and generation efficiency, with increasingly larger gains as the context length grows.

title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
author: Xiaopeng Ke; Zhixin Wang; Xuebo Liu; Xinyu Ma; Xing Zheng; Bowen Song; Weiqiang Wang; Min Zhang
abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{ANT-A Benchmark}, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss’ \kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose \textbf{ANT-OR}, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@\ge2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss’ \kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.

title: Unveiling Latent Cognitive Bias Constructs in Large Language Models
author: Bezawit Lake Tilaye; Huw Day; Chris McWilliams; Telmo M Silva Filho
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in decision-making, there is a growing need to better understand the behavioural patterns underlying their reasoning. Evaluation is one of the primary approaches used to study model behaviour. However, most existing LLM evaluations rely on task-based benchmarks that summarise performance through aggregate scores. While effective for comparing model performance, such approaches provide limited insight into the latent behavioural tendencies that drive biased reasoning. In this paper, we propose a construct-based evaluation framework for studying cognitive bias in LLMs grounded in psychometric evaluation. We systematically perturb prompts across controlled conditions to analyse reasoning behaviour. From model responses, we derive behavioural features capturing susceptibility, robustness, correction, and variability, and apply latent variable modelling to infer underlying behavioural constructs. Our findings show that cognitive bias in LLMs is structured and dynamic, varying across bias type, model families, and scale.

title: Controlling Creativity in Concept Space: A Framework for Generative Models
author: Dana Levin; Dafna Shahaf
abstract: Generative models, such as text-to-image models, excel at taking textual prompts and producing semantically faithful outputs. However, the user’s ability to control the level of creativity of the output remains limited. We introduce Concept-Level Temperature (Concept-τ ), a novel framework for controlling creativity in generative models. Unlike existing methods that operate on low-level features (tokens, noise, etc.), Concept-τ operates at a higher level of abstraction; it systematically identifies decisions left underspecified by the prompt and realizes them according to a creativity parameter, creating a structured exploration space. In this work, we design general criteria for a creativity parameter, and implement an interpretable, model-agnostic method to satisfy them. We demonstrate our ideas on the text-to-image domain; empirical evaluation, both qualitative and quantitative, shows that Concept- significantly outperforms baseline methods in creative modulation and enhancement.

title: Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance: Training-Free Localized Accent Control for Code-Switching Text-to-Speech
author: Che Hyun Lee; Sangkwon Park; Donghun Kang; Dongwook Lee; Youngho Cho; Heeseung Kim; Sungroh Yoon
abstract: Current speech synthesis struggles with code-switching, which mixes a foreign language phrase into a primary language utterance, causing the phrase to be spoken with the primary language’s accent rather than its native one. We propose Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance (LCG), a training-free inference framework that restores a native accent to code-switched phrases in cross-lingual text-to-speech. LCG replaces the single language guidance applied across the whole utterance with a separate guidance for each region, so each part is guided by its own language. To choose where to apply this localized guidance, we propose a self-attention probing technique that finds the phrase boundaries without external alignments. Together, these components generate speech in which each region carries the accent of its own language, requiring no fine-tuning or auxiliary models. Across diverse language pairs, LCG robustly increases the nativeness of the code-switched phrase while suppressing accent leakage, and preserving overall speaker identity and naturalness.

title: SCOPE-RL: Optimizing Reasoning Paths Before and After Success
author: Xiaojian Liu; Han Xu; Jianqiang Xia; Zhixuan Li; Ke Xu; Yiwei Dai; Xinran Chen; Changwo Wu; Yuchen Li
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) optimizes LLMs using sparse verifiable final-answer rewards. This sparse anchor reliably verifies whether a trajectory succeeds but provides no direct feedback on the reasoning path that produced it. Before success, prerequisite progress on hard problems receives no reward signal; after success, outcome rewards cannot distinguish well-organized correct trajectories from redundant or locally flawed ones. We introduce SCOPE-RL (Scaffolded Chain Optimization with Process Efficiency), a two-stage framework that densifies this anchor while retaining the GRPO update: Adaptive Scaffolded RL adds prefix-decomposed verifiable rewards on answer-hidden sub-question chains before success, and Quality-Aware Process RL applies correctness-gated process-shape rewards to refine correct trajectories after success. An expert-validated Step-Quality Evaluation Protocol evaluates useful-step density, error localization, and token efficiency beyond final-answer accuracy. On Qwen3-8B-Instruct trained on DAPO-Math and Big-Math, SCOPE-RL improves average accuracy by up to 11.2 pp and reduces reasoning tokens by up to 27.1% over outcome-only GRPO; the gains hold under GSPO and on Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct, indicating that reward-signal densification is complementary to policy-update-level RLVR advances.

title: Leveraging Teacher-Forcing Token-Level Anomaly Signals for Heterogeneous Backdoor Filtering in LLMs
author: Tianxu Han; Jiangming Wang; Chunyi Zhou; Binbin Zhao; Tianyu Du
abstract: Generative backdoor attacks pose a growing threat to the instruction tuning of large language models (LLMs), where attackers poison a few training samples to induce malicious payloads on triggered inputs while preserving normal behavior on clean ones. However, existing backdoor-poisoned sample filtering methods typically rely on global sample representations and clustering-based separation, and such global signals can become fragile when heterogeneous target-side malicious payloads scatter poisoned samples or low poisoning rates prevent poisoned samples from forming stable clusters. This motivates us to move beyond cross-sample separability and instead exploit localized token-level target-side anomalies induced by malicious payload tokens under teacher forcing. Building on this intuition, we propose TTAF, a Teacher-forcing Token-level Anomaly Filtering framework which introduces a token-level anomaly score under teacher forcing and aggregates localized evidence to filter suspicious poisoned samples before fine-tuning. Experiments across multiple datasets, representative backdoor attacks, and different LLMs show that TTAF consistently achieves strong filtering performance within this payload-injection setting, with efficient runtime and no external dependencies. Code is available at https://github.com/Sam-Han2020/TTAF.

title: FailureMem: A Failure-Aware Multimodal Framework for Autonomous Software Repair
author: Ruize Ma; Yilei Jiang; Shilin Zhang; Zheng Ma; Yi Feng; Zhi Wang; Xiangyu Yue; Chuanyi Li; Vincent Ng; Lewei Lu
abstract: Multimodal Automated Program Repair (MAPR) extends traditional program repair by requiring models to jointly reason over source code, textual issue descriptions, and visual artifacts such as GUI screenshots. While recent LLM-based repair systems have shown promising results, existing approaches face several limitations: rigid workflow pipelines restrict exploration during debugging, visual reasoning is often performed over full-page screenshots without localized grounding, and failed repair attempts are rarely transformed into reusable knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose FailureMem, a multimodal repair framework that integrates three key mechanisms: a hybrid workflow–agent architecture that balances structured localization with flexible reasoning, active perception tools that enable region-level visual grounding, and a Failure Memory Bank that converts past repair attempts into reusable guidance. Experiments on SWE-bench Multimodal demonstrate FailureMem improves the resolved rate over GUIRepair by 3.7%.
