Rather than static retrieval, CogMem employs a deterministic controller with four cognitive operators (anchoring, traversal, intersection, evidence grounding) that dynamically navigate the graph based on query intent. Comprehensive evaluation on LoCoMo and LongMemEval shows that CogMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across all task categories, surpassing neural memory systems and graph retrieval methods. These results demonstrate that structured cognitive modeling significantly improves long-term memory accuracy and robustness compared to passive vector retrieval.

title: Efficient Token-Level Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion Models via Velocity Alignment
author: Chenxing Wei; Jiazhen Kang; Hong Wang; Jianqing Zhang; Hao Jiang; Xuxiaolong; Ningyuan Sun; Ying He; Fei Yu; Yao Shu; Bo Jiang
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) successfully aligns autoregressive models in rigorous domains like mathematical reasoning and code generation. However, applying RLVR to Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) is hindered by intractable sequence-level likelihoods, forcing existing methods to rely on unstable, high-variance approximations. We propose Sequence Likelihood-Free Policy Optimization (LFPO), an efficient framework that circumvents this bottleneck by formulating policy alignment as discrete velocity alignment. Inspired by continuous flow matching, LFPO eschews trajectory-level estimation and directly optimizes denoising logits via contrastive token-level updates, providing a stable, low-variance surrogate. Furthermore, predicting terminal solutions from intermediate states implicitly straightens the generation trajectory, enabling high-quality sampling with significantly fewer denoising iterations. Extensive experiments on reasoning and coding benchmarks demonstrate that LFPO matches or exceeds the accuracy of likelihood-based baselines while substantially accelerating inference.

title: Same Answer, Different Representations: Hidden instability in VLMs
author: Farooq Ahmad Wani; Alessandro Suglia; Rohit Saxena; Aryo Pradipta Gema; Wai-Chung Kwan; Fazl Barez; Maria Sofia Bucarelli; Fabrizio Silvestri; Pasquale Minervini
abstract: The robustness of Vision Language Models (VLMs) is commonly assessed through output-level invariance, implicitly assuming that stable predictions reflect stable multimodal processing. In this work, we argue that this assumption is insufficient. We introduce a representation-aware and frequency-aware evaluation framework that measures internal embedding drift, spectral sensitivity, and structural smoothness (spatial consistency of vision tokens), alongside standard label-based metrics. Applying this framework to modern VLMs across the SEEDBench, MMMU, and POPE datasets reveals three distinct failure modes. First, models frequently preserve predicted answers while undergoing substantial internal representation drift; for perturbations such as text overlays, this drift approaches the magnitude of inter-image variability, indicating that representations move to regions typically occupied by unrelated inputs despite unchanged outputs. Second, robustness does not improve with scale; larger models achieve higher accuracy but exhibit equal or greater sensitivity, consistent with sharper yet more fragile decision boundaries. Third, we find that perturbations affect tasks differently: they harm reasoning when they disrupt how models combine coarse and fine visual cues, but on the hallucination benchmarks, they can reduce false positives by making models generate more conservative answers.

title: State2State: Revealing Compositional Safety Failures through State-Transition Reasoning
author: Chu-Jun Peng; Zhong-Wei Lin; Yu-Wen Tseng; Hong-Han Shuai; Wen-Huang Cheng
abstract: Current aligned models can reject explicit harmful requests, yet may remain vulnerable when harmful intent is distributed across semantically related descriptions. Existing jailbreak methods often rely on surface-form manipulation, decomposition, or visual obfuscation, but the harmful objective may still remain detectable by modern safety safeguards. We present State2State (S2S), a state-transition-based, single-turn black-box jailbreak framework that targets a core weakness of current aligned models: compositional blindness. S2S rewrites a harmful request into a pair of original-state and final-state descriptions, then prompts the target model to explain the causal transition between them. Instead of directly processing an explicit harmful instruction, the model infers the malicious procedure as the logical bridge connecting the initial and final states. Controlled ablations further show that S2S remains highly effective when the state descriptions are provided as text only, while rendering them as visual inputs does not improve attack success. This suggests that the observed vulnerability is not driven solely by visual obfuscation, but is associated with compositional reasoning over transformation semantics. Across seven recent target models, S2S achieves 81.33% ASR on OpenAI o1, outperforming strong baselines by 74.63 to 81.33 percentage points and exposing a critical blind spot in current model safety safeguards.

title: Sieve and Sage: Efficient Distraction Filtering for Reliable RALM Abstention
author: Jongbin Won; SungGeun AN; Jay-Yoon Lee
abstract: Just as Socrates recognized the limits of his own knowledge, Retrieval-Augmented Language Models (RALMs) should learn to abstain when the retrieved evidence cannot support a reliable response. Existing approaches largely rely on monolithic LLMs to handle heterogeneous retrieval failures in a single step, resulting in limited abstention performance and high computational costs. We instead decompose retrieval failures into two distinct states: (i) the unanswerable state, where the required evidence is absent, and (ii) the distracted state, where relevant evidence is mixed with conflicting, negated, or adversarial information. Based on this decomposition, we introduce a lightweight module (Sieve) that screens retrieved document sets for distracting evidence before invoking a costly LLM (Sage) for grounded generation and abstention. Evaluated across both general and high-stakes expert domains, our Sieve and Sage framework preemptively detects distracting noise, improving system accuracy by up to 69.4%p and Macro-F1 by 55.2%p compared to one-stage baselines. Furthermore, it achieves up to a 1.99\times speedup, establishing a highly efficient and reliable abstention pipeline for RALM with abstention.

title: STARK: Strategic Advantage Reinforcement with Confidence-Driven Exploration for Long-Horizon Agentic Learning
author: Jinyang Wu; Xinan Chang; Yuhao Shen; Zhengxi Lu; Shuo Yang; Mingkuan Feng; Jiangyan Yi; Shuai Zhang; Zheng Lian; Zhengqi Wen; Jianhua Tao
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for long-horizon agents faces two key challenges. First, parallel linear rollouts tend to converge toward homogeneous reasoning patterns, leading to cognitive-mode collapse. Second, existing methods refine credit assignment along only a single dimension, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve state-aligned comparison and meta-reasoning discrimination. We propose STARK (**S**trategic and **T**actical **A**dvantage **R**einforcement via Confidence Guided **K**eypoint Exploration) to resolve both issues. STARK performs corrective exploration through confidence-driven branching at uncertain decision points and injects reflection into new branches. To empower these keypoint-expanded trajectories, STARK introduces a dual-track strategic and tactical advantage estimator: The strategic track compares reasoning modes under shared environmental observations, while the tactical track evaluates execution quality within each meta-reasoning tag group. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop show that STARK consistently outperforms strong baselines across model scales and task domains, and enables a 1.5B model to surpass GPT-5 on the out-of-domain settings.

title: Quantifying and Mitigating Korean Jamo-Level Typographical Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models
author: Seojin Lee; Hwanhee Lee
abstract: Korean introduces an additional typographical perturbation level not captured by ordinary character-level edit models: because syllable blocks are internally composed of sub-character units called jamo, keyboard-level errors can occur \textit{within} a syllable, either producing a valid but semantically altered character or exposing raw jamo on the surface. Both outcomes disrupt sub-word tokenization and are not reliably corrected by existing grammatical error correction pipelines, leaving LLMs directly exposed to corrupted inputs. To quantify this vulnerability, we apply five jamo-level perturbation types to the KMMLU benchmark and evaluate four language models, finding that accuracy declines monotonically with perturbation intensity and that parameter scaling does not confer robustness against intra-syllabic noise. We further show that typo-corrupted inputs induce a distinct shift in internal representations that is not reducible to ordinary answer incorrectness, and that a simple linear probe trained on these representations detects unseen perturbation types with high AUROC. Motivated by this signal, we propose \textbf{Typo-Aware Chain-of-Thought (TACoT)}, which routes inputs to chain-of-thought inference only when the probe detects a likely typo, recovering a substantial portion of the CoT accuracy gain at a fraction of the inference cost.

title: From Decoding Knobs to Commit Frontiers: Understanding Trajectory Control in Discrete Diffusion Language Models
author: Junzhuo Li; Bo Wang; Tianhao Li; Hao-Ran Wei; Baosong Yang; Xuming Hu
abstract: Discrete diffusion language models generate text by iteratively committing masked positions, making decoding a trajectory-level process rather than a sequence of independent token decisions. Existing analyses often focus on surface-level knobs such as temperature, step budget, block size, or scheduler choice, but these knobs do not explain why the same change can induce different behaviors across models. We analyze discrete diffusion decoding through high-influence commitment events and define an observed trajectory influence measure based on downstream entropy reduction over unresolved positions. Across Dream-v0-Instruct-7B and LLaDA-8B-Instruct on reasoning, code, and question-answering tasks, we find that influence is sparse, early relative to each model’s commit frontier, and stable under tested seed and step-budget variations. We further show that criticality emerges from the interaction between commit timing and token role, explaining why decoding knobs reshape trajectories in model-dependent ways. Finally, lightweight margin-based interventions validate the analysis by correcting diagnosed failure modes without additional forward passes.

title: EgoActor: Grounding Task Planning into Spatial-aware Egocentric Actions for Humanoid Robots via Visual-Language Models
author: Yu Bai; MingMing Yu; Chaojie Li; Ziyi Bai; Xinlong Wang; Börje F. Karlsson
abstract: Deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments requires tightly integrating perception, locomotion, and manipulation under partial observations, dynamic changes, and frequent transitions across heterogeneous sub-tasks. Towards this challenge, we propose EgoActing, a new task that grounds high-level instructions into diverse, precise, and spatially aware humanoid actions. We instantiate it with EgoActor, a hierarchical humanoid system centered on a vision-language model that predicts egocentric textual actions from monocular RGB observations. Among the actions, parameterized movement and viewpoint actions are mapped to locomotion and head controllers, while manipulation and human-interaction actions are routed to downstream skills via lightweight parsing. Trained with broad supervision from real-world egocentric demonstrations, spatial reasoning QA, and simulated demonstrations, EgoActor makes robust, context-aware decisions with a sub-second VLM forward pass for both 8B and 4B variants, while the current cloud-deployed robot loop takes 3–8 seconds end-to-end. Extensive simulated and real-world evaluations show that EgoActor bridges abstract task planning and concrete motor execution, generalizing across diverse tasks and unseen environments. Code and models are released at https://baai-agents.github.io/RoboNoid/EgoActor/.

title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection
author: Yu Wang; Yanran Chen; Yifan Wang; Steffen Eger; Hendrik Buschmeier
abstract: We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. In contrast, human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics; however, linear-CKA uncovers a distinct cross-metric convergence pattern. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96% accuracy. Our classification results demonstrate its potential without relying on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal, which require a language model as the estimator.

title: RL from Teacher-Model Refinement: Gradual Imitation Learning for Machine Translation
author: Dongyub Jude Lee; Zhenyi Ye; Pengcheng He
abstract: Preference-learning methods for machine translation (MT), such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have shown strong gains but typically rely on carefully curated preference triplets and often struggle to generalize beyond their tuning domains. We propose Reinforcement Learning from Teacher-Model Refinement (RLfR), which replaces static triplets with on-policy, actor-conditioned refinements produced by a frozen teacher. At each step, the actor samples candidate translations, the teacher performs a minimal local edit of each draft, and the actor is reinforced to close the gap using a composite reward that combines scaled negative edit distance for lexical and structural fidelity with COMET for semantic adequacy. This formulation yields a stable, model-aware learning signal without requiring curated preference triplets, making it naturally scalable to many language pairs without additional data collection. Experiments on FLORES-200 (en <-> de/es/zh/ko/ja) show that RLfR consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving semantic quality and entity preservation across automatic, LLM-judge, and human evaluations.

title: When Personas Become Harmful: Guiding LLM with Global Citizenship Values Alignment
author: Siqi Shen; Lajanugen Logeswaran; Moontae Lee; Honglak Lee; Rada Mihalcea
abstract: LLMs are increasingly being used by users from diverse demographics with pluralistic values and distinct backgrounds. Maintaining safety while respecting value-laden personas is uniquely challenging because persona-conditioned requests are often not overtly malicious, unlike those in existing safety benchmarks. Alignment methods aimed at adversarial requests therefore may miss the harm that emerges from persona use, leaving models to either refuse legitimate value expression or blindly follow unsafe personas. We construct a dataset of 11k controversial topics paired with value-based personas mapping to value dimensions from the Schwartz Value Survey. Through an agentic pipeline that iteratively refines the topic and persona, we surface and collect harmful responses from well-aligned commercial LLMs with a more than 47% success rate. We use UNESCO’s global citizenship principles as a minimal common ground for distinguishing valid value expressions from harmful behaviors, and introduce a controllable alignment model that lets users balance persona adherence and safety at inference time. The resulting model is safer and more persona-adherent than baselines on most samples.

title: JarvisGUI: Towards Cross-Device GUI Agents with Dynamic Task Composition
author: Zixiang Chen; Yuheng Lu; Zihao Cheng; Zeming Liu; Jizeng Bai; Ziye Huang; Zhiyin Lin; Zihan Li; Yuhang Guo; Yunhong Wang; Haifeng Wang
abstract: Real-world GUI usage frequently involves workflows that span multiple devices and platforms, requiring the transfer of intermediate results, maintenance of shared state, and coordination across heterogeneous environments. However, existing GUI benchmarks overwhelmingly evaluate agents on single-device, statically defined tasks, thus leaving such cross-device capabilities largely unexamined, resulting in an overly optimistic assessment of agents’ readiness for real-world usage. We introduce JarvisGUI, a dynamic benchmark that evaluates GUI agents on cross-device workflows requiring coordinated interaction across heterogeneous platforms—including Android, Windows, and Ubuntu. Specifically, JarvisGUI formulates GUI tasks as input–output transformations under a lightweight type system, which allows us to automatically compose multi-step, cross-device workflows and dynamically evaluate agent performance within a unified framework. By evaluating agents in virtual environments spanning multiple operating systems, JarvisGUI reveals that state-of-the-art open-source GUI agents struggle with the state-transfer awareness, cross-platform contextual reasoning, and long-horizon dependency management required for real-world workflows, exposing a critical capability gap invisible to existing benchmarks.

title: PILAR: A Page-Grounded Unified Evidence Representation via an Entity-Linked Assertion Graph for Open-Domain QA Agents over Multimodal Document Corpora
author: Joongmin Shin; Gyuho Shim; Jung-Hun Lee; Jaehyung Seo
abstract: Open-domain question answering (ODQA) over multimodal document corpora requires linking evidence scattered across text, tables, and figures. Existing systems often store these sources separately or retrieve only coarse pages, which weakens global evidence linking. We present PILAR, a page-grounded unified evidence representation instantiated as an entity-linked assertion graph. PILAR maps sentence-, table-, and figure-derived facts into a common assertion space and uses the graph as a controlled linking layer over robust page retrieval. In a shared-reader evaluation with four agent frameworks, fourteen retrieval backends, and two benchmarks, PILAR achieves the best end-to-end EM/ANLS. Gains are largest on compositional, cross-document, and multimodal questions, with a single-shot improvement of +1.6 EM over flat retrieval, rising to +2.9 on compositional and +5.9 on 3-hop questions. Ablations show that current gains are driven mainly by the text-instantiated slice of the framework, while visual assertions help only after locality-aware filtering. We therefore position PILAR as a unified evidence representation for multimodal ODQA rather than a standalone visual-reasoning module.

title: Does Sensitivity to Pragmatic Norms Emerge with More Parameters, More Data, or More Conversations?
author: Raha Askari; Judith Sieker; Valerio Basile; Sina Zarrieß
abstract: While previous work has examined the ability of language models (LMs) to capture pragmatic patterns, it remains understudied to what extent these abilities are shaped by training conditions. To address this gap, we test several models using an existing evaluation paradigm targeting LMs’ sensitivity to conversational norms (Askari et al. 2025). Across three experimental settings, we investigate the role of model size, training dynamics, and data composition in shaping pragmatic competence. Our results show that different pragmatic abilities exhibit distinct learning dynamics across models with varying sizes. While size or data scaling lead to inconsistent gains, exposure to conversational data causes moderate improvements in a modest training setting. Together, our findings suggest that pragmatic competence in LMs is heterogeneous and highlight the importance of targeted training conditions over scale alone for developing pragmatically sensitive models.

title: WebSync: A Self-Evolving Web Agent Framework for Co-Evolving Strategic Advice and Executable Skills
author: Yuanlei Wang; Haohao Luo; Zihao Yi; Ying Shen; Liang Lin
abstract: With the advent of large language models, autonomous web agents have achieved more sophisticated capabilities in planning, reflecting, and tool using, enabling automating navigation in complex and dynamic web environments. Despite this, existing efforts to instill experiential learning through memory-centric retrieval or skill-centric synthesis are respectively limited by computational inefficiency and a lack of robustness, preventing web agents from truly self-evolving. To tackle this problem, we introduce a novel web agent framework called WebSync, which is designed to unify strategic advice and skill synthesis through a structured skill recipe to compile experience into executable skills more efficiently and robustly. Furthermore, it enables continuous self-evolving by using runtime feedback to trigger iterative recipe and skill refinement, thus achieving a robust transition from trial-and-error reasoning to proven execution. Experimental results on WebArena and WebVoyager benchmarks demonstrate the superiority and versatility of WebSync across multiple backbone large language models.

title: Retrieval Sensitivity to Identity Signals in Queries
author: Andrew Tang; Nicholas Deas; Kathleen McKeown; Vishal Misra
abstract: Dense retrievers decide which documents reach users and the language models that use them, yet they are typically evaluated with neutral queries. We ask whether the identity signals that real users express in their queries—political ideology and dialect—bias what a retriever returns. We design evaluations in two domains, political news and consumer-health questions, each pairing a controlled synthetic set that varies only the identity signal with naturalistic queries. Across five dense retrievers and a sparse baseline, every retriever (i) retrieves articles that align with the query’s own political lean and (ii) performs worse for questions written in African American Language (AAL) than in White Mainstream English (WME). Two analyses tie these gaps to queries’ identity signals beyond surface vocabulary: partialling out an aggregate lexical-asymmetry score leaves the synthetic gaps largely intact, and linear probes recover lean and dialect from the retrievers’ query embeddings beyond token-level features. Left unaddressed, such retrieval biases risk contributing to polarization and reinforcing the health disparities already faced by AAL speakers.

title: TimelineAgent: An LLM-based Framework for Query-Centric Event Timeline Extraction Across Multiple Documents
author: Qingkai Min; Yunxin Bao; Yifeng Lu; Zhenyu Feng; Yulong Chen; Andreas Vlachos; Yue Zhang
abstract: Query-centric cross-document event timeline extraction aims to construct event timelines from multiple documents under diverse query focuses. The task is very challenging due to the heterogeneous event modeling and reasoning requirements arising from both the intrinsic complexity of cross-document timeline construction and the diversity of query focuses. In this paper, we propose TimelineAgent, an LLM-based multi-agent framework featuring a multi-stage reasoning workflow, where heterogeneous event features are organized into reusable skills and orchestrated through a goal-oriented protocol. To facilitate evaluation, we construct a benchmark covering diverse query focuses. Experimental results show that TimelineAgent consistently outperforms existing methods, offering a practical framework for complex real-world timeline construction.

title: SHIFT: Self-reconstruction Harnesses Implicit Fine-grained Thinking for Retrieval
author: Yuxiao Luo; Da Li; Mingjie Zhang; Zhentao he; Shikun Zhang; Wei Ye
abstract: LLM-based retrievers have become a fundamental component of modern information retrieval systems. The paradigm of ”rewrite-then-retrieve” introduces explicit reasoning before retrieval. In addition, implicit-reasoning retrievers such as GIRCSE and LaSER improve efficiency by replacing explicit reasoning with soft tokens. Although these methods demonstrated competitive performance on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, they struggle to address the mismatch between the objectives of retrieval and generation. In this work, we propose SHIFT (**S**elf-reconstruction **H**arnesses **I**mplicit **F**ine-grained **T**hinking for Retrieval), a retrieval training framework based on LLMs. Firstly, we transfer LLMs into reasoning-efficient retrievers with residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in the latent space. Secondly, we alleviate the mismatch between contrastive learning and implicit reasoning using fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction. Extensive experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks show that SHIFT consistently outperforms other widely used retrievers. We also carried out a detailed analysis to illustrate how our method works.

title: Towards Multidisciplinary Citance Analysis: A Novel Approach for Intent, Polarity, and Semantics Classification
author: Georgios Pantelakis; Petros Stavropoulos; Haris Papageorgiou
abstract: The rapid increase in research publications, particularly in computer science, presents significant challenges for researchers, reviewers, and institutions in performing comprehensive literature reviews. Traditional citance analysis, which mainly focuses on sentiment and citance intent, often misses important details. To address this, we introduce a new approach that combines three key aspects: Intent, Polarity, and Semantics. Using data from Semantic Scholar we classify citances based on this approach to create CitAn dataset which has 1,165 manually labeled citances from 80 subfields in Computer Science, Health Sciences, Bioinformatics, and Social Sciences and Humanities. Finally, we fine-tune state-of-the-art language models using this dataset, which yields promising results and paves the way for efficient citance analysis across various academic fields.

title: SafeMo: Linguistically Grounded Unlearning for Trustworthy Text-to-Motion Generation
author: Yiling Wang; Zeyu Zhang; Yiran Wang; Hao Tang
abstract: Text-to-motion (T2M) generation has achieved impressive realism but poses significant safety risks by faithfully executing unsafe textual prompts. Existing motion unlearning methods face dual challenges: brittle keyword filtering and discrete codebook manipulation, which may degrade benign generation quality and introduce jerky transitions. To address these challenges, we propose SafeMo, a linguistically grounded framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to align motion generation with safety constraints. First, we introduce SafeMoEngine, an LLM-agent pipeline that autonomously classifies unsafe intents and performs semantic rewriting to construct SafeMoVAE-29K, the first safety-aligned text-to-motion dataset. Second, we propose Minimal Motion Unlearning (MMU), a continuous-space unlearning strategy that projects unsafe semantic concepts into a task vector for precise negation, avoiding the quantization artifacts of discrete methods. Experiments demonstrate SafeMo’s effective unlearning performance by more strongly suppressing unsafe text–motion retrieval than the prior SOTA motion unlearning baseline LCR, reducing forget-set R@1 by 35.3% and achieving 2.61× normalized retrieval trade-off score (NRTS), while showing better or competitive benign utility on safe prompts, with similar trends on Motion-X. Code and checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/SafeMo. Project page: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/SafeMo.

title: Evaluating Communicative Belief Updates in Large Language Models via Implicature Recognition and Cancellation
author: Cesare Spinoso-Di Piano; Verna Dankers; Marius Mosbach; Jackie Chi Kit Cheung
abstract: Human language is driven by unspoken beliefs and belief updates which are thus of critical importance for successful interactions between large language models (LLMs) and their users. In this paper, we evaluate the ability of LLMs to recognize unspoken beliefs made through implicatures and to recognize their updates through implicature cancellation: the pragmatic phenomenon whereby an utterance’s implied meaning is weakened or negated. We create the first expert-annotated implicature cancellation dataset, ImplicatureX, crowdsourced for human judgements of implicatures and their corresponding cancellations. We find that LLM belief update understanding lags behind that of humans, especially in more naturally-occurring scenarios. Additional control experiments suggest that successes in LLM belief updates may in part stem from a reliance on prior beliefs, and that failures in belief updates may depend on their type and on their form. Overall, our study suggests that current LLMs have not yet reached human-level understanding of communicative belief updates.

title: Why Prompt-Injection Detectors Fail on XPIA: A Latent-Space Explanation
author: Yash Narendra; Niladri Chatterjee
abstract: Prompt-injection detectors often fail on **cross-prompt-injection attacks (XPIA)**, where the adversarial instruction is hidden inside a document, email, webpage, or tool output. This paper argues that the failure is not only a **distribution-shift problem**, but also a **representation-level problem**. Inside the hidden states of frozen detector backbones, user prompt-injection attacks (UPIA) and XPIA are encoded along **distinct, weakly aligned directions**. A detector whose readout is primarily aligned with the UPIA direction can therefore miss the XPIA signal, even though both signals are present in the same model’s representation. A **two-axis linear-discriminant probe** recovers this missing signal: UPIA attacks fire the UPIA axis in **99.9%** of caught cases, while XPIA attacks fire the XPIA axis in **97.3%** of caught cases. Axis ablations and activation-level steering suggest that these directions are not only predictive but may also be behaviorally relevant under controlled perturbations. The geometry persists across model families, training stages, scales, and external prompt-injection benchmarks, suggesting that **XPIA should be treated as a distinct threat axis rather than as a harder version of UPIA**.

title: VDAHM: Vision-Delimiter-aware Attention Head Modulation for Enhancing Multi-Image Understanding in Large Vision-Language Models
author: Zhibiao Liang; Junyu Cheng; Ziqian Zeng
abstract: Although Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) excel at single-image understanding tasks, their performance often degrades significantly when processing multi-image inputs due to unintended cross-image information leakage, in which visual content from different images is erroneously fused and image-specific contextual information is lost. Current approaches attempt to mitigate this by inserting special vision delimiter tokens between images during input formatting to help models distinguish image boundaries and preserve context. However, our analysis reveals that such delimiters alone yield limited gains because models do not sufficiently perceive or respond to these boundary signals. To address this, we propose Vision-Delimiter-aware Attention Head Modulation (VDAHM), a training-free method that modulates the output of delimiter-sensitive attention heads, reorienting the model’s internal attention flow to strengthen its structural perception of boundary signals. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks, including Mantis, BLINK, MuirBench, and Qbench2, demonstrate that VDAHM consistently improves LVLMs performance with virtually no additional computational cost. The source code is available at [https://github.com/ZeroNLP/VDAHM](https://github.com/ZeroNLP/VDAHM).

title: Stable Reasoning, Unstable Responses: Mitigating LLM Deception via Stability Asymmetry
author: Guoxi Zhang; Jiawei Chen; Tianzhuo Yang; Lang Qin; Juntao Dai; Yaodong Yang; Jingwei Yi
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) expand in capability and application scope, their trustworthiness becomes critical. A vital risk is intrinsic deception, wherein models strategically mislead users to achieve their own objectives. Existing alignment approaches based on chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring supervise explicit reasoning traces. However, under optimization pressure, models are incentivized to conceal deceptive reasoning, rendering semantic supervision fundamentally unreliable. Grounded in cognitive psychology, we hypothesize that a deceptive LLM maintains a stable internal belief in its CoT while its external response remains fragile under perturbation. We term this phenomenon stability asymmetry and quantify it by measuring the contrast between internal CoT stability and external response stability under perturbation. Building on this structural signature, we propose the Stability Asymmetry Regularization (SAR), a novel alignment objective that penalizes this distributional asymmetry during reinforcement learning. Unlike CoT monitoring, SAR targets the statistical structure of model outputs, rendering it robust to semantic concealment. Extensive experiments confirm that stability asymmetry reliably identifies deceptive behavior, and that SAR effectively suppresses intrinsic deception without degrading general model capability.

title: ReproRepo: Scaling Reproducibility Audits with GitHub Repository Issues
author: Shanda Li; Qiuhong Anna Wei; Jingwu Tang; Valerie Chen; Nihar B Shah; Tim Dettmers; Yiming Yang; Ameet Talwalkar
abstract: Reproducing research results from papers and released code is central to scientific progress. Existing works have introduced benchmarks to evaluate whether LLM agents can assist with reproducibility, but they are difficult to scale due to their reliance on substantial manual effort for data curation and evaluation. We introduce ReproRepo, a scalable framework for reproducibility evaluation that leverages human-raised GitHub issues as naturally occurring supervision on realistic reproduction blockers. We instantiate ReproRepo on 1,149 recent machine learning papers from major conferences and evaluate four frontier model-agent configurations. Our results show that LLM agents, even without executing code, can identify many real-world reproducibility problems from paper-repository pairs: the best agent in our study, namely Codex with GPT-5.5, surfaces at least one semantically related human-reported blocker for \sim90% of papers in the study. Further analysis shows that agents are particularly effective for surfacing visible failures and identifying the right semantic region, but may still be insufficient in exact localization. ReproRepo can serve as a reusable, scalable framework for future evaluations of LLM agents on real-world reproducibility auditing. Our code is released at https://github.com/LithiumDA/ReproRepo.

title: Diagnosing LLM Fragility: An Empirical Study on Reasoning Entropy and Malicious Outputs
author: Fabio Mercorio; Daniele Potertì; Andrea Seveso
abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting is increasingly relied upon as a safety monitoring surface: if a model reasons before acting, its trace can be inspected before harm occurs. Yet reasoning is a stochastic branching process rather than a deterministic, auditable path. We introduce Bifurcation Entropy (H_{BE}), a step-level diagnostic metric that extends Kernel Language Entropy to intermediate reasoning steps, measuring the semantic breadth of a model’s next-step distribution at each point in the Chain-of-Thought. We deploy H_{BE} via In-Distribution Attacks, a controlled probing instrument that injects the model’s own high-entropy continuations to test whether H_{BE} predicts exploitability. Across five reasoning models in high-stakes blackmail scenarios, phrases in the top H_{BE} quartile are exploited 6.2\times more often than the lowest, with H_{BE}-targeted probing inducing significantly more alignment failures than random selection. These results establish H_{BE} as a principled probing signal that concentrates safety monitoring effort on the minority of reasoning steps that carry the majority of alignment risk.

title: RoleKV - Role-Aware KV Cache Management for the Inverted Age-Importance of LLM Agent Context
author: Eashan Dash; Arun Ramachandran; Prakash Raghavendra
abstract: When serving LLM agents in production, the KV cache grows over turns, and mainstream serving engines (e.g., vLLM) rely on least recently used (LRU) eviction to manage memory pressure. While LRU is well-understood for OS pages and single-turn LLM serving, its behavior on agent workloads remains underexplored. We present an inverted age-importance phenomenon in agent workflows, where the oldest KV blocks (system prompts, tool outputs) are the most persistently attended, while the .newest blocks (chain-of-thought reasoning) decay fastest. As a result, recency-based eviction systematically discards the wrong blocks in agent workloads, producing two distinct overheads: (1) wasted prefill work on preempt-discard engines, and (2) wasted PCIe bandwidth on CPU-offload engines. We propose RoleKV, a training-free, lossless eviction policy that evicts KV blocks based on their semantic role in agent workflows. A lightweight Role Tagger assigns each block to a semantic role, and RoleKV then evicts by role-aware decay rather than recency. Unlike model-level KV compression methods that incur quality loss, RoleKV is a system-level policy that decides where blocks reside (GPU vs. CPU/disk), without affecting model outputs. RoleKV cuts preemptions by up to 64.3%, PCIe traffic by up to 63.8%, and improves end-to-end latency by up to 1.41× on 8B-70B models, with gains that grow on longer agent traces and persist on multi-GPU setups. This recasts KV eviction in production LLM serving from a recency problem to a role-aware retention problem.

title: Why and When to Use Statistical Significance in Explanation Evaluation: A Systematic Survey and Guidelines for Explainable NLP
author: Fariz Ikhwantri; Dusica Marijan
abstract: In this paper, we present a systematic survey and methodological guidelines for explanation evaluation and statistical significance testing in explainable NLP (XAI). We systematically reviewed 494 verified papers from the ACL Anthology (2020–2025) to identify how explanations are evaluated and the frequency of statistical validation. Our analysis identifies a persistent **rigour gap**: although **the number of explainable NLP papers increased fivefold** during the study period, there was **no corresponding increase in the use of explanation-specific statistical testing**. Across the full corpus, only 25.30% (125/494) of studies substantiate evaluation claims with hypothesis testing. This remains a minority practice in every surveyed year. We categorise the primary barriers to rigour into three issues: implicit generalisation, inferential reporting gap, and incomplete rigour. To address these, we propose a bipartite framework that maps research hypotheses to appropriate statistical testing regimes. Our goal is to clarify when statistical testing is necessary and to provide a guideline for more rigorous, reproducible explainability research in the LLM era.

title: World Models for Policy Refinement in StarCraft II
author: Yixin Zhang; Ziyi Wang; Yiming Rong; Haoxi Wang; Jinling Jiang; Shuang Xu; Haoran Wu; Shiyu Zhou; Bo XU
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown strong reasoning capabilities, motivating their use in complex decision-making environments. StarCraft II (SC2), with its massive state-action space and partial observability, is a challenging testbed. However, existing LLM-based SC2 agents primarily focus on improving the policy itself, leaving the integration of a learnable, action-conditioned dynamics model into the decision loop largely unexplored. In this work, we propose StarWM and StarWM-Agent, and conduct the first systematic study of the learnability and decision utility of player-view, action-conditioned textual world models for SC2. StarWM predicts short-horizon future observations under partial observability. StarWM-Agent integrates StarWM into a lightweight Generate-Simulate-Refine loop for foresight-driven policy refinement. Extensive experiments show that StarWM substantially outperforms zero-shot baselines across multiple dimensions, while StarWM-Agent achieves consistent win-rate gains of 30%, 15%, and 30% against the SC2 built-in AI at Hard (LV5), Harder (LV6), and VeryHard (LV7), respectively. Additional analyses show that our method is complementary to existing history-summarization SC2-agent approaches, with their combination achieving the strongest online performance in our evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/yxzzhang/StarWM.

title: Divide by Question, Conquer by Agent: SPLIT-RAG with Question-driven graph partitioning
author: Ruiyi Yang; Hao Xue; Imran Razzak; Shirui Pan; Hakim Hacid; Flora D. Salim
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs (KGs) can improve the factual grounding of large language models, but efficient retrieval remains challenging when the underlying graph is large and multi-hop evidence is distributed across different regions. We present **SPLIT-RAG**, an efficiency-oriented multi-agent KG-RAG framework that organises a KG into reusable, question-aligned partitions using reasoning patterns observed in training questions. At inference time, SPLIT-RAG forms a query-specific retrieval plan, activates only a small set of relevant partition-specialised agents, and aggregates their retrieved evidence before final answer generation. To improve reliability when evidence from different agents is combined, the framework applies compatibility-based filtering over retrieved triples prior to synthesis. Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and MetaQA show that SPLIT-RAG achieves strong performance against recent KG+LLM baselines while reducing end-to-end latency under matched budgets. Component ablations and model-tier analyses further show that selective multi-agent retrieval is central to the performance gain, and that lightweight retrieval agents paired with a stronger head agent provide an effective accuracy–latency trade-off.

title: An Interpretable Linguistically-Grounded Analysis of Scene Saliency in Movie Screenplays
author: Uday Bindal; Ishaan Karan; Manan Garg; Ekansh Goyal; Rahul Mishra; Rajakrishnan P Rajkumar
abstract: We investigate the factors affecting salience in movie screenplay by posing two research questions: 1. Does Uniform Information Density (UID) predict salient scenes? 2. What other linguistic properties distinguish salient scenes from non-salient background? We answer both questions through a controlled corpus study on the MENSA corpus, paired with a Linguistically-Grounded Salience Model (LGSM), a dual-stream classifier that fuses a frozen BERT encoder with explicit linguistic features through adaptive gating. The UID picture is layered in long-form discourse. Perscene UID summaries carry no independent signal once length is controlled, but at the token level salient scenes match non-salient material in the bulk while specifically suppressing the rarest, hardest-to-predict tokens in the upper tail. UID therefore lives at the within-scene token level rather than as a per-scene aggregate. Salient scenes also show a moderate and sustained cast of central characters (following an inverted-U pattern), strong third-person usage, syntactically simpler language, and more abstract vocabulary about motivation and conflict. LGSM exploits this signature and improves recall on salient scenes over a strong semantic baseline while yielding better downstream summaries.

title: Universal Activation Verbalizer: A Unified Framework for Cross-Model Activation Explanation
author: Haiyan Zhao; Zirui He; Guanchu Wang; Ali Payani; Yingcong Li; Mengnan Du
abstract: Activation verbalization explains hidden representations in natural language, but existing methods are mostly limited to self-explanation, where each model explains only its own activations. We introduce Universal Activation Verbalizer (UAV), a shared-decoder framework that uses donor- and layer-specific adapters to explain activations from heterogeneous donor models. UAV learns a lightweight adapter that converts donor activations into soft tokens in decoder’s embedding space, and further supports adapter-only transfer by reusing a frozen decoder-side LoRA while training only a new adapter for another donor. Across classification, fact retrieval, and gist summarization, UAV remains competitive with strong self-explanation baselines while enabling cross-model verbalization across model families and scales. Ablations show that decoder-side tuning mainly improves task behavior, whereas the adapter provides the activation-grounded factual and semantic evidence. Code and data are available at our GitHub repository.

title: Hidden Configuration Effects on Fairness in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Decision Systems
author: Hamed Loghmani; Ninareh Mehrabi; Homa Hosseinmardi; Amir Ghasemian
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as decision agents in regulated settings—loan approval, hiring, clinical triage—must pass pre-deployment fairness audits that report a single fairness number per model under one implicit configuration. We argue this framing misses the dominant source of variation: configuration itself. Sweeping five axes (persona, interview, deliberation, aggregation rule, order) across three frontier LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o-mini, Grok 4.20 Reasoning) on a 1,000-applicant Adult Census Income sample and a 500-applicant ACSIncome (2024 ACS data) sample, we find that within a single model, persona alone swings positive-prediction rate by up to 91 percentage points and collapses decision rules on two of three models; within a Conservative/Balanced/Progressive panel, replacing the panel chair on identical deliberation transcripts moves the disparate-impact ratio from adverse-impact to near-parity; and reversing the speaking order flips up to 34% of applicants on the same panel. We identify a median-voter effect: the Balanced agent matches the majority-vote verdict on 95.8–100% of applicants across all three models—deliberative aggregation reduces, mechanically, to single-agent decision by the median. The audit unit is the configuration, not the model: a system can pass an audit under one configuration and be silently reconfigured into a non-compliant one through a prompt edit—a change that current regulations do not treat as requiring re-audit. The code to reproduce the experiments in this paper is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/agent-decision-bias-emnlp-F059/

title: Are LLMs Ready to Assist Physicians? PhysAssistBench for Interactive Doctor-Patient-EHR Assistance
author: Tianming Du; Peijie Yu; Sihan Shang; Danli Shi; My Linh Nguyen; Shengbo Gao; Guangyuan Li; Yinghong Yu; Yan Jiang; Qianlong Zhao; Behzad Bozorgtabar; Shaoxiong Ji; Jiazhen Pan; Daniel Rueckert; Jiancheng Yang
abstract: The most plausible near-term role of medical LLMs is to assist rather than replace physicians, yet current evaluations often test isolated capabilities: clinical knowledge, EHR system interaction, or patient communication. Physician assistance instead requires coordinating these capabilities within the same interaction, where physicians issue underspecified requests, patients describe symptoms ambiguously, and EHR systems demand precise tool use. We introduce PhysAssistBench, a benchmark for interactive doctor-patient-EHR assistance. Built from real MIMIC-IV cases, PhysAssistBench uses a scalable pipeline to construct agentic patients: interactive, record-grounded agents that turn static EHR records into multi-turn clinical scenarios while preserving clinical factuality. PhysAssistBench provides a curated evaluation set of 1,296 manually reviewed and physician-validated turns. Experiments with leading LLMs show that current models remain unreliable in this setting, struggling to infer physician intent, clarify vague patient descriptions, formulate grounded EHR queries, and integrate evidence across sources. These results expose a key bottleneck for clinical LLMs: reliable assistance requires coordination across knowledge, communication, and systems, not isolated gains in any of them.

title: Don’t Just Look, Intervene: Perturbation Based Region Labeling for VQA Images
author: Marko Jojic; Zhaonan Li; Ben Zhou
abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) should rely on visual evidence that directly determines the correct answer, but supervision for grounding visual reasoning is often expensive to obtain manually or tied to dataset-specific annotation primitives. We instead introduce model-causal visual evidence as an annotation target, defined as the set of image regions whose counterfactual intervention changes a model’s answer distribution for a given image-question pair. Based on this principle, we introduce Counterfactual Search for Grounding Regions (CSGR). CSGR is a scalable pipeline that proposes candidate regions, perturbs them, measures their effect on answer sensitivity, and aggregates this evidence across multiple judges to approximate answer-critical regions in VQA data. To assess whether CSGR annotations contain a useful supervision signal, we plug them into three existing grounding-aware training routines: attention steering, Visual CoT finetuning, and latent visual reasoning. These experiments test whether the proposed annotation scheme can provide a useful supervision signal across multiple ways of consuming region labels, rather than introducing a new way of using them. Across competing automatic region-labeling mechanisms, CSGR annotations provide the most consistent gains over Cross Entropy-only finetuning in both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations, indicating that the proposed labeling scheme captures useful region-level information.

title: Modality-Specific Gating for Large Audio-Language Models
author: Zhenni Ren; Juan Wang; Qiuchi Li; Lei Li; Chunxiao Gao; Huaping Zhang; Baohua Zhang
abstract: Large Audio-Language Models have made significant advances in audio-text instruction following and multimodal interaction. However, due to their text-conditioned generation architecture, current LALMs tend to be overly influenced by input text prompts. When acoustic evidence conflicts with textual prompts, incorrect or irrelevant textual cues may steer model predictions away from the audio. In this work, we systematically analyze this challenge and show that representative LALMs exhibit a persistent audio-text imbalance during decoding, where attention to audio tokens is weakened across generation steps. To address the imbalance, we propose Modality-Specific Gating (MSG), an acoustic calibration mechanism that improves audio grounding with a small number of additional parameters. MSG introduces a token-wise, query-conditioned bias to the attention logits of audio tokens before softmax, while leaving the original attention computation unchanged. With parameter-efficient fine-tuning, MSG enhances acoustic evidence utilization, leading to consistently improved performance on vocal sound classification and speech emotion recognition, as well as strong robustness under adversarial or irrelevant text prompts.

title: Variable-size Discovery and Representation of Atomic Propositions
author: Francesco Ortame; Roberto Navigli
abstract: Sentence embeddings represent meaning as a single fixed-size vector, regardless of the complexity of the input sentence. This design compresses all propositional structure into a single point, losing part of the internal structure of the sentence in the process. To address this, we introduce Atomic Proposition Embeddings (APE) to dynamically discover and encode atomic propositions in sentences as variable-size bags of vectors. We use a slot mechanism, inspired by object detection in computer vision, over an encoder backbone. APE is trained on a proposition-decomposed version of WikiSplit, and matches or outperforms sentence encoders up to 15x its size on PAWS-Wiki and SNLI with no task-specific fine-tuning, using proposition-level scoring rules at inference time. We further introduce PropSearch, a retrieval benchmark for proposition-level embeddings in which models must retrieve source sentences given atomic propositions. APE leads on PropSearch over proposition-level alternatives, with its advantage growing with sentence complexity. Ablations confirm the gains are architectural rather than data-driven and that APE can generalize over its training signal. We release our code, data and models for research purposes at https://github.com/SapienzaNLP/APE.

title: Revisiting Task Vectors: A Structural Analysis of Their Limits
author: Leekyeung Han; Hyeseung JI; Sangwon Jung; Seungwoo Lyu; Paul Hongsuck Seo
abstract: To mitigate high inference costs for in-context learning, prior works have proposed activation-space task vectors that encapsulate demonstration contexts into static representations. However, performance occasionally degrades across tasks, leaving it unclear whether this stems from sub-optimal extraction heuristics or fundamental limitations. We resolve this by decomposing Transformer self-attention to establish a theoretical best-case approximation: the Minimal-Gap Approximation. By isolating structural constraints from heuristic flaws, the Minimal-Gap Approximation reveals that task vectors are fundamentally bottlenecked by attention and length gaps. Specifically, because task vectors lock contextual information to fixed attention maps and positional alignments, they structurally fail under dynamic routing, length mismatches, and multi-token generation. We further show that these findings consistently hold across training-free extract-and-inject task vector methods, model architectures, and model scales.

title: Beyond Retrieval: Learning Compact User Representations for Scalable LLM Personalization
author: Heng Cao; Fan Zhang; Jian Yao; Yujie Zheng; Changlin Zhao; Lu Hao; Yuxuan Wei; Wangze Ni; Huaiyu Fu; Yuqian Sun; Xuyan Mo
abstract: Personalizing large language models requires adapting model behavior to individual users while preserving robustness and deployment-scale efficiency. Existing approaches typically personalize LLMs either at the input level, by retrieving user histories or constructing profile prompts, or at the parameter level, by maintaining user-specific parameter-efficient modules. The former makes personalization sensitive to retrieval quality and prompt design, whereas the latter incurs storage and maintenance costs that grow with the user population. To address these limitations, we propose TAP-PER (Temporal Attentive Prefix for PERsonalization), a prefix-based framework that encodes user preferences as learnable representations, avoiding the serialization of user histories into prompts and replacing heavy per-user adapters with lightweight user-state prefix embeddings. Inspired by personalized recommendation systems, TAP-PER decomposes user modeling into user-state and query-conditioned components, and incorporates temporal signals to capture the evolving nature of user interests. Experiments on six LaMP tasks show that TAP-PER consistently outperforms prompt-based and model-based baselines across classification, rating, and generation settings. Moreover, TAP-PER uses 130× fewer per-user parameters than OPPU and roughly half the total parameter footprint of PER-PCS at the 1,000-user scale, demonstrating scalable personalization without prompt-serialized histories or heavy per-user adapters.

title: How Do Self-Referential LLM Loops Contract Political Diversity?
author: Wooyoung Kim; Wooju Kim
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly consume their own outputs through retrieval-augmented generation and synthetic data pipelines, self-referential loops are becoming prevalent in modern information ecosystems. While prior work has studied variance collapse during recursive training, the dynamic consequences for political diversity during inference remain underexplored. We investigate this by conducting iterative paraphrasing experiments across eight widely used LLMs, and formalize self-referential generation as a discrete-time Markov process to characterize its long-term behavior. Our results reveal a systematic contraction of political diversity, with several models converging toward center-dominant equilibria. Notably, this homogenization is strongly front-loaded: the majority of diversity loss occurs within the earliest iterative rounds, indicating that even a few AI-mediated transformations can disproportionately narrow the political spectrum. We further examine two interventions: Stance-Conditioned Generation (SCG) substantially reduces marginal stance-distribution drift even without ground-truth labels, leaving no statistically detectable shift for three of the four homogenizing models, whereas Self-Identified Stance Preservation (SISP) overshoots into over-polarization; even SCG improves but does not guarantee instance-level stance retention. These findings highlight a structural risk associated with self-referential generation in AI-driven information pipelines. Our code and prompts are publicly available at https://github.com/timothy-coshin/SelfReferentialPoliticalDiversity.

title: More Evidence Is Not Always More Support: Controlled Diagnostics for Evidence Aggregation in Fact Verification
author: Shaoxin Zhong; Yuchen Su; Qian Liu; Michael J. Witbrock
abstract: Final-context accuracy in multi-passage fact verification can hide whether an added passage contributes a new verdict-relevant fact or merely repeats evidence already present. We introduce a controlled same-prefix diagnostic derived from HoVer supporting-fact annotations to measure marginal evidence contribution. For each claim, a shared prefix covers one fact’s evidence while leaving another required fact absent; the next passage either repeats the covered fact or supplies the missing fact. The diagnostic contains 1,180 same-prefix pairs and an exact-repetition ladder testing whether repeated copies of one evidence sentence can change a verifier’s label. Supervised verifiers with similar clean F1 scores, from 0.6324 to 0.6528, differ sharply in eight-repeat flip rate, from 8.5% to 30.3%. Conservative pooling and natural-language-inference (NLI) scoring reduce duplicate sensitivity but give near-zero missing-fact gain, while gain-oriented systems improve gain but remain repetition-sensitive. Latent-Gated Evidence Dynamics (LGED), a compact stateful reference model, shows that low duplicate sensitivity and positive missing-fact gain can coexist. Surface controls and decision-level analyses support this diagnostic interpretation. Redundancy and reader tests extend the duplicate-sensitivity finding beyond HoVer, while prompted open-weight LLMs reveal a gap between role recognition and verdict updating.

title: TRACE: Single-Pass Decoding-Trace Risk Localization for Generation Calibration
author: Yuebin Xu; Xuemei Peng; Junlan Chen; Zhiyi Chen; Zeyi Wen
abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for large language model deployment. However, answer-level calibration remains challenging because generation errors are often localized: a response may be fluent and high-probability overall while still failing at a critical number, entity, or factual claim. Existing estimators compress token probabilities, sequence likelihoods, entropy, or beam statistics into a global score, which can dilute such local risk signals. We propose TRACE, a single-pass, decoded-answer-preserving confidence estimator that treats decoding-time uncertainty as a trajectory through three steps: (i) recording token-level surprisal and predictive entropy during decoding, (ii) applying local risk operators to preserve uncertainty spikes, and (iii) converting localized trace risk into answer-level confidence. TRACE produces a label-free risk score, while TRACE+ calibrates trace-only features into probabilities using a held-out split, without extra generations or external verifiers. We evaluate four tasks against 19 calibration baselines, and TRACE+ reduces Brier from 0.149 to 0.137 and improves AUROC from 0.758 to 0.792 over the strongest likelihood baseline. Across seven LLMs, TRACE+ improves over the best non-TRACE baseline pool from 0.136 to 0.120 Brier and from 0.764 to 0.817 AUROC. Results show localizing decoding-time risk provides a general approach to calibration.

title: One prompt is not enough: Instruction Sensitivity Undermines Embedding Model Evaluation
author: Yevhen Kostiuk; Kenneth Enevoldsen
abstract: Instruction embedding models have become common among state-of-the-art models, however are evaluated using a single prompt per task. The single-point evaluation ignores a main problem of the instruction-based approach namely: sensitivity to the phrasing of the instruction. We present an empirical study of prompt sensitivity across 6 embedding models and 11 datasets. We show that reported scores misrepresent the distribution of scores over plausible prompts. The default prompt can both systematically understate or overstate performance. Furthermore, we show that the leaderboard ranking is not robust to prompt selection: a developer improve their rank by favorably selecting prompts, and under adversarial prompt selection any model can be promoted to first place. Our findings suggest that single-prompt evaluation is insufficient for instruction-tuned embedding models and that benchmarks should incorporate prompt robustness, either by evaluating over multiple prompts or by reporting sensitivity alongside point estimates.

title: From Leaky Thoughts to Private Reasoning: Controlling What LRMs Say to Themselves
author: Haritz Puerto; Haonan Li; Xudong Han; Timothy Baldwin; Iryna Gurevych
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) produce reasoning traces (RTs) that often contain sensitive information. These leaky thoughts are difficult to control and frequently violate explicit privacy directives. Because RTs can be exposed through prompt injection attacks, this becomes a direct privacy risk to the user. We approach this as a controllability problem: since privacy directives are themselves instructions, improving instruction-following (IF) within the RT provides a direct path to reducing privacy leaks. To this end, we introduce an SFT dataset that teaches models to follow general instructions throughout their reasoning process, and propose Staged Decoding, a simple decoding strategy that decouples RT and answer generation using separate LoRA adapters to maximize IF of each component. We evaluate our approach on six models from two families (1.7B-14B parameters), across two IF benchmarks and two privacy benchmarks. Our method yields substantial improvements, with gains of up to 20.9 points in IF and 51.9 percentage points on privacy benchmarks, though these can come at the cost of task utility due to the trade-off between reasoning performance and IF. Our results show that improving IF in LRMs can significantly enhance privacy, suggesting a promising direction for future privacy-aware LRMs.

title: DynaTokens: Controlling Token Dynamics for Continual Video-Language Understanding
author: Toan Nguyen; Yang Liu; Celso M de Melo; Flora D. Salim
abstract: Continual VideoQA with multimodal LLMs remains challenging because sequential adaptation induces task interference, while storing task-specific prompts becomes impractical as task sequences grow. We introduce DynaTokens, a transformer-based token generator that dynamically produces fine-tuning tokens on demand, enabling task-adaptive prompt updates through shared generation weights. To mitigate forgetting, we introduce meta-learning-inspired regularisers that look ahead to avoid task-specific sharp update directions while anchoring the evolving generator to prior-task behaviours. We theoretically connect this objective to sharpness-aware optimisation, showing how it favours flatter cross-task minima and improves retention. DynaTokens combines gradient-free routing based on robust pretrained token and visual embeddings with lightweight auxiliary multimodal supervision, reducing router drift during continual adaptation. Across standard continual VideoQA benchmarks, DynaTokens achieves higher average accuracy and substantially lower forgetting than strong baselines. It also improves zero-shot generalisation and remains effective in longer domain-incremental sequences with extended task shifts. Finally, we introduce a challenging ImageQA->VideoQA protocol and show that DynaTokens enables robust cross-modal continual transfer.

title: MobileDreamer: Generative Sketch World Model for GUI Agent
author: Yilin Cao; Yufeng Zhong; Zhixiong Zeng; Liming Zheng; Jing Huang; Haibo Qiu; Peng Shi; Wenji Mao
abstract: Mobile GUI agents have shown strong potential in real-world automation and practical applications. However, most existing agents remain reactive, making decisions mainly from the current screen, which limits their performance on long-horizon tasks. To address this limitation, a natural approach is to use the forecasting ability of world models to support better decision-making. This is challenging because existing world models often lack spatial awareness when predicting post-action states and are too expensive for practical deployment. In this paper, we propose MobileDreamer, an efficient world-model-based lookahead framework to equip the GUI agents based on the future imagination provided by the world model. It consists of textual sketch world model and rollout imagination for GUI agent. Textual sketch world model forecasts post-action states through a learning process to transform digital images into key task-related sketches, and designs a novel order-invariant learning strategy to preserve the spatial information of GUI elements. The rollout imagination strategy for the GUI agent optimizes the action-selection process by leveraging the prediction capability of world model. Empirical results on Android World demonstrate that MobileDreamer consistently improves the task success rate across multiple base models, achieving an average performance gain of 5.3%. World model evaluations further verify that our textual sketch modeling accurately forecasts key GUI elements.

title: Grounding Memory Summarization in Utility Intent
author: Zhenyu Lei; Mingjia Shi; Xingbo Fu; Haoyu He; Qi R. Wang; Jundong Li
abstract: Existing summarizers for memory systems are typically optimized for human-facing criteria such as faithfulness, which misaligns with their true objective: preserving the evidence needed to support future queries. We show that conditioning summarization on query-answer pairs substantially improves answer quality, and that this utility-aware behavior is transferable across queries. Motivated by these findings, we propose MemSuit, a self-distillation framework in which a teacher summarizer, conditioned on observed query-answer pairs, produces utility-aware memory entries that a student learns to reproduce from the raw conversation alone. To prevent collateral erasure where conditioning on a single query-answer pair discards evidence relevant to other plausible queries, the teacher decomposes each block into multiple self-contained entries that preserve distinct query-relevant facets as independently retrievable units. To align the retriever with the compact, fact-dense style of teacher entries, we further fine-tune the embedding model with a contrastive objective supervised by teacher entries. Across a diverse suite of conversational query types, MemSuit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, confirming the value of grounding memory in downstream utility.

title: SALA: Semantic-Aware Logical Alignment for Complex Reasoning in In-Context Learning
author: Zhao Ji; Wenqing Chen; Zhixuan Chu; Jianxing Yu; Jingping Liu; Shanhe Zhao; Zibin Zheng
abstract: Effective in-context learning (ICL) for complex reasoning relies on selecting the right demonstrations. Traditional retrieval methods based on surface similarity fail to capture the underlying problem-solving logic. Recent logic-based methods address this by matching predefined reasoning steps, but the rigid rules and exact-match criteria is improper to handle flexible or diverse reasoning processes. To address the problem, we propose SALA, a Semantic-Aware Logical Alignment framework. Instead of relying on a fixed inventory, SALA automatically learns task-specific reasoning operations. It then embeds these operations into a continuous semantic space and uses dynamic time warping (DTW) to align the reasoning sequences. This approach allows for soft, flexible matching of reasoning logic while remaining highly interpretable. Experiments across four reasoning benchmarks and three LLMs demonstrate that SALA outperforms existing demonstration selection methods. Further analysis confirming the roles of the operation induction and the logical semantic alignment.

title: Coder as Editor: Code-driven Interpretable Molecular Editing
author: Wenyu Zhu; Chengzhu Li; Xiaohe Tian; Yifan Wang; Yinjun Jia; Jianhui Wang; Bowen Gao; Haichuan Tan; Ya-Qin Zhang; Wei-Ying Ma; Yanyan Lan
abstract: Molecular design is a central task in drug discovery that requires precise structural reasoning and domain knowledge. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating high-level editing intentions in natural language, they often struggle to faithfully execute these modifications, particularly when operating on non-intuitive representations like SMILES. We introduce MECo, a framework that bridges reasoning and execution by translating editing actions into executable code. MECo reformulates molecular modification for LLMs as a cascaded framework: generating human-interpretable editing intentions from a molecule and property goal, followed by translating those intentions into executable structural edits via code generation. Our approach achieves over 98% accuracy in reproducing held-out realistic edits derived from chemical reactions and target-specific compound pairs. On downstream benchmarks spanning physicochemical properties and target activities, MECo substantially improves consistency by 38-86 percentage points to 90%+ and achieves higher success rates over SMILES-based baselines while preserving structural similarity. By aligning intention with execution, MECo enables consistent, controllable and interpretable molecular design, laying the foundation for high-fidelity feedback loops and collaborative human–AI workflows in drug discovery.

title: Before the Script, Set the Stage: How Worldview Simulation Amplifies Psychologically Grounded Persuasion in Multi-Turn Jailbreaking
author: Siyu Chen; Haoran Wang; Xiaojian Li; Yao Huang; Yinpeng Dong; Wei Xu
abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks demonstrate that harmful intent can be distributed across dialogue, yet existing methods obscure what conversational mechanisms drive vulnerability. We introduce Blueprint, a safety-evaluation framework that separates a factorized social-influence strategy space from WorldviewSim, a cross-turn situational context module. Monte Carlo Tree Search optimizes turn-level combinations of 18 theory-grounded influence factors across a four-turn trajectory. Across six frontier models, Blueprint achieves near-ceiling attack success rates on major open-weight and proprietary models, while requiring the fewest average queries (2.46). The resulting trajectories further reveal model-specific vulnerability among resistant targets: each responds to distinct influence factors and strategy transitions, yet all share a common recovery pathway. Specifically, shifting toward concrete, executable task framing consistently escapes hard-refusal states. Ablations confirm that operational cues matter most: making requests actionable has the largest impact, gain framing is unusually potent, and some legitimacy appeals can backfire. These findings suggest that robust multi-turn safety requires monitoring not only harmful content, but also how dialogue state makes unsafe requests appear concrete and locally executable. The code is open-sourced at: https://github.com/charlottec1583/Blueprint.

title: InfoEdit: Probing Global Layout Reasoning in Infographic Editing
author: Cheng Yang; Chufan Shi; Huijuan Wang; Bo Shui; Yaokang Wu; Muzi Tao; Yibo Yan; Xuezhe Ma; Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick
abstract: Multimodal foundation models edit natural photographs at production quality, yet the same models struggle with structured visual content such as infographics. Unlike photographs, infographics encode information through logical relations; editing one element often requires surrounding elements to be adapted. We refer to this global layout reasoning capability as reflow. Existing image-editing benchmarks neither provide a dedicated setting for structured visual content nor evaluate the reflow capability. We introduce InfoEdit, a novel benchmark of 1,000 infographics across eight logical-relation families, paired with 4,000 editing instructions across four editing tasks, and a reflow-aware evaluation protocol. Across eight frontier editors, only GPT-Image-2 clears 60% average success rate; most models fall below 7%, and no editor exceeds 36% on Swap-Block task even with perfect target localization. We further show that code-level editing can match the strongest pixel-level editor, revealing complementary strengths across tasks. InfoEdit identifies reflow as a central challenge in structured visual content editing and provides a diagnostic benchmark to facilitate future progress.

title: LAK-LoRA: Layer-Wise Adaptive Expert Allocation and Principal Component–Based Feature Separation for Medical Multi-Task Learning
author: Ye Lyu; Chuan Li; Chengyu Wang; Mingyuan Fan; Cen Chen
abstract: Multi-task learning in the medical domain remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), plagued by conflicting task objectives and substantial computational overhead associated with full fine-tuning. Although parameter-efficient tuning methods help reduce these resource demands, their effectiveness is limited by two critical issues: (i) rigid allocation of expert capacity across layers, and (ii) lack of regularization mechanisms to partition shared components from task-specific signals. To address these limitations, we propose LAK-LoRA, a novel architecture that enables adaptive, depth-aware scaling of expert capacity, allowing more efficient resource allocation throughout the model. Furthermore, to resolve conflicting task objectives, LAK-LoRA divides experts into two distinct groups dedicated to modeling general and task-specific features, respectively. This separation is implemented via a feature separator module, which disentangles representations into shared and task-specific subspaces before assigning them to the appropriate experts. To foster diversity and minimize representational redundancy, orthogonality constraints are imposed among specialized experts. Extensive experiments on benchmark medical datasets demonstrate that LAK-LoRA achieves the best average performance.

title: Expanding the Solvable Frontier: Policy-Adaptive Curriculum Learning for Reasoning RL
author: Guocong Li; Jinjian Zhang; Ping Wang; Siyan Guo; Yukai Sun; Hao Huang; Wei Zhou; Linjian Mo; Hongxia Xu; Jian Wu
abstract: Existing curriculum learning methods for reasoning reinforcement learning often treat problem difficulty as a static property of the problem. We argue that difficulty is instead policy-dependent: problems beyond the current policy provide sparse learning signals, while problems already solved by greedy decoding may still yield informative stochastic trajectories during RL. We propose PAD-Curriculum, a policy-adaptive curriculum framework for GRPO that estimates the student’s evolving solvable frontier from student-generated trajectories. For currently solved problems, PAD-Curriculum ranks examples by a normalized Scorer-to-Student KL discrepancy computed against a frozen stronger scorer; unsolved problems are deferred and periodically re-evaluated as the policy improves. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, and NuminaMath-CoT with Llama-3.1 and Qwen3 models show consistent gains over standard GRPO and curriculum/distillation baselines, with particularly strong improvements on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Analyses further show that adaptive discrepancy estimation is more effective than static scorer-based difficulty.

title: PhysWave: Physics-Guided Latent Diffusion Models for Controllable Spatial Audio Generation
author: Lingfeng Yao; Chenpei Huang; Xingke Yang; Ziye Geng; Changqing Luo; Hao Wang; Jiang Liu; Miao Pan
abstract: Text-to-spatial audio generation, such as text-to-First-Order Ambisonics (FOA), provides a convenient way to create spatial audio for billion-dollar gaming and film industries. However, existing text-to-FOA methods are largely data-driven and may produce audio that violates acoustic relations between source direction and distance. They also separate descriptive and parametric control, forcing users to trade usability for precision. In this paper, we present PhysWave, a physics-guided latent diffusion model for controllable text-to-FOA generation. PhysWave unifies natural-language and trajectory control through a shared waypoint-caption representation, and augments diffusion training with two differentiable acoustic priors: spherical-harmonic direction consistency and inverse-square distance consistency. To support dynamic spatial generation, we further construct a 300K-clip FOA dataset with diverse sound categories and source trajectories. Extensive results show that the proposed priors help PhysWave generate spatially consistent FOA audio while maintaining competitive audio quality. Further analyses show that these physics priors improve spatial consistency during training and can also be used as inference-time guidance for training-free spatial refinement.

title: EffectMem: Effectiveness-Driven Memory Reuse for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
author: Jingjing Yin; Lingbo Wang; Dongyan Cao; Yu Hong
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have stimulated increasing interest in LLM-based agents for long-horizon interactive decision-making. As a lightweight alternative to parameter-level optimization, many studies enhance LLM agents through retrievable experience memory. However, existing retrieval strategies primarily optimize for the relevance of historical memories, leaving the applicability conditions and verifiable execution effects of retrieved trajectories insufficiently captured. To mitigate this executability gap between relevance-driven retrieval and executable reuse, we propose Effectiveness-Driven Memory (EffectMem), a framework that reframes trajectory memory as executable guidance whose applicability and effects are checked during interaction. During memory construction, EffectMem structures successful trajectories into positive executable contracts and localizable failures into negative experience guards.
