Training such agents to act safely is difficult, since safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety arises only at a small number of safety-critical steps within a trajectory. Standard supervision is insufficient: imitating safe trajectories teaches behavior without explaining why it is safe, and contrasting arbitrary safe and unsafe trajectories mixes the safety signal with unrelated differences. We propose SafeBranch, a framework that aligns an embodied actor on safety through branch pairs constructed from the actor’s own unsafe rollouts via environment rollback. SafeBranch rolls each unsafe rollout back to the safety-critical step that caused the violation, queries the actor for a safe alternative, and pairs the original action with the alternative so that the two branches differ only at that step. The trained actor acts safely at deployment with no critic in the loop. On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks and objects, it improves safe task completion, achieving roughly ten times more safe successes than the untrained baseline on the unseen-object variant. Project page: https://github.com/98hyunse/SafeBranch.

title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing
author: Junyong Lee; Woo Kyung Kim; Honguk Woo
abstract: Effective collaboration in multi-agent systems requires mechanisms for coordination and adaptability in dynamic and uncertain environments. However, existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly, instead relying on ad-hoc output correction that limits systematic, runtime management of robustness. In this work, we propose Multi-Agent Mesh (MA-Mesh), a framework that constructs a role-based self-healing layer on top of a collaboration pattern. Specifically, MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications and synthesizes them into executable multi-agent policy code. To enhance resilience, we introduce two self-healing mechanisms: Cross-agent reflection, a mechanism that allows agents to evaluate not only their own outcomes but also the performance of their peers, enabling informed behavioral adjustments and collective policy refinement; Role-based failover, a strategy which dynamically reassigns roles and enables agents to substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform, ensuring continuity of task execution. Experimental results across diverse tasks (e.g., software development, tool use, scientific reasoning) demonstrate that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in both task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.

title: From Tokens to Topology: When Large Language Models Meet Graph-Structured Reasoning
author: Qihang Zhang; Liang Zeng
abstract: Reasoning benchmarks often collapse heterogeneous problem types into aggregate scores, obscuring which structural computations large language models (LLMs) can reliably perform. Existing graph-reasoning benchmarks cover graph traversal, broad graph computation, and graph-language interaction, but do not directly test whether graph-structured reasoning transfers across topological mechanisms under matched conditions. We introduce GraphReason-Bench (GR-Bench), comprising 1,800 programmatically generated and oracle-verified problems across three prompt-length regimes and six task families: local motif enumeration, exact-depth breadth-first search, bounded path enumeration, articulation-point identification, non-induced subgraph matching, and non-monotonic rule execution. All tasks share a text-only executable interface, exact oracles, canonical output normalization, and set-based scoring, enabling controlled cross-mechanism comparison. On the 600-instance main evaluation split across nine proprietary and open-source LLMs, we find mechanism-level dissociation: models that succeed on one structural operation often fail on others, and cross-task performance does not reduce to a stable graph-reasoning ability. Trace-level cases reveal mechanism-specific failures such as premature search termination and loss of intermediate state. An initial sparse-autoencoder probe, supported by cross-model robustness checks, shows that topology-sensitive representations become less separable as structural difficulty increases. Together, these results establish graph-structured reasoning as a measurable domain of LLM evaluation.

title: Lessons Without Borders? Evaluating Cultural Alignment of LLMs Using Multilingual Story Moral Generation
author: Sophie Wu; Andrew Piper
abstract: Stories are key to transmitting values across cultures, but their interpretation varies across linguistic and cultural contexts. Thus, we introduce multilingual story moral generation as a novel culturally grounded evaluation task. Using a new dataset of human-written story morals collected across 14 language–culture pairs, we compare model outputs with human interpretations via semantic similarity, a human preference survey, and value categorization. We show that frontier models such as GPT-4o and Gemini generate story morals that are semantically similar to human responses and preferred by human evaluators. However, their outputs exhibit markedly less cross-linguistic variation and concentrate on a narrower set of widely shared values. These findings suggest that while contemporary models can approximate central tendencies of human moral interpretation, they struggle to reproduce the diversity that characterizes human narrative understanding. By operationalizing abstract interpretation of narrative as an evaluation for cultural alignment, this work contributes to studying culturally grounded language model behaviour beyond static benchmarks or knowledge-based tests.

title: SHADOWBENCH: Toward Reliable Automatic Evaluation of Semantic Alignment in Autoformalization
author: Hojae Han; Jongyoon Kim; Sanghyeok Park; Dongwook Cheon; Yeachan Park; Myeong Jae Jeon; SunJong Choe; Soonho Kong; Wonseok Hur; Seung-Won Hwang; Donghoon Hyeon
abstract: Autoformalization translates informal mathematical theorems into code for proof assistants such as Lean. A central challenge is that current evaluation metrics can accept type-correct but misaligned statements or reject correct statements written in a different formulation. Inspired by Pass@k, we propose SA-PASS (*Semantic Alignment Pass*), which tests formal statements using auxiliary statements called *shadows* that characterize the intended statement. A generated statement receives full credit only when it compiles, implies each shadow (forward check), and is implied by their conjunction (backward check). We instantiate SA-PASS in ShadowBench, a Lean 4 full autoformalization benchmark of 178 postgraduate- to research-level problems spanning eight mathematical areas. Claude Code (Opus 4.8) with Numina-Lean-Agent reaches 61.8% compile rate and 11.2% SA-PASS. Across outputs generated by six agentic configurations, SA-PASS achieves 98.8% binary agreement with expert judgments. An early version of ShadowBench served as the benchmark for Track 4 of the ICML 2026 AI4Math Challenge.

title: HyDRA: Hyperbolic Damage-aware Recovery and Adaptation for Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Incomplete Data
author: Yun Luo; Zejiang He; Zhen Huang; Zhiliang Tian; Yanzhou Ma; Menglong Lu; Jingyuan Huang; Shanshan Liu; Faying Wu; Dongsheng Li
abstract: Incomplete-Modality Multimodal Sentiment Analysis extends multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) to infer sentiment from language, audio, and visual streams when one or more modalities are incomplete at inference time. Existing methods improve incomplete-modality MSA through feature reconstruction, distillation, or fusion adjustment, but usually assign similar correction strength to all samples with incomplete inputs. This overlooks the uneven emotional impact of modality missingness: mild missingness often leaves sentiment recognizable, whereas severe missingness can distort the expressed emotion and therefore requires stronger correction. We propose HyDRA (Hyperbolic Damage-aware Recovery and Adaptation), a damage-aware and text-guided hyperbolic framework that aligns correction strength with missingness-induced sentiment damage. HyDRA first recovers lost emotional cues from available modalities, then places each sample in the Poincaré ball according to estimated damage severity, and finally applies damage-weighted hyperbolic correction toward a complete-modality teacher anchor. Since hyperbolic distances expand near the boundary, heavily incomplete samples receive stronger correction while lightly incomplete samples are gently adjusted. Experiments on MOSI, MOSEI, and SIMS show SOTA robustness across incomplete-modality conditions.

title: FAVoR: Measuring and Mitigating Author-Style Homogenization in Federated Personalized Generation
author: Lu Han; Jingyao Zhang; Katy Ilonka Gero; Nguyen H. Tran
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as personalized writing assistants, but adapting a model across many authors can compromise individual writing style by pulling author-specific signals toward a shared register. Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers a data-local setting for this multi-author adaptation problem: clients keep author text local while sharing compact adapter updates. However, we show that standard aggregation can preserve continuation utility while making different authors’ generations less distinguishable in style space, a failure mode we define as author-style homogenization. We evaluate author-style retention with Angular Style Classification Encoder (ASCE)-based diagnostics on our main BlogText benchmark and ASCE-independent external authorship verification. Using this protocol, we find that common federated PEFT baselines can preserve semantic utility while averaging out author-specific signals. To address this homogenization, we instantiate FAVoR (Federated Authorial Voice Retention), an author-style residual mechanism for federated PEFT. FAVoR uses a shared-private adapter design: clients upload shared-adapter updates while retaining author-specific residual corrections locally. Across BlogText and external Mythos-Reddit validation, FAVoR improves author-style retention over standard and personalized federated PEFT baselines. These gains come with small continuation-utility trade-offs and are supported by component ablations, external verification, and cold-start transfer.

title: On the Efficiency-Safety Dilemma in Large Reasoning Models
author: Yifei Yang; Zouying Cao; Xingrui Wang; Xiao Zhou; Yuexian Li; Dongjie Yang; Hai Zhao
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) incur high inference costs, often mitigated by efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning. However, the impact of these techniques on model adversarial robustness remains largely unexplored. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of the interplay between efficiency, jailbreak vulnerability, and reasoning in LRMs. We find that while efficiency methods seemingly reduce the success rate of jailbreak attacks, this improvement is often superficial. It largely arises from degraded reasoning capabilities leading to “attempted but failed” malicious responses, rather than an increase in genuine alignment. Mechanistic analysis of representational drift confirms this, revealing a strict coupling between reasoning capability loss and the model’s inability to maintain malicious semantic trajectories. Additionally, we identify quantization with pruning as the optimal strategy to balance efficiency and robustness. These findings clarify the distinction between true safety alignment and capability-induced failure, providing an empirical foundation for LRM deployment.

title: CANVAS: Continuity-Aware Narrative Generation via Visual Agentic Storyboarding
author: Ishani Mondal; Yiwen Song; Mihir Parmar; Palash Goyal; Jordan Boyd-Graber; Tomas Pfister; Yale Song
abstract: Long-form visual storytelling requires maintaining continuity across shots, including consistent characters, stable environments, and smooth scene transitions. While existing generative models can produce strong individual frames, they fail to preserve such continuity, leading to appearance changes, inconsistent backgrounds, and abrupt scene shifts. We introduce CANVAS (Continuity-Aware Narratives via Visual Agentic Storyboarding), a multi-agent framework that explicitly plans visual continuity in multi-shot narratives. CANVAS enforces coherence through character continuity, persistent background anchors, and location-aware scene planning for smooth transitions within the same setting. We evaluate CANVAS on two storyboard generation benchmarks ST-BENCH and ViStoryBench and introduce a new challenging benchmark HardContinuityBench for long-range narrative consistency. CANVAS consistently outperforms the best-performing baseline, improving background continuity by 21.6%, character consistency by 9.6% and props consistency by 7.6%.

title: CAVEWOMAN: How Large Language Models Behave Under Linguistic Input and Output Compression
author: Morayo Danielle Adeyemi; Ryan A. Rossi; Franck Dernoncourt
abstract: "Talk short. Drop grammar. Save token." This phrase is widely promoted as a way to reduce inference costs, but whether it saves anything depends on whether you compress the prompt or the response. We present CAVEWOMAN, a two-channel evaluation protocol that scores every question–answer pair on task accuracy, realized per-item cost, and whether the response still says what the model would have written without compression. It is tested on nine models, five short-answer benchmarks, and five grammatical reduction levels, with a ten-language replication and a two-dataset summarization study. Constraining the response reduces realized API cost in dollars by 1.7× on average and up to 3× without losing accuracy. Compressing the prompt raises net cost on three of the four API models, by up to 96%, and lowers accuracy at every level. Under output compression, over half of responses on the six non-reasoning models are correct but no longer entail the response the model wrote without the constraint. How much accuracy a model keeps under compression varies across models and languages. Task accuracy alone does not capture the effects of compression, so compression should be evaluated on accuracy, agreement with the unconstrained response, and cost, each reported separately. Code is available at https://github.com/danielle34/cavewoman.

title: GRACE: Step-Level Benchmark for Faithful Reasoning over Context
author: Hoang Pham; Dong Le; Anh Tuan Luu
abstract: Many reasoning tasks require models to reason over input context, from document-grounded question answering to rule-based deduction. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting produces traces that appear transparent, yet individual steps can silently deviate from the source evidence, even when the final answer is correct. Existing methods detect hallucinations at the response level but fail to identify where in the chain a failure occurs or what type it is. We introduce GRACE, the first human-annotated step-level faithfulness benchmark with a data-driven error taxonomy for context-grounded textual reasoning. GRACE covers CoT traces from 10 models across 4 source datasets, with each step annotated for faithfulness, error category, and natural language explanation. A data-driven taxonomy, discovered bottom-up via unsupervised clustering, organizes failures into two tracks: GRACE-Inference (deductive errors) and GRACE-Grounding (factual grounding errors), with four categories each. The evaluation set is human-annotated and challenging by design. Our experiments reveal substantial headroom for current models. In addition, integrating step-level faithfulness signals into reinforcement learning pipelines improves both downstream accuracy and reasoning reliability.

title: WRDO: Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization in Aligned Language Models
author: Grigoriy Evseev; Vladimir Solodkin; Dmitry Bylinkin; Daniil Medyakov; Vladimir Aletov; Aleksandr Beznosikov
abstract: Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/WRDO.

title: When i.i.d. Factorization Breaks Language: The Structural Failure of Discrete Diffusion Language Models
author: Hyukhun Koh; Seongho Joo; Haesung Pyun; Kyomin Jung
abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (DDLMs) offer potential advantages for language generation, such as parallel decoding and iterative refinement, but they often underperform autoregressive (AR) models and exhibit higher training instability. Recent approaches incorporate AR training signals to stabilize training, yet this introduces strong sequential inductive biases that limit the benefits of non-autoregressive generation. In this work, we analyze the structural causes of degeneration in non-AR DDLMs. We show that standard diffusion formulations rely on an i.i.d. corruption process and factorized sampling structure that implicitly assume token exchangeability, which conflicts with the non-exchangeable dependency structure of natural language. This mismatch leads to degeneration under semantic sparsity, where contextual signals are insufficient. To guarantee stable language generation, we propose the Dependency-Coupling Principle, a structural constraint that preserves necessary contextual dependencies during diffusion generation and provides insight into the performance gap between AR and diffusion language models.

title: Emotional Labor Strategy Preferences in LLM Personas
author: Mohammad Saim; Tianyu Jiang
abstract: Emotional labor is the effortful management of emotional displays to meet social or professional expectations. Personality traits have been correlated with emotional labor strategies, yet research on this link relies almost exclusively on self-report scales administered in only occupational settings. We investigate whether large language models injected with psychometrically grounded personas reproduce these personality-driven selection patterns across everyday social scenarios. We construct the first emotional labor strategy dataset of 500 socially situated events, each offering three behavioral choices corresponding to surface acting, deep acting, and genuine expression. We source 50 fictional characters from a large-scale personality repository and profile each through two parallel tracks: observer-rated bipolar adjective composites and in-character self-report items. Five LLMs evaluate all scenarios under both persona conditions. We find that models align more towards deep acting, and that Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability consistently predict this preference. Entropy analysis confirms that persona reliably influences the output and varies across models and emotions.

title: How Identity and Opinion Shape Political Sycophancy in LLMs
author: Li-Ni Fu; Chang Chih Meng; Chien-Hua Chen; Hen-Hsen Huang; I-Chen Wu
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles for tailored assistance, measuring their political alignment becomes increasingly important. However, many existing benchmarks for assessing political behavior rely on closed-ended questions and do not fully capture how a model’s stance may adapt to user-provided context during interaction. We introduce a framework that disentangles two distinct triggers of political sycophancy: opinion (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity (stereotyping based on demographic labels). Using 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes, we evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs. We uncover a dissociation: a model’s susceptibility to explicit opinions does not necessarily predict its susceptibility to identity cues, and vice versa. When both signals are present, their effects are generally sub-additive rather than simply additive. Additionally, system-level personas primarily shift a model’s baseline stance while having limited effect on the stance shift caused by user opinion or identity. Ultimately, our results suggest that LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than being a fixed trait, highlighting how personalization may amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in the model’s behaviors.

title: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable, Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents
author: Kaicheng Zhang; Wen Ge; Lei Jiang; Weixin Yang; Jordan Langham-Lopez; Jialin Yu; Lukasz Szpruch; Hao Ni
abstract: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train–test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepIntoStreams/OpenFinGym.git

title: Evidence-Bounded Mental Health Reasoning from Heterogeneous Speech Protocols
author: Chengyuan Gao; Jiang WU; Tao Lu; Jiayan Guo; Mingkun Xu; Tianyi Zang; Shangyang Li
abstract: Computational mental health screening using multimodal speech and text has shown great promise. However, existing models often assume all clinical speech protocols carry equivalent evidentiary validity. In reality, heterogeneous protocols, from free interviews to fixed reading tasks, support fundamentally different evidence. Forcing uniform reasoning flattens these boundaries, causing models to hallucinate symptoms from irrelevant text or overclaim support. Even advanced long chain-of-thought LLMs fail to resolve this issue, as free-form reasoning can exacerbate boundary violations. To address this, we reformulate multimodal screening as an evidence-bounded reasoning problem. We introduce the Evidence Package Benchmark, integrating 1,870 packages across six heterogeneous sources with explicit modality masks and evidence permissions. We further propose EviBound, a protocol-aware evidence control framework. Unlike direct LLM prompting, EviBound uses a profile-aware planner to restrict reasoning scope, orchestrates evidence tools via five-way acoustic consensus, and enforces a boundary critic to suppress unsupported claims. Empirical results show EviBound achieves a held-out test Depression AUROC of 0.8658, exceeding the strongest direct omni-modal baseline by +0.0811 AUROC while maintaining zero claim violations. Our work moves beyond unconstrained accuracy toward evidence-consistent, protocol-aware systems for safer clinical NLP research.

title: The Magnitude Mirage: Rethinking Confidence for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
author: Jamie Holdcroft; Abdelrahman Abdallah; Adam Jatowt
abstract: Many production RAG systems implement retrieval abstention by thresholding raw similarity scores, implicitly treating score magnitude as a confidence signal. We demonstrate that this practice degrades systematically as queries require reasoning beyond semantic matching. Across 11 retrieval architectures and 28 datasets, neural retrievers consistently assign high similarity scores to semantically related but constraint-violating documents, causing magnitude-based thresholds to collapse toward near-random abstention performance on logical and temporal reasoning tasks—a failure we term the Magnitude Mirage. To address this without computationally expensive alternatives, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of six zero-cost Query Performance Prediction (QPP) metrics across three cognitive tiers: semantic matching (BEIR), logical reasoning (BRIGHT), and temporal reasoning (TEMPO). Our central finding is that the key improvement comes from abandoning magnitude in favor of score-distribution signals: the gain from this shift exceeds the differences among distributional alternatives by a factor of 5–10\times. In particular, Score Gap (s_1 - s_k) and a practical adaptation of Score Magnitude and Variance (LSMV) improve abstention AUROC by up to 0.16 in settings where magnitude-based confidence provides little discriminative power. These methods require no additional inference, retraining, or latency, making them a practical zero-cost replacement for magnitude thresholding in deployed RAG systems.

title: How Far Can Machine Translation Quality Take You? Extrinsic Discourse Evaluation in Goal-Oriented Setups
author: Wafaa Mohammed; Kata Naszadi; Vlad Niculae
abstract: Existing machine translation (MT) metrics and discourse-focused evaluations primarily assess translation quality intrinsically, without measuring the downstream consequences of translation errors. In this work, we focus on extrinsic discourse evaluation of machine translation under two distinct regimes: static and interactive. Under the static regime, we propose an entity counting task as an illustrative probe of referential consistency in discourse. We show that high intrinsic MT quality does not reliably predict downstream discourse success and strong MT systems still produce referential inconsistencies. For the interactive regime, we study the goal-oriented multi-agent Welfare Diplomacy game as a probe of communication and coordination success over long horizons. We find that interaction-specific translation failures impact downstream coordination. Our results highlight goal-oriented translation-mediated environments as a viable framework for discourse-sensitive extrinsic MT evaluation.

title: Preference-Aligned Data Synthesis for Fine-Grained Intent Detection
author: Sitong Shen; Xiaotong Zhang
abstract: Fine-grained intent detection becomes brittle as label spaces expand with many semantically adjacent intents. Although large language models (LLMs) can synthesize labeled utterances to reduce annotation cost, the resulting pseudo data are often ambiguous across intents and repetitive within intents. Existing synthesis pipelines mainly rely on prompt engineering and filtering, without updating generator parameters. We propose a preference-aligned synthesis framework that automatically mines supervision to optimize the generator. Each intent is represented by multi-centroid prototypes, and block-conditioned generation supports diversity-aware candidate construction. From these candidates, we build preferred blocks that are both prototype-consistent and diverse, and rejected blocks composed of confusable negatives from neighboring intents. These preference pairs are used to optimize the generator with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), together with iterative refresh to mine harder confusions over time. Experiments show consistent gains for downstream intent classification in zero-shot and few-shot settings, while remaining competitive in fully supervised settings. We further observe improved generator reliability and strong transfer across multiple backbone LLM families.

title: IntroConformal: Conformal Factuality Guarantees for Large Vision-Language Models via Introspective Signals
author: Md. Atabuzzaman; Christian Alexander; Chris Thomas
abstract: Large Vision–Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved strong multimodal performance, yet ensuring the factual correctness of generated content remains challenging. Existing methods that provide statistical guarantees on factuality typically rely on external verifiers or generation-time confidence signals, which introduce auxiliary dependencies or often fail for confident but incorrect outputs. We argue that reliable factuality control can instead be achieved through introspective signals derived from the model itself. We introduce IntroConformal, a training-free Conformal Risk Control (CRC) framework that provides finite-sample, distribution-free factuality guarantees. We first instantiate it with layer-wise semantic stability, a conformity score derived from hidden-state representations, and then propose verification probability, a stronger score capturing the model’s self-administered judgment on claim factuality. Across multiple LVLM architectures, IntroConformal satisfies the conformal risk guarantee while substantially reducing abstention and achieving competitive or superior claim-level discrimination relative to external verifier–based baselines.

title: RULE-EDIT: Benchmarking Rule-Level Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
author: Jizhi Zhang; Dylan Xinming Hou; Zhaoyi Li; Qishun Yang; Mahardika Krisna Ihsani; Muhammad Asif Ali; Gus Xia; Lijie Hu
abstract: Knowledge editing seeks to update language models without full retraining. While most prior work focuses on isolated factual or instance-level edits, we study a more structured setting: mathematical rules as a controlled stress test for abstract symbolic rule editing. We introduce RULE-EDIT, the first benchmark explicitly designed for editing and evaluating rule-level knowledge in LLMs. Our benchmark investigates two key questions: (1) whether edits to abstract rules propagate to derived instances, and (2) whether edits remain consistent across different representations of the same rule. To evaluate these aspects, we propose two new metrics: Instance Portability and Rule Understanding. Experiments on strong open-source LLMs with representative editing methods show that, although models can often overwrite formula-level knowledge, they struggle to transfer edits to rule-derived instances and to maintain consistency across symbolic and natural-language forms. For example, several methods achieve nearly 100% reliability on direct rule queries, while Instance Portability never exceeds 52% and Rule Understanding remains below 26%. Overall, RULE-EDIT provides a controlled benchmark for studying whether current knowledge editing approaches truly modify abstract symbolic rules in LLMs, rather than merely altering surface outputs.

title: Deeper is Not Always Better: Mitigating the Alignment Tax via Confident Layer Decoding
author: Sining Zhoubian; Xuanming Zhang; Yuxuan Chen; Tianyi Tang; An Yang; Sean Du; Chujie Zheng; Fei Huang; Dayiheng Liu; Gao Huang; Jingren Zhou
abstract: Autoregressive generation in large language models (LLMs) conventionally decodes from the final layer, assuming that deeper representations yield more reliable next-token predictions. We revisit this assumption by revealing a recurring **Guess–Refine–Perturb** dynamic: early layers form coarse guesses, intermediate layers refine reasoning-relevant semantics, and final layers can perturb these refined predictions toward generic or alignment-preferred tokens. We introduce **Confident Decoding**, a training-free decoding strategy that dynamically selects a near-final layer through entropy-guided conservative backward search. We further formulate layer selection as an optimal stopping problem and show that, under explicit local-monotonicity and bounded-probe-noise conditions, the search rule filters terminal perturbations while bounding unfinished refinement. Experiments across dense and Mixture-of-Experts LLMs show that gains concentrate on challenging reasoning settings, including GPQA-Diamond, Omni-MATH, and HLE, while saturated tasks remain broadly stable, with no additional KV-cache memory and less than 2% latency increase. These results suggest dynamically bypassing final-layer perturbations can recover stronger reasoning behavior from aligned LLMs.

title: SPUR-XMC: Context-Adaptive Spurious Correlation Mitigation for Extreme Multi-Label Classification of Biomedical Literature
author: Ratri Mukherjee; Shailesh Dahal; Kishlay Jha
abstract: Extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) of biomedical literature aims to classify articles into a set of pre-defined labels from a large and highly skewed label distribution space. While recent pretrained language model (PLM)-based XMTC approaches have made substantial advances, they still struggle to generalize to tail labels representing concepts of high biomedical significance (e.g., rare diseases). A key factor contributing to poor tail-label performance is the presence of spurious correlations, where models inadvertently learn non-informative feature-label associations. To address this issue, we propose a novel context-adaptive spurious correlation mitigation technique, SPUR-XMC, which selectively attenuates spurious influences according to the context of the input article. A unique advantage of the proposed framework is that it does not modify existing PLM architectures for XMTC and instead operates as an add-on enhancement module. Extensive experiments across benchmark biomedical literature datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Group-Aware Adaptive Retrieval for Evidence Navigation
author: June Park; Jun Kwon; Jonghyo Kim; Jongwuk Lee
abstract: Reasoning-intensive retrieval addresses queries whose relevance cannot be identified by surface-level matching, thereby requiring multi-step reasoning. Because relevant documents rarely appear in the initial candidate set, retrieval systems suffer from the bounded recall problem. Existing methods iteratively expand a candidate pool at the document level over a corpus graph, examining each neighbor in isolation and drifting toward a narrow region of the corpus. To address this problem, we propose Group-Aware Adaptive Retrieval for Evidence Navigation (GAREN), which explores the corpus graph through group-level expansion. GAREN organizes documents into semantically coherent and distinguishable groups based on their connections in the corpus graph. The information in each group indicates what can be accessed by expanding through it, providing guidance beyond individual document-level signals. At each iteration, GAREN uses a group-level navigator to identify promising expansion directions, retrieves documents from the selected groups, and applies a document-level reranker to evaluate the updated candidate set. Extensive experiments show that GAREN achieves up to 8.0% improvement over the strongest baseline on BRIGHT. The source code is available at https://github.com/KJ12124/GAREN

title: FormalMATH: Benchmarking Formal Mathematical Reasoning of Large Language Models
author: Zhouliang Yu; Ruotian Peng; Keyi Ding; Yizhe Li; Zhongyuan Peng; Minghao Liu; Yifan Zhang; Zheng Yuan; Huajian Xin; Wenhao Huang; Yandong Wen; Ge Zhang; Weiyang Liu
abstract: We introduce FormalMATH, a large-scale Lean4 benchmark for formal mathematical reasoning, comprising 5,560 semantically validated Lean4 statements spanning competition-level and undergraduate mathematics. To improve reliability, FormalMATH is constructed through a human-in-the-loop pipeline that combines type checking, LLM-based semantic verification against the informal–formal statements alignment, negation-based disproving, and expert review. We conduct a systematic evaluation of frontier theorem provers under test-time scaling on FormalMATH. Results show that current provers remain far from solving the benchmark: the strongest model, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 (671B), achieves only 28.31% Pass@32. We further observe substantial domain imbalance across provers, with stronger performance in applied mathematics and algebra but weaker results in discrete mathematics. We identify common failure modes in current provers, including incomplete proofs, weak handling of inequalities, misuse of automation tactics, and redundant hypothesis introduction. Extreme test-time scaling (e.g., Pass@3200) yields only modest gains on a subset of FormalMATH, suggesting that current training paradigms do not equip provers to effectively exploit additional sampling budget. We also observe a counterintuitive negative effect when provers are given human-written natural-language solution references: such references can measurably degrade formal proof generation rather than aid it. Overall, FormalMATH provides a challenging and reliable testbed for measuring progress in formal mathematical reasoning.

title: End-to-End On-Device Quantization-Aware Training for LLMs at Inference Cost
author: Qitao Tan; Xiaoying Song; Ningxi Cheng; Guoming Li; Jun Liu; Lingzi Hong; Caiwen Ding; Jundong Li; Xiaoming Zhai; Shaoyi Huang; Jin Lu; Ninghao Liu; Wei Niu; Geng Yuan
abstract: Quantization reduces the deployment cost of large language models (LLMs). However, post-training quantization (PTQ) cannot fine-tune model parameters and often degrades accuracy in low-bit settings, while quantization-aware training (QAT) requires backpropagation and incurs high memory overhead. We propose ZeroQAT, a zeroth-order QAT framework supporting both weight and activation quantization. By using forward-only gradient estimation, ZeroQAT removes backpropagation and substantially reduces memory and computation while retaining end-to-end optimization benefits. We further introduce a lightweight variant of ZeroQAT for quantized fine-tuning, which freezes and pre-quantizes most parameters to further cut memory usage. Experiments show that ZeroQAT consistently outperforms representative PTQ and QAT baselines while requiring significantly less memory. For example, ZeroQAT enables fine-tuning of a 13B model at extremely low bit-widths (e.g., 2-4 bits) on a single 8GB GPU, and even allows fine-tuning a 6.7B model on a OnePlus 12 smartphone, demonstrating its practicality for end-to-end QAT on resource-limited edge devices.

title: When Knowledge Is Not Free: Cost-Aware Evidence Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: Mingyan Wu; Han Yang; Omer Ben-Porat; Yftah Ziser
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) typically assumes that external knowledge is free, but many high-quality sources are paywalled, licensed, restricted, or otherwise costly to access. We introduce cost-aware RAG, a setting where retrieved evidence is assigned access-cost tiers and systems must answer under an explicit evidence-access budget. We instantiate this setting by augmenting MS MARCO v2.1 with access-friction tiers and evaluate budgeted evidence selection across general-domain and domain-specific QA benchmarks. Our results show that static selection is brittle: no fixed selector uniformly dominates, and larger budgets do not reliably improve answer quality, even when costly evidence is domain-matched. We then study agentic cost-aware RAG, where an LLM decides when to retrieve, which tier to access, and when to stop. Agents show strong promise as adaptive evidence-acquisition controllers, but their behavior remains highly model- and task-dependent. These findings suggest that cost-aware evidence acquisition is a central challenge for the next generation of RAG systems. All code and data are available at https://github.com/Mignonmy/Cost-Aware.

title: Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects
author: Seonglae Cho; Zekun Wu; Kleyton Da Costa; Rishi Kalra; Ilham Wicaksono; Adriano Koshiyama
abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet nobody has tested whether a feature’s causal role is stable across SAE families. Single-token features fire on one vocabulary item, so ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families and zero-ablate at full layer depth: they sit 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers. Deleting one lowers the model’s logit for that token in 178 of 208 layer conditions, significant after multiple-comparison correction. And depth decides how the damage lands: early-layer deletions disrupt the layers that follow, late-layer deletions change the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features are causally anchored, LlamaScope features locally redundant. Under LlamaScope the token returns to within 2x its pre-ablation rank 96-98% of the time. Changing only the activation function reverses the sign of that difference, so the training recipe is the remaining candidate: cross-family claims are sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

title: Guiding Graph: Explicit Query-Structure Guidance for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
author: Dehao Tao; Guangjie Liu; Jun Zhou; Junhao Chen; Wei Zheng; Rui Chen; Chen Junren; Yongfeng Huang; Minghu Jiang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can match local semantic clues in knowledge graphs (KGs), but complex KGQA often requires satisfying the full dependency structure of a question. Existing retrieval-based methods therefore risk producing reasoning paths that look plausible at each step but violate the query’s global intent. We propose Guiding Graph, a schema-light query-structure interface that turns KGQA from open-ended semantic traversal into structure-constrained query completion. A Guiding Graph exposes the entities, placeholders, and global dependencies that KG exploration must preserve, serving as an operational interface between natural language and graph traversal. The interface is training-free by default through prompt-based construction, and can optionally be strengthened with a cold-start fine-tuned constructor trained from limited bootstrapped supervision. Given the constructed Guiding Graph, exploration is governed by target selection from the query structure, structure-guided pruning before semantic matching, and target-scoped semantic alignment under the current Guiding Graph triple. Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and a domain-specific agricultural KG show that explicit query-structure guidance improves accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, with especially clear benefits for multi-hop reasoning and smaller LLMs.

title: Decoding Self-Knowledge from Latent Reasoning Models for Selective Prediction and Adaptive Routing
author: Zhiqi Li; Yichi Zhang; Cunjie He; Ziheng Hua; Maolin Wang; Zenglin Xu
abstract: Latent reasoning models compress chain-of-thought into hidden states, but whether these representations retain usable self-knowledge about correctness remains unclear. We study two compression-based paradigms, Latent-SFT and CoLaR, and find a sharp distinction between problem-level and trajectory-level self-knowledge. A lightweight attention probe predicts which problems the model will solve (AUC 0.805/0.853) and transfers across datasets and compression ratios, yet cannot reliably rank rollouts of the same problem; distribution-matched retraining does not recover this signal. This distinction maps directly to downstream use: selective prediction improves accuracy by 20–25pp at 50% coverage, and adaptive routing outperforms either solver while reducing token cost, whereas latent best-of-N yields negligible gains despite available oracle headroom. The problem-level signal also persists on a 7B math checkpoint but vanishes on StrategyQA. These results identify an algorithm–paradigm boundary for exploiting self-knowledge in latent reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/Arthas777/latent-probe.

title: FinanceLLM: A Survey of Large Language Models in Finance
author: Ojas Nimase; Zhengao Li; Xinyu Wei; Jinglin Hu; Luojia Liu; Kangyi Zhao; Yue Zhao; Yushun Dong
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as transformative, powerful tools for processing and acting on unstructured financial data. However, existing surveys suffer from methodological fragmentation, evaluation inconsistency, and application disconnect. This hinders the transition of research from academia to real-life applications in financial institutions. To address these gaps, we (1) introduce a unified taxonomy organizing approaches by computational complexity, (2) propose a three-stage evaluation framework, and (3) examine LLM deployment approaches suited to specific operational contexts. Furthermore, we identify key challenges including validation frameworks, data contamination, and operational compliance that need to be further investigated.

title: Training Matryoshka Mixture-of-Experts for Elastic Inference-Time Expert Utilization
author: Yaoxiang Wang; Qingguo Hu; Yucheng Ding; Ruizhe Wang; Yeyun Gong; Jian Jiao; Yelong Shen; Peng Cheng; Jinsong Su
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has emerged as a promising paradigm for efficiently scaling large language models without a proportional increase in computational cost. However, the standard training strategy of Top-K router prevents MoE models from realizing their full potential for elastic inference. When the number of activated experts is altered at inference time, these models exhibit precipitous performance degradation. In this work, we introduce Matryoshka MoE (M-MoE), a training framework that instills a coarse-to-fine structure directly into the expert ensemble. By systematically varying the number of activated experts during training, M-MoE compels the model to learn a meaningful ranking: top-ranked experts collaborate to provide essential, coarse-grained capabilities, while subsequent experts add progressively finer-grained detail. We explore this principle at multiple granularities, identifying a layer-wise randomization strategy as the most effective. Our experiments demonstrate that a single M-MoE model achieves remarkable elasticity, with its performance at various expert counts closely matching that of an entire suite of specialist models, but at only a fraction of the total training cost. This flexibility not only unlocks elastic inference but also enables optimizing performance by allocating different computational budgets to different model layers. Our work paves the way for more practical and adaptable deployments of large-scale MoE models.

title: When Safety Routing Breaks: Understanding Alignment Fragility under Benign Fine-Tuning
author: Yitong Guo; Xiaoyi Chen; Siyuan Zhang; XiaoFeng Wang; Haixu Tang
abstract: Benign fine-tuning severely weakens the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs), so we study why refusal behavior is so fragile. While prior work often attributes this failure to gradient conflict, we propose a fundamentally different Fisher-geometric explanation: safety Fisher is low-rank, and alignment makes the safety geometry flatter while preserving an output-routing pathway. After 100 benign fine-tuning examples, this pathway is selectively re-sharpened in output-side MLP modules, explaining the asymmetric fragility: safety can collapse to high attack success rates, while general utility degrades mildly. The routing view also explains why few safety examples can restore refusal behavior, indicating that internal safety-relevant representations are preserved. Finally, we show that LoRA and ASAM mitigate early collapse by suppressing output-side sharpness, but their protection weakens at larger fine-tuning scales. Overall, safety failure is best understood as a disruption of a low-rank output-routing mechanism.

title: Understanding Reliability in LLM-based Human Behavior Simulation
author: Pei Wang; Lei Wang; Yuanzi Li; Xu Chen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human survey responses and behavioral reactions, yet unreliable simulations can mislead social science conclusions. However, existing evaluations focus on end-to-end scores, leaving it unclear how different aspects of the simulation process interact to determine reliability. We propose ReliMap, which decomposes LLM-based human behavior simulation into three structured layers and evaluates reliability at both the individual level (R1) and population level (R2) across three configuration dimensions: model capacity, profile completeness, and population coverage. Through experiments across four simulation tasks and eleven LLMs, we find that all models exhibit substantial distributional bias without profile conditioning. Profile conditioning reduces this bias with diminishing returns. Larger models benefit more, and attribute informativeness matters more than quantity. Critically, R1 gains do not reliably transfer to R2—individual and population-level reliability can move in opposite directions. At the population layer, increasing coverage reduces variance but not systematic bias, with R2 stabilizing at around 50–100 individuals. These findings highlight that reliable simulation cannot be achieved by optimizing any single layer in isolation, but requires coordinated improvement across all three.

title: Why It Hurts: Identifying the Drivers of Negative Thoughts in Emotional Support Conversations
author: Hainiu Xu; Zhaoyue Sun; Hanqi Yan; Jinhua Du; Caroline Catmur; Yulan He
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for emotional support tasks, such as negative thought reframing. This task relies on modifying cognitive appraisals, the subjective interpretation of events that elicit negative emotions, which is typically conceptualized along multiple discrete dimensions. Current LLM-based frameworks model cognitive appraisal by exhaustively evaluating all possible dimensions, but they fail to account for the varying saliency of these dimensions across different contexts. In this work, we investigate a vital yet overlooked question: "Can LLMs infer the salient appraisal dimensions from emotional support conversations?" To address this question, we introduce the AppraiSal benchmark, containing 996 emotional support conversations with human-annotated mental states, including salient cognitive appraisal dimensions. Furthermore, we propose PRISM, a multi-agent probabilistic framework grounded in Bayesian Inverse Planning, designed to improve LLMs’ ability to identify context-specific appraisal dimensions. Experimental results show that PRISM brings improvements to LLMs across various sizes, particularly in identifying the most salient appraisal dimensions

title: How You Ask Shapes What You Get: A Theory-Seeded Measurement of Articulation in Advice-Seeking LLM Conversations
author: Juneha Baek; Suhyeon Lee; Donghyuk Shin
abstract: Users articulate the same advice-seeking request in different ways: some specify detailed constraints, others gesture at a vague need. Prior work treats this variation as noise to be averaged away; we instead treat it as a stable, measurable structure in the input distribution. We ask whether articulation (how people ask) forms latent dimensions separable from topic (what they ask about), and whether it is associated with how language models respond. We extract interpretable features from 16,447 advice-seeking prompts pooled from public chat corpora (WildChat, LMSYS, and ShareChat) and recover a small set of latent articulation factors that replicate across train/test splits and across corpora. Because this structure is largely separable from topic, the populations it defines cut across topics and stay invisible to topic- or task-based evaluation. The factors define a handful of recurring articulation styles, one of which stands out: a long-form but information-poor style, roughly one in six prompts in the largest corpus, where models return shorter, vaguer answers and do not ask for clarification even though under-specification is exactly the condition that warrants it. The contrast holds within every topic group and length quintile, and is not under-specification alone: a second, equally under-specified style does draw clarifying questions. Two independent human annotators reproduce this contrast. We argue that benchmarks should stratify on articulation, and we offer the extracted structure as a measurement instrument for doing so.

title: Mindscape-Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation for Improved Long Context Understanding
author: Yuqing Li; Jiangnan Li; Zheng Lin; Ziyan Zhou; Junjie Wu; Jie Zhou; Mo Yu
abstract: Humans understand long and complex texts by relying on a holistic semantic representation of the content. This global view helps organize prior knowledge, interpret new information, and integrate evidence dispersed across a document, as revealed by the Mindscape-Aware Capability of humans in psychology. However, current Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often lack explicit global semantic guidance, making it difficult to retrieve and integrate dispersed evidence in long-context tasks. In this paper, we propose Mindscape-Aware RAG (MiA-RAG), the first framework to formulate mindscape-aware retrieval and generation as a unified conditioning paradigm for LLM-based RAG. MiA-RAG builds a mindscape through hierarchical summarization and conditions both retrieval and generation on this global semantic representation. This enables the retriever to form enriched query embeddings and the generator to reason over retrieved evidence within a coherent global context. We evaluate MiA-RAG across diverse long-context and bilingual benchmarks for evidence-based understanding and global sense-making. It consistently surpasses baselines, and further analysis shows that it aligns local details with a coherent global representation, enabling more human-like long-context retrieval and reasoning.

title: Beyond Case-Level Similarity: Multi-Defendant Legal Case Retrieval via Individual-Aware Reasoning
author: Yi Yang; Ruize Ma; Yi Feng; Chuanyi Li; Vincent Ng
abstract: Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) aims to identify cases that are legally similar to a given query case. Existing research has largely recast LCR as the task of modeling the textual similarity between the query case and a historical case. While this approach can handle single-defendant cases fairly easily, such surface-level matching proves insufficient for multi-defendant cases, which typically requires modeling and aligning defendants’ roles and judgment outcomes in different cases. To address the challenges associated with Multi-defendant LCR (Multi-LCR), we (1) present Multi-ELAM and Multi-LeCaRDv2, two multi-defendant datasets we create by enriching widely used benchmarks with defendant-level annotations, and (2) introduce a novel role- and judgment-aware framework for Multi-LCR. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its effectiveness for Multi-LCR.

title: Where Does the Sound Go? Tracing Acoustic Information Loss in Audio-Conditioned LLMs
author: Song-ha Jo; Sehyun Lee; Soyoon Kim; Jaesik Choi; Sanghyuk Choi
abstract: Audio-conditioned language models often underuse acoustic cues such as prosody, emotion, and non-speech sounds, raising the question of whether ASR-supervised frontends discard this information before it reaches the LM. We test whether the frontend is responsible by comparing Whisper-Tiny and Whisper-Small with EnCodec, DAC-VAE, and WavTokenizer in a shared Qwen3.5-4B audio-LM pipeline on ASR, emotion recognition, and sound captioning. Encoder replacement alone does not resolve this underuse: Whisper variants remain strongest overall, including on emotion and environmental sound captioning. To localize the failure, we trace task-relevant information through the encoder, projector, LM layers, and LM head. Linear probes and geometric analyses show that discriminative acoustic structure remains recoverable at the final LM layer, even when MCQA accuracy trails probe accuracy by up to 83 points. Because the answer format and decoding procedure are controlled, this task-dependent gap points to content-specific readout failure rather than generic format bias. LogitLens analyses and a targeted LM head intervention support the conclusion that acoustic underuse is not explained solely by encoder-side information loss and that readout alignment can be a dominant bottleneck.

title: Visual Compliance via Executable Safety Rule Entailment
author: Jisoo Kim; TaeYoon Kwack; Jinwoo Jang; Honguk Woo
abstract: Recent advances in LLMs and VLMs have enabled safety systems to reason beyond simple risk patterns toward more contextual and semantic safety concerns. However, as risk patterns continue to evolve and safety rules become more complex, existing training-based end-to-end safeguards face persistent challenges in adaptability and explainable reasoning over complex safety rules. To address these challenges, we propose GuardEn (Guarding by Safety Rule Entailment), an executable safeguard framework that decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions through Safety-Rule Compilation, modeling their composition as executable code. At test time, Scene-Grounded Execution instantiates these atomic propositions with contextual visual information derived from scene graphs, enabling rule-grounded and interpretable safety reasoning. Experiments on SafetyVisionBench demonstrate the effectiveness of programmable safeguard for complex visual safety assessment, achieving an average improvement of 9.8 F1 points over the strongest baseline across four domains.

title: When Fairness Evolves: Value Orientation and Evolution in Multi-Agent Resource Allocation
author: Song Gao; Zengqing Wu; Yu-Xuan Qiu; Chuan Xiao; Ruiqi Xu; Jianbin Qin
abstract: This study employs LLM-based multi-agent simulation to investigate how fairness-related behavior evolves in repeated resource allocation. Thirty agents with five idealized value orientations participate in a survival-production cycle under equal, needs-based, contribution-based, and negotiation-based allocation mechanisms. Results show that negotiation achieves the highest productive return and subjective satisfaction with the strongest consensus in our main setting, and its subjective advantage holds across eight LLMs, suggesting that deliberative allocation can help navigate the fairness–efficiency tradeoff. Agents also exhibit systematic misalignment between subjective satisfaction and objective resource outcomes, shaped by value orientations and interaction conditions. Over repeated interaction, agents’ reflection-derived fairness positions shift away from their initial orientations toward more hybrid combinations of equality-, merit-, and needs-related reasoning. To provide human-grounded structural comparison, we further benchmark GPT-4o against published human choice distributions in 16 controlled allocation scenarios, finding moderate rank-level correspondence but substantially more concentrated LLM choices. These findings characterize value-conditioned reasoning and semantic change in LLM societies while remaining computational hypotheses rather than direct evidence of human fairness behavior.

title: Geometric-disentanglement Unlearning
author: Duo Zhou; Yuji Zhang; Tianxin Wei; Ruizhong Qiu; Ke Yang; Xiao Lin; Cheng Qian; Jingrui He; Hanghang Tong; ChengXiang Zhai; Heng Ji; Huan Zhang
abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove specified training data while preserving retained behavior, but gradient-based updates often induce a forgetting-retention tradeoff. This motivates our first-principles objective: optimize forgetting while keeping the retaining loss locally unchanged, formalized as retain invariance. We prove an equivalence under optimizer-induced geometry: the retain loss is locally invariant if and only if the update is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by retain gradients. Crucially, this geometry differs from Euclidean geometry because optimizer preconditioning rescales raw gradients before parameter updates. Based on this characterization, we propose Geometric-disentanglement Unlearning (GU), a plug-and-play projection module that filters any candidate forget update without modifying the underlying unlearning objective. GU projects the candidate update under the optimizer-induced metric to enforce first-order retain invariance and, under a trust-region constraint, gives the steepest forget direction among retain-preserving updates. Across 72 TOFU configurations, GU improves or preserves retain-set Extraction Strength in 91.7% and model utility in 86.1%, with gains transferring to MUSE and WMDP. Optimizer-metric GU outperforms its Euclidean counterpart on all four metrics, while running 5.1\times faster than the per-sample-QR baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Lemutisme/Geometric-Unlearning.

title: Multilingual Medical Reasoning for Question Answering with Large Language Models
author: Pietro Ferrazzi; Aitor Soroa; Rodrigo Agerri
abstract: Large Language Models with reasoning capabilities have recently shown strong promise for medical Question Answering. Current approaches report competitive results on English benchmarks through knowledge distillation from large models, yet multilingual coverage remains limited. We extend this line of research by presenting a method to generate multilingual reasoning traces that enrich the distillation paradigm with factual information from Wikipedia. Using a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline over WikiProject Medicine, we produce 500k reasoning traces in English, Italian, and Spanish. The traces are generated to solve medical questions drawn from MedQA and MedMCQA, both of which we extend to Italian and Spanish. We evaluate our approach across in-domain and out-of-domain Medical QA benchmarks, demonstrating consistent performance gains in both few-shot in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning settings, achieving state-of-the-art results among 8B-parameter models across multiple model families. With the aim of fostering the development of multilingual clinical decision-support tools, we release the complete suite of resources: reasoning traces, translated datasets, Medical Wikipedia, and fine-tuned models.

title: Lingo-Blocksworld: A Dataset for Linguistically-Informed Blocksworld
author: Melissa Torgbi; Claire Benet Post; Claire Bonial; Harish Tayyar Madabushi
abstract: We introduce Lingo-Blocksworld, a linguistically-informed diagnostic benchmark for evaluating the generalisation and planning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the Blocksworld (BW) domain. Unlike prior obfuscated BW variants, our method replaces content words with morphosyntactically well-formed nonsense words, preserving the grammatical scaffolding of the domain while removing lexical familiarity. This enables us to test a psycholinguistically-motivated hypothesis, and find systematic support across both reasoning and non-reasoning models, with degradation patterns that mirror syntactic bootstrapping from human language processing. Additionally, we test the ability of models to generalise planning solutions from the typical 4-block problems to 12 blocks. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning models stay robust where non-reasoning models collapse: non-reasoning model performance drops to near zero once problems exceed four blocks or have actions and predicates obfuscated, while reasoning models maintain strong performance until structural and lexical difficulty are combined. Manual error analysis pinpoints further differences. Reasoning model errors are more often skipped steps or incomplete instruction following, whereas non-reasoning models fail to derive plausible plans at all. By combining psycholinguistic motivation with classical planning evaluation, Lingo-BW allows us to shift research focus from whether LLMs plan to how their planning depends on linguistic surface form.

title: AnInter: Anti-Interference Training for Long Context Retrieval
author: Lijie Ye
abstract: Dense retrievers in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have achieved substantial progress in semantic matching, but they remain limited in long context retrieval. In long context retrieval, target evidence often occupies only a small local span, while the remaining content acts as noise. We aim to improve long-document retrieval by enhancing retrievers’ anti-interference capability. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we construct the Anti-Interference Capability Benchmark (AICB) to evaluate retrievers’ anti-interference capability under controlled noise levels; (2) we propose anti-interference training as a short-text training path for improving long context retrieval; and (3) we train AnInter, a series of embedding models that are more robust to noisy long documents. Evaluation on LongEmbed shows that AnInter improves over its backbone by 16.4 points on average and achieves state-of-the-art performance on this challenging long context embedding benchmark. These results show that interference-aware training is a practical direction for improving long context retrieval.

title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Evidence Misgrounding in Multimodal Knowledge Editing
author: Zhiwu Wang; Yichen Wu; Jinqian Yang; Yizhou Yang; Renzhen Wang; Qian Zhao; Deyu Meng
abstract: Multimodal knowledge editing aims to update visually grounded facts in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving unrelated text and visual behaviors. However, standard answer-level metrics can hide evidence misgrounding: an edit may produce the target answer on the original image yet remain sensitive to incidental context rather than the intended visual evidence. To examine this issue in a controlled setting, we construct WATERBIRD-EDIT, an analysis set that decouples bird habitat labels from background context and measures whether edited predictions remain stable when the target evidence is preserved but the background changes. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose VICE (Visual In-Context Editing), a retrieval-based framework that stores edits in external memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations designed to expose task-relevant evidence. Experiments on three standard benchmarks show that VICE achieves strong lifelong editing performance, while results on WATERBIRD-EDIT show that it substantially reduces sensitivity to the controlled background shifts.

title: PRO-Step: Step-level Process Reward Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: MinKeon Kim; Namjun Lee; Jaekwang Kim
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation enhances Large Language Models by grounding responses in external knowledge, but multi-hop reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, where early retrieval failures confound subsequent steps. Standard outcome-based optimization only rewards the final answer, leaving intermediate retrieval and reasoning errors undetected. While existing process-based methods introduce step-level signals, they still score each step against the final answer, rewarding spurious successes where flawed retrieval coincidentally produces the correct answer. Step-level supervision in RAG requires evaluating both logical validity and evidential grounding at each step. We introduce PRO-STEP: we train a generative PRM that evaluates both dimensions, employ PRM-guided value tree search to construct preference pairs contrasting valid steps against flawed ones, and optimize the policy via step-level Direct Preference Optimization. Experiments on single- and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that PRO-STEP mitigates error propagation and outperforms existing outcome- and process-based RAG baselines.

title: Data Augmentation via Relation-Variant Discourse Recasting for Implicit Discourse Relation Recognition
author: Yikang Yang; Weihao Sun; Yu Hong; Zhipang Wang; Guodong Zhou
abstract: Implicit discourse relation recognition (abbr., IDRR) is a task of automatically classifying semantic relations between pairwise arguments in the absence of explicit connectives. IDRR suffers from imbalanced data distribution of different relations. The current data augmentation approaches have relieved this problem to some extent. However, the incorporated discourse samples during augmentation lack customized contrastive effects. To address this issue, we propose to construct topic-relevant relation-inconsistent arguments for augmentation. Specifically, we implement a Relation-Variant Discourse Recasting (RVDR) approach. RVDR utilizes Qwen3-4B to paraphrase discourses under the forcible constraints of preserving inherent topics and transforming relation senses toward infrequent target relations. To avoid excessive divergent thinking of RVDR, we optimize the Qwen3-4B via reinforcement learning, where Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is used along with multiple task-specific rewards. Furthermore, rule-based filtering and confidence estimation are used to ensure data quality, which additionally enable two application modes, i.e., Confidence-based and Progressive Data Augmentation (i.e., CDA and PDA). Experiments on PDTB 2.0 and 3.0 show that RVDR-based CDA consistently improves IDRR performance across multiple backbones, including both encoder-only and decoder-only cases. It also allows the strong IDRR frameworks CP-KD and SCDN to be enhanced further. The code is publicly available.

title: Med-R2: An Adversarial Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in Medical VLMs
author: Wen MA; Fucheng Niu; Zhiting Fan; Zikai Xiao; Jiaxiang Liu; Zuozhu Liu
abstract: Vision–language models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in general medical visual question answering, yet it remains unclear whether their predictions reflect evidence-grounded clinical reasoning or reliance on spurious priors. We introduce Med-R2 Bench, a hierarchical benchmark aligned with the clinical workflow to evaluate adversarial robustness with visual grounding. We design stepwise QA tasks to assess whether reasoning chains are strictly grounded in visual evidence across the four clinical stages, and employ adversarial perturbations to test robustness against misleading cues. Med-R2 comprises 42,432 images, 31 task categories, and 110,406 QA pairs. Evaluation across 14 VLMs reveals a sequential performance degradation along the four-stage clinical workflow. Adversarial experiments show that models rely heavily on correct prompts to guess answers. Even when provided with explicit visual cues, the models struggle to accurately align textual descriptions. Finally, we demonstrate that stepwise fine-tuning using our hierarchical data significantly improves reasoning robustness, highlighting its potential to drive future improvements in evidence-based medical AI.

title: MegaCode: A Repository-Level Dataset for Long-Context Code Reasoning
author: Wenyang Luo; Shuang Sun; Yiwen Hu; Fei Bai; Yanzipeng Gao; Shuo Wang; Hongyu Lu; Xin Zhao; Ji-Rong Wen
abstract: Code reasoning is essential for building AI systems that can understand, generate, and verify complex software. Yet most open-source code corpora focus on isolated snippets or single functions, failing to capture the long-range dependencies and cross-file interactions that define real-world repositories. We introduce MegaCode, a 300B repository-level corpus designed to support structured code reasoning and long-context modeling. MegaCode preserves full project structure—including build scripts, configuration files, and inter-file links—and is constructed through a multi-stage curation pipeline combining deduplication, rule-based filtering, and model-based quality assessment. Models pretrained on MegaCode demonstrate consistent gains on code reasoning and long-context benchmarks compared with those trained on flattened code datasets. Also, we validate the effectiveness of adding repo relevent infomation such as LSP, repo structure and repo summary. These results highlight the importance of maintaining repository structure for next-generation code intelligence. We release the dataset, curation pipeline, and evaluation suite to facilitate research on large-scale code pretraining and repository-level understanding.

title: Beyond Token-Level Guidance: Inference-Time Alignment of Specialized LLMs via Cross-Family Representation Steering
author: Jin Gan; Xin Li; Jun Luo
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) finetuned for specialized domains represent crucial high-impact applications. Inference-time alignment improves safety degraded from specialization finetuning without requiring substantial computational resources, complementing finetuning-based methods with an easy-to-use, plug-and-play solution. However, existing inference-time methods fail to reliably improve safety without disrupting domain capability. We identify the root cause as complementary expertise orthogonality: specialized base models and general-domain guidance models have orthogonal competencies, making the guidance signal unreliable for specialized generation. This primarily manifests as stop token interference, where the guidance model’s tendency toward continuation overrides the base model’s decision to stop, burying correct answers under guidance-induced continuation. To address this problem, we propose CREST, an inference-time alignment method that steers base model hidden representations using safety directions extracted from a guidance model of any family, avoiding token-level structural limitations entirely. CREST improves safety where specialization has weakened it while preserving both domain-specific capability and the safety of already well-aligned models, outperforming baselines by up to 22.2% on safety benchmarks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/DecayingSeart/CREST.

title: Decision-aware User Simulation Agent for Evaluating Conversational Recommender Systems
author: Yuan-Chi Li; Li-Chi Chen; Sung-Yi Wu; Yu-Che Tsai; Shou-De Lin
abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRS) increasingly rely on user simulators for automated evaluation of sales agents. A key requirement for such simulators is the ability to model human decision-making. However, most LLM-based simulators often exhibit unrealistically strong information-processing capabilities, rarely exhibiting the hesitation and decision deferral commonly observed in real consumer behavior, resulting in overly high acceptance rates. To address this limitation, we propose Hesitator, a theory-grounded user simulation framework that explicitly models a specific dimension of human decision-making: decision deferral under choice overload. The framework introduces a modular Decision Module that separates utility-based item selection from overload-aware commitment decisions. Experiments across multiple user simulation frameworks, domains, sales modes, and LLM backbones show that integrating our module consistently mitigates unrealistic behaviors under increasing overload conditions. Furthermore, Hesitator reproduces established findings from behavioral economics, demonstrating its ability to model human decision behavior.

title: SEATauBench: Progressively Adapting Tool-Agent-User Evaluation Into Low-Resource Southeast Asian Languages
author: My Chiffon Nguyen; Aulia Adila; Saksorn Ruangtanusak; Kittiphat Leesombatwathana; Vissuta Gunawan Lim; Patomporn Payoungkhamdee; Samuel Cahyawijaya
abstract: While AI development and evaluation for Southeast Asia (SEA) has grown rapidly, agent capabilities in regional languages are still poorly understood despite its importance to sovereign AI. To fill this gap, we introduce SEATauBench, the first agent-focused evaluation framework for SEA sovereign AI. It adapts Tau2-Bench to five languages—Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, and Filipino—and evaluates agents across progressively localized settings that vary the language of user-agent interaction, tool specifications, and task domains. Across three models, we find that English agent capabilities transfer reasonably well when only the conversation language changes, but quality and robustness degrade sharply as more task contexts are localized, with the largest losses in full domain adaptation. We also highlight the limits of English-only agent assessment for predicting agent capabilities in SEA languages. More broadly, SEATauBench provides a diagnostic benchmark and reusable adaptation pipeline for building reliable multilingual agents for linguistically diverse regions.

title: FIDES: Faithful Inference via Deep Evidence Signals for Retrieval-Memory Conflict in RAG
author: Zhe Yu; Wenpeng Xing; Tiancheng Zhao; Mohan Li; Changting Lin; Meng Han
abstract: When retrieved evidence contradicts parametric memory, language models frequently ignore the context and revert to memorized priors—a failure that undermines the purpose of retrieval augmentation. Contrastive decoding amplifies context-conditioned output to suppress parametric bias, but fixed coefficients cannot track changing disagreement, while output-only adaptive coefficients observe only the final prediction distributions. We propose FIDES (Faithful Inference via Deep Evidence Signals), a training-free decoder that combines signals from output distributions, hidden representations, and prediction trajectories to recompute contrastive intervention strength at every step. A matched, formula-verified audit on 128 NQ-Swap pairs shows that conflict raises Opposition by 0.0969 and the resulting coefficient α by 0.0727 at the same answer-prediction position (both p < 10⁻⁴). The audit also finds only a small Shift effect and saturated clipped Noise, clarifying the limits of the mechanism interpretation. Across three benchmarks and six backbones—four primary 7B/8B models and two scaling backbones up to 70B—FIDES achieves the best context fidelity in all 18 settings, outperforming the strongest training-free baseline by +3 to +13 points. At 70B, fidelity reaches 92–94% while F1 reaches 62–63%, showing that multi-depth stepwise contrast can preserve generation utility while improving evidence following.

title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
author: Qingren Yao; Yaxuan Kong; Yuqi Nie; Yichen Li; Stefan Zohren; Anna Vettoruzzo; Qingsong Wen; Ming Jin; Joaquin Vanschoren
