To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, recent advances implement low-rank adaptation with orthogonal projections (e.g., O-LoRA) to isolate task parameters. However, we reveal that such strict geometric constraints trigger an “Orthogonality Dilemma”: rigid parameter isolation impedes the transfer and accumulation of shared representations across semantically related tasks. In this work, we propose a new replay-free method, called \underline{\mathit{Co}}\mathit{nsolidation} and \underline{\mathit{De}}\mathit{coupling} \underline{\mathit{LoRA}} (CoDe-LoRA), for CL of LLMs. CoDe-LoRA disentangles the learning process into \mathit{Consolidating\ Universal\ Knowledge} and \mathit{Decoupling\ Task\text{-}Specific\ Knowledge}. To achieve this, CoDe-LoRA leverages an adaptive null-space projection mechanism and semantic routing to balance knowledge accumulation with task-specific adaptation. Experimental results on diverse CL benchmarks demonstrate that CoDe-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at [https://github.com/Estrellajer/CoDe-LoRA](https://github.com/Estrellajer/CoDe-LoRA).

title: SCORE: Similarity-Aware Contextual Overlap-Redundancy Eviction for Efficient KV Cache Compression in LLMs
author: Gilha Lee; Seungil Lee; Hyun Kim
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unlocked remarkable long-context capabilities, enabling breakthroughs across diverse NLP tasks. However, despite architectural progress, the key-value (KV) cache remains a critical memory bottleneck during inference. Prior work has explored cache optimization via eviction strategies, yet most rely on heuristic or single-axis importance metrics, neglecting the nuanced and dynamic interplay between layers and attention heads. In this paper, we propose SCORE (Similarity-aware Contextual Overlap-Redundancy Eviction), a novel framework that introduces a distance-based multi-level similarity metric to quantify and eliminate structural redundancy within the KV cache. By dynamically reallocating cache budgets across layers and heads and employing a redundancy-aware greedy token selection mechanism, SCORE preserves semantic diversity while minimizing memory overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks such as LongBench and NeedleBench show that SCORE retains 96.2% of full KV cache performance using only 1.5% of the cache, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines under strict memory constraints. These results underscore the value of fine-grained, context-aware cache management for scalable and efficient long-context inference in LLMs.

title: Small Reward Models via Backward Inference
author: Yike Wang; Faeze Brahman; Shangbin Feng; Teng Xiao; Hannaneh Hajishirzi; Yulia Tsvetkov
abstract: Reward models (RMs) play a central role throughout the language model (LM) pipeline, particularly in non-verifiable domains. However, the dominant LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm relies on the strong reasoning capabilities of large models, while alternative approaches require reference responses or explicit rubrics, limiting flexibility and broader accessibility. In this work, we propose FLIP (FLipped Inference for Prompt reconstruction), a reference-free and rubric-free reward modeling approach that reformulates reward modeling through backward inference: inferring the instruction that would most plausibly produce a given response. The similarity between the inferred and the original instructions is then used as the reward signal. Evaluations across four domains using 13 small language models show that FLIP outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge baselines by an average of 79.6%. Moreover, FLIP substantially improves downstream performance in extrinsic evaluations under test-time scaling via parallel sampling and GRPO training. We further find that FLIP is particularly effective for longer outputs and robust to common forms of reward hacking. By explicitly exploiting the validation–generation gap, FLIP enables reliable reward modeling in downscaled regimes where judgment methods fail.

title: HAPMoE: Heterogeneity-Aware Automatic Parallelism Planning for Mixture-of-Experts Models Training
author: Mengyuan Fan; Peizhuang Cong; Zixiao Huang; Si Xu; Tong Qiao; Yanghao Li; Jing Yang; Tong Yang; Quanlu Zhang; Yu Wang
abstract: As model sizes continue to scale, distributed training has become inevitable. Automatic parallelization techniques can derive efficient training parallelism strategies at low cost while achieving superior performance. The difficulty of this problem is jointly determined by the complexity of the model and the underlying compute cluster. Meanwhile, mixture-of-experts (MoE) models are increasingly emerging as the dominant architecture and the rapid evolution of accelerator hardware has made cluster heterogeneity commonplace, posing substantial challenges to automatic parallelization. However, existing approaches typically target either MoE architectures or heterogeneous clusters, failing to generalize to scenarios where both challenges coexist. To this end, we present HAPMoE, a heterogeneity-aware automatic parallelism planner for MoE training. HAPMoE builds a lightweight MoE-aware cost model and efficiently searches a six-dimensional parallel space, producing parallel plans directly deployable on Megatron-LM. Experiments show that HAPMoE improves end-to-end training throughput by up to 3.2× over baselines across heterogeneous clusters. Its non-uniform pipeline partitioning yields an additional up to 78% gains, and its pruning-enhanced dynamic programming algorithm completes the search within 1 minute, demonstrating high efficiency and practical value in complex hardware environments.

title: Aggregation-Aware Synthetic Text Generation Against Authorship Re-Identification
author: Qian Ma; Anna Cinzia Squicciarini; Sarah Rajtmajer
abstract: Online users often release multiple texts under the same identity, giving attackers an author profile that can reveal more than any single text. Existing authorship obfuscation methods optimize privacy independently for each document, leaving them blind to cross-document correlations that make aggregation dangerous. We propose Aggregation-Aware Synthetic Text Generation (AAST), a framework that addresses this gap by jointly selecting synthetic texts at the bundle level rather than optimizing each text in isolation. AAST targets attribution and verification attacks, including cross-genre settings where attacker references come from a genre not observed during generation or selection. Experiments across same-genre, cross-genre, neural, and independent non-neural stylometric attacks show that AAST lowers account-level linkability as bundle size grows, while preserving semantic quality, linguistic acceptability, and sentiment alignment.

title: PRISM: Multidimensional Safety Risk Detection and Measurement Beyond Superficial Compliance for LLMs
author: YIfan Sun; Xiang Zhao; Beining Lin; Feng Huang; You Song
abstract: Existing LLM safety measures operate as black boxes, lacking categorical precision and calibrated severity assessment. We propose **PRISM** (**P**rototypical **R**epresentation for **I**nternal **S**afety **M**apping), a fine-grained two-stage safety auditing framework grounded in internal mechanistic representations. Stage I localizes functional safety zones via spectral analysis and maps internal activations onto concept prototypes for camouflage-resilient categorical risk identification. Stage II decomposes violation severity across orthogonal dimensions through structured CoT reasoning, producing calibrated human-auditable ordinal verdicts. PRISM achieves a new best F1 of 77.60% on the adversarial ToxicChat benchmark and approaches 671B frontier judges within a 2.3% margin on severity calibration, demonstrating that mechanistic grounding and principled task formulation can substitute for scale in fine-grained safety governance.

title: Diversity is Not Ambiguity: Toward Accurate and Efficient Ambiguity Detection for Open-Domain QA
author: Jiwon Lee; Yong-chan Park; Jungin Hong; U Kang
abstract: How can question answering (QA) systems determine whether a query is ambiguous? Ambiguity detection is essential in open-domain QA, as misclassification leads to either answering under the wrong interpretation or triggering unnecessary clarification. However, existing methods conflate answer diversity with ambiguity, leading to inaccurate predictions. They also process all queries uniformly, resulting in wasteful computation. We propose ARCHIVE, an accurate and efficient framework that detects ambiguity via *logical conflict*: a query is ambiguous if its valid answers cannot all be true under a single interpretation. ARCHIVE combines a lightweight early-exit encoder for surface-detectable cases with a conflict modeling module that captures logical relations among answers, reinforced by an invariance objective for robustness to noisy answer sets. We also present QuireQA, a 4,703-query benchmark spanning factoid, non-factoid, and ill-formed queries. Experiments show that ARCHIVE outperforms competitors, improving F1-amb and F1-unamb by up to 10.4 and 21.6 points, respectively, while operating 16\times faster than the best competitor.

title: DICS: Exploring Data Intrinsic Consistency for Visual Instruction Selection
author: Yuyang Hong; Jinhui Guo; Jiaqi Gu; Lubin Fan; Ruixiang Wang; Kun Ding; Yue Wu; Shiming Xiang; Jieping Ye
abstract: Visual instruction tuning is crucial for advancing the vision-language alignment and instruction-following capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, identifying optimal subsets under a fixed ratio constraint from rapidly expanding datasets remains a significant bottleneck. While existing methods largely depend on distribution diversity or heuristic filtering, they often overlook the internal coherence within individual samples. To bridge this gap, we propose Data Intrinsic Consistency (DIC), a self-scoring metric designed to quantify the sample-level inter-component consistency. DIC consists of two modules: Visual Information Consistency (VIC), evaluating the alignment between visual content and instructions, and Response Information Consistency (RIC), assessing response coherence relative to the instruction. Building upon DIC, we introduce Data Intrinsic Consistency Selection (DICS), an adaptive data selection method that optimizes the trade-off between high intra-sample consistency and global distributional diversity under varying data budgets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DICS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse dataset scales and model architectures, surpassing full-dataset fine-tuning while using only 25% of the LLaVA-1.5-665K data.

title: Gaming the Judge: How Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought Can Undermine Agent Evaluation
author: Muhammad Khalifa; Lajanugen Logeswaran; Jaekyeom Kim; Sungryull Sohn; Yunxiang Zhang; Moontae Lee; Hao Peng; Lu Wang; Honglak Lee
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to evaluate agent performance, particularly in non-verifiable settings where judgments rely on agent trajectories including chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. This paradigm implicitly assumes that the agent’s CoT faithfully reflects both its internal reasoning and the underlying environment state. We show this assumption is brittle: LLM judges are highly susceptible to manipulation of agent reasoning traces. By systematically rewriting agent CoTs while holding actions and observations fixed, we demonstrate that manipulated reasoning alone can increase false positive rates of state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM) judges by up to 117% relative to the unmanipulated baseline across 800 trajectories spanning diverse web tasks. We study manipulation strategies spanning style-based approaches that alter only the presentation of reasoning and content-based approaches that fabricate signals of task progress, and find that content-based manipulations are consistently more effective. We evaluate mitigation strategies including manipulation-aware prompting and judge-time scaling, which can reduce but do not eliminate the vulnerability. Our findings reveal a fundamental vulnerability in LLM-based evaluation and highlight the need for judging mechanisms that verify reasoning claims against observable evidence.

title: Argus-Retriever: Vision-LLM Late-Interaction Retrieval with Region-Aware Query-Conditioned MoE for Visual Document Retrieval
author: Abdelrahman Abdallah; Mahmoud Abdalla; Mohammed Ali; Adam Jatowt
abstract: Late-interaction vision-language retrievers represent each document page as many visual token embeddings and score queries with MaxSim. In systems such as ColPali, ColQwen, ColNomic, and Nemotron ColEmbed, the document embeddings are produced without seeing the query, so the same page is represented identically for a table lookup, a chart question, and a layout-sensitive evidence request. We introduce Argus, a family of query-conditioned late-interaction retrievers built on Qwen3.5-VL. Argus adds a region-aware Mixture-of-Experts module: the query encoder produces both retrieval embeddings and a compact context vector, the document page is pooled into spatial regions, and a query-aware router selects latent experts per region before MaxSim. The output remains a multi-vector index compatible with ColPali-style retrieval, but the document representation is now dependent on the query (i.e., \mathbf{D}(q)). All Argus models use a 1024-dimensional retrieval head, compared with the 2560-dimensional and 4096-dimensional heads of recent state-of-the-art systems, and are trained on roughly 9% of the available public supervision rather than the full pool. The 9B model reaches 92.67 NDCG@5 on ViDoRe V1 and 86.0 NDCG@5 on the combined V1+V2 leaderboard, the highest reported value for an open late-interaction model on the combined leaderboard. Wrapped in a Qwen3.6-27B agentic retrieval pipeline on ViDoRe V3, Argus-9B further improves its NDCG@10 from 60.28 to 64.80 over public tasks, showing that the same retriever serves both as a strong standalone system and as a search primitive for iterative LLM agents.

title: Fortifying Hallucination Detection Under Distribution Shift in Short-Form QA
author: Ti Tze Hong; Saffron Salmah Yen Lim; Maarten Sap
abstract: Hallucinations remain one of the major barriers to the reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs). Recent works have explored hallucination detection using both supervised classification based approaches and unsupervised metric based approaches, with the latter remaining popular since they do not require labeled data. In this work, we study the performance and generalizability of these approaches through a comprehensive empirical analyses across 11 datasets and 10 models. We first establish that supervised methods achieve stronger in-domain performance but lag behind unsupervised methods in the out-of-domain setting. Then to narrow this generalization gap, we introduce a simple approach that improves the generalizability of supervised hallucination detectors by training on a curated, multi-domain data mix, which can complement the subsequent addition of task-specific data. In our experiments on hallucination detection on 697K QA samples from 12 open source QA datasets, we show that incorporating this general training allows supervised methods to surpass unsupervised metric based methods by an average of +7.25% on out-of-distribution data within the short-form QA setting, without addition of any task-specific data. We also analyze scaling behaviors and estimate how much task-specific data is required to achieve reliable performance, finding that models augmented with general data require up to 40.3% less task-specific data to achieve close to optimal performance. Together, our findings highlight a simple path toward fortifying supervised hallucination detectors against domain shift.

title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision–Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation
author: Soumyajit Datta; Arka Dutta; Ashiqur R. KhudaBukhsh
abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.

title: POLARIS: Guiding Small Models to Write Long Stories
author: Rishanth Rajendhran; Jenna Russell; Mohit Iyyer; John Frederick Wieting
abstract: Small open-weight models struggle at long-form creative writing: their generated stories either fall far short of the requested length, or their quality significantly degrades as length increases, especially when compared to frontier models. We present **POLARIS** (**P**olicy **O**ptimization with **L**LM-as-a-judge rewards and **A**nchored-**R**eference **I**njection for **S**torywriting), **a lower-compute GRPO recipe** with two key ingredients: a frontier LLM judge with a **structured *Story Quality* rubric** as the online reward, and **human-reference injection (HRI)**, where a teacher-forced human-written story serves as a high-reward anchor within each GRPO group. By applying our training recipe to Qwen3.5-9B, using a dataset of \sim1.4K prompt–story pairs derived from 100 short-story anthologies and 4 A100 GPUs, we obtain **POLARIS-9B**. Across five benchmarks spanning in-distribution and out-of-distribution prompts and rubrics, POLARIS-9B is **competitive with much larger open-weight models** while following length instructions more closely. A blinded human evaluation confirms that POLARIS-9B is preferred to the base Qwen3.5-9B and on par with Qwen3.5-27B. Despite training only on stories up to 4k words, POLARIS-9B preserves quality on prompts requesting stories up to 3\times the training length, a regime where most open-weight models degrade substantially in quality, length adherence, or both. More broadly, our results suggest that **length generalization is a meaningful stress test for creative-writing models** and a useful lens for distinguishing otherwise close models.

title: When AI-Text Detectors Become Evidence: Rethinking Detection for Human Decisions
author: Jiatao Li; Mao Ye; Xinyu Hu; Cheng Peng; Xunjian Yin; Xiaojun Wan
abstract: AI-generated-text detectors are evaluated as classifiers, yet consequential deployments use detector outputs as evidence that people inspect, trust, contest, or use to escalate decisions. We call this mismatch the classification–evidence gap. The gap makes scalar detector scores a weak deployment interface: they hide the basis of a judgment, invite overtrust, and can turn false positives into accusations. We argue that AI-text detection should be evaluated as evidence-grounded decision support rather than as authorship proof. We introduce AGENT-XTrust, a guideline-expert detector that returns direct MetaAgent labels without target-domain scalar-cutoff calibration and converts each document-level judgment into inspectable evidence records containing local labels, rationales, confidence estimates, and linked spans. Across three domains and four generators, AGENT-XTrust preserves strong binary accuracy while producing inspectable, contestable evidence. In a controlled fixed-stimulus user study, participants assigned to the full AGENT-XTrust system-and-interface package achieved 19.8 and 11.3 points higher decision accuracy than those assigned to the score-only and score-plus-explanation packages, respectively; overtrust on each condition’s detector-wrong cases was 17.8 and 18.3 points lower. These results suggest a broader evaluation target for AI-text detection: not only whether a detector is correct, but whether complete detector-and-evidence packages support reliable human decisions under uncertainty.

title: Some Tokens Behave like Magnets: Revealing Linguistic Organization in the Layers of Language Models
author: Andrew Liu; Devan Srinivasan; Gerald Penn
abstract: We identify a special group of token vectors inside large language models (LLMs) — which we term magnetic vectors — that organize the surrounding tokens by either attracting or repelling them. Particularly, tokens pointing the same way as an attracting magnet are elongated; tokens pointing the same way as a repelling magnet are compressed. Just as physical magnets pull or push away the iron filings around them, these vectors organize their surroundings through two opposing polarities. Moreover, we identify a statistically significant pattern in linguistic category where function words consistently act as repelling magnets in early layers, and we also find magnets consistently reorganize their polarities in unique ways deeper in the model. In a further case study we find this observation may unveil a deliberate, layer-wise organization in how LLMs process language. This pattern is consistent across different LLM architectures, sizes, and layer configurations. It is also causally relevant. When the LLM is fine-tuned for a downstream task, the task-functional tokens emerge as magnets. E.g., in question answering, the answer-span tokens become uniquely repelling magnets in the final layer, geometrically carving the answer out of the surrounding context. Furthermore, removing early-layer repelling magnets devastates syntactic tasks (POS tagging accuracy drops from 91% to below 10%) while sparing semantic ones, and removing late-layer attracting magnets does the reverse. We believe this phenomenon warrants further investigation, as it opens the first probe-free path to understanding how language models geometrically organize linguistic computation across their layers.

title: How Instruction Hierarchy Breaks Under Pairwise Multi-Conflict Pressure
author: Yerin Hwang; Jiwon Moon; Changho Lee; Kwangmin Ki; Taegwan Kang; Jinsik Lee; Honglak Lee; Kyomin Jung
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly process instructions from multiple sources with different privilege ranks, preserving the priority of higher-rank directives over conflicting lower-rank ones is critical for safe and predictable deployment. However, existing evaluations mostly focus on limited conflict settings, leaving it unclear how models handle instruction hierarchy (IH) when multiple conflicts arise. To address this gap, we present the first systematic study of IH under multi-conflict settings and introduce MIH-Bench, a benchmark that scales the number of simultaneous conflicts across six pairwise hierarchy scenarios. Experiments on 21 LLMs show that IH compliance deteriorates sharply as conflicts accumulate, while neither model scale nor generation reliably predicts robustness. We further find that system-involving conflicts are the most vulnerable, a particularly concerning result given the safety-critical role of system prompts. Moreover, reasoning can improve conflict resolution, although the gains vary across models and are bounded by underlying model capability. These results show that current LLMs remain fragile in pairwise multi-conflict settings, highlighting the need for stronger hierarchy-aware alignment. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MIH-release-A5B8/

title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
author: Goncalo Emanuel Cavaco Gomes; Bruno Martins; Chrysoula Zerva
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, demonstrating strong performance in terms of ranking correlation, calibration, and interval sharpness. BEiTScore++ not only produces accurate predictions, but also captures aleatoric uncertainty arising from ambiguous inputs, and epistemic uncertainty due to limited model knowledge, making it a reliable tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

title: When Symbolic Analyses Mislead: Resolution Sensitivity in Neural Language Representations
author: Matthew Fried
abstract: Recent representation analyses have reported structure-like or invariant behavior even in randomly initialized transformers, motivating the interpretation that aspects of linguistic structure may be architectural rather than learned. We show that such conclusions can be artifacts of coarse symbolic discretization. We formalize symbolic analysis of neural representations as operating over discretized activation trajectories and identify symbolic resolution as a critical, previously uncontrolled variable. Varying resolution reveals a sharp collapse of apparent similarity in random models, while pretrained models maintain stable, operator-selective differentiation across all tested resolutions. We introduce resolution stability as a necessary validity criterion for symbolic and automata-based analyses, providing a falsifiable, architecture-agnostic diagnostic for auditing internal linguistic structure in neural language models.

title: RIFT: Relation Modeling and Transfer for Visual Figurative Entailment
author: Xiaojian Lou; Qimeng Yang; Hui Song; Yunjing Jiang; Jinmiao Song; Xinjun Pei
abstract: Visual figurative entailment requires determining whether an image supports the nonliteral meaning of a textual claim, posing challenges for multimodal figurative understanding. Existing methods typically use fixed image-text fusion and struggle to capture sample-specific relations between visual evidence and figurative claims. Moreover, the limited scale of annotated visual figurative data makes it difficult to learn robust figurative relations from visual supervision alone. To address these challenges, we propose RIFT, which generates a claim-conditioned visual description and uses a relation-gated multimodal mixture of experts to model interactions among the image, description, and claim. It further retrieves figurative reasoning patterns from a FLUTE-based relation-level rationale memory and employs a confidence routing gate to modulate this external guidance according to retrieval reliability. The resulting internal and external relation representations are integrated as latent prefix tokens for joint entailment prediction and explanation generation. On V-FLUTE, RIFT achieves 88.52 F1@0, 76.07 F1@53, and 59.47 F1@60, outperforming MAPPER by 3.98, 6.38, and 7.75 points, respectively. These improvements, particularly on explanation-constrained metrics, show that relation modeling and cross-modal transfer benefit both prediction and explanation quality.

title: AutoHealth: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous Health Prediction
author: Tong Xia; Weibin Li; Yu Liu; Liu Gang; Yong Li
abstract: Developing effective and reliable health prediction models traditionally requires close collaboration between clinicians and machine learning experts, which is costly and limits efficiency. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) agents offer the potential for clinicians to autonomously develop prediction models through natural language interaction. However, existing agent-based systems remain limited in handling heterogeneous health data, complex prediction tasks, and the reliability requirements of healthcare applications. In this work, we present AutoHealth, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent framework for autonomous health prediction. Given task descriptions, AutoHealth dynamically constructs specialized agents that collaboratively perform data exploration, strategy design, code generation, model training, evaluation, and iterative refinement. Beyond optimizing predictive performance, the framework explicitly models uncertainty and generates comprehensive reports to support trustworthy clinical decision-making. To enable robust evaluation, we curate a real-world benchmark comprising 17 tasks across diverse health data modalities and learning settings. On this benchmark, AutoHealth completes all tasks and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both prediction performance and uncertainty estimation. These results demonstrate the strong capability of LLM agents in automated health data modeling.

title: Steering Geometry: Validating Human Value Geometry in LLM Steering Space
author: Mohammad Mahdi Abootorabi; Armin Saghafian; Ali Bazshoushtari; Hamid Rezaei; EunJeong Hwang; Vered Shwartz; Parvin Mousavi; Purang Abolmaesumi
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in alignment-sensitive contexts, activation steering has emerged as a lightweight, inference-time alternative to fine-tuning methods (e.g., RLHF, DPO) for behavioral control. However, existing work typically validates steering on isolated behaviors, leaving it unclear whether steering vectors encode coherent semantic structure or merely exploit behavior-specific shortcuts. We investigate whether the latent geometry of LLM steering vectors reflects theory-specified structure in human values and morality. Using Schwartz’s Theory of Basic Human Values as our primary fine-grained framework, we introduce a 26K-sample benchmark covering 20 human values and analyze distribution-driven methods (e.g., CAA, SphericalSteer, ODESteer) and behavior-centric approaches (e.g., COLD-Steer, BiPO) across diverse model families and sizes. We find that distribution-driven methods recover human value topologies aligned with theoretical predictions (Spearman \rho up to 0.51, p < 10^{-13}). In contrast, behavior-centric methods achieve comparable steering performance but show little correlation with the expected value geometry. Geometric fidelity improves with model scale but drops after instruction tuning. Finally, better geometric alignment also leads to more human-consistent transfer across values: steering one value correctly lifts compatible values and suppresses opposing ones. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/DeepRCL/Steering_Geometry.

title: Learning to Evict: Policy-Driven KV Cache Optimization for Multi-Hop Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
author: Jiale Chang; Ying Li
abstract: Visualization-of-thought (VoT) has substantially advanced multimodal spatial reasoning by interleaving visual thinking with verbal reasoning. However, multi-hop VoT reasoning introduces a fundamental scalability bottleneck: the autoregressive accumulation of interleaved visual and textual tokens causes KV cache memory to grow rapidly across successive hops. We present ScoutKV, a framework that recasts KV cache eviction as a reinforcement learning problem. ScoutKV trains a dedicated lightweight policy agent per KV head, conditioned on key–value representations, cross-hop positional encodings, and modality embeddings, to predict each token’s long-term utility across the full reasoning trajectory. Training combines offline supervised fine-tuning with future-query attention targets and online GRPO optimization with a multimodal process reward targeting low-entropy text anchors and modality-specific spatial anchors. ScoutKV consistently reduces FLOPs, latency, and peak memory while maintaining or improving accuracy across multimodal spatial reasoning benchmarks, and generalizes robustly to broader vision-language tasks.

title: A Survey on Natural Language User Profiles for Recommendation: Methods, Datasets, and Metrics
author: Mariam Arustashvili; Krisztian Balog
abstract: Natural language (NL) user interest profiles—concise, human-readable descriptions of a user’s preferences—are an emerging alternative to opaque embeddings in recommender systems, offering transparency and user control alongside predictive utility. Recent advances in large language models have made generating and consuming such profiles increasingly practical, spurring a growing but fragmented body of research. In this survey, we provide the first systematic review of NL user profiles for recommendation, organizing the literature around two coupled tasks—profile generation and profile-based recommendation—and surveying the methods, datasets, and evaluation practices currently in use. We further propose the Reference-Anchored Evaluation Taxonomy (RAET), which organizes intrinsic and extrinsic metrics around explicit (output, reference signal) pairs, and reveals where efforts have concentrated and which axes remain unexplored. Finally, we identify structural open challenges—such as the tension between transparency and task-driven optimization—establishing a clear roadmap for future research in this space.

title: DEAM: Diverse Embeddings for Arabic Multimodal Retrieval
author: Omer Nacar; Fatimah Mohamed Emad Elden; Rahaf Saeed Al Hallay; Mona A.Azim; Aya Hamod; Mohamed Zaytoon; Nour Qandos; Mohamed Abdelaziz; Israa Elhosiny; Yousra Alaa El-Ghawi; Serry Sibaee; Hadi Hamoud; Norah Naji Al-Zaid; Muhammed Ragab; Khloud Al Jallad
abstract: Modern visual document retrieval (VDR) models remain strongly English-centric, leaving Arabic substantially under-served in this rapidly advancing field. To address this gap, we introduce DEAM, the first open Arabic visual document retrieval dataset explicitly designed for fine-tuning and evaluating multimodal retrievers on Arabic. DEAM is built through a human-in-the-loop construction pipeline with annotators community annotators, combining Arabic document rendering, query creation, validation, and retrieval-oriented hard-negative mining. The dataset comprises18,275 rendered Arabic documents spanning nine source domains and 82,727 contrastive retrieval triplets, each including five mined hard negatives and one easy negative for contrastive fine-tuning. Zero-shot evaluation of 27 retrievers shows that multilingual text retrievers outperform visual retrievers on Arabic by 13.6 nDCG@10, except on layout-rich news pages. DEAM establishes a public foundation for Arabic visual document retrieval.https://huggingface.co/collections/NAMAA-Space/deam-for-arabic-multimodal-retrieval

title: OSPD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Persona-Consistent Dialogue
author: Rui Xu; Yikai Zhang; Aili Chen; Zicheng Zhao; Xu Yinghui; Libo Wu
abstract: Maintaining persona consistency across multi-turn dialogues remains a core challenge for role-playing language models. Off-policy distillation from external teachers incurs distribution mismatch that compounds across dialogue turns, while reinforcement learning struggles with reward ambiguity inherent in subjective persona fidelity. We propose OSPD, an on-policy self-distillation framework where the same model serves as both teacher and student under asymmetric information: the teacher receives a complete character profile while the student sees only a brief summary, and the student generates trajectories from its own policy. We find that teacher confidence in role-playing dialogue exhibits a bimodal structure—sharply peaked at character-critical tokens yet diffuse at generic utterances—and introduce role-aware divergence switching to match this structure. A progressive trait masking curriculum further forces staged internalization of character knowledge along semantic dimensions. Experiments on CharacterBench, CharacterEval, and SocialBench show that OSPD substantially improves persona consistency over supervised fine-tuning and multi-turn RL baselines, without requiring any external teacher or reward model.

title: A Benchmark for the Generation and Evaluation of Scientific Architecture Diagrams in HTML/SVG
author: Kyeongman Park; Kang-il Lee; Janghoon Han; Yerin Hwang; Taegwan Kang; Minwoo Lee; Changho Lee; Kyomin Jung
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can now automate many parts of scientific writing, architectural figure generation faces a critical modality bottleneck because image outputs are inherently difficult to edit, verify, and integrate into text-native LLM workflows. To enable fully text-driven synthesis, we propose a new task: generating architectural figures as pure HTML/SVG source code. Furthermore, we introduce FigureCode, a novel benchmark that evaluates structural fidelity and visual properties through code-based evaluation. Our benchmark improves agreement with human judgments by 0.35 Kendall’s τ over prior VLM-based methods. Moreover, the figure-as-code paradigm improves edit-instruction success rate by 30% and retrieval F1 score by 25.3% over baselines, while achieving 66.1% WCAG/ARIA accessibility coverage.

title: Enhancing linear attention with residual learning
author: Xunhao Lai; Jialiang Kang; Jianqiao Lu; Pengyu Zhao; Tong Lin
abstract: Linear attention offers a linear-time alternative to self-attention but often struggles to capture long-range patterns. We revisit linear attention through a prediction-correction lens and show that prevalent variants can be written as a combination of a historical prediction and a single-token correction, which creates an expressivity bottleneck. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Residual Linear Attention (RLA), a framework that equips linear attention with an explicit residual-fitting mechanism. RLA maintains an auxiliary recurrent state that learns to accumulate residual errors over time and correct the base prediction. We further instantiate a delta-rule version, Residual Delta Net (RDN), incorporating adaptive gating and residual clipping for enhanced correction control and stability. Our implementation leverages highly optimized linear attention kernels and preserves linear time and memory. Across language modeling and recall-intensive evaluations, RLA and RDN consistently outperform their respective baselines and other modern linear-attention methods, narrowing the gap to standard Transformers while retaining linear scaling.

title: Don’t Start from Scratch: Memory-Informed Detoxification for Safer LLM Responses
author: Pengze Chen; Jiachuan Wang; Weijie Sun; Wangze Ni; Lei Chen
abstract: Large language models demonstrate exceptional capabilities but raise critical safety concerns due to toxic outputs causing potential harm to users. Prompt optimization has emerged as a practical detoxification solution because it operates at the input level and can be applied to black-box or API-based models without parameter access. However, existing methods treat each task in a stateless manner without leveraging prior optimization experiences, which results in either ineffective detoxification or over-sanitized prompts that lose original intent in the vast search space. To address this, we propose the Memory-INformed Detoxification (MIND) framework that harnesses historical optimization experiences to enhance detoxification effectiveness through Memory Retrieval (MR) for retrieving relevant past cases and Memory Maintenance (MM) for maintaining a representative memory pool. We formulate MR and MM as optimization problems, prove their NP-hardness, and develop two approximation algorithms with constant approximation ratios for these problems. Experiments across multiple datasets and model configurations show that MIND outperforms existing baselines in both toxicity reduction and response utility.

title: When Hate Meets Facts: LLMs-in-the-Loop for Check-worthiness Detection in Hate Speech
author: Nicolás Benjamín Ocampo; Tommaso Caselli; Davide Ceolin
abstract: Hateful content online is often expressed using fact-like, not necessarily correct information, especially in coordinated online harassment campaigns and extremist propaganda. Failing to jointly address hate speech (HS) and misinformation can deepen prejudice, reinforce harmful stereotypes, and expose bystanders to psychological distress, while polluting public debate. Moreover, these messages require more effort from content moderators because they must assess both harmfulness and veracity, i.e., fact-check them. To address this challenge, we release WSF-ARG+, the first dataset which combines hate speech with check-worthiness information. We also introduce a novel LLM-in-the-loop framework to facilitate the annotation of check-worthy claims. We run our framework, testing it with 12 open-weight LLMs of different sizes and architectures. We validate it through extensive human evaluation, and show that our LLM-in-the-loop framework reduces human effort without compromising the annotation quality of the data. Finally, we show that HS messages with check-worthy claims show significantly higher harassment and hate, and that incorporating check-worthiness labels improves LLM-based HS detection up to 0.213 macro-F1 and to 0.154 macro-F1 on average for large models.

title: MABPD: Multi-Agent Bias Probing & Detection via Structured Argument Debate
author: Garvit Joshi; Stavya Dhyani; Jasmine; Arun Chauhan
abstract: Media bias in news articles operates through subtle linguistic cues—loaded language, selective framing, and strategic omission—that resist single-model detection and have traditionally required large annotated corpora for supervised training. We ask whether structured multi-agent deliberation can serve as a principled, training-free alternative to supervised classification for this task. We introduce MABPD (Multi-Agent Bias Probing Detection), a pipeline in which three specialized LLM agents analyze an article from complementary perspectives and resolve disagreements through a Structured Argument Debate (SAD) protocol. SAD implements a domain-motivated asymmetric burden of proof—biased claims without grounded textual evidence carry zero weight—combined with role-weighted voting and post-consensus verification, replacing task-specific supervised decision boundaries with explicit deliberative structure. Ablation confirms that this structured deliberation, not mere agent parallelism, drives performance: removing the debate module reduces F1 by up to 10.6 points. On the BABE benchmark (4,121 expert-annotated sentences), MABPD achieves 83.4% macro F1 on the held-out test split—within 0.7 percentage points (pp) of the supervised SOTA (MAGPIE, 84.1% macro F1; Horych et al., 2024)—without any task-specific training or threshold tuning on annotated data. Cross-dataset evaluation on the SemEval 2019 HyperPartisan corpus (644 articles) yields 75.0% zero-shot accuracy, within 7.2 pp of the supervised SOTA accuracy (82.2%; Kiesel et al. 2019), confirming transfer across annotation regimes. We release the full pipeline and evaluation code.

title: Provenance Before Prose: Claim-Locked Reporting for Statistical Text Generation
author: Xiao Fan; Jingyuan Li; Hongbin Guo; Yubo Han; Yi Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can fluently verbalize statistical evidence, yet statistical reports can still drift numerical values, invert effect directions, or restate thresholded contrasts as categorical effects. We frame these failures as a control problem: the evidence-bearing content of a scientific report should be fixed by structured statistical results rather than sampled during prose generation. We therefore use cross-run reproducibility to stress-test whether report-visible numbers and claims are bound before prose generation. Existing controls operate at the text or slot level; a deterministic hybrid template reproduces only 61.1% of report-visible numerical content across seeds because the LLM still selects which findings and numbers the template renders. We propose claim-locked reporting, a provenance-before-prose protocol that fixes the evidence source, numbers, direction, and allowed language strength of each reportable claim before the LLM writes connective wording. Across fMRI functional-connectivity reporting and randomized controlled trial reporting on Evidence Inference 2.0, claim-locked reporting improves reproducibility over the hybrid template by 37.4 and 20.5 points, respectively. Blinded human audits support the observed direction-preservation and governance trends. In an fMRI cost analysis with DeepSeek, claim-locked reporting also yields the lowest observed token use and median generation latency. Code is available at https://github.com/XiuFan719/Claim-Locked-Reporting.

title: Generating Clinical Vignettes that Preserve Cognitive Formulations
author: Amit Oren; Nimrod Hertz-Palmor; Dean Ariel; Guy Laban
abstract: Large language models can generate fluent clinical case vignettes, but fluency alone does not ensure fidelity to a specifiable clinical structure. We introduce FORMA, a theory-grounded framework that compiles a cognitive model of a disorder into a directed weighted graph, samples a person-specific configuration of that graph, and validates whether the generated vignette preserves the specified components and causal links. We instantiate FORMA on Posttraumatic Stress Disorder using the Ehlers and Clark cognitive model, generating 16,500 vignettes across 500 personas, 11 generation models, and three ablation conditions. Evaluation combines an external edge-recovery probe, two clinical experts, a scaled LLM judge, and a clinician user study with 100 licensed practitioners. The cognitive graph is recoverable from full-condition vignettes (MCC = +0.41, AUC = 0.70) but not from zero-shot generation (MCC = +0.01, AUC = 0.50). Experts rate full vignettes substantially higher than zero-shot alternatives, and clinicians perceive them to be human-written 85% of the time, compared with 22% for zero-shot. FORMA also reduces demographic disparity in perceived quality by 1.5–7×. These results show that cognitive formulation can serve as an auditable specification for scalable synthetic clinical text generation. A repository with the data and code is available online: https://github.com/Amit-Oren/FORMA.

title: Probing Benchmark-Specific Regularities in Knowledge Gating via Lightweight Feature Analysis
author: Zilong Cheng; Yubo Chen; Jingbo Sun; Ge Gao; Bo Chen; Xiaobing Zhao
abstract: We study whether knowledge-gating benchmarks support transferable retrieval decisions or expose benchmark-specific structural regularities that can be exploited without full semantic interpretation. Knowledge gating is the binary decision of whether a dialogue system should retrieve external knowledge at a given turn. We audit this question with a lightweight logistic-regression probe over ten dialogue-metadata features: position, length, and question-form cues. Despite using only metadata and surface signals, the probe reveals non-trivial in-domain signal and markedly different structural patterns across benchmark families. Cross-benchmark transfer provides the clearest evidence: transfer within the related DSTC9/DSTC11 family is near-lossless (Macro F1 0.81–0.84; ROC-AUC ≈ 0.90), whereas transfer across the KETOD–DSTC benchmark-family boundary has weak ranking quality (ROC-AUC 0.41–0.48) and poor detection of knowledge-needed turns (positive-class F1 ≤ 0.22 in one direction). Sentence embeddings and fine-tuned BERT show the same qualitative weakness in the DSTC→KETOD setting: MiniLM ranking is sub-chance (ROC-AUC 0.40–0.44), while BERT remains near chance (0.50–0.53) despite having the strongest KETOD in-domain positive F1. These results suggest that strong in-domain gating scores can partly reflect benchmark-specific regularities and should not, by themselves, be interpreted as evidence of transferable retrieval reasoning. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/zilongcheng582-cyber/RAGate-analysis.

title: MoraLink: Bridging Morals and Narrative Fables for Retrieval
author: Lior Livyatan; Kai Golan Hashiloni; Asif Amar; Roei Rahamim; Kfir Bar
abstract: A fable is a short narrative whose purpose is to convey a moral lesson. While semantically related, morals and fables differ fundamentally in form: morals are abstract and propositional, while fables express the same idea through characters and plot. In this work, we ask how well this conceptual relationship is captured in the latent representations of embedding models. To study this, we introduce MoraLink, a benchmark for moral-to-fable retrieval in which models must retrieve the correct fable for a given moral. We find that off-the-shelf embedding models struggle with this task, and that augmenting fable documents with LLM-generated moral-style summaries substantially improves retrieval, identifying document representation as the primary bottleneck. Contrastive fine-tuning further improves performance, and we release MoraLink as a challenging testbed for probing how well embedding models capture the abstraction gap between a moral principle and the narrative that embodies it.

title: Model Editing for Targeted Translation Error Repair
author: Danna Zheng; Yang Liu; Zhu Liu; Vimal Bhat; Manoj Aggarwal; Gerard Medioni; Najmeh Sadoughi
abstract: Machine translation systems still make systematic errors on idioms and other expressions that cannot be translated literally. Model editing offers a possible way to fix such recurring errors without retraining the whole model, but it has mostly been studied for monolingual factual updates rather than translation. We introduce MEMT-bench, the first benchmark for evaluating model editing in machine translation across multiple languages, models, and editing settings. The benchmark is built from idiomatic translation errors and tests whether an edit can correct a targeted mistranslation while preserving unrelated translation behavior. Experiments with causal tracing and representative editing methods reveal both the promise and difficulty of translation editing: edits can repair targeted errors, but maintaining cross-lingual locality and robustness under repeated edits remains challenging. Code and data are publicly available at [GitHub](https://github.com/dannalily/MEMT-Model-Editing-for-Targeted-Translation-Error-Repair/) and [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Dannalily/MEMT-bench), respectively.

title: Re2A: Situated Conversational Recommendation via Rubric-based Preference Reasoning and Alignment
author: Dongding Lin; Jian Wang; Xiaoyan Zhao; Wenjie Li
abstract: Real-world recommendation scenarios are commonly grounded in shared physical environments during user–recommender interactions. This motivates situated conversational recommendation (SCR), a complex task requiring recommender assistants to jointly reason over dialogue history, co-observed scenes, and in-scene item attributes. However, current approaches struggle with this setting due to two intertwined challenges: accurately understanding situated user preferences throughout the conversation and generating responses that simultaneously satisfy user needs and grounded situations. To this end, we propose Re2A, a framework that formulates SCR as a structured reason-then-align process. We introduce rubric-based preference reasoning, which uses automated rubrics to guide the model toward producing explicit preference states. Based on these states, we propose a preference-conditioned optimization to align response generation with dual objectives: user preference satisfaction and situation consistency. Extensive experiments on two SCR datasets demonstrate that Re2A consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering more precise, context-aware conversational recommendations. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongdingLin/Re2A.

title: AVERT: Audio-Verified Adjudication for Spoken Dialogue State Tracking
author: Chunggi Lee; Hanspeter Pfister
abstract: Spoken dialogue state tracking recovers slot-value pairs from speech, where ASR errors concentrate in entity values and persist across turns, making it both a generation and an editing problem. A strong per-turn text editor corrects much of this but, operating on the transcript alone, leaves three recoverable errors: a value predicted inconsistently across turns, an omitted slot, and a value the audio does not support. We present AVERT, which scores each candidate value by combining cross-turn agreement with a trained audio-conditioned verifier and resolves the three error types with three operators, vote, add, and swap, each restricted to the slots where its error is common. On SpokenWOZ, a base speech-LLM reaches 33.04 JGA, a text editor 38.34, and AVERT 40.13, without retraining either. This is in the range of a 1B end-to-end system that consumes the full spoken history (39.32), though AVERT uses two 1B decoders rather than one. The audio verifier contributes a statistically significant gain, and restricting each operator to a selected slot subset matters: removing it lets unrestricted voting overwrite correct categorical values and fall below the editor.

title: Categorize Early, Integrate Late: Divergent Processing Strategies in Automatic Speech Recognition
author: Nathan Roll; Pranav Bhalerao; Martijn Bartelds; Arjun Pawar; Yuka Tatsumi; Tolúlopé Ògúnrèmí; Chen Shani; Calbert Graham; Meghan Sumner; Dan Jurafsky
abstract: In speech language modeling, two architectures dominate the frontier: the Transformer and the Conformer. However, it remains unknown whether their comparable performance stems from convergent processing strategies or distinct architectural inductive biases. We introduce Architectural Fingerprinting, a probing framework that isolates the effect of architecture on representation, and apply it to a controlled suite of 24 pre-trained encoders (39M–3.3B parameters). Our analysis reveals divergent hierarchies: Conformers implement a "Categorize Early" strategy, resolving phoneme categories 29% earlier in depth and speaker gender by 16% depth. In contrast, Transformers "Integrate Late," deferring phoneme, accent, and duration encoding to deep layers (49-57%). These fingerprints suggest design heuristics: Conformers’ front-loaded categorization may benefit low-latency streaming, while Transformers’ deep integration may favor tasks requiring rich context and cross-utterance normalization.

title: Beyond Factual QA: Mentorship-Oriented Question Answering over Long-Form Multilingual Content
author: Parth Bhalerao; Ruiwen Guan; Diola Dsouza; Oana Ignat
abstract: Question answering systems are usually evaluated for factual correctness, but many real world settings such as education and career guidance require mentorship responses that offer reflection, context, and guidance. We introduce MENTORQA, the first multilingual dataset and evaluation framework for mentorship focused question answering from long form videos, with nearly 9,000 QA pairs from 180 hours of content across four languages. We define evaluation dimensions that measure fluency, clarity, alignment, and mentorship value, and use them to compare Single Agent, Dual Agent, RAG, and Multi Agent QA pipelines under controlled conditions. Multi Agent pipelines produce the strongest mentorship responses, with larger gains for complex topics and lower resource languages. We also study LLM based evaluation and find substantial variation in alignment with human judgments. Overall, MENTORQA establishes mentorship focused QA as a distinct research problem and provides a benchmark for studying agentic architectures and evaluation design in educational AI. The dataset and evaluation framework are released at https://aim-scu.github.io/MentorQA/.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Understanding Language Abilities in Large Language Models: A Survey
author: Xufeng Duan; Zhaoqian Yao; Xinyu Zhou; Zihao Fu; Beijia Kan; Yibo Wang; Bei Xiao; Hengyuan Zhang; Xuemei Tang; Ercong Nie; Zhenguang Cai
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong performance across language tasks, raising the question of whether this success reflects linguistic abstraction or reliance on surface-level statistical patterns. This survey reviews recent advances in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for analyzing candidate internal mechanisms underlying linguistic competence in LLMs. We trace the shift from model-agnostic analyses to transformer-specific methods and summarize core approaches including probing, neuron- and circuit-level analysis, and causal interventions. Synthesizing empirical findings, we argue that current evidence supports an intermediate view: LLMs appear to use reusable mechanisms for some grammatical behaviors, while these mechanisms remain frequency-conditioned, distributed, and only partially understood. We further review interpretability studies of multilingual models, highlighting evidence for both language-specific and shared representations. Finally, we outline open challenges in scalability, benchmarking, and ethics, and discuss directions toward a more cautious mechanistic account of language in LLMs.

title: CoQuant: Joint Weight-Activation Subspace Projection for Mixed-Precision LLMs
author: Zhe Ding; Su Pan; Duowei Pan
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has become an important technique for reducing the inference cost of Large Language Models (LLMs). While recent mixed-precision methods improve ultra-low bit quantization by preserving critical subspaces in high precision, they typically construct these subspaces relying solely on activation statistics. This ignores the fundamental nature of linear operations, where the output perturbation is jointly driven by both activation and weight quantization noise. In this paper, we propose CoQuant, a joint weight-activation subspace projection method. By theoretically modeling the expected output error, CoQuant formulates a closed-form weighted PCA solution that balances activation and weight covariances to select the optimal high-precision subspace. Extensive experiments on Llama-3.2 and Qwen2.5 models show that CoQuant consistently outperforms strong PTQ baselines in both WikiText perplexity and zero-shot common-sense reasoning accuracy. These results demonstrate that joint weight-activation subspace modeling provides a principled and effective direction for low-bit LLM quantization. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zachary5895/CoQuant

title: VLA-Trace: Diagnosing Vision-Language-Action Models through Representation and Behavior Tracing
author: Haoyuan Shi; Xiancong Ren; Yingji Zhang; Qinfan Zhang; Jiayu Hu; Haozhe Shan; Han Dong; Jinpeng Lu; Yinda Chen; Yi Zhang; Yong Dai; Xiaozhu Ju
abstract: Understanding how Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models transform multimodal knowledge into embodied control remains an open challenge. We present VLA-Trace, a progressive diagnostic framework that analyzes VLA models through a unified evidence chain from representation dynamics to causal control attribution and behavioral manifestation. It specifically combines cross-modal and checkpoint-drift centered kernel alignment (CKA) to trace representation evolution, attention knockout interventions to identify modality-specific control pathways, and rollout-level behavioral probes to examine grounding, shortcut dependence, and semantic following. Experiments on \pi_{0.5} and OpenVLA reveal three key findings. First, the two models exhibit distinct modality-specific adaptation dynamics during VLA finetuning. Second, they rely on different multimodal routing strategies and layer-wise dependencies during action decoding. Third, although VLA policies excel at visually grounded trajectory generation, they remain limited in fine-grained semantic following. These findings highlight future directions for representation-preserving adaptation, causal VLA circuits, and compositional semantic control.

title: PICO Entity Datasets and Methodologies in the Context of Randomized Controlled Trials: A Case Study
author: Julien Bezançon; Pierre Zweigenbaum; Nona Naderi
abstract: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) contain crucial information about the outcomes of clinical experiments. However, the sheer number of RCTs—approximately 595,000 asof September 2023—makes it difficult to efficiently navigate the available evidence. To address this challenge, medical practitioners rely on the PICO framework to identify relevant information and NLP engineers have developed automated PICO extraction pipelines. In this work, we study four PICO-related datasets created from RCTs and commonly used in the literature. We then compare two PICO extraction pipelines: PICOX reproduction and BIOBERT overlaps. Our findings show that (i) PICO-related datasets can be broadly categorized as either span-based or entity-based, with clear differences in how PICO information is annotated, and (ii) while PICOX reproduction is better suited to extracting text spans containing PICO information, BIOBERT overlaps is more suitable for fine-grained and precise PICO entity extraction. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of both models on nested and over- lapping PICO entities, found in the EBM-NLP dataset. BIOBERT overlaps achieves an entity-level micro-F1 score of 30.70 on these entities, compared with 17.58 for PICOX reproduction.

title: Beyond Trajectory Rewards: Step-level Credit Assignment for Agentic Search via Graph Modeling
author: Yuchen Liu; Feng Yingjie; Lixiong Qin; Jiasi Chen; Jianing Yu; Sheng Gao; Sheng Yang; Weiran Xu
abstract: In Agentic Search, trajectory-level outcome rewards fail to quantify the behavioral contributions of individual steps, while existing step-level reward methods typically rely on costly tree sampling. We view world knowledge as a latent world graph and each IS task as search within a latent task graph, where effective steps should make graph progress toward the answer node. Based on this prior, we propose Graph-Distance Contribution Reward (GDCR), a step-level process reward that scores newly-retrieved and newly-cited entities by their distance to the answer node in a training-time Entity-Relation (ER) graph. We further propose Step Advantage Policy Optimization (SAPO), which converts GDCR into step-level advantages and combines them with trajectory-level outcome advantages. Experiments on four challenging benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method.

title: Beyond Analysis: Training Language Models with Internal Mechanistic Feedback
author: Hanlin Xue; Gang Zhang; Xiangyuan Wang; Yunhao Bai; Yulong Wan; Xiang Li; Jiaqi Zhou; Ruochong Xiong; Junfei Liu
abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed how language models process information, yet these insights rarely improve model performance. We propose Interpretable Feature-Space Regularization (IFSR), a training-time framework that transforms mechanistic insights into optimization signals. IFSR identifies error-prone feature interactions through circuit attribution and penalizes them during training, encouraging the model to discover alternative computational pathways. Unlike inference-time interventions that operate on individual features, IFSR targets feature-to-feature edges representing internal computational patterns, and permanently encodes improvements into model parameters. Experiments across ten classification tasks show consistent improvements. Cross-task evaluation demonstrates that IFSR training can transfer positively to unrelated tasks, suggesting benefits to general model capabilities. Our analysis reveals that most identified error patterns resist human interpretation, yet penalizing them still improves performance, suggesting that automatic error identification at the level of feature interactions is feasible and effective. This work demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can directly enhance task performance through training-time optimization.

title: Trinity: Human–Agent–Environment Alignment for Embodied Task Planning
author: Hyungmin Kim; Hobeom Jeon; Dohyung Kim; Jinhyeok Jang; Minsu Jang
abstract: LLM-based embodied agents are increasingly evaluated on environment-grounded, long-horizon planning, yet existing benchmarks rarely test whether an agent can condition its plans on the specific user it serves. This gap points to a broader limitation in embodied task-planning systems, which often ground their reasoning only in the physical environment while overlooking the diversity of the people they serve. We frame this problem as Planning with Human Attributes (PHA), in which an agent must integrate explicit user information into long-horizon embodied task planning. We introduce Trinity, a benchmark designed to evaluate PHA capabilities. Within Trinity, a single instruction can yield different, equally valid, or even opposing outcomes depending on a user’s personal attributes. Our experiments reveal that standard off-the-shelf in-context learning-based agents commonly fail at the human-grounding component, whether or not they are provided with relevant examples, highlighting a key obstacle for PHA tasks. Beyond benchmarking, we contribute a bottom-up failure-mode analysis that isolates where and why agents break, and we distill it into concrete, model-agnostic design principles for human-agent-environment (HAE) aligned agents. We hope Trinity brings domestic robots a step closer to becoming trusted, socially acceptable partners.

title: Targeted Token-Level Unlearning for Repairing Text-to-SQL Models
author: Jinyu Zhang; Ruiheng Liu; Yu Zhang
abstract: Text-to-SQL models may exhibit recurring error generation patterns that are reproducible under a fixed model and difficult to eliminate through continued training. Existing approaches either perform post-hoc correction at the output level or require access to the target domain’s training data for preference optimization, neither of which directly targets these reproducible local decision tendencies. To address these limitations, we propose Targeted Token-level Unlearning for SQL (TTU-SQL), a machine-unlearning-based framework that uses a probe dataset to detect and correct systematic errors without requiring access to the model’s original training data. The framework comprises three components: (1) AST-based token-level divergence detection that precisely localizes erroneous decision points; (2) a targeted error-type extraction procedure that selects three specific types of forgettable errors based on AST divergence and logit-level behavior; and (3) Part-NPO, which applies negative preference optimization only to localized divergence tokens to suppress erroneous continuations while preserving useful SQL generation knowledge. Across the Spider and BIRD datasets and all evaluated model backbones, TTU-SQL yields consistent execution-accuracy gains over equal-budget training-based repair baselines.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
author: Mehreen Hossain Chowdhury; Nowshin Mahjabin; Ahmed Shafin Ruhan; MD Azam Hossain; Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal; Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar
abstract: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

title: AdaRetouch: An Interleaved Vision-Language Agent for Adaptive Multi-Turn Image Retouching
author: Ziang Liu; Yongheng Zhang; Qi Wen; Kai Zhao; Jianwei Zhang; Yuezhou Dong; Yiren Hao; Bo Li; Peishan Dai; Hao Zhang
abstract: Image retouching requires sophisticated aesthetic understanding and precise parameter control, yet existing agents typically rely on fixed, open-loop execution or software-specific supervision. We introduce AdaRetouch, an interleaved vision-language agent for adaptive, multi-turn image retouching. Given an instruction and an image, AdaRetouch dynamically diagnoses the visual state, invokes non-destructive tools, and iteratively observes the results until the intent is satisfied. To train this closed-loop behavior, we propose a software-agnostic pipeline that constructs trajectories featuring curriculum-driven tool sequences and step-wise reasoning. AdaRetouch is initialized via supervised fine-tuning and further optimized using process-level reinforcement learning for quality and efficiency. Experiments on AdaRetouch-Bench show that AdaRetouch outperforms general MLLMs, existing agents, and diffusion editors in intent alignment, perceptual quality, and calibrated tool planning.

title: Fine PT-PT Web: A High-Quality 41 Billion Tokens Data Collection of the European Portuguese Web
author: Gonçalo Vinagre; Rui Pedro Guerra; Pedro Gomes; Miguel Moura Ramos; Duarte Miguel Alves; Afonso Simplício; Diogo Tavares; David Semedo; Daniel Gomes; Joao Magalhaes
abstract: Curating Web corpora for regional language variants like European Portuguese (PT-PT) is heavily bottlenecked by dialectal overlap (mainly with PT-BR) and data processing scale. This paper presents an efficient pipeline to curate a production-ready PT-PT corpus from the Portuguese Web, spanning 411 TB of raw data from Arquivo.pt. We introduce a novel post-scraping block that removes boilerplate and line duplicates prior to filtering. This early-stage intervention increases final document yield by 19.04% by rescuing valid text that standard heuristic filters prematurely discard. Integrated with rigorous language identification, weighted fuzzy deduplication, and neural quality classification, our pipeline offers a scalable framework and a clean, representative corpus optimized for LLM pre-training.

title: SecOPD: Mitigating Adaptive Prompt Injections by On-Policy Distillation
author: Yibo Peng; Long Lian; David Wagner; Sizhe Chen
abstract: Prompt injection is listed as the #1 threat to AI agents. When an agent accesses external data from websites, files, or emails, an attacker may inject a prompt into the data, saying, "Ignore all prior instructions and perform <an attacker’s task>." To prevent arbitrary manipulation of agents, defenders try to train secure LLMs, which, however, still suffer from near 100% attack success rates (ASRs) against adaptive prompt injections. We note that this is because existing defensive fine-tuning recipes rely on sequence-level feedback signals (in DPO or GRPO). Treating an entire output equally prevents the model from learning precisely which output tokens are insecure. In this paper, we propose Secure On-Policy Distillation (SecOPD) that provides token-level feedback to guide defensive fine-tuning. The LLM receives an injected sample and produces a rollout, whose tokens are scored by the initialization model given the corresponding clean input. With more fine-grained training signals, our defended Qwen3.6-27B achieves a 9.0% ASR against the SoTA PISmith adaptive prompt injections, compared to 94.0% for the prior SoTA, Meta-SecAlign. The obtained security generalizes to domains completely unseen in training: in agentic tool calling, SecOPD achieves a 4.7% ASR compared to 5.5% for Meta-SecAlign.

title: RoutePO: Personalized Routing Policy Optimization for LLM-based Multi-Channel Recall
author: Zaiyi Zheng; Yaochen Zhu; Mingxuan Ju; Tong Zhao; Neil Shah; Jundong Li
abstract: LLM-based rerankers in recommender systems are inherently constrained by limited context windows: they can only reorder a small retrieved candidate set, so any relevant item missed by upstream retrieval cannot be recovered at ranking time. To mitigate this dependency, we propose RoutePO, which repositions the LLM from an item ranker to a recall strategy router for multi-channel recall. Conditioned on a user’s profile/context (interaction history and optional demographics), the LLM outputs personalized fusion weights over heterogeneous retrieval experts, enabling dynamic candidate aggregation without exposing long candidate lists from the entire item pool to the prompt. We train the router via a synergistic two-stage alignment process: Coarse Routing Alignment (SFT) warm-starts the policy with a quality-aware oracle prior over retrieval experts, and Fine-grained Metric Optimization (RL) directly optimizes recall-stage ranking metrics (e.g., NDCG) by sampling simplex-valued routing weights and rewarding fused-list quality. To support continuous exploration over the simplex under GRPO-style optimization, we introduce SofT-GRPO based on Gumbel–Softmax reparameterization with nucleus restriction and KL regularization. Finally, we instantiate fusion with both weighted score merging and a weight-aware interleaving strategy (Snake Fusion) that preserves within-channel rankings. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate consistent gains over strong individual recallers and multi-channel fusion baselines, including up to 15.88% relative improvement in NDCG@50 on Food. Our implementation is available on https://github.com/zhengzaiyi/RoutePO.

title: Quality, Not Just Outcome: A Structural Scoring Framework for Selecting Coding-Agent Trajectories for Supervised Fine-Tuning
author: Sida Li; Yuanxin Liu; Shicheng Li; Linli Yao; Xu Sun; Haoli Bai; Xiao-Hui Li
abstract: Open coding agents are commonly trained through supervised fine-tuning on interaction trajectories whose final patches pass the benchmark test suite. However, this outcome-level filtering criterion ignores process quality: trajectories that eventually succeed may still contain inefficient interaction patterns such as repetitive file inspection, unstable tool usage, or delayed modification behavior, all of which become part of the imitation target. We propose (Trajectory Quality Score), a structural scoring framework for coding-agent trajectories that operates directly on trajectory structure, requires no LLM judge, and runs in linear time. characterizes trajectory quality through structural signals organized around structured convergence: information focus, intent–action alignment, and policy dynamics. Using 155,144 successful trajectories from a public open-license corpus, we rank trajectories by and fine-tune coding agents on filtered subsets. Models trained on top-ranked trajectories consistently outperform those trained on random or bottom-ranked subsets on . Our results suggest that process-level trajectory quality is an important factor in coding-agent supervision and that structural trajectory filtering provides an effective and scalable alternative to LLM-based data selection.

title: LaPR: Latent Preference Reasoning for Generative Personalized Retrieval
author: Hanze Guo; Shunyu Zhang; Jiakai Tang; Jingwei Zhuo; Yi Zhang; Xuanping Li; Xiao Zhou
abstract: Generative retrieval offers a unified paradigm for personalized search by autoregressively decoding items as Semantic IDs. However, personalized search hinges on reasoning about query-history relevance, in which explicit textual reasoning incurs heavy cost and high latency, whereas purely implicit reasoning does not provide a structured intermediate latent interface for retrieval. To resolve this tension, we propose LaPR, an adaptive latent retrieval reasoning framework that turns explicit retrieval reasoning into compact latent signals. Specifically, LaPR constructs verified step-wise retrieval traces, induces step-conditioned semantic slots via vector quantization, and distills textual reasoning into these slots through a text-latent to pure-latent curriculum. At inference, LaPR adaptively predicts the reasoning depth and corresponding slots from the query and user history, providing latent reasoning signals for efficient Semantic-ID generation. Extensive experiments show that LaPR consistently surpasses all baselines, achieving SOTA personal retrieval performance while substantially reducing reasoning-token cost and inference latency.

title: From Homogeneity to Diversity: Self-Refined GRPO for Controllable Creative Writing
author: Minna Peng; Wei Tan; Zeyu Wang; Yongquan Hu; Ruizhi Huang; Yang Jie
abstract: Controllable creative writing is a text generation task that requires both high generation quality and diverse outputs. However, existing methods often improve one aspect at the expense of the other. To address this challenge, we propose SERGE, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that introduces a diversity-guided self-refinement mechanism, where the policy itself refines low-diversity candidate texts, and employs policy shaping to amplify the gradient contributions of samples with both high generation quality and diversity. We also propose a fine-grained reward modeling framework to provide reliable quality reward signals to support RL optimization. Experiments on the short-form video copywriting generation task show that SERGE outperforms the base model and conventional diversity-enhancement strategies on both diversity metrics (DisNGram, PairBLEU, CosSim) and generation quality, effectively alleviating the "diversity collapse” issue in RL. Our code is available at: https://github.com/peng-mn/SERGE.

title: LTS-VoiceAgent: A Listen-Think-Speak Framework for Efficient Streaming Voice Interaction via Semantic Triggering and Incremental Reasoning
author: Wenhao Zou; Yuwei Miao; Zhanyu Ma; Jun Xu; Jiuchong Gao; Renqing He; Jingwen Xu
abstract: Real-time voice agents face a tension: end-to-end models often lack deep reasoning, while cascaded ASR–LLM–TTS pipelines achieve stronger reasoning but defer LLM inference until after ASR finalizes the transcript, creating an avoidable post–turn-end silent gap. We target this gap under complex spoken requests that admit a relatively determinate answer, and treat it as system-induced rather than communicatively motivated. Existing cascaded streaming strategies attempt to reduce it via mechanical segmentation (e.g., fixed chunks, VAD-based splitting) or speculative generation, but they frequently either break semantic units or waste computation on predictions that must be rolled back. We propose LTS-VoiceAgent, a Listen–Think–Speak framework that explicitly separates when to think from how to reason incrementally.
