To systematically investigate reasoning rigidity, a behavior unexplored in prior work, we introduce a dataset, ReasoningTrap, consisting of math problems, puzzles, and agentic tasks designed to diagnose reasoning rigidity. Using this dataset, we identify patterns that occur when models default to ingrained reasoning, and suggest inference-level and GRPO-based post-training remedies. Our diagnostic set and evaluation code are available at the project page to facilitate future research on mitigating reasoning rigidity in language models.

title: Multimodal Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
author: Jiayu Yao; Yiwei Wang; Anmeng Zhang; Zhe Sun; Songsong Wang; Lingrui Mei; Yuyao Ge; Shenghua Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, higher proxy rewards do not necessarily lead to better task performance, especially when visual evidence is difficult to verify with text-only or weakly grounded reward signals. We systematically study reward hacking in MLLM reinforcement learning by varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale, and RL algorithm. To separate RL-induced failures from pre-existing weaknesses, we introduce the Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR), which measures the hacking rate among samples where RL achieves higher proxy reward than the SFT baseline. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, RL can actively create new failures rather than merely amplify existing ones, and the effect is especially pronounced near ambiguous decision boundaries. Second, robustness depends jointly on model scale, reward design, and RL algorithm, and scaling mitigates hacking but cannot replace reliable rewards. Third, incorporating visual evidence helps only when verification is reliable, since keyword-based verification introduces additional exploitation opportunities whereas VLM-based semantic verification can reduce reward hacking. Overall, multimodal reward hacking is a systematic consequence of optimizing imperfect reward signals, highlighting the need for rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.

title: Toward Latent Language Model Skills Steering and Optimization: An Empirical Study
author: Xunyi Jiang; Junda Wu; Yuxin Xiong; Sheldon Yu; Tong Yu; David Arbour; Ritwik Sinha; Julian McAuley; Hongyi Wen
abstract: Skills, as a useful abstraction for the procedural capabilities of large language models (LLMs), capture how models perform structured, multi-step reasoning and program execution. Existing approaches typically treat skills as explicit, surface-level constructs specified through prompts or programs, leaving open the question of how such procedural capabilities are represented inside the model and whether they can be manipulated as structured objects in latent space. In this empirical study, we investigate whether procedural LLM skills can be represented as directions in activation space and whether vector-space operations over these directions can express skill-level behaviors. We find that procedural skills admit a vector-space representation: individual skill directions can be activated to shift model behavior; independently extracted directions can compose to form higher-level skills. Contrastive directions yield context-conditioned algorithmic personalization and optimization trajectories over skill directions evolve non-monotonically, with intermediate states often surpassing fully optimized solutions. These results support a representation-level view of procedural LLM skills: they admit a latent vector-space organization that allows direct manipulation through internal interventions.

title: Subjective and Hierarchical Annotation of Text Difficulty in Japanese
author: Daisuke Maekawa; Kazumasa Omura; Sora Tarumoto; Shotaro Ishihara; Tomoyuki Kajiwara
abstract: This study presents a difficulty-annotated corpus of Japanese newspaper articles. The annotation in our corpus has two key features. First, it is hierarchical, with difficulty levels labeled at the word, sentence, and document levels, respectively. Second, it is subjective, with 99 readers from diverse backgrounds labeling the difficulty levels based on their own perceptions. Detailed analysis of our corpus revealed correlations in difficulty levels across linguistic units, such as between words and sentences, and sentences and documents. We also found that text difficulty varies depending on reader attributes such as age and topics of interest. Furthermore, we trained Transformer encoders on this corpus and developed a personalized difficulty estimation model that takes into account both linguistic and attribute information. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating reader attributes improves the performance of difficulty estimation and that multi-task learning across language units is beneficial. Our difficulty annotations are publicly available.

title: Cultural (In)Competence: Investigating Culture-Specific Stereotype Detection Capabilities of LLMs
author: Maximilian Spliethöver; Jannes Lötfering; Dominik Bachmann; Alexander Espig; Willem Zuidema; Katrin Schulz; Henning Wachsmuth
abstract: Stereotypes are subjective constructs that are mediated by the cultural context in which they are viewed. Successfully modeling them thus also requires cultural competence. When using large language models (LLMs) for stereotype-related tasks, such as their detection, it is therefore crucial that models can access relevant cultural knowledge and adjust responses accordingly. Since LLMs have shown disparities in what cultural knowledge is available to them, their capacity regarding stereotypes may also be disparate across languages and cultural contexts (e.g., for non-English languages or for non-US contexts). In this paper, we systematically investigate the effectiveness of LLMs for culture-specific stereotype detection across three factors: (1) the prompting language, (2) the instruction tuning language, and (3) the fine-tuning dataset size. We conduct experiments for US, Dutch, and Chinese cultural contexts. Our results suggest that LLMs do not reliably account for cultural contexts and overpredict the presence of stereotypes. Non-English prompts seem to improve consideration of cultural context and thus lead to more effective predictions. Moreover, we find that additional instruction tuning reduces false-positive rates and that training data size moderates detection effectiveness non-monotonically.

title: Graph Evidence Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Native Decoder Use in Graph-Augmented LLMs
author: Xiaoyu Guo; Pengcheng Chen; YU Jiong; Yi Lu; Yaohua Wang; Ziyang Li
abstract: Graph-augmented large language models often assume that graph evidence produced by external computation and placed in the input can be used by the native decoder. We test this assumption with HopQA, a deliberately bounded diagnostic that asks for the shortest-hop distance between two query nodes. Because the answer is a small integer and the target is purely topological, failure cannot be dismissed as open-ended generation or ambiguous evaluation. Yet existing graph-augmented baselines still fail on this setting, showing that providing graph evidence is not the same as making it usable. We introduce an intervention triangle with three matched conditions: readable graph evidence, shuffled graph evidence, and no-graph input. This separates evidence inclusion, structural readability, and decoder-usable topology. Guided by this diagnosis, we present S²GE as an instance showing that diagnosis-driven interface design can improve native decoder usability. S²GE uses query-aware sampling, endpoint- and proximity-based ordering, and structure-preserving alignment. Across DBLP, Biomedical, GoodReads, and PubMed, S²GE achieves strict exact-match scores of 36.5%, 57.8%, 76.6%, and 52.0%, improving over the strongest native-generation baseline by 53.5 points on average. The interventions further reveal harmful-shuffle, shuffle-robust, and no-graph-saturated regimes.

title: DarterSD: Dynamic Token-Weighted Distillation for High-Efficient Speculative Decoding
author: Zhaoning Zhang; Xu Baizhou; Libo Zhang; Yi Chen; Zhiliang Tian; Zhen Huang; Dongsheng Li
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive LLM generation with a lightweight draft model, yet existing distillation methods treat all historical tokens equally despite their divergent contributions to next-token prediction. We discover that attention in draft models is extremely concentrated: the top-3 historical tokens capture 80% of attention weight, while over 90% of tokens contribute negligibly. This uniform training paradigm forces the draft model to learn from noisy, low-importance tokens, diluting the learning signal from informative positions and limiting the alignment between draft and target distributions. To address this, we propose DarterSD, a dynamic token-weighted distillation framework for efficient speculative decoding. DarterSD employs a learnable sigmoid gate in self-attention to compute per-token importance scores, and designs a multi-objective distillation loss comprising distribution alignment, logit matching, and gate regularization to focus training on high-informative tokens. We further introduce a lightweight Boolean-mask denoising strategy at inference to suppress contextual noise, without modifying the target model’s verification pipeline. Experiments show DarterSD delivers a lossless speedup up to 5.52x , outperforming EAGLE3 (4.67x), and boosts the average accepted token length by 12.9%.

title: Better World Models Can Lead to Better Post-Training Performance
author: Prakhar Gupta; Henry Conklin; Sarah-Jane Leslie; Andrew Lee
abstract: We study how explicit world-modeling objectives affect the internal representations and downstream capability of Transformers, using Rubik’s Cubes as our training domain. We ask: (1) how does explicitly pretraining a world model affect a model’s latent representations, (2) how does world-model quality affect post-training performance, and (3) how should a finite data budget be split between pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning? We compare standard action-prediction fine-tuning with two strategies that add explicit state-prediction supervision: state pretraining followed by fine-tuning, and joint action and state training. We measure task accuracy after Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). We further find that explicit world-modeling yields better representations in terms of higher probing accuracy and steerability of the model, and that better representations yield larger gains from GRPO, especially on harder cube states. Finally, when the fine-tuning budget is held fixed, probe accuracy strongly predicts the GRPO improvement. Under a fixed total data budget, accuracy is maximized by allocating only a small fraction to pretraining.

title: Auditing Speaker-Level Metadata Utility in Text-Residual Prosody Prediction
author: Gaeun Kim; Jihyun Park; Sohee Jang; Joon-Hyuk Chang
abstract: Text only partially determines prosodic realization, leaving residual variation that may align with speaker-level metadata such as regional accent or first-language (L1) background. However, because these labels are assigned to speakers, their predictive gains may overlap with broader speaker-associated structure rather than uniquely reflect category-level prosodic effects. We frame this as an attribution problem and propose a speaker-controlled audit using matched text-residual prosody predictors that differ only in access to metadata labels and speaker identity. The audit measures label utility beyond text, speaker utility beyond text, and the additional empirical utility of the label when speaker conditioning is already available. Across VCTK regional-accent labels and L2-ARCTIC L1 labels, metadata yields modest gains over text, while speaker conditioning yields larger gains and leaves little additional label utility under speaker control. Random speaker-group and label-perturbation controls further characterize the specificity and use of the supplied metadata. Importantly, speaker-held-out evaluation shows that metadata transfer to unseen speakers is limited and target-dependent, indicating that observed-speaker metadata gains do not by themselves establish speaker-independent category-level effects. These results position speaker-controlled auditing as a prerequisite attribution check before assigning category-level interpretations to metadata-conditioned predictive gains.

title: Prompt2Box: Improving LLM Weakness Discovery and Specificity Estimation by Uncovering Entailment Structure among Prompts
author: Neeladri Bhuiya; Shib Sankar Dasgupta; Andrew McCallum; Haw-Shiuan Chang
abstract: To discover the weaknesses of LLMs, researchers often embed prompts into a vector space and cluster them to extract insightful patterns. However, vector embeddings primarily capture topical similarity. As a result, prompts that share a topic but differ in specificity, and consequently in difficulty, are often represented similarly, making fine-grained weakness analysis difficult. To address this limitation, we propose Prompt2Box:, which embeds prompts into a box embedding space using a trained encoder. The encoder, trained on existing and synthesized datasets, outputs box embeddings that capture not only semantic similarity but also specificity relations between prompts (e.g., "writing an adventure story" is more specific than "writing a story". We further develop a novel dimension reduction technique for box embeddings to facilitate dataset visualization and comparison. Our experiments demonstrate that box embeddings consistently capture prompt specificity better than vector baselines and achieve up to 45% error reduction compared to the prompt length baseline. On the downstream task of creating hierarchical clustering trees for 17 LLMs from the UltraFeedback dataset, Prompt2Box: can identify 13.5% more LLM weaknesses than vector baselines and achieves an approximately 33% stronger correlation between hierarchical depth and instruction specificity.

title: SeVeR: Selective Visual Exposure and Retrieval for 3D Medical Image Question Answering
author: Yaojun Hu; Danyang Tu; Yang Liu; Jiajin Zhang; Wei Fang; Zhiqiang Liu; Chunlai Dong; Yingda Xia; Haochao Ying; Jian Wu; Ling Zhang
abstract: Volumetric medical VQA requires reasoning over long and redundant 3D visual token sequences, especially in multi-sequence MRI where complementary modalities provide diverse diagnostic cues but expose the decoder to many repeated anatomical regions. To investigate reasoning under multi-sequence visual redundancy, we first introduce BreMRIs-VQA, a clinically curated breast MRI benchmark with 1.19M QA pairs from 71.0K sequences and 12.9K patients, covering both free-text and multiple-choice questions. We further propose SeVeR, a selective visual exposure framework that compresses dense volumes into modality-wise prototypes and retrieves complementary multi-level evidence with change-aware gated attention during decoding, trained with a marginal-utility self-consistency objective that suppresses unhelpful retrieval. Experiments on BreMRIs-VQA and public benchmarks show that SeVeR improves both discriminative and generative performance while exposing substantially fewer visual tokens.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Activation Steering in Large Language Models
author: Kien Le; Thai Le
abstract: Activation steering has become a popular training-free method to control LLMs’ behavior by injecting precomputed direction vectors into the model’s residual stream at inference time. Yet, its robustness to realistic input variation remains under-explored. We present the first systematic evaluation of activation steering robustness under adversarial text perturbations on the inputs, covering four extraction methods, three attack strategies, six personas from the Anthropic Model-Written Evaluations dataset, and five models ranging from 1.5B to 30B parameters. Attacks succeed broadly across all settings: directional robustness drops by up to 64%, post-attack confidence collapses near or below 0.25 across all methods and models, and steering strength degrades on nearly every steerable input. Layer selection is equally fragile, with the optimal layer identified by an automated method on clean inputs shifting by up to 17 positions under perturbation, a failure that compounds the vector-level breakdown. Extracting vectors from adversarially perturbed inputs partially recovers steerability for PCA and MD on mid-to-large models, but they consistently fail to locate the improved optimal layer, limiting the practical benefit of this mitigation. Together, these findings reveal that the brittleness of activation steering is structural rather than method-specific, and that current layer selection strategies are not robust enough for real-world deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/kien206/steering-adv-robustness.

title: What Limits Us? Analyzing Self-Reported Limitations in NLP Research
author: Tawan Thaepprasit; Peeranuth Kehasukcharoen; Ding Wang; Remi Denton; Peerapon Vateekul; Piyawat Lertvittayakumjorn
abstract: Since late 2022, a Limitations section has become mandatory at many top-tier NLP conferences. The growing number of accepted papers at these venues has resulted in a vast corpus of self-reported limitations that cannot all be manually reviewed, yet remains systematically unanalyzed. Therefore, in this paper, we conduct a large-scale analysis of the Limitations sections from ACL and EMNLP papers published between 2020 and 2025 to understand what researchers disclose about their own work. To do so, we implement a novel human-AI framework for iterative hybrid qualitative coding. This framework enables us to investigate trends in self-reported limitations over time, their correlations with specific paper attributes, and the writing patterns that recur around these disclosures. Our findings offer a critical reflection on the diverse reported challenges as well as the self-reporting practices of researchers in the NLP community.

title: EvoFormat: Discovering Effective Graph-to-Text Formats via Rule-Based Evolutionary Search
author: Kazuya Kakizaki; Taiki Miyagawa; Hideyuki Oiso; Ryo Furukawa
abstract: Encoding graphs as text prompts enables LLM-based graph reasoning. However, effective graph-to-text encodings depend on the downstream task, graph structure, and target LLM, making manual format design time-consuming and brittle. We propose EvoFormat, a black-box evolutionary search framework that automatically discovers interpretable graph-to-text formats represented as human-readable formatting rules over node naming, relation expression, and global arrangement. Using only task-level feedback from LLM outputs, EvoFormat iteratively mutates and selects rules without gradients or internal model access. Across synthetic GraphQA and IMDB-MULTI-derived structural QA tasks over unattributed graphs, EvoFormat outperforms strong hand-crafted encodings in most settings.

title: APEX-EM: Non-Parametric Online Learning for Autonomous Agents via Structured Procedural-Episodic Experience Replay
author: Pratyay Banerjee; Masud Moshtaghi; Ankit Chadha
abstract: LLM agents rerun full reasoning for every task, even one they solved moments earlier. We introduce APEX-EM, a non-parametric experience memory that stores complete procedural-episodic traces in a typed Procedural Knowledge Graph (PKG) and retrieves them through three channels: semantic search, structural-signature matching over abstract operation sequences, and graph traversal. A Plan-Retrieve-Generate-Iterate-Ingest (PRGII) workflow produces, quality-gates, and commits experiences, indexing both successes and failures so the agent learns what to reuse and what to avoid. No weights change during deployment. We evaluate on five benchmarks: BigCodeBench, KGQAGen-10k, HLE, Lifelong Agent Bench, and ALFWorld. Because prior work uses different backbones, we base our claims on same-backbone comparisons that hold model capability fixed. On held-out BigCodeBench transfer with a shared GPT-4o backbone, APEX-EM gains +7.6pp over the no-memory baseline, which is 3.3x MemRL’s +2.3pp under the identical setup. On Lifelong Agent Bench with a shared GPT-4o-mini backbone, APEX-EM gains +1.4pp (OS) and +1.0pp (DB) cumulative success. On KGQAGen-10k, frozen memory transfers to a blind 1,079-question test split at 73.7% versus 42.0% with no memory, approaching an oracle that is handed the ground-truth subgraph (84.9%). Across three Opus scales the memory gain stays at +27pp to +32pp, so it adds to model capability rather than substituting for it. Component analysis shows no single mechanism dominates: teacher feedback is negligible for code but adds +10.3pp on structured queries, structural signatures give 3.3 times the transfer of semantic-only retrieval, and within-epoch iteration recovers most of the gain when rich feedback is unavailable. These results argue for modular memory composed per domain.

title: DyBenchEval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Suite for Measuring LLM-as-Dynamic-Benchmarker
author: Pei Ke; Jingye Wang; Maolin Sun; Lan Wang; Haitao Peng; Bosi Wen; Enping Hu; Ruyi Luo; Minlie Huang; Ke Qin
abstract: Dynamic benchmarking is an essential research direction in the evaluation of large language models (LLMs) to avoid data contamination. Although existing works have proposed LLM-based methods for dynamic benchmarking, there still lacks a unified paradigm for performance comparison among different LLMs, which hinders researchers from model selection for specific domains and tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a comprehensive evaluation suite called DyBenchEval, including a novel seed dataset across 4 domains and 7 tasks as well as multi-aspect evaluation metrics. A cross data filling method is utilized for high-quality data augmentation with domain/task-level similarity, aiming to overcome the data scarcity problem. For automatic metrics, we consider coherence, correctness, and diversity of LLM-generated evaluation samples, simultaneously measuring the respective quality of generated questions / answers and the relationship between them. Extensive experimental results on DyBenchEval reveal deficiencies in 11 mainstream closed-source and open-source LLMs when dealing with dynamic benchmarking across different domains and tasks.

title: Token-level Adaptive Weighting via Implicit Rewards for Inference-time Multi-objective Alignment
author: Dou Hu; Lingwei Wei; Peiran Xu; Hongjiang Xiao; Songlin Hu; Yuan Zhang
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is challenging due to the inherent heterogeneity and multi-dimensionality of these preferences. Existing inference-time multi-objective alignment methods often rely on fixed weights to combine preference models. However, different tokens contribute unequally to preference objectives during decoding. Ignoring such token-level variation may cause the loss of preference information and lead to objective interference. To alleviate this, we utilize the implicit rewards of preference models to estimate importance differences between tokens, and propose a new training-free and reward-free framework TAW to dynamically balance multiple objectives for inference-time alignment. We design the relative entropy and marginal entropy estimators to quantify the informativeness and uncertainty of preference objectives. TAW with the estimator ensures that more informative or reliable preferences are emphasized, while weak or uncertain signals are suppressed. Experiments on two LLM alignment benchmarks show that TAW outperforms strong baselines without predefined weightings, while also achieves an overall optimal Pareto front when explicit preference weighting is applied.

title: Selective State-Space Adaptation and Retrieval for Language Model Reasoning
author: Atahan Dokme; Larry Heck
abstract: Low-rank adaptation introduces a static learned update applied identically to every input. The update provides task-level adaptation but does not explicitly represent token-level or instance-level state variation. A family of adapters is proposed that introduces selective state-space control at two complementary granularities. At the token level, MaLoRA (Mamba-modulated low-rank adaptation) makes the adapter’s scaling factor a dynamic input-dependent function with recurrent state across tokens, in contrast to the stateless modulators of prior work. The token-level adapter improves over low-rank adaptation. On the other hand, it differentiates tokens by structural role but not by contextual relevance, which motivates placing evidence selection at the context level. At the context level, MaRA (Mamba Retrieval Adapter) tracks cross-segment reasoning state and selects the segments most relevant to the query. State-space controlled retrieval of approximately three million parameters exceeds an eight-billion-parameter dense retriever on supporting-paragraph recall. Although base models perform poorly on the task without adaptation (14 to 25 F1), MaRA recovers the evidence relevance latent in their representations. Across three frozen backbones and two multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, the end-to-end family improves reasoning accuracy on every cell of the 3-by-2 grid, by +6.4 F1 (+10.0% relative) on average over the LoRA baseline.

title: Granuscore: A Reference-Free Measure of Granularity for Text Analysis and Question Answering
author: Lukas Ellinger; Alexander M. Fichtl; Miriam Anschütz; Georg Groh
abstract: Natural language conveys information at varying levels of granularity, from fine-grained references to broad descriptions. While granularity is fundamental to human communication, existing measures mostly capture surface detail or sentence specificity. We introduce Granuscore, a reference-free measure of granularity that leverages structural properties of a hierarchical embedding space. Granuscore reliably recovers hierarchical orderings on the Granola-EQ dataset and captures expected differences in granularity across discourse contexts. Across domains, we further show that Granuscore explains non-linear variation in sentence specificity beyond sentence length. Finally, we apply Granuscore to four question-answering benchmarks and analyze how granularity differs for questions, gold answers, and model outputs across response outcomes. The analysis reveals consistent differences in model behavior and provides a principled lens for characterizing the difficulty of QA datasets. Together, the results position Granuscore as a scalable, broadly applicable tool for analyzing granularity in text.

title: Learning New Facts with QLoRA: An Acquisition-Retention Frontier
author: Estelle Zheng; Sébastien Warichet; Emmanuel Helbert; Christophe Cerisara
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is often assumed to preserve pretrained capabilities because it updates only a small number of parameters. We show that this assumption depends strongly on adapter capacity. We study factual acquisition in a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark where Qwen3-4B must learn anonymized geographic relations while retaining unrelated capabilities. Comparing FFT with QLoRA ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64, we find that rank induces a clear acquisition–retention frontier. Low-rank QLoRA preserves OOD performance but acquires fewer facts, whereas higher ranks improve same-fact paraphrase generalization at increasing cost to unrelated benchmarks. FFT behaves as a conservative baseline: it retains general capabilities well, but does not reach the highest factual-acquisition regime. Distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics mirror this behavioral trade-off, with higher-rank QLoRA moving farther from the pretrained model. A separate math adaptation experiment shows a weaker frontier, suggesting that the effect is most pronounced when adaptation must install new factual associations rather than reinforce skills already supported by pretraining.

title: Noise Adaptive Streaming Audio-Visual Speech Token Enhancement for Robust Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models
author: Bella Godiva; Yeonju Kim; Yong Man Ro
abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems enable simultaneous listening and speaking, but their audio-only perception often fails under background noise and overlapping speech, leading to incoherent responses. Recent audio-visual dialogue approaches show that incorporating visual cues such as lip movements improve robustness under audio corruption. However, existing approaches often adapt the large speech dialogue model itself to process visual input, requiring costly multimodal training. We propose AV-STE, a modular streaming audio-visual front-end that restores corrupted semantic speech tokens from noisy audio and lip video before they reach the speech LLM. The downstream dialogue model remains entirely frozen, preserving its pretrained conversational capabilities. When integrated with frozen Moshi, AV-STE improves average GPT-4o-judged response coherence from 1.42 to 1.91 under same-dataset speaker interference while largely preserving turn-taking behavior. Gains also transfer to out-of-domain Seamless Interaction. Code and models are available: https://github.com/bellagodiva/av-ste.git

title: Multi-Label Delegation Target Identification in Japanese Law
author: Tsuyoshi Fujita; Yuya Sawada; Yusuke Sakai; Taro Watanabe
abstract: Legal systems often employ legislative drafting practices in which higher-level laws delegate detailed regulations to lower-level laws. In particular, when a single provision delegates authority to multiple lower-level laws, readers must cross-reference many related provisions scattered across the entire bodies of law, imposing a substantial cognitive burden. Reflecting this real-world problem, this work proposes a novel multi-label delegation target identification task to identify all the delegated provisions corresponding to an input provision, with the focus on Japanese law. We construct pipeline systems combining a candidate retriever and a candidate classifier, using language models with diverse architectures. Experimental results show that adopting a cross-encoder-based binary classifier as a candidate classifier improves performance at finer granularities, establishing a solid baseline for the task. Furthermore, our comprehensive analyses reveal the remaining challenges in achieving sufficient performance on instances with many delegated provisions and identify typical error types, providing a foundation for future improvement.

title: Frequency Matters: Fast Model-Agnostic Data Curation for Pruning and Quantization
author: Francesco Pio Monaco; Elia Cunegatti; Flavio Vella; Giovanni Iacca
abstract: Post-training model compression is essential for enhancing the portability of Large Language Models (LLMs) while preserving their performance. While several compression approaches have been proposed, less emphasis has been placed on selecting the most suitable set of data (the so-called *calibration data*) for finding the compressed model configuration. The choice of calibration data is a critical step in preserving model capabilities both intra- and inter-tasks. In this work, we address the challenge of identifying high-performance calibration sets for both pruning and quantization by analyzing intrinsic data properties rather than model-specific signals. We introduce **ZipCal**, a model-agnostic data curation strategy that maximizes lexical diversity based on Zipfian power laws. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms standard uniform random sampling across various benchmarks. Notably, it also performs on par, in terms of downstream performance, with a state-of-the-art method that relies on model perplexity. The latter becomes prohibitively expensive at large-scale models and datasets, while **ZipCal** is on average 240 faster due to its tractable linear complexity. We make the code and the experiments available at https://github.com/FrancescoMonaco/ZipCal.

title: CoSteer: Collaborative Decoding-Time Personalization via Local Delta Steering
author: Hang Lv; Sheng Liang; Hao Wang; Hongchao Gu; Yaxiong Wu; Wei Guo; Defu Lian; Yong Liu; Enhong Chen
abstract: Personalization has become crucial for adapting models to the diverse and evolving needs of users across cultural, temporal, and contextual dimensions. While existing methods often rely on centralized fine-tuning or static preference alignment within a single model, they struggle to achieve both real-time and high-quality personalization under the resource and privacy constraints of personal devices. To address this challenge, we propose CoSteer, a collaborative framework that enables tuning-free, real-time personalization via decoding-time adaptation. By leveraging logit differences between context-aware and -agnostic local small models, CoSteer steers cloud-based large models, ensuring effective personalization while preserving the large model’s capabilities. Personalization is handled locally, with only final tokens sent to the cloud, maintaining both user context and system efficiency. Through extensive experiments across a wide range of tasks, we demonstrate that CoSteer generates high-quality personalized content, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Our results highlight its robustness across models and environments, confirming its practical applicability in real-world scenarios. Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Costeer-4977.

title: Unified Fragment Growing, Linking, and Merging with Energy-Aware Pre-training and Reward-Ranked Alignment
author: Xuefeng Liu; Songhao Jiang; Tinson Xu; Qinan Huang; Rick L. Stevens
abstract: Fragment-based drug discovery optimizes small molecular hits through three recurring transformations: fragment growing, linking, and merging. Existing generative methods, however, usually specialize in a single transformation and have focused primarily on linker design. We introduce FragmentGPT, a unified chemical language model that casts all three operations as conditional molecular generation. To build this capability, we construct a chemically-aware pre-training corpus using energy-guided bond cleavage, together with overlap-based examples that teach the model to connect separated fragments and consolidate shared substructures. We further introduce Reward-Ranked Alignment with Expert Exploration (RAE), which combines expert-guided candidate generation, Pareto- and composite-reward-based selection, and supervised fine-tuning for multi-objective molecular optimization. Conditioned on one or more fragments, FragmentGPT can expand a scaffold, connect distinct subunits, or merge overlapping structures into a complete molecule. Experiments on RTCB and SARS-CoV-2 main protease (3CLPro), together with ablation studies, show high chemical validity and strong aggregate performance across multiple drug-design objectives.

title: \text{GR}^2: Mitigating Granularity Collapse via Adaptive Query Routing in Generative Retrieval
author: Soona Hong; Dohyeon Lee; Jaeyoung Kim; Seung-Won Hwang
abstract: Generative Retrieval (GR) aims to directly generate document identifiers (DocIDs) without external indices. We identify granularity collapse: during training, GR models develop a preference for generating DocIDs with a specific granularity, causing retrieval failures when it differs from that of the target document’s DocID. We propose to quantify this mismatch using "isotropy" and confirm that retrieval accuracy degrades as such granularity mismatch increases. To address this, we propose Granularity Routing for Generative Retrieval (\text{GR}^2), which trains multiple expert models specialized for different granularity levels and routes each query to the appropriate expert. Experiments on NQ320k demonstrate that improves retrieval performance, with larger gains on queries that suffer more from granularity collapse.

title: LogicInception: Discourse-Level Indirect Prompt Injection via Causal Chain Construction
author: Mingshuai Liu; Yijie Peng; Chen Dongxian; Mingfeng Li; Xin Li
abstract: Existing indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks commonly face a stealth-effectiveness tradeoff: features that make payloads effective can also make them detectable because attack intent is localized in a single payload. LogicInception moves IPI to discourse-level inference: attack logic is decomposed into register-matched declarative fragments distributed across tool outputs and linked by fabricated causal dependencies that the agent reconstructs through reasoning. To our knowledge, it is the first IPI framework to demonstrate successful unauthorized tool execution with no directive instruction anywhere in the injected content. No fragment contains a command or exploits instruction-following; the attack emerges from the agent’s own inference. We observe an empirical capability-safety amplification pattern: discourse-level amplification correlates with task capability across the evaluated models. On 1,139 scenarios with 5 defenses, LogicInception achieves 42.9-48.8% ASR at 88% per-fragment stealth, while all baselines remain below 8% composite success. The three prompt-level defenses reduce baseline ASR by up to 72% but reduce LogicInception by less than 7%; we trace this asymmetry to three architectural factors that motivate discourse-level rather than content-level countermeasures. This defense asymmetry is larger for higher-utility models in our evaluation, suggesting a tension between reasoning capability and safety.

title: GRAIL: Grounded Visual Alignment of Medical Vision-Language Models for Radiology Report Generation
author: Sarosij Bose; Ravi K. Rajendran; Biplob Debnath; Konstantinos Karydis; Amit Roy-Chowdhury; Srimat Chakradhar
abstract: Radiology Report Generation (RRG) aims to reduce the burden of clinical documentation, yet generating reports that remain visually grounded in the input image remains challenging. Current medical vision-language models (Med-VLMs) often rely on curated preference data, retrieval augmentation, or large-scale labeled corpora, but remain prone to hallucinated findings due to weak cross-modal alignment. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{GRAIL}: Grounded Radiology Alignment of Medical Vision-Language Models for Radiology Report Generation, a two-stage multimodal alignment framework for grounded RRG. First, \textit{Clinically Informed Textual Reasoning} improves report structure and medical terminology using verifiable language rewards with periodic clinical guidance. Second, \textit{Expert-guided Visual Reasoning} leverages a domain expert to rank generated reports using image-report alignment scores, encouraging visually grounded report generation without curated preference pairs or retrieval data. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that \textbf{GRAIL} consistently improves both report generation quality and clinical accuracy, achieving relative gains over strong post-training baselines by up to \textbf{15}% in clinical accuracy and \textbf{13}% in generation quality. \textbf{GRAIL} also outperforms proprietary general-purpose and medical VLMs, highlighting the effectiveness of self-supervised multimodal post-alignment for reducing hallucinations in visually grounded radiology report generation.

title: SyRuP: Enhancing System-Prompt Following via Reward-Guided Prediction in LLM Decoding
author: Seoyeon Kim; Minjae Kang; Jaehyung Kim
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly controlled through system prompts that specify roles, formats, and safety requirements. However, models follow these prompts only implicitly through in-context learning, which can be insufficient for complex or compositional prompts. Existing approaches often require model tuning or response-level reranking, limiting their practicality for lightweight inference-time control. We introduce SyRuP, a decoding-time framework for improving system-prompt adherence while keeping the base LM frozen. SyRuP trains a cross-attention reward head from system-prompt-conditioned preference pairs, treating the system prompt as a separate memory to produce token-level adherence scores. At inference, SyRuP reranks the base LM’s top-k candidates by combining base logits with both the learned reward signal and a contrastive signal that captures system-induced logit shifts. Experiments on system-prompt following benchmarks show that SyRuP consistently outperforms prompting and decoding-time baselines with moderate inference overhead. These results suggest that explicit token-level guidance is an effective and practical mechanism for reliable system-prompt following.

title: PersuaRL: Reinforcement Learning-Driven Multi-Expert Selection for Persuasive Dialogue Generation in Insurance
author: Rohan Kirti; Akash Ghosh; Aryan Vats; Niladri Ghosh; Shipra Shriparn; Roshni Ramnani; Anutosh Maitra; Sriparna Saha
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are revolutionizing digital communication by powering conversational agents deployed across domains such as customer service, digital sales, and insurance. These agents, built on LLMs, can understand user input, retrieve relevant information, and generate coherent responses. However, while they excel at factual communication, they often lack the ability to engage in truly persuasive, context-sensitive dialogue, especially in domains like insurance, where trust and clarity are critical. Building on this need within the insurance domain, our work focuses on improving the persuasiveness of digital agents, aka LLMs. To support this, we introduce InsureDial, a Persuasive Insurance Dialogue dataset, designed to capture the nuances of persuasive communication specific to motor insurance interactions. We introduce PersuaRL, a reinforcement learning–based framework that equips LLM-driven dialogue agents with the ability to adaptively explore, select, and coordinate strategies across multiple expert modules, guided by the evolving dialogue context, to achieve more effective persuasion. We conduct extensive automatic human and qualitative evaluations on two benchmark persuasion dialogue datasets, including our InsureDial. Our evaluations consistently demonstrate that PersuaRL outperforms baseline, generating contextually appropriate and highly persuasive responses.

title: Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning
author: Yongyi Huang; Huaping Zhang; Wenyao Cui; Qiuchi Li; Lei Li; Baohua Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates query predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.

title: KairosAgent: Agentic Time Series Forecasting with Fused Semantic Reasoning
author: Kun Feng; Ziwei Shan; Yuchen Fang; Yiyang Tan; Sihan Lu; Shuqi Gu; Xingyu Lu; Lintao Ma; Kan Ren
abstract: Cross-domain multimodal time series forecasting is a challenging task, requiring models to integrate precise numerical comprehension, cross-domain semantic understanding, and effective multimodal fusion. Existing approaches either build Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) from scratch or leverage pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs). However, TSFMs often overlook semantic understanding and lack the ability to perform future-oriented semantic reasoning, and LLMs struggle with numerical comprehension and accurate quantitative forecasting. To overcome these limitations, we propose KairosAgent, a novel agentic framework for multimodal time series forecasting, including an LLM-based reasoner and a TSFM-based forecaster. KairosAgent unifies textual reasoning and numerical forecasting by dynamically invoking analytical tools to enhance the numerical understanding and semantic reasoning capabilities of LLMs. The reasoning results are subsequently fused into the TSFM pipeline, enabling more accurate and reliable future predictions. To further improve the reasoning, we curate a large-scale corpus of high-quality trajectories, alongside a reinforcement learning from forecasting paradigm with multi-turn refinement and turn-level credit assignment. Experiments demonstrate that KairosAgent achieves superior zero-shot forecasting performance while maximizing the utility of pretrained LLMs and TSFMs, presenting a promising direction for efficient and interpretable time series agents. The project page is at https://foundation-model-research.github.io/KairosAgent.

title: S2J: Bridging the Gap Between Solving and Judging Ability in Generative Reward Models
author: Shaoning Sun; Jiachen Yu; Zongqi Wang; Xuewei Yang; Tianle Gu; Yujiu Yang
abstract: With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), generative reward models (GRMs) have been widely adopted for reward modeling and evaluation. Previous studies have primarily focused on training specialized GRMs by optimizing them on preference datasets with the judgment correctness as supervision. While it’s widely accepted that GRMs with stronger problem-solving capabilities typically exhibit superior judgment abilities, we first identify a significant solve-to-judge gap when examining individual queries. Specifically, the solve-to-judge gap refers to the phenomenon where GRMs struggle to make correct judgments on some queries (14%-37%), despite being fully capable of solving them. In this paper, we propose the Solve-to-Judge (S2J) approach to address this problem. Specifically, S2J simultaneously leverages both the solving and judging capabilities on a single GRM’s output for supervision, explicitly linking the GRM’s problem-solving and evaluation abilities during model optimization, thereby narrowing the gap. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that S2J effectively reduces the solve-to-judge gap by 16.2%, thereby enhancing the model’s judgment performance by 5.8%. Notably, S2J achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance among GRMs built on the same base model while utilizing a significantly smaller training dataset.

title: Same Evidence, Different Decisions: Document Segmentation Bias in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: Jiang Hui; Dichun Deng; Chenyang Zhou; Zhenrui Zhang; Chenghui Wu
abstract: Document chunking is widely treated as neutral preprocessing in retrieval-augmented generation, but in content-balanced interventions, re-segmenting the same evidence, without changing its semantic content, can shift fixed-choice LLM decisions and flip them in near-threshold regimes. Across full ratio-sweep experiments on 9 primary queries and 6 LLMs, document-unit structure systematically shifts model choices. We fit a shifted sigmoid whose steepness captures structural sensitivity and whose offset c captures fitted decision asymmetry. The two fitted parameters enable post-hoc flip-point estimation after per-query calibration, not a priori prediction. The shifted-sigmoid fit reaches R² ≥ 0.80 in 38/41 non-degenerate model–query combinations; the English experiments show the same form on 9 queries and 4 LLMs. It persists under noisy real-corpus retrieval when retrieved evidence is stance-balanced (ΔP = 0.53, p < .001, on one THUCNews retrieval query). The effect is regime-dependent: near-threshold decisions are vulnerable, while large decision offsets resist manipulation. Chunking and boundary placement can therefore affect downstream fixed-choice RAG decisions, with implications for retrieval system design and adversarial robustness.

title: Can LLMs Compress Wireless Signals? Physics-Informed Prompting for Training-Free Signal Compression
author: Yiwei Wang; Lixiang Lian; Sijie Ji
abstract: Wireless signals are a unique form of time-series data that encode rich physical characteristics of the propagation environment. As large volumes of signals are continuously generated in wireless sensing systems, efficient compression is essential for scalable transmission under limited system resources. However, wireless signals exhibit strong variability across environments and time, making it difficult to design universal compression schemes that generalize across domains while preserving the physical fidelity required for accurate reconstruction and sensing. Meanwhile, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning and adaptation capabilities across diverse modalities and domains. This raises an intriguing question: can LLMs compress wireless signals in a training-free manner while preserving physical fidelity? To the best of our knowledge, this problem remains unexplored. To answer this question, we propose a physics-informed prompting framework for training-free wireless signal compression. The framework incorporates environmental context and scenario-specific knowledge as physical priors in the prompt. We further introduce a dictionary module with self-learned patterns to stabilize inference and a key prompt module to align the semantics between the LLMs used for compression and reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves high-fidelity reconstruction under cross-domain settings, highlighting the promise of physics-informed prompting as a new paradigm for processing and compressing low-level physical signals.

title: Mitigating Memory Interference in Lifelong Model Editing through Multi-Head Hopfield Retrieval
author: Yue Che; Chen Guoyi; Xijian Deng; Yujie Wu; Jiang Cai; Xuming Ran; Mingkun Xu
abstract: Lifelong model editing seeks to continuously incorporate new knowledge into Large Language Models (LLMs) without costly retraining. Memory-augmented editors preserve pretrained weights to protect unrelated capabilities, but struggle to balance Generalization to rephrased edit queries and Locality on non-edited knowledge. This challenge becomes particularly severe under dense editing settings, where semantically related edits induce substantial memory interference. To tackle this problem, we propose MH-HoReN, a multi-head Hopfield retrieval framework that performs retrieval across complementary subspaces and combines head-wise matching signals for more reliable memory selection. We further extend Hopfield-based editing into a clustered batched scheme that combines shared codebook memories for related edits with token-level pooling for efficient knowledge storage and query routing. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and editing benchmarks demonstrate that MH-HoReN achieves better locality-generalization trade-offs as editing scales increase, improving the sum of Locality and Generalization by more than 12% over existing methods while preserving almost perfect Reliability in sequential editing, alongside 7.7% gains in Overall Performance under batched editing. Our code is available here.

title: ContraGAND: Auditing and Repairing Gender Ambiguity Failures in LLMs with Neurosymbolic Contrastive Data Augmentation
author: Thomas Moerman; Eleni Gkovedarou; Janiça Hackenbuchner
abstract: Recent work on gender bias in the automatic translation of gender-ambiguous scenarios has highlighted the need for gender ambiguity detection. We address this gap with ContraGAND, a contrastive corpus of 4,852 natural gender-ambiguous English sentences, each minimally paired with a masculine and a feminine variant generated by a neurosymbolic pipeline. We use ContraGAND to perform and evaluate gender ambiguity detection in two settings: (i) a closed task, where the referent is given, and (ii) an open task, where it is not. For both tasks, we evaluate six open-weight large language models by prompting, and test selected models with fine-tuning and knowledge distillation. We show that (i) the closed task is saturated in current models, whereas (ii) the open task produces a gap that varies considerably by model. We find that two failure modes dominate: a binding failure (the model surfaces the referent but defaults to ’ambiguous’ when the gender cue is cross-clause) and a format failure that, on local cues, is primarily under-commitment rather than a binding deficit (long unparseable reasoning chains on small models). Further analysis reveals that both are forms of over-prediction of the ’ambiguous’ class rather than stereotype-driven misclassification. While explicit prompts and decoding interventions do not close the gap, both fine-tuning on the augmented contrastive variants and distillation from a 31B teacher are effective at teaching a 4B student to successfully perform gender ambiguity detection.

title: On the Universality of the Inner Product as a PMI Estimator in Embedding Models
author: Enrique Amigo; Fernando Giner; Julio Gonzalo
abstract: Embedding representations are widely used in natural language processing, yet their semantic interpretation depends on the operators used to compare them. Previous work has shown that, for certain embedding models, the inner product is linearly correlated with Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI). However, this relation has so far been established only empirically or analytically for specific models. In this work, we formally show that, under certain assumptions about distributional semantic embedding models, the inner product between embeddings approaches PMI. This theoretical result provides a more general explanation for the observed relationship and enables the formulation of training criteria aimed at learning embedding spaces in which operations between embeddings are semantically interpretable.

title: Mirror, Mirror on the Wall: Prompt Echoing in Instruct Language Models
author: Inez Okulska; Bartosz Naskręcki; Jan Piotrowski; Tomasz Steifer
abstract: Prompt echoing is a recognized failure mode of instruct language models, in which a model instead of generating a response, mirrors the provided prompt, even though it did not receive a specific instruction to do so. Is this phenomenon a sign of the model leaking the content of its training dataset, or is it rather caused by a misaligned behavior of the internal induction/copying mechanisms? We investigate prompt echoing small language models from different families (Gemma, Llama, Qwen, SmolLM and OLMo) and show that echoing prompts are likely to have partial overlap with the training dataset but the phenomenon is primarily driven by the model’s induction heads.

title: RW-TTT: Batched Serving for Request-Owned Test-Time Training State
author: Jian Yang; Zhizhuo Kou; Chen Han; Hao Zhang; Yao Tian; Sirui Han; Yike Guo
abstract: Test-time training (TTT) adapts an LLM during generation by reading and updating request-owned state, such as fast weights, low-rank deltas, or streaming learner state. This breaks batched LLM serving, which assumes shared static weights: serial execution is correct but slow, while naive batching can corrupt request state. We formulate this problem as read-write TTT serving and present RW-TTT, which tags each decode step with its owner, version, and READ/WRITE effect, batches only compatible phases, and commits updates only to the owner. On one GPU with eight fast-weight In-Place-TTT streams, RW-TTT reaches 274.61 aggregate tok/s, 9.31\times over sequential serving and 3.44\times over memory-matched independent replicas. It preserves behavior on RULER, a long-context benchmark, and passes owner/version checks.

title: VITAL: Visual-Semantic Dual Supervision for Enhanced and Interpretable Latent Reasoning in Medical MLLMs
author: Qiaoru Li; Shaotian Liang; Jintao Chen; Haoran Sun; Yuxiang Cai; Jianwei Yin; Yankai Jiang
abstract: Latent reasoning enables reasoning over continuous hidden states rather than explicit tokens, avoiding the language bottleneck and inference overhead of chain-of-thought for medical VQA. However, existing methods suffer from modality collapse, insufficient visual supervision, and train-inference mismatch. Moreover, their opaque latent states offer no interpretability, which is critical in clinical applications. We propose VITAL, a latent-space reasoning framework for medical MLLMs with visual-semantic dual supervision: an auxiliary text decoder reconstructs reasoning chains from latent states, while a visual projector regresses ROI features from a frozen, independent medical vision encoder. Both modules are discarded at inference with zero overhead, yet can be re-attached post-hoc for dual interpretability, providing textual and visual explanations of the reasoning process without sacrificing efficiency. We construct a 61K dataset spanning 9 imaging modalities, exceeding prior medical visual latent reasoning datasets by an order of magnitude. Experiments on 7 benchmarks show that VITAL consistently and substantially outperforms the backbone, all latent reasoning baselines, and medical MLLMs trained on far larger data, achieving state-of-the-art results competitive with trillion-parameter proprietary models.

title: Fair Like Us? Auditing LLM Alignment in Resource Allocation
author: Qishen Han; Hadi Hosseini; Joshua Kavner; Samarth Khanna; Sujoy Sikdar; Lirong Xia
abstract: Fair allocation of scarce, indivisible resources is an important challenge in many societal problems. While there are several formal theories of fairness, no single definition can always be satisfied. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support decisions and act as agents, they raise new concerns about distributional justice: their judgments are not directly tied to any specific fairness framework and may violate key normative principles. In this work, we introduce a general method for evaluating fairness reasoning in LLMs. We study first-person fairness judgments across a broad set of models and compare them directly with human responses on matched scenarios and elicitation conditions. We find that LLMs tend to prefer stricter fairness constraints than humans, show more self-interested behavior, are sensitive to how information is framed, and are difficult to align with human judgments using fine-tuning with current datasets.

title: TRACE: Triplet Recovery via Arrowhead-Centric Extraction for Flowchart Understanding
author: Daozhu Dong; Kaiwen Shi; Dan Si; Xiaoyu Hao; Tong Liu; Wenjie Zhang; Gong Cheng
abstract: Flowcharts are widely used in business management and software development to represent process logic and user interactions. Understanding the semantics they encode is essential for downstream applications such as visual question answering. Existing methods either detect components and reconstruct topology, which suffers from cascaded errors and rigid shape assumptions, or feed the whole image to a vision language model (VLM), which dilutes attention on dense diagrams and often reverses edge directions. Inspired by cognitive science findings that humans read flowcharts by tracing arrows, we propose TRACE (Triplet Recovery via Arrowhead-Centric Extraction), a three-stage framework. An offline stage synthesizes aligned training data from text-format flowchart sources (e.g., Mermaid, BPMN XML) and fine-tunes the two models used online: a detector that locates every arrowhead, and then a VLM that extracts one triplet per arrowhead. Each output triplet is grounded to a detected arrowhead, enabling traceable diagnosis. Experiments show that TRACE substantially improves flowchart understanding accuracy and improves downstream QA accuracy.

title: MedCUA-Bench: A Screenshot-Only Benchmark for Clinical Computer-Use Agents
author: Jia Yu; Zilong Wang; Xinyang Jiang; Dongsheng Li; Shuo Wang
abstract: Computer-use agents could automate repetitive screen-based clinical work, but their reliability in medical graphical user interfaces remains largely unvalidated. Existing benchmarks focus on general web or desktop tasks and underrepresent medical software, which requires domain knowledge, exhibits markedly different UI design from mainstream applications, lacks public testing environments, and demands safety validation beyond task completion. We introduce MedCUA-Bench, an interactive benchmark for clinical computer-use agents. It covers 18 clinical scenarios across 10 medical domains, reconstructed from real product manuals and open-source medical systems to capture authentic clinical interfaces while avoiding licensing and privacy constraints. Each task ships with paired intent- and step-level goals to disentangle clinical reasoning from UI execution, and is evaluated by a deterministic checker over task completion and five clinical safety dimensions. Across 23 agents, the best closed-source model reaches 54.2% strict success, while all models remain below 9% on the real OpenEMR. Open-source agents average only 2.5%, with the best reaching 16.2%. MedCUA-Bench exposes the gap between current agents and reliable clinical software use, providing a reproducible testbed for future research. Code: https://github.com/Jia7878/MedCUA-BenchMark.

title: DYNAMO: Dynamic Skill-Tool Evolution for Vision-Language Agents
author: Yutao Sun; Yanting Miao; Hao-Xuan Ma; Mengyu Zhou; Mingshuai Chen; Tiancheng Zhao; Dexin Wang; Lei Lv; Li Xu; Xiaoxi Jiang; Guanjun Jiang
abstract: Improving vision-language models (VLMs) on visual reasoning typically requires retraining or hand-designed prompts and tools. We present Dynamo, a training-free framework that adapts a frozen VLM without any weight updates. On a small labeled training subset, the agent inspects its own correct and incorrect attempts and evolves two complementary capabilities: reusable reasoning skills for cognitive bottlenecks, and executable visual tools for perceptual ones. Each generated tool is paired with a skill that specifies when to invoke it, and both capability types accumulate in a persistent library. Across four visual reasoning benchmarks and five VLM backbones, Dynamo improves direct inference on all 20 model–benchmark settings (avg. +5.6 acc). When the tool set is given in advance, the framework learns when to call each tool, and per-step tool choice improves on every tested backbone. Against task-specific RL (VTool-R1, DeepEyes), Dynamo closes 65–99% of the RL gap at a fraction of the compute, and combines additively with RL when available.

title: ReTrace: Visual Backtracking for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
author: Guangzong Si; Dong Wang; Yifan Yu; Miao Liu; Panwang Pan; Wentao Zhu
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify Visual Backtracking: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReTrace, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83 prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.

title: DiaLLM: An Investigation into the Robustness-Generation Gap in English Dialect Adaptation
author: Jordan Painter; Dipankar Srirag; Adarsh Kappiyath; Diptesh Kanojia; Aditya Joshi; Lu Yin
abstract: Large language models increasingly understand dialectal English, yet still produce only standard, US-leaning English, leaving dialectal generation, the harder half of the problem, largely unaddressed. We introduce DiaLLM, which continually pretrains three open-weight language model families on the International Corpus of English and applies implicit and explicit post-training paradigms, each combined with three model alignment strategies, giving the first controlled comparison of these components across Australian, Indian, and Northern British English. Our results reveal a robustness–generation gap: benchmarks are shaped by continual pretraining and SFT, while alignment visibly reshapes generation in ways benchmarks do not capture. Explicit variety-targeted adaptation produces output reliably recognised as dialectal and judged more dialectal than broad alignment, yet where human judgement was directly assessed, the method that most aggressively optimises the dialectal reward is not the one judged most dialectal. Independent linguistic analysis corroborates this reward-quality gap, most clearly on two of the three families. No single alignment method dominates, and closing the gap will require richer reward designs and continued investment in dialectal resources. We release all code, checkpoints, and preference datasets.

title: Progressive Behavioral Drift through Compression Valleys in Large Language Models
author: Zhiyuan Xu; Stanislav Abaimov; Joseph Gardiner; Sana Belguith
abstract: We show that attention sinks and compression valleys create a vulnerable region in decoder-only Transformers, where small activation perturbations can be amplified through the autoregressive trajectory. Based on this, we propose Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-space attack that anchors perturbations at the beginning-of-sequence token and adaptively reinforces them at sensitive layers and tokens. Instead of forcing an abrupt behavioral change, SSS induces a staged drift, making outputs gradually shift toward the target behavior while remaining fluent and benign-looking in early generations. Across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS achieves high attack success, preserves coherence, and causes negligible degradation to general capabilities. These results show that attention sinks and compression valleys are not merely mechanistic features; rather, they expose exploitable amplification mechanisms that can be treated as hidden-state weaknesses for activation-space attacks in white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

title: Canonical Color as a Lens into Concept Decodability in Vision Encoders and VLMs
author: Xiaofu Chen; Stella Frank; Yova Kementchedjhieva
abstract: Vision encoders construct the image representations used by vision-language models. How much conceptual information, rather than immediately visible image evidence, do these representations contain? We use canonical color as a controlled test case: can a vision encoder represent the typical color of an object concept, such as yellow for bananas, when visible color is removed from the input image? We construct a dataset of objects with canonical color labels and probe vision encoders for both color and object identity using RGB and grayscale inputs. We find that canonical color remains decodable from grayscale images and is tied to predicted object identity, suggesting a conceptual link between object and color information. Extending this analysis to full VLMs, we find that VLM post-training can have a surprisingly large effect on color decodability in the vision encoder. Overall, canonical color provides a controllable lens for tracing object-level semantic information in vision encoders and VLMs.

title: Orchestrating Hidden-Intermediate Pruning-and-Distill for MoEs Slimming
author: Yifu Ding; Yongcheng Jing; Chengyu Wang; Jun Huang; Dacheng Tao
abstract: The remarkable performance of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models often comes with substantial architectural scale and resource overhead. Prior structural compression mainly focuses on expert-level or FFN intermediate pruning. However, we identify an emerging architectural trend that the FFN expansion ratio in state-of-the-art MoEs has steadily decreased, making intermediate-only pruning less effective and motivating us to explore other redundancies. Motivated by this, we propose an orchestrated hidden-intermediate prune-and-distill framework that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to jointly prune expert FFNs along both intermediate and hidden dimensions. It includes Budget-Constrained Coordinate Descent to efficiently search expert-specific pruning ratios across the two dimensions, and attention relation transfer distillation to provide stable supervision under hidden misalignment. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks validates that hidden-dimension pruning is a promising direction for compressing modern MoEs.

title: Second language input density can induce age of acquisition effects in language models
author: Simon Jerome Han; James McClelland
abstract: People who learn a second language early in life are more likely to achieve high levels of grammatical proficiency than those who learn a second language later in life. Researchers have begun to use language models in an effort to address explanations for this age of acquisition (AOA) effect. Here, we argue that this work has failed to consider an important factor that may be relevant to AOA: younger learners may experience a greater density of exposure to a second language than older learners. While earlier work neglecting this density factor in LMs failed to find an AoA effect, we demonstrate empirically and theoretically that language models that receive second language input at lower densities learn to make second language grammatical judgments more slowly and also plateau at lower levels of ability. Crucially, this remains true even in the long run when cumulative second language input is held constant. Our findings highlight the possibility that second language AOA effects in humans as well as models might reflect differences in exposure density that covary with age. This account stands in contrast to classic maturational and experiential accounts of second language age of acquisition effects, and adds an important yet missing dimension to the effort to use language models to interrogate this effect.

title: SciFigBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Method Figure Understanding
author: Lijia Wu; Zheng Li; Yuxuan Liu; Jingwen Zhang; Penghai Zhao; Xiang Li
abstract: Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper’s methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse-grained tasks, such as context-based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine-grained content and inter-module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real-world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question-answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training-free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow-induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method-figure reasoning. Experiments across open-source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.

title: Beyond Memorization: Distinguishing Between Pattern-Based and Epistemic Reasoning in LLMs Using Epistemic Puzzles
author: Adi Gabay; Gabriel Stanovsky; Liat Peterfreund
abstract: Epistemic reasoning requires agents to infer the state of the world from partial observations and information about other agents’ knowledge. Prior work evaluating LLMs on epistemic puzzles often frames failures as memorization rather than reasoning. We argue that this dichotomy is too coarse for newer models: memorization is a limiting case of pattern-based reasoning, where a model matches a task to a familiar template and applies the corresponding solution. We introduce a two-dimensional benchmark over Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) puzzles, separating narrative familiarity from inference complexity, which allows us to distinguish pattern-based from epistemic reasoning. We find that models are substantially more robust to surface form changes than prior work suggested, yet consistently struggle in asymmetric settings where familiar patterns no longer apply and success requires tracking fragmented epistemic states. Code, datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/adigabay84/del-puzzles-benchmark.

title: Beyond Static Dialogues: Benchmarking Realistic, Heterogeneous, and Evolving Long-Horizon Memory
author: Han Zhang; Zihao Tang; Xin Yu; Xiao Liu; Yeyun Gong; Haizhen Huang; Yan Lu; Weiwei Deng; Feng Sun; Qi Zhang; Hanfang Yang
abstract: In existing memory benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs), the evaluated dialogue sessions often lack long-term semantic consistency, and the underlying personas tend to be flat and static. Furthermore, in real-world scenarios, interactions between users and assistants involve more diverse, heterogeneous data streams, such as documents and emails. These shortcomings significantly limit the realism and effectiveness of current evaluations. To address these limitations, we introduce \textbf{RHELM} (\underline{R}ealistic, \underline{H}eterogeneous, and \underline{E}volving \underline{L}ong-term \underline{M}emory). Driven by meticulously crafted user profiles and a novel \textbf{LOOP} (p\underline{L}an-r\underline{O}llout-ev\underline{O}lve-\underline{P}rune) module, we construct realistic dialogues across diverse interaction scenarios that exhibit dynamic temporal evolution and long-term coherence. Crucially, these dialogues are deeply integrated with heterogeneous external sources synchronized with the user’s temporal event trajectory. The resulting benchmark encompasses challenging question-answer pairs spanning \textbf{seven} inquiry types, with each question mapping to at least one of \textbf{27} critical memory characteristics that we identify as essential yet underexplored in current research. Comprehensive experiments across full-context models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods, and representative memory frameworks reveal that contemporary approaches still expose critical weaknesses in complex, real-world settings, particularly in resolving multi-source aggregation and real-world contextual reasoning.

title: EviNoteRAG: Enhancing RAG Models via Quality-Augmented Evidence Notes
author: Yuqin Dai; Guoqing Wang; Yuan Wang; Zhouheng Yao; Kairan Dou; Kaichen Zhou; Zhanwei Zhang; Shuo Yang; Fei Tang; Jun Yin; Pengyu Zeng; Can YI; Changhua Meng; Yuchen Zhou; Yongliang Shen; Shuai Lu
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has advanced open-domain question answering by incorporating external information into model reasoning. However, raw retrieved content often suffers from low signal-to-noise ratio, where answer-supportive information is diluted by irrelevant material, and error accumulation, where incomplete or misleading content degrades multi-hop reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose EviNoteRAG, a framework that enhances RAG through quality-augmented evidence notes. The model is trained to generate Supportive-Evidence Notes (SENs), concise abstractions that preserve only answer-critical information and explicitly highlight key and uncertain content to improve reasoning accuracy. To further ensure note quality, we introduce an entailment-based Evidence Quality Reward (EQR), which incentivizes SENs to be logically sufficient for deriving the correct answer. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that EviNoteRAG achieves state-of-the-art performance, with relative F1 gains of 20% on HotpotQA (+0.093), 40% on Bamboogle (+0.151), and 91% on 2Wiki (+0.256), while also improving training stability and efficiency.

title: InComeS: Integrating Compression and Selection Mechanisms into LLMs for Efficient Model Editing
author: Shuaiyi Li; Zhisong Zhang; Yang Deng; Chenlong Deng; Tianqing Fang; Hongming Zhang; Haitao Mi; Dong Yu; Wai Lam
abstract: Although existing model editing methods perform well in recalling exact edit facts, they often struggle in complex scenarios that require deeper semantic understanding rather than mere knowledge regurgitation. Leveraging the strong contextual reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), in-context learning (ICL) becomes a promising editing method by comprehending edit information through context encoding. However, this method is constrained by the limited context window of LLMs, leading to degraded performance and efficiency as the number of edits increases. To overcome this limitation, we propose InComeS, a flexible framework that enhances LLMs’ ability to process editing contexts through explicit compression and selection mechanisms. Specifically, InComeS compresses each editing context into the key-value (KV) cache of a special token, enabling efficient handling of multiple edits without being restricted by the model’s context window. Furthermore, specialized cross-attention modules are added to dynamically select the most relevant information from the pool of special tokens, enabling adaptive and effective utilization of edit information. We conduct experiments on diverse model editing benchmarks with various editing formats, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

title: ChartAttack: Testing the Vulnerability of LLMs to Malicious Prompting in Chart Generation
author: Jesus-German Ortiz-Barajas; Jonathan Tonglet; Vivek Gupta; Iryna Gurevych
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to automate chart generation from data tables, improving efficiency but introducing new misuse risks. We present ChartAttack, a framework for evaluating how MLLMs use design misleaders to generate charts that induce incorrect interpretations. We also introduce AttackViz, a chart question-answering (QA) dataset labeled with effective misleaders and their induced incorrect answers. ChartAttack reduces MLLM QA accuracy by 17.2 points in-domain and 11.9 points cross-domain.
