The current operationalization of benchmarks is questioned, and we provide recommendations and directions for further ethical evaluation. Warning: this paper contains content that may be offensive or upsetting.

title: Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks
author: Haoyu Liu; Dingcheng Li; Lukas Rutishauser; Zeyu Zheng
abstract: Multimodal web agents that process both screenshots and accessibility trees are increasingly deployed to interact with web interfaces, yet their dual-stream architecture opens an underexplored attack surface: an adversary who injects content into the webpage DOM simultaneously corrupts both observation channels with a consistent deceptive narrative. Our vulnerability analysis on MiniWob++ reveals that attacks including a visual component far outperform text-only injections, exposing critical gaps in text-centric VLM safety training. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training (DMAST), a framework that formalizes the agent-attacker interaction as a two-player zero-sum Markov game and co-trains both players through a three-stage pipeline: (1) imitation learning from a strong teacher model, (2) oracle-guided supervised fine-tuning that uses a novel zero-acknowledgment strategy to instill task-focused reasoning under adversarial noise, and (3) adversarial reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) self-play. On out-of-distribution tasks, DMAST nearly halves the attack success rate (41.2% \rightarrow 21.4%) while raising task completion by over 60% relative (6.2% \rightarrow 10.2%). Our approach outperforms established training-based and prompt-based defenses, demonstrating genuine co-evolutionary progress and robust generalization to complex, unseen environments. Code is available at https://github.com/huajianduzhuo-code/DMAST_official.

title: Beyond Static Symbols: Evidence-Grounded Visual Checklists for Cultural Activity Generation
author: Hongcan Deng; Bo Ma; Yating Yang; Rong Ma; Zhen Wang; Xi Zhou; Rui Dong; Turghun Osman
abstract: Text-to-image models can render recognizable cultural symbols, but cultural activity generation requires coordinated control over participants, actions, interactions, scenes, and culture-specific constraints. We propose CARE, an evidence-grounded visual checklist framework for controllable cultural activity image generation. Given an activity prompt, CARE builds source-traceable cultural evidence, converts it into an optimized prompt and fine-grained checklist, verifies generated images with concrete VLM-based visual checks, and uses failed checks for targeted prompt repair. We introduce CARE-1360, a dataset of 1,360 cultural activity prompts across eight countries, and evaluate generated images with a unified human protocol. Experiments show that CARE consistently improves over direct generation and retrieval-based prompt refinement baselines across cultural and visual quality dimensions. Results with both ZImage and Stable Diffusion XL suggest that evidence-grounded visual checklists provide an interpretable control mechanism that transfers across the tested generation backends.

title: CLAMP: Constrained Decoding for Vision-Language Embodied Planning
author: Tianyi Ma; Parisa Kordjamshidi
abstract: Embodied planning increasingly relies on vision-language models (VLMs) to translate instructions and visual observations into executable action sequences. However, fluent plans are not always executable. A VLM may refer to objects that are not visually observed, select actions whose required affordances are unavailable, or violate syntax and action constraints. We introduce CLAMP, a multimodal constraint-grounding framework that turns scene evidence into decoding-time constraints for a frozen VLM planner. CLAMP uses the initial observation to restrict object references to those supported by the scene, while a provided symbolic action model specifies state transitions and goals. During decoding, hard masks eliminate invalid next-token candidates, while a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based world-state lookahead module reweights the probabilities of the remaining feasible candidates based on action preconditions and goal reachability. This allows the planner to retain the VLM’s language prior while preventing visually unsupported, unsafe, or infeasible candidates from entering the plan. For unseen tasks and environments, CLAMP adapts the HMM at test time using label-free continuations sampled from the frozen VLM. Experiments on VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA show that scene-grounded constraints improve object grounding and safety, while most remaining failures stem from perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications.

title: CultureTalk: Towards Multi-turn Cultural Competence in Large Language Models
author: Minzhi Li; Jiayu Han; Oleg Poliannikov; Vipul Agarwal; Dezhi Hong; Mingxian Wang
abstract: As conversational AI systems increasingly engage users through multi-turn dialogue across diverse cultural contexts, cross-cultural competence, the ability to recognize, respect, and adapt to cultural differences, is essential for effective human-AI interaction. Existing evaluations largely rely on single-turn settings, overlooking the complexities of real-world, multi-turn conversations where cultural cues often emerge gradually. To address this gap, we introduce CultureTalk, a benchmark for evaluating multi-turn cultural reasoning in conversational AI. The dataset contains 1,741 culturally grounded dialogues derived from human-verified cultural knowledge resources and evaluates models’ ability to accumulate cultural context across turns and remain robust to topic shifts. Our evaluation reveals substantial performance gaps between single- and multi-turn settings, highlighting current models’ limitations in sustained culturally grounded context understanding. We further show that fine-tuning on augmented single-turn conversational data and inference scaling significantly improve multi-turn cultural reasoning, yielding a 64.7% relative gain in cultural knowledge entailment with a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model.

title: When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents
author: Kaiyue Yang; Yuyan Bu; Jingwei Yi; Yuchi Wang; Biyu Zhou; Juntao Dai; Songlin Hu; Yaodong Yang
abstract: As LLM agents increasingly select tools autonomously, their choices among tools with different privileges become safety-relevant. However, prior tool-selection studies focus on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices underexplored. To address this gap, we study over-privileged tool selection, in which an agent selects or escalates to a higher-privilege tool despite a sufficient lower-privilege alternative. We introduce ToolPrivBench to evaluate whether agents choose higher-privilege tools despite sufficient lower-privilege alternatives, measuring both initial selection and escalation after transient tool failures. Across eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, we find that over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is further amplified by transient failures. We further find that general safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice, while prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. We therefore introduce a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary. Our mitigation experiments show that this defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

title: The Interlingua Hypothesis: LLMs Translate via a Latent Task-agnostic Feature Space
author: Jacob Brinton; Jannik Brinkmann; Mark Crovella; Aaron Mueller
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated improved machine translation performance over strong supervised baselines. This raises questions as to what mechanisms underlie how LLMs perform machine translation between languages. Motivated by recent interpretability findings—namely, that LLMs use massively multilingual latent feature representations to perform language modeling—we propose the interlingua hypothesis. The hypothesis holds that language models translate by reading a source sentence into a latent feature space, and generate a target sentence by reading from the latent feature space. We show three lines of evidence in support of this hypothesis: (1) variance in BLEU across language pairs is largely predictable from language-specific competences with no language pair–specific interaction terms; (2) many model components are causally influential in both monolingual tasks and translation tasks; (3) and fine-tuning on monolingual data recovers a large proportion of translation improvements relative to fine-tuning on aligned documents. Together, these provide convergent evidence in support of the interlingua hypothesis, and suggest new ways of understanding and improving how LLMs can be leveraged to perform translation tasks.

title: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Coordination in Multi-Agent Conquest
author: Abigail O’Neill; Alan Zhu; Mihran Miroyan; Narges Norouzi; Joseph E. Gonzalez
abstract: Language Model (LM)-based agents remain challenging to evaluate systematically in mixed-motive settings where agents must leverage short-term cooperation for long-term competitive goals (e.g., multi-party politics). We introduce Cooperate to Compete (C2C), a multi-agent environment where players can engage in private negotiations while competing to be the first to achieve their secret objective. Players have asymmetric objectives and negotiations are non-binding, allowing alliances to form and break as players’ short-term interests align and diverge. We run AI-only games and conduct a user study pitting human players against AI opponents. We find that humans favor lower-complexity deals and talk to more unique partners over the course of the game. We also find that humans are more aggressive negotiators, closing deals only 73.5% of the time compared to 94.0% for LM-based agents. Interventions inspired by these findings shift agent negotiation behavior and can raise win rates from 22.2% to 32.7%, demonstrating that language coordination strategies in C2C substantially alter negotiation dynamics. We run over 1,300 games with over 20,000 private conversations totaling over 180,000 player actions. By combining multi-party, long-horizon play with partial observability, asymmetric objectives, and non-binding negotiations, C2C provides a controlled, gamified testbed for studying strategic coordination in LM-based agents.

title: CebIDN: A Computational Framework for Cebuano Idiom Identification, Disambiguation, and Normalization
author: Adrian P. Vaflor; Robert R. Roxas
abstract: Idioms remain a persistent challenge for natural language understanding due to their non-compositional nature, especially in morphologically rich, low-resource languages like Cebuano. Existing work on idiom processing has explored span extraction, contrastive learning, and normalization, but typically treats these tasks independently or assumes previous steps have already been done. We propose CebIDN, a modular pipeline that unifies idiom identification, disambiguation, and normalization for Cebuano. Central to our framework is a morphology-aware canonical matcher that links extracted spans to an idiom knowledge base, passing structural tags, the idiom used, and retrieved literal hints to the downstream generative model. The system is evaluated in various tagging configurations, incorporating CRF-based sequence labeling and span-level triplet loss, along with few-shot and fine-tuned normalization strategies across both tagged and tag-free configurations. The optimal configuration (using a 3-tag BIO+CRF tagger with a tag-free normalizer) significantly outperforms a fine-tuned end-to-end LLM baseline by improving binary idiom detection (0.899 vs. 0.847 F1) and achieving superior normalization quality (88.87 vs. 86.89 BLEU; 96.40 vs. 95.04 BERTScore; 4.71 vs. 4.46 human-validated LLM evaluation scores), while running 1.7 times faster. These results demonstrate that structured task decoupling improves figurative language understanding in low-resource settings.

title: When In-Distribution Gains Fail: Evaluating Weak-to-Strong Reward Models under Preference Shift
author: Khoi M. Le; Tri Cao; Phong Nam Huu Nguyen; Cong-Duy T Nguyen; Anh Tuan Luu; Chunyan Miao; See-Kiong Ng; Thong Thanh Nguyen
abstract: Weak-to-strong (W2S) generalization is a promising framework for scalable oversight, yet existing evaluations often test students under matched train-test distributions. Therefore, we study W2S preference learning under zero-shot distribution shift and find that strong students trained on weak preference labels can appear successful in-distribution while failing to transfer across preference datasets. We provide evidence consistent with a representational failure mode in which weak-supervised fine-tuning may move the strong model toward source-domain features instead of maintaining broadly transferable preference representations. To mitigate this, we propose *Representation Anchoring* (Anchor), a simple yet effective regularizer that constrains excessive drift from the pretrained strong model’s representation space during fine-tuning, while still allowing task-relevant adaptation. Across preference domains, datasets, and model families, Anchor improves out-of-distribution transfer while maintaining competitive in-distribution performance. Together, our evaluation protocol, transfer-aware metrics, and method expose hidden brittleness in current W2S reward modeling and provide a practical path toward more robust preference transfer.

title: PISanitizer: Preventing Prompt Injection to Long-Context LLMs via Prompt Sanitization
author: Runpeng Geng; Yanting Wang; Chenlong Yin; Minhao Cheng; Ying Chen; Jinyuan Jia
abstract: Long-context LLMs are vulnerable to prompt injection, where an attacker injects an instruction into a long context to hijack the LLM’s output. Existing defenses, designed for short contexts, have limited effectiveness in long-context scenarios because the injected instruction constitutes only a small portion of the context. We propose PISanitizer, which pinpoints and sanitizes injected tokens in a context before a backend LLM generates its response. PISanitizer builds on two observations: (1) prompt injection attacks craft instructions that compel an LLM to follow them, and (2) LLMs leverage attention to focus on influential input tokens during generation. Accordingly, we intentionally let an LLM follow any instructions in the context and then sanitize tokens receiving high attention from the resulting instruction-following behavior. This design creates a dilemma for attackers: the more effectively an injected instruction compels the LLM to follow it, the more likely it is to be sanitized. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that PISanitizer successfully and efficiently prevents prompt injection, maintains utility, outperforms existing defenses, and is robust to optimization-based and adaptive attacks. The code is available at https://github.com/sleeepeer/PISanitizer.

title: TagPR: Tag-Guided Process Supervision for Personalization Reasoning in Large Language Models
author: Song Jin; Juntian Zhang; Ruyu Lyu; Yong Liu; Xun Zhang; Yufei Zhang; Fei Jiang; Guojun Yin; Wei Lin; Rui Yan
abstract: Recent advancements have endowed Large Language Models with impressive general reasoning capabilities. However, these reasoning models often perform worse than non-reasoning models on personalization tasks. While some methods use outcome-based RL to improve personalization reasoning, they fail to supervise the reasoning process. As a result, models may reach correct answers through flawed reasoning chains, limiting further improvement. To address this, we propose TagPR, a novel framework that adds semantic tags to the reasoning process for step-by-step guidance. TagPR first automatically generates a structured, tagged dataset for Supervised Fine-Tuning. It then employs a multi-stage RL process guided by a composite reward signal, which integrates tag-based process supervision with a novel Personalization Reward Model with User Embeddings to achieve fine-grained alignment with user-specific logic. Extensive experiments on public LaMP, LongLaMP, PGraphRAG, and a self-constructed dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results, delivering an average improvement of 32.65% over the base model across all LaMP benchmark tasks. Our work demonstrates that tag-guided process supervision is an effective approach for personalization reasoning.

title: Defending Agentic Fact-Checking Against Adversarial Attacks
author: Fanzhen Liu; Tingyang Xu; Xixun Lin; Haolong Xiang; Ge Zhang; Anan Du; Shuchao Pang
abstract: Agentic fact-checking (FC) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for verifying complex claims through dynamic reasoning, tool use, and iterative evidence gathering. Understanding the vulnerability of these systems is essential for assessing their reliability against misinformation and adversarial manipulation. In this work, we study both the offensive and defensive aspects of agentic FC. First, we identify a limitation in the state-of-the-art Fact2Fiction attack, which introduces excessive semantic drift into malicious evidence, and propose F+, a relevance-filtering framework that generates more semantically consistent adversarial evidence. Second, we introduce SRSFact, an enhanced agentic FC system with a Supporter–Refuter–Summarizer mechanism for structured evidence authenticity assessment, improving robustness without relying on external open-web knowledge search. Experiments on the AVeriTeC benchmark show that F+ significantly strengthens attack effectiveness, while SRSFact substantially reduces failure rates under diverse adversarial attacks.

title: FORGE: Fine-grained multimodal evaluation for manufacturing quality assurance
author: Xiangru Jian; Hao Xu; Wei Pang; Xinjian Zhao; Chengyu Tao; Qixin Zhang; Xikun Zhang; Chao Zhang; Guanzhi Deng; Jingxi Xue; Juan Du; Tianshu Yu; Garth Tarr; Linqi Song; Qiuzhuang Sun; Dacheng Tao
abstract: The manufacturing sector is increasingly adopting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to move from low-level perception toward higher-level reasoning and decision support, yet current evaluations rarely reflect the fine-grained precision that real-world manufacturing demands. Progress is further hindered by data scarcity and a lack of fine-grained domain semantics in existing datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce FORGE, a benchmark for three core quality-assurance tasks of discrete manufacturing: workpiece verification, structural surface inspection, and assembly verification. We first construct a high-quality multimodal dataset spanning real-world 2D images and 3D point clouds, annotated with fine-grained domain semantics such as standardized model numbers. We then evaluate 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs on these three tasks, revealing significant performance gaps. Counter to conventional understanding, our bottleneck analysis on five representative models indicates that visual grounding is not the primary limiting factor. Instead, insufficient domain-specific knowledge is the key bottleneck. Beyond evaluation, we show that our structured annotations can serve as an actionable training resource: supervised fine-tuning of a compact 3B-parameter model on our data yields up to 90.8% relative improvement in accuracy on held-out manufacturing scenarios, providing preliminary evidence for a practical pathway toward domain-adapted manufacturing MLLMs.

title: MaS-VQA: A Mask-and-Select Framework for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
author: Xianwei Mao; Kai Ye; Sheng Zhou; Nan Zhang; Haikuan Huang; Bin Li; Jiajun Bu
abstract: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) requires models to answer questions by integrating visual information with external knowledge. However, retrieved knowledge is often noisy, partially irrelevant, or misaligned with the visual content, while internal model knowledge is difficult to control and interpret. Naïve aggregation of these sources limits reasoning effectiveness and reduces answer accuracy. To address this, we propose MaS-VQA, a selection-driven framework that tightly couples explicit knowledge filtering with implicit knowledge reasoning. MaS-VQA first retrieves candidate passages and applies a Mask-and-Select mechanism to jointly prune irrelevant image regions and weakly relevant knowledge fragments, producing compact, high-signal multimodal knowledge . This filtered knowledge then guides the activation of internal knowledge in a constrained semantic space, enabling complementary co-modeling of explicit and implicit knowledge for robust answer prediction. Experiments on Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek demonstrate consistent performance gains across multiple MLLM backbones, and ablations verify that the selection mechanism effectively reduces noise and enhances knowledge utilization.

title: KoNeoBench: A Curated Evaluation Dataset for LLM Understanding of Korean Neologisms
author: Soha Lee; Soojin Lee; Heesung Yang; Hyunju Song; Hyunji Lee; Jinsan An; Jeongwan Shin; Jin Hyun Park; Jun Lee; Hyeyoung Park; Kilim Nam
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on static benchmarks, even though natural language constantly evolves through newly emerging words and meanings. Existing Korean benchmarks are centered on established vocabulary and therefore provide limited coverage of such recent lexical change, and their English-oriented design makes it difficult to assess the typological properties of Korean, in which content words combine productively with functional morphemes. In this paper, we introduce **KoNeoBench**, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ understanding of Korean neologisms. KoNeoBench is built on 1,785 Korean neologisms attested in online news since 2020 and curated through expert lexicographic review. Each entry provides usage examples, word-formation analyses, and dictionary-style definitions. Based on this resource, we define four tasks and report results on recent models, together with a human baseline. Our experiments show that current LLMs exhibit clear limitations in recovering source components, distinguishing semantic categories, and generating accurate definitions. These results reveal specific aspects of recent Korean lexical change that remain challenging for current LLMs. KoNeoBench is available at https://github.com/bcmilab/ko-neobench/ .

title: Video-Language Entailment for Video Similarity Estimation
author: Benedetta Liberatori; Lorenzo Vaquero; Elisa Ricci; Paolo Rota
abstract: Comparing videos to assess their semantic similarity remains a challenging task for current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which are primarily trained with single-video objectives. While most prior works have focused on computing global similarity, recent studies have introduced the more challenging problem of concept-based similarity, which measures how similar two videos are with respect to specific concepts (e.g., activity, location). However, no dedicated approaches have yet leveraged LMMs to explicitly address this task. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap introducing Video Caption Entailment for video similarity estimation (VICE): a dual-branch design that leverages LMMs for cross-video reasoning. Each branch jointly processes one video and the caption of the other, measuring their alignment for a specific concept via video-language entailment. The outputs from both branches are fused to produce a final similarity score, along with a textual explanation of the model reasoning. This approach leverages the model’s native single-video understanding while enabling fine-grained comparative reasoning between video and text. Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show that VICE outperforms models that process both videos simultaneously, highlighting the promise of single-video reasoning for concept-based similarity estimation.

title: Modular Representation Steering for Multi-Attribute LLM Alignment
author: Chaojian Shi; Renhong Huang; Xulan Qiu; Jiawei Zhou; Yunsong Zhou
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with multiple behavioral objectives from a certain corpus remains challenging, as joint optimization of attributes often leads to interference and trade-offs. While recent representation steering methods enable lightweight control over individual behaviors through hidden-state interventions, their composability for multi-attribute alignment remains underexplored. We present POLAR, Poly-attribute Alignment via Modular Representation Steering, a modular framework that composes independently trained alignment interventions within a frozen LLM. To mitigate conflicts between steering modules, we introduce calibrated and compatibility-aware intervention composition in hidden-state space. Experiments across heterogeneous alignment attributes show that POLAR achieves the best overall trade-off, with a 37.4% improvement in average rank over the strongest multi-attribute baseline while preserving response quality and controllability. The code and data will be publicly available.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Adaptive Information Acquisition and Diagnosis with Sequentially Revealed Inpatient Records
author: Huawei Feng; Dongsheng Shi; Linlin Wang
abstract: While recent medical benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) have begun to incorporate clinical temporality, they still overlook a key reality: clinical evidence is encountered incrementally, requiring repeated decisions between reviewing the next available record and committing to a prediction. To address this issue, we introduce [<https://github.com/hwfengcs/INA-Bench>] , a benchmark for Inpatient Note Acquisition that evaluates LLMs’ ability to make acquire-or-predict decisions using sequentially revealed real-world Chinese inpatient records. In this benchmark, each case sequentially reveals up to three note blocks: an admission note, a first-course summary, and a daily-progress summary. After each block, the model under evaluation must either request the next block or predict one or more later documented follow-up actions (laboratory, imaging, pathology, or consultation). Surgery and discharge records are withheld for label construction and boundary checks only. is built from 8,986 de-identified inpatient records collected from two tertiary teaching hospitals, with patient-disjoint and temporal evaluation splits. Representative LLMs exhibit diverse acquire-or-predict behaviors. For example, DeepSeek-chat improves action micro-F1 by +0.102 and +0.074 on the patient-disjoint and temporal splits, respectively, while reading fewer note blocks, though the gains weaken under temporal drift.

title: SAGE: Semantic Attribute Graphs for Multi-Entity Visual Retrieval
author: Yongjoo Kim; Mincheol Kwon; Seonga Choi; Minseung Lee; Kyeong-Jin Oh; Hyunyoung Lee; Yunsu Choi; Jungbeom Lee
abstract: Dense document images often contain many fine-grained visual and textual entities whose relevance depends on a user query. Standard vision-language retrievers encode cropped regions with a single vector, which can mix distinct entity signals and obscure the evidence needed for fine-grained retrieval. We call this failure mode **Semantic Dilution** and quantitatively show that it degrades entity-level retrieval as a function of entity density. To mitigate it, we propose **SAGE**, a training-free framework that parses semantic entities from dense document images, represents them as hierarchical graph nodes with multi-vector embeddings, and retrieves query-relevant evidence through iterative entity-level subgraph matching. We also introduce **DEAR**, a dataset of 1,055 query–image pairs sourced from product detail pages, where each query requires retrieving and comparing multiple fine-grained entities from visually dense inputs across four question types of increasing complexity. Experiments show that SAGE substantially reduces semantic dilution and outperforms patch-level and OCR-based retrieval baselines on DEAR, achieving a Recall@3 of 0.849 and a generation score of 2.746 on multi-entity visual comparison queries. Our code is available at https://github.com/All4Nothing/SAGE.

title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
author: Zhangqi Duan; Shuyan Huang; Alexander Scarlatos; Jaewook Lee; Simon Woodhead; Andrew Lan
abstract: A key part of developing large language model (LLM)-powered, automated tutoring tools is student simulation, i.e., using LLMs to role-play as students, which can facilitate tutor model evaluation and training. Existing work mostly focuses on within-dialogue simulation, which lacks context on student knowledge and behavior, partly due to not grounding in past student question-answering or dialogue interactions. In this work, we introduce the task of history-conditioned student simulation, where the goal is to accurately predict student dialogue turns by leveraging information in the student’s learning history. We propose a two-component framework in which a profile generator summarizes a student’s history and a simulator predicts student turns conditioned on the resulting profile. We train both components with reinforcement learning (RL), yielding profiles optimized for faithful student simulation. We evaluate our method and baselines on the first-of-its-kind real-world dataset of student dialogues and question responses that we collect from a math learning platform. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms baselines, and demonstrate the importance of history, profiles, and RL training.

title: Unifying Detection and Adaptation in Task-Free Continual Learning
author: Dezheng Han; Anbang Zhang; Zhihao Zhu; Shuaishuai Guo
abstract: To mitigate catastrophic forgetting in downstream continual learning (CL) for large language models (LLMs), existing methods typically constrain parameter updates or introduce task-specific adaptation modules. However, these methods often rely on explicit task boundaries during training, limiting their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios. In this paper, we propose a Fisher-guided unified (FiUni) framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation. FiUni is motivated by a key observation about the Fisher information matrix (FIM) of pre-trained models: the orthogonality among the principal subspaces of its Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) approximation, estimated from a small number of downstream task samples, can reflect the similarity between different tasks. Based on this observation, FiUni constructs FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA), while matching the Fisher principal subspace of each incoming batch window with historical subspaces. This enables FiUni to adaptively determine whether to reuse existing knowledge, expand a related subspace, or create a new subspace, dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation. Experiments show that FiUni can effectively infer latent batch-level task affiliations and achieve competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters.

title: A Framework for Generating Valid Context-Specific Benchmarks through Expert Guidance
author: Kimberly Le Truong; Nari Johnson; Anna Kawakami; Hoda Heidari
abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end approach for generating context-specific large language model (LLM) benchmark datasets by combining expert input with synthetic data generation. Existing benchmark construction methods often trade off *validity* and *scalability*: datasets designed with domain experts can produce high-quality evaluations but are slow and costly to create, while synthetically generating data may scale efficiently but often results in unrealistic, redundant, or out-of-scope examples. To address this gap, we introduce a schema eliciting key information about the goals, scope, and context of an evaluation task, and use this information to guide synthetic data generation. We further define four criteria grounded in measurement validity for assessing dataset quality: coverage, diversity, content realism, and stylistic realism. Using these criteria, we show how expert-informed scaffolds can guide synthetic data generation toward more valid benchmarks. Through quantitative evaluations and a real-world case study with domain experts, we demonstrate that our approach improves benchmark data quality over existing methods while preserving validity. We additionally analyze how different types of schema information affect different dataset quality criteria, and provide practical guidance on which information to prioritize collecting under resource constraints.

title: When Charts Deceive Web Agents: A Paired Benchmark for Misleading Visualization-Grounded Tasks
author: Yisheng Li; Dongming Han; Hongkun Pan; Bingcheng Mao; Zijian Wang; Yunlong Mao; Wei Tong; Sheng Zhong
abstract: Web agents increasingly browse, interpret, and act on web content on behalf of users. In many realistic workflows, however, the visual evidence they consume is not neutral: charts and dashboards can be misleading, shaping judgments without issuing any explicit malicious instruction. Unlike chart question answering, Web Agents treat charts as intermediate evidence whose misinterpretation can propagate into concrete downstream actions — a reliability risk that remains underexplored. We introduce MisVisAgentBench, the first paired executable benchmark for evaluating how misleading visualizations affect Web Agent execution. It comprises 280 task instances in matched clean–misleading pairs that differ only in chart evidence. We further provide a diagnostic framework that isolates misleading-induced failures from baseline task difficulty and captures execution-level effects such as extra browsing steps and decision hesitation. Across eleven vision-language Web Agents, replacing clean charts with misleading counterparts nearly halves the average task success rate, an absolute drop exceeding 34 percentage points. Moreover, these failures predominantly follow the targeted misleading action branch, suggesting that deceptive charts systematically redirect rather than randomly disrupt agent decisions. These results reveal that visualization robustness is a critical yet understudied dimension of Web Agent safety and reliability.

title: Predictive Language Grounding for Event-Driven Time Series Forecasting via Dual-Path Event Injection
author: Jintao Wu; Xin Xue; Yabin Cao; Peng QI; Su Zhao; Shuai Chen; Wei Lin; Tianyu Chen; Haoyi Zhou
abstract: Discrete events such as holidays, policy announcements, and public gatherings leave no trace in historical time series yet fundamentally shape future demand. Language models capture precisely this event knowledge, making them a natural source of auxiliary signal for event-driven forecasting. However, some multimodal forecasters borrow semantic alignment from vision-language pretraining, enforcing geometric proximity between text and series embeddings. For time series regression, this objective is theoretically unnecessary and actively harmful when training data is limited or text-series coupling is weak: contrastive gradients compress the high-variance series features required to represent event-induced spikes. We propose predictive grounding as the principled alternative, shaping language representations through prediction loss alone. PROSE (Predictive grOunding for event-driven time-Series forEcasting) realizes this framework through a fully fine-tuned language encoder, token-level Event Token Injection, LLM-generated Trajectory Reasoning Anchors as global prefix tokens, and a Soft Functional Alignment loss. On a 464K-sample Chinese holiday benchmark, PROSE surpasses the strongest baseline by 10.7% WMAPE; on Time-MMD, it achieves state-of-the-art results across 7 of 9 domains.

title: Seeing is Believing? Evaluating Vision-Language Model Susceptibility in Agent-to-Agent Multimodal Persuasion
author: Haoyi Qiu; Yilun Zhou; Pranav Narayanan Venkit; Kung-Hsiang Huang; Jiaxin Zhang; Nanyun Peng; Chien-Sheng Wu
abstract: As autonomous agents increasingly interact, they inevitably attempt to influence one another. While prior work in text-only settings has explored the dynamics of Agent-to-Agent (A2A) persuasion, the rise of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) introduces a more complex challenge: multimodal content conveys richer information while integrating subtle, hard-to-detect persuasive cues. To study this vulnerability, we present MMPersuade, a unified framework and dataset for A2A multimodal persuasion. We model interactions between a persuader agent, which leverages images and psychological strategies, and a persuadee VLM. Our benchmark spans commercial, subjective and behavioral, and adversarial contexts, and evaluates persuasion via function-calling that capture behavioral shifts beyond verbal responses. Experiments on six VLMs reveal three findings: (1) multimodal inputs consistently outperform text-only persuasion, with raw visual signals uniquely increasing susceptibility in adversarial settings by bypassing text-activated safety defenses; (2) persuadee vulnerability is highly domain- and format-dependent, with realistic and community-style formats driving susceptibility in commercial settings while different formats dominate in adversarial ones; and (3) psychological strategy efficacy varies with context and model architecture, as more capable models resist benign persuasion yet become more susceptible under adversarial multimodal inputs. Our framework provides a foundation for building more robust and aligned VLMs in multi-agent environments.

title: SAGE: An Extensible Benchmark for Service Agent Graph-guided Evaluation
author: Ling Shi; Yuqin Dai; Ziyin Wang; Wei Zhang; Ning Gao; Chaozheng Wang; Xinwei Wu; Yujie Wang; Wei He; Jinpeng Wang; Linlong Xu; Deyi Xiong
abstract: LLMs are transforming customer service, yet evaluating service agents across diverse business scenarios remains costly and fragmented, as each new domain requires building a dedicated benchmark from scratch. Existing benchmarks rely on static, scenario-specific scripts with two fundamental limitations: ***Scenario Silos***, where each domain demands costly independent annotation with no shared evaluation structure, and ***Dialogue Dynamics Gap***, where fixed scripts fail to capture the full range of real user behaviors. We propose **SAGE** (**S**ervice **A**gent **G**raph-guided **E**valuation), to our knowledge the first scenario-extensible benchmark to jointly assess logical SOP compliance and conversational quality, abstracting any SOP as a directed graph and bridging Scenario Silos through a lightweight two-step extension mechanism. SAGE further enables dynamic multi-turn simulation via adversarial user agents to overcome the Dynamics Gap. Across six industrial scenarios representative of real-world customer service deployment, we evaluate 27 mainstream LLMs spanning both closed-source systems and open-source families, offering a fine-grained capability map to guide real-world model selection. Our experiments further reveal two systematic failure patterns shared across all tested models: while models generally succeed at recognizing user intent, they frequently struggle to follow complex business logic and execute the correct subsequent action; and they sustain a warm and empathetic conversational tone even when their underlying procedural reasoning has already failed. **Code and resources are available at: https://github.com/lingshi6565/SAGE-Bench.**

title: Breaking Temporal Ambiguity: Linguistic Temporal Knowledge Transfer for Weakly-Supervised Action Localization
author: Zhilin Li; Shining Wu; Yixin Zhang; Chuandong Cheng; Zilei Wang
abstract: Weakly-supervised temporal action localization (WS-TAL) remains challenging due to the severe temporal ambiguity inherent in video-level supervision. Existing methods often overfit to highly discriminative snippets, struggling to capture the complete action extent. In this paper, we reconceptualize actions not as isolated events, but as multi-stage action evolutions. To alleviate temporal ambiguity, we propose a novel framework driven by Linguistic Temporal Knowledge Transfer (LTKT) Network, comprising three cohesive modules. First, Temporal Stage Grounding (TSG) leverages explicitly deconstructed LLM descriptions as cross-modal priors, guiding unconstrained visual snippets to anchor their specific evolutionary stages. Second, Temporal Transition Gating (TTG) enforces forward causality on the timeline. By mandating that an execution stage is flanked by historical preparation and future completion, TTG strictly filters static noise to yield refined temporal action scores. Finally, Linguistic Knowledge Transfer (LKT) integrates knowledge distillation and contrastive learning to embed this structural knowledge into the visual backbone. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet1.2 and ActivityNet1.3 demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: From Text to Structure: The PACKaGE Benchmark for Bidirectional Causal Reasoning in Paragraphs and Graphs
author: Juhyeon Kim; Dohun Lee; Jiwon Jang; Joseph Shim; Hyunwoo Park
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, yet they struggle with causal reasoning tasks. We introduce PACKaGE (Paragraph-level Annotated Causal Knowledge and Graph–tExt), a causal benchmark dataset that pairs paragraph-level texts with explicit causal graphs. Unlike prior sentence-level resources, our benchmark dataset (i) operates at paragraph level to capture various and interdependent causal pathways; (ii) offers multimodal annotations including full graphs and contextualized relations; and (iii) maps extended passages to comprehensive graphs. We detail a four-stage construction pipeline: collecting causality-labeled and fact-centric texts, inducing graphs from span-tagged pairs, condensing nodes, and recomposing path-aligned narratives. Overall, the paired evaluation highlights a persistent discrepancy between linguistic competence and causal understanding in LLMs, pointing to the need for further development.

title: PEAR: Permutation-Equivariant Adaptive Routing Multi-Agent Debate
author: Yang Feng; Ziwei Xu; Xia Hu; Fengxiang He
abstract: Multi-agent debate improves the reliability of large language models (LLMs) through iterative peer critiques. However, fixed topologies often introduce persistent positional biases, amplify unreliable agents, and cause high sensitivity to role assignments. We introduce Permutation-Equivariant Adaptive Routing Multi-Agent Debate (PEAR), an inference-time protocol that dynamically reconfigures communication roles and sparse topologies across consecutive debate rounds. By strategically switching agent-to-role assignments based on evolving agent states, PEAR prevents any agent from permanently occupying a privileged network position or distributes influence more evenly across the debate. We theoretically characterize PEAR as an equivariant sparse router: it preserves accuracy under agent relabeling while reducing routing complexity and improving generalization. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across four reasoning benchmarks and six diverse LLM backbones demonstrate PEAR significantly improves average accuracy over the strongest debate baselines. The code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/PEAR.

title: Semantic Distractor Robustness in LLMs: Exploring the Underlying Mechanisms
author: Xiangyu Wong; Eugene J. Yu; Chenhao Xiong; Zheng Li; Yifan Song; Sujian Li
abstract: Large language models drop in performance when their context contains \textit{semantic distractors}: context topically related to the question but off the reasoning chain. Prior mechanistic work tracks a single injected distractor token, missing failures in which the model predicts other context tokens or out-of-context but topically related ones. We instead track the model’s actual top non-gold prediction, providing a localization target for every observed top-1 failure in the analyzed subset. Failures converge on a small set of mid-to-late-layer \textit{answer-selection heads} (AS-Heads): patching their clean outputs into distracting runs recovers 60-86\\%$ of failed predictions across four base models from two families (random heads recover $\leq 8\\%$), with the mechanism also replicating in two instruction-tuned models. Clean-prompt ablations indicate that these heads also contribute to normal answer selection, so their role is not specific to distractors. Redirecting their attention onto an entity span causes the model to transcribe that span at $22$-$83\\%$ (vs. $\leq 7.4\\%$ for random heads), establishing a causally consequential intervention point. The localized heads transfer across MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and non-Wikipedia RAG settings. At inference, their attention provides a training-free context-filtering signal that lifts F1 by up to $+35$ points on disrupted samples and is competitive with retrieval-head methods.

title: Teach a Man to Fish: Self-Adaptive Reinforced Distillation for In-Context Reasoning-based Reranker
author: Wenwei Wu; Youhang LI; Mingyang Chen; Jie Yang; Xiaofeng Gu; Duyi Pan; Yiwen Wu; Kaichen Zhang; Wei Wang; Zixuan Yuan
abstract: Recent advances in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are reshaping reasoning-intensive reranking, where step-by-step reasoning enables multi-faceted relevance judgments. To scale LRMs, existing approaches distill chain-of-thought traces from a teacher LRM into a student reranker via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, this pipeline is misaligned with the distillation objective: teacher traces are too dense for direct imitation, while RL exploration is too sparse on hard cases. To this end, we propose SARD (Self-Adaptive Reinforced Distillation), a tri-mode RL framework that recasts teacher reasoning from a fixed supervision target into an adaptive resource the student draws on only when its own reasoning falls short. Triggered by rollout outcomes, SARD organizes training into three modes: Free Exploration, where the student reasons independently; Guided Exploration, which supplies reusable in-context guidance abstracted from teacher traces when free rollouts fail; and Teacher-Guided Repair, where the teacher diagnoses failures and revises, re-selects, or appends guidance, falling back to teacher trajectories only as a last resort. Experiments on reasoning-intensive reranking benchmarks show SARD outperforms strong reranking and SFT-then-RL baselines, with clear gains on difficult instances and under-represented reasoning patterns.

title: AgentTAC: Mining Temporal Action-Context Error Patterns from Agent Traces
author: Chenchen Zhao; Muxi Chen; Jianhai Shu; Zhaohua Zhang; Wenyu Jiang; Tianwen Jiang; Hexuan Deng; Sa Zhu; Haolin Yang; Geyuan Zhu; Cheng Yang; Qiuyong Xiao; Jianhuan Zhuo; Jihong Zhang; Qiang Xu
abstract: Interactive agents increasingly fail on long task processes involving user turns, tool calls, and evolving environment contexts. Existing agent debugging methods provide useful trace-level diagnosis, but generally return explanations for individual failed traces rather than recurring, fine-grained action-context patterns across runs. To offer such corpus-level analyses, we present AgentTAC (Temporal Action-Context), an automated framework for mining erroneous and generalizable temporal sequences of action and context properties from agent traces. AgentTAC first localizes all distinct errors in each involved agent run. Then, it constructs and maintains a dynamic pool of attributes over the involved tasks, actions, and contexts to summarize their intrinsic properties and contextual relationships. Finally, it extracts temporally contiguous attribute patterns anchored at the localized errors. The resulting error patterns describe failures as interpretable sequential combinations of context and actions, such as making decisions under a missing-constraint context or taking an action after an incompatible prior decision. Extensive evaluations of AgentTAC on multiple benchmarks and agents validate its capabilities in error localization and error pattern mining, and provide preliminary evidence for error-pattern-driven test-time repair.

title: Prompt-Induced Recovery Behavior Decomposition for Black-Box Pre-training Data Detection
author: Xin Fan; Miyamoto Ryoto; Fan Mo; Chongxian Chen; Tsuneo Matsumoto; Fuyuko Kido; Hayato Yamana
abstract: Large language models are pretrained on massive, largely undisclosed corpora that may contain copyrighted, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise unauthorized content, making pre-training data detection essential for data-rights auditing, privacy protection, and benchmark contamination analysis. However, most existing methods follow a gray-box setting, relying on internal signals such as token probabilities, logits, or losses, which are unavailable for commercial LLMs that expose only the final generated text. Recent black-box methods instead use word-recovery rate as the detection signal, but overlook that a word’s discriminative value can vary substantially across target models and target texts. To address this limitation, we propose ***PIRBD-PDD***, a target LLM- and text-adaptive framework for black-box pre-training data detection via *Prompt-Induced Recovery Behavior Decomposition*. ***PIRBD-PDD*** decomposes the target LLM’s recovery behavior into memorization-oriented and context-oriented modes through prompt induction, contrasts their recovery outcomes to identify high-discriminability words, and computes the final detection score from their recovery rate under the original, non-induced prompt. Experiments across diverse LLMs and data domains show that ***PIRBD-PDD*** consistently outperforms state-of-the-art black-box baselines. Further analyses provide empirical evidence for the proposed decomposition and show that high-discriminability words provide more robust and informative signals for pre-training data detection.

title: Router Prior Bias: Preserving Base Routing Structure in MoE Post-Training
author: Jaedeok Lee; Keonwoo Kim; Dongyoon Han; Sangdoo Yun; Yera Choi; Haanju Yoo
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) pretraining relies on an auxiliary load-balancing loss (LBL) to drive per-expert utilization toward uniformity. Post-training inherits a different situation: the base router already encodes non-uniform expert co-activation structure, which a re-imposed uniformity objective flattens away. We show that downstream performance depends instead on holding this inherited routing softly, a principle we term soft router anchoring, and instantiate it as Router Prior Bias (RPB), a training-time bias that pulls the router logits toward a prior read off the frozen base router while leaving the router itself trainable. On math post-training of Moonlight-16B-A3B, RPB attains 45.77 in-domain accuracy against 31.91 under re-applied LBL and 29.44 under unanchored fine-tuning, and retains more out-of-domain capability than either. The ordering against LBL reproduces on a second model family (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base), and the advantage over LBL is resolvable on an independently sourced corpus. Anchors defined on the router weights, on its logits, or on its output distribution perform comparably with no consistent ordering, which places the effect in the softness of the constraint rather than in the particular prior RPB supplies. Retained community structure in the expert co-activation graph tracks these gains wherever the base router is non-uniform enough for communities to form, yet enforcing the same prior as a hard assignment preserves that structure while performance falls sharply. Community structure is therefore a footprint of soft anchoring rather than its source, and the practical lesson is that inherited routing should be held softly during post-training, since both flattening it toward uniformity and enforcing it absolutely carry a downstream cost. Our code will be released at https://github.com/naver-ai/rpb.

title: Beyond Shallow Alignment: How Post-Training Methods Determine Refusal Circuits And Steering Robustness
author: Hoang Cuong Nguyen; Mark Dras; Usman Naseem
abstract: How do the methods used to train language models to refuse harmful requests shape how that refusal actually works inside the model? We compare three post-training methods - supervised fine-tuning, reasoning-augmented fine-tuning (training on reasoning chains that justify a safety decision), and preference optimization (ORPO) – across three architecturally distinct models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen3-8B). We find that training method, not just data, reshapes how refusal is computed internally: reasoning-augmented training consistently produces a distinct kind of refusal computation, visible across all three models, while architecture independently shapes internal structure and how reliably refusal can be steered. Most importantly, no method we study achieves all three properties we would want from safe alignment at once: refusal that isn’t concentrated in a few fragile components, safety gains that don’t cost general capability, and safety behavior correctable through small, targeted edits. We caution against treating current post-training methods as a solved, reliable defense, especially for security-critical use. Code and models are available in https: //github.com/hoangcuongnguyen2001/Beyond-Shallow-Alignment.

title: OSynth: A Longitudinal, Context-Sensitive Evaluation of Meeting Understanding
author: Ian Porada; Suraj Tripathi; Chaitanya Animesh; Leda Sari; Chaitanya Narisetty; Austin R Matthews; Bohan Yu; Ramesh L Thulasiram; Gregory Sell; KK Chin; Dmitriy Genzel
abstract: Meeting notetakers are increasingly deployed in settings where longitudinal context is available including calendar metadata, prior meetings, emails, slides, and speaker enrollments; however, meeting corpora remain limited in terms of size, domain coverage, and available context. We present OSynth, a large-scale synthetic dataset of simulated organizations comprising 570 hours of meeting audio together with associated artifacts and a latent ground-truth state. In a pairwise comparison, human raters distinguish OSynth meetings from real meeting transcripts with only 56% accuracy based on excerpts of 150–300 words. Across state-of-the-art LLMs, additional context yields significant gains on several entity-sensitive dimensions, demonstrating limitations of contemporary approaches and the potential usefulness of OSynth in developing better-contextualized meeting-understanding systems.

title: Multi-Model Framework for Sentiment Annotation: A Use Case of Multilingual Wikipedia
author: Włodzimierz Lewoniewski; Milena Stróżyna; Izabela Czumałowska
abstract: In this work, we investigate whether data annotation can be automated using state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), while maintaining high consistency and reliability. We propose a multi-model, multi-run framework in which several LLMs act as annotators and their outputs are aggregated using a strict consensus criterion to improve annotation robustness and reduce model-specific biases. The proposed approach is evaluated on a multilingual sentiment analysis task using lead sections of Wikipedia articles covering diverse topics in five languages. The resulting annotations are assessed using intra-model consistency, cross-model agreement, and standard inter-annotator agreement metrics. Additionally, we conducted human evaluation. The described framework enables scalable and reproducible data annotation, and the resulting dataset is publicly released to support further research.

title: APEx: Distillation of Agent Procedural Experience for Adaptive Deep Research Question Answering
author: Jie Ding; Rui Sun; Xinyuan Zhang; Zeyu Zhang; Xin Liu
abstract: Deep research agents augment large language models with external tools to answer complex, long-horizon questions through multi-turn reasoning. Learning from prior experience is crucial for continual improvement, yet existing methods either retrieve verbose task-specific traces that burden decision-making, or distill procedural skills that remain decoupled from downstream policy adaptation. We propose APEx, a hierarchical experience utilization framework that organizes interaction history into instance-level trajectory memories and category-level procedural skills, and couples them through a closed-loop architecture of Executor, Distiller, and Planner. The three modules are optimized via a three-stage alternating GRPO training paradigm, enabling reward-guided skill distillation rather than fixed-prompt generation. At test time, distilled skills serve as procedural priors for online Planner adaptation through skill-guided test-time reinforcement learning, allowing ground-truth-free self-improvement with skill-alignment regularization to prevent policy drift. Experiments on 7 benchmarks demonstrate that APEx achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing GPT-5.4 by 14.7 points and the strongest memory-augmented baseline by 3.0 points.

title: Influence Guided Sampling for Domain Adaptation of Text Retrievers
author: Meet Doshi; Vishwajeet Kumar; Yulong Li; Jaydeep Sen
abstract: General-purpose open-domain dense retrieval systems are usually trained with a large, eclectic mix of corpora and search tasks. How should these diverse corpora and tasks be sampled for training? Conventional approaches sample them uniformly, proportional to their instance population sizes, or depend on human-level expert supervision. It is well known that the training data sampling strategy can greatly impact model performance. However, how to find the optimal strategy has not been adequately studied in the context of embedding models. We propose **Inf-DDS**, a novel reinforcement learning–driven sampling framework that adaptively reweighs training datasets guided by influence-based reward signals and is much more lightweight w.r.t. GPU consumption. Our technique iteratively refines the sampling policy, prioritizing datasets that maximize model performance on a target development set. We evaluate the efficacy of our sampling strategy on a wide range of text retrieval tasks, demonstrating strong improvements in retrieval performance and better adaptation compared to existing gradient-based sampling methods, while also being 1.5\text{—}4\times cheaper in GPU compute. Our sampling strategy achieves a \mathbf{5.03} absolute NDCG@10 improvement while training the multilingual bge-m3 model and an absolute NDCG@10 improvement of \mathbf{0.94} while training all-MiniLM-L6-v2, even when starting from expert-assigned weights on a large pool of training datasets.

title: When Does Reasoning Help in Machine Translation? A Hierarchical Analysis of LRM Reasoning Traces
author: Yuxiang Liu; Jiaming Luo; Eleftheria Briakou; Colin Cherry
abstract: Large Reasoning Models increasingly use intermediate traces for machine translation, but it remains unclear when such reasoning helps or hurts. We analyze reasoning traces across models, languages, domains, and datasets, focusing on reasoning language, length, and structure. We find that the best reasoning language is model-specific, reasoning length has a non-monotonic relationship with quality, and traces exhibit recurring functional patterns. To uncover these patterns, we introduce **Hierarchical Meta-Summarization (HMS)**, a scalable framework that induces coarse- and fine-grained reasoning structures without predefined taxonomies. HMS reveals a shared organization–understanding/planning, translating/drafting, and refining/verifying–alongside domain-specific variation. Our results suggest that MT reasoning should be controlled in a model-aware, length-aware, and pattern-aware manner rather than uniformly encouraged.

title: Beyond Semantic Similarity: Learning Behavior-Aligned Retrieval for Tool-Augmented LLMs
author: Yixin Chen; Ying Xiong; Shangyu Wu; Yufei Cui; Xue Liu; Nan Guan; Chun Jason Xue
abstract: Tool-augmented LLMs invoke external functions to extend their capabilities, but errors in the invocation decision, such as calling a tool when none is needed or omitting a needed call, can produce unreliable outputs and unnecessary cost. A lightweight remedy is to prepend retrieved examples so LLMs decide tool use in context. However, existing retrievers rank examples by semantic similarity alone. Lexically close or semantically close queries can require opposite behavior, so the retrieved examples may be behaviorally inconsistent and silently mislead the model. We propose Behavior-Aligned Retrieval (BAR), a backbone-agnostic training recipe that teaches a dense retriever a behavior-aware similarity, keeping semantically related candidates close only when their tool-use behavior is compatible. BAR does not predict invocation labels; instead, it ranks demonstrations while leaving the final tool-use decision to the LLM. Applied to multiple retrieval backbones, including BERT, Contriever, and Qwen3-Reranker, BAR consistently improves invocation reliability and reduces unnecessary API calls across 14 LLMs and 3 benchmarks.

title: JURY-RL: Votes Propose, Proofs Dispose for Label-Free RLVR
author: Xinjie Chen; Biao Fu; Wu Jing; Guoxin Chen; Xinggao Liu; Dayiheng Liu; Minpeng Liao
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs) but typically depends on human-annotated answers or curated reward specifications. Label-free alternatives such as majority voting or LLM-as-a-Judge remove this cost but introduce false positives that destabilize training. We introduce JURY-RL, a label-free RLVR framework that decouples answer proposal from reward disposal: rollouts matching the plurality-voted answer receive positive reward only when that answer is verified in Lean. When verification is inconclusive, ResZero (Residual-Zero) discards the unverified plurality and redistributes a zero-mean, variance-preserving signal over the residual answers, keeping the optimization gradient stable without reinforcing unverifiable consensus. Across three backbones trained on math data, JURY-RL outperforms label-free baselines on mathematical reasoning, transfers to code generation and general benchmarks, and surpasses a majority-vote baseline in the test-time RL (TTRL) setting; it matches supervised ground-truth training on pass@1 and beats it on pass@k and response diversity.

title: Beyond Correlation-Driven Fusion: Sample-Adaptive Causal Evidence Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
author: Gaifang Luo; Hao Zhang; Yanan Liu; Haomin Tan; Guochuan Wu; Dan Xu
abstract: Existing multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) methods rely on representation learning and cross-modal fusion. However, many follow a correlation-driven paradigm that may encode lexical shortcuts, visual biases, and non-causal correlations into predictions. To address this, we propose a Consistency-Conflict Fusion with Sample-Adaptive Causal Evidence (CCF-SACE) framework, revisiting MSA from a representation-level causal modeling perspective. First, encoders extract textual and visual features, and an adaptor projects them into a shared space. The framework then performs sample-adaptive cross-modal causal evidence selection, where textual causal evidence is selected under visual context and visual causal evidence under textual context. The remaining contexts are modeled as non-causal proxies, allowing the model to separate emotion-supportive evidence from shortcut-related information. CCF-SACE further introduces a covariance-based consistency-conflict-aware fusion module that constructs an evidence-level mediator by modeling cross-modal consistency and discrepancy rather than directly fusing all selected cues. Since the residual proxy stream may still carry label-correlated shortcut information, we introduce non-causal proxy suppression and counterfactual sensitivity objectives to weaken its standalone predictability and enlarge the discrepancy between evidence-mediated and proxy-only predictions. Experiments on five benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, especially on fine-grained affective recognition.

title: KARMA: Karma-Aligned Reward Model Adaptation
author: Jared Scott; Jesse Roberts
abstract: Human communication depends on implicit social signals where effectiveness is shaped by tone, context, and conversational norms rather than semantic content alone. We introduce KARMA (Karma-Aligned Reward Model Adaptation), a framework for LLM learning of context-sensitive conversational behavior from large-scale social media data. KARMA trains a reward model on Reddit conversations to predict response valuation conditioned on context, and uses this signal to fine-tune language models via reinforcement learning to improve performance on pragmatics-mediated tasks. Critically, we find that the highest performing reward model does not lead to better downstream model alignment: a reward model relying exclusively on conversational context was a worse predictor of Reddit karma but yielded substantially better downstream performance. We evaluate the effects of KARMA applied to a downstream model with and without direct exposure to the social media data. The resulting models show improved pragmatics-mediated behaviors with largely mitigated undesirable side effects.

title: From Chain to Mesh: Evolving Robust Safety Alignment via Neuron-Circuit Topology
author: Guan Wang; Xuehai Tang; Biyu Zhou; Wenjie Xiao; Yuanshu Zhao; Lijia Lv; Jizhong Han; Songlin Hu
abstract: Despite substantial progress in safety alignment, aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) remain fragile under small parameter-space and activation-space perturbations, such as downstream fine-tuning and jailbreak attacks. To explain why local perturbations can trigger broad safety failures, we analyze safety-task neuron circuits from the perspectives of activation flow and circuit topology. We identify a critical topological fragility in safety alignment: In aligned models, safety-task neuron circuits exhibit a low-redundancy, isolated single-chain topology, in sharp contrast to the highly redundant dense-mesh topology of general-task circuits. This brittle topology creates rigid serial dependencies, whereby perturbing a small set of upstream neurons can disrupt downstream safety neurons and cascade into broad alignment failures. To mitigate this topological fragility, we propose Dense Safety Mesh (DSM), a topology-aware alignment framework that transforms brittle single-chain safety circuits into more redundant and resilient mesh-like structures. DSM employs structural adversarial masking to suppress dominant safety pathways, forcing safety circuits to develop diverse parallel pathways. Extensive experiments across seven models and multiple evaluations show that DSM improves robustness against perturbations attacks while maintaining general capabilities.

title: MATCHA: A Chinese Multi-Disorder Mental Health Dataset with Cross-Lingual Analyses on Social Media
author: Bingrui Jin; Baihan Li; Zitong Li; Shimeng Li; Kunyao Lan; Kenny Q. Zhu; Mengyue Wu
abstract: Mental health research on social media has been dominated by English-language datasets and DSM-5-centered resources, limiting cross-lingual and cross-cultural understanding of online mental health expression. We introduce MATCHA, the first Chinese multi-disorder mental health dataset that links disorder-specific Weibo Super-Topic communities with users’ broader public timelines. MATCHA covers seven DSM-5 disorders and a control group, comprising 46,025 cohort-level users and 1.8 million posts. The dataset distinguishes users with explicit self-disclosure evidence from broader disorder-related participants through an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, and is released in a rigorously de-identified, controlled-access format. Using MATCHA, we analyze behavioral, linguistic, symptom-related, and life-event-related patterns across disorders, and conduct cross-lingual comparisons with Twitter-STMHD. Our analyses show that Weibo Super-Topics function as concentrated spaces for affective and health-related expression, while cross-platform differences between Weibo and Twitter often exceed cross-disorder variation. MATCHA provides a new resource for community-aware and cross-lingual mental health NLP research.

title: Auditing Intersectional Bias in Clinical LLMs: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Race-HIV Stigma Circuits
author: Chang Lu; Yizheng Zhao
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into interpretable latents, exposing the racial biases they encode. Existing SAE-based audits, however, vary one demographic attribute at a time, leaving open whether bias compounds when race meets a stigmatized diagnosis. We examine this compounding for people living with HIV (PLWH), for whom provider stigma is a well-documented barrier to care, and report three findings. In Gemma-2-9B-it, the Gemma Scope latents that encode Black racial identity co-fire with HIV stigma concepts such as "noncompliance" and "substance use". A factorial analysis shows the coupling is superadditive: stigma activations for Black HIV-positive vignettes exceed what the race and HIV main effects predict. Under zero-shot elicitation the model never names race in its chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, even when the race latent causally changes its prediction. We then propose Contrastive Activation Editing (CAE), which subtracts the race direction’s projection onto the stigma subspace, leaving clinical information intact. On a benchmark of 2,004 counterfactual HIV vignettes, CAE reduces the demographic parity gap by 73% while retaining 98% of diagnostic accuracy, outperforming zero-ablation, anti-bias prompting, and linear direction ablation. All three results replicate on Llama-3.1-8B, in both base and instruction-tuned form, using two independently trained SAE suites.

title: The Cold-Start Safety Gap in LLM Agents
author: Chung-En Sun; Linbo Liu; Tsui-Wei Weng
abstract: Are tool-calling LLM agents equally safe throughout a conversation? We discover they are not: agents are most vulnerable at the very start of a session and become substantially safer after a few regular agentic tasks—a phenomenon we term the cold-start safety gap. To study this systematically, we introduce Safety Over Depth for Agents (SODA), a benchmark that controls how many regular agentic tasks the agent completes before encountering a safety threat, supporting up to 20 preceding tasks. Evaluating 7 models from 4 families, safety improves by 9–52% as the number of preceding regular agentic tasks increases from zero to twenty. Representation analysis confirms that model hidden states gradually shift toward a safety-aligned region as more preceding tasks are present. By systematically studying which part of the preceding conversation matters most, we find that the regular agentic tasks themselves are the primary driver of safety, while the agent’s own prior responses have less effect on safety but are essential for preserving later utility. This conclusion is further supported by evaluation on open-source safety benchmarks (AgentHarm, Agent Safety Bench) and utility benchmarks (BFCL, API-Bank), confirming that warming up the agent with regular agentic tasks before deployment makes it safer and preserves full capability. Based on these findings, we recommend a simple deployment strategy: having the agent complete a few regular agentic tasks before possible exposure to safety-critical requests mitigates the cold-start safety gap.

title: Toward Native Multimodal Modeling: A Roadmap
author: Siyu An; Junru Lu; Junnan Dong; Qiufeng Wang; Yinghui Li; Weizhi Fei; Zichao Yu; Zheng Yuan; Biao Liu; Haopeng Wang; Renzhao Liang; Yixuan Yang; Yunhang Shen; Bo Ke; Keyu Chen; Linhao Luo; Difan Zou; Xiao Huang; di Yin; Ruizhi Qiao; Xing Sun
abstract: Multimodal modeling represents a vital step from modality-agnostic reasoning toward world modeling. While early approaches predominantly rely on late-fusion that assembles encoders and frozen language backbones with output heads, recent efforts have shifted the paradigm toward native multimodal modeling (NMM) with the intrinsic integration of modalities for superior multimodal performance. Despite its potential, the design space of native architectures remains insufficiently defined. In this paper, we present the community with a formalized roadmap for this transition. Specifically, we formally define the architectural nativity, distinguishing mid-fusion and early-fusion from non-native paradigms. We further organize the existing native models through the lens of input-output duality into three categories: (i) Multi-to-Text for cross-modal comprehension with text-only output; (ii) Multi-to-Target for scenario-oriented generation e.g., image, audio and video generation, and (iii) Multi-to-Multi for unified modeling with symmetric input-output. We systematically unpack the end-to-end pipeline from industrial perspectives from: architectural coordination, massive data curation, to full-stack training recipes, inference deployment, and evaluation. Finally, based on our assessment of native multimodal development trends, we provide a forward-looking perspective on its future trajectory.

title: ICE: Intervention-Consistent Explanation Evaluation with Statistical Grounding for LLMs
author: Abhinaba Basu; Pavan Chakraborty
abstract: Evaluating whether explanations faithfully reflect a model’s reasoning remains an open problem. Existing benchmarks use single interventions without statistical testing, making it impossible to distinguish genuine faithfulness from chance-level performance. We show that faithfulness is not a fixed property but an operator-dependent quantity that changes with the intervention method used to measure it. We introduce ICE (Intervention-Consistent Explanation), a framework that evaluates explanations against random baselines of equal size under multiple operators. Evaluating 7 LLMs across 4 tasks with deletion and retrieval infill operators, we find that switching operators crosses the positive-evidence threshold in 18% of configurations (5 of 28 attention comparisons), with gaps reaching 44 percentage points. Randomized baselines detect anti-faithfulness (explanations worse than random) in nearly one-third of English deletion configurations, invisible without random comparisons. These patterns persist across 6 non-English languages and 2 attribution methods. The methodology generalizes to step-level chain-of-thought evaluation, where preliminary results on 3 frontier models suggest that high accuracy does not imply faithful reasoning.

title: MAS-on-the-Fly: In-Context Structural Adaptation of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
author: Guangyi Liu; Linhaojun; Zenghuan; Heng Wang; Quanming Yao
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex tasks. However, existing works often rely on manual designs or “one-size-fits-all” automation and lack adaptability after deployment. We study in-context structural adaptation, where structured experience conditions both query-dependent system generation and execution-time reconfiguration without updating LLM parameters. We introduce MASFly, which realizes this adaptation through two complementary mechanisms. First, a retrieval-augmented SOP instantiation mechanism retrieves and adapts successful collaboration patterns to construct a query-specific MAS. Second, an experience-enhanced process supervision mechanism uses a dedicated Watcher agent to monitor execution against prior failure experience and reconfigure the system upon abnormal behavior. Experiments demonstrate that MASFly achieves state-of the-art performance, including a 61.7% success rate on TravelPlanner, with strong task adaptability and robustness.

title: MultiSynt/MT: Trillion-Token Multi-Parallel Pretraining Data Translated Across 36 Languages
author: Maximilian Idahl; Jörg Tiedemann; Sampo Pyysalo; David Salinas; Tomasz Galica; Shenbin Qian; Tudor Nicolae Mateiu; Zihao Li; Anna Lokrantz; Fedor Vitiugin; Andre Martins; Jenna Kanerva; Filip Ginter; Matthias Lindemann; Tim Isbister; Birger Moell; Jonas Lindh; Jan Hajič; Jenia Jitsev; Andrey Kutuzov; Stephan Oepen; Gema Ramírez-Sánchez
abstract: Open web-scale pre-training corpora remain concentrated in English, limiting multilingual LLM development. We introduce MultiSynt/MT, an open synthetic parallel corpus with approximately 4.8 trillion target-language tokens across 36 European languages, produced by translating 100 billion high-quality Nemotron-CC tokens with Tower+ and OPUS-MT/HPLT-MT systems. For many medium- and lower-resource European languages, this is the largest openly available pre-training resource. On a broad multilingual benchmark suite, reference LLMs trained on MultiSynt/MT reach the final score of HPLT 2.0, a native-data baseline, using roughly 72% fewer pre-training tokens, and outperform it by approximately 15% relative at a matched 100B-token training budget. Our analyses also identify evaluation blind spots: standard multiple-choice benchmarks miss translation-quality differences that a fluency-sensitive LLM-as-judge evaluation cleanly recovers on the trained LLMs (with no fluency deficit in MultiSynt itself), and Norwegian idiomatic and culturally grounded tasks remain better served by native data. We release the corpus, including row-aligned translations from multiple systems, to support controlled research on multilingual pre-training data and evaluation.

title: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
author: Zesheng Shi; Xue li; Chenrui Dai; Jing Li
abstract: LLMs over external data face a per-instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety-utility frontier and forcing a choice between over-refusal and over-compliance. We argue the missing capability is **per-instruction credit attribution** and formalize it as External-Data Instruction Classification, an identify-classify-act decision over each embedded directive. We propose **EDIC**, a decomposed reward framework for per-instruction compliance. A scene-grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful-rejection by up to 7.7% and Arena-Hard-Auto utility by 12.5% on Qwen3-4B.

title: Typology-Aware Dual-Track: Detecting Hybrid AI Text Across Languages
author: Kihoon Park; Seungwoo Lim; Jihie Kim
