However, their robustness remains insufficiently understood in the presence of large language models (LLMs), which can generate fluent and deceptive content at scale. This work investigates the vulnerability of neural ranking models to corpus poisoning attacks, in which an adversary injects a small number of maliciously crafted documents into the corpus to distort ranking behavior. We propose VerTox, the first framework to formulate corpus poisoning as a verifiable reward-guided reinforcement learning (RLVR) problem. By explicitly coupling ranking distortion with factual corruption through specialized reward shaping, we fine-tune compact LLMs into adversarial generators. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves near-perfect attack success rates, producing adversarial documents that frequently rank higher than target documents across major neural ranking architectures, as well as a proprietary commercial embedding model. The generated adversarial documents are fluent and exhibit low perplexity, making them difficult to detect. Furthermore, by explicitly encouraging factual corruption, our adversarial documents significantly degrade the performance of a downstream RAG application.

title: ArgSum-X: A Structure-Aware Benchmark for Argument Summarization and Key Point Analysis
author: Zhiqiang Shi; Oana Cocarascu
abstract: Argument summarization requires capturing semantic content while preserving the underlying argumentative structure. We present ArgSum-X, a dataset supporting both argumentative text summarization (ATS) and key point analysis (KPA) . To construct the dataset, we propose constructed via a multi-stage annotation framework with hybrid LLM–human annotation and quality tiers, and provide a detailed analysis of annotation quality. We propose a comprehensive evaluation framework for argument summarization covering structural, faithfulness, and semantic aspects, and conduct an empirical analysis of structure-aware modeling, revealing the unique properties and challenges of argument summarization.

title: Beyond Ranking: Role-Specific Signals for Token-Budgeted SFT Data Selection
author: Haocheng Zhu; Tianqi Wang; Jun Suzuki
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a core stage in post-training general-purpose language models, but modern SFT training corpora are often large, heterogeneous mixtures, making data selection important under fixed token budgets. Simple ranking approaches can be informative yet insufficient: ranking alone does not determine how to allocate a fixed token budget across examples. We study the role-specific use of likelihood-derived signals for token-budgeted subset construction. An external instruction-tuned reference model computes response-side negative log-likelihood scores to rank training examples. We then combine this ranking with base model likelihood filtering to restrict the candidate region and response-side cosine filtering to reduce redundancy in the selected subset. In the OLMo fine-tuning setting studied here, ranking examples only by reference-model likelihood underperforms the random baseline, whereas the same ranking becomes more effective when combined with base model likelihood filtering and cosine-based redundancy control. Our results support viewing token-budgeted SFT data selection as a budget-allocation problem rather than only as an example-ranking problem.

title: SnapBench: Benchmarking Snap-and-Ask Multimodal Retrieval for Mobile Interactions
author: Zirong Chen; Fuda Ye; Kuan Zhang; Enjun Du; Junfu Pu; Xinlei Wang; Xinyu Zuo; Lisheng Duan; Jin Ma; Yongqi Zhang
abstract: Mobile AI acts as a visual oracle, empowering users to snap a picture of something and ask for information. Snap-and-ask retrieval is now one of the most common entry points for mobile AI, yet photos are often blurry, while text questions may be short or mistyped. Existing benchmarks only test on clean inputs or do not isolate paired robustness in snap-and-ask retrieval. Therefore, we introduce SnapBench, the first paired benchmark for robust snap-and-ask multimodal retrieval, spanning 1,145 queries, 9,085 gallery items under 53 controlled corruption conditions with human annotations. We evaluate 16 multimodal retrievers, covering dual-tower encoders and embedding-based VLMs. Results show that image corruptions substantially degrade retrieval, while text corruptions mainly affect text-only retrieval and have limited impact on joint retrieval. Clean image-only retrieval often outperforms joint retrieval, indicating the coarse-text drag and the lack of cross-modal fallback under noisy inputs. SnapBench provides a controlled testbed for evaluating robust retrieval in snap-and-ask scenarios. We further propose MOOR (Modality-anchored, Outlier-aware, Optimal Reweighting), a simple adaptive fusion approach, highlighting the need for reliability-aware modality calibration in snap-and-ask retrieval. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/zrchen03/SnapBench.

title: K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts
author: Nahyun Lee; Dongkeun Yoon; Guijin Son; Geewook Kim; Dayoon Ko; Jeonghun Park; Haneul Yoo; Jaewon Cho; Junghun Park; Changyoon Lee; Kyochul Jang; Jaeyeon Kim; Eunsu Kim; Seungone Kim
abstract: Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00–45.67%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea’s Proprietary AI Foundation Model program achieve at most 10.33%. We further construct a 100-problem Synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code at https://github.com/prometheus-eval/K-BrowseComp.

title: CITAR-NER-Br: A Unified NER Dataset for Fine-Grained Legal Citation Extraction in Brazilian Portuguese
author: Arthur Elwing Torres; Altigran da Silva; Hidelberg Oliveira Albuquerque; Ellen Polliana Ramos Souza Pereira; Héldon José Oliveira Albuquerque; Nádia Félix Felipe Da Silva; Márcio De Souza Dias; Douglas Vitório; Andre Suslik Spritzer; Laura Pereira de Gouveia; Rafael Pereira de Gouveia; Breno Gabriel De Melo Lima
abstract: We present CITAR-NER-Br, a unified NER dataset for direct extraction of fine-grained legal citation subcomponents in Brazilian Portuguese. CITAR-NER-Br annotates six citation subcomponents over 270 legal documents from LeNER-Br and Ulysses Tesemõ, capturing the overlapping and discontinuous spans intrinsic to legal citations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified NER dataset for the legal domain specifically designed to represent discontinuous entities, which account for 44.8% of annotations, the highest proportion among existing legal NER corpora. We establish baselines using four configurations across three LLM-based and non-LLM NER methods to support future research. Our experiments demonstrate that, while non-LLM methods achieve strong performance, they remain heavily reliant on high-quality training data. Conversely, LLM-based methods achieve overall lower performance, but require only few-shot supervision. Moreover, the traditional exact-match NER evaluation approach significantly penalizes LLM-based methods even when their outputs preserve semantic accuracy.

title: TreeFlash: Parallel AR-Approximation for Faster Speculative Decoding
author: Peer Rheinboldt; Frédéric Berdoz; Roger Wattenhofer
abstract: One-shot block drafters for speculative decoding generate the full draft in a single forward pass, achieving strong throughput by eliminating sequential token generation. However, they predict each draft token conditioned only on the prefix context, with no dependence on previously drafted tokens. This non-autoregressive conditioning causes the drafter’s distribution to diverge from the verifier’s true autoregressive distribution as draft depth grows. This problem becomes more severe in tree-based drafting, where distinct branches are forced to share the same marginal distribution for subsequent tokens. We propose TreeFlash, which addresses this by incorporating an MLP layer conditioned on the drafter’s hidden state and the previous token to approximate an autoregressive distribution. TreeFlash retains the \mathcal{O}(1) decoding time complexity of one-shot drafters by employing a two-stage approximation mechanism. TreeFlash achieves state-of-the-art performance across a variety of tasks and models, improving over marginal tree drafting by 12% higher block efficiency and 9% higher speedup at a drafting budget of 64.

title: UDSS-BWE: Uncertainty- and Decision-Science Inspired Swin BandWidth Extension
author: Tarikul Islam Tamiti; Sajid Fardin Dipto; David Vergano; Luke Baja-Ricketts; Anomadarshi Barua
abstract: Bandwidth extension (BWE) is fundamentally localized: the most perceptual distortions are not average-case distortions, but rare high-frequency (HF) transients that standard, risk-neutral objectives tend to smooth away. To close this gap, we seek solutions in the risk-sensitive and uncertainty-aware decision science rules and present UDSS-BWE, which introduces five decision-science and uncertainty-aware dicriminators: CVaRD (does tail pooling to amplify HF artifacts), CCD (a primal-dual augmented Lagrangian to prevent HF overboost), MCUD (a learnable utility over spectral flatness/ centroid/ rolloff), EDD (captures epistemic uncertainty), and DROD (captures entropic KL-DRO aggregation). UDSS-BWE is also designed as a complex-valued adversarial BWE framework that uses Swin-based generators, a lightweight dual-stream shifted-window backbone, to capture local and long-range structure efficiently, while learnable lattice coupling provides controlled cross-stream exchange. UDSS-BWE is optimized extensively and achieves better performance across a total of 13 different evaluation metrics with 3.89x fewer parameters (72M vs. 18M) over two English and French datasets under clean and noisy conditions. To best of our knowledge, this work shows how multi disciplinary decision-science and uncertainty theories can be successfully used to design efficient discriminators for producing more nuanced audios, establishing a new baseline in the BWE task.

title: DeepSearch-World: Self-Distillation for Deep Search Agents in a Verifiable Environment
author: Xinyu Geng; Xuanhua He; Sixiang Chen; Yanjing Xiao; Fan Zhang; Shijue Huang; Haitao Mi; Zhenwen Liang; Tianqing Fang; Yi R. Fung
abstract: Training tool-use agents to improve from their own experience remains challenging, as supervised fine-tuning relies on fixed teacher-distilled trajectories, while sparse-reward reinforcement learning provides weak supervision for long-horizon interactions. We present DeepSearch-Evolve, a self-distillation framework for web agents built on DeepSearch-World, a deterministic and verifiable environment with reproducible search and page-reading tools. DeepSearch-World contains 420K multi-hop QA tasks constructed from entity-level random walks and supports key agentic cognitive behaviors useful for self-evolving, including progress verification, grounded reflection, and failure recovery. DeepSearch-Evolve iteratively performs trajectory generation, filtering, data mixing, and fine-tuning to train stronger agents. Without distillation from more capable models, DeepSearch-World-9B achieves competitive performance compared with open-source agents, reaching 31.2% on BrowseComp, 61.5% on GAIA, and 93.4% on HotpotQA, showing that verifiable environments enable scalable self-evolution for long-horizon web agents. We will release the environment, 420K training pool, validation set, model, and code to facilitate future research on self-improving deep search agents.

title: MetaGAI: A Large-Scale and High-Quality Benchmark for Generative AI Model and Data Card Generation
author: Haoxuan Zhang; Ruochi Li; Yang Zhang; Zhenni Liang; Junhua Ding; Ting Xiao; Haihua Chen
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative AI has created a pressing need for rigorous documentation standards that support transparency and governance. Manual creation of Model and Data Cards, however, is difficult to scale, and automated approaches lack the large-scale, high-fidelity benchmarks required for systematic evaluation. We introduce MetaGAI, a benchmark of 2,541 semantically matched document triplets constructed from academic papers, GitHub repositories, and Hugging Face artifacts. Reference cards are produced by a multi-agent pipeline of specialized Retriever, Generator, and Editor agents, and the pipeline is assessed through a four-part validation protocol. We further propose an evaluation framework that combines reference-based automated metrics with a multi-model LLM-as-a-Judge protocol, together with explicit agreement and sensitivity analyses. Among the evaluated baselines, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct achieves the best observed cost–quality trade-off, and the results reveal a recurring tension between faithfulness and completeness. MetaGAI provides a testbed for benchmarking, training, and analyzing automated Model and Data Card generation at scale. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/haoxuan-unt2024/MetaGAI-Benchmark.

title: Diagnosing CFG Interpretation in LLMs
author: Hanqi Li; Lu Chen; Kai Yu
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly integrated into agentic systems, they must adhere to dynamically defined, machine-interpretable interfaces. We evaluate LLMs as in-context interpreters: given a novel context-free grammar, can LLMs generate syntactically valid, behaviorally functional, and semantically faithful outputs? We introduce RoboGrid, a framework that disentangles syntax, behavior, and semantics through controlled stress-tests of recursion depth, expression complexity, and surface styles. Our experiments reveal a consistent hierarchical degradation: LLMs often maintain surface syntax but fail to preserve structural semantics. Despite the partial mitigation provided by CoT reasoning, performance collapses under structural density, specifically deep recursion and high branching, with semantic alignment vanishing at extreme depths. Furthermore, Alien lexicons reveal that LLMs rely on semantic bootstrapping from keywords rather than pure symbolic induction. These findings pinpoint critical gaps in hierarchical state-tracking required for reliable, grammar-agnostic agents.

title: LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning
author: Ye Tian; Zihao Wang; Onat Gungor; Xiaoran Fan; Tajana Rosing
abstract: Personalized lifestyle health analysis requires long-horizon, multi-dimensional reasoning over heterogeneous lifestyle signals, and recent advances in mobile sensing and large language models (LLMs) make such support increasingly feasible. However, the capabilities of current LLMs in this setting remain insufficiently understood due to the lack of systematic benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce LifeAgentBench, a large-scale QA benchmark for long-horizon, cross-dimensional, and multi-user lifestyle health reasoning, containing 22,573 questions spanning from basic retrieval to complex reasoning. We release an extensible benchmark construction pipeline and a standardized evaluation protocol, deriving verifiable answers through executable queries and programs to support reliable assessment. We then systematically evaluate 13 representative LLMs on LifeAgentBench and identify key bottlenecks in long-horizon aggregation and cross-dimensional reasoning. Motivated by these findings, we propose LifeAgent, a tool-augmented reasoning baseline that decomposes complex queries, performs multi-step evidence retrieval, and invokes tools for deterministic aggregation. LifeAgent substantially enhances LLMs’ capabilities on challenging reasoning tasks, achieving clear improvements over widely used baselines and showing potential for health reasoning in everyday scenarios. The benchmark is publicly available.

title: Syntactic Belief Update as the Driver of Garden Path Processing Difficulty
author: Alan Zhou; Miloš Stanojević; John T. Hale
abstract: Garden path sentences present a processing difficulty for humans— the sentence prefix leads the listener towards one interpretation, until the listener hears a critical word that shows that the initial interpretation was wrong. Lexical surprisal, a measure that usually predicts sentence processing difficulty quite well, fails to provide good predictions for garden path sentences. We propose an alternative that actively predicts a distribution over syntactic trees (its syntactic belief) and updates that distribution after each new word. If a processor is led down a garden path, syntactic beliefs will be wrong, requiring a large update at the critical word. The magnitude of the update is measured with a Rényi divergence. Crucially, this metric is dependent on lexical items, but is distinct from lexical probability and measures a degree of belief update over non-lexical syntactic structure only. This Syntactic Belief Update provides a better fit to human reading time data on garden path sentences, suggesting a new research direction examining non-lexical alternatives to surprisal for psycholinguistics.

title: Advancing Fact-Checking for Large Language Models via Argumentative Reasoning
author: Zirong Chen; Xiangwei Lv; Zhaoqun Li; Wenwei Ke; Jinxiong Chang; Linjian Mo; Beishui Liao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in high-stakes domains, yet their unfaithful or non-factual outputs create serious risks and hinder trustworthy deployment. Rigorous fact-checking is therefore essential to mitigate these risks. Most existing factuality verification methods improve evidence acquisition, but fail to capture complex logical relations between claims and multi-source evidence, especially when different evidence sources are inconsistent or incomplete. Moreover, current benchmarks rarely capture such realistic conflict scenarios. To address this, we introduce MAVEN, a real-world benchmark for verifying complex claims against heterogeneous and conflicting web evidence with fine-grained explanations. We further propose ArgCheck, an argumentation-based fact-checking framework. It models claims and retrieved evidence as arguments linked by attack relations, resolving conflicts through formal argumentation semantics. To avoid incomplete evidence, ArgCheck incorporates adversarial web retrieval to gather balanced multi-source evidence and grounds its verdicts and explanations in accepted arguments. Experiments on MAVEN and the public fact-checking benchmark AVeriTeC show that ArgCheck improves Macro-F1 over the strongest baseline by 5.39 and 11.10 points, respectively, while generating more faithful and evidence-grounded explanations. Our code and dataset are available online https://github.com/ZyraChen/ArgCheck.

title: LLMpedia: A Transparent Framework to Materialize an LLM’s Encyclopedic Knowledge at Scale
author: Muhammed Saeed; Simon Razniewski
abstract: Benchmarks like MMLU suggest flagship language models approach factuality saturation above 90%. LLMpedia shows this picture is incomplete. We materialize ~1.3M encyclopedia articles entirely from parametric memory across three model families, then audit every claim against Wikipedia and curated web evidence. For gpt-5-mini, the verifiable true rate is 68.4% on Wikipedia-covered subjects — more than 21pp below MMLU — and the gap is driven by unverifiability (30.5%), not refutation (1.2%). Beyond Wikipedia, frontier articles audited against curated web evidence reach 57.6%; Wikipedia covers only 56.7% of model-surfaced subjects, and three model families overlap in just 7.3% of subject choices. In a retrieval-trap benchmark inspired by prior analysis of Grokipedia, LLMpedia is more factual at roughly half the textual similarity to Wikipedia. Every prompt, article, and verdict is released. Data, code, interface: https://llmpedia.net

title: MOSAIC: A Large-Scale Multimodal Open-Course Segmentation and Alignment Corpus in Chinese
author: Yuming Ai; Shuai Fan; Hua Xu; Fang Kong
abstract: Real-world lectures follow a predefined topic inventory (e.g., a syllabus), but instructors often reorder, paraphrase, or skip items, creating mismatches between the outline and the spoken content. Lectures also contain non-topical utterances (openings, transitions and wrap-ups) that should not be assigned to any topic, yet existing corpora rarely model both challenges. We present **MOSAIC** (**M**ultimodal **O**pen-course **S**egmentation and **A**lignment corpus **I**n **C**hinese), a large-scale Chinese MOOC corpus for *topic-guided segmentation and alignment* under predefined inventories, with explicit *non-topical* labels and matched slide resources. MOSAIC includes **MOSAIC-G** (human-annotated gold benchmark with utterance-level topic alignment and video-level links to matched slide resources) and **MOSAIC-S** (automatically labeled silver data), collectively covering 179 courses and 14,942 videos. To scale annotation, we propose **DORA** (**D**ual-stage **O**utline **R**efinement and **A**lignment), a two-stage pipeline that refines noisy inventories and then performs joint segmentation and topic assignment. Experiments show that silver supervision substantially improves the performance of local models and that incorporating slides consistently benefits knowledge-point extraction, a lecture-comprehension proxy.

title: Social Caption: Evaluating Social Understanding in Multimodal Models
author: Leena Mathur; Bhaavanaa Thumu; Gaoussou Youssouf Kebe; Louis-Philippe Morency
abstract: Social understanding abilities are crucial for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret human social interactions. We introduce Social Caption, a framework grounded in interaction theory to evaluate social understanding abilities of MLLMs along three dimensions: Social Inference (SI), the ability to make accurate inferences about interactions; Holistic Social Analysis (HSA), the ability to generate comprehensive descriptions of interactions; Directed Social Analysis (DSA), the ability to generate relevant information from interactions. We analyze factors influencing model performance in social understanding, such as scale, architectural design, and spoken context. Experiments with MLLM judges demonstrate a path towards scaling automated evaluation of multimodal social understanding.

title: How to Solve Noise and Hard Samples: Filtering and Difficulty-adaptive Augmentation for Fine-grained Negative Emotion Classification
author: Lianxi Wang; Siting Lin; Chao Liang; Yuying Li; Xinfeng Liao; Nankai Lin
abstract: Fine-grained negative emotion classification suffers from subjective annotation noise and semantically ambiguous hard samples, which severely degrades model performance. Most existing methods cannot distinguish valid hard samples from noise and lack strategies to improve hard sample learnability. To address these issues, we propose a Noise Filtering and Difficulty-adaptive Hard Sample Augmentation (NF-DHSA) framework for fine-grained negative emotion classification. It first mines high-risk candidates using a hybrid score of normalized loss and predictive entropy, then applies a multi-view logic-guided filtering mechanism to reliably separate noise from valid hard samples. Further, difficulty-adaptive dynamic augmentation generates moderate-difficulty, label-stable augmented samples, and prototype-guided dual-granularity contrastive learning aligns original-augmented pairs while strengthening global category boundaries. The results reported on three benchmark datasets show that NF-DHSA outperforms the baseline methods overall, with Macro-F1 scores improved by 1.25%, 2.47%, and 3.53% on the VIRUS, NLPCC, and COVID datasets, respectively.

title: Long-Context Demonstration Selection Using State Space Models
author: Ziniu Zhang; Zhenshuo Zhang; Ruoxuan Xiong; Gene Cooperman; Hongyang R. Zhang
abstract: We study the problem of demonstration selection, which involves selecting a subset of examples for pre-pending to a query to a language model. This problem is closely related to in-context learning and model inference. Since the inference cost of a transformer model scales quadratically with sequence length, the selection problem becomes especially challenging in a long-context scenario. In this paper, we tackle this problem by building on state space models (SSMs), which has linear inference time given the input embeddings. Our approach works in two stages. First, we learn a small set of SSMs through a distillation procedure — given a (trained) transformer model, we partition all the layers into consecutive (layer) groups — for each group, we learn one SSM to mimic the input-output behavior, thereby capturing structural similarity in adjacent layers. Second, we map the SSM outputs to a small set of tokens, and apply them for downstream demonstration selection. We run extensive experiments in both synthetic and real-world datasets to validate this approach. We show that the SSMs trained from distillation incur a relative approximation error of less than 0.7%. As for downstream demonstration selection, we find that on several text classification and reasoning tasks, our approach reduces FLOPs by 14.2\times and improves accuracy by 6.48% relative to baseline selection methods.

title: AIMER: Calibration-Free Task-Agnostic MoE Expert Pruning
author: Zongfang Liu; Guangyi Chen; Yifan Shen; Shengkun Tang; Huan Wang; Xin Yuan
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models increase parameter capacity without proportional per-token computation, yet deployment still requires storing the full expert pool, making expert pruning important for reducing memory and serving overhead. Existing task-agnostic expert-pruning methods are typically calibration-dependent: they estimate expert importance from routing or activation statistics on a calibration set, making pruning decisions sensitive to calibration-data variation while introducing substantial preprocessing cost. We propose AIMER (Absolute mean over root mean square IMportance for Expert Ranking), a simple calibration-free criterion that identifies more distinct experts by capturing the concentration pattern of expert weights, making it well suited for task-agnostic expert pruning. Across 7B to 47B MoE language models with distinct architectures and 16 diverse benchmarks, AIMER consistently delivers stronger capability balance across diverse tasks than existing calibration-free methods. Surprisingly, AIMER also achieves better balance than strong calibration-based expert-pruning baselines calibrated on the widely used task-agnostic C4 corpus, while requiring only 0.22–2.06 seconds to score all experts.

title: Phonological Abstraction and Exception Memorization in Noisy Tone Learning
author: Yi Yang; Yiming Wang; Jiahong Yuan
abstract: Transformer-based speech models have recently been shown to perform well under impoverished and ambiguous supervision, a setting motivated by poverty-of-the-stimulus arguments, yet their learning dynamics remain unclear. In this work, we study this question with wav2vec2.0 on Mandarin tone classification, using 70 scale–noise configurations, capacity interventions, and perturbation probes to examine the dynamics of abstraction-consistent generalization and exception memorization, yielding representative regimes of Robust Generalization, Abrupt Transition, and High-noise Collapse. We find a consistent abstraction–exception trajectory: when phonological recovery is possible, the model first exhibits phonologically abstraction-consistent behavior and only later fits corrupted labels as empirical exceptions. Capacity analyses show that this trajectory is not merely a large-model artifact: it persists under truncated Transformer encoders, while acoustic rank compression modulates but does not selectively separate abstraction from exception memorization. Finally, acoustic perturbations show different local robustness: abstraction-consistent predictions remain stable under stronger waveform perturbations, whereas fitted exceptions behave as fragile local overrides on top of the broader abstraction-consistent behavior.

title: Boundary-Aware Expert Ordering Preservation with Next-Router Supervision for MoE Quantization
author: Hancheol Park; Geonho Lee; Tae-Ho Kim
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity through sparse expert activation, but their large parameter footprint remains costly to deploy. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical compression strategy; however, quantization errors can alter router decisions and cause the quantized model to activate experts different from those selected by its full-precision counterpart. Prior router-aware PTQ objectives mitigate such expert-shift by aligning router outputs or preserving top-k expert orderings and margins at a given router. Yet sequential block-wise PTQ introduces an additional failure mode: quantizing a decoder block changes the representations received by the next MoE router, potentially causing downstream expert-shift that is not directly optimized by existing objectives. To address this issue, we propose MENDS-MoE (Margin-Preserving Expert Orderings with Next-Router Decision Supervision), an auxiliary calibration objective that supervises current-block quantization using routing decisions at the next MoE router. MENDS-MoE further introduces a boundary-aware margin loss that preserves orderings among selected experts while maintaining their separation from unselected experts near the top-k boundary. It is applied only during calibration and adds no inference-time computation. Across three MoE language models under 4-bit and 3-bit-average weight-only quantization, MENDS-MoE achieves the best average downstream accuracy and the lowest perplexity in most evaluated model–bit settings. Ablation studies further support the contributions of both next-router supervision and boundary-aware margin preservation.

title: Benchmarking LLM-as-a-Judge for Long-Form Output Evaluation
author: Junjie Chen; Yuxi Dong; Haitao Li; Weihang Su; Yujia Zhou; Min Zhang; Yiqun Liu; Qingyao Ai
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for long-form generation, reliably evaluating long-form outputs has become a critical challenge. LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to human evaluation, yet its reliability in long-form output evaluation remains underexamined: existing meta-evaluation benchmarks focus mainly on short-form outputs. Compared with short-form evaluation, long-form evaluation is not merely a matter of output length; it often requires judges to handle more complex document-level demands. In this work, we introduce LongJudgeBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM judges on long-form outputs across diverse real-world scenarios and judging protocols. We systematically evaluate a broad range of LLM judges, covering multiple base models and judging settings. Our results reveal a substantial reliability gap: current LLM judges remain unstable across scenarios, and rubrics or references are helpful but not always sufficient. We hope LongJudgeBench will support future research on more robust, context-aware, and human-aligned LLM-as-a-judge methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/cjj826/LongJudgeBench.

title: OUTLETS: Output-Length Prediction from Speculative Decoding Backbones
author: Weihuang Wen; Yingying Liu; Yichuan Liu; Wenqi Zeng; Li Zhou; Chumin Sun; Jie Sun; Tianshu Yu
abstract: The heavy-tailed distribution of output lengths in Large Language Model (LLM) serving poses major challenges for resource provisioning and cluster scheduling. Although output-length prediction can mitigate these issues, existing approaches have key drawbacks: external proxy models add substantial latency and often have limited fidelity, whereas internal state-based methods are efficient but rely on shallow probes of current model states. We identify a structural connection between speculative decoding (SD) and length prediction: latent representations produced by the draft decoder in advanced frameworks (e.g., EAGLE-3) encode signals that are predictive of generation length. Building on this insight, we introduce **OUTLETS** (**Out**put-**Le**ng**t**h Prediction from **S**peculative Decoding Backbones), which repurposes the speculative backbone as a trajectory-aware length predictor. When its draft representations are already computed for speculative decoding, OUTLETS adds only a lightweight regression head and achieves lower MAE than the evaluated methods. Under saturated disaggregated serving, OUTLETS predictions enable standard scheduling policies to prioritize shorter requests and distribute requests more evenly across decoding instances, reducing short-request P99 latency by **34.8%**.

title: From Instance Selection to Fixed-Pool Data Recipe Search for Supervised Fine-Tuning
author: Haodong Wu; Jiahao Zhang; Lijie Hu; Yongqi Zhang
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data selection is commonly formulated as instance ranking: score each example and retain a top-k subset. However, effective SFT training subsets are often produced through ordered curation recipes, where filtering, mixing, and deduplication operators jointly shape the final data distribution. We formulate this problem as fixed-pool data recipe search: given a raw instruction pool and a library of grounded operators, the goal is to discover an executable recipe that constructs a high-quality selected subset under a limited budget of full SFT evaluations, without generating, rewriting, or augmenting training samples. We introduce AutoSelection, a two-layer solver that decouples fixed-pool materialization based on cached task-, data-, and model-side signals from expensive full evaluation, using warmup probes, realized subset states, local recipe edits, Gaussian-process-assisted ranking, and stagnation-triggered reseeding. Experiments on a 90K instruction pool show that AutoSelection achieves the strongest in-distribution reasoning average across three base models, outperforming full-data training, random recipe search, random top-k, and single-operator selectors. Additional held-out reasoning, instruction-following, graph-reasoning, search-stability, structural-ablation, and 1.5B-to-7B transfer results further show that recipe structure matters beyond individual selection operators. Code is available at https://github.com/w253/AutoSelection.

title: SEAR: Self-Judging Agentic Reward Models
author: Bingqian Li; Chuan Hao; Junyi Li; Ran Tao; Jian Yang; Xin Zhao
abstract: Agentic reward models enhance large language model (LLM) evaluation by incorporating external tool-use capabilities. However, their training is heavily constrained by coarse-grained outcome supervision and the high cost of process-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose SEAR (Self-judging agentic reward models), a novel training framework that enables agentic reward models to self-judge their own judging processes. SEAR introduces a dual-role adversarial co-evolution framework, where the model alternates between a judger and a self-judger within a single generation process: the judger is optimized to produce more rigorous reasoning trajectories that maximize self-judgment scores, while the self-judger learns to provide critical and discriminative evaluations. Moreover, SEAR further enables agentic RMs to self-evolve without relying on external human annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SEAR consistently improves the reliability of agentic reward models across diverse benchmarks.

title: OmniInteract: Benchmarking Real-World Streaming Interaction for Real-Time Omnimodal Assistants
author: Xudong Lu; Xueying Li; Annan Wang; Yang Bo; Jinpeng Chen; Zengliang Li; Nianzu Yang; Rui Liu; Xue Yang; Jingwen Hou; Hongsheng Li
abstract: We introduce OmniInteract, a streaming benchmark for real-time omnimodal large language models evaluated through native online inference over audio-visual streams. Unlike offline video understanding or text-prompted streaming QA, OmniInteract preserves the original audio-visual stream and requires models to process it online, without access to future content. User queries and ambient sounds are embedded in the audio track, requiring models to detect multimodal triggers, decide when to respond, and answer while the stream unfolds. OmniInteract contains 250 videos with 1,430 temporally grounded response slots: 1,062 1Q1A slots across real-time, proactive, and nested scenarios, and 368 1QnA slots for continuous task monitoring and step guidance. Each slot includes a trigger, response window, and target answer. We evaluate response correctness, timing, invalid outputs, interruption handling, and context continuity using Interaction-Aware Quality-Timeliness F1, Interruption Diagnostic Suite, and Nested Chain Completion Score. Experiments show that current models remain weak in streaming interaction, with the best overall IA-QTF1 reaching only 0.368 and the best 1QnA IA-QTF1 only 0.052. Further study on mathematical reasoning in full-duplex settings shows that offline capability does not necessarily transfer to online interaction. Code and datasets will be made publicly accessible at https://github.com/Lucky-Lance/OmniInteract.

title: Unsupervised Domain Specialization for Multimodal Embeddings
author: Ruifeng Hu; Jianxun Lian; Mingqi Wu; Mingyang Zhou; Hao Liao; Naipeng Chao
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have enabled powerful generic embeddings. However, real-world applications—such as e-commerce or healthcare—rely on domain-specific patterns that these generic models often fail to capture precisely. Adapting them without readily available labeled data remains a critical challenge. In this paper, we propose MM-UDA, a robust unsupervised domain adaptation framework designed to systematically convert a generic multimodal embedding model into a domain expert using only unlabeled target data. Our framework employs a two-stage strategy. First, we introduce a within-modality pseudo-labeling task refined by Gaussian Mixture Model filtering, which rapidly adapts the model to domain-specific features while suppressing label noise. Then, we align modalities through a score-guided learning scheme to refine cross-modal pairing. Extensive evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MM-UDA both significantly enhances various backbone models and consistently outperforms competitive baselines, confirming its effectiveness for cross-modal retrieval in specialized domains. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/hrf516/MM-UDA.

title: Beyond Similarity: Coverage-Aware Prompt Selection for Time Series Forecasting with LLMs
author: Daeun Ji; Minkyoung Kim; Dongkuk Kim; Yohan Lee; Beomsoo Kim; Beakcheol Jang
abstract: Similarity-based retrieval is the dominant rule for conditioning large language models (LLMs) in in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and prompt-based time series forecasting. The rule concentrates on near-duplicate candidates, an issue that has motivated diversity-aware retrieval but remains unexamined in other retrieval-conditioned pipelines. We study this issue using prompt-based time series forecasting as a test bed, where a learned prompt pool is retrieved by similarity. Dominant methods in this setting retrieve top-K entries by cosine similarity without redundancy control, producing a bias toward dominant temporal patterns while overlooking rare but informative events. We propose CASP-LLM, a coverage-aware semantic prompting framework that addresses this prompt selection bias by combining usage-tracking and saturating-gate techniques into a coverage regularizer that adds no learnable parameters. On six long-term benchmarks and the M4 short-term benchmark, CASP-LLM matches or improves on similarity-based LLM forecasters on most dataset-horizon settings, with the exceptions of Electricity, M4-Monthly, and the few-shot long-horizon setting. A controlled study locates the failure mode at the cross-batch usage level rather than per-retrieval redundancy: within-retrieval diversification such as MMR does not help, whereas regularizing anchor usage across training does.

title: To Answer or Not to Answer? Reliability-Oriented Reinforcement Learning for Visual Language Models
author: Paul Jian; Julian Wu; Leo Wei; Dylan Chen; Garvin Guo; Qingpei Guo; Jianing Li
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently demonstrated substantial gains in reasoning capabilities of vision–language models (VLMs). However, existing RLVR paradigms rely on deterministic rewards that implicitly penalize uncertainty expression and abstention, causing VLMs to overproduce speculative answers and degrading reliability. Through quantitative analysis, we find that vanilla RLVR, while effective in improving reasoning accuracy, significantly impairs VLMs’ ability to appropriately abstain from unanswerable queries. To systematically address this, we introduce Reliable-V-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate VLMs’ abstaining capacity on challenging and realistic unanswerable visual questions. We further propose Reliable-V-RL, a reliability-aware RL framework that incorporates unanswerable and ambiguous visual questions into training, guided by a fine-grained, rubric-based reward mechanism that encourages VLMs to jointly optimize reasoning accuracy and reliable judgment. Experimental results demonstrate that Reliable-V-RL substantially improves the reliability and abstention capability of VLMs without sacrificing performance on standard multimodal benchmarks.

title: Fine-Tuning for Social-Media User Simulation: A Study Across Models and Evaluators
author: Sneheel Sarangi; Aurélien Bück-Kaeffer; Maximilian Puelma Touzel; Zachary Yang; Jean-François Godbout; Reihaneh Rabbany
abstract: Does fine-tuning on a user’s social-media history make an LLM a better simulator of that user? We study this question using QLoRA, conditioning models on a user’s chronological action history and a reply thread before generating that user’s reply. Across 12 matched baseline–QLoRA pairs from four model families (0.8B–32B), plus a baseline-only 122B model, LLM-as-judge believability evaluations show that QLoRA improves several smaller models, has mixed effects on stronger models, and does not lift a sub-10B model into the strongest large-model tier. However, a real-versus-generated classifier gives a different result: QLoRA makes Qwen, OLMo, and Llama replies much less detectable, while Gemma remains readily detectable. Contextual believability and detector AUC are uncorrelated across systems. We further explore LLM evaluations: strong LLM judges agree on broad quality tiers, and a blind 200-comparison audit finds human–judge agreement of 66% when three strong judges agree and 47% when they split. The measured effect of QLoRA therefore depends on the evaluation axis.

title: Watch Your Norms: On Test-Time Expert Reduction in Multilingual MoEs
author: Benedikt Ebing; Goran Glavaš
abstract: Test-time expert reduction (top-k reduction) is a popular way to cut inference cost in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, avoiding the expensive model retraining. Existing work, however, analyzes the effects of top-k reduction almost exclusively on English benchmarks. In this work, we provide the first systematic multilingual study of test-time top-k reduction across three contemporary MoE models, 100 languages, and 5 downstream tasks. We show that down to 75% of retained experts, the models degrade gracefully, but overall retention collapses sharply at low k and widens a structural multilingual gap: low-resource languages degrade much faster than high-resource ones. We trace the gap to a renormalization-induced norm overshoot in the MoE block, where the renormalization over the surviving expert weights inflates the MoE contribution to the residual stream. This inflation harms low-resource languages disproportionately due to their smaller residual norms. As a remedy, we propose two training-free and latency-free interventions: (i) a grid-searched global scalar to rescale the representations output by the MoE layer (global α) and (ii) a parameter-free per-token correction (token α) of expert weights derived from the routing. The proposed interventions substantially improve overall retention and reduce the multilingual gap.

title: Alignment or Formatting? Dissecting What On-Policy DPO Actually Learns
author: Keyu Wen; Yang Song; Lijun Yang; Rui Lin
abstract: On-policy Direct Preference Optimization is commonly evaluated using held-out pairwise accuracy and LLM-judge win rate, but these metrics can reward different behaviors. In controlled Qwen3-4B ablations, interventions that improve a log-prob preference probe do not necessarily improve judged generations, and interventions that win generation judging need not improve the probe. The clearest gains in judge win rate come from direction correction, which strongly improves generation evaluation while leaving pairwise accuracy nearly unchanged. Output-level analysis shows that this advantage is driven primarily by response organization: the judged-winning model wins formatting on 40/50 prompts but wins instruction-following on only 11/50. Stripping markdown does not remove the advantage, suggesting that the effect is not merely markdown decoration but broader response organization. These results suggest that in this setting, on-policy DPO can optimize judge-preferred response organization without corresponding gains on a held-out preference probe.

title: Surprisal Theory is Tautological (without Rational Grounding)
author: Ryan Cotterell
abstract: Surprisal theory holds that the human processing difficulty of a linguistic unit is an affine function of its surprisal in context under some language model. I argue this claim is tautological, i.e., for any non-negative difficulty measure over units in context, there exists a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it under mild technical conditions. Therefore, because any pattern of difficulty is consistent with some language model, without an additional constraint on the language model itself, surprisal theory makes no falsifiable predictions. I further claim that the tautology was obscured by an assumption implicit in two decades of psycholinguistic work – that the language model relevant for studying human sentence processing is the distribution that generated the training corpus. Recent empirical work, however, has undermined this assumption, demonstrating that better corpus models can be worse predictors of processing difficulty. I conclude that breaking the tautology requires a rationalist intervention, i.e., the language models used for the study of human sentence processing must be derived from an independently motivated model of the comprehender, which could be based on, for instance, memory constraints or processing goals, and that, crucially, does not depend on the behavioral data surprisal theory is meant to explain.

title: Safety Sentry: Context-Aware Human Intervention via EXECUTE–ASK–REFUSE Routing
author: Tianyu Chen; Chujia Hu; Wenjie Wang
abstract: LLM agents act on real-world environments through tool calls, and a single misjudged action can cause irreversible harm. The standard safeguard is a guard model that labels each proposed action as safe or unsafe, but this binary view conflates two distinct decisions: whether the action is harmful in itself, and whether it is appropriate given the user’s context. It also operates at the granularity of action categories rather than individual instances, producing routine interruptions that erode autonomy and train users to wave through the most consequential alerts. We reframe the problem as a per-instance three-way routing decision over Execute, Ask, Refuse and instantiate it with Safety Sentry, a lightweight guard model whose inference reduces to a single decoding call. A single decoding-time threshold lets one fixed checkpoint be re-positioned across deployments of differing risk tolerance without retraining. Safety Sentry outperforms a broad set of open-weight and frontier closed-source baselines on overall accuracy and safety-related recall, while controlling both directional error rates simultaneously.

title: MacAgentBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Real-World macOS Desktop
author: Yikun Fu; Bowen Fu; Zhenyu Wu; Shuang Cheng; Xiaowei Sun; Bowen Yang; Zehao Li; Yibo Zhao; Zichen Ding; Zhoumianze Liu; Shijie Wang; Biqing Qi; Bowen Zhou
abstract: Computer use agents (CUAs) have advanced rapidly in desktop automation, and a growing number of users deploy CUAs such as OpenClaw on Mac Mini for always-on automation. However, existing benchmarks, including those for macOS, evaluate agents without framework augmentation and rely on binary evaluation. As a result, they fail to capture both the framework capabilities leveraged by modern CUAs and the partial progress on long-horizon, multi-application tasks. We present MacAgentBench, a comprehensive macOS agent benchmark comprising 169 seed tasks expanded into 676 task instances across 25 applications, with nearly 60% involving both GUI and CLI interaction. The benchmark adopts deterministic rule-based evaluation and introduces fine-grained multi-checkpoint scoring with capability annotations for multi-application tasks. Experiments across three frameworks and 16 models show that the best configuration, Claude Opus 4.6 on OpenClaw, attains 73.7% Pass@1, while this advantage is primarily driven by the skill library rather than by framework design. Fine-grained metrics further reveal that models with similar Pass@1 can differ substantially in sub-goal completion.

title: Efficient Agentic Reinforcement Learning with On-Policy Intrinsic Knowledge Boundary Enhancement
author: Dingwei Chen; Zefang Zong; Zhipeng ma; Leo Luo; Yang Li; Chengming Li; Peng Chen; Jie Jiang
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has proven effective for training LLM-based agents with external tool-use capabilities. However, we identify that agentic RL training induces increasing redundant tool calls and blurs the model’s intrinsic knowledge boundary, where the model fails to distinguish when tools are needed versus when parametric knowledge suffices. Existing solutions based on reward shaping create coarse-grained optimization targets that tend to incentivize indiscriminate tool-call suppression, leading to reward hacking. In this paper, we propose **AKBE** (**A**gentic **K**nowledge **B**oundary **E**nhancement), an on-policy method that dynamically probes the model’s intrinsic knowledge boundary through dual-path (with-tool and no-tool) rollouts during training. We define the knowledge boundary as the per-instance determination of whether tools are required and the minimum tool calls necessary. By comparing correctness across paths, AKBE categorizes trajectories and constructs targeted supervisory signals that guide efficient tool-use patterns for each question. These signals are integrated seamlessly into the agentic RL training loop. Experiments on seven QA benchmarks demonstrate that AKBE improves task accuracy by on average +1.85 and reduces tool calls by 18% over standard agentic RL, yielding 25% higher tool productivity without any accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Further analysis suggests its plug-and-play compatibility across different RL algorithms and the mechanism of each signal category.

title: Validity Is Not Visibility: A Lifecycle FSM for Agent Memory
author: Shuo Zhou; Pengcheng Xu; Shaotong qi; Li Que; Ming Sun; Han Li
abstract: Long-term memory for LLM agents must answer two questions for every stored fact: whether the fact is still true and whether it should be surfaced for a given query. We refer to these two dimensions as validity and visibility, respectively. Existing memory systems often collapse these two decisions into a single scalar score. However, current and historical queries may require opposite retrieval decisions for the same fact: a superseded fact should be hidden for a current-intent query but surfaced for a historical-intent one. This creates a structural failure mode: superseded and expired facts are collapsed onto the same validity axis. To address this problem, we propose MemFSM, a training-free retrieval-side layer that separates validity from visibility through a memory-lifecycle finite-state machine. Along the validity axis, a four-state FSM tracks whether each fact has been superseded and expired. Along the visibility axis, an intent-aware router decides whether to surface or hide a fact based on its state and the query intent. By decoupling visibility from validity, MemFSM improves performance across heterogeneous memory benchmarks and diverse LLM backbones. To evaluate memory systems under fact conflicts and diverse query intents, we further introduce ValidMem, a benchmark that annotates each fact with both supersedure and expiry labels and pairs each memory store with both current-intent and historical-intent queries.

title: Beyond Single-Attribute Auditing: A Configurable Multi-Attribute Benchmark for Intersectional Fairness in LLMs
author: Zheng Zhang; Yifan Wu; Yuxiang Zhou; Qi Liu; Qingyang Mao; Ning Li; Weibo Gao; QiYuan Shi; Zhenya Huang; Baosheng Yu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for fairness, yet most existing benchmarks audit one sensitive attribute at a time. This single-attribute paradigm can miss intersectional harms, where multiple attributes interact non-additively and produce failures that are invisible under marginal evaluation. We introduce ComFair, a configurable benchmark that converts existing fairness data into 479,066 controlled Dual- and Multi-attribute instances and pairs every augmented instance with its task-equivalent source. Across Recognition, Selection, Continuation, and Conversation, this pairing supports a unified audit of performance or bias-score shifts, how often added attributes introduce new errors or mask existing ones, and model-ranking stability. Experiments on ten LLMs show task- and subgroup-dependent sensitivity: discriminative tasks expose both transition directions even when aggregate changes are modest, generative tasks exhibit larger and directionally asymmetric shifts, and rankings vary with attribute composition. ComFair therefore provides a scalable controlled sensitivity audit—rather than a model of the natural joint distribution of identities—for testing the robustness of fairness-benchmark conclusions beyond single-attribute settings.

title: Self-Corrected Speech Reasoning: Diagnosing and Improving Condition Updating via PACER
author: Zijie Zeng; Liwen Shi; Yunji; Bowen Wang; Nanjie Li; Xiaoyong Guo; Zeyu Chen; Xinzheng Sun; Xuyang Xiong; Haoyang Wu; Sheng Zhang
abstract: Speech large language models (Speech LLMs) are increasingly expected to reason in everyday spoken interactions, where users often revise task conditions through self-correction. Unlike ordinary disfluencies, self-corrections alter the premise structure of a problem: obsolete conditions must be discarded, while final corrected conditions must guide reasoning. We formulate this setting as self-corrected speech reasoning and study it as a condition-update problem. We construct SCUR-Bench (Spoken Condition-Update Reasoning Benchmark), a controlled Chinese benchmark of 13,295 instances organized by reasoning difficulty and self-correction difficulty, and introduce a three-path diagnostic protocol to analyze speech-side recovery, condition use, and reasoning. Our analysis reveals a recurrent failure pattern in current Speech LLMs: corrected conditions may be perceived, transcribed, or even mentioned, yet still fail to serve as active premises in reasoning. We term this final-condition adoption failure. A controlled English parallel evaluation exhibits the same recovery–adoption gap, providing preliminary evidence that this failure is not unique to Chinese. To mitigate it, we propose PACER, a perception-aware condition-enhanced reinforcement framework based on GRPO. On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, PACER reduces end-to-end error and condition-related errors by 39.8% and 67.5%, respectively, relative to the untrained baseline.

title: Poly-FEVER: A Multilingual Hallucination Detection Benchmark
author: Hanzhi Zhang; Sumera Anjum; Heng Fan; Weijian Zheng; Yan Huang; Yunhe Feng
abstract: We present Poly-FEVER, an open-source large-scale multilingual benchmark for hallucination detection through controlled factuality judgment in large language models. Poly-FEVER extends FEVER, Climate-FEVER, and SciFact to 77,973 Supported/Refuted claims aligned across 11 languages. We augment each claim with topic metadata from a 22-topic LDA model, enabling topic-aware analysis of multilingual factuality behavior. Translations are produced with Google Cloud Translation and validated by a targeted human audit, GEMBA, and COMETKiwi. We benchmark ChatGPT-3.5, LLaMA-2/3, Phi-3.5, and Mistral across three prompt families and evaluate robustness to model-generated rephrasing. We further analyze resource imbalance using web presence as a proxy for online claim availability, and evaluate retrieval-augmented factuality judgment with DPR over Wikipedia. Results show pronounced cross-lingual disparities under aligned claims, with stronger accuracy in high-resource languages such as English and Chinese and weaker accuracy in lower-resource languages such as Amharic and Tamil. Topic-aware prompting and retrieval provide selective gains, especially in Arabic and Amharic, while their effects vary across languages and can conflict with model priors. Poly-FEVER establishes a rigorous resource for responsible, language-adaptive hallucination detection and language-sensitive factuality evaluation. The proposed Poly-FEVER is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/HanzhiZhang/Poly-FEVER.

title: PAGE: Progress-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Advantage for Long-Horizon GUI Agents
author: Qingliang Zhang; Yongqian Sun; Yuanhong Cai; Xiaohui Nie; JiaJu Wang; Yu Luo; Jiamin Jiang; Zhekang Chen; Yaozheng Fang; Meng Wang; Chaobo Xian; Peng Li; Dan Pei
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) perform well on long-horizon GUI tasks, but their high inference costs make small VLMs (SVLMs) attractive for cost-effective local deployment despite a substantial capability gap. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a widely used RL algorithm for improving SVLMs, yet its binary outcome rewards provide no intermediate progress signal across trajectories and its uniform advantages lead to semantically-blind credit assignment within each trajectory. We propose PAGE, an RL training method built on automatic progress reward construction and hierarchical advantage computation. The former derives structured evaluation criteria from successful trajectories through iterative extraction and produces stable continuous progress rewards through multi-round aggregation, while the latter combines progress-based inter-rollout advantages with intra-rollout subtask-level advantages obtained through LVLM-driven segmentation and completion verification. Across three long-horizon GUI scenarios, PAGE achieves a 79.3% average success rate with an 8B SVLM, a 16.0 pp gain over the GRPO baseline, and competitive performance against the evaluated closed-source LVLMs.

title: SCAMBENCH: A Multi-Dimensional Scam Benchmark through Human-AI Collaborative Data Construction
author: Huaye Li; Siyu Huang; Jinkyung Katie Park
abstract: Online scams are a growing form of digital harm, yet scam research remains constrained by fragmented datasets and limited annotation depth. We introduce SCAMBENCH, a benchmark of 1,836 authentic scam messages curated from victim-reported incidents across six scam types: employment, investment, imposter, sweepstakes/lottery/prizes, tech support, and advance fee loan scams, along with 1,834 real-world non-scam examples from legitimate sources. SCAMBENCH provides multi-dimensional annotations that capture persuasion strategies from the scammer perspective, red flags from the user perspective, and severity levels reflecting potential harm and urgency. These annotations are produced through a human-AI collaborative pipeline that uses expert-labeled examples to calibrate and validate LLM-assisted annotation at scale. Our analysis shows that these signals vary significantly across scam types, highlighting substantial scam-type heterogeneity. We further use annotated evidence spans to generate cue-removed hard scam examples by rephrasing explicit persuasion and red-flag cues. Evaluating five LLM-based detectors on original and rewritten scams shows that all five detectors perform worse on cue-removed examples, and the performance drop persists on a human-validated subset, suggesting sensitivity to surface-level cues. A qualitative case study identifies five recurring failure patterns. SCAMBENCH provides a resource for scam detection, robustness evaluation, and scam education, publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Shouninger/ScamBench.

title: Not All Subjectivity Is the Same! Defining Desiderata for the Evaluation of Subjectivity in NLP
author: Urja Khurana; Michiel T. van der Meer; Enrico Liscio; Antske Fokkens; Pradeep K. Murukannaiah
abstract: Subjective judgments are part of several NLP datasets and recent work is increasingly prioritizing models whose outputs reflect a diversity of perspectives. Such responses allow us to shed light on minority voices, which are frequently marginalized or obscured by dominant perspectives. It remains a question whether our evaluation practices align with these models’ objectives. This position paper proposes seven evaluation desiderata for subjectivity-sensitive models, rooted in how subjectivity is represented in NLP data and models. The desiderata are constructed in a top-down approach, keeping in mind the user-centric impact of such models. We scan the experimental setup of 64 papers and show that various aspects of subjectivity are still understudied: the distinction between ambiguous and polyphonic input, whether subjectivity is effectively expressed to the user, and a lack of interplay between different desiderata, amongst other gaps.

title: Typological Feature Prediction with Large Language Models: An In-Context Learning Approach
author: Qianwen Wang; York Hay Ng; Aditya Khan; En-Shiun Annie Lee
abstract: Typological features are widely used in multilingual NLP, and the prediction of such features holds downstream utility. However, existing methods to predict missing values lack interpretable justifications for predictions, while their performance across resource levels and feature types remains underexplored. Given LLMs’ abilities in meta-linguistic reasoning and in providing rationales, we investigate LLMs’ performance in typological feature prediction via an in-context learning approach with linguistic data from URIEL+ and Glottolog. We find that zero-shot prompting is insufficient, but when given phylogenetic and geographic neighbour evidence, LLMs substantially outperform all baselines without disadvantaging low-resource languages. We further find that most LLM rationales are consistent with the provided evidence, offering a step toward explainable typological feature prediction.

title: MathDebugger: A Benchmark for Type-Aware Error Detection in Synthetic Math Data
author: Hao Liang; Meiyi Qiang; Yuying Li; Zefeng He; Xiaochen Ma; Ruichuan An; Yongzhen Guo; Zhengzhou Zhu; Bin Cui; Wentao Zhang
abstract: Synthetic math data is widely used to scale LLM training, but its correctness is not guaranteed. We introduce MathDebugger, the first text-only, type-aware benchmark for jointly detecting *and* classifying errors in synthetic mathematical questions and answers. MathDebugger contains 2,000 correct questions, 2,000 erroneous questions (balanced across four fine-grained error types), and 2,000 annotated answers (610 erroneous, across three error types), each annotated with both a correctness label and an error-type label, with per-error-type Fleiss’ \kappa ranging from 0.69 to 0.88. On 14 SOTA LLMs (6 closed-source, 8 open-source, 1.5B–72B) and 3 process reward models, even advanced systems such as GPT-o3 and DeepSeek-R1 remain far from saturating the benchmark, particularly on fine-grained error-type detection; we further surface a *solving-vs-verifying* gap that causes math-tuned and long-chain-reasoning models to trail their general-purpose siblings. Error-type annotations also provide actionable supervision for correction, with gains that are significant under paired bootstrap (p<0.01). Code and data: [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MathDebugger-7C4A/README.md](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MathDebugger-7C4A/README.md)

title: On the Robustness of Knowledge Editing for Detoxification
author: Ming Dong; Shiyi Tang; Ziyan Peng; Guanyi Chen; Tingting He
abstract: Knowledge-Editing-based (KE-based) detoxification has emerged as a promising approach for mitigating harmful behaviours in Large Language Models. Existing evaluations, however, largely rely on automatic toxicity classifiers, implicitly assuming that reduced toxicity scores reflect genuine behavioural suppression. In this work, we propose a robustness-oriented evaluation framework for KE-based detoxification that examines its reliability beyond standard classifier-based metrics along three dimensions: optimisation robustness, compositional robustness, and cross-lingual robustness. We identify pseudo-detoxification as a common failure mode, where apparent toxicity reductions arise from degenerate generation behaviours rather than meaningful suppression of unsafe content. We further show that detoxification effectiveness degrades when multiple unsafe behaviours are edited jointly, and that both monolingual and cross-lingual detoxification remain effective only under specific model–method combinations. Overall, our results indicate that KE-based detoxification is robust only for certain models, limited numbers of detoxification objectives, and a subset of languages.

title: I Know What You Meme, Even If it Emerged Today: Understanding Evolving Memes through Open-World Knowledge Acquisition
author: Shanhong Liu; Rui Cao; Pai Chet Ng; De Wen Soh
abstract: Multimodal memes are dynamic and often require up-to-date background knowledge for interpretation. Existing methods often overlook such knowledge or rely on fixed parametric knowledge of pre-trained models that may be incomplete, outdated, or unavailable for emerging memes. We introduce Query-Retrieve-Conclude, a zero-shot framework that identifies missing knowledge, retrieves open-web evidence, and synthesizes evidence-grounded background knowledge for meme understanding and detection. We also introduce a curated meme understanding benchmark of recent memes from 2024–2026 with external background knowledge annotations. Experiments on three meme understanding datasets and five meme detection tasks show that our framework improves knowledge recovery, meme understanding and downstream detection over zero-shot baselines.

title: IFMTBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multilingual Translation Instruction Following
author: Mingrui Sun; Mao Zheng; Zheng Li; Mingyang Song
abstract: Modern translation workflows demand more than semantic equivalence. Users routinely require models to preserve JSON or HTML schemas, honor curated glossaries, disambiguate with provided context, and match prescribed registers, often several at once. Conventional metrics such as BLEU and xCOMET capture semantic fidelity but provide little signal on constraint adherence, while general instruction following benchmarks ignore the cross-lingual nature of translation. We introduce IFMTBench, a benchmark for multilingual translation instruction following covering seven high-resource languages, with 4,506 single-constraint and 2,838 multi-constraint items spanning seven constraint dimensions and five compositional patterns with instructions issued in all seven languages. Constraints are split into a gating subset verified by deterministic checkers and a continuous subset scored by a rubric-based LLM judge, combined under a multiplicative rule that resists reward hacking. Evaluating 15 models reveals systematic gaps that prior protocols miss: Instruction following scales with size more sharply than translation quality, glossary and structured-format constraints dominate the difficulty gradient, and general instruction following rankings correlate only weakly with translation behavior. Our benchmark is available at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT2/tree/main/IFMTBench.

title: SABER-Math: An Automated Reranking Benchmark for Mathematical Information Retrieval
author: Nikolay Georgiev; Maria Drencheva; Kseniia Ibragimova; Ivo Petrov; Dimitar Iliev Dimitrov; Martin Vechev
abstract: As agentic AI systems tackle more complex mathematical tasks, they increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) to search problem databases, theorem libraries, and educational resources. However, choosing the right retriever remains difficult, as it is infeasible to isolate its effect on downstream performance. On the other hand, existing retrieval-specific benchmarks often fail to capture fine-grained mathematical relevance, penalizing systems that retrieve useful documents. We address this gap with SABER-Math, the first fully automated reranking benchmark for mathematical IR, built without expert annotation. Starting from 283K high-school-level problems with solutions, it builds challenging tasks in three steps: (i) LLMs extract concise solution summaries and topics for each problem; (ii) candidates are discovered per query using ontology-based topic similarity and lexical overlap between solution summaries; and (iii) a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament assigns every candidate a graded relevance rating. Over these judged candidate pools, we evaluate retrievers across all major paradigms, from lexical and math-specific systems to modern embedding, late-interaction, and reranking models. Reasoning embedders lead, followed by general-purpose models, both far outperforming classical and math-specific baselines. Yet, all still struggle in symbol-heavy domains such as Algebra and Calculus. Importantly, we show that generic IR benchmarks, such as MTEB, track mathematical performance broadly but are less discriminative among the strongest models, highlighting the need for domain-specific evaluation.

title: Steering Vectors are an Adversarial Attack Surface
author: Abzal Aidakhmetov; Donato Crisostomi; Tommaso Mencattini; Adrian Robert Minut; Iacopo Masi; Emanuele Rodolà
abstract: Activation steering has become a popular way to control Large Language Model (LLM) behavior without fine-tuning. Since the technique is plug-and-play, users share datasets and precomputed vectors to steer model activations. However, we show that a stealth data poisoning attack silently compromises this pipeline. By substituting 4{-}6\% of tokens in the steering dataset, an attacker can silently align the resulting vector with an anti-refusal direction. This jailbreaks the target model while preserving the intended steering effect on benign prompts. Under this threat model, a malicious actor can distribute an apparently safe bundle containing texts, vectors, and weights, alongside an equivalence certificate that the end-user can verify. We test the attack on two open-weight model families and eight model-attribute combinations, observing that poisoned vectors reach an absolute attack success rate (ASR) of 20{-}55\%, +19\% to +51\% over a clean reference. The vulnerability is not an artefact of scale or of access to the victim: it persists natively at 70B, and a poisoning optimised once on a small surrogate transfers to unseen models that recompute their own vectors from the shared texts. Finally, we find that a refusal-direction orthogonalization defense can recover {\approx}82\% of the ASR gap without harming benign behavior.

title: Discover, Then Diversify: Phase-Aware Control of Tree-of-Thought Search
author: Atkia Mahila; Avinash Maurya; M. Mustafa Rafique; Bogdan Nicolae
abstract: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) reasoning has significantly enhanced the problem-solving capabilities of Language Models by enabling the structured exploration of reasoning trajectories. However, the efficiency of these frameworks is often bottlenecked by search algorithms that struggle to navigate vast reasoning spaces at a reasonable inference cost. In this work, we address the challenge of optimizing LLM performance on mathematical reasoning tasks under limited token budgets. A key limitation of existing search strategies is that they apply the same exploration and selection rule throughout the entire search, which under a finite budget, often leads to token exhaustion with suboptimal or no candidate answers. Effective search instead requires different behavior at different stages. We introduce PACE (Phase-Aware Controller for Exploration), a strategy that adjusts its behavior based on the current state of the search: it prioritizes progress toward a first complete answer when none exists, and broadens exploration toward structurally distinct regions later on. Across GSM8K and Math500, two model scales, and token budgets from 3k to 10k, PACE consistently matches or improves over recent state-of-the-art baselines. On GSM8K with Llama-3.2-3B at a 3k budget, PACE delivers roughly a 56% relative accuracy improvement over the strongest tree-search baseline, and an early-stopping variant achieves comparable accuracy using about two-thirds of the tokens.

title: Agent-Trident: A Three-Level Progressive Diagnostic Benchmark for Tool-Use Hallucination in LLM Agents
author: Jiaqing Li; Du Xuehui; Liu Aodi; Jiaxi Shi; Jiangpeng Cui
abstract: Tool-use hallucination has become a critical obstacle to agent deployment. It can emerge and propagate across judgment, planning, and execution. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on final task completion or individual tool-use capabilities, making fine-grained failure attribution difficult. We propose Agent-Trident (TRIDENT), a three-level progressive diagnostic benchmark for tool-use hallucination. TRIDENT decomposes the agent tool-use process into judgment, planning, and execution, supporting stage-level attribution of tool-use failures. The dataset contains 1,120 samples across 20 subdomains and 7 task structures. We further propose the Cross-level Composite Metric (CCM), a bottleneck-sensitive aggregate metric that measures models’ overall reliability across the tool-use chain. Evaluating 29 mainstream large language models (LLMs), we find that even the best model reaches only 42.79% CCM, indicating that current LLM agents remain far from reliable tool use. Our analysis further identifies model behaviors and stage-level differences overlooked by conventional evaluations. These results show that TRIDENT complements final-outcome evaluation with stage-level diagnosis, revealing reliability limitations in solvability judgment, tool-use planning, and dynamic execution while supporting agent model selection, error analysis, and safe deployment.

title: Lost in Speech: Benchmarking, Evaluation, and Parsing of Spoken Bilingual Conversational Language Beyond Standard UD Assumptions
author: Nemika Tyagi; Olga Kellert; Holly Hendrix; Nelvin Licona-Guevara; Justin Mackie; Phanos Kareen; Megan Michelle Smith; Tatiana Gallego Hernandez; Samhitha Harish; Chitta Baral
abstract: Spoken bilingual conversations pose substantial challenges for syntactic parsing because they often include disfluencies and discourse-driven structures that complicate dependency parsing under standard Universal Dependencies (UD) assumptions and evaluation practices. To systematically study these challenges, in this work, we first introduce a linguistically grounded taxonomy of conversational bilingual phenomena, together with SpokeBench, an expert-annotated English-Spanish benchmark for structurally complex speech. To address the limitations of existing evaluation practices, we propose Flex-UD, an ambiguity-aware evaluation metric that distinguishes catastrophic structural failures from linguistically acceptable variations. Finally, we introduce DECAP, a decoupled agentic parsing framework that separates spoken-phenomena handling from core syntactic analysis, enabling robust and interpretable dependency parsing without retraining. Experiments across both proprietary and open-weight LLMs show that DECAP substantially improves performance on complex conversational phenomena and achieves over 60% improvements in UPOS-F1 Score over baselines, while Flex-UD evaluations reveal gains that otherwise remain partially hidden under standard attachment-based metrics.

title: Breaking Failure Cascades: Step-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Medical Multimodal Reasoning
author: Junha Jung; Minbyul Jeong; Suhyeon Lim; Sungwook Jung; Jaehoon Yun; Taeyun Roh; Mujeen Sung; Jaewoo Kang
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have shown great promise in clinical image reasoning, but existing post-training pipelines remain predominantly outcome-centric, relying on final answer correctness or sequence-level preferences. This approach suffers from sparse credit assignment, making it difficult to optimize the internal reasoning process essential for clinical applications. Our analysis reveals that cascading errors from early-stage reasoning failures are a leading cause of incorrect predictions in medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmarks. Motivated by this, we propose Medical Reasoning-aware Policy Optimization(MRPO), an RL algorithm that incorporates step-wise process rewards. When the final answer is incorrect, MRPO assigns exponentially larger penalties to tokens in earlier invalid reasoning steps, breaking failure cascades without compromising successful paths. Across three multimodal LLM backbones, MRPO consistently outperforms standard GRPO and a recent RL baseline, and on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct even outperforms substantially larger medical MLLMs such as HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B by 2.79 points. Moreover, MRPO reduces early-stage reasoning failures from 64.0% to 13.0%, demonstrating that targeted mitigation of cascading failures improves both reasoning quality and final answer accuracy.

title: Cross-lingual Self-Consistency for Multilingual Reasoning with Language Models
author: Ahmed Elhady; Eneko Agirre; Mikel Artetxe
abstract: Despite expanding their multilingual coverage, the advanced reasoning capabilities of LLMs remain largely confined to a few high-resource languages like English.
