The adaptive module explicitly captures horizontal, vertical, diagonal, and global spatial priors, enabling the model to better handle heterogeneous writing systems and layouts. Extensive experiments show that HoloDP delivers consistent gains on underrepresented and mixed-script benchmarks while remaining competitive on high-resource Chinese and English documents. Ablation studies confirm that the benchmark resources, direction-aware adaptation, and script-conditioned modeling provide complementary benefits. We will release the code, models, and benchmarks for further research.

title: Chart-EARL: Improving Chart Reasoning of Vision LLMs via Early Anchoring in Reinforcement Learning
author: Gongyao Jiang; Qiong Luo
abstract: Chart reasoning poses a significant challenge for Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs). While Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a promising solution, existing outcome-based RL methods overlook intermediate errors, whereas process-based approaches remain difficult in verifying abstract logical steps. We therefore analyze chart-reasoning failures to identify an intermediate supervision signal that is both relevant to the task and amenable to objective verification. Our pilot study suggests that early visual-perception errors constitute a prominent source of failure in the chart-reasoning setting. Guided by this insight, we propose Chart-EARL, which constructs verifiable early visual anchors for targeted chart-reasoning supervision. We first build a structured training corpus that explicitly decouples visual perception from logical deduction. Building upon this structure, our approach optimizes the model with rewards for both accurate extraction of descriptive visual features and final-answer correctness. This strategy provides direct and verifiable feedback on early visual grounding while keeping supervision on the final reasoning objective. Experiments show clear performance improvements on complex chart reasoning benchmarks.

title: Brain Translation: Multitask Sequence-to-Sequence Modeling for Intracortical Attempted Speech Decoding
author: Michał Olak; Tommaso Boccato; Matteo Ferrante
abstract: Decoding language from intracortical activity is a sequence transduction problem that stress-tests modern NLP methods: inputs are high-dimensional and nonstationary, alignment to linguistic units is unknown, and training data are orders of magnitude smaller than in standard translation or speech recognition. We study attempted-speech decoding from intracortical recordings as a neural-to-language translation task and ask what contextual sequence-to-sequence modeling contributes beyond the framewise connectionist temporal classification (CTC) pipelines that dominate this domain. We introduce a multitask Transformer encoder–decoder that jointly predicts phonemes, words (via a BART-initialized decoder), and auxiliary acoustic features, together with a day-conditioned calibration module (Neural Hammer Scalpel, NHS) that combines a global affine transform with feature-wise linear modulation to handle session-level distribution shift. On the Willet et al. dataset, our model achieves state-of-the-art phoneme error rate (14.3%); direct word decoding reaches 25.6% WER, falling to 19.4% with rescoring, however still trailing multi-stage systems with heavy language-model refinement. Ablations and held-out-day experiments quantify the contributions of multitask supervision and NHS and the cost of session drift, while attention analyses reveal recurring temporal chunking that phoneme and word decoders consume differently. Together, these results position seq2seq modeling as both a competitive decoder and an interpretable probe for how language evidence is organized in neural inputs.

title: CopyShield: A Cross-Level Benchmark of Copyright Defenses in LLMs
author: Maryam Alshehyari; Dushyant Singh Chauhan; Samuele Poppi; Martin Takáč; Salem Lahlou; Nils Lukas
abstract: Large language models can reproduce memorized text verbatim, yet copyright defenses are usually evaluated under incompatible protocols. We introduce CopyShield, a controlled benchmark comparing three representative defenses at distinct intervention levels: contrastive decoding (output), Direct Preference Optimization (behavioral), and activation intervention (representation). We evaluate CopyShield on two model families, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, using controlled memorization over five public-domain books and a shared protocol measuring literal leakage, calibrated non-literal leakage, utility, and degeneracy. Across these methods, intervention level is associated with distinct compliance–utility trade-offs. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, contrastive decoding remains near-degeneracy-free (0–2%) but reaches a literal-suppression floor at NV-Recall 0.192–0.203. DPO nearly eliminates literal leakage (0.263 to 0.002) but induces paraphrase-loop degeneracy in 58% of QA outputs, with no utility gain over the SFT baseline. Activation intervention attains the lowest non-literal flagging rate (1/200) by blocking 84% of non-literal queries before generation. Human evaluation confirms that DPO has low coherence, whereas activation lowers perceived copyright risk through broad refusal. On Mistral-7B-v0.3, the output- and representation-level patterns persist, while DPO degeneracy falls to 10–14%, showing that its severity is model-dependent. Together, CopyShield provides cross-level reference baselines and identifies targeted non-literal suppression as an open challenge. The code is available at https://github.com/spotai-mbzuai/CopyShield.git.

title: SlidesGen-Bench: Evaluating Slides Generation via Computational and Quantitative Metrics
author: Yunqiao Yang; Wenbo Li; Houxing Ren; Zimu Lu; Ke Wang; Zhiyuan Huang; Zhuofan Zong; Mingjie Zhan; Hongsheng Li
abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has fostered diverse paradigms for automated slide generation, ranging from code-driven layouts to image-centric synthesis. However, evaluating these heterogeneous systems remains challenging, as existing protocols often struggle to provide comparable scores across architectures or rely on uncalibrated judgments. In this paper, we introduce SlidesGen-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate slide generation through a lens of three core principles: universality, quantification, and reliability. First, to establish a consistent evaluation framework, we ground our primary analysis in the visual domain, treating terminal outputs as visual renderings for consistent comparison, while acknowledging format-conditional ceilings in structural editability. Second, we propose a structured computational approach that quantitatively assesses slides across three distinct dimensions—Content, Aesthetics, and Editability. Finally, we ensure high correlation with human preference for the highly subjective aesthetic dimensions by constructing the Slides-Align1.5k dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that SlidesGen-Bench achieves a significantly higher degree of alignment with human judgment than existing evaluation pipelines. Our code and data are released to support further research.

title: SWITCH: Benchmarking Modeling and Handling of Tangible Interfaces in Long-horizon Embodied Scenarios
author: Juntao Cheng; Wanyue Zhang; Zhiwei Yu; Shuo Ren; Zheqi He; Shaoxuan Xie; Guocai Yao; Jieru Lin; Börje F. Karlsson; Jiajun Zhang
abstract: Tangible control interfaces (TCIs), such as appliance panels, remotes, elevators, and embedded GUIs, are a fundamental component of everyday human-built environments. Interacting with these interfaces requires agents not only to ground language in visual observations, but also to execute actions, track temporally evolving state changes, and verify whether intended outcomes have been achieved. However, existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate open-loop perception or single-step action execution, failing to capture this continuous cycle of interaction, feedback, and correction. We introduce SWITCH, a benchmark for closed-loop interactive reasoning with TCIs inrealistic egocentric environments1. SWITCH comprises 1,170 temporally interactive videos across diverse functional categories, providing structured annotations of instructions, actions,state transitions, outcomes, and recovery behaviors over time. To probe generative world modeling, SWITCH also evaluates video generation models on interaction-centered tasks using both LLM-as-judge and human evaluation.Experiments with frontier proprietary and opensource multimodal models reveal persistent weaknesses in fine-grained visual-temporal perception, outcome verification, and error recovery, highlighting SWITCH as a testbed for closed-loop embodied intelligence

title: Benchmarking Argument Identification and Ellipsis Recovery in Chinese Comparative Constructions
author: Wenjing Xu; Hongzhi Xu
abstract: Ellipsis in comparative constructions provides a challenging test of semantic interpretation because comprehenders must reconstruct implicit constituents that are not overtly expressed. This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can capture the structured semantic inferences required for understanding Chinese comparative constructions. We introduce a linguistically motivated evaluation framework targeting two essential components of comparative interpretation: (i) identification of comparative arguments and (ii) recovery of elliptical constituents. Based on 2,076 naturally occurring Chinese bi-comparative sentences, we construct an annotated resource with comparative argument boundaries, recovered elliptical constituents, and five comparison dimensions representing distinct semantic bases of comparison. We evaluate several representative LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-4o, and Gemini-2.0-Flash. While all models reliably identify overt comparative arguments, they exhibit substantial degradation when reconstructing implicit constituents. These results suggest that current LLMs can capture surface-level structural regularities but still face challenges in recovering implicit semantic representations required for human-like interpretation. Our resource provides a controlled linguistic testbed for studying the relationship between linguistic structure, semantic inference, and computational models of language understanding.

title: Structured Claim-Level Discourse Representations for Dense Health Narratives
author: Farnoush Nili; Elham Pourabbas Vafa; Shirin Nilizadeh; Eduard Dragut
abstract: Health discourse in social media videos often contains densely entangled claims spanning multiple thematic aspects, stances, evidential frames, and rhetorical functions within short conversational spans. Existing approaches largely rely on coarse topic-level, sentiment-based, or stance-oriented representations that do not adequately capture this structure. Our analysis identifies an average of 13.22 atomic claims per minute, motivating richer claim-level discourse representations. We introduce a structured framework for claim-level discourse analysis in dense health narratives. Our framework models discourse through tuples linking atomic claims with thematic aspects, stance, and multidimensional pragmatic discourse attributes. To support this setting, we construct a benchmark spanning four health domains with 1,191 manually annotated claims from 60 videos. Using this framework, we evaluate automated structured discourse analysis under different discourse context settings. Results show that current LLMs achieve strong performance on thematic categorization and stance prediction, but struggle with high-dimensional pragmatic profiling. We also find that different discourse tasks benefit from different forms of contextual reasoning, suggesting that future systems may require task decomposition and specialized inference strategies.

title: MedRAGChecker: Claim-Level Verification for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: Yuelyu Ji; Min Gu Kwak; Hang Zhang; Xizhi Wu; Chenyu Li; Yanshan Wang
abstract: Biomedical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) produces long-form answers that mix supported, under-evidenced, and contradicted claims, demanding fine-grained verification. We propose MedRAGChecker, a claim-level diagnostic framework that combines textual natural language inference (NLI) with a biomedical knowledge-graph (KG) compatibility signal. Its asymmetric selective-gating rule preserves the textual prediction for most claims and applies KG adjustment only to confident textual entailments assigned low plausibility by the KG back-end. We distill GPT-4.1 claim decompositions and NLI pseudo-labels into compact student models and evaluate three biomedical generators on PubMedQA, MedQuAD, LiveQA, and MedRedQA. The student-ensemble results show that selective BioPortal gating increases macro-averaged faithfulness from 60.8% to 64.4% and reduces the contradiction rate from 19.9% to 15.0%. On 172 annotations of 86 claims whose decisions change after fusion, agreement with human evidence judgments increases from 63.4% to 69.8%. A comparison with DRKG shows that fusion behavior varies substantially with KG coverage, entity linking, score construction, and calibration; the comparison therefore characterizes back-end effects rather than isolating a causal effect of coverage.

title: When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs
author: Anna Mosolova; Djamé Seddah
abstract: Quiz rooms, trivia nights, and quiz shows challenge human knowledge across a wide range of topics, from canonical facts to everyday culture. In this paper, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can perform competitively in such settings, using quiz-style questions to test them on both common and niche topics. We introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark designed to evaluate everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge across 288 topics. The benchmark contains 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages and additional 5,340 French-only questions for a more fine-grained case study. We evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs from European, Asian, and North American providers, covering models from 7 to 70B parameters. We find that models are strong on knowledge-intensive topics such as history, geography, and mathematics, but substantially weaker on everyday popular-culture topics such as celebrities, music, movies, and news. Moreover, model performance varies across languages even for the same underlying questions, suggesting that access to factual knowledge is not always language-independent. In sum, our dataset and experiments demonstrate an important knowledge gap which is not captured by existing academic-based saturated benchmarks.

title: DIP: Dynamic In-Context Planner For Diffusion Language Models
author: Yang Li; Han Meng; Chenan Wang; Zhenyu Bi; Xuan Wang; Haipeng Chen
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have shown strong potential for general natural language tasks with in-context examples. Existing In-Context Learning (ICL) approaches largely inherit the practice of autoregressive language models (ARLMs), incorporating all examples into a fixed prompt. However, applying this rigid, static-prompt paradigm to DLMs incurs substantial computational overhead, as the model must evaluate the maximum context length at every step. We address this inefficiency with a key discovery: the block-wise KV-cache mechanism inherent to DLM inference enables the \textit{low-cost dynamic adjustment of the context}. Following this intuition, our core idea is to start generation with a minimal prompt and progressively insert additional examples on the fly only when the generated tokens are of low confidence. Through rigorous empirical evaluations, we observe that average verified token confidence correlates strongly with generation accuracy, making it a reliable and computationally efficient signal of token quality. Formally, we propose \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{I}n-Context \textbf{P}lanner (DIP), a context-optimization algorithm based on average verified confidence that dynamically ranks and inserts in-context examples during generation, rather than providing all examples up front. Experimental results on math and coding benchmarks with LLaDA-1.5 and LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DIP achieves up to 1.59\times and 1.36\times speedups, respectively, while largely preserving the generation quality of the fixed-prompt baseline. Code: https://github.com/wmd3i/DIP

title: PEAM: Parametric Embodied Agent Memory for Continual Skill Learning via Internalization of Experience in Minecraft
author: Yuchen Guo; Junli Gong; Weicheng Wang; Hongmin Cai; Yiu-ming Cheung; Weifeng Su
abstract: We present PEAM, a Parametric Embodied Agent Memory framework in Minecraft that transforms agent memory from inference-time retrieval into parameter-resident skills internalized through experience. PEAM pairs a slow deliberative LLM for open-ended reasoning with a fast parametric module for reflexive execution of consolidated skills. The fast module is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts LoRA architecture with per-category physically isolated adapters, enabling parameter-level continual learning with structural resistance to cross- category forgetting. We treat failure as a first-class training signal: failure–correction trajectory pairs are internalized through a joint behavioral-cloning and contrastive objective, so the agent learns not only what succeeds but also how corrected actions differ from failed ones. To govern consolidation, PEAM introduces a parameterization-worthiness score for deciding which experience should be internalized, and a scale-free self-triggered consolidation mechanism for deciding when to internalize without task-specific hand-tuned thresholds, making the agent self-evolving as the trigger transfers across task distributions without re-tuning. Experiments in Minecraft show that PEAM improves long-horizon task performance, mitigates forgetting on previously consolidated skills, and improves parametric-versus-retrieval efficiency over retrieval-based embodied agents and parametric memory variants.

title: All Leaks Count, Some Count More: Interpretable Temporal Contamination Detection and Mitigation in LLM Backtesting
author: Zeyu Zhang; Bradly Stadie
abstract: Backtesting LLMs on resolved events assumes models reason only from pre-cutoff knowledge, yet pretrained models inevitably leak post-cutoff knowledge. We introduce a claim-level evaluation framework that decomposes prediction rationales into atomic claims and applies Shapley values to quantify each claim’s decision impact, yielding Shapley-DCLR (Shapley-weighted Decision-Critical Leakage Rate)—an interpretable metric measuring what fraction of decision-driving reasoning is contaminated. We further propose TimeSPEC (Time-Supervised Prediction with Extracted Claims), an inference-time architecture that interleaves temporally-filtered retrieval with claim-level supervision, producing predictions grounded entirely in pre-cutoff evidence. Across three LLMs, the ablation experiments confirm retrieval and supervision are jointly necessary; and a three-task probe further illustrates that the performance cost of temporal enforcement scales with each task’s reliance on post-cutoff information.

title: The Language of Evidence: Robustness and Bias in Code-Switched RAG
author: Medha Hira; Joel Mire; Maarten Sap
abstract: Many people code-switch, mixing multiple languages within a single conversation, text or both in everyday communication and increasingly in interactions with AI systems. While prior work has examined how code-switching affects LLM outputs, its impact on RAG systems remains largely unexplored. We present a systematic study of multilingual retrieval under code-switched queries. First, we introduce a retrieval evaluation framework jointly measuring ranking accuracy, language alignment, and bilingual coverage, revealing language preferences that standard metrics obscure. In particular, the strongest relevance-performing retrievers tend to exhibit an English preference. Second, we propose Language-Targeted Contrastive Training to mitigate this retrieval bias, but find a fundamental trade-off: improving alignment reduces exposure to relevant content across languages. Third, controlled RAG experiments show that generation quality depends on retrieval language, with the preferred evidence language varying across query languages. Together, our findings expose tensions between retrieval accuracy, language coverage, and fairness in multilingual RAG, arguing for evaluation protocols that account for query-language coverage.

title: Revisiting the Estimation of Unigram Surprisal in Computational Psycholinguistics
author: Zachary Hopton; Francesco Ignazio Re; Samuel Kiegeland; Andreas Opedal; Eleanor Chodroff; Ryan Cotterell
abstract: Contextual and unigram surprisal are standard predictors of reading time in computational psycholinguistics. While contextual surprisal is typically derived from neural language models, unigram surprisal is usually obtained from independent corpus counts. Although both quantities are deterministic functionals of a single underlying distribution—capturing conditional and marginal structure respectively—this practice breaks their probabilistic link and may introduce estimation error from the mismatch. We propose three principles for estimating unigram surprisal in psycholinguistic research, including the requirement that both quantities be derived from the same language model. We operationalize this principle by introducing a Monte Carlo estimator of unigram surprisal from a language model, along with a marginalized variant that has lower variance empirically. When unigram surprisal is re-estimated under this unified framework, we find evidence that predictors change in their predictive contribution to reading time. We also confirm prior findings that frequency can be a stronger predictor of processing effort than contextual surprisal under this unified framework.

title: R²Edit: Mastering Relation Replacement Editing via Target-Smoothed Forgetting and Self-Paced Learning
author: Xu Cao; Xinrui Chen; Qing Liu; Mengyang Li; Ou Wu; Yi Du
abstract: Knowledge editing updates facts in large language models while preserving unrelated knowledge. Most prior work studies object editing, which modifies the object under a fixed subject–relation pair. We instead study relation replacement editing, where an obsolete relation must be suppressed as a new one is introduced. We systematically study this setting with a dedicated benchmark and method. We introduce \textbf{ReEditBench} to evaluate replacement rather than association addition. Existing editors exhibit two major failures: obsolete-relation retention remains as high as 98.20% after successful edits, and difficult samples often destabilize editing. To address this, we propose \textbf{R$^2$Edit}, a two-stage framework for relation replacement. Its target-smoothed Forget stage reduces obsolete-relation activation without fixed/random pseudo-target bias, while its curriculum-guided Edit stage progressively injects new relations from easy to hard samples. Across multiple LLMs, \textbf{R$^2$Edit} improves replacement success, reduces retention, and preserves generalization. Stress tests on difficult subsets further demonstrate the robustness of the Edit stage. Code is available at: https://github.com/caoxu0109/R2Edit.

title: Internalizing Meta-Experience into Memory for Guided Reinforcement Learning in Large Language Models
author: Shiting Huang; Zecheng Li; Yu Zeng; Qingnan Ren; Zhen Fang; Qisheng Su; Kou Shi; Ziao Zhang; Lin Chen; Zehui Chen; Feng Zhao
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite its efficacy, RLVR faces a meta-learning bottleneck: it lacks mechanisms for error attribution and experience internalization intrinsic to the human learning cycle beyond practice and verification, thereby limiting fine-grained credit assignment and reusable knowledge formation. We term such reusable knowledge representations derived from past errors as meta-experience. Based on this insight, we propose **M**eta-**E**xperience **L**earning (**MEL**), a novel framework that incorporates self-distilled meta-experience into the model’s parametric memory. Building upon standard RLVR, we introduce an additional design that leverages the LLM’s self-verification capability to conduct contrastive analysis on paired correct and incorrect trajectories, identify the precise bifurcation points where reasoning errors arise, and summarize them into generalizable meta-experience. The meta-experience is further internalized into the LLM’s parametric memory by minimizing the negative log-likelihood, which induces a language-modeled reward signal that bridges correct and incorrect reasoning trajectories and facilitates effective knowledge reuse. Experimental results demonstrate that MEL achieves consistent improvements on benchmarks, yielding 3.92%–4.73% Pass@1 gains across varying model sizes.

title: HachiWare: One-Shot Selective SVD in a Dual-Branch Framework for KV Cache Compression
author: Hsiao-Ting Shao; Xiaolin Lin; Yu-Chen Lu; Grace Li Zhang; Kai-Chiang Wu; Ning-Chi Huang
abstract: Long-context inference is increasingly limited by the memory and access cost of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing KV cache compression methods face a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and information preservation. Eviction-based methods are efficient but may discard critical tokens, whereas low-rank-based methods preserve all tokens at the cost of substantial computational overhead. We propose HachiWare, a dual-branch framework that applies one-shot selective SVD to semantic-critical cache states while handling less critical states with lightweight eviction. It stores these states in a Semantic-Critical Branch (SCB) using low-rank factors, while assigning the remaining states to an Eviction Branch (EB) for cheaper eviction. During decoding, bounded active-cache refresh selectively reconstructs only active SCB entries, avoiding reconstruction of the full SCB cache. On the RULER benchmark with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, HachiWare incurs only a 3% accuracy drop compared with the full KV cache baseline at a KV cache compression ratio of up to 16x, while improving accuracy by 5% over existing compression methods. For decoding efficiency, HachiWare achieves up to 9.44x and 16.50x throughput speedups over Full KV at 64K and 128K context lengths. These results highlight selective allocation of reconstructability as an effective way to improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of KV cache compression.

title: Beneath the Surface of Chains-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Reasoning Operations in LLMs
author: Seogyeong Jeong; Jaehui Hwang; Dongyoon Han; Geonmo Gu; Alice Oh; Taekyung Kim
abstract: Reasoning in large language models unfolds through diverse functional operations, such as problem formulation, goal decomposition, and deduction. Although these operations are explicitly distinguished in text, little is known about how they are geometrically organized in representation spaces. To this end, we investigate whether distinct reasoning operations exhibit corresponding geometric structure in hidden representations. We find that operations are separable in held-out representations, with separability peaking in middle layers, and verify that this structure is not explained by lexical or positional confounds. Across layers, token-wise operation-alignment becomes more distributed over spans, while identical surface tokens are represented differently depending on the operation of its surrounding chunk. Attention-masking interventions further show that operation-aligned representations at chunk onset depend on preceding reasoning context. Consequently, our work demonstrates that language models maintain representational correspondence between linguistic reasoning expressions and their internal geometric structures. Code and project materials are available at https://github.com/naver-ai/beneath-cot.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Robust Rubric Rewards
author: Ya-Qi Yu; Hao Wang; Fangyu Hong; Xiangyang Qu; Gaojie Wu; Qiaoyu Luo; Nuo Xu; Huixin Wang; Wuheng Xu; Yongxin Liao; Zihao Chen; Haonan Li; Ziming Li; Dezhi Peng; Minghui Liao; Jihao Wu; Haoyu Ren; Dandan Tu
abstract: While RLVR is effective for deterministically verifiable tasks, many vision-language tasks are only *partially verifiable*, demanding multi-criterion supervision. To bridge this gap, we propose *Reinforcement Learning with Robust Rubric Rewards (\text{RLR}^3), extending RL with criterion-level rewards. To ensure faithful scoring, \text{RLR}^3 routes each criterion to one of two execution paths: an LLM-as-an-extractor paired with a verifier, or an LLM-as-a-Judge for fuzzy criteria. We also introduce a minimal exposure strategy that masks verifier targets from extractors and source images from the GenRM. Furthermore, \text{RLR}^3 employs decoupled normalization to mitigate score saturation and hierarchical aggregation to prioritize essential criteria. Evaluated on Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B across 15 benchmarks, \text{RLR}^3 consistently outperforms RLVR, yielding a 4.7-point improvement over the base model and exceeding the official instruct-to-thinking model gap. Controlled audits show that deterministic verifier and minimal exposure strategy reduce exploitable false positives.

title: CauSight: Learning to Supersense for Visual Causal Discovery
author: Yize Zhang; Meiqi Chen; Sirui Chen; Bo Peng; Yanxi Zhang; Tianyu Li; Chaochao Lu
abstract: Causal thinking enables humans to understand not just what is seen, but why it happens. To bring this ability to modern AI systems, we introduce visual causal discovery, the task of inferring visually verifiable direct causal dependencies among entities in a single static image. We construct the Visual Causal Graph dataset (VCG-32K), a large-scale collection of over 32,000 images annotated with entity-level causal graphs, and develop Causight, a causally aware vision-language model for this task. Our training recipe combines data curation from VCG-32K, Tree-of-Causal-Thought (ToCT) reasoning synthesis, and reinforcement learning with a graph-structured causal reward. Experiments show that Causight outperforms GPT-4.1, achieving over a threefold performance boost (21% absolute gain).

title: Investigating Linear Probe Robustness to Linguistic Register, Medical Specialty, and Corpus Shifts in Medical QA
author: Nishant Mishra; Ameen Abu-Hanna; Iacer Calixto
abstract: Linear classifiers trained on hidden states of a large language model (LLM)—*linear probes*—can flag factual errors from a single forward pass. Geometrically, that implies that true and false statements separate along a stable direction in hidden state space, i.e., the *truth direction*. Prior work disagrees on whether this generalises across input shifts, but the disagreement is hard to interpret because cross-dataset probe transfer experiments confound several kinds of input change at once. We isolate three such variables in medical question-answering (QA): writing style (register), domain (medical specialty), and corpus (dataset). We build a benchmark using 500 MedQA entries, each rewritten into four styles (textbook, patient, clinical note, colloquial), annotated with clinical specialty, and grouped with two other exam corpora, MedMCQA and MMLU-medical, for cross-dataset evaluation. Probing four open-weight LLMs (2–8B), we find that the truth direction is largely robust to writing style (mean \Delta_\text{register} \approx 0.10 AUROC on held-out facts) and to medical specialty (\Delta_\text{specialty} \approx 0.03), but degrades unevenly across corpora: by 0.12 AUROC on MMLU-medical and by 0.21 on MedMCQA, roughly twice the register gap. The register result replicates with a second generator and carries over to human-written patient questions. The truth direction is therefore largely stable within the medical domain but breaks under some corpus shifts, and question format does not explain the break, which suggests that the signal a linear probe recovers is partly bound to dataset structure rather than to medical knowledge alone.

title: Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
author: Cen Zhao; Haibo Ruan; Wenjie Chen; Pei-fen Tu; Usman Abbasi; Joel Hesch
abstract: LLM tool agents can be improved without retraining by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model: prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. We study this setting as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, with the search surface scoped to prompts and tool-boundary middleware: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary, not arbitrary rewriting of agent execution logic. Our optimizer-agnostic protocol reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of the held-out gain of the harness selected under budget B. We instantiate the protocol with prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search. On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM obtains mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points and positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks, and a component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, the results show that some search procedures can occasionally find large gains but still choose brittle updates, so the reliability of the chosen harness should be reported alongside average held-out lift.

title: Visual Framing for News Stance Detection via Image Generation
author: Dahyun Lee; Jiyoung Han; Kunwoo Park
abstract: Article-level news stance detection aims to identify the perspective of news articles toward social issues. Despite advances in stance detection and its importance for trustworthy media environments, news articles pose distinct challenges because their stances are often implicit, subtly conveyed through journalistic framing, and embedded in long, structurally complex texts. To address these challenges, we introduce VFStance, which leverages visual framing to make implicit stance cues more explicit via image generation. In evaluation experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of VFStance over existing methods and the contribution of visual framing to its performance. Finally, a controlled user study (N=200) in a snippet-based news consumption setting further demonstrates that VFStance can make stance signals visually salient and highlights its potential use beyond automated stance detection.

title: Calibrating Hierarchical Memory Utilization for Long-Term Memory QA
author: Hang Lv; Xuyang Zhi; Hongchao Gu; Hao Wang
abstract: Long-term memory systems increasingly organize interaction histories into hierarchical contexts, where coarse summaries, mid-level events, and fine-grained evidence provide complementary signals for future queries. Yet after retrieval, these signals are often collapsed into a single generation context and used implicitly. We ask how retrieved hierarchical memory should shape generation after access, framing it as a post-retrieval calibration problem. We propose HiR, a training-free inference-time framework that contrasts full-hierarchy decoding with a coarse-only reference view, preserving the complete hierarchy while tempering over-reliance on broad abstractions. Extensive experiments and analyses show that HiR enables more effective and robust use of hierarchical memory without changing memory construction or retrieval; more broadly, our results suggest that memory research should consider not only what to store or retrieve, but also how retrieved information shapes generation.

title: Bridging the Consistency Gap: A Noun Bank Augmented Framework for Low-Cost Long Text Translation
author: Tao Chen; Mao Zheng; Zheng Li; Zhang Zheng; Bo Lv
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced machine translation, yet long-text translation still faces a practical tension between document-level lexical consistency and inference cost. Recent document-level methods improve coherence by expanding context, maintaining multi-level memories, or injecting multi-granularity knowledge, but such broad context mechanisms often introduce substantial prompt redundancy and limit parallel inference. We propose \textbf{NoBAT} (\textbf{No}un \textbf{B}ank \textbf{A}ugmented \textbf{T}ranslation), a lightweight framework that distills document-level lexical constraints into a compact global Noun Bank. NoBAT first constructs and disambiguates the Noun Bank serially, and then retrieves only relevant noun constraints for local, parallel translation. Experiments on IWSLT2017 and Novels-XL with multiple LLM backbones show that NoBAT consistently improves lexical translation consistency while maintaining competitive COMET scores. Compared with DELTA, NoBAT further reduces total token consumption by \textbf{6.3$\times$}, demonstrating a cost-effective trade-off among consistency, translation quality, and efficiency.

title: GSAR: Goal-State-Anchor Rewards for Mobile GUI Agents with Self-Evolving Data Synthesis
author: Long Zhang; Yuhan Chen; Chaoran Zhang; Wanxia Cao; Kun Huang; Pengzhi Gao; Wei Liu; Jian Luan; Chenliang Li; Lixin Zou
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) based GUI agents stand to benefit significantly from online reinforcement learning (RL). However, their training is bottlenecked by two fundamental issues: current data synthesis methods for GUI Agents rely on specific environments and struggle to generate diverse data, while existing evaluators either suffer from limited scalability or provide inaccurate and unreliable reward signals. To overcome these challenges, we introduce GSAR (Goal-State-Anchor Reward), a RL reward framework that supports scalable task generation and delivers reliable reward signals for stable and efficient policy optimization. Our approach features self-evolving data synthesis, which produces multiple environments through task execution and generates diverse tasks and goal states. Complementing this, a state-anchor mechanism automatically annotates task-relevant UI elements in successful goal states as reference anchors. During RL training, these reference anchors provide accurate, scalable reward signals that substantially enhance efficiency. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves over 90% accuracy on offline trajectory verification and performs closest to rule-based methods. Furthermore, agents trained using our reward framework exhibit strong performance on both AndroidWorld and our constructed benchmark, establishing a scalable approach for GUI agent training.

title: Do Language Models Follow Occam’s Razor? An Evaluation of Parsimony in Inductive and Abductive Reasoning
author: Yunxin Sun; Abulhair Saparov
abstract: Non-deductive reasoning, encompassing inductive and abductive reasoning, is essential in addressing complex real-world questions. One key feature of inductive and abductive reasoning is that there are many valid hypotheses; the simplest ones (those that adhere to Occam’s razor) are often most useful. However, this aspect is ignored in recent work that evaluates the non-deductive reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). This work fills this gap, focusing on understanding whether the inductive and abductive reasoning capabilities of LLMs adhere to Occam’s razor, while also examining the correctness of their reasoning. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a framework to synthetically generate reasoning questions that *(a)* require inductive reasoning and abductive reasoning simultaneously; *(b)* is readily extended to produce any abductive/inductive reasoning question expressible in first-order logic. The task for the intelligent agent is to produce hypotheses to *explain* observations under a given world model. We also propose a new automated metric to assess whether hypotheses quantitatively adhere to Occam’s razor; those hypotheses that are correct and simplest are considered *high-quality*. Our findings on state-of-the-art LLMs suggest that LLMs can perform inductive and abductive reasoning in simple scenarios, but struggle with complex world models and with producing *high-quality* hypotheses, even with popular reasoning-enhancing techniques such as in-context learning and RLVR.

title: Cross-lingual Biography Enrichment via Claim Extraction and Alignment
author: Yifei Song; Ziyang Chen; Emil Sayilov; Claire Gardent
abstract: English Wikipedia is often treated as the default encyclopedic source, yet non-English Wikipedia editions can contain richer locally grounded information for long-tail figures. We study cross-lingual biography enrichment: enriching an existing English biography with facts supported by a non-English biography about the same person. Focusing on women from non-English-speaking contexts, we introduce CLAW-4L, a benchmark consisting of 300 Wikipedia biography pairs linking an English biography with its French, Chinese or Azerbaijani counterpart, along with claim annotations and a fine-grained claim-pair relation corpus. We propose a claim-based enrichment framework that extracts English claims from both biographies, aligns them to identify enrichment evidence from the non-English biography, and rewrites the English biography using the selected claims. Our results show that non-English Wikipedia biographies provide valuable evidence for improving English biography coverage, while lower-resource settings remain challenging.

title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
author: Abir Harrasse; Florent Draye; Punya Syon Pandey; Zhijing Jin; Bernhard Schölkopf
abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why do multilingual performance gaps persist? To address this question, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal a consistent three-phase structure across models: early layers encode language-specific information, middle layers converge to highly shared multilingual representations, and final layers re-specialize for language-specific decoding. Training models without English produces the same shared multilingual structures, suggesting that these representations emerge independently of English dominance. We further show that decoding relies on a small set of high-frequency late-layer features that linearly encode language identity from earlier layers, and that intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, through a Model-Diffing experiment, we show that non-English failures arise from weak late-layer decoding features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer fragmentation that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual performance gaps.

title: Neither Here Nor There: Cross-Lingual Representation Dynamics of Code-Mixed Text — A Hindi–English Case Study
author: Debajyoti Mazumder; Divyansh Pathak; Prashant Kodali; Jasabanta Patro
abstract: Multilingual encoder-based language models are widely used for code-mixed analysis, yet their internal representations of code-mixed inputs—and their relationship to the constituent languages—remain poorly understood. Using Hindi–English as a case study, we construct a unified trilingual corpus of parallel English, Hindi (Devanagari), and Romanized code-mixed sentences. We then probe cross-lingual representation alignment in standard multilingual encoders and their code-mix-adapted variants using CKA, token-level saliency, and entropy-based uncertainty analysis. We find that while standard models align English and Hindi well, code-mixed inputs remain loosely connected to either language — and that continued pre-training on code-mixed data improves English–code-mixed alignment at the cost of English–Hindi alignment. Interpretability analyses further reveal a clear asymmetry: models process code-mixed text through an English-dominant semantic subspace, while native-script Hindi provides complementary signals that reduce representational uncertainty. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a trilingual post-training alignment objective that brings code-mixed representations closer to both constituent languages simultaneously, yielding more balanced cross-lingual alignment and downstream gains on sentiment analysis and hate speech detection — showing that grounding code-mixed representations in their constituent languages meaningfully helps cross-lingual understanding. Code is available at: https://github.com/debajyotimaz/tri_align_EMNLP_2026.

title: Cognitive-Level Prefix-MoE Reward Modeling for Curriculum Alignment of Medical Language Models
author: Hao Wang; Wendi Feng; Chun Kang; Yanting Wang; Rui Li; Lei Sha
abstract: Medical language models are increasingly evaluated on open-ended clinical reasoning, where good responses must combine factual recall, evidence integration, decision making, and synthesis. However, standard reward models compress these different standards into one reward score, while medical RL with answer keys mainly rewards multiple-choice correctness. This makes it difficult to improve non-multiple-choice medical reasoning without losing performance on exam-style benchmarks. In this paper, we propose a Prefix Mixture-of-Experts Reward Model (Prefix-MoE RM), which routes each query-response pair across recall, analysis, decision, and synthesis prefix experts, softly fuses their trainable prefixes, and then predicts one reward score. The MoE structure allows different abilities to use different scoring experts to reduce reward conflicts, while continuous prefixes provide a more expressive conditioning signal than fixed hard prompts. The reward model is trained on non-multiple-choice medical preferences and then used in mixed-data curriculum GRPO, where multiple-choice prompts provide additional answer-key feedback. On held-out reward-model evaluation, Prefix-MoE RM improves pairwise accuracy from 79.8 to 93.0 over a shared RM; with the RL pipeline fixed, replacing it with a shared RM or soft expert-head MoE lowers HealthBench from 43.8 to 24.8 and 34.6, respectively. With Qwen3-8B as the policy backbone, the full system outperforms the larger Qwen3-32B base on MedXpertQA and HealthBench, while the Qwen3-32B version reaches 50.1 HealthBench and 4.55 LLMEval-Med, remaining competitive with stronger closed general models and retaining an advantage on non-multiple-choice metrics.

title: Human Inputs, Model Outputs: Dual Sources of Variability in Stance Mining on Gun Rights/Control
author: Niranjana Sathish Avilery; Soumyajit Datta; Ashini Anantharaman; Ashiqur R. KhudaBukhsh
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science, both to analyze human-generated web content and to act as human surrogates capable of answering substantive research questions. As these uses expand, a critical methodological question arises: how stable and reliable are the answers LLMs produce? We examine this question through the lens of stance mining on gun control and gun rights, a mature and widely used NLP task applied to one of the most extensively studied and polarized political issues in the United States. Using a multi-platform dataset spanning diverse online communities, we evaluate the stability of LLM-predicted stance across model families, prompt designs, and conversational contexts. Despite strong expectations of robustness in this setting, we observe substantial variability in predicted stance across LLMs and prompts. To contextualize these findings, we compare model-induced variability with human variability by analyzing annotations from raters with differing political affiliations. We find that political priors and annotator disagreement persist even in this ostensibly straightforward classification task. As a useful resource, we release a stance dataset annotated by raters with diverse political affiliations. Our results show that outcomes in stance mining depend jointly on which LLM is used and which humans provide the inputs, underscoring dual sources of variability that have important implications for using LLMs as research instruments in computational social science.

title: Skill Retrieval Augmentation for Agentic AI
author: Weihang Su; Jianming Long; Qingyao Ai; Qiaozhi He; Yichen Tang; Changyue Wang; Yiteng Tu; Yingbo Wang; Yiqun Liu
abstract: Agentic AI systems powered by large language models are increasingly expected to solve capability-intensive tasks by using reusable external skills, which package instructions, tool-use procedures, executable code, and auxiliary resources. However, mainstream skill-based systems typically assume that available skills can be directly placed in the prompt. As skill libraries grow, this assumption becomes impractical: large corpora cannot be fully exposed to the model, while excessive candidate exposure can distract the agent and degrade skill selection. Therefore, scalable skill augmentation requires retrieving a small set of task-relevant skills from a large corpus before incorporating them into the agent’s context. We formulate this paradigm as Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA), where agents dynamically retrieve, incorporate, and apply reusable skills from large external corpora on demand. To systematically study SRA, we introduce SRA-Bench, which enables decomposed evaluation across three stages: skill retrieval, skill incorporation, and skill application. SRA-Bench contains 5,400 capability-intensive instances from six domains, 636 manually constructed gold skills, and a corpus of 26,262 skills. Experiments across multiple LLM and skill-use strategies show that SRA can consistently improve agent performance, but current agents struggle to realize this promise in practical pipelines. Specifically, they remain sensitive to distractor skills, lack need-aware skill loading, and often fail to translate relevant skills into correct task execution. Together, these results establish SRA as a distinct research problem and provide a foundation for developing scalable skill-augmented agents.

title: LintEval: Benchmarking LLMs on Linter-Guided File Refactoring
author: Tongwei Deng; Jinyu Zhu; Yue Cao; Chenxu Wang; Yanzhen Zou; Bing Xie
abstract: Linters are widely used in code maintenance and real-time IDE editing to surface lint alerts related to performance, style, error-prone, and other patterns in source files. However, existing code benchmarks do not explicitly evaluate linter-guided file refactoring, where models must reduce lint alerts in source files with correct initial functionality while satisfying functionality preservation. We introduce LintEval, a multilingual benchmark for linter-guided file refactoring across C++, Python, and Java, comprising 13,061 programs with correct initial functionality and 171,662 lint alerts extracted using language-specific linters. LintEval jointly evaluates functionality preservation, lint alert reduction, new alert avoidance, and edit minimality. Experiments reveal a persistent trade-off: closed-source commercial models reach up to 90.4% Reduction@P but achieve only 67.1%–68.3% Pass@1, while several open-source small models show low or negative Reduction@P. A controlled fine-tuning study further shows that supervision format matters: refactoring-oriented SFT raises Qwen2.5-Coder-7B Reduction@P from 24.7% to 76.0%. LintEval enables controlled evaluation of models that improve source files under functionality preservation.

title: MemPro: Agentic Memory Systems as Evolvable Programs
author: Qingshan Liu; Guoqing Wang; Wen Wu; Jingqi Huang; Xinqi Tao; Dejia Song; Jie Zhou; Liang He
abstract: Long-horizon autonomous agents require memory systems to retain historical information, track evolving states, and reuse relevant knowledge beyond finite context windows. Existing agentic memory systems typically follow a memory construction–retrieval (MCR) pipeline, but often adapt mainly the memory bank while keeping the surrounding pipeline fixed after deployment. This fixed-pipeline design struggles to handle heterogeneous task-specific failure modes and can become misaligned with memory banks that evolve in scale and structure over time. To address these limitations, we propose MemPro, a system-level evolution framework that treats the entire MCR pipeline as an evolvable program rather than adapting only the memory bank or prompt text. MemPro maintains a version tree of runnable memory-system implementations, where an Evolving Agent iteratively selects promising versions, diagnoses recurring failures, and creates improved child versions through failure-mode-guided edit–debug refinement. Experiments on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, HotpotQA, and NarrativeQA show that MemPro consistently outperforms strong static and prompt-level evolving baselines within a few iterations, continues to improve with evolution, and achieves a favorable performance–cost trade-off. Code is available at https://github.com/wanghai673/MemPro.

title: Bias Before the Model: Detecting and Removing Cognitive Bias Triggers in Financial Text
author: Triantafillos Papadopoulos; Venetis Charilaos; John Pavlopoulos; Ion Androutsopoulos; Sophia Ananiadou
abstract: Financial text frequently contains cognitive bias triggers, such as an authority cue like “according to Goldman Sachs”, that can distort sentiment judgments without altering the underlying facts. While prior work has established that LLMs are susceptible to cognitive biases, existing evaluations treat bias exclusively as a property of the model, overlooking triggers already present in the input text. We ask whether LLMs can (i) detect such triggers, (ii) rewrite text to remove them, and (iii) whether doing so improves sentiment predictions, a task central to automated financial decision-making. We introduce TriggerBank, a dataset of 3,006 financial sentences with six types of synthetically injected bias triggers, and evaluate 11 LLMs across tasks (i)–(iii). Detection remains challenging, with framing and overconfidence hardest to detect, and removal fails for anchoring. Despite this, rewriting outperforms all instruction-based defenses for most models in downstream sentiment classification, while chain-of-thought prompting generally degrades performance. Debiasing the input text via rewriting is thus a more robust strategy than prompt-based approaches.

title: Is my model perplexed for the right reason? Contrasting LLMs’ Benchmark Behavior with Token-Level Perplexity
author: Zoë Prins; Samuele Punzo; Frank Wildenburg; Giovanni Cinà; Sandro Pezzelle
abstract: Standard evaluations of Large language models (LLMs) focus on task performance, offering limited insight into whether correct behavior reflects appropriate underlying mechanisms and risking confirmation bias. We introduce a simple, principled interpretability framework based on token-level perplexity to test whether models rely on linguistically relevant cues. By comparing perplexity distributions over minimal sentence pairs differing in one or a few ‘pivotal’ tokens, our method enables precise, hypothesis-driven analysis without relying on unstable feature-attribution techniques. Experiments on controlled linguistic benchmarks with several open-weight LLMs show that, while linguistically important tokens influence model behavior, they never fully explain perplexity shifts, revealing that models rely on heuristics other than the expected linguistic ones.

title: Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Block Diffusion Language Models in Complex Reasoning
author: Yi Lu; Deyang Kong; Jianing Wang; Linsen Guo; Xue Wang; Qi Guo; Tao Gui; Xuanjing Huang; Wei Ye; Shikun Zhang; Wei Wang
abstract: Recent advances in block diffusion language models have demonstrated competitive performance and strong scalability on reasoning tasks. However, their test-time compute allocation remains largely unexplored, leaving a critical speed-effectiveness trade-off unresolved in long Chain-of-Thought reasoning. To address this, we propose a unified test-time compute allocation framework that introduces adaptivity in both step-wise decoding and blockwise generation. At the decoding level, we propose Bounded Adaptive Confidence Decoding (BACD), a difficulty-aware sampling strategy that dynamically adjusts denoising based on model confidence, accelerating inference while controlling error accumulation. Beyond step-wise adaptivity, we introduce the Think Coarse, Critic Fine (TCCF) paradigm that allocates large block sizes for exploratory thinking and smaller block sizes for precise refinement. To stabilize training under varying block configurations, we adopt Progressive Block Size Extension, which mitigates quality degradation when scaling up block sizes. Extensive evaluations on six benchmarks show that our TDAR-8B model with BACD and TCCF achieves a 2.38 speedup and +3.4% average accuracy over the strong TraDo-8B baseline, unlocking the potential of block diffusion in complex reasoning.

title: Parallelism Strategy Chaining for Fast Training Convergence
author: Minchul Kang; Changyong Shin; Younghun Go; Hyunho Lee; Jinwoo Jeong; Chuck Yoo; Gyeongsik Yang
abstract: Selecting a parallelism strategy—the configuration of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism degrees together with micro- and global-batch sizes—largely determines the training efficiency of large language models. State-of-the-art methods search for a parallelism strategy offline and select the single strategy that minimizes per-iteration time. But we find that they neglect the target validation perplexity and time-to-perplexity (TTP). In particular, our analysis reveals that the best strategy yielding the fastest perplexity improvement changes multiple times during training. As a result, state-of-the-art methods are 1.8–11.4× slower in TTP than the strategy sequence that selects the best strategy at each iteration. This paper proposes CONA, a new training method that introduces online strategy chaining. Instead of a single strategy selected offline, CONA ranks candidate strategies during training using a surrogate metric built from compute throughput and gradient statistics, and switches the current strategy to a new strategy with a higher metric. In our evaluation with GPT-3 1.3B, BERT-Large, and Llama-3.2-1B, CONA reaches the target validation perplexity 1.4–9.6× faster than state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, CONA closely tracks the perplexity achieved by the sequence that selects the best strategy at each iteration, within 2.6%.

title: Padamitra: Grounded Glossary Generation for Classical Sanskrit
author: Manoj Balaji Jagadeeshan; Sai Pragnaan Marala; Pawan Goyal
abstract: We introduce grounded glossary generation, a structured task requiring models to recover semantically meaningful Sanskrit phrases and produce translation-grounded meanings from a śloka-translation pair, formalizing the traditional pāṭha-commentary practice as an evaluable NLP objective. We construct a benchmark of 31,316 śloka-translation-glossary triples from the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, paired with two metrics: Jaccard for phrase recovery and Meaning Faithfulness for semantic consistency. Across zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction fine-tuned variants of Gemma-3n-E4B, Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4, and Qwen3.5-9B, instruction fine-tuning substantially outperforms prompting, while explicit segmentation yields gains. Error analysis identifies over-segmentation of sandhi and samāsa compounds as the dominant failure mode, pointing to morphological modeling as the key bottleneck for faithful Sanskrit lexical decomposition.

title: Entropy-Adaptive Fine-Tuning: Resolving Confident Conflicts to Mitigate Forgetting
author: Muxi Diao; Lele Yang; Wuxuan Gong; Yutong Zhang; Zhonghao Yan; Yufei Han; Kongming Liang; Weiran Xu; Zhanyu Ma
abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is the standard paradigm for domain adaptation, yet it frequently incurs the cost of catastrophic forgetting. In sharp contrast, on-policy Reinforcement Learning (RL) effectively preserves general capabilities. We investigate this discrepancy and identify a fundamental distributional gap: while RL aligns with the model’s internal belief, SFT forces the model to fit external supervision. This mismatch often manifests as "Confident Conflicts"—tokens characterized by low probability but low entropy. In these instances, the model is highly confident in its own prediction but is forced to learn a divergent ground truth, triggering destructive gradient updates. To address this, we propose Entropy-Adaptive Fine-Tuning (EAFT). Unlike methods relying solely on prediction probability, EAFT utilizes token-level entropy as a gating mechanism to distinguish between epistemic uncertainty and knowledge conflict. This allows the model to learn from uncertain samples while suppressing gradients on conflicting data. Extensive experiments on Qwen and GLM series (ranging from 4B to 32B parameters) across mathematical, medical, and agentic domains confirm our hypothesis. EAFT consistently matches the downstream performance of standard SFT while significantly mitigating the degradation of general capabilities.

title: DRFLOW: A Deep Research Benchmark for Personalized Workflow Prediction
author: Md Tawkat Islam Khondaker; Raymond Li; Muhammad Abdul-Mageed; Laks V. S. Lakshmanan; Issam H. Laradji
abstract: Deep research (DR) systems are increasingly used for complex information-seeking tasks, but existing works mainly focus on generating reports and summaries. In contrast, many enterprise tasks instead require an agent to identify concrete workflows which is a sequence of action-steps. For example, rather than summarizing budgeting policies, an agent should be able to determine the steps needed to answer a question such as: "How do I request new headcount given a fixed budget?". Therefore, we introduce DRFLOW, a benchmark for evaluating personalized workflows predicted by agents from heterogeneous sources. Each task requires the agent to identify relevant evidence from scattered sources, then use that evidence to predict the correct action-step sequence for the user’s task. DRFLOW contains 100 tasks across five domains, with 1, 246 reference workflow steps grounded in more than 3, 900 sources. We define seven diagnostic metrics covering factual grounding, step recovery, structural ordering, condition resolution, and personalization. We further present DRFLOW-Agent (DRFA), a workflow-oriented reference agent to predict personalized workflow. We show that although DRFA improves over strong baseline agents (upto 10.02% average F1 score), there is substantial room for improvement remains across these workflow metrics, indicating that predicting complete and correct personalized workflows remains a challenging frontier for deep research.

title: DUPO: Dual-Mode Unified Policy Optimization for Tool-Using Agents
author: Zexin Hu; Mu Hu; Lijuan Yang; Yisen Wang; Xiaogang Zhu; KangJian Jiao; Yu Fu; Lihong Gu; Zhiyong Wang; Kun Hu
abstract: Tool-using large language models (LLMs) have improved at producing executable API calls, but reliable tool use requires coordinating semantic intent with executable invocation, especially in multi-step settings. Existing tool-learning objectives and traces collapse these two roles into a single homogeneous generation stream, so the learning signal cannot distinguish a flawed plan from a flawed call. We propose Dual-Mode Unified Policy Optimization (DUPO), a typed trajectory optimization framework that represents each step with a PLAN span for the current subgoal and a TOOL span for the API invocation. DUPO follows a PLAN-to-TOOL rollout factorization, optimizes the two modes with mode-separated policy ratios, and introduces Chain-Aware Upstream Advantage, so that early planning errors, which propagate through the rest of the trajectory, receive stronger credit than later steps. To support this optimization, we introduce PlanArena, a human-annotated dataset of 20,646 trajectories across 7,941 scenarios with explicit PLAN–TOOL supervision. Experiments on BFCL, API-Bank, and Tau2 show that DUPO improves tool-use performance, with gains concentrated in multi-step settings. Our code and dataset will be released upon publication.

title: Perceive-Then-Adjudicate: A Multi-Agent Framework for Resolving Knowledge-Evidence Conflicts in LLM Fact-Checking
author: Yongcheng Zhang; Xin Zhang; Fei Li; Chong Teng; Jiang-Ming Yang; Donghong Ji; Zhuang Li
abstract: Fact-checking has transitioned from traditional semantic matching toward active reasoning powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), manifesting as the interplay between internal parametric knowledge and external grounded evidence. However, this paradigm introduces two critical challenges: (i) excessive reliance on external evidence even when it conflicts with correct internal judgment, and (ii) uncritical acceptance of a consensus even when both sources are erroneous. To address these limitations, we propose a Multi-Agent Arbitration Framework where a meta-cognitive Adjudication Agent (AA) orchestrates a Knowledge Agent (KA) and an Evidence Agent (EA). Through hybrid reinforcement and imitation learning, the AA perceives conflict signals between KA and EA to adaptively calibrate judgmental autonomy against evidentiary support. Upon detecting a potentially erroneous consensus, the AA invokes a Reflective Rejection mechanism to scrutinize and disrupt deceptive alignment. Empirical evaluations on Snopes and PolitiFact demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, it effectively mitigates over-reliance errors while maintaining high fidelity in correct-consensus scenarios, recovering 26.2% of dual-error cases where static systems typically succumb to superficial consistency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Zhang-Gorden/Perceive-Then-Adjudicate.

title: MulEG: Multi-Level Explanation-Guided Feature Attribute Graph for Zero-Shot Tabular Classification
author: Jiayang Zhang; Yunxiao Zhao; Xin Kang; Zhichao Yan; Boxiang Ma; Qinghua Chai; Xingtong Yu; Ru Li
abstract: Zero-shot classification for structured tabular data has attracted increasing attention in recent years. An important line of research is leveraging textual explanations as supervision to improve the modeling of tabular attribute features. Previous studies usually serialize tabular data into flattened explanation sequences, or employ logical rules to model directional associations between tabular attributes and labels. However, these methods often suffer from two major limitations: the former disrupts the inherent row-column topological structure of tables, while the latter mainly represents relations with fixed logical operators or aggregation weights, making it difficult to model learnable dependencies among features. To address these issues, we propose a novel method (MulEG), which harnesses multi-level textual explanations with a feature attribute graph to model both tabular topology and cell-element relations. Specifically, to preserve the intrinsic row-column topological structure of tables, we propose a multi-level textual explanation modeling with sample-level, attribute-level, and label-level perspectives. Moreover, to capture fine-grained feature dependencies, we propose a differentiable message-passing mechanism using a feature attribute graph that allows heterogeneous features to propagate through message passing. Finally, extensive experimental results on datasets covering sixteen tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Stateful Visual Encoders for Vision-Language Models
author: Zirui Wang; Junwei Yu; Adam Yala; David M. Chan; Joseph E. Gonzalez; Trevor Darrell
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in multi-image, multi-turn agentic settings where decisions depend on visual changes. However, in existing open-weight VLMs, visual comparisons happen only inside the language model, while the visual encoder itself remains stateless: each image is encoded independently, without access to the prior visual context. As a result, small but task-critical changes may be attenuated before the language model has a chance to compare them, especially when those changes do not affect the high-level semantics of the scene. We introduce a Stateful Visual Encoder, which conditions each visual representation on prior visual features. Under supervised finetuning, VLMs equipped with stateful encoders achieve consistent improvements on controlled tasks involving cross-image spatial aggregation, multi-object visual differencing, and visual trajectory behavior cloning. These improvements are consistent across input resolutions, language model sizes, and VLM backbones. Finally, we validate our model on real-world tasks, including longitudinal radiology, fine-grained image comparison, and remote sensing, where stateful encoders consistently improve generalist VLM baselines and can match or surpass specialized models in selected domains.

title: SCP-ISA: Spatial Cross-attention Projection for Textual Spatial Semantic Anomaly Detection and Attribution
author: Bei Xu; Mengqi Ding
abstract: Textual spatial semantic anomaly detection and attribution requires deciding whether a sentence contains an implausible spatial relation and assigning the corresponding attribution label. Prior prompting and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning methods rely on raw tokenlevel representations, leaving spatial roles and cross-triple conflicts implicit. We propose SCP-ISA, a Spatial Cross-attention Projection (SCP) method with an Inter-Slot Attention (ISA) layer that uses a frozen MacBERT-large encoder to build input-conditioned spatial slots and injects the projected slots into Qwen2.5 as soft prefix embeddings. The ISA layer enables structured cross-slot interaction that collapses co-referring spatial mentions into a shared entity-anchored representation before generation. On the CRSARC benchmark, SCP-ISA improves test cascade attribution F1 (Attr-F1) by 22.7 percentage points (0.509 to 0.736) over Direct LoRA, and detection macro-F1 (Det-F1) from 0.846 to 0.881.

title: HINT-SD: Targeted Hindsight Self-Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
author: Woongyeong Yeo; Yumin Choi; Taekyung Ki; Sung Ju Hwang
abstract: Training long-horizon LLM agents with reinforcement learning is challenging because sparse outcome rewards reveal whether a task succeeds, but not which intermediate actions caused the outcome or how they should be corrected. Recent methods alleviate this issue by generating rewards or textual hints from turn-level action-output signals, or by using feedback-conditioned self-distillation. However, generating feedback at every turn is inefficient when many intermediate turns are already successful or neutral, and applying feedback at a fixed or misaligned turn often fails to supervise the actions that contributed to the failure. To bridge this gap, we propose HINT-SD, a targeted self-distillation framework that uses full-trajectory hindsight to select failure-relevant actions and applies feedback-conditioned distillation only to targeted action spans. Experiments on BFCL v3 and AppWorld show that our method outperforms the dense per-turn feedback baseline by up to 13.60 percentage points on average while achieving a 2.26\times reduction in time per training step, suggesting that selecting where to distill is key to effective and efficient long-horizon agent training.

title: Routing-Free Mixture of Experts
author: Yilun Liu; Jinru Han; Sikuan Yan; Volker Tresp; Yunpu Ma
abstract: Standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) designs rely heavily on centralized routing mechanisms that introduce rigid inductive biases. We propose Routing-Free MoE, which eliminates all hard-coded centralized components, including external routers, Softmax, TopK, and fixed load balancing. All related functionalities become encapsulated within individual experts, allowing each expert to determine its activation entirely on its own. We introduce a unified, adaptively scheduled load-balancing framework to simultaneously optimize both expert-balancing and token-balancing objectives through a customizable interpolation, letting optimal resource allocation pattern emerge locally during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Routing-Free MoE achieves consistently better performance, efficiency, and robustness than baseline approaches at both training and deployment. We further analyze its emergent behavior in detail and offer insights that may facilitate future MoE design and optimization. Code is available at https://liuyilun2000.github.io/RoutingFreeMoE/.

title: ParaBridge: Bridging Paralinguistic Perception and Dialogue Behavior in Speech Language Models
author: Yuxiang Wang; Qinke Ni; Shengbo Cai; Wan Lin; Liqiang Zhang; Zhizheng Wu
abstract: Speech carries more information than just words: a child’s voice, a fearful tone, or a noisy background should all lead a sufficiently competent spoken-dialogue assistant to different replies. Current Speech Language Models (SLMs) can recognize such paralinguistic cues but often ignore them in open-ended dialogue. We observe that a simple paralinguistic instruction scaffold at the inference stage narrows this perception-behavior gap, suggesting that the relevant cues are already latent in the model. Such scaffolds, however, remain brittle under multi-turn context and competing instructions. Therefore, we propose **ParaBridge**, an on-policy self-distillation method that turns a brittle inference-time scaffold into stable model behavior. During training, the scaffold serves only as a temporary privileged view; the scaffold-free model rolls out its own response, while the scaffolded view supplies dense, full-vocabulary next-token targets along its trajectory. This supervision teaches when non-lexical cues should affect the reply without the need for curated dialogues, human labels, or external reward models. On Qwen3-Omni-thinking, ParaBridge raises scaffold-free VoxSafeBench SAR from 14.6% to 40.3% and improves EchoMind average rating from 3.27 to 3.92. It also preserves general ability, with MMAU-Pro, VoiceBench, and GPQA all within 0.4 points of the original model. Beyond the training distribution, ParaBridge generalizes to unseen paralinguistic cues, transfers from safety-oriented training to empathy-oriented dialogue, and works on a different SLM backbone. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/AmphionTeam/ParaBridge.

title: SYNAPSE: Neuro-Symbolic Visual Thought-to-Text Decoding via Topological Semantic Denoising
author: Akshaj Murhekar; Abhijit Mishra
abstract: Recent advances in large language models have accelerated open-vocabulary EEG-to-imagined-text decoding, where non-invasive neural activity recorded during visual perception is translated into coherent natural language descriptions of viewed stimuli. However, existing systems remain highly vulnerable to biological noise, where corrupted neural projections induce hallucinated or semantically unstable generation in frozen language models. We introduce SYNAPSE (Symbolic Neural Alignment for Precise Semantic Extraction), a lightweight neuro-symbolic framework that stabilizes neural text generation through inference-time symbolic regularization. By purifying EEG-derived semantic candidates using commonsense graph structure and latent exemplars, SYNAPSE improves semantic stability without end-to-end LLM fine-tuning. Experiments across popular EEG decoding benchmarks and multiple frozen LLM backends demonstrate consistent gains over unconstrained prompting baselines, robustness under object-label ablation, and performance commensurate with substantially more resource-intensive fine-tuned systems, while preserving biometric privacy by localizing raw EEG processing entirely within the encoder stack.

title: Localizing Cross-Lingual Generalization in Parameter Space
author: Yeoreum Lee; Jaeseong Lee; Seung-Won Hwang
abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is uneven across tasks, succeeding for natural language understanding but often failing for mathematical reasoning. We argue that this asymmetry is governed by the geometry of parameter space. Specifically, cross-lingual generalization is determined by whether English and target-language LoRA adapters share a low-error basin. To test this, we use linear mode connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language adapters, evaluating on three tasks. We find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected, whereas mathematical reasoning (Math) pairs are not, indicating that basin geometry is task-dependent. Such disconnection in Math is “local” rather than global. A small target-language task sample, applied only to the English adapter’s language encoding or semantic composition layers, is enough to repair it. Cross-lingual generalization is also factorizable into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each supplied separately from a cheaper signal. English task data routed to the composition layers and an unlabeled target-language corpus routed to the language encoding layers each alleviate it on their own for nearly every pair. Composition is the more influential of these, and it needs no target-language data. Together, these results suggest that cross-lingual generalization decomposes into language-specific and language-agnostic components in parameter space. This decomposition offers a practical route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.

title: When LLMs Say No: Diagnosing and Mitigating Conservative Bias in Authorship Verification
author: Nicholas Wlezien; Rakesh M Verma
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been used for zero-shot authorship verification, where a model must determine whether two texts share an author. We show that evaluated zero-shot prompting methods exhibit a conservative bias, often over-predicting different authorship. This behavior is especially pronounced when the texts of the same author differ in topic or content. Through qualitative and quantitative analyses, we find evidence that LLMs confuse differences in content with differences in authorship. To test whether this failure can be reduced, we introduce lightweight prompt interventions that instruct the model to focus on style rather than content. Across four datasets and five open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, the best intervention improves same-author accuracy by 13.1 points while also increasing macro-F1 by 3.1 points on average across all 20 experimental settings. Our findings show that zero-shot authorship verification is sensitive to the separation of content and style and that small framing changes can meaningfully change the direction of LLM errors.
